Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
(Docket ID OCC-2026-0694, RIN 1557-AF57; FDIC RIN 3064-AG31)

Dear Sir or Madam,

The San Joaquin Valley Housing Collaborative appreciates the opportunity to comment on the
proposed amendments to the agencies' Community Reinvestment Act regulations published in
the Federal Register on August 12, 2026. The Collaborative is a regional nonprofit serving the
eight counties of California's San Joaquin Valley. Our members include affordable housing
developers, local governments, lenders, and community organizations working together to
expand the supply of safe, affordable homes in one of the most housing-burdened regions in the
country.

Some context on our region may be helpful. The San Joaquin Valley is home to more than four
million people and produces much of the nation's food, yet it has some of the lowest household
incomes and highest poverty rates in California. Large philanthropic institutions are scarce here.
Bank participation motivated by CRA is not a supplement to other capital in our region. In many
cases it is the capital. That is why we are writing about two elements of the proposal that would,
in our experience, pull investment and support away from the very communities the statute
directs banks to serve.

First, we are concerned about the proposal to reclassify banks with assets between $1.65 billion
and $10 billion as intermediate banks no longer subject to the investment test. The Low-Income
Housing Tax Credit is the primary tool for building affordable homes in our region, and the
banks that invest in Valley LIHTC projects are disproportionately mid-size and regional
institutions in this asset range. The investment test is a meaningful part of why they do. If these
banks can receive the same CRA consideration for ordinary market-rate lending, many will have
little reason to continue purchasing housing credits. Fewer investors mean weaker equity
 pricing, and weaker pricing means fewer homes built per credit dollar. Our region already sees
thinner LIHTC pricing than coastal markets, so we would feel this change first and hardest. We
ask the agencies to retain a community development investment component for banks above the
current large bank threshold, or at minimum to structure the intermediate bank evaluation so
that LIHTC and other community development investments receive distinct, meaningful
recognition rather than being blended into general lending performance.

Second, we are concerned about the proposed treatment of community development grants.
Limiting consideration to grants directly used for a specific plan, project, or initiative, and
requiring banks with assets over $10 billion to document that grantees hold overhead costs to 15
percent or less, would sharply curtail bank support for organizations like ours and for the
housing counselors, CDFIs, and community-based nonprofits we work alongside. General
operating support is often the most valuable grant a community organization can receive,
because it funds the staff who put projects together in the first place. The 15 percent overhead
figure has no basis in how effective nonprofits actually operate, and it penalizes small rural
organizations that run lean but cannot spread fixed costs across a large budget. In practice, we
expect the documentation burden would lead many banks to simply stop making grants rather
than police their grantees' cost structures. We ask the agencies to withdraw the overhead
documentation requirement and to preserve CRA consideration for grants, including operating
support, made to organizations whose work has a community development purpose.

We recognize and support the agencies' goals of clarity, continuity, and reduced burden for
community banks. But these two provisions would not reduce burden on communities. They
would reduce investment in them. We would welcome the chance to discuss our experience in
the San Joaquin Valley with agency staff, and we thank you for considering these comments.

Sincerely,

Miguel Arambula
Executive Director
San Joaquin Valley Housing Collaborative

To Whom It May Concern,

On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the Community
Reinvestment Act.

OFN is the nation's leading network and intermediary focused on community development
investment, managing over $1 billion in total assets and a membership of more than 500
community development financial institutions (CDFIs). OFN's membership includes community
development loan funds, credit unions, banks, and venture capital funds, many of whom
partner with banks who are motivated by the CRA to invest in low- and moderate-income
(LMI) communities.

Since its founding in 1986, OFN members have originated $136 billion in financing, helping to
create or maintain more than 3.8 million jobs, start or expand more than 1.2 million
businesses and microenterprises, and support the development or rehabilitation of nearly 3
million housing units and more than 16,000 community facility projects in rural, urban, and
Native communities across the United States. With cumulative net charge-off rates near one
percent, OFN members lend prudently and productively in the LMI communities.

The Notice of Proposed Rulemaking spans over four hundred pages and proposes significant
changes to the CRA framework with far-reaching implications for banks, community
development partners, and the low- and moderate-income communities they serve. In
addition, the review period covers the final month of Summer when significant portions of
Washington D.C.-based policy organizations are short staffed due to summer vacations ahead
of back-to-school obligations. Given these factors, the proposed 60-day comment period
at this time, and for a regulation of this complexity, does not provide sufficient time
for stakeholders to fully analyze, assess, and understand a rulemaking of this
magnitude. While the agencies have spent considerable time developing the proposal,
regulated institutions and community stakeholders require adequate time to evaluate its

Page 2
 operational, economic, and community impacts, consult with internal and external experts, and
develop meaningful, evidence-based feedback.
Previous major CRA rulemakings have provided 90 days for public comment. For instance, in
2022, when the federal banking regulators jointly proposed substantial changes to the CRA
regulations, they provided a 90-day comment period. A rulemaking of this scope with a 60-
day comment period would be insufficient to meaningfully evaluate the proposal, consult
affected parties, and develop data-driven recommendations. For organizations like ours and
the CDFIs we represent, a meaningful review also requires engaging with members nationwide
to understand how the proposal would affect institutions of varying sizes, business models,
and markets. Providing additional time for this analysis will ultimately result in comments that
are more substantive, data-driven, and useful to the agencies as they consider a final rule.
Accordingly, we respectfully urge the agencies to extend the comment period by at
least 30 days. An extension would encourage broader participation from banks, community
organizations, CDFIs, and other stakeholders, leading to a more complete administrative
record and a more informed final regulation.
The CRA is one of the nation's most consequential community development statutes, shaping
billions of dollars in lending, investment, and services that support low- and moderate-income
communities. Changes to its implementing regulations warrant careful deliberation and
meaningful stakeholder engagement. Experience has shown that complex regulatory overhauls
developed under compressed timelines are more likely to require subsequent revisions,
clarification, or litigation. Allowing additional time for public input will help ensure that any
modernization of the CRA framework is thoughtful, durable, and effective for both regulated
institutions and the communities the Act was designed to serve.
Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Sincerely,
Dafina Williams
EVP, Chief Policy Officer and Head of Government Affairs
Opportunity Finance Network

AG31

To the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation:
For Small Business Only LLC strongly supports the agencies' proposed amendments to the Community
Reinvestment Act regulations. The proposal appropriately returns the focus of CRA administration to
demonstrable community credit needs, direct local benefit, transparent use of grant funds, and clear
standards for banks and community organizations.
For Small Business Only LLC (FSBO) is a Virginia limited liability company and a technical-assistance and
capital-readiness intermediary working with nonprofit organizations and financial institutions to prepare
small businesses to become bankable, creditworthy, and lender-ready. FSBO develops and delivers
business-credit, cash-flow, compliance, financial-literacy, and capital-readiness programming. Our
operating premise is straightforward: access to capital improves when businesses receive disciplined
technical assistance before they apply for financing.

Strong support for capital-readiness technical assistance

FSBO particularly supports the proposed economic-development category covering technical assistance
and support services for qualifying small businesses and farms. The proposal recognizes an operational
fact seen across community-development ecosystems: many viable small businesses are not yet
prepared to obtain traditional bank financing and require structured assistance before they can present
an underwriter-ready application.
This clarification should be retained in the final rule. Capital-readiness assistance can improve
compliance, financial records, cash-flow management, credit profiles, loan documentation, and
understanding of lender requirements. These activities reduce preventable application failures and
create a more qualified pipeline for responsible lenders. They advance CRA's objective more directly

 For Small Business Only LLC | Page 1
 CRA Comment | For Small Business Only LLC

than programming that promotes access without preparing applicants to use credit safely and
successfully.

Strong support for direct community-development grants

FSBO also strongly supports the proposal's express recognition that a grant or donation to a local
nonprofit providing small-business technical assistance or financial-literacy programming may receive
CRA consideration. This language gives banks greater confidence to support organizations that directly
serve communities and gives nonprofit recipients a clearer standard around which to design programs,
budgets, records, and outcomes.

We likewise support requiring a direct connection between grant funds, qualifying activities, and the
bank's assessment area. The written commitment, program budget, geographic evidence, and closeout
documentation contemplated by the proposal will help distinguish direct service from pass-through
arrangements in which excessive administrative layers reduce the resources reaching businesses and
residents.

Strong support for the 15% indirect-cost guardrail

FSBO supports the proposed 15% indirect-cost limit for community-development grants made by large
banks. A clear ceiling protects community benefit, disciplines program design, and permits reasonable
recovery of necessary operating expenses. The use of the Uniform Guidance framework or a comparable
standard also gives recipients a recognizable method for classifying costs.

The final rule should preserve this guardrail. To improve consistent implementation without weakening
the standard, FSBO respectfully requests that the agencies clarify the following points in final regulatory
text, official commentary, or implementation guidance:

 New nonprofit documentation. A newly formed nonprofit that has not yet filed an IRS Form 990
 should be permitted to substantiate compliance through its current operating budget, program
 budget, board-approved cost-allocation policy, recent financial statements, formation
 documents, and written attestation.

 Specialized curriculum and intellectual property. A reasonable, documented, arm's-length
 license fee for curriculum actually used to deliver the funded program should be treated as a
 direct program cost when the license is necessary to provide the qualifying service, separately
 stated, properly approved, and supported by a written agreement.

 Outcome measurement and required reporting. Costs incurred to collect eligibility, assessment-
 area, service-delivery, and outcome evidence required by the bank or agencies should be
 treated as direct costs when they are allocable to the funded program.

 Related-party safeguards. Where a nonprofit licenses curriculum or purchases services from an
 affiliated entity, the agencies should recognize the cost if the relationship is disclosed, the
 interested director or officer recuses, the governing body determines the terms are fair and
 reasonable, and the recipient maintains documentation supporting the programmatic necessity
 and value.

 For Small Business Only LLC | Page 2
 CRA Comment | For Small Business Only LLC

 Comparable standards. The final rule should confirm that a recipient may use a consistently
 applied cost-allocation methodology comparable to 2 CFR part 200 even when the recipient is
 not a federal grantee.

Financial literacy and workforce development

FSBO supports the continued treatment of financial-literacy and workforce-development activities as
community development when they serve low- or moderate-income individuals and families. Financial
capability affects employment stability, household resilience, responsible credit use, and the ability to
retain income gains from workforce participation. The proposal appropriately preserves these activities
while improving categorical clarity.

Recommended final-rule implementation

The agencies can strengthen implementation by encouraging banks and recipients to use a standardized
but scalable evidence package. At minimum, that package should identify the qualifying purpose,
assessment-area nexus, eligible population or business size, approved budget, direct and indirect costs,
service outputs, outcomes, and budget-to-actual reconciliation. Smaller organizations should not be
required to create costly systems disproportionate to the grant, but every recipient should be capable of
demonstrating where the funds went and whom they benefited.
The final rule should also continue to make clear that technical assistance does not require or guarantee
a subsequent loan. The value of capital-readiness programming lies in improving the quality of the
applicant, the completeness of the documentation, and the appropriateness of the financing request.
Individual lending decisions must remain with lenders applying safe and sound underwriting standards.

Conclusion

For Small Business Only LLC strongly supports the proposed rule because it recognizes that community
credit needs are not met by capital alone. Communities also need local organizations capable of
preparing residents and small businesses to understand, qualify for, obtain, and responsibly use financial
products. The proposal's recognition of technical assistance, financial literacy, direct nonprofit grants,
assessment-area benefit, and transparent indirect-cost limits provides a sound framework for
accountable bank-community partnerships.
We urge the OCC and FDIC to adopt the proposal with the limited implementation clarifications
described above. Those clarifications would preserve the proposal's guardrails while enabling newly
formed and specialized nonprofit providers to demonstrate compliance through reliable, proportionate
documentation.

Respectfully submitted,
Sandy E. Day, MSL, PA, CFEI
Managing Director
For Small Business Only LLC | FSBOnly.com | seday@fsbonly.com

The National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) and Rise Economy are submitting a joint letter (attached) requesting an extension of the comment period for the newly proposed Community Reinvestment Act rule.

We believe that the significant changes suggested by the proposal necessitate a comment period of at least one hundred and twenty (120) days. 

This letter has been endorsed and signed by over 370 community partners and organizations.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0009_09000064b948f6e1.pdf:
August 24, 2026

Travis Hill, Chair
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
550 17th Street NW,
Washington, DC 20429
Via email: comments@FDIC.gov

Jonathan V. Gould, Comptroller
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
400 7th St. SW,
Washington, DC 20219
Via: https://regulations.gov/

Re: Community groups request an extension of the CRA comment period
RIN 3064-AG31, Docket ID OCC-2026-0694

Dear Chair Hill and Comptroller Gould,

The National Community Reinvestment Coalition, Rise Economy, and 374
community groups and national partners formally request the OCC and FDIC
extend the sixty (60) day comment period relating to the recently proposed
changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. We believe that
the significant changes suggested by the proposal necessitate a comment
period of at least one hundred and twenty (120) days.

The 60-day comment period is not sufficient for effective examination of and
comment on the over 350 pages of material and over 60 questions posed in
this complex proposed rule. It proposes to reclassify over 1200 banks and
we are concerned that many of the numerous proposed changes, if finalized
in substantially the same form, would lead to considerably less reinvestment
in the low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities meant to be served by
the CRA. More specifically, we are concerned that proposed changes will lead
to significant outcomes, including: less support for affordable housing via
the Low Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) and other community

 1




development activity, less transparency of small business lending, fewer
community development loans and investments that support small
businesses, fewer branches in LMI and rural communities, less access to
affordable bank accounts and higher fees for unbanked and underbanked
consumers, less capacity for community based organizations to play their
critical role in supporting communities and the financial service ecosystem,
and less scrutiny of redlining and discrimination by banks.

The NPRM does not appear to clearly quantify or address the costs to, and
impacts on, communities of the various changes proposed. This lack of
analysis of community impacts makes it difficult for the public to comment
meaningfully on the proposal and puts the burden on communities to
identify and quantify the proposal's impacts. More time is needed to conduct
research and analysis to understand what the agencies' proposed changes to
the Community Reinvestment Act will actually mean for communities,
including Native American and Tribal communities.

We note that in 2020, when the FDIC and the OCC similarly proposed a new
CRA rule, the agencies agreed to extend the comment period.1

For these reasons, the undersigned community organizations urge the FDIC
and the OCC to extend the comment period on this proposal to one-hundred
twenty (120) days in total.

1 https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/news-releases/2020/nr-ia-2020-19.html

 2




Thank you for your consideration of this request. Should you have any
questions, please feel free to contact Kevin Stein at Rise Economy, at
kstein@rise-economy.org or Kevin Hill at National Community Reinvestment
Coalition at khill@ncrc.org.

Very Truly Yours,


Kevin Stein
Chief of Legal and Strategy
Rise Economy

Kevin Hill
Senior Policy Advisor
National Community Reinvestment Coalition

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations Joint Notice of Proposed Rulemaking

Dear Sir/Madam:

The National Association of Development Companies (NADCO) submits these comments
in response to the joint Notice of Proposed Rulemaking and request for comment from the
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and Department of the Treasury, Office of
the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC).

NADCO represents over 190 Certified Development Companies (CDCs) and their industry
partners that deliver the Small Business Administration (SBA) Development Company
Program, commonly known as the 504 Loan Program (and referred to as the "SBDC"
program in the proposed rule). Since 1986, CDCs have provided over 224,000 small
businesses with $146 billion in Section 504 financing, representing a total capital
investment of over $418 billion and creating or retaining over 3.4 million jobs in local
communities throughout the United States.

The SBA Development Company Program is authorized by Section 501(a) of the Small
Business Investment Act of 1958, P.L. 85-699, as amended, which states: "The Congress
hereby finds and declares that the purpose of this title is to foster economic development
and to create or preserve job opportunities in both urban and rural areas by providing long-
term financing for small business concerns through the development company program
authorized by this title."

The 504 Loan Program advances this congressionally established economic development
mission through a public-private partnership. In a typical 504 financing, a private-sector
lending institution provides a first mortgage loan in conjunction with financing provided
through a CDC and backed by an SBA-guaranteed debenture. This structure enables small
businesses to obtain long-term financing for major fixed assets, including land, buildings,
machinery, and equipment, while leveraging private-sector capital to support economic
development and job creation in communities throughout the country.
 Proposed Economic Development Definition
NADCO strongly supports the agencies' proposed revisions to the definition of "economic
development." In particular, NADCO supports the proposed third category of economic
development, which would include "Federal, State, local, or Tribal government programs,
projects, or initiatives that serve small businesses or small farms, as defined by those
programs."

NADCO particularly supports the agencies' specific identification of the SBA Development
Company Program as an example of a federal program meeting this economic
development category. The 504 Loan Program is a congressionally established economic
development program specifically designed to foster economic development and create or
preserve employment opportunities through long-term financing for small businesses.

As the agencies recognize in the proposed rule, expressly identifying these government
programs will provide greater clarity and encourage continued participation in and support
of programs providing small business and small farm financing. The agencies further
recognize that aligning CRA economic development activities with government programs
addressing identified small business needs can encourage coordination among banks,
government agencies, and other program participants. NADCO strongly agrees with this
approach.

This clarification is particularly appropriate for the 504 Loan Program because the program
is built upon precisely this type of public-private coordination. Bank lending partners are
integral to 504 financing, providing private-sector capital alongside CDC/SBA financing to
support small-business investment and economic development. Greater certainty
regarding CRA consideration for qualifying 504-related lending can encourage continued
bank participation in the program and expand access to long-term capital for small
businesses in communities throughout the country.

Elimination of the Purpose Test
NADCO also supports the agencies' proposal to eliminate the existing "purpose test"
applicable to economic development activities. Under current guidance, an otherwise
qualifying small-business activity must satisfy additional requirements related to job
creation, retention, or improvement for low- or moderate-income individuals or in
qualifying geographic areas.

The proposed approach would instead establish more objective criteria for determining
whether an activity qualifies as economic development. As the agencies explain, banks
would no longer need to demonstrate, for example, low- or moderate-income job creation
for a qualifying small-business loan and could instead demonstrate that the activity or
government program through which the activity was made is identified as economic
development under the regulation.

 For the SBA 504 Loan Program, this approach appropriately recognizes the economic
development purpose of a federal program specifically established by Congress to foster
economic development and create or preserve employment opportunities, while providing
greater certainty for participating banks.

Response to Question 26
In response to Question 26, NADCO strongly supports retaining the SBA Development
Company Program in the non-exhaustive list of Federal, State, local, or Tribal government
programs, projects, or initiatives included in the proposed definition of economic
development.

Explicit recognition of the SBA Development Company Program will provide greater
regulatory certainty to bank lending partners, encourage continued bank participation in
the 504 Loan Program, and help expand access to long-term capital for small businesses
throughout the United States. It also appropriately recognizes the role of CDCs and their
bank lending partners in carrying out a congressionally established federal economic
development program.

NADCO therefore urges the agencies to adopt the proposed revisions to the economic
development provisions and retain the specific reference to the SBA Development
Company Program in the final rule.

NADCO appreciates the opportunity to provide these comments and the agencies'
recognition of the important role the SBA Development Company Program, Certified
Development Companies, and their bank lending partners play in supporting economic
development in communities throughout the United States.

Executive Summary

VeloxVFX LLC respectfully supports the agencies' effort to refocus CRA implementation on
community credit needs, improve clarity, ensure that community-development grants reach their
intended communities, and modernize data and public access.

The proposal's most consequential opportunity is to connect institutional CRA consideration to a
reviewable record of demonstrable community benefit without converting banks into government
benefit authorities or altering safe-and-sound underwriting.

The agencies should distinguish institutional activity from completed public benefit. A loan, grant,
investment, service, website, referral, or program relationship may be CRA-relevant, but the
evaluation framework should be capable of showing, proportionately, the qualifying purpose,
intended population or geography, amount or service committed, amount or service delivered,
material returns or reversals, and a reasonable outcome measure. Complexity and transaction size
should not substitute for beneficiary reach or verified delivery.

Consumer access should also be visible. Where a bank provides or supports a housing-resource,
counseling, or community-assistance pathway, the access point should be prominent, accessible,
neutral, and consent-based. Any program matching should communicate potential relevance rather
than final eligibility. Government agencies and authorized program administrators must retain
benefit-eligibility authority, and banks must retain independent underwriting and credit decisions.

Where legally permitted and affirmatively authorized by the consumer, verified information may
support a neutral referral to separately authorized housing, counseling, rental-stability, utility-
assistance, or other community resources. A mortgage denial should not itself establish eligibility for

  VELOXVFX LLC | OCC-2026-0694 | RIN 1557-AF57 | FDIC RIN 3064-AG31

another program, and no referral should guarantee funding. Existing agency and institutional
systems may satisfy these objectives; no particular technology platform is requested.

Principal Recommendations

 Connect CRA consideration to attributable activity and outcome records while distinguishing bank
 capital, public funding, guarantees, grants, and other sources.

 Preserve grant guardrails and add recipient, use, geography, beneficiary, disbursement, indirect-cost,
 amendment, return, and outcome fields.

 Distinguish institutional activity from completed community benefit; complexity, transaction size,
 advertising, or portal availability should not substitute for evidence of beneficiary reach or delivery.

 Recognize accessible, neutral, consent-based consumer discovery and referral infrastructure where it
 demonstrably improves access to qualifying community resources.

 Keep potential program matching, governmental eligibility, lender underwriting, and completed benefit
 delivery as separate states.

 Permit consumer continuity after an unmet credit request through voluntary referral to separately
 authorized resources, without guaranteeing eligibility or funding.

 Use annual records and evaluation-period outcomes together; late-period activity should not erase
 earlier gaps.

 Publish accessible maps, strategic plans, comment-response records, CRA files, and machine-readable
 data with meaningful non-digital alternatives.

Responses to Questions 1-63

Each agency question is reproduced in substance from the proposal and followed by VeloxVFX LLC's direct

Response to Question 1

Question 1: To better align with agency policies that establish an asset size of less than $30 billion as a
threshold for certain supervisory approaches, such as being considered a community bank or being
subject to the continuous examination process, should the agencies consider adjusting the intermediate
bank asset size threshold to include all banks with an asset size of less than $30 billion that do not
qualify as small banks? If the agencies establish $30 billion as the appropriate threshold to delineate
between intermediate banks and large banks, should the agencies also adopt a larger threshold for
small banks, such as the $10 billion currently proposed as the intermediate bank threshold?
VeloxVFX does not possess representative examination, operating-cost, or market data sufficient to
recommend a $10 billion or $30 billion boundary. The agencies should select the threshold using
evidence about supervisory burden, community-development activity, geographic reach, and the
loss of data visibility created by reclassification. Supervisory labels used for other purposes should
not automatically control CRA categories. Whatever threshold is selected, institutions whose scale or
geographic reach can materially affect multiple communities should preserve proportionate,
machine-readable community-development records.

Response to Question 2

Question 2: Should the agencies clarify in the rules that designation as a wholesale or limited purpose
bank or election of a strategic plan does not override the bank's asset-based definition (e.g., a bank can
be both a large bank and a wholesale bank)?
Yes. Asset category, business-model designation, and evaluation method should remain separate
attributes. The final rule should state that selecting a strategic plan or receiving a wholesale or
limited-purpose designation does not erase the bank's independently determined asset classification
or the data obligations attached to it.

Response to Question 3

Question 3: Should the final rules include a definition for 'assets' to be used in setting asset size
thresholds and assessing a bank's position relative to these thresholds? For example, should the
agencies define 'assets' to mean a bank's total assets as reported in Schedule RC of the Consolidated
Reports of Condition and Income (Call Report), or Schedule RAL for U.S. branches and agencies of
foreign banks, as applicable?
Yes. Use total assets reported on the applicable Call Report or Schedule RAL, with a stated
measurement date, averaging convention, treatment of mergers and conversions, and correction
procedure. A common source record will reduce interpretive disputes and preserve consistent year-

applicable law and safe-and-sound underwriting. No particular technology, platform, or proprietary
architecture should be required.

Conclusion

The proposed rule can improve CRA clarity while making the public purpose more visible. The final
framework should not equate institutional activity with completed public benefit. It should preserve
a proportionate, attributable record capable of showing what was committed, who or what
qualifying population was intended to benefit, what was delivered, what did not proceed, what was
returned or corrected, and what outcome followed.
Large and complex community-development transactions can produce substantial public value, and
direct household or small-business assistance can produce substantial public value. CRA evaluation
should be capable of seeing both. Transaction size, structural complexity, or eligibility for
consideration should not, by themselves, substitute for evidence of responsiveness, beneficiary
reach, delivery, and outcome. Information may interoperate, but eligibility authority, credit
authority, supervisory authority, institutional responsibility, and consumer rights must remain
attributable.

To Whom It May Concern:

The [Independent Bankers Association of Texas ("IBAT") appreciates the
opportunity to submit this comment letter regarding the joint Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) on July
31, 2026, to amend the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.

Representing community banks across Texas, IBAT is dedicated to preserving
the health and vitality of local financial banks that serve as the economic
engines of our communities.

IBAT and its member banks have a long, proven track record of meeting the
credit needs of our local communities, long predating the original 1977 CRA
statute. While we appreciate the agencies' intent to modernize the
framework, reduce unnecessary burdens, and provide greater transparency,
we have both positive feedback and significant concerns regarding the
specific structural impacts of this proposal on community banking.

Support for Regulatory Relief and Streamlined Frameworks

IBAT welcomes several provisions within the proposal that offer necessary
relief to community banks:

Realignment of Asset Thresholds: Raising the asset thresholds is a highly
consequential and positive adjustment. Re-categorizing small banks to
include banks under $1 billion in assets (up from the previous $412 million
threshold) and establishing the intermediate bank category between $1
billion and $10 billion provides critical regulatory relief. Exempting banks
under $10 billion from excessive data collection, maintenance, and reporting
requirements represents a substantial reduction in unnecessary overhead.
 Refocus on Core Lending Activities: Community banks excel at traditional relationship-based lending. By
refocusing the evaluation framework more heavily on measurable lending activities and primary credit
products, the proposal aligns evaluations with what community banks do best: funding local families, small
businesses, and agriculture.

Exclusion of Retail Deposit Services: Limiting the retail service test to primary credit products and explicitly
excluding retail deposit services from evaluation acknowledges that digital and physical deposit gathering
have evolved significantly. This eliminates subjective and burdensome evaluations of retail service metrics
that do not accurately measure community impact.

Objective Qualification Criteria: The effort to bring greater clarity, transparency, and objectivity to what
qualifies for community development consideration will provide community banks with greater certainty
prior to making long-term investment or lending commitments.

Critical Concerns with the Joint Proposal

Despite these positive developments, IBAT is deeply concerned by several structural aspects of the
proposal that threaten to disrupt the banking ecosystem and introduce operational challenges:

A Fractured Regulatory Framework: The most glaring deficiency of this proposal is that the Board of
Governors of the Federal Reserve System did not join it. A fractured framework where OCC- and FDIC-
supervised banks operate under a new rule while Federal Reserve-regulated state member banks remain
under the legacy 1995 framework is unworkable. This division disrupts competitive equity, complicates
holding company supervision, and creates confusion for community partnerships that rely on consistent
interagency rules.

Regulatory Whiplash and Uncertainty: The banking industry has endured substantial regulatory shifting
since 2020, ranging from the 2023 final rule to subsequent litigation, rescission proposals, and now this
completely new framework. Community banks require a durable, long-term, and fully unified interagency
standard. This cyclical rulemaking forces community banks to redirect finite compliance resources away
from actual community lending to handle continuous administrative changes.

Constraints on Community Development Infrastructure: While community banks support verifying that
community development funds reach their intended beneficiaries, specific new restrictions--such as rigid
indirect cost caps or narrow definitions of qualifying economic development--may inadvertently penalize
long-standing partnerships with local nonprofits. Local nonprofits in rural or smaller Texas markets heavily
depend on general operating support grants from community banks, and overly restrictive tracking
mandates could choke off this vital infrastructure.

IBAT urges the OCC and the FDIC to pause finalization of this proposal until a fully unified, interagency rule
can be reached in conjunction with the Federal Reserve. While the tiered asset thresholds and lending
focus represent positive steps toward meaningful regulatory relief, a split regulatory landscape
undermines the core statutory goal of providing a consistent, predictable environment for community
investment. We look forward to ongoing engagement with the agencies to establish a workable, durable
CRA framework that truly supports economic growth across Texas.
 Sincerely,

/s/

Christopher Williston
President and CEO
Independent Bankers Association of Texas

 work identified several regulatory and process problems, including the risk that banks could be penalized

led by Lord Santiago LLC have identified better pathways for addressing this regulatory obstacle while
improving net access to capital for borrowers who do not meet conventional bank underwriting standards.

Lord Santiago LLC's involvement in minority depository institution revitalization also highlighted the need to

that they do not possess the internal infrastructure available to their larger counterparts. We are pleased
that regulators are increasingly sensitive to this economies-of-scale challenge and to the need for
supervisory expectations that remain rigorous but proportionate to institutional capacity.

Lord Santiago LLC's founder, Dennis Santiago, also authored a substantial response to the June 3, 2022,
interagency notice of proposed rulemaking on Community Reinvestment Act regulations while serving as a
member of the Board of Directors of the National Diversity Coalition. That response provided detailed input
on numerous specific questions posed by the regulators and reflected direct engagement with the
proposal's major policy choices.

We support the regulators' objective of ensuring that CRA-qualified activities demonstrably benefit the
communities Congress intended the CRA to serve. We also support efforts to make CRA qualification more
predictable and to focus CRA evaluation on the provision of credit and meaningful community-development
activities.

In particular, we support the concept underlying Options 1 and 2 for determining major product lines: CRA
retail lending evaluation should concentrate principally on the lending products that represent meaningful
components of a bank's business. We believe this approach can make CRA evaluation more relevant to
how financial institutions actually operate while allowing banks and regulators to devote greater attention
to activities capable of producing meaningful community impact.

We also agree with the regulators that rent extraction is a legitimate concern in evaluating community-
development grants. CRA consideration should not encourage structures in which successive layers of
intermediaries consume grant resources without producing commensurate benefits for the communities
the CRA is intended to serve.

These two policy objectives are related. If banks are encouraged to concentrate their direct retail lending
efforts on the major products in which they possess scale, systems, expertise, and demonstrated capacity,
Treasury-certified CDFIs can provide a complementary channel for reaching borrowers and credit needs
that fall outside those products or below conventional bank underwriting standards.

Direct bank partnerships with Treasury-certified CDFIs can therefore improve the efficacy of CRA programs
while simultaneously addressing the regulators' concern about unnecessary intermediary costs.

I. Treasury-certified CDFIs should be distinguished from generic intermediaries.

CDFIs are not simply intermediaries between banks and ultimate beneficiaries. A certified CDFI is a
specialized financial institution whose primary mission is community development and whose certification
is subject to standards administered by the U.S. Department of the Treasury.

CDFIs perform financial functions that conventional lenders frequently cannot perform economically at
comparable scale. These functions include borrower identification and development, technical assistance,
underwriting of nontraditional credits, loan origination, loan servicing, portfolio monitoring, compliance,
loan-loss management, and recycling of repaid capital into subsequent community-development loans.

These functions are not ancillary to community-development lending. They are the process by which
community-development lending occurs.

 Page 2
 Banks appropriately establish credit standards--or "buy boxes"--designed to define borrowers and
transactions that satisfy their risk, underwriting, profitability, regulatory and portfolio requirements.
Inevitably, otherwise viable borrowers exist whose financial condition, collateral, credit history, transaction
size, stage of development or other characteristics place them below those conventional bank financing
thresholds.

Serving that population is one of the essential functions of a CDFI. A CDFI identifies prospective borrowers,
prepares them for financing, provides technical assistance where appropriate, performs underwriting
adapted to the characteristics of underserved markets, originates and services loans, monitors credit
performance, and works with borrowers after closing.

The objective is not merely to make loans that conventional banks will not make. It is to develop qualified
borrowers and viable credits in markets where conventional bank underwriting alone may not economically
support that development process.

We recommend that the regulators establish a rebuttable presumption or safe harbor under which a loan,
investment, grant, or other qualifying financial commitment to a Treasury-certified CDFI is considered to
have a community-development purpose when the funds are committed to activities otherwise qualifying
under the CRA and the CDFI maintains reasonable records demonstrating the use and geographic
distribution of those funds.

II. Major product lines: We support the fundamental direction of Options 1 and 2

We support the regulators' proposal to focus CRA retail lending evaluation on a bank's major product lines.

Banks differ substantially in business model, market, expertise, and lending capacity. A bank substantially
engaged in small-business lending should be evaluated meaningfully on its small-business lending
performance. Similarly, an institution whose principal retail credit activity consists of mortgage lending
should receive appropriate scrutiny of that activity.

Requiring equal regulatory attention to incidental lending activities can consume both bank and regulatory
resources without necessarily producing a corresponding community benefit.

Accordingly, we support the fundamental concept reflected in both Options 1 and 2: CRA evaluation should
identify and meaningfully evaluate the lending activities that are actually significant to the institution or the
markets in which it operates.

At the same time, concentrating evaluation on major products should not cause credit needs outside those
products to disappear from CRA policy.

This is precisely where strategically working with U.S. Treasury-certified CDFIs can improve the
effectiveness of a bank's CRA program. CDFIs can complement the bank's major product lending by
reaching qualified community-development borrowers and activities outside the bank's primary business
lines and by serving prospective borrowers below the bank's conventional credit thresholds.

III. Response to Question 4: A de minimis threshold is reasonable.

Question 4 asks whether the regulators should establish a de minimis threshold for determining major
product lines, including whether a threshold such as 30 loans would appropriately exclude incidental
lending.

We believe a de minimis threshold is reasonable and appropriate.

A bank may originate a small number of loans in a particular category for reasons unrelated to a sustained
product strategy. Inadvertently, treating such incidental activity as a major product line could distort CRA

 Page 3
 evaluation and impose examination and compliance costs disproportionate to the community significance
of the activity.

The threshold should distinguish a genuine lending business from incidental activity while avoiding a level
so high that it excludes meaningful lending by smaller institutions. We encourage the regulators to consider
both loan count and the institution's overall lending activity when defining the threshold and to evaluate
experience under the final rule to determine whether the chosen threshold produces the intended result.

Importantly, exclusion of incidental lending from the major-product test should not imply that the
corresponding community credit need is unimportant. Banks should be encouraged to address credit
needs outside their major products through community development lending and strategic partnerships
with Treasury-certified CDFIs possessing specialized capacity in those markets. This provides a practical
means of focusing on major products while preserving broader CRA impact.

IV. Response to Question 5: Consumer lending should be evaluated by individual type.

We recommend that consumer lending be evaluated by individual product type rather than treated as a
single undifferentiated category.

Consumer lending encompasses a particularly broad variety of credit structures, purposes, borrower
populations, risk characteristics, and pricing models.

Historically, "consumer lending" has often functioned as a catch-all reporting category, including for
regulatory Call Report purposes. That broad categorization may be useful for certain financial-reporting
purposes, but CRA evaluation requires a more granular understanding of how credit is actually being
provided to communities.

For example, automobile lending, credit-card lending, other revolving credit, unsecured installment
lending, and other forms of consumer credit can present substantially different borrower populations,
pricing structures, underwriting criteria, and community impacts.

For CRA purposes, consumer lending should therefore be examined with a finer degree of product-level
differentiation. This would allow regulators to determine whether a particular consumer product represents
a meaningful component of the bank's lending activity rather than allowing a broad aggregate category to
obscure the significance--or insignificance--of individual lending products.

Here again, Treasury-certified CDFIs can serve as strategic partners. Where a particular consumer-credit
need is material to a community but does not constitute a major product for the bank, a qualified CDFI with
appropriate lending authority and expertise may provide a more effective channel through which the bank
can support responsible access to credit.

V. Response to Question 6: Both dollar volume and loan count should determine major
product lines.

Question 6 asks whether regulators should rely on dollar volume, loan count, or both in determining a
bank's major product lines.

We recommend using both dollar volume and loan count. Neither metric alone adequately captures the
significance of a lending product.

This is particularly evident in small-business lending. Small-business loans frequently have substantially
smaller principal balances than residential mortgages and other large-balance credit products. A bank
could originate a significant number of small-business loans, serve a substantial number of businesses,
and generate meaningful community impact, while the aggregate dollar balance of those loans remains
relatively modest compared with its mortgage portfolio.

 Page 4
 A dollar-volume-only test could consequently understate the importance of small-business lending.
Conversely, loan count alone could understate the significance of a product involving fewer but
substantially larger extensions of credit.

Using both metrics provides regulators with a more complete picture of the bank's actual lending business
and avoids systematically penalizing products characterized by smaller, more numerous loans.

This principle is particularly relevant to CDFI partnerships. CDFI lending frequently consists of
comparatively small loans whose aggregate community impact is better reflected by considering both
dollars deployed and borrowers served. Banks working strategically with Treasury-certified CDFIs should
therefore be encouraged to report both dollar volume and loan count, together with appropriate information
concerning borrower characteristics and community impact.

VI. Response to Question 7: Apply Option 1 to small and intermediate banks and consider
Option 2 for large banks.

Question 7 asks whether, if Option 1 is adopted, major product lines should be determined by assessment
area rather than at the institution level.

We believe the answer should depend substantially on institution size and geographic complexity.

For small and intermediate banks as defined under the proposed rule, we believe the institution-level
methodology contemplated by Option 1 is generally the preferable approach. These institutions are more
likely to have relatively cohesive business models and geographic footprints. Determining their major
product lines at the institution level should provide regulators with meaningful information while avoiding
unnecessary compliance and examination burden.

For large banks, particularly institutions operating across numerous and materially different geographic
markets, the assessment area analysis contemplated by Option 2 may provide useful additional
information.

A large geographically dispersed institution may operate in markets with significantly different economic
conditions, demographic characteristics, credit needs, and product demand. A product that is relatively
insignificant at the consolidated institution level may nevertheless be important in a particular assessment
area. Accordingly, an assessment-area approach may provide greater insight into whether the bank is
responding to the credit characteristics of particular communities.

However, this additional analytical granularity comes at a cost. The regulators should therefore evaluate the
cost-benefit relationship associated with imposing assessment-area-level major-product analysis on large
institutions.

The relevant question should be whether the additional data collection, systems, compliance activity,
examination work, and regulatory resources required by the assessment-area methodology produce a
commensurate improvement in community outcomes and CRA effectiveness.

We recommend that the regulators incorporate a mechanism to assess this return on regulatory investment
after implementation. Such an assessment could examine whether the additional analytical work materially
improves identification of unmet credit needs, changes bank lending behavior, or produces measurable
benefits for communities.

If experience demonstrates that assessment-area analysis produces meaningful incremental benefits, its
continuation would be supported by evidence. If the additional burden produces little difference in
community outcomes, the regulators should retain the flexibility to simplify the methodology.

Treasury-certified CDFIs can also contribute to this analysis. Because CDFIs frequently possess detailed
knowledge of credit gaps within individual communities, strategic bank-CDFI relationships can provide

 Page 5
 banks and regulators with market information that may complement quantitative assessment-area
analysis.

VII. Further Regarding Questions 4 to 7: The major product framework strengthens the
case for direct bank-CDFI partnerships.

Questions 4 through 7 should not be considered independently from the community development
provisions addressed later in the proposal.
A major product framework necessarily acknowledges that no bank can specialize in every form of lending
required by every community it serves.
The logical regulatory objective should therefore be twofold: first, evaluate banks rigorously on the lending
products that constitute meaningful components of their business; second, provide effective channels
through which banks can address legitimate community credit needs outside those major products.
Treasury-certified CDFIs provide one such channel.
Bank major-product lending supports direct lending in areas where the bank possesses scale, systems, and
expertise. Bank-CDFI partnerships support specialized borrower development, technical assistance,
underwriting, and lending in areas outside the bank's principal products or conventional credit parameters.
The major product framework and CDFI partnerships should therefore be viewed as complementary
components of an efficient CRA architecture rather than unrelated policy questions.

VIII. Response to Question 9: Address rent extraction by distinguishing intermediaries
from direct CDFI financial activity

Question 9 asks: "Are there alternative standards the regulators should consider relying on in the context of
limiting indirect costs for CD grants? Do the proposed guardrails do enough to ensure the majority of grant
and donation funds go directly towards benefiting the bank's assessment area(s)?"
We agree with the regulators' underlying concern. CRA consideration should not encourage arrangements
in which organizations function principally as intermediaries, transferring resources through multiple layers
while extracting administrative costs at each stage. Regulators have a legitimate interest in ensuring that
CRA-motivated grants actually produce measurable community-development benefits.
We believe that direct relationships between banks and Treasury-certified CDFIs engaged in actual
economic-development lending provide one appropriate regulatory response to this concern.
A Treasury-certified CDFI that identifies borrowers, develops those borrowers, performs underwriting,
originates loans, services those loans, and monitors their performance is not merely passing funds to
another organization. It is performing the financial activity for which the community-development resources
were provided.
The distinction between intermediation and financial production is therefore critical.
Where an organization merely receives a grant and passes substantially the same funds through to another
organization, the regulators' concern about intermediary costs may appropriately receive heightened
scrutiny. Where a certified CDFI uses bank resources to identify, prepare, underwrite, finance, service and
monitor borrowers that fall outside conventional bank credit parameters, those expenditures are
fundamentally different. They are costs incurred to produce community-development credit.

 Page 6
 IX. The 15 percent limitation should principally address true general-and-administrative
costs.

We believe the regulators' proposed 15 percent limitation is better understood and more appropriately
applied as a limitation on general and administrative (G&A) costs, rather than as a broad limitation on all
operating expenditures that do not directly become loan principal.

A distinction should be drawn between (1) general institutional overhead, consisting of costs that are not
reasonably allocable to a particular lending or community-development program, and (2) direct program
costs, consisting of expenditures necessary to identify, prepare, underwrite, originate, service, monitor and
manage qualifying community-development credit.

The regulators' concern regarding rent extraction is most relevant to the first category. True G&A expenses
may include corporate governance, certain executive and administrative functions, general office
administration, non-program-specific legal or accounting expenses, and other costs supporting the
organization as a whole without a direct nexus to qualifying community-development activity.

The second category represents the operational cost of producing and maintaining the very financial activity
the CRA is intended to encourage.

We therefore recommend that any percentage limitation adopted in the final rule apply principally to true
general-and-administrative costs, and not to reasonable direct program costs necessary to create,
administer and monitor qualifying community-development loans.

X. Borrower development, lending infrastructure and technology are direct program
costs.

For a CDFI loan fund, borrower development, underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, portfolio
management, loan-loss monitoring, impact reporting, and appropriate financial controls are essential
components of the lending process.

A dollar cannot responsibly be deployed as a small-business loan merely by transferring it from a bank to a
borrower. The prospective borrower must be identified. The business must be evaluated. The borrower may
require assistance with financial statements, bookkeeping, cash-flow projections, or other elements
necessary to be prepared for financing.

The credit must then be underwritten, approved, documented, and closed. After closing, the loan must be
serviced and monitored. Delinquencies and credit deterioration must be identified and managed. These are
direct costs of producing and maintaining community-development loans.

The technology supporting those functions is equally integral. Direct program costs should expressly
include reasonable expenses associated with:

 loan application platforms used for borrower intake and document collection.
 underwriting platforms used for credit analysis, risk assessment, and approval.
 loan servicing platforms used to administer loans after closing; and
 portfolio surveillance systems used to monitor credit performance, covenant compliance, delinquency,

 concentration, and risk migration.
These systems are not administrative conveniences. They are lending infrastructure. A platform used to
originate or monitor hundreds of qualifying loans should not become an indirect expense merely because
the technology supports multiple borrowers.

 Page 7
 XI. Banks should document CDFI performance rather than rely solely on an overhead
percentage.

The regulators can address rent extraction through accountability for outputs and outcomes, rather than
relying exclusively on an overhead ratio.

Banks receiving CRA consideration for CDFI support could reasonably request periodic reports concerning:

 number and dollar amount of loans originated.
 communities and populations served.
 borrower characteristics relevant to CRA qualification.
 borrowers receiving technical assistance.
 borrowers prepared for financing.
 lending to borrowers outside conventional bank underwriting thresholds.
 geographic distribution.
 loan and portfolio performance.
 direct program expenses associated with borrower development and lending.
 technology costs reasonably allocable to qualifying lending; and
 where practicable, borrowers subsequently graduating to conventional financial products.
The CDFI-bank relationship is inherently symbiotic. Banks provide capital, grants, investments, and
financial expertise. CDFIs provide specialized market access and the borrower-development, underwriting
and servicing capabilities necessary to responsibly extend credit deeper into underserved markets.

The appropriate regulatory question therefore should not simply be: "What percentage did the CDFI spend
on administration?"

A more meaningful question is: "What did the CDFI produce with the bank's support, whom did it
finance, what financial-development activities and systems were required to produce those loans,
and did the resulting activity demonstrably benefit the communities the CRA is intended to serve?"

XII. The proposed 15 percent indirect cost limitation should be modified for certified
CDFIs. G&A costs should be controlled. Certain program costs should be classified as
direct costs.

We appreciate the regulators' objective of preventing excessive administrative expenses from absorbing
funds intended for community development. However, a rigid 15 percent test does not accurately reflect
the economics of community-development finance.

The Uniform Guidance de minimis indirect-cost rate provides a mechanism for recognizing and recovering
legitimate indirect costs. Its existence should not imply that organizations exceeding that percentage are
inefficient or engaged in rent extraction.

We recommend that the 15 percent limitation apply principally to G&A expenses after reasonable direct
program costs have been identified and allocated.

For Treasury-certified CDFIs, direct program costs should include reasonable expenses associated with
borrower identification and preparation, technical assistance, underwriting, origination, closing, servicing,
portfolio surveillance, loan-loss management, and lending technology--including loan applications,
underwriting, servicing, and portfolio-surveillance platforms.

This concept is similar to the use of cost allocation agreements used in other areas of federal contracting.
We believe they principles are applicable and recommend regulators consider codifying this guidance as
part of the final rule.

 Page 8
 Alternatively, the regulators could establish 15 percent as an administrative safe harbor rather than an
absolute ceiling. Organizations within the safe harbor would require no additional demonstration. A
certified CDFI exceeding it could establish qualification through documentation demonstrating the nature
of its costs and the qualifying lending produced.

XIII. Response to Question 10: Grants and donations should remain eligible.

Question 10 asks: "As an alternative, should the regulators eliminate all grants and donations from CRA
consideration?"
We strongly recommend that grants and donations remain eligible.
Loan capital finances assets expected to produce repayment. Grants finance many of the activities
required to create the pipeline through which that loan capital can responsibly reach underserved
borrowers.
These include borrower preparation, technical assistance, underwriting assistance, outreach, loan-loss
support, post-closing assistance, lending systems, and institutional capacity.
Eliminating CRA consideration for grants could therefore reduce precisely the activities that help
prospective borrowers become capable of obtaining responsible financing and, ultimately, conventional
financing.

XIV. Geographic flexibility for CDFI activities

CDFI service territories frequently do not correspond precisely with bank assessment areas.
CDFIs may manage lending programs across metropolitan, regional, or statewide markets. Excessively
narrow geographic restrictions can fragment capital pools, increase reporting burdens, and inhibit
deployment based on actual borrower demand.
CDFIs should therefore be permitted to establish geographic benefit through reasonable methodologies
including loan-level information, portfolio allocations, borrower addresses, census-tract data, or
proportional allocation.
Exact tracing of every dollar should not be required where a reasonable methodology reliably demonstrates
community benefit.

XV. Strategic plans should incorporate CDFI knowledge.

CDFIs work directly with borrowers who frequently cannot obtain conventional financing and therefore
possess information about unmet credit demand that may not appear in traditional bank lending data.
We recommend expressly recognizing consultation with certified CDFIs as potentially relevant evidence
when banks identify community credit needs and develop measurable CRA strategic-plan objectives.
Such consultation should not be mandatory or exclusive, but it represents a meaningful source of market
intelligence.

XVI. Recommended CDFI safe harbor

We encourage the regulators to consider language substantially similar to the following:
Certified CDFI Safe Harbor

 A loan, investment, grant, deposit, or other financial commitment provided to a Community
 Development Financial Institution certified by the U.S. Department of the Treasury shall be

 Page 9
  presumed to have a community-development purpose to the extent that the recipient CDFI commits
 the funds to activities satisfying the community-development requirements of this part.

 Reasonable costs directly associated with identifying and preparing prospective borrowers and with
 originating, underwriting, closing, administering, servicing, monitoring, or providing technical
 assistance in connection with qualifying community-development loans shall constitute direct
 program costs.

 Direct program costs shall include reasonable costs allocable to loan application platforms,
 underwriting and credit-analysis platforms, loan servicing platforms, portfolio-surveillance and risk-
 management systems, and other technology infrastructure necessary to originate, manage and
 monitor qualifying community-development credit.

 Any percentage limitation on indirect costs should apply principally to general-and-administrative
 expenses remaining after reasonable direct program costs have been identified and allocated.

 A certified CDFI may establish geographic benefit through loan-level information, portfolio
 allocations, proportional methodologies, beneficiary information, or another reasonable and
 consistently applied methodology.

 A regulated financial institution relying upon this safe harbor should maintain reasonable
 documentation of the recipient CDFI's qualifying activities and outcomes, including lending volumes,
 borrower and geographic characteristics, technical-assistance activity, portfolio performance, and
 direct program expenditures.

XVII. The future role of national intermediaries

National intermediaries remain a valuable resource within the broader ecosystem serving communities.
Their value should increasingly be understood not as that of rent-extracting conduits, but as outcome-
enhancing resources capable of improving the efficiency, reach, and accountability of community-
development activity.

We believe national intermediaries can reduce friction costs for both regulators and banks by helping
identify opportunities for direct relationships with Treasury-certified CDFIs, facilitating appropriate
introductions and due diligence, and monitoring the efficiency and outcomes of service delivery to the
American public. Properly structured, this role can complement rather than displace direct bank-CDFI
relationships.

We therefore recommend that the regulators initiate a study of how national intermediaries can best be
utilized on a going-forward basis. We respectfully suggest that this study be conducted as a public-private
partnership between regulators and banks, with structured input from CDFIs and national intermediaries,
and that it focus on measurable outcomes, reduced transaction friction, and the efficient delivery of capital
and services to communities.

XVIII. Conclusion and recommendations

We support the regulators' movement toward a CRA framework that concentrates examination resources
on meaningful lending activity while improving accountability for community-development expenditures.

We respectfully recommend that the regulators:

 1. adopt the major product concept reflected in Options 1 and 2.
 2. establish a reasonable de minimis threshold under Question 4 to exclude truly incidental lending.
 3. under Question 5, evaluate consumer lending by individual product type rather than as a single catch-all

 category.
 4. under Question 6, use both dollar volume and loan count when identifying major product lines.

 Page 10
  5. under Question 7, generally employ Option 1's institution-level methodology for small and intermediate
 institutions while considering Option 2's assessment-area methodology for large, geographically dispersed
 institutions.

 6. evaluate whether the incremental compliance and examination costs of assessment-area analysis for large
 institutions produce commensurate improvements in community outcomes.

 7. recognize strategic partnerships with Treasury-certified CDFIs as a complementary mechanism for
 addressing credit needs outside banks' major products and conventional underwriting parameters.

 8. retain grants and donations as CRA-eligible community-development activities.
 9. address rent extraction by distinguishing unnecessary intermediary costs from the direct costs of producing

 community-development credit.
 10. apply the proposed 15 percent limitation principally to true G&A expenses.
 11. recognize borrower identification, preparation, technical assistance, underwriting, origination, servicing and

 monitoring as direct program costs.
 12. expressly recognize reasonable loan-application, underwriting, servicing, and portfolio-surveillance

 technology as direct program costs.
 13. create a safe harbor or rebuttable presumption for qualifying activity conducted directly through Treasury-

 certified CDFIs.
 14. encourage outcome-oriented reporting by CDFIs receiving CRA-motivated bank support.
 15. preserve reasonable geographic flexibility for qualifying CDFI activity; and
 16. recognize CDFIs as an appropriate source of information concerning community credit needs.
 17. initiate a public-private study, in partnership with banks and informed by CDFIs, on how national

 intermediaries can reduce transaction friction, facilitate direct bank-CDFI relationships, and
 strengthen outcome monitoring.
These recommendations share a common principle: CRA regulation should concentrate resources where
they can produce measurable credit outcomes.
We agree with regulators that banks should be evaluated for CRA performance with an emphasis on the
lending they either directly provide or leverage delivering to the community. Direct partnerships with
Treasury-certified CDFIs should complement in-house activity, extending the financial system's reach to
borrowers, products and communities that fall outside conventional bank credit channels.
That division of labor can simultaneously improve regulatory efficiency, reduce opportunities for rent
extraction, strengthen accountability, and increase the amount of responsible credit ultimately reaching
underserved communities.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this important rulemaking.
