To Whom It May Concern,

On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA). CRA has helped create a durable incentive for banks to provide loans, investments, grants, and
services in communities that have historically lacked access to capital. As such, we wish to offer
comments on the proposed regulation from the perspective of an emerging community development
financial institution (CDFI).

While we support some of the agencies' provisions that could improve the CRA and increase accessible
and responsible capital in economically distressed communities, we are concerned about the asset
thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated, as well as proposed restrictions on grants. There
are also provisions that we feel could weaken community development incentives across geographic
areas.

CDFI Friendly Bloomington, Inc. (CFB) serves a rural 13-county region in Southwest Central Indiana with
a population of 516,000. We are a newly certified CDFI (as of July 2025) that works to attract
investment from CDFI partners in our designated target markets serving geographic Investment Areas
(Ias) and Low-Income Targeted Populations (LITP). Since our founding in 2018, our organization has
helped facilitate more than $29 million in CDFI investment to our region as part of more than $74
  2

million in projects. This includes affordable housing, small business, childcare and nonprofit
organizations who have benefitted from CDFI investment. Our area of Indiana has historically lacked
access to non-traditional financing, and our organization serves as a connector to help fill financial gaps
where they exist for community development projects.

Our banking partners are a critical ally in these efforts. We have relationships with banks that provide a
range of services benefiting our organization and our region. These include service on our board of
directors, technical expertise and networking, grants and lending capital investments such as lines of
credit and Equity Equivalent (EQ2) investments. These investments not only assist our organization in
providing critical technical assistance and outreach/education on access to financing, but they help
weave together the important components of community development finance in our region. These
financial partnerships, estimated at nearly $400,000 in grant support and in partnership with other
entities including the CDFI Fund, have helped CFB assist with the creation or retention of 425 units of
affordable housing and, over the last three years, with more than 700 hours of technical assistance.

These partnerships speak to the longstanding, mutually beneficial relationship that CDFIs like ours have
with our banking partners, due in part to the CRA and its tools that help our organizations create a
more seamless financing network. In order for this to continue, we wish to comment on three CRA
provisions that are under review.

1. Raised Asset Thresholds That Could Jeopardize Community Development Finance: Section IV.A,
 "Asset Thresholds"; Questions 13

The proposal defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets, intermediate banks
as institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as institutions with more than
$10 billion. About 800 banks that currently face a separate community development test as
intermediate small banks would become small banks and lose that requirement. Another
approximately 400 banks that are currently evaluated as large banks would become intermediate
banks, losing the separate large-bank lending, investment, and service tests and many associated
data-reporting requirements.

In Indiana, it is estimated that more than 40 percent, or 34 of our 84 banks, would no longer be
required to reinvest in local community development projects such as affordable housing, small
business support and healthcare. About 16 banks, comprising 40 percent of all banks in the state,
would lose their large bank status, thereby jeopardizing more than 30 percent of branches located in
LMI areas. In our rural region, the loss of even one or two CRA-motivated bank partners can materially
affect whether projects are financed. In an already tough environment to meet the demand for
housing, childcare and a ready workforce, increasing barriers to financing will exacerbate these
challenges.

Page 2
  3

The asset threshold changes would also substantially reduce the number of institutions subject to
large-bank CRA data requirements. This would make it harder for communities, CDFIs, policymakers,
and regulators to identify credit gaps, compare bank performance, assess geographic disparities, and
understand whether community credit needs are being met. We are concerned that aggregate
community development finance data is already difficult to track and the proposal would decrease
clarity on data gathering, making it difficult to identify and understand where credit is flowing. This is
especially important in our rural region, where the Federal Reserve Bank of New York has determined
that seven of our 13 counties are credit-constrained.

Recommendation

For all the reasons cited above, we urge the agencies to retain the current thresholds and reject all
alternatives offered (including the substantially higher thresholds raised for consideration in Question
1).

2. Restrictions on Community Development Grants: Section IV.C, "Community Development
 Activities -- CD Grants"; Questions 911

We strongly oppose the proposed restrictions on community development grants which: 1) requires a
qualifying CD grant to be directly used by the recipient for a program, project, or initiative with a
primary purpose of community development; 2) for large banks, caps grant recipient's indirect
administrative costs to 15%; 3) requires that large banks obtain documentation from grant recipients
including written commitments regarding use of funds, indirect-cost attestations, IRS Form 990s, and
operating and program budgets. We also strongly oppose the alternative contemplated in Question 10
to eliminate grants and donations from CRA consideration entirely.

While we share the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants meaningfully benefit
communities, these requirements would restrict many forms of effective grantmaking and
misunderstand the role that flexible operating support plays in community development finance. For
CDFIs, staffing, underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, risk management, data systems,
financial management, technical assistance, and product development are not ancillary to community
development. They are the infrastructure that makes community development lending possible.

As an organization focused on outreach and technical assistance, our operations are our programming
in many ways. Our audited financial statements show that our organization spends just 23% of our
assets on operations, with 77% dedicated to programming. The majority of our staff time is focused on
providing direct interaction with clients and projects, and focused on the logistical preparation to assist
seeing more community development projects to the finish line. It is also critical that organizations like
ours be administered in a professional manner, ensuring we have the funds available to obtain
professional financial accounting and audit services, as well as qualified staff who can perform the
necessary duties grantmakers are interested in funding. Over the last three years, CFB has provided

Page 3
  4

more than 700 hours of technical assistance and has increased our loan portfolio to more than $1
million. In addition, during this time we have helped increase CDFI investment in our region by nearly
$4 million.

Therefore, we strongly oppose using a fixed 15% indirect-cost limit as a condition of CRA eligibility. An
organization's administrative-cost percentage is not an appropriate proxy for community impact. Costs
vary depending on an organization's size, geography, product mix, regulatory obligations,
technical-assistance model, and populations served. The cap could disproportionately affect small and
emerging CDFIs, rural CDFIs, CDFIs making small-dollar loans, organizations providing intensive
borrower technical assistance, CDFIs developing new products or entering underserved markets and
organizations making necessary investments in technology, compliance, data, and risk management.
CDFI Friendly Bloomington meets all of the above criteria.

Recommendation

The agencies should preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-building grants as
currently is in place under the 1995 framework. CRA should encourage flexibility for banks to provide
the form of support that best responds to the identified community needs instead of imposing undue
compliance burdens.

3. Geographic flexibility for CD activities outside assessment areas: Section IV.E, "Consideration of
 Community Development Activities -- CD Activities Outside Assessment Areas"; proposed
 __.13(e); Question 34

We support the goal of enabling CRA-motivated capital to reach communities with significant unmet
needs but relatively few bank assessment areas. Greater geographic flexibility could be particularly
beneficial for reaching CRA deserts.

CDFI Friendly Bloomington serves what is known as a CDFI desert. According to data from the CDFI
Fund, over the last 20 years, the per capita investment from CDFIs in our region was just $22,
compared to $714 nationally. While that number has more than doubled in the past few years, we still
have a long way to go in filling financing gaps in our 13 counties.

Flexibility with CRA capital should supplement rather than displace CD activity in banks' own
assessment areas. The agencies are considering both quantitative and qualitative approaches for
determining when a bank has sufficiently served its assessment areas to receive consideration for
outside-AA activity.

Page 4
  5
Recommendation
With respect to Question 34, we support greater geographic flexibility where it can help direct
CRA-motivated capital to rural communities, Indian Country, and other underserved areas that may fall
outside traditional assessment areas.
In conclusion, CRA has helped create a powerful partnership among banks, CDFIs, and the communities
we serve. We appreciate the agencies' efforts to improve clarity and flexibility. Modernization,
however, should result in more responsible capital reaching communities with unmet credit needs, as
the CRA statute was intended. In doing so, maintaining flexible, yet structured criteria that is easily
understood in communities that also support emerging CDFIs is essential to making community
development work.
We urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the raised asset thresholds proposed, the restrictions on CD
operating grants and to maintain geographic flexibility with CRA-motivated capital.
Thank you for considering these comments and for considering the impact of the proposed changes on
our communities.

John C. Zody

Habitat for Humanity Susquehanna submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Corey Leon submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency
(OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)1 because it would
significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the
complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, I also request that the OCC and FDIC,
before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low-
and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis
and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current
comment deadline by 60-days.

I have over 30 years of professional experience working at the national, state, and local
levels in community development finance. From investments in Low-Income Housing
Tax Credits and New Markets Tax Credits to funding local community development
corporations, I have seen how the CRA encourages regulated institutions to pay attention,
tract and monitor and even dedicate staff to making loans, investments and grants in
underserved communities. I am proudly a member of the National Community
Reinvestment Coalition.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).

 1
 in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal
access to mainstream financial services.

The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and
would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and
support for nonprofit organizations. I am concerned that these changes are being
considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-
income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination
and disinvestment.

CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. Most of my
work is in Michigan and Ohio. In metro Detroit, from 2010-2024, banks made
$28,964,420,000 in CRA qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census
tracts and $25,352,603,000 in CRA qualified lending to small businesses.

I am concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1
capital devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough
to receive a passing CRA rating.2 However, that percentage is far lower than the
percentage the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the
largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.

NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the
OCC and FDIC supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these
banks currently conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community development
loans and investments inside their assessment areas, and that the median percentage of
annual community development lending in assessment areas was 6.8% of tier 1 capital,
and a median of 3.6% of tier 1 capital for annual CRA qualified investments.3 If each
bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet separate thresholds of 0.625%
of Tier 1 capital for community development lending and investments, combined activity
would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually -- a decrease of approximately $87.1
billion, or 85%. Similarly, the proposal encourages banks to use strategic plans to make
their CRA compliance easier and more predictable. Previous proposed guidance also set
strategic plan benchmarks for CRA performance well-below historical levels of
community development activity.4

effect of this proposal is that the benchmark will serve not as a floor, but a ceiling.

communities. For example, in my community, many small businesses have a hard time
finding growth capital. It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to
meet community needs. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether
the proposed changes would reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and
moderate-income communities and whether communities that have experienced historic
discrimination or disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.

The proposal would substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small
banks, while banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be
evaluated under the less demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more
comprehensive tests applied to large banks.5 The proposal would also eliminate several
CRA data collection and reporting requirements currently applicable to large banks for
institutions with $10 billion or less in assets, including reporting on small-business,
small-farm and community development lending.6

Approximately 800 banks would no longer receive a community development evaluation
because the proposal would raise the small-bank threshold from $412 million to $1
billion.7 The 417 banks newly classified as intermediate rather than large would no
longer be examined under separate CRA investment and services tests and instead would
be evaluated based on their combined community development loans, investments and
services. These reclassifications and resulting eliminations of community development
obligations for over 800 banks and separate investment evaluations for 400 banks, may
worsen the housing crisis by reducing the demand for Low-Income Housing Tax Credits
(LIHTC).

Michigan will lose 15 of its 64 banks with CRA obligations if this proposal goes through.
Of those 64 banks, 29 have "large" bank status but this proposal would reduce that to
only 19 banks. Furthermore, this proposal jeopardizes 64 branches in low- and moderate-
income areas and 19 branches in communities of color.

This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and
moderate-income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to
affordable mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain

because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the
CRA obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify
the banks that would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the
communities those institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development
activity that would receive less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be
concentrated in low- and moderate-income communities or communities that have
experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

I am also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants
and nonprofit organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-business

other community-based services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with
nonprofit organizations. These resources can be particularly important to local
organizations that have deep relationships with residents and understand the specific
needs of their communities.

For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect
costs and new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for
smaller organizations.8 For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be
unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other operating expenses
are often necessary to deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also
have fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs. In addition,
many community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain
financial records, budgets or program documentation in the precise format a bank would
need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations
are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger

consequences well beyond the banks themselves.

redirect bank support away from smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those with

reducing perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also determine
what the changes mean for the communities CRA is intended to serve.

Under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying small business does not
automatically constitute economic development. The activity must also satisfy a
requirement known as the "purpose test," meaning it must promote economic
development by supporting permanent job creation, retention, or improvement for low- or
moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income communities.9

The proposed rule would eliminate the "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks
could earn CRA credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or
improves jobs for low- and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income
communities. Instead, financing could qualify as economic development based primarily
on the type and size of the business and whether the financing expands, improves or
preserves the business's productive capacity, physical presence or employment base.10

I am concerned that this change would weaken the connection between CRA economic-
development credit and the people and communities CRA is intended to benefit.
Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying business expand does not necessarily create
jobs, increase economic opportunity in an underserved neighborhood or address the needs
of low- and moderate-income communities.

Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens
a qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank
to demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or
neighborhoods.11 The agencies themselves acknowledge that eliminating the purpose test
would expand the universe of activities eligible for CRA credit.12

Before eliminating the purpose test, the agencies should analyze what additional activities
would qualify under the new definition, where those activities are likely to occur, and
whether bank financing could shift away from activities that create or retain jobs for low-
and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income communities. The agencies
should also explain why eliminating the existing connection to these outcomes is

wouldchange the standard by allowing credit for infrastructure that "benefits or serves" a
targeted area, even when the project delivers little meaningful benefit to LMI residents
and does not help preserve or strengthen the community.13

This means that a bank could seek CRA credit for financing a large regional
infrastructure project that only incidentally serves an LMI neighborhood, even if most of
the project's benefits flow to affluent communities or private companies. For example, a
data center located in or connected to an LMI tract could qualify despite creating few
permanent jobs and providing little direct benefit to residents.

Before expanding what infrastructure projects qualify for CRA credit in this way, the
agencies should analyze the impact of expanding the types of projects that qualify for
CRA credit on people with low- and moderate-incomes or low- and moderate-income
communities, including whether it could result in a reduction in projects that preserve or
strengthen LMI communities. In addition, the agencies should explain why changing the

the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income

 identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA
 scrutiny under the proposal;

 assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or
 populations, including rural communities and communities of color;

 consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without
 sacrificing meaningful community accountability; and

materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are

Attached is a comment letter from California Intertribal Alliances opposing the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act regulations. Our letter addresses how the proposal could reduce access to responsible lending, community development investment, banking services, and support for grassroots nonprofits, small businesses, and underserved Central Valley communities.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0065_09000064b95f674f.pdf:
2547 W. Shaw Ave., Suite 108

 559-448-7515

September 30, 2026

Travis Hill, Chair
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
550 17th Street NW,
Washington, DC 20429
RIN 3064-AG31
Via email: comments@FDIC.gov

Jonathan V. Gould, Comptroller
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)

Via: https://regulations.gov/

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

California Intertribal Alliances writes to object to the harmful changes proposed to
the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed by Congress in
1977 in response to redlining and creates an affirmative obligation for banks to help
meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of communities, including low and
moderate income (LMI) communities. While the CRA has successfully encouraged
banks to lend, invest and provide services in underserved communities, challenges
related to redlining, discrimination, underinvestment, and lack of access remain.
  California Intertribal Alliances is a California 501(c)(3) public benefit nonprofit
serving Indigenous and other underserved communities throughout California's
Central Valley. Our culturally grounded programs and activities support cultural
preservation, community wellness, food access, creative expression, and
cross-cultural solidarity. We also strive to encourage community entrepreneurship
by sharing information, creating supportive connections, and empowering people
who dream of becoming business owners to pursue their goals.

As a relatively new nonprofit led by a founder who is also building a small local
business, we have experienced how difficult it can be to access financial support,
responsible credit, and meaningful banking relationships. California Intertribal
Alliances does not currently receive CRA-related funding or institutional support
from financial institutions. This is not because community need or potential impact
is absent. New and grassroots organizations frequently encounter complicated and
resource-intensive application processes, limited information about available
opportunities, capacity requirements that tend to favor larger or more established
organizations, and systems that depend heavily on existing institutional
relationships.

These barriers make it difficult for newer community-led organizations, small
businesses, and emerging entrepreneurs to access the investments, responsible
lending opportunities, grants, banking services, and partnerships intended to
benefit underserved communities. We need clearer, more transparent, and more
accessible pathways to CRA-related support. Weakening CRA obligations would not
eliminate the barriers we already face; it could significantly reduce opportunities in
Central Valley communities that continue to experience underinvestment and
limited financial access.

The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift.
The proposal does not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on
LMI communities. We request an extension of the comment period for an additional
60 days so we have time to better understand how much CRA activity may be lost
to communities because of this proposal an analysis the regulators did not
conduct or provide.
The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved
communities in several ways.

 1) Community development (CD) activities for affordable housing
 and small businesses will drop dramatically.

As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities
that support critically needed affordable housing and economic development
projects. These activities often provide the greatest CRA impact in communities as
 they strengthen economic stability and mobility, quality of life, and social health of
residents and communities.

The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large"
Banks, such that many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and
expectation to serve the community development needs of their communities.[1]
According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70
California banks would see their reinvestment obligations reduced under the
proposal. Twenty-five California banks would shed their Community Development
Test responsibilities entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer be subject to
the Investment Test.[2]

The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical
community development programs that have had large impacts in LMI
communities. These include Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) which are a
key driver of affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) which
fuel economic development projects in tribal and other areas; and EQ2 equity
equivalent investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs)
that provide small business lending in underserved areas that banks cannot reach,
and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that take property off of the speculative
market.

Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting
the critical importance of the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable
housing.[3] Approximately half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from CRA
motivated banks.[4] The regulators will even further weaken CD obligations if they
adopt the alternative proposal that Large Banks be defined as those with over $30
billion in assets.

Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance
even where they remain subject to the Community Development and Investment
Tests. The regulators signal to all banks that they can do significantly less CD
lending and investment and still pass their CRA examinations, all while seeking CRA
credit for activity outside of their CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests
that a bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1
capital were devoted to CD loans and CD investments. That percentage is far lower
than the percentage that NCRC determined banks currently devote to community
investments and loans. If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary
to meet the proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by approximately
$87.1 billion, or 85%.[5]

Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have
tremendous negative impacts on affordable housing and small business
development in our state. Asset thresholds should not be raised.
  2) Banks will shed branches and BankOn.

The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and maintain
branches in LMI and BIPOC neighborhoods. By increasing the asset threshold for a
Large Bank to over $10 billion, forty-five banks in California will no longer be
subject to the Services Test and reviewed to ensure that their branches are serving
LMI communities. In California alone, NCRC estimates that 245 branches in LMI
areas and 497 branches in neighborhoods of color would be vulnerable to closure
due to this proposal.[6]

Branch presence has been tied to increased small business lending in communities.
Fewer branches will result in less small business lending. These changes will be
particularly hard hitting in rural areas of our state where smaller banks originate a
larger portion of the small business loans.

The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to
offer deposit products that are accessible to LMI residents.[7] Deposit accounts are
a gateway to credit access, financial stability, and wealth building, especially for
families who are otherwise preyed upon by predatory financial institutions. As one
important example, the BankOn program has provided access to no or low fee bank
accounts for over fourteen million people.[8] California is home to several BankOn
coalitions that establish effective partnerships among banks, community-based
organizations, and local governments. The proposal jettisons this work.

Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million
are underbanked.[9] National banks regulated by the OCC charged billions of
dollars in overdraft and non-sufficient fund fees in 2025, and in California alone,
state-chartered banks charged over fifty-six million dollars ($56 million) in OD and
NSF fees to California consumers in 2025.[10]

 3) Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.

Another consequence of the proposal's drive to raise asset thresholds is that fewer
banks will be required to report data regarding their small business, small farm,
and community development lending activities. Such data is critical to
understanding not only individual bank performance, but also the needs of local
markets. Rise Economy and its member organizations routinely analyze this CRA
data when meeting with banks and commenting on CRA exams and mergers. The
loss of such data is particularly harmful at a time when the Administration is
walking back efforts to collect and disclose detailed small business lending data
under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank Act. These changes will disproportionately
impact rural communities in our state where banks up to $10 billion in assets make
up a larger part of the small business and small farm lending markets.
  4) Native American communities and Tribal Nations will not see
 sufficient benefits.

The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the needs
of Native American communities and Tribal Nations which have been poorly served
by banks. The current rules focus CRA obligations in areas where banks have
branches, even though there are far fewer bank branches near Tribal lands and in
rural areas where Native Americans may reside. The proposal seeks to address this
CRA gap by encouraging banks to engage in community development and related
activities in "Indian Country" and on "Tribal and Native lands," even if outside of
bank CRA assessment areas. But many members of Tribes in California will not
benefit from this proposal as they do not live in Indian Country or on Tribal or
Native lands, as defined.

CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring within
particular geographies, given the challenges and impacts associated with historic
dispossession and federal policy. Instead, CRA evaluations should also consider
whether banks have established meaningful relationships with, and provided direct
benefits to, federally recognized Tribes as well as non-federally recognized Tribes.
Non-federally recognized Tribes have been acknowledged by, and are able to access
programs and contracts with, various local and state entities.[11] Such processes
exist.

More specifically, the CRA rules should encourage banks to serve Tribes, nonprofit
organizations or other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned businesses
that are majority owned and controlled by Native American entrepreneurs by
providing:

 Active outreach and engagement
 Community development loans and investments for affordable housing and

 economic development projects
 Small farm and small business loans
 Home mortgage loans
 Grants to meet community needs, including for capacity building for Tribes

 and support for Tribes seeking federal recognition if desired
 Support for cultural, health and other programs
 Bank branches
 Deposit products such as affordable bank accounts, and
 The provision of financial services such as financial literacy, apprenticeship

 programs and technical assistance support

While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities
outside of their branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made to
encourage banks to engage in CRA related activity to directly benefit Tribes,
nonprofit organizations and other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned
 businesses that are majority owned and controlled by Native American
entrepreneurs.

A better approach is needed. All banks should be subject to an impact and
responsiveness review factor during their CRA exams that evaluates and tracks
whether banks have engaged in any CRA activity directly with Tribes, Tribally
controlled entities and Native owned businesses.[12] If banks know they will be
examined for their work with Tribes, they will find mutually beneficial ways to work
with Tribes.

 5) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will
 suffer.

The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by
requiring a demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating
that large banks and their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more
than 15% of these grants on overhead.[13] As if this wasn't enough, the FDIC and
OCC question whether they should end CRA eligibility for bank grantmaking to
nonprofits entirely.

Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian
measures will be except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller
groups, may be impacted.[14]

Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local
needs. They also can be key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and
investment products into communities inclined to trust long established local
organizations. Many nonprofit organizations and programs, such as downpayment
assistance programs, that support CRA related activity, rely on bank contributions
to operate. Smaller, local, and rural organizations will be least able to meet new
reporting obligations, and they risk losing bank support as a result. The proposal
would also end impactful contributions from banks for general operating support,
sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.

Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their
communities on their own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps
in their own capacity seeking assistance with community outreach, borrower
education, credit building and repair, technical assistance, legal services, job
training and placement, tax assistance, affordable housing and other services and
programs which help residents become stable and bankable so that banks can
attract new deposits and make new loans in LMI communities.

The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and will
focus grantmaking on larger organizations that can help them more easily meet
their new FDIC and OCC-imposed regulatory burdens.
 Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15%
overhead restriction will negatively affect operations and organizational success. As
one example, in order to secure CRA grants from Large Banks, CDFIs will need to
pare down costs for critical operational expenses such as underwriting, servicing,
compliance, technology, impact measurement, product development, and borrower
technical assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions,
organizations are put at risk.

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA
activity that contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large
negative impact it will have on nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding,
the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are meant to benefit from the CRA,
and the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

 6) Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.

There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link
between CRA and LMI impact in the name of easing bank burden.

Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their
top two major product lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in,
and profiting from, communities, this lending by banks, subsidiaries and affiliates
must be evaluated. Further, certain products, such as small farm and consumer
loans, are important in many communities, but may not be among a bank's largest
product lines. If regulators give banks a pass and exempt smaller product lines
from CRA oversight, banks will have less incentive to consider how those products
are offered.

Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and
soundness, encourages banks to meet community needs, and engenders greater
trust in banks by the community. Eliminating categories of loan products from
scrutiny will have the opposite effect.

No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test,
which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the
definition of economic development. The CRA should create greater incentives for
banks to support the creation of jobs that pay family sustaining wages for LMI
workers and in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to provisions that would provide
CRA credit for job creation and economic development that may only benefit
middle- and upper-income workers and communities. Such provisions ignore the
purpose of CRA.

Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA
credit for large scale community infrastructure products that generate profits for
 banks, would likely be financed without CRA credit, and provide only incidental
benefits to LMI residents and communities. Such an expansion of what qualifies for
CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities.
For example, banks might choose to more profitably earn CRA credit by financing
larger scale infrastructure projects, like bridges, in lieu of financing less lucrative,
smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local community needs (such as
childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or resilience
projects).

Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA
should require banks to focus their CRA activities on their CRA assessments
areas,[15] where they are subject to more rigorous regulatory oversight (with an
exception made to encourage banks to better serve Tribes, as noted above). Banks
are not doing enough currently to meet the credit and deposit needs in the areas
where they have CRA responsibility, a problem the regulators tried to address in the
2023 CRA Rule.[16] Yet the proposal further encourages banks to seek CRA credit
for projects in areas away from their branches, lending and CRA responsibility. This
will enable banks to get credit for activity outside of their assessment areas, while
providing no accompanying CRA obligation to better serve these areas.

Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal goes
out of its way to encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan option to meet
their CRA responsibilities. The Strategic Plan was meant for financial institutions
that operated under a unique business model that the CRA rules were not designed
to address. The Strategic Plan option provides for minimal public input and
regulatory scrutiny and allows banks to determine the level of reinvestment activity
they need to engage in to earn a passing CRA grade. In our experience, banks with
Strategic Plans tend to reinvest less in the community and in less impactful ways.
The OCC's guidance establishing low community development thresholds for banks
opting for the Strategic Plan, [17] validates this perspective.

Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community
development efforts with little benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing,
where units are affordable at a point in time but not encumbered by deed or rent
restrictions, are a feature of today's housing market. But CRA rules should not give
banks credit for financing such activities where the benefit to LMI residents and
communities is unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it
can be a driver of bank investment in problematic landlords and displacement. CRA
credit should be given for financing of NOAH only if the project is owned and
operated by mission-driven organizations, where a majority of residents are LMI
tenants, and the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are
compliant with tenant rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents
can reasonably be expected to retain their housing.
  7) Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA
 ratings downgrades.

The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and redline
should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding"
ratings. Under the Biden Administration, at least a dozen banks that passed their
CRA exams were accused of redlining. This proposal will only increase that number
by narrowing what constitutes evidence of discrimination that may be considered
for the purpose of downgrading a bank's CRA rating. Here, regulators should
consider any evidence that a bank, its affiliates, or subsidiaries engaged in
discrimination, redlining, or illegal credit practices as part of their lending, deposit,
branching, or other activities. This evidence should be considered regardless of its
source (public or private parties), or its form (informal complaints, research based
on data, testing results, comment letters, administrative actions, private litigation,
etc.). We also urge the regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity
Act authorizes Special Purpose Credit Programs, and to once again encourage banks
to develop SPCPs to better serve communities that have been redlined, excluded,
and underserved. This is the essence of CRA.

Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information to
allow for meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of
entities and activities, and will undoubtedly harm the communities that the CRA
was meant to support. If finalized in substantially the same form as proposed,
communities will suffer significantly decreased investment in affordable housing and
CDFI support, more LMI branch closures, higher bank account fees, fewer
community serving nonprofit organizations, and increased bank discrimination and
redlining with no CRA consequence. The CRA will become further removed from its
purpose of encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and
the OCC to reconsider this proposal.

Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Respectfully submitted,

Naomi Isabel Ortega-Singh

Founder and Chief Executive Officer


California Intertribal Alliances

On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, proposing
major revisions to the regulations of the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). We offer this comment letter in
response.

We appreciate the agencies' efforts to reform the CRA regulations, and we support some of the agencies'
provisions that could improve the CRA's implementation framework to increase responsible capital in
underserved communities. However, we have real concerns with the increases in the asset thresholds that
determine how banks are evaluated under CRA and the restrictions on operating grants. We also have concerns
with several interacting provisions that could further weaken community development incentives that will likely
impair the flow of much needed capital to the most underserved communities.

Allies for Community Business (A4CB) is a community development finance institution (CDFI) serving all of Illinois
and Indiana. We believe that entrepreneurs from any background can start and grow businesses that create
generational wealth for their families and communities. Our mission is to provide the capital, coaching, and
connections entrepreneurs need to grow great businesses that create jobs and wealth in their communities. Since
our founding in 1994, we have provided over $1B in grants and loans primarily to underserved entrepreneurs and
have served over 100K business owners eager to grow.

Banks are critical partners in our work. They provide low-cost loans, operating grants, and referrals to the
entrepreneurs with whom they have depository relationships but do not qualify for debt. We have borrowed and
relent hundreds of millions of dollars that have created or retained tens of thousands of jobs in our communities.
We could not have done so without CRA-motivated bank partners.

These partnerships are mutually reinforcing. In addition to providing critical capital to CDFIs, banks rely on CDFIs
to reach underserved communities, develop borrowers, and cultivate future bank borrowers. The CRA has long
helped create the incentives for banks to build and sustain these relationships, strengthening the broader
community development ecosystem. We are therefore concerned that several provisions in the proposal could

 A4CB.org | info@A4CB.org | (312) 275-3000 | 135 N. Kedzie Avenue, Chicago IL 60612
 weaken these incentives, reducing bank engagement with CDFIs and ultimately the flow of capital to the
communities we serve.

Raised Asset Thresholds Jeopardize Community Development Finance: Section IV.A, "Asset Thresholds";
Questions 13

The proposal defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets, intermediate banks as
institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as institutions with more than $10 billion.
About 800 banks that currently face a separate community development test as intermediate small banks would
become small banks and lose that requirement. Another approximately 400 banks that are currently evaluated as
large banks would become intermediate banks, losing the separate large-bank lending, investment, and service
tests and many associated data-reporting requirements.

In the states where we serve, it is estimated that approximately 40% of banks in Illinois and Indiana would no
longer be required to reinvest in local community development projects including small business support. About
62% of banks in Illinois and 40% of banks in Indiana would lose their large bank status.

The consequences may be especially significant in rural and smaller markets throughout our two states, where
there are fewer financial institutions and fewer alternative sources of capital. In these communities, the loss of
even one or two CRA-motivated bank partners can materially affect whether projects are financed. For
communities with fewer financial institutions and fewer sources of private capital to begin with, losing even a
handful of CRA-motivated lenders and investors could have an outsized effect on whether small businesses get
financed.

These thresholds determine whether and how a bank's community development performance is evaluated and
therefore affect the strength of banks' incentives to engage in community development. The agencies
acknowledge in the proposal that when banks become subject to a CD test under the current framework, the
explicit evaluation of their CD activities typically results in banks adjusting their CRA programs.

We expect that banks moving down asset sizes and losing incentives for community development activities will
have a direct impact on our partnerships. It is difficult to quantify the size of that effect, but we think it would be
substantial.

The threshold changes would also substantially reduce the number of institutions subject to large-bank CRA data
requirements. This would make it harder for communities, CDFIs, policymakers, and regulators to identify credit
gaps, compare bank performance, assess geographic disparities, and understand whether community credit
needs are being met. We are concerned that aggregate community development finance data is already difficult to
track and the proposal would exacerbate the coverage of data, making it difficult to identify and understand
where credit is flowing and where A4CB's services are needed most.

Recommendation

For all the reasons cited above, we urge the agencies to retain the current thresholds and reject all alternatives
offered (including the substantially higher thresholds raised for consideration in Question 1). The current

 A4CB.org | info@A4CB.org | (312) 275-3000 | 135 N. Kedzie Avenue, Chicago IL 60612
 thresholds are already annually indexed to CPI-W, so they are not beholden to 1995 asset levels. Moreover, the
justification of "restoring proportionality to 1995" that the agencies use in the proposal does not adequately
explain why raising asset thresholds will better serve the statutory intent of the CRA, which is to ensure that credit
needs of LMI communities are met. For the small bank threshold, the proportionality metric rests on the
distribution of the number of banks such that nearly 80% of all banks would be considered small, similar to what it
was in 1995. While that's true, by the same logic, nearly 20% of banks in 1995 were considered large, whereas
under the proposed large bank threshold only a little over 2% of all banks would be considered large. Instead, the
agencies selectively use total banking industry share to justify the large bank threshold. Matching a 1995
distribution through either method does not necessarily demonstrate that the resulting categories are appropriate
for the modern banking system. The industry has consolidated dramatically, and bank business models and
geographic reach have changed. Banks with several billion dollars in assets today may have substantially greater
lending, investment, data, and operational capacity than institutions that were treated as small or intermediate
three decades ago. The fact that assets happen to sit above a chosen threshold does not by itself establish that
banks below that threshold should lose the separate investment/service tests or associated data requirements.

Restrictions on Community Development Grants: Section IV.C, "Community Development Activities -- CD
Grants"; Questions 911

We strongly oppose the proposed restrictions on community development grants which
 1) requires a qualifying CD grant to be directly used by the recipient for a program, project, or initiative with a
 primary purpose of community development;
 2) for large banks, caps grant recipient's indirect administrative costs to 15%; and
 3) requires that large banks obtain documentation from grant recipients including written commitments
 regarding use of funds, indirect-cost attestations, IRS Form 990s, and operating and program budgets.

We also strongly oppose the alternative contemplated in Question 10 to eliminate grants and donations from CRA
consideration entirely.

While we share the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants meaningfully benefit communities, these
requirements would restrict many forms of effective grantmaking and misunderstand the role that flexible
operating support plays in community development finance. For CDFIs, staffing, underwriting, servicing,
compliance, technology, risk management, data systems, financial management, technical assistance, and
product development are not ancillary to community development. They are the infrastructure that makes
community development lending possible. A4CB uses operating grants to hire and retain staff, cover critical
technology and infrastructure costs, and research how we can improve our services.

We also strongly oppose using a fixed 15% indirect-cost limit as a condition of CRA eligibility. An organization's
administrative-cost percentage is not an appropriate proxy for community impact. Costs vary depending on an
organization's size, geography, product mix, regulatory obligations, technical-assistance model, and populations
served. The cap could disproportionately affect small and emerging CDFIs, rural CDFIs, CDFIs like A4CB that make
small-dollar loans, organizations providing intensive borrower technical assistance, CDFIs developing new
products or entering underserved markets and organizations making necessary investments in technology,
compliance, data, and risk management.

 A4CB.org | info@A4CB.org | (312) 275-3000 | 135 N. Kedzie Avenue, Chicago IL 60612
 Recommendation

The agencies should preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-building grants as currently is
in place under the 1995 framework. CRA should encourage flexibility for banks to provide the form of support that
best responds to the identified community needs instead of imposing undue compliance burdens.

Interacting Provisions That Could Further Reduce Community Development Incentives

Preserve meaningful consequences for intermediate-bank CD performance: Section IV.B, "Performance
Tests -- Intermediate Bank Ratings"

Under the current framework, an intermediate small bank generally must receive at least a Satisfactory rating on
both its lending test and its CD test to receive an overall Satisfactory rating. The proposal would require a
Satisfactory or better lending-test rating but would allow lending performance to compensate for weaker CD
performance.

This change is particularly concerning when combined with the proposed asset thresholds, which would move
hundreds of banks currently evaluated under the large-bank framework into the intermediate category. If weak CD
performance does not prevent an overall Satisfactory rating, banks may have less regulatory incentive to make
CDFI loans and investments, provide grants, or undertake other community development activities. We urge the
agencies to retain a requirement that intermediate banks demonstrate at least Satisfactory CD performance to
receive an overall Satisfactory rating.

Prevent ordinary retail lending from substituting for specialized CD lending: Section IV.B, "Retail Lending
Product Lines," Questions 47; and Section IV.C, "CD Loans"

The proposal would evaluate retail lending only in a bank's major product lines. It would also allow a loan in a
retail product line that is not evaluated as a major product line to receive consideration as a CD loan if the loan
otherwise satisfies the community development definition. We agree that genuinely community-development-
oriented financing should not lose CRA consideration simply because a product line is excluded from the retail
evaluation.

However, this interaction creates a risk that ordinary-course small-business, small-farm, or other retail lending
could substitute for more specialized community development lending that depends more directly on CRA
incentives. The agencies should require a meaningful community development nexus and ensure that the
provision does not allow banks to satisfy CD expectations primarily through activity they would undertake in the
ordinary course of business.

Strategic plans require strong guardrails: Section IV.F, "Strategic Plan"; particularly Questions 3853

We support efforts to provide greater clarity regarding strategic plans and measurable goals. However, because
strategic plans allow banks to develop individualized CRA performance standards, strong guardrails are essential
to ensure that banks do not circumvent rigorous and reasonably consistent expectations applied to similarly
situated institutions.

 A4CB.org | info@A4CB.org | (312) 275-3000 | 135 N. Kedzie Avenue, Chicago IL 60612
 The agencies should require strategic-plan goals to be responsive to demonstrated community needs, sufficiently
rigorous to approximate performance expected under the standard CRA tests, transparent and measurable,
subject to meaningful public engagement and evaluated against clear standards for determining whether the
goals adequately address assessment-area credit needs.

We particularly urge the agencies to establish strong standards in responding to Question 53, which asks when
measurable goals should be considered inadequate to address assessment-area needs.

Provisions That Could Strengthen Community Development Finance

Consider prior-period community development loans: Section IV.C, "CD Loans"; Question 8

We strongly support providing CRA consideration for qualifying CD loans that remain outstanding from prior
evaluation periods, similar to the existing treatment of prior-period investments. Community development
borrowers frequently need long-term, patient financing. CRA should encourage banks to structure loans around
community needs rather than examination cycles.

With respect to Question 8, we recommend evaluation period-based consideration because it better recognizes
patient, long-term CD financing and provides a more representative measure of capital committed throughout the
CRA examination period than an annual snapshot and brings parity to the treatment of loans and investments.
The agencies should base consideration on the average outstanding balance or otherwise account for both the
amount and duration of the outstanding exposure, and should treat repeated renewals of substantially the same
loan as a single exposure.

Establish an illustrative list and advance-confirmation process: Section IV.E, "Illustrative List" and
"Confirmation of CD Activity Eligibility"; Questions 3233

We strongly support establishing a publicly available, non-exhaustive illustrative list of eligible CD activities and a
formal process for advance confirmation of eligibility. The OCC, FDIC, and Federal Reserve should seek to maintain
consistent standards and, ideally, a single interagency illustrative list.

With respect to Questions 3233, we support requiring banks to retain eligibility determinations for as long as the
applicable activity remains on their balance sheet and establishing a maximum 30-day extension beyond the
proposed 90-day review period.

We also encourage the agencies to pair this with a confirmation process that provides timely certainty while
maintaining accountability for genuine community development impact. Eligibility determinations should include
a clear written rationale and, where appropriate, identify the facts or conditions on which eligibility depends. The
agencies should provide a process for reconsideration where banks or community development partners can
supply additional information, as well as a mechanism for community stakeholders to raise material concerns
regarding activities that have been determined eligible. Nonconfidential or anonymized determinations and their
rationales should be made public to promote transparency and consistent treatment across institutions. Eligibility

 A4CB.org | info@A4CB.org | (312) 275-3000 | 135 N. Kedzie Avenue, Chicago IL 60612
 determinations should also remain subject to verification during CRA examinations where the activity is ultimately
implemented differently than represented.
Recognize disaster preparedness and resilience: Section IV.D, "Revitalization and Stabilization -- Designated
Disaster Areas"; Question 31
We support expressly recognizing qualifying activities that help communities prepare for, adapt to, and withstand
natural disasters. CDFIs frequently provide financing before and after disasters to affordable housing
developments, homeowners, small businesses, and community facilities. CRA should recognize responsible
investments that strengthen vulnerable communities before disasters occur, not only financing provided after
damage occurs.
Conclusion
CRA has helped create a powerful partnership among banks, CDFIs, and the communities we serve. We appreciate
the agencies' efforts to improve clarity and flexibility. Modernization, however, should result in more responsible
capital reaching communities with unmet credit needs, as the CRA statute was intended.
We therefore urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the raised asset thresholds proposed and to withdraw the
restrictions on CD operating grants. We also urge you to adjust the interacting provisions as I have recommended
above.
Thank you for evaluating these comments and for considering the impact of the proposed changes on the
communities we serve.
Sincerely,

Brad McConnell
CEO
Allies for Community Business

From: Stephanie Murphy, NFC Executive Director and approved by NFC Board of Directors

The Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) has been an important tool for community
development since 1977. Neighborhood Finance Corporation (NFC), a 36-year nonprofit
mortgage company and Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI), was founded on
partnerships developed as the result of CRA.

The NFC staff and Board of Directors believe it is important to share our key concerns
regarding the impact if the proposed changes were to be implemented. Please note, we do
have other concerns, but these are the primary concerns.

The proposed rule raises the asset thresholds under CRA significantly
As a nonprofit Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI), NFC relies on bank
investment commitments to fund first-mortgage purchase and refinance loans as well as
home-improvement loans. NFC's renovation lending helps homebuyers and owner-occupants
purchase, improve, and maintain homes, supporting pathways to homeownership, housing
supply, neighborhood revitalization, and the local tax base that funds public services. NFC
currently has more than $20 million in commitments providing critical capital to expand
homeownership and housing supply in our communities. We understand that banks
participate in our lending pools because of their broader commitment to the communities
they serve; at the same time, CRA credit has contributed materially to NFC's ability to raise
more than $140 million over the past 36 years.

Raising the asset thresholds results in 46 of 109 (42.2 percent) Iowa banks no longer have
obligations to report their community development investments and 18 of 37 (48.6 percent)
Iowa banks losing their large bank status. NFC's 36-year history informs our understanding that
 our long-term viability relies on the CRA community development obligations to keep these
relationship strong, predictable and ongoing.

Restricts CRA credit for grants that pay basic nonprofit operating costs
NFC receives capital for our lending from community banks, most of these banks are under the
$10 billion asset size. The other financial support NFC receives is from larger, national banks in
the form of community development grants to support operating costs. The pairing of capital
with the operational support is key to NFC being able to efficiently and effectively deploy the
raised capital to our homeowners and homebuyers.

Flexible operating support enables nonprofits to retain qualified staff, maintain programs, and
respond to changing community needs. NFC is concerned that the proposal may reduce banks'
willingness to provide this support, particularly to smaller organizations. For example, under
the proposal, a large bank could receive no CRA credit when 25% of a grant covers internal
expenses, even if the remaining 75% supports direct service costs. This structure may lead
nonprofits to devote more time to securing narrowly restricted, project-specific grants and less
time to delivering CRA-eligible community-development services, including expanding
pathways to homeownership and providing homeowners with critical capital to maintain their
homes.

For these reasons, NFC respectfully asks the FDIC and OCC to reconsider the proposed asset-
threshold changes and the treatment of grants supporting essential nonprofit operating costs.
We encourage the agencies to preserve meaningful community development incentives while
pursuing a framework that is clear, proportionate, and workable for banks of different sizes.

Stephanie Murphy, Executive Director
Neighborhood Finance Corporation
