Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations -- Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (Docket ID OCC
20260694). Comment on the Potential Effects of Proposed Changes to CRA Asset Thresholds,
Investment Test Weighting, and Community Development Eligibility on Investment Demand and LMI
Communities.

Dear Chair Hill and Comptroller Gould,

On behalf of Community Capital Management, LLC ("CCM"), the registered investment advisor to the CCM
Community Impact Bond ("CIB") Fund ("the Fund"), we respectfully submit these comments on the joint
notice of proposed rulemaking issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (the "OCC") and the
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (the "FDIC") (together, the "agencies") to amend the regulations
implementing the Community Reinvestment Act ("CRA").

The CCM Community Impact Bond Fund (formerly the CRA Qualified Investment Fund) was launched in
1999 with the specific purpose to help banks make CRA qualified investments to support low- and
moderate-income ("LMI") people and communities across their assessment areas. Today the Fund is one
of the nation's largest community development mutual funds and has assisted approximately 640 banks
with access to qualified community development investments, in a safe and sound manner, through over
1,900 CRA examinations. These banks range in size and sophistication from the largest money center
banks to small community banks. The Fund has a lengthy record of community development success and
in 27 years has invested approximately $13.9 billion in vital community development investments on behalf
of banks and other impact investors.

As Chair of the Board and Trustee of the Community Capital Trust, which consists of the CIB Fund, and
CEO & President of Community Capital Management, LLC, the registered advisor to the Fund, we
appreciate the opportunity to provide substantive and constructive comments to assist the agencies in
crafting a CRA rule that reduces unnecessary burden while not weakening its primary purpose of helping
LMI people and communities. We write, however, to offer perspective on several aspects of the proposal
which we believe could have unintended consequences for LMI people and communities nationwide.

877.272.1977 www.ccminvests.com Community Capital Management, LLC
 I. The proposed asset size thresholds remove the investment incentive from a large share of

 the banking industry

While the CRA statute does not require the agencies to tailor the performance tests by asset size, the
current regulation and the proposal both use a bank's asset size as a determination of which performance
test a bank is subject to. Under the current rules, a bank with more than $1.649 billion in assets is a "large
bank" evaluated under separate lending, investment, and service tests with the investment test alone
generally accounting for 25 percent of the institution's overall rating. A bank between $412
million and $1.649 billion is an intermediate small bank subject to a community development ("CD") test
that expressly considers qualified investments. The proposal would raise every threshold and as a result
have two compounding effects that reduce demand for community development investments:

 Loss of the standalone investment test for banks between $1.649 billion and $10 billion.
 Institutions in this range are large banks today, subject to a rigorous, separately weighted
 investment test that measures the dollar amount and responsiveness of their qualified
 investments. Under the proposal, they become "intermediate banks," no longer subject to any
 standalone investment test. By the agencies' own estimates, approximately 126 OCC-supervised
 banks and 250 FDIC-supervised banks, roughly 376 institutions, would be reclassified from large to
 intermediate and would no longer be subject to the large bank data, investment, and service test
 requirements.

 Loss of the CD test entirely for banks between $412 million and $1 billion. Institutions in this
 range are intermediate small banks today, whose CD test explicitly evaluates qualified investments.
 Under the proposal they become "small banks" subject only to a lending test with no CD test and
 therefore no examination driven reason to hold qualified investments at all. The agencies estimate
 that up to 194 OCC banks and 604 FDIC banks, roughly 798 institutions, would move into this
 category.

A third change amplifies the effect. For the intermediate banks that do remain subject to a CD test, the
proposal would amend Appendix A so that a bank can achieve an overall "satisfactory" rating on the
strength of its lending test alone, even if its CD performance is weaker. Removing the requirement that
intermediate banks earn at least a "satisfactory" on the CD test further dilutes the incentive to make
qualified investments.

II. The investment test is a distinct and irreplaceable channel of capital to LMI communities

Retail lending and community development investment are not interchangeable. The investment test drives
bank demand for the fixed income securities that finance affordable housing production and preservation
including agency mortgage-backed securities supporting LMI homeownership, agency commercial
mortgage-backed securities backing affordable multifamily rental properties, Low Income Housing Tax
Credit financing, and taxable municipal housing bonds, as well as small business and community facility
financing. This is patient, long-term capital that a lending only framework does not capture. When banks
are no longer examined on their investments, that demand does not migrate to lending; it simply

 877.272.1977 www.ccminvests.com Community Capital Management, LLC
 disappears, and with it the capital that reaches LMI households and communities, rural and underserved
areas, small businesses, and small farms.

The agencies acknowledge this risk. The proposal's own economic analysis concedes that the changes
could produce "a possible shift in CRA motivated activity toward lending and credit services and away from
certain CD activities," and identifies "reduced CRA incentives" and "potential geographic reallocation away
from assessment areas" as secondary burdens. The CIB Fund's direct experience confirms the concern: a
meaningful share of the community development capital we deploy on behalf of banks originates from
institutions in precisely the $1 billion to $10 billion range that the proposal would relieve of the investment
test. Reducing that demand will translate into fewer affordable housing units financed and less community
development capital reaching LMI neighborhoods nationwide.

The Fund's experience illustrates the scale and geographic reach of community development investment
supported by bank demand. Since inception, the Fund has invested more than $10.2 billion in CRA-
qualified investments on behalf of banks. The majority of this community impact (approximately $5.3
billion) was made on behalf of approximately 500 banks under $10 billion in assets. This community impact
was made across 49 states and 739 counties. Additionally,

 Over $2.3 billion has been invested to provide affordable homeownership to over 16,400 LMI
 households;

 Over $2.3 billion has been invested in affordable multifamily housing for LMI households;
 Approximately $139 million has been invested in CDFI investments and other economic

 development projects benefiting LMI communities; and
 Approximately $134 million has been invested in supporting small businesses.

The Fund's experience also demonstrates the important role that banks with less than $10 billion in assets
play in directing community development capital to rural areas. Investments made by the CIB Fund in rural
communities on behalf of these banks represent 3.2 percent of the total investment amount, compared
with 2.0 percent for banks with more than $10 billion in assets. These investments reached rural
communities across 44 states and 380 counties and include more than 1,000 loans financing affordable
homeownership for LMI households. Withdrawing the investment incentive from hundreds of banks will
deepen, not relieve, "CRA deserts". As the agencies consider how best to address "CRA deserts," these
findings underscore the importance of preserving a meaningful investment incentive for the community
banks that help direct capital to rural and other underserved areas.

 III. The Investment Test Amplifies Community Development Lending Through Capital Market
 Liquidity

The investment test also serves an important capital markets function that extends beyond the dollars
represented by any individual investment. Community development lending cannot reach its full potential
if loans and other community development assets remain permanently on the balance sheets of the
institutions that originate them. A robust market for CRA-qualified investments creates additional investor
demand for these assets and provides an avenue for community development credit to access the broader
capital markets. This enables capital to be recycled and redeployed, expanding the capacity of financial

877.272.1977 www.ccminvests.com Community Capital Management, LLC
 institutions and other community development lenders to finance additional affordable housing,
homeownership, small businesses, and other activities that benefit LMI people and communities.

This connection between community development and the capital markets is one of the important
functions of maintaining a distinct investment test component within the CRA. The availability of
investment capital can create a multiplier effect: capital used to finance one pool of community
development loans can be replenished through the sale or financing of those assets and redeployed to
support additional lending. Access to deep and efficient capital markets has long been an important driver
of economic growth and prosperity. LMI communities should benefit from that same financial
infrastructure.

Our own experience provides a tangible illustration of how access to capital for affordable homeownership
can support long term household asset building. Over CCM's 27 year history we have invested
approximately $5.6 billion in more than 36,000 loans supporting affordable homeownership for LMI
households. Based on our analysis, these mortgages have generated an estimated median homeowner
wealth of approximately $80,000 per household.

Weakening the CRA investment test risks not only reducing the amount that banks invest directly, but also
diminishing the liquidity and investor demand that enable community development lenders to continue
originating new credit in underserved communities. Preserving a meaningful investment test can therefore
expand access to affordable homeownership and other forms of community development credit that help
LMI households build assets and strengthen their long term financial stability.

 IV. The proposed community development definition should retain a clear and demonstrable
 connection to LMI people and communities

We support the agencies' effort to provide banks with clearer and more objective standards for determining
when an activity qualifies for community development consideration. Greater certainty can help banks
identify and finance projects that respond to community needs. However, several proposed changes would
allow activities to receive CRA credit without requiring clear evidence that LMI people or communities are
the primary beneficiaries. We are concerned that these changes could reduce the amount of CRA
motivated capital available for activities that directly address the needs of LMI households and
communities.

The proposal generally retains the requirement that a loan, investment, grant, or service have a primary
purpose of community development. However, it would broaden the underlying categories that may satisfy
that standard. As a result, an activity could qualify under the revised definition of community development
without having a clear and demonstrable purpose of benefiting LMI people or communities. Areas of
particular concern include:

 Economic development activities. Eliminating the purpose test for economic development
 activities could redirect CRA motivated financing towards conventional business expansion that

877.272.1977 www.ccminvests.com Community Capital Management, LLC
  may have occurred without CRA support. This could leave fewer resources for businesses that
 create accessible employment and economic opportunities for LMI people.
 Government designated redevelopment areas. Expanding CRA eligibility to activities within
 government designated redevelopment areas could have unintended consequences for existing
 LMI residents of a community. Large redevelopment projects may increase property values,
 expand the tax base, or attract higher-income residents and businesses. Although these outcomes
 may provide general economic benefits, they may offer limited direct benefit to existing LMI
 residents and, in some circumstances, contribute to rising housing costs or displacement. Without
 an appropriate LMI safeguard, CRA motivated capital could support redevelopment without
 adequately addressing the needs of the people and communities the CRA is intended to serve.

 Together, these changes could permit banks to satisfy a greater portion of their community
 development obligations through activities that provide broad, indirect, or geographically assumed
 benefits, without demonstrating that LMI people and communities are primary and meaningful
 beneficiaries. This could redirect limited CRA motivated capital away from affordable housing,
 employment opportunities for LMI people, neighborhood small businesses, community services, and
 other activities specifically designed to address the needs of communities that continue to face the
 greatest barriers to credit and investment.

 V. Recommendations

We share the agencies' commitment to a clear, workable CRA framework and to reducing unnecessary
burden on community banks. We believe these objectives can be achieved while preserving the
examination driven incentives that have helped channel significant capital into community development
activities. With that goal in mind, we respectfully offer the following recommendations:

 1. Do not raise the large bank threshold to $10 billion. Retain the current $1.649 billion large bank
 threshold (subject to continued inflation indexing) so that banks already familiar with the
 standalone investment test remain subject to a consistent examination framework. Although the
 proposal is intended to reduce regulatory burden, changing the applicable performance test for
 these institutions could create new burdens by requiring revisions to internal policies, procedures,
 compliance processes, and data systems. Maintaining the current threshold would provide
 regulatory continuity while preserving an established incentive for qualified community
 development investment.

 2. Preserve a distinct, separately weighted qualified investment component. For any bank that
 remains an intermediate bank, retain a meaningful CD test that gives explicit weight to qualified
 investments, and do not adopt the Appendix A change that would allow strong lending performance
 to fully offset weak CD performance. The investment component should remain a genuine, ratings
 relevant obligation, not an optional enhancement.

 3. Retain the CD test for banks between $412 million and $1 billion. Do not raise the small bank
 threshold to $1 billion in a manner that eliminates the CD test for these institutions. It has been our
 experience that banks in this current Intermediate Small Bank category appreciate the flexibility
 that the community development test affords them to meet the needs of LMI households and

877.272.1977 www.ccminvests.com Community Capital Management, LLC
  communities within their assessment areas. Removing the option for the community development
 test for many banks may have the unintended consequence of creating increased burden.
 4. Retain annual inflation indexing of the thresholds. A fixed $10 billion threshold that is not
 indexed will steadily erode coverage as the industry grows. Continued CPI-W indexing preserves the
 intended balance over time.
 5. Decline to raise the thresholds further toward $30 billion. The agencies should not expand the
 intermediate or small categories to include banks up to $30 billion (Question 1), which would leave
 only the very largest institutions subject to the investment test and would compound the
 disinvestment described above.
 6. Keep Community Development Activities focused on LMI people and communities. Retain LMI
 benefit as the organizing principle of the community development definition and apply it
 consistently across all four categories. Maintaining this focus preserves the clarity the proposal is

Dear Sir/Madam:

The National Association of Development Companies (NADCO) submits these
comments in response to the joint Notice of Proposed Rulemaking and request for
comment from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and Department of
the Treasury, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC).

NADCO represents over 190 Certified Development Companies (CDCs) and their
industry partners that deliver the Small Business Administration (SBA) Development
Company Program, commonly known as the 504 Loan Program (and referred to as the
"SBDC" program in the proposed rule). Since 1986, CDCs have provided over 224,000
small businesses with $146 billion in Section 504 financing, representing a total capital
investment of over $418 billion and creating or retaining over 3.4 million jobs in local
communities throughout the United States.

The SBA Development Company Program is authorized by Section 501(a) of the Small
Business Investment Act of 1958, P.L. 85-699, as amended, which states: "The
Congress hereby finds and declares that the purpose of this title is to foster economic
development and to create or preserve job opportunities in both urban and rural areas
by providing long-term financing for small business concerns through the development
company program authorized by this title."

The 504 Loan Program advances this congressionally established economic
development mission through a public-private partnership. In a typical 504 financing, a
private-sector lending institution provides a first mortgage loan in conjunction with
financing provided through a CDC and backed by an SBA-guaranteed debenture. This
structure enables small businesses to obtain long-term financing for major fixed assets,
including land, buildings, machinery, and equipment, while leveraging private-sector
capital to support economic development and job creation in communities throughout
the country.
 Proposed Economic Development Definition
NADCO strongly supports the agencies' proposed revisions to the definition of
"economic development." In particular, NADCO supports the proposed third category of
economic development, which would include "Federal, State, local, or Tribal
government programs, projects, or initiatives that serve small businesses or small
farms, as defined by those programs."

NADCO particularly supports the agencies' specific identification of the SBA
Development Company Program as an example of a federal program meeting this
economic development category. The 504 Loan Program is a congressionally
established economic development program specifically designed to foster economic
development and create or preserve employment opportunities through long-term
financing for small businesses.

As the agencies recognize in the proposed rule, expressly identifying these government
programs will provide greater clarity and encourage continued participation in and
support of programs providing small business and small farm financing. The agencies
further recognize that aligning CRA economic development activities with government
programs addressing identified small business needs can encourage coordination
among banks, government agencies, and other program participants. NADCO strongly
agrees with this approach.

This clarification is particularly appropriate for the 504 Loan Program because the
program is built upon precisely this type of public-private coordination. Bank lending
partners are integral to 504 financing, providing private-sector capital alongside
CDC/SBA financing to support small-business investment and economic development.
Greater certainty regarding CRA consideration for qualifying 504-related lending can
encourage continued bank participation in the program and expand access to long-term
capital for small businesses in communities throughout the country.

Elimination of the Purpose Test
NADCO also supports the agencies' proposal to eliminate the existing "purpose test"
applicable to economic development activities. Under current guidance, an otherwise
qualifying small-business activity must satisfy additional requirements related to job
creation, retention, or improvement for low- or moderate-income individuals or in
qualifying geographic areas.

The proposed approach would instead establish more objective criteria for determining
whether an activity qualifies as economic development. As the agencies explain, banks
would no longer need to demonstrate, for example, low- or moderate-income job
creation for a qualifying small-business loan and could instead demonstrate that the
activity or government program through which the activity was made is identified as
economic development under the regulation.

For the SBA 504 Loan Program, this approach appropriately recognizes the economic
development purpose of a federal program specifically established by Congress to

 Page 2 of 3
 foster economic development and create or preserve employment opportunities, while
providing greater certainty for participating banks.
Response to Question 26
In response to Question 26, NADCO strongly supports retaining the SBA Development
Company Program in the non-exhaustive list of Federal, State, local, or Tribal
government programs, projects, or initiatives included in the proposed definition of
economic development.
Explicit recognition of the SBA Development Company Program will provide greater
regulatory certainty to bank lending partners, encourage continued bank participation in
the 504 Loan Program, and help expand access to long-term capital for small
businesses throughout the United States. It also appropriately recognizes the role of
CDCs and their bank lending partners in carrying out a congressionally established
federal economic development program.
NADCO therefore urges the agencies to adopt the proposed revisions to the economic
development provisions and retain the specific reference to the SBA Development
Company Program in the final rule.
NADCO appreciates the opportunity to provide these comments and the agencies'
recognition of the important role the SBA Development Company Program, Certified
Development Companies, and their bank lending partners play in supporting economic
development in communities throughout the United States.
Sincerely,

Wayne Williams
Executive Vice President
Regulatory Affairs & Training

Parkview Services opposes the proposed Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. We urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the proposal, publish a thorough analysis of its impacts for public comment, and extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

Please include the attached letter from Parkview Services, dated October 2, 2026, in the public comment record. We incorporate that letter in full as part of this comment. The following summarizes our principal concerns.

Founded in 1967, Parkview Services is a Washington nonprofit that creates inclusive housing solutions promoting stability, opportunity, and community. We develop and preserve affordable rental housing for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD), provide supported living services, and deliver statewide homeownership counseling, down payment assistance, and foreclosure prevention. In 2025, our Homeownership Program served 1,039 households, and 14 households became homeowners with Parkview’s down payment assistance loans.

Raising the small-bank threshold to $1 billion and the large-bank threshold to $10 billion would reduce community development scrutiny and weaken incentives to support affordable housing and housing counseling. The need for these resources does not diminish when a bank is reclassified.

Our experience illustrates the urgency of maintaining investment. Parkview’s scattered-site operating and maintenance support declined from approximately $110,000 in 2022 to $35,000 in 2025, with a 2026 award of only $3,400. A typical three-bedroom home serving tenants at 30 percent of area median income can lose approximately $8,000 annually without operating subsidy. Many of our tenants have incomes closer to 15 percent of area median income. Reduced bank investment incentives would compound the pressure on this essential housing.

We also oppose a rigid 15 percent indirect-cost limit for community development grants. Accounting, technology, compliance, and supervision are necessary to deliver reliable housing services and safeguard funds. Grant rules should allow reasonable, documented administrative costs and proportionate reporting requirements.

CRA examinations should assess important local mortgage credit needs even when mortgages are not a bank’s major lending product. Strong community development reporting and meaningful investment expectations should remain in place.

Before advancing these changes, the agencies should identify affected banks and communities, quantify the lending and investment that would receive less scrutiny, and assess impacts on rural communities, communities of color, and low-income people with disabilities. Any revised rule should preserve meaningful accountability and support lasting housing stability.

Marc G. Côté
Executive Director
Parkview Services

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Parkview Services opposes the proposed Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rule because it would weaken
incentives for banks to support affordable housing, responsible mortgage lending, and the nonprofit
organizations that help households achieve and sustain housing stability. We urge the OCC and FDIC to
withdraw the proposal, publish a thorough analysis of its community impacts for public comment, and
extend the comment period by at least 60 days, to a total of at least 120 days.

Founded in 1967, Parkview is a Washington nonprofit whose mission is to create inclusive housing solutions
that promote stability, opportunity, and community. We develop and preserve affordable rental housing,
with a focus on people with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD), and provide statewide
homeownership counseling, down payment assistance, and foreclosure prevention. Our supported living
services also support people with IDD in their homes. These roles give us a direct understanding of the
financing and ongoing support necessary to make housing accessible to households with limited incomes.

In 2025, our Homeownership Program served 1,039 households and helped 14 households with special
needs become homeowners. We work with people who need assistance navigating mortgage requirements,
addressing financial hardship, and preparing for sustainable ownership. Bank lending and community
investment should reinforce these efforts. CRA evaluations must continue to hold banks accountable for
meeting the needs of low- and moderate-income households, including those whose disabilities create
additional barriers to housing.

The proposal would raise the small-bank asset threshold to $1 billion and the large-bank threshold to $10
billion, reducing community development scrutiny and eliminating separate investment and service
evaluations for banks moved out of the large-bank category. We are concerned that these changes would
reduce incentives to finance affordable housing and support housing counseling. Community needs do not
diminish when a bank is reclassified. The agencies should identify the affected institutions and communities
and analyze the investment, lending, and services that would receive less scrutiny before changing these
thresholds.

For Parkview's rental housing, the need for sustained investment is especially acute. Our scattered-site
operating and maintenance support declined from approximately $110,000 in 2022 to $35,000 in 2025, with
a 2026 award of only $3,400. A typical three-bedroom home serving tenants at 30 percent of area median
income can lose approximately $8,000 annually without operating subsidy; many of our tenants have
incomes closer to 15 percent of area median income. These are homes where people can live in their

 Parkview Services | CRA comments | 1
 communities with the support they need. Reducing bank investment expectations while public operating
resources are shrinking would place additional pressure on housing that is already difficult to sustain.

CRA policy should encourage financing for acquisition, preservation, rehabilitation, and new housing
production, including small scattered-site properties serving people with IDD. The agencies should evaluate
whether the proposed community development benchmarks would reduce activity below current levels and
whether smaller projects serving households with extremely low incomes would be particularly affected.
Predictable standards should reflect documented community needs and preserve strong incentives for banks
to meet them.

We also oppose a rigid 15 percent limit on indirect costs for community development grants. Housing
counseling and affordable housing programs require accounting, technology, compliance, supervision, and
reliable administrative systems. Those functions help ensure that funds are used responsibly and services
remain available. A uniform cap can underfund the capacity needed to deliver the very outcomes CRA is
intended to support. Additional documentation requirements could also discourage banks from partnering
with community-based nonprofits. The agencies should allow reasonable, documented administrative costs
and use proportionate reporting requirements.

The proposed focus on a bank's major lending product lines raises another concern. Affordable mortgage
credit remains essential to the households we serve even when mortgage lending represents a smaller share
of a particular bank's business. CRA examinations should assess important local credit needs and gaps rather
than allow a bank's business mix to determine which needs receive meaningful review. Strong public
reporting on community development lending should also remain available so communities can assess bank
performance.

Parkview works with housing advocates and other organizations to expand inclusive housing development
across Washington, and participates in the Black Home Initiative Leadership Council. We ask the agencies to
examine how the proposal would affect communities facing historic racial discrimination and disinvestment,
as well as low-income people with disabilities. Public input from the people affected should guide that
analysis.

Before advancing a revised rule, the agencies should identify which communities would lose scrutiny;
quantify changes in lending, investment, and services subject to evaluation; assess geographic and
population impacts, including rural communities and communities of color; and consider alternatives that
reduce administrative burden while preserving accountability. The present proposal does not provide an
adequate basis for accepting the risks to the households we serve.

We urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw this proposal and maintain meaningful CRA expectations while
undertaking that analysis. We also request at least a 60-day extension of the October 13, 2026 comment
deadline. Community organizations need time to assess these extensive changes and contribute evidence
from their work. Any future rule should strengthen banks' responsiveness to community needs and support
lasting housing stability.

obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks
that would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the communities
those institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development activity that would
receive less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and
moderate-income communities or communities that have experienced historic
discrimination and disinvestment.

PROPOSAL WILL MAKE HOLDING BANKS ACCOUNTABLE HARDER
Under the current rule, banks above the large bank threshold annually collect and report data
on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans. The proposal
would limit these requirements to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. Over 400 banks
with assets of $10 billion or less would no longer be required to annually collect and report
CRA data on small business loans, small-farm loans, and community development loans.
Without meaningful data, communities,regulators, and researchers would have less
information toidentifycredit deserts, compare bank performance or understand whether
local credit needs are being met. Our educational programs for bankers often point to
banking and other economic data to demonstrate where credit markets are successfully or
inadequately meeting community needs. We rely on CRA-related and other regulatory data to
provide visibility into industry trends so we can design and test solutions that help banks
develop more inclusive practices. Without loan and investment data, it will also become
much harder for banks themselves to understand their own markets, competitive landscape,
and impact.

According to NCRC, the proposal would eliminate 11% of CRA small business lending data
reporting nationwide. Specifically in California, where we are headquartered, the loss of small
business data would eliminate a critically important dataset, as small businesses represent

(June 22, 2022). https://kinder.rice.edu/research/2022-state-housing-harris-county-and-houston

 5
 99.9% of all businesses in the state and employ nearly half of all employees in the state.11

hinder state, regional, and local efforts to track and improve economic development
outcomes.

Before reducing reporting requirements, the agencies should analyze the impact doing so will
have for people with low- and moderate-incomes or low- and moderate-income
communities, including whether it could result in a reduction in small business, small farm, or
community development lending. In addition, the agencies should explain why changing the
standard is consistent with the CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the
credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities.

Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:

 identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA
 scrutiny under the proposal;

 quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and
 community development activities subject to CRA evaluation;

 assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or
 populations, including rural communities and communities of color;

 consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without
 sacrificing meaningful community accountability.

believes that the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of
its impacts is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs
considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for
meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially
weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with
CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods.

We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days.
The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant
changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations,

my firm, Ally Community Development, works with nonprofit organizations and tribes all over
the State of Washington to develop affordable housing projects. Over the past 30 years I have
worked with over 40 organizations to develop over 1,300 affordable housing units.

The projects that I have worked on have benefitted from the Community Reinvestment Act in a
number of ways. Many of my clients have received grants from banks that are incentivized by
the CRA. Many have received construction and permanent loans, either directly from banks or
through consortia like the WA Community Reinvestment Association, that are motivated by the
banks' CRA responsibilities. Many have received Low Income Housing Tax Credit and Historic
Tax Credit investments. It has been clear in banks' investment offers that banks are more
willing to invest in projects that are perceived as higher risk, and are willing to pay more per
dollar of credit, when they can get CRA credit for those investments. I am very concerned that
the bank participation that has made many of these projects possible will not be available for
future projects because of the proposed changes in the CRA.

I am concerned that the proposed new rule reduces the CRA expectations by increasing the
asset limits that put banks in the Small, Intermediate and Large bank categories that determine
what level of investment and scrutiny that the banks received under the CRA. For my past
projects, it has often been smaller local banks that are the most flexible and helpful in providing

 exempted from any CRA responsibilities. For large banks, the amount of community

Intermediate and Small banks remain at their current levels, and that the percentage of
Community development investment and lending that are required also remain unchanged.

operating support grants from lenders. These organizations are generally small and medium

reporting requirements. The requirement that CRA related grant be project-specific and show

accountability.

evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. Given the
complexity and impact of the rule, additional time is warranted. An extension would allow
affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather examples from
the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more complete record on which
to base any final rule.

Sincerely,

Philippa Nye
Ally Community Development

communities. We support that goal, and we believe financial education is part of how it is achieved, not
a distraction from it. Borrowers who understand budgeting, credit, and repayment are better positioned
to qualify for credit and to repay it.

The research supports this. A 2022 meta-analysis in the Journal of Financial Economics reviewed 76
randomized experiments covering more than 160,000 people and found that financial education
programs produce positive causal effects on both financial knowledge and downstream financial
behavior. A Federal Reserve Board study of Georgia, Idaho, and Texas found that young adults who
were in school after those states adopted financial education requirements had higher relative credit
scores and lower relative delinquency rates than peers in comparison states. The same research shows
that results depend on rigorous, carefully implemented programs, which is why we recommend below
that the agencies give weight to programs that measure outcomes.

 Page 1

 For these reasons, we encourage the agencies to treat well-designed financial education for LMI
 individuals as a complement to the proposal's lending focus. Clear rules for when such programs
 qualify will help banks invest in them with confidence.

 Recommendations

 1. Keep financial literacy expressly named in the community development definition.
 The proposed definition lists financial literacy among the forms of support that qualify under civic
 assistance for LMI individuals, and the preamble gives a grant to a nonprofit providing financial
 literacy programming as an example. We support both and ask that the final rule retain them. Naming
 financial literacy in the rule text, rather than only in guidance, gives banks durable certainty across
 examination cycles.

 2. Include financial education delivered through technology in the illustrative list in proposed 12
 CFR 25.13(a) and 345.13(a).
 The proposed public list of qualifying activities, and the confirmation process in proposed paragraph
 (b) of the same sections, are among the most useful features of the proposal. We ask that the list include
 at least one example of financial education for LMI individuals delivered through a digital or adaptive
 platform, such as a program offered in schools where a majority of students qualify for free or
 reduced-price meals. Many community banks lack the staff to teach classes in person, and technology
 lets them reach more learners at lower cost. Without an example, banks may hesitate to use these
 programs until an examiner rules on them.

 3. Confirm that bank employees who facilitate a technology-delivered program can earn
 community development service consideration.
 Under current guidance, community development services are generally volunteer services by bank
 staff that relate to financial services. We ask the agencies to confirm in the rule or preamble that this
 includes bank employees who lead, host, mentor, or support sessions of a financial education program
 delivered through software, even when the curriculum itself comes from a third party. The service is the
 employees' time and financial expertise, and the delivery method should not disqualify it.

 4. Specify how the 15 percent indirect cost limit is calculated, and treat learner-facing program
 costs as direct costs.
 The proposed community development grant definition and proposed 12 CFR 25.42(a)(3) and
 345.42(a)(3) limit a large bank grant recipient's indirect costs to 15 percent, calculated consistent with 2
 CFR part 200 or a comparable standard. The Uniform Guidance measures indirect costs against
 modified total direct costs, while the preamble applies the limit to the grant or donation dollar amount.
 We ask the agencies to state the calculation base directly in the rule and to explain what qualifies as a
 comparable standard. We also ask them to confirm that curriculum, platform, and instructional costs
 that directly serve LMI learners count as direct program costs, not indirect administrative costs.
 Otherwise, a school foundation or nonprofit that uses a bank grant to provide financial education may
 be unable to tell whether the grant qualifies.

 5. Name financial education as an example of what small banks can do voluntarily.
 Under the proposal, banks below $1 billion in assets would no longer be evaluated under a community
 development test. We take no position on that threshold. We support two provisions that keep a modest,
 voluntary incentive in place for these banks: proposed appendix A, paragraph (d)(3)(ii)(B), which lets a

 Page 2

 small bank that exceeds the lending standards be considered for an "outstanding" rating based in part on
 its community development activities, and the new performance context factor in proposed 12 CFR
 25.21(b)(7) and 345.21(b)(7) for community development activities not considered under another test.
 We ask that the final rule retain both and that the preamble or illustrative list name financial education
 for LMI individuals as an example of activity that may be considered under them. This encourages
 small banks to continue these programs without adding any new requirement or burden.

 Responses to specific questions
 Question 9 (alternative standards for limiting indirect costs). We support the goal of ensuring grant
 funds reach the intended communities. As an alternative or supplement to a fixed percentage, the
 agencies could accept documented outcome measures for grant-funded education programs, such as the
 number of LMI participants served and measured gains in financial knowledge. Evidence of what a
 grant delivered is a stronger safeguard than overhead ratios alone.

 Question 11 (guidance on determining primary purpose). Yes. For financial education, we suggest
 guidance stating that a program has a primary purpose of community development when it is targeted
 to LMI individuals, for example through schools where a majority of students qualify for free or
 reduced-price meals, or through programs located in and directed to residents of LMI census tracts.
 These methods already appear in the Interagency Questions and Answers and would be more durable if
 codified.

 Question 16 (defining innovativeness). If the agencies define innovativeness, we suggest it include
 new delivery methods that expand the reach of community development services to more LMI
 individuals at lower cost per person, such as adaptive digital education. The definition should reward
 measurable reach and outcomes, not novelty of technology alone.

 Question 58 (addressing the Interagency Questions and Answers going forward). As the agencies
 codify or retire portions of the Interagency Questions and Answers, we ask that they preserve the
 existing methods for showing that a community service is targeted to LMI individuals, including
 service at schools where a majority of students qualify for free or reduced-price meals. Banks and their
 partners rely on these methods to document financial education programs, and losing them without a
 replacement would create the very uncertainty the proposal seeks to reduce.

 Conclusion
 Clear, durable rules for financial education will help community banks of every size invest in programs
 that build creditworthy borrowers in LMI communities. Our recommendations ask for clarity, not new
 burden, and would apply equally to every provider and bank. We appreciate the agencies' work on this
 proposal and would welcome the opportunity to answer questions.

 Respectfully submitted,

 Kevin Allen Ringler

To Whom It May Concern:

Thank you for the opportunity to provide feedback on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
(OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposal to reform Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. Our company R4 Capital provides capital solutions to create
and preserve affordable housing nationwide. We are an affordable housing investor with proven
expertise in LIHTC equity syndication, underwriting, asset management, tax-exempt lending, and
development. Our growing $14.5 billion LIHTC equity and debt portfolio is distributed throughout
49 U.S. states, Washington, D.C., and territories representing more than 82,000 units of
affordable housing. R4 Capital has offices in New York, NY, Boston, MA, Newport Beach, CA,
and Austin, TX.

For nearly half a century, CRA has driven banks to extend private capital financing to local
communities they serve, combating the legacy of redlining, promoting equitable lending, and
facilitating reinvestment in low- and moderate-income places and people. CRA has spurred
lending and investments in homeownership, small businesses, healthcare, childcare, and other
community needs, but nowhere is its impact more pronounced than in the effect CRA has had on
the production of affordable rental housing through the Low Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing
Credit) program.

The Housing Credit, our nation's most important tool for the production of affordable rental
housing, relies heavily on investments from banks subject to CRA. In fact, approximately 80
percent of equity investments in the Housing Credit each year come from CRA-motivated bank
investors, according to a 2025 study by the accounting firm CohnReznick.1 Banks make these
investments not only to receive the modest return provided by the tax advantages associated with
investing in Housing Credit properties, but also because the full CRA examination for large banks
includes a distinct investment test. Because Housing Credit investment yields are typically
modest, large banks often could get a more substantial yield from making other forms of
investment, but often still choose to invest in the Housing Credit because Housing Credit
investments help banks meet their CRA obligations.

We are concerned that OCC and FDIC's proposal to reclassify banks with assets ranging from
$1.649 billion to $10 billion as intermediate banks rather than large banks subject to the full CRA
examination, including the investment test, could reduce competition in the Housing Credit equity
market, leading to lower pricing on credits and less housing produced. Of the 642 banks currently

banks with assets in the $1.649 billion to $10 billion range invested at least $1.6 billion in Housing

market, banks in this asset range invested up to $2 billion in Housing Credit equity over the past
five years.

If the OCC/FDIC proposal is made final, newly classified intermediate banks would no longer need
to invest in the low and moderate-income communities they are supposed to serve because they
would no longer be subject to the investment test, despite still having more general community
development obligations as an intermediate-sized bank. This is because, for various reasons, it
is often easier for banks to support community development activities through lending rather than

Moreover, the CRA Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) undercuts recent congressional action
to strengthen and expand the Housing Credit and facilitate more bank investment in the program.

The consequences of this proposal would be most damaging to smaller communities that now

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57
FDIC RIN 3064-AG31

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the OCC and FDIC's proposed amendments to the
Community Reinvestment Act regulations.

I want to begin by acknowledging the agencies for taking another thoughtful look at CRA and
asking how the regulation can be clearer, more workable and better aligned with today's
financial system.

I agree that modernization is necessary.

I also agree that regulatory complexity does not automatically produce better outcomes. Banks
need to understand what is expected of them. Examiners need clear and consistent standards.
Community banks should not be overwhelmed by requirements designed for institutions many
times their size. And the rules should provide greater certainty about which activities qualify for
CRA consideration. But as we simplify CRA, we cannot simplify away the accountability that
makes CRA work.

I offer these comments from a perspective that has allowed me to see the Community
Reinvestment Act from three very different seats. I started my career as a bank regulator with the
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. I subsequently spent much of my career as a banker,
including leading community development and community reinvestment work. Today, I serve as
President and CEO of Opportunity Resource Fund, a Michigan statewide Community
Development Financial Institution. I have been the regulator evaluating performance. I have been
the banker responsible for delivering it. And today I lead a CDFI working alongside banks and
communities to turn capital into homeownership, affordable housing, small-business growth and
economic opportunity.

I remember when CRA examinations placed considerably more emphasis on good effort. I have
also seen what happens when expectations are clear, performance is measured and institutions
are accountable for results.

 Behavior changes
  Capital moves
 Products change
 Partnerships develop

Institutions become more intentional about understanding and responding to the needs of the
communities they serve.

That is the value of CRA.

The question before us in 2026 should therefore not simply be how to make CRA easier to
administer.

The question should be how we make CRA more effective at producing responsible
lending, investment, financial services and economic opportunity in a financial marketplace
that looks very different from the one in which CRA was created.

Against that standard, I believe several provisions of the proposal should be strengthened.

A fragmented CRA supervisory framework creates its own uncertainty.

I am also concerned that this proposal is being advanced by two of the three federal prudential
banking regulators rather than through a unified interagency CRA framework. Banks and
communities benefit when the OCC, FDIC and Federal Reserve operate from consistent
standards for evaluating community reinvestment performance. A framework in which similarly
situated institutions may be evaluated under different CRA rules depending on their charter or
primary federal regulator risks creating unnecessary complexity, inconsistent expectations and
uneven accountability.

If the goal of this rulemaking is greater clarity, predictability and reduced regulatory burden,
fragmentation among the prudential regulators works against that objective. Regulatory
simplification should not come at the cost of regulatory consistency.

Recommendation: The OCC and FDIC should continue working toward alignment with the
Federal Reserve and, wherever statutory authority permits, preserve a consistent interagency
approach to CRA standards, definitions, examination expectations and performance
measurement. The financial system benefits from proportional regulation--but it also benefits
from one clear and durable framework for community reinvestment.

1. Asset thresholds: proportionality should not mean less accountability. The proposal
would define small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets, intermediate banks as
institutions with $1 billion to $10 billion, and large banks as institutions with more than $10
billion. I understand the agencies' rationale.

A $500 million community bank should not necessarily have the same data, staffing and
examination requirements as a $500 billion institution.
 But the proposed thresholds would move a significant number of institutions into examination
categories with reduced data collection, reporting and more flexible performance standards.

That deserves careful consideration.
A $5 billion or $9 billion bank can be one of the most important financial institutions in the
communities it serves.

Recommendation: Retain proportionality, but do not allow asset thresholds to materially reduce
accountability for community credit needs. Before finalizing the $10 billion threshold--or
considering an even higher threshold--the agencies should quantify the amount of mortgage
lending, small-business lending, community development financing, investments and services
that would become subject to less rigorous measurement and reporting. And rather than simply
asking less of community banks, regulators should help them do more.

Provide technical assistance. Create clearer pathways for CDFI partnerships. Help community
banks understand affordable-housing finance, small-business lending, guarantees, loan
participations, credit enhancements and other tools that allow them to serve their communities
more effectively. Proportionality should change how responsibility is measured--not whether
responsibility exists.

2. Major product lines: CRA cannot become an "in-and-out" lending test The proposal
would evaluate all banks primarily on their major retail lending product lines and offers
alternative methodologies for determining which products receive examination.
I understand the desire to focus examination resources where an institution conducts meaningful
business.

My concern is what we stop seeing. A bank may not consider mortgage lending or small-
business lending one of its largest product lines precisely because it has not built the products,
expertise, risk appetite or partnerships necessary to serve those markets. If those products then
receive less examination attention because the bank does relatively little of them, CRA risks
reinforcing the very gap it should encourage institutions to address.

A meaningful CRA examination should not simply ask:
What does this bank already do?

It should also ask:
What does this community need, and what is the institution capable of responsibly doing to meet
that need?

Recommendation: Major-product-line methodology should not allow material gaps in
mortgage, small-business or other important community credit needs to disappear from CRA
evaluation.
Performance context and documented community needs must remain meaningful components of
the examination.

3. Lending evaluation: do not allow meaningful analysis to collapse into ratios
 The proposal appropriately recognizes that some lending datasets may be too small to support
meaningful statistical conclusions. However, where data are limited, the proposal contemplates
relying on other measures, including loan-to-deposit and in-out ratios and performance context.
Those measures can be useful. They should not become substitutes for understanding whether an
institution is actually serving its community.

A bank can have an acceptable loan-to-deposit ratio without adequately serving low- and
moderate-income borrowers, small businesses or communities with significant housing needs.

Recommendation: Where transaction volume is insufficient for statistical analysis, examiners
should conduct a substantive assessment of community credit needs, product availability,
underwriting practices, partnerships and the institution's capacity to respond--not simply default
to ratios.
CRA should evaluate performance, not just mathematical compliance.

4. Retail banking services: do not remove deposit services from meaningful consideration
I have significant concerns with the proposal to revise the service test so that the range of
services evaluated focuses only on credit services, rather than deposit products and services.

Credit matters enormously.
But access to responsible banking begins before someone needs a loan.
Checking accounts matter.
Savings products matter.
Affordable transaction services matter.
Branch access matters.
Digital access matters.

And the CRA statute itself recognizes that community convenience and needs include both credit
and deposit services. This becomes even more important as branches disappear.

Recommendation: Retain meaningful consideration of deposit products and services,
particularly where they expand access to responsible banking for low- and moderate-income
households and communities with limited banking access.
A modern CRA framework should not narrow our understanding of financial access at the same
moment the ways consumers access banking are becoming more complex.

5. Banking deserts: measure access, not simply the presence of a branch or an app. The
proposal's treatment of retail banking services must also confront the growth of banking deserts.
Branches still matter. A branch can provide access to a mortgage lender, small-business banker,
financial advice and relationships that are difficult to replace. But I also recognize that every
solution does not require a physical branch.

Technology can help.
Mobile delivery can help.
Community partnerships can help.
CDFIs can help.
 What matters is whether people are actually being served.

Recommendation: CRA examinations should evaluate how banks respond when communities
lose meaningful access to financial services. When branches close, institutions should
demonstrate how they will continue to provide meaningful access to credit and financial services.

An app alone should not constitute community access.

The measurement should be whether consumers and businesses in the affected community are
actually using and benefiting from the alternative delivery model.

6. Community development grants: reject the 15 percent indirect-cost limitation. The
proposal would require, for a grant from a large bank to qualify for CRA consideration, that the
recipient's indirect costs for administering the grant not exceed 15 percent. I strongly disagree
with this approach.

I understand what the agencies are trying to prevent. CRA consideration should not reward
arrangements in which resources intended for communities are consumed by unnecessary layers
of administration. But an arbitrary 15 percent threshold is not an effective measure of
organizational efficiency or community impact. I run a CDFI. Responsible deployment of capital
requires underwriting, compliance, servicing, financial management, audit, cybersecurity,
technology, risk management, impact measurement and talented people. Those functions are not
waste.
They are what allow an organization to responsibly manage and leverage millions of dollars of
private, public and philanthropic capital. The proposed standard could unintentionally penalize
sophisticated organizations that have invested in the infrastructure necessary to manage capital
responsibly while rewarding organizations that underinvest in those capabilities.

Recommendation: Remove the 15 percent indirect-cost limitation. Instead, require
reasonable documentation that grant funds support a legitimate community development purpose
and evaluate the recipient's stewardship, effectiveness and measurable outcomes.
Measure impact--not an arbitrary overhead ratio.

7. Preserve grants, but do not allow grants to substitute for lending. The proposal raises
important questions about how grants should qualify for CRA consideration.
Grants matter. They fund homebuyer education, small-business technical assistance, financial
capability, predevelopment work, product development and the operating capacity necessary for
CDFIs and nonprofits to deliver programs effectively.

In many cases, grants help make lending possible. But philanthropy should complement--not
substitute for--lending and investment. A sponsorship cannot compensate for a significant
mortgage lending gap. A grant cannot substitute for a bank failing to develop a viable small-
business lending strategy.
 Recommendation: Preserve meaningful CRA consideration for grants that respond to
documented community needs while ensuring that philanthropy cannot substitute for strong
lending, investment and service performance.

8. Treat CDFIs as financial infrastructure--not simply grant recipients. CDFIs should not
be viewed primarily as organizations to which banks make CRA-qualified grants or investments.
CDFIs can make banks better lenders.

We aggregate transactions that may be inefficient for conventional institutions.
We provide technical assistance.
We structure subordinate and patient capital.
We understand local markets.
We prepare borrowers.
We originate loans banks can purchase or participate in.

We can help institutions responsibly test new products and reach borrowers who may fall outside
conventional credit boxes. The relationship should therefore be evaluated based on what the
partnership accomplishes.

Recommendation: CRA should strongly encourage loans, deposits, EQ2s, investments,
guarantees, participations, loan purchases, grants and other substantive partnerships with
certified CDFIs when those activities expand responsible access to credit.

Ask: not simply whether a bank invested in a CDFI.
Ask: What did that partnership allow the bank and the CDFI to accomplish that neither could
have accomplished as effectively alone?

9. CRA should encourage banks to responsibly expand their credit boxes One of the most
important things CRA can accomplish is encouraging institutions to become better lenders. This
does not mean asking banks to make unsafe loans. Safety and soundness must remain
fundamental. But there is a significant difference between unsafe lending and unnecessarily
narrow lending. Banks should continually evaluate whether there are responsible ways to say yes
to more borrowers.

Can underwriting consider additional evidence of repayment capacity?
Can guarantees or credit enhancements mitigate risk?
Can a CDFI partnership allow an institution to reach a borrower it cannot efficiently serve
directly?
Can a Special Purpose Credit Program address a demonstrated market gap?
Can technology identify creditworthy borrowers that traditional models overlook?

Recommendation: CRA performance should recognize responsible product and underwriting
innovation that demonstrably expands access to credit while maintaining safety and soundness.
The standard should never be "make bad loans."
It should be: Have you exhausted the responsible tools available to make more good loans?
 10. Small-business lending must remain a meaningful measure of performance. Access to
affordable small-business capital remains uneven. That has consequences beyond individual
entrepreneurs. Small businesses create jobs, stabilize commercial corridors and create household
and community wealth.

The major-product-line approach should not allow small-business lending to escape meaningful
scrutiny simply because an institution has chosen not to make it a significant part of its business.

Recommendation: Preserve meaningful evaluation of small-business lending where there are
documented market needs, even when it is not among an institution's largest product lines.
Maintain sufficient data and recordkeeping to understand where capital is flowing, what types
and sizes of businesses are being served and where meaningful gaps remain. And encourage
banks to partner with CDFIs and other responsible community lenders when conventional
economics make smaller transactions difficult.

11. Affordable housing: use CRA to bring more tools to the problem. I appreciate that the
proposal continues to recognize affordable housing as a core community development activity
and specifically asks whether affordable-housing consideration should extend to middle-income
households in high-cost areas. That is an important conversation. Housing affordability is no
longer a challenge confined to the lowest-income households. At the same time, we cannot
broaden eligibility in a way that unintentionally diverts resources from communities with the
greatest need.

We need more affordable rental housing.
We need to preserve naturally occurring affordable housing.
We need home repair.
We need neighborhood stabilization.
And we need responsible pathways to homeownership.

Recommendation: Maintain a strong focus on LMI households while allowing carefully defined
consideration of middle-income housing needs in demonstrably high-cost markets. CRA should
encourage banks to use multiple tools--senior debt, subordinate capital, guarantees, credit
enhancements, CDFI partnerships and responsible mortgage products--to expand both
affordable rental housing and sustainable homeownership.

12. Geographic consideration should recognize how community development actually
work. I appreciate the proposal's attempt to provide greater clarity around activities benefiting
multiple assessment areas and regional activities. CDFIs do not always operate according to
bank assessment-area boundaries. Affordable-housing funds, small-business programs and
community development initiatives frequently operate statewide or regionally. Rural
communities in particular may have fewer banks and fewer sources of capital.

Recommendation: Preserve meaningful flexibility for statewide and regional CDFI and
community-development activities while requiring banks to demonstrate that they are first
meaningfully responding to needs within their own assessment areas. Geographic accountability
and regional collaboration can coexist.
 13. Strategic plans: make the process easier, not the performance easier. I support the
agencies' effort to make strategic plans more accessible. Different business models may require
different approaches to CRA. Community banks in particular may benefit from greater certainty
about expectations. But flexibility cannot become a path to lower performance. Measurable goals
should reflect community needs, an institution's capacity and historical performance.
Community input should be meaningful and occur early enough to influence the plan. And an
Outstanding rating should represent performance meaningfully stronger than Satisfactory.

Recommendation: Simplify the strategic-plan process while maintaining strong, transparent
measurable goals, meaningful community participation and accountability for performance over
the life of the plan.

14. Modern financial services require modern accountability. This is where I believe the
agencies--and ultimately Congress--must look beyond this rulemaking. The financial
marketplace has fundamentally changed. Consumers increasingly receive financial products
through internet banks, fintech companies and emerging AI-enabled platforms. Some institutions
can gather deposits nationally without a significant physical presence. Other companies provide
financial products that look increasingly similar to traditional banking services.

I recognize the statutory limits of CRA. The OCC and FDIC cannot simply extend the statute to
every nonbank financial-services provider through regulation. But policymakers cannot ignore
the accountability gap created by the changing marketplace. If you accept deposits, there is a
responsibility that comes with that privilege. And as more entities provide bank-like financial
services and derive profits from consumers and communities, we need a broader policy
conversation about what responsibility comes with that economic benefit.
Recommendation: Apply CRA fully and meaningfully to digital and branchless insured
depository institutions based on their actual business models and economic reach. The agencies
should also work with Congress and other regulators to develop appropriate community-
investment, financial-inclusion and consumer-protection responsibilities for significant nonbank
financial-services providers. Innovation should expand access. It should not create an
accountability loophole.

15. Recordkeeping: reduce unnecessary paperwork, not the ability to measure performance
I support eliminating reporting that is duplicative or produces little useful information. I have
been a regulator and a banker. I understand the cost of regulatory requirements that do not
improve supervision or outcomes. But I also know this:

What we do not measure is difficult to manage and almost impossible to hold accountable. Data
allow regulators to identify gaps. They allow banks to understand their own performance. They
allow communities to see where capital is flowing. And they allow all of us to distinguish
meaningful performance from good intentions.

Recommendation: Reduce unnecessary reporting while preserving sufficient loan-level,
geographic, borrower, small-business and community-development information to meaningfully
 evaluate performance. Every proposed reporting reduction should be evaluated against a simple
question:

What will we no longer be able to know? If the answer is something necessary to determine
whether a bank is meeting community credit needs, we should retain it.

16. Measure outcomes, not simply activity. Ultimately, this is where I believe CRA should go.
At the end of an examination, we should be able to answer more than how many qualifying
transactions occurred.

Did more qualified families become homeowners?
Was affordable rental housing created or preserved?
Did small businesses obtain affordable capital?
Did a bank responsibly expand its credit box?
Did communities losing branches retain meaningful financial access?
Did a CDFI partnership allow an institution to reach borrowers it could not previously reach?
Did an institution identify a credit gap and change its products, underwriting or partnerships to
address it?

That is performance.

Recommendation: Maintain strong quantitative measures while giving meaningful
consideration to responsiveness, responsible innovation, leverage, partnerships and demonstrated
outcomes.

accomplish with the 2026 proposal.
CRA can be clearer.
It can be more predictable.
Some unnecessary administrative burdens can be reduced.
Community banks can be given greater flexibility. And institutions should have greater certainty
about what qualifies for CRA consideration. But those improvements should enable better
performance--not lower expectations.

Today, housing affordability is one of the most significant economic challenges facing American
families. Small businesses still struggle to obtain appropriately structured capital. Communities
are losing bank branches. Technology is fundamentally changing financial services. And CDFIs
are being asked to solve increasingly difficult market gaps.

We are also confronting the possibility that the next generation may have less opportunity to own
a home, build wealth and achieve economic security than their parents.

it better.

Large banks have a role.
Community banks have a role.
 CDFIs have a role.
Nonprofit Community Development Entities and community organizations have a role.
Technology providers and the expanding financial-services ecosystem have a role.
Regulators have a role.

And policymakers have a responsibility to make sure that as financial services evolve,
accountability evolves with them.

lead a CDFI working alongside banks to put capital to work in communities. From all three seats,
I have learned the same thing:

Help community banks build capacity.
Encourage responsible expansion of credit.
Strengthen CDFIs as partners in the financial system.
Preserve accountability for small-business lending.
Bring more capital and more tools to affordable rental housing and homeownership.
Address banking deserts.

And ensure that changes in technology and the way consumers access financial services do not
result in less responsibility to the communities from which financial institutions derive their
strength.

That is the modernization I believe communities--and our financial system--need.

Respectfully submitted,

Opportunity Resource Fund
