Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the OCC and FDIC's proposed amendments to the
Community Reinvestment Act regulations.

I want to begin by acknowledging the agencies for taking another thoughtful look at CRA and
asking how the regulation can be clearer, more workable and better aligned with today's
financial system.

I agree that modernization is necessary.

I also agree that regulatory complexity does not automatically produce better outcomes. Banks
need to understand what is expected of them. Examiners need clear and consistent standards.
Community banks should not be overwhelmed by requirements designed for institutions many
times their size. And the rules should provide greater certainty about which activities qualify for
CRA consideration. But as we simplify CRA, we cannot simplify away the accountability that
makes CRA work.

I offer these comments from a perspective that has allowed me to see the Community
Reinvestment Act from three very different seats. I started my career as a bank regulator with the
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. I subsequently spent much of my career as a banker,
including leading community development and community reinvestment work. Today, I serve as
President and CEO of Opportunity Resource Fund, a Michigan statewide Community
Development Financial Institution. I have been the regulator evaluating performance. I have been
the banker responsible for delivering it. And today I lead a CDFI working alongside banks and
communities to turn capital into homeownership, affordable housing, small-business growth and
economic opportunity.

I remember when CRA examinations placed considerably more emphasis on good effort. I have
also seen what happens when expectations are clear, performance is measured and institutions
are accountable for results.

 Behavior changes
  Capital moves
 Products change
 Partnerships develop

Institutions become more intentional about understanding and responding to the needs of the
communities they serve.

That is the value of CRA.

The question before us in 2026 should therefore not simply be how to make CRA easier to
administer.

The question should be how we make CRA more effective at producing responsible
lending, investment, financial services and economic opportunity in a financial marketplace
that looks very different from the one in which CRA was created.

Against that standard, I believe several provisions of the proposal should be strengthened.

A fragmented CRA supervisory framework creates its own uncertainty.

I am also concerned that this proposal is being advanced by two of the three federal prudential
banking regulators rather than through a unified interagency CRA framework. Banks and
communities benefit when the OCC, FDIC and Federal Reserve operate from consistent
standards for evaluating community reinvestment performance. A framework in which similarly
situated institutions may be evaluated under different CRA rules depending on their charter or
primary federal regulator risks creating unnecessary complexity, inconsistent expectations and
uneven accountability.

If the goal of this rulemaking is greater clarity, predictability and reduced regulatory burden,
fragmentation among the prudential regulators works against that objective. Regulatory
simplification should not come at the cost of regulatory consistency.

Recommendation: The OCC and FDIC should continue working toward alignment with the
Federal Reserve and, wherever statutory authority permits, preserve a consistent interagency
approach to CRA standards, definitions, examination expectations and performance
measurement. The financial system benefits from proportional regulation--but it also benefits
from one clear and durable framework for community reinvestment.

1. Asset thresholds: proportionality should not mean less accountability. The proposal
would define small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets, intermediate banks as
institutions with $1 billion to $10 billion, and large banks as institutions with more than $10
billion. I understand the agencies' rationale.

A $500 million community bank should not necessarily have the same data, staffing and
examination requirements as a $500 billion institution.
 But the proposed thresholds would move a significant number of institutions into examination
categories with reduced data collection, reporting and more flexible performance standards.

That deserves careful consideration.
A $5 billion or $9 billion bank can be one of the most important financial institutions in the
communities it serves.

Recommendation: Retain proportionality, but do not allow asset thresholds to materially reduce
accountability for community credit needs. Before finalizing the $10 billion threshold--or
considering an even higher threshold--the agencies should quantify the amount of mortgage
lending, small-business lending, community development financing, investments and services
that would become subject to less rigorous measurement and reporting. And rather than simply
asking less of community banks, regulators should help them do more.

Provide technical assistance. Create clearer pathways for CDFI partnerships. Help community
banks understand affordable-housing finance, small-business lending, guarantees, loan
participations, credit enhancements and other tools that allow them to serve their communities
more effectively. Proportionality should change how responsibility is measured--not whether
responsibility exists.

2. Major product lines: CRA cannot become an "in-and-out" lending test The proposal
would evaluate all banks primarily on their major retail lending product lines and offers
alternative methodologies for determining which products receive examination.
I understand the desire to focus examination resources where an institution conducts meaningful
business.

My concern is what we stop seeing. A bank may not consider mortgage lending or small-
business lending one of its largest product lines precisely because it has not built the products,
expertise, risk appetite or partnerships necessary to serve those markets. If those products then
receive less examination attention because the bank does relatively little of them, CRA risks
reinforcing the very gap it should encourage institutions to address.

A meaningful CRA examination should not simply ask:
What does this bank already do?

It should also ask:
What does this community need, and what is the institution capable of responsibly doing to meet
that need?

Recommendation: Major-product-line methodology should not allow material gaps in
mortgage, small-business or other important community credit needs to disappear from CRA
evaluation.
Performance context and documented community needs must remain meaningful components of
the examination.

3. Lending evaluation: do not allow meaningful analysis to collapse into ratios
 The proposal appropriately recognizes that some lending datasets may be too small to support
meaningful statistical conclusions. However, where data are limited, the proposal contemplates
relying on other measures, including loan-to-deposit and in-out ratios and performance context.
Those measures can be useful. They should not become substitutes for understanding whether an
institution is actually serving its community.

A bank can have an acceptable loan-to-deposit ratio without adequately serving low- and
moderate-income borrowers, small businesses or communities with significant housing needs.

Recommendation: Where transaction volume is insufficient for statistical analysis, examiners
should conduct a substantive assessment of community credit needs, product availability,
underwriting practices, partnerships and the institution's capacity to respond--not simply default
to ratios.
CRA should evaluate performance, not just mathematical compliance.

I have significant concerns with the proposal to revise the service test so that the range of
services evaluated focuses only on credit services, rather than deposit products and services.

Credit matters enormously.
But access to responsible banking begins before someone needs a loan.
Checking accounts matter.
Savings products matter.
Affordable transaction services matter.
Branch access matters.
Digital access matters.

And the CRA statute itself recognizes that community convenience and needs include both credit
and deposit services. This becomes even more important as branches disappear.

Recommendation: Retain meaningful consideration of deposit products and services,
particularly where they expand access to responsible banking for low- and moderate-income
households and communities with limited banking access.
A modern CRA framework should not narrow our understanding of financial access at the same
moment the ways consumers access banking are becoming more complex.

5. Banking deserts: measure access, not simply the presence of a branch or an app. The
proposal's treatment of retail banking services must also confront the growth of banking deserts.
Branches still matter. A branch can provide access to a mortgage lender, small-business banker,
financial advice and relationships that are difficult to replace. But I also recognize that every
solution does not require a physical branch.

Technology can help.
Mobile delivery can help.
Community partnerships can help.
CDFIs can help.
 What matters is whether people are actually being served.

Recommendation: CRA examinations should evaluate how banks respond when communities
lose meaningful access to financial services. When branches close, institutions should
demonstrate how they will continue to provide meaningful access to credit and financial services.

An app alone should not constitute community access.

The measurement should be whether consumers and businesses in the affected community are
actually using and benefiting from the alternative delivery model.

6. Community development grants: reject the 15 percent indirect-cost limitation. The
proposal would require, for a grant from a large bank to qualify for CRA consideration, that the
recipient's indirect costs for administering the grant not exceed 15 percent. I strongly disagree
with this approach.

I understand what the agencies are trying to prevent. CRA consideration should not reward
arrangements in which resources intended for communities are consumed by unnecessary layers
of administration. But an arbitrary 15 percent threshold is not an effective measure of
organizational efficiency or community impact. I run a CDFI. Responsible deployment of capital
requires underwriting, compliance, servicing, financial management, audit, cybersecurity,
technology, risk management, impact measurement and talented people. Those functions are not
waste.
They are what allow an organization to responsibly manage and leverage millions of dollars of
private, public and philanthropic capital. The proposed standard could unintentionally penalize
sophisticated organizations that have invested in the infrastructure necessary to manage capital
responsibly while rewarding organizations that underinvest in those capabilities.

Recommendation: Remove the 15 percent indirect-cost limitation. Instead, require
reasonable documentation that grant funds support a legitimate community development purpose
and evaluate the recipient's stewardship, effectiveness and measurable outcomes.
Measure impact--not an arbitrary overhead ratio.

7. Preserve grants, but do not allow grants to substitute for lending. The proposal raises
important questions about how grants should qualify for CRA consideration.
Grants matter. They fund homebuyer education, small-business technical assistance, financial
capability, predevelopment work, product development and the operating capacity necessary for
CDFIs and nonprofits to deliver programs effectively.

In many cases, grants help make lending possible. But philanthropy should complement--not
substitute for--lending and investment. A sponsorship cannot compensate for a significant
mortgage lending gap. A grant cannot substitute for a bank failing to develop a viable small-
business lending strategy.
 Recommendation: Preserve meaningful CRA consideration for grants that respond to
documented community needs while ensuring that philanthropy cannot substitute for strong
lending, investment and service performance.

CDFIs can make banks better lenders.

We aggregate transactions that may be inefficient for conventional institutions.
We provide technical assistance.
We structure subordinate and patient capital.
We understand local markets.
We prepare borrowers.
We originate loans banks can purchase or participate in.

We can help institutions responsibly test new products and reach borrowers who may fall outside

Ask: What did that partnership allow the bank and the CDFI to accomplish that neither could

9. CRA should encourage banks to responsibly expand their credit boxes One of the most

does not mean asking banks to make unsafe loans. Safety and soundness must remain
fundamental. But there is a significant difference between unsafe lending and unnecessarily

Can guarantees or credit enhancements mitigate risk?
Can a CDFI partnership allow an institution to reach a borrower it cannot efficiently serve

Can a Special Purpose Credit Program address a demonstrated market gap?
Can technology identify creditworthy borrowers that traditional models overlook?

Recommendation: CRA performance should recognize responsible product and underwriting
innovation that demonstrably expands access to credit while maintaining safety and soundness.
The standard should never be "make bad loans."
It should be: Have you exhausted the responsible tools available to make more good loans?
 10. Small-business lending must remain a meaningful measure of performance. Access to
affordable small-business capital remains uneven. That has consequences beyond individual
entrepreneurs. Small businesses create jobs, stabilize commercial corridors and create household
and community wealth.

The major-product-line approach should not allow small-business lending to escape meaningful
scrutiny simply because an institution has chosen not to make it a significant part of its business.

Recommendation: Preserve meaningful evaluation of small-business lending where there are

Maintain sufficient data and recordkeeping to understand where capital is flowing, what types
and sizes of businesses are being served and where meaningful gaps remain. And encourage
banks to partner with CDFIs and other responsible community lenders when conventional
economics make smaller transactions difficult.

proposal continues to recognize affordable housing as a core community development activity

households in high-cost areas. That is an important conversation. Housing affordability is no
longer a challenge confined to the lowest-income households. At the same time, we cannot
broaden eligibility in a way that unintentionally diverts resources from communities with the
greatest need.

We need more affordable rental housing.
We need to preserve naturally occurring affordable housing.
We need home repair.
We need neighborhood stabilization.
And we need responsible pathways to homeownership.

Recommendation: Maintain a strong focus on LMI households while allowing carefully defined
consideration of middle-income housing needs in demonstrably high-cost markets. CRA should
encourage banks to use multiple tools--senior debt, subordinate capital, guarantees, credit
enhancements, CDFI partnerships and responsible mortgage products--to expand both
affordable rental housing and sustainable homeownership.

work. I appreciate the proposal's attempt to provide greater clarity around activities benefiting
multiple assessment areas and regional activities. CDFIs do not always operate according to
bank assessment-area boundaries. Affordable-housing funds, small-business programs and

the life of the plan.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Michigan Community Capital (MCC), and its affiliate, Magnet Lending Corporation (MLC) submit these
comments on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations
issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC) (together, "the agencies") on July 31, 2026.1

For nearly fifty years, CRA has given banks a durable reason to provide loans, investments, grants, and
services in communities that have historically lacked access to capital. We appreciate the agencies' efforts to
update the CRA rules, and we support several provisions that could make the framework work better.
However, we have serious concerns about three central issues: the proposal would create different CRA
rules for different banks because the Federal Reserve did not join it; it would raise the asset thresholds
that determine how banks are evaluated; and it would restrict community development grants. We are
also concerned about several other provisions that, taken together, could further weaken banks' incentives to
invest in the communities that need it most.

Given the size and scope of the proposal, we also ask the agencies to extend the comment period by at
least 60 days and, before finalizing any changes, to analyze and publish for public comment the likely effects
on low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities.

WHO WE ARE
Michigan Community Capital is a 501(c)3 nonprofit, certified Community Development Entity (CDE); and
Magnet Lending Corporation, an affiliate of MCC, is a certified Community Development Financial Institution

1Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52114 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 (CDFI). Our mission is to promote community and economic development, create wealth and job
opportunities, and bring private and public capital to Michigan communities. We focus on expanding
economic mobility for LMI Michigan residents and on community development through impactful real estate
lending, real estate development and New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) financing. Statewide -- in rural and
urban communities -- we invest in job-creating manufacturing businesses, for-sale and rental housing,
community revitalizing mixed-use developments, and projects that expand access to healthy food from retail
grocery stories to agricultural farms.

Banks are critical partners in our CDE and CDFI work. Our bank partners provide direct loans, bonds,
and equity and Equity Equivalent Investments (EQ2s). Since 2017:

 Bank partners have provided about 95% ($32.7 million) of MLC's total borrowed capital.
 MLC has provided more than $43 million in construction, bridge, and permanent loans.
 That lending has leveraged more than $152 million in additional private investment in LMI communities

 across the state.
 Bank partners have provided more than $115 million in NMTC equity, leveraging more than $1.33

 billion in private investment in Michigan communities.
 Together, this capital has supported the creation of 1,894 new LMI residential units, created and

 retained more than 8,100 jobs, and activated more than 7.5 million square feet of real estate.
These partnerships benefit banks, too. Banks rely on CDFIs like MLC to reach underserved communities,
prepare borrowers, and develop future bank customers. A perfect example is Thompson Block, a small-scale
development in Ypsilanti, Michigan. This development, led by two restaurant entrepreneurs, utilized MLC
funding to bridge historic tax credits, and it eventually utilized traditional community bank lending for
permanent loans. CRA has long given banks the incentive to build and sustain these relationships. We are
concerned that several provisions in the proposal would weaken that incentive, reduce bank engagement
with CDFIs, and ultimately reduce the amount of capital reaching the communities we serve.

Provisions of issue

1. All three banking agencies should follow the same CRA rules

For decades, the OCC, the FDIC, and the Federal Reserve have evaluated banks' CRA performance under
a generally consistent interagency framework. This proposal breaks from that practice. It was issued by only
two of the three federal banking agencies. The Federal Reserve did not join it. If finalized, the proposal would
apply to banks supervised by the OCC and the FDIC, while banks supervised by the Federal Reserve would
continue to be evaluated under different rules.

As a result, two similar banks serving the same Michigan community could face different CRA expectations
based only on their charter or their primary federal regulator. For example:

 An investment in MLC could count one way for an OCC- or FDIC-supervised bank and different way for
 a Federal Reservesupervised bank.

 A grant to a CDFI could be subject to the 15% indirect-cost cap and new documentation requirements
 from one bank partner, but not from another.

 Banks could be measured against different asset thresholds, performance tests, and lists of eligible
 activities, even when they compete in the same market.

We are concerned that this split would create confusion for banks and communities, weaken accountability,
and invite regulatory arbitrage, where a bank chooses its charter or regulator based on which CRA rules are
easier to meet. The agencies say the central goal of this rulemaking is greater clarity, predictability, and

 Page 2
 reduced burden. A fragmented system works against every one of those goals. Regulatory simplification
should not come at the cost of regulatory consistency.

This matters to CDFIs like MLC because we work with many bank partners at once, and they are supervised
by different federal regulators. MLC's partners include large national banks supervised by the OCC, such as
Huntington and U.S. Bank, as well as banks supervised by the Federal Reserve, such as Independent Bank,
a mid-size regional bank based in Grand Rapids, and Chelsea State Bank, a small community bank. Under
the proposal, U.S. Bank would follow the new OCC and FDIC rules, while Independent Bank and Chelsea
State Bank would continue under the Federal Reserve's rules. An investment, loan, or grant to MLC could
qualify for CRA credit at one partner but not another or come with different documentation requirements.
That would make it harder to bring several banks together on a single project, harder to explain to partners
what will qualify, and harder for communities to compare how banks are performing.

Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should explain how banks, CDFIs, and communities would operate
under two different CRA frameworks, identify which Michigan and national markets would have banks
evaluated under different standards, and explain why that result is consistent with CRA's purpose of
ensuring that every bank meets the credit needs of its entire community.

What we ask: The OCC and FDIC should continue working with the Federal Reserve toward one

consistent interagency CRA framework. Wherever the law allows, the agencies should keep consistent
standards, definitions, examination expectations, and performance measures, including a single
interagency illustrative list of eligible activities.

2. Raising the asset thresholds would cut community development finance

Proposal reference: Section IV.A, "Asset Thresholds"; Questions 13

What would change

The proposal would classify banks with less than $1 billion in assets as small, banks with $1 billion to $10
billion as intermediate, and only banks with more than $10 billion as large.2 As a result:

 About 800 banks that now receive a separate community development evaluation as intermediate small
 banks would become small banks and lose that evaluation.3

 417 banks now evaluated as large banks would become intermediate banks, losing the separate
 lending, investment, service tests, and many data-reporting requirements.

What it means for Michigan

In Michigan, an estimated 15, or 23.4% of the banks in the state, would no longer be required to reinvest in
local community development projects, such as affordable housing, grocery stores and mixed-use facilities.
10 of the existing 29 (34.5%) large banks in Michigan will lose their large-bank status.4 This will overall
reduce the pool of CRA dollars flowing to LMI communities in Michigan.

2Id. at 52,12023.
3NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3, 2026), https://ncrc.org/2026-
cra-rollbacks/.
4National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC), Interactive CRA Map, https://ncrc.org/cra/.

 Page 3
 The effects will be felt most in rural and smaller markets, where there are fewer banks and other sources of
capital. In these places, losing even one or two CRA-motivated bank partners can decide whether an
affordable housing project, small business, or community facility gets financed. MLC's experience is that
most projects in rural communities rely on Michigan's robust network of CDFI's and very small community
banks. Loans recently financed by those groups include food clubs, Habitat for Humanity homes, and mixed-
use community development projects. Rules related to concentration weighting for assessment areas
already diminish appetite by OCC/FDIC banks. This rule would further limit work in these communities.

What it means for our partnerships

The agencies acknowledge in the proposal that when banks become subject to a community development
test, they typically adjust their CRA programs in response. The reverse is also true: when the test goes
away, much of the incentive goes with it. The result would be fewer CRA-motivated dollars overall, and more
organizations competing for them. Under less pressure, banks will reasonably look for the simplest way to
meet their remaining obligations. That favors large, routine transactions over the smaller, more complex, and
more patient financing that CDFIs provide and that LMI and rural communities depend on.

Earlier this year, MLC provided a construction loan to Bridgeview Housing III, located in the West Village
neighborhood of Detroit, with CRA funds borrowed from U.S. Bank. Funds provided much needed capital
improvements for two family townhome rental communities, originally LIHTC projects that were well beyond
year 15. Total investment was just over $5 million and rehabbed 22, two-bedroom and three-bedroom rental
units. If CRA thresholds are reduced and the CRA dollars shrink, projects like Bridgeview Housing III won't
be able to compete with less complicated transactions in the same census tract. CDFIs depend on regional
and community banks for patient loans, deposits, investments, lines of credit, and grants that let us reach
borrowers and projects conventional lenders cannot serve efficiently.

What it means for tax credit investments

The change would also undercut Congress's recent, bipartisan work to expand the Low-Income Housing Tax
Credit (LIHTC) and make the New Markets Tax Credit permanent. Today, large banks' investments,
including LIHTC and NMTC equity and Equity Equivalent Investments (EQ2s) in CDFIs are evaluated under
a separate investment test that carries 25% of their CRA rating. Large banks reclassified as intermediate
would lose that dedicated incentive, reducing demand for the patient, equity-like capital these programs
depend on. Tax credit equity and CDFI lending work together in the same projects: when tax credit
investment weakens, financing gaps grow, and fewer projects move forward.

MCC has seen this firsthand. Currently classified large, OCC regulated banks have provided more than $115
million in NMTC equity in MCC's transactions. MCC provided $3 million NMTC allocation to the Habitat for
Humanity of Kent County project that is creating 27 affordable for-sale homes. Project financing was
provided by Chase, Mercantile Bank, IFF, and with CRA dollars borrowed from Huntington. Leveraging
NMTC to development more for-sale housing has been identified as a top priority of the Trump
Administration and reducing CRA bank obligations is going to make achieving those goals even harder.

The "1995 proportionality" rationale does not hold up

The agencies justify the change as restoring the balance of bank sizes that existed in 1995. But the current
thresholds are already adjusted every year for inflation (CPI-W), so they are not stuck at 1995 levels. And
the agencies apply the 1995 comparison selectively:

 Page 4
  For the small-bank threshold, they point to the share of banks: about 80% of banks would be small, as in
 1995.

 By that same measure, about 20% of banks were large in 1995. Under the proposal, only a little over 2%
 would be.

 For the large-bank threshold, the agencies switch measures and point to the share of industry assets:
 large banks would hold about 85% of assets, as in 1995.

Matching a 1995 distribution by either measure does not show that the new categories fit today's banking
system. The industry has consolidated dramatically, and a bank with several billion dollars in assets today
has far more lending, investment, data, and operational capacity than a similarly classified bank three
decades ago. More importantly, the agencies have not explained how higher thresholds would better serve
CRA's purpose: meeting the credit needs of LMI communities.

What we ask: Keep the current asset thresholds and reject all alternatives, including the even higher

thresholds raised in Question 1.

3. Grant restrictions would undercut the work grants make possible

Proposal reference: Section IV.C, "Community Development Activities CD Grants"; Questions 911

The proposal would:

 Require a qualifying grant to be used directly by the recipient for a program, project, or initiative whose
 primary purpose is community development.

 For large banks, cap the recipient's indirect administrative costs at 15%.5
 Require large banks to collect written commitments on the use of funds, indirect-cost attestations, IRS

 Form 990s, and operating and program budgets from grant recipients.
The agencies also ask, in Question 10, whether grants and donations should lose CRA consideration
entirely. We strongly oppose all these changes.

We share the goal of making sure CRA-motivated grants truly benefit communities. But these rules
misunderstand how community development finance works. For a CDFI, staffing, underwriting, loan
servicing, compliance, technology, risk management, data systems, financial management, technical
assistance, and product development are not overhead to be minimized. They are the infrastructure that
makes community development lending possible.

MLC has used grants to support additional staff, to adopt technology that improves compliance reporting for
borrowers, and to reduce the cost of borrowing by blending grant funds with borrowed bank capital, allowing
us to offer more attractive loan interest rates and longer terms.

A fixed 15% cap on indirect costs is not a sound measure of community impact. Costs vary with an
organization's size, geography, products, regulatory obligations, technical assistance model, and the people
it serves. The cap would hit hardest CDFIs similarly situated to MLC:

 Small and emerging CDFIs
 Organizations that provide intensive technical assistance to borrowers
 CDFIs developing new products or entering underserved markets

5Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,129 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).

 Page 5
  Organizations investing in needed technology, compliance, data, and risk management

What we ask: Keep CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-building grants, as under the

current rules. CRA should give banks the flexibility to provide the kind of support that best meets community
needs, rather than adding unnecessary compliance burdens.

4. Other provisions that could further weaken community development

Several additional provisions could, especially in combination with the higher thresholds, further reduce
banks' incentives to invest in community development.

Keep real consequences for weak community development performance

Proposal reference: Section IV.B, "Performance Tests Intermediate Bank Ratings"

Today, an intermediate small bank generally must earn at least a Satisfactory rating on both its lending test
and its community development test to receive an overall Satisfactory rating. The proposal would still require
Satisfactory lending but would let strong lending make up for weak community development performance.

Because the new thresholds would move hundreds of large banks into the intermediate category, this
change matters even more. If weak community development performance no longer blocks a Satisfactory
rating, banks will have less reason to lend to and invest in CDFIs, make grants, or pursue other community
development. MLC has seen firsthand how the ability to purchase investment-grade rated bonds and
profitable tax credits have undermined the real risk-taking behavior that many communities need. In the case
of one institution, a single large community center project was funded with federal tax credits, and the bank
used one economic investment to avoid or avert additional loans and investments in the mid-Michigan
market for the full three years of its assessment cycle. That is an unreasonable result and avoids the
substance of the rule. Elements of the proposed rule would likely incentivize this behavior.

What we ask: Keep the requirement that intermediate banks show at least Satisfactory community

development performance to receive an overall Satisfactory rating.

5. Don't define "complexity" only by its link to a loan

Proposal reference: Section IV.C, "Qualitative Factors"; Questions 1217

The proposal would judge whether a community development investment, grant, or service is "complex"
primarily by whether it is part of a larger financing deal involving a loan. We oppose this narrow, lending-
centered definition. Investments in CDFIs can be complex on their own because they involve specialized
expertise, layered capital, subordinate positions, public subsidies, risk sharing, guarantees, tax-credit
structures, or patient repayment terms. We also oppose requiring investments or services to be complex
(Question 14), or treating complexity as automatically more valuable than innovation, flexibility, or impact
(Question 15). As an example, we recently provided a long-term bridge loan secured by a tax increment
financing stream to a new single-family housing development in Port Huron, Michigan. While the project was
relatively simple, the developer could not identify a lender willing to accept the long-term risk tied to the
variable tax payments. The analysis was complex not because of the loan itself but because of the collateral
and repayment variability and the long duration of the timeline. Under the new guidelines, this project would
not be considered complex.

What we ask: Evaluate complexity, innovation, flexibility, impact, and responsiveness based on the

activity itself and the value it brings to the community, not on whether it is tied to a loan.

 Page 6
 6. Don't let routine retail lending substitute for community development
 lending

Proposal reference: Section IV.B, "Retail Lending Product Lines," Questions 47; Section IV.C, "CD Loans"

The proposal would evaluate retail lending only in a bank's major product lines. A loan in a product line that
is not evaluated could instead count as a community development loan if it meets the community
development definition. We agree that truly community-development-oriented loans should not lose CRA
credit just because their product line is not reviewed. But this creates a risk that ordinary small-business,
small-farm, or other retail lending, which banks would do anyway, could stand in for the specialized
community development lending that depends on CRA incentives.

What we ask: Require a real community development connection and make sure banks cannot meet

community development expectations through business they would do in the ordinary course. Banks must
connect a community development loan to a demonstrated community need.

7. Put strong guardrails on strategic plans

Proposal reference: Section IV.F, "Strategic Plan"; Questions 3853

We support making strategic plans clearer and their goals measurable. But because strategic plans let
banks set their own CRA performance standards, strong guardrails are needed so banks cannot sidestep
the expectations applied to similar institutions.

What we ask: Require strategic-plan goals to be:

 Responsive to documented community needs
 Rigorous enough to match the performance expected under the standard CRA tests
 Transparent and measurable
 Subject to meaningful public input
 Evaluated against clear standards for whether they meet assessment-area credit needs
We especially urge the agencies to set strong standards in response to Question 53, which asks when
measurable goals should be considered inadequate.

8. Allow flexibility outside assessment areas only after banks serve their own

Proposal reference: Section IV.E, "CD Activities Outside Assessment Areas"; proposed __.13(e); Question
34

We support the goal of enabling CRA-motivated capital to reach places with significant unmet needs outside
of a bank's assessment areas, including rural communities, Indian Country, and other "CRA deserts." Most
of Michigan's upper peninsula and northern lower peninsula suffer from having very few if any institutions
that demonstrate any level of concentration which might drive CRA assessment. In areas like Grayling, there
are branches of federally regulated banks, but because deposit concentrations are higher in Detroit and
Grand Rapids, banks often ignore areas like Grayling once they "win" in the higher concentration areas. This
leaves little incentive for banks to focus on areas where they indeed have a high concentration of deposits
for the area but generally smaller overall levels when compared to major metros in the State.

But this flexibility should add to, not replace, banks' community development obligations in their own
assessment areas, and it should only become available after a bank has done meaningful work there. The

 Page 7
 standard proposed under Option 1 sets that bar too low. A large bank could get credit outside its assessment
areas once it reaches 0.625% of allocated Tier 1 capital in community development loans and 0.625% in
community development investments and grants. The agencies themselves say these levels generally reflect
the minimum needed to avoid a "Needs to Improve" rating, not satisfactory performance.

The gap between that benchmark and what banks do today is large. The National Community Reinvestment
Coalition (NCRC) analyzed all 69 OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks among the 100 largest banks by
assets:6

 These banks currently provide about $102 billion a year in community development loans and
 investments inside their assessment areas.

 If each did only enough to meet the 0.625% thresholds, that would fall to about $14.9 billion, a drop of
 about $87.1 billion, or 85%.

 Median community development lending is 6.8% of Tier 1 capital, and median qualified investments are
 3.6%, both far above 0.625%.

What we ask: Set the standard at satisfactory community development performance, not the minimum

to avoid a failing rating, and consider both the amount of activity and how well it responds to community
needs. Any "substantially met" exception should be narrow and limited to cases where a documented lack of
opportunities or other performance-context factors explains the shortfall. It should not let weak performance
in one assessment area be offset by activity elsewhere.

Allocate multi-area investments where the capital actually goes

Proposal reference: Section IV.E, "CD Activities in Assessment Areas, Assessment Area Allocation,
Assigning Assessment Area Weights"

We support more flexibility in allocating community development activities that serve several assessment
areas. This would better reflect statewide and regional CDFIs, whose impact is not captured by the location
of their headquarters. For example, MLC is headquartered in Lansing, Michigan but 90% of our financing has
been in other markets urban and rural throughout the state. Assigning a bank's entire investment to our
headquarters would misrepresent the communities that actually benefit.

Provisions we support

1. Give credit for community development loans from prior periods

Proposal reference: Section IV.C, "CD Loans"; Question 8

We strongly support giving CRA credit for qualifying community development loans still outstanding from
earlier evaluation periods, as is already done for investments. Community development borrowers often
need long-term, patient financing. CRA should encourage banks to structure loans around community needs,
not exam cycles.

What we ask: In response to Question 8, use evaluation-period-based consideration. It better

recognizes patient, long-term financing, better reflects the capital committed across the exam period than an
annual snapshot and treats loans and investments the same way. The agencies should base consideration

6NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 85% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk (Sept. 10, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-development-activity-at-risk/.

 Page 8
 on the average outstanding balance or otherwise account for both the amount and duration of the
outstanding exposure and should treat repeated renewals of substantially the same loan as a single
exposure.

2. Create an illustrative list and a way to confirm eligibility in advance

Proposal reference: Section IV.E, "Illustrative List" and "Confirmation of CD Activity Eligibility"; Questions
3233

We strongly support a public, non-exhaustive list of eligible community development activities and a formal
process for confirming eligibility in advance. Ideally, the OCC, FDIC, and Federal Reserve would share one
interagency list.

What we ask: In response to Questions 3233:

 Require banks to keep eligibility determinations for as long as the activity stays on their balance sheet.
 Allow no more than a 30-day extension beyond the proposed 90-day review period.
 Give each determination a clear written rationale and, where appropriate, name the facts or conditions it

 depends on.
 Provide a reconsideration process where banks or community partners can submit more information,

 and a way for community members to raise concerns about activities already found eligible.
 Publish nonconfidential or anonymized determinations and their reasoning, so treatment is transparent

 and consistent.
 Keep determinations subject to review during CRA exams if the activity ends up being carried out

 differently than described.

Conclusion

CRA has built a strong partnership among banks, CDFIs, and the communities we serve. We appreciate the
agencies' work to make the rules clearer and more flexible. But modernization should put more responsible
capital into communities with unmet credit needs, as the CRA statute intended, not less.

We therefore urge the OCC and FDIC to:
 Work with the Federal Reserve toward one consistent interagency CRA framework.
 Withdraw the proposed increase in asset thresholds.
 Withdraw the restrictions on community development grants, including the 15% indirect-cost cap.
 Keep the requirement that intermediate banks show Satisfactory community development performance.
 Don't allow a Satisfactory rating in one category to compensate for poor performance in another.
 Evaluate complexity and impact based on the activity itself, not its link to a loan.
 Prevent routine retail lending from substituting for community development lending.
 Don't allow for the purchase of investment grade rated bonds on the open market to be considered

 responsive to a community's needs.
 Set strong guardrails for strategic plans.
 Allow credit outside assessment areas only after satisfactory performance inside them.
 Adopt the proposed credit for prior-period loans and the illustrative list and confirmation process, with the

To Whom It May Concern,

On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies")
promulgated a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the
regulations of the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).

CRA has helped create a durable incentive for banks to provide loans, investments,
grants, and services in communities that have historically lacked access to capital.
We appreciate the agencies' efforts to reform the CRA regulations, and we support
some of the proposals that could improve the CRA framework and increase access to
responsible capital in underserved communities.

However, we are concerned about increases in the asset thresholds that determine
how banks are evaluated under CRA and the restrictions on operating grants. We also
have concerns with several interacting provisions that could further weaken
community development incentives that will undoubtedly impair the flow of much
needed capital in the most underserved communities.

Craft3 is a nonprofit Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) located in
Oregon and Washington. Through commercial and consumer loans, we serve low-to-
moderate income and low-wealth borrowers, and communities that lack sufficient
access to mainstream capital, including rural and tribal communities. CDFIs are an
important part of the U.S. financial system, providing access to capital to areas often
underserved by the traditional financial sector. Banks are critical partners in our
work, providing loans, investments, and grants that capitalize loans and fund
programs important to a thriving regional economy. These include business services
and access to capital to rural and urban residents, small businesses that provide
goods and services and create jobs, and tribes and nonprofits that provide essential
services to struggling families.

CDFI-bank partnerships are mutually reinforcing. In addition to providing critical
capital and resources to CDFIs, banks rely on CDFIs to reach underserved
communities, develop borrowers, and cultivate future bank customers. The CRA has
long helped create the incentives for banks to build and sustain these relationships,
strengthening the broader community development ecosystem. We are therefore
concerned that several provisions in the proposal could weaken these incentives,
reducing bank engagement with CDFIs and ultimately the flow of capital to the
communities we serve.

 1
 Raised Asset Thresholds Jeopardize Community Development Finance: Section IV.A,
"Asset Thresholds"

One of the most consequential proposed changes is to raise the asset-threshold. By
the agencies' own estimates, the proposal would move 800 banks from intermediate-
small to small, meaning they are no longer subject to the Community Development
(CD) test. More than 75% of all banks could be exempt due to this proposed change.
Another approximately 400 banks that are currently evaluated as large banks would
become intermediate banks, losing the separate large-bank lending, investment, and
service tests and many associated data-reporting requirements.

In Oregon and Washington, it is estimated that out of the 31 banks with the large or
intermediate designations under current rules, 15 would be moved to small, meaning
almost 50% of banks in the state would be exempt from the Community
Development test under the proposed rules. Weakening CRA incentives in this way
means less investment in underserved areas not just across Oregon and Washington,
but nationwide. The consequences are especially significant in rural and smaller
markets, where there are fewer financial institutions and fewer alternative sources of
capital. In these communities, the loss of even one or two CRA-motivated bank
partners can materially affect whether projects are financed. For communities with
fewer financial institutions and fewer sources of private capital to begin with, losing
even a handful of CRA-motivated lenders and investors could have an outsized effect
on whether affordable housing, small businesses, and community facilities get
financed.

Banks moving down asset sizes and losing incentives for community development
activities would have a direct impact on our partnerships. We estimate that $7.7
million of our debt would be at risk from our bank funders that are currently
considered large or intermediate that would transition into lower asset categories.
This represents 22% of our total bank funding.

Recommendation

We urge the agencies to retain the current thresholds and reject all alternatives
offered (including the substantially higher thresholds raised for consideration in
Question 1). The current thresholds are already annually indexed to CPI-W, so they
are not beholden to 1995 asset levels. Moreover, the justification of "restoring
proportionality to 1995" that the agencies use in the proposal does not adequately
explain why raising asset thresholds better serve the statutory intent of the CRA--
which is to ensure that credit needs of LMI communities are met. For the small bank
threshold, the proportionality metric rests on the distribution of the number of banks
such that nearly 80% of all banks would be considered small, similar to what it was
in 1995. While that's true, by the same logic, nearly 20% of banks in 1995 were
considered large whereas under the proposed large bank threshold, only a little over
2% of all banks would be considered large. Instead, the agencies selectively use total
banking industry share to justify the large bank threshold saying large banks would
under this proposal, and similar to 1995, cover about 85% of all total bank industry's
assets. Matching a 1995 distribution through either method does not necessarily
demonstrate that the resulting categories are appropriate for the modern banking
system. The industry has consolidated dramatically and bank business models and
geographic reach have changed. Banks with several billion dollars in assets today may
have substantially greater lending, investment, data, and operational capacity than

 2
 institutions that were treated as small or intermediate three decades ago. The fact
that assets happen to sit above a chosen threshold does not by itself establish that
banks below that threshold should lose the separate investment/service tests or
associated data requirements.

Restrictions on Community Development Grants: Section IV.C, "Community
Development Activities -- CD Grants"

We strongly oppose the proposed restrictions on community development (CD) grants
which: 1) requires a qualifying CD grant to be directly used by the recipient for a
program, project, or initiative with a primary purpose of community development; 2)
for large banks, caps grant recipient's indirect administrative costs to 15%; 3) requires
that large banks obtain documentation from grant recipients including written
commitments regarding use of funds, indirect-cost attestations, IRS Form 990s, and
operating and program budgets. We also strongly oppose the alternative
contemplated in Question 10 to eliminate grants and donations from CRA
consideration entirely.

While we share the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants
meaningfully benefit communities, these requirements would restrict many forms of
effective grantmaking and misunderstand the role that flexible operating support
plays in community development finance. For CDFIs, staffing, underwriting, servicing,
compliance, technology, risk management, data systems, financial management,
technical assistance, and product development are not ancillary to community
development. They are the infrastructure that makes community development
lending possible.

Craft3 has received over $10 million in grants from banking partners over the last five
years, nearly 10% in the form of general operating grants, which has given us the
flexibility and discretion to support capacity building to meet our community
development mission. These awards have supported the creation of new positions,
development of new financing products, evaluation of programs to improve them and
deliver greater impact in underserved communities, and delivery of critical technical
assistance to small businesses, increasing capital delivery and borrower success.

Moreover, we strongly oppose using a fixed 15% indirect-cost limit as a condition of
CRA eligibility. An organization's administrative-cost percentage is not an appropriate
proxy for community impact. Costs vary depending on an organization's size,
geography, product mix, regulatory obligations, technical-assistance model, and
populations served. The cap could disproportionately affect small and emerging
CDFIs, rural CDFIs, CDFIs making small-dollar loans, organizations providing intensive
borrower technical assistance, CDFIs developing new products or entering
underserved markets and organizations making necessary investments in technology,
compliance, data, and risk management.

Recommendation

The agencies should preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-
building grants as currently is in place under the 1995 framework. CRA should
encourage flexibility for banks to provide the form of support that best responds to
the identified community needs instead of imposing undue compliance burdens.

In closing, CRA has helped create a powerful partnership among banks, CDFIs, and
the communities we serve. We appreciate the agencies' efforts to improve clarity and

 3
 flexibility. Modernization, however, should result in more responsible capital reaching
communities with unmet credit needs, as the CRA statute was intended.
We therefore urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the raised asset thresholds
proposed and to withdraw the restrictions on Community Development operating
grants.
Thank you for considering these comments and for considering the impact of the
proposed changes on the communities we serve.
Sincerely,

Elisabeth Zeller
Chief Executive Officer
Craft3

To Whom It May Concern:

I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the notice of proposed rulemaking issued by the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation on July 31, 2026, and
published in the Federal Register on August 12, 2026. As a banking professional who works at an institutio
subject to CRA examinations, I support the agencies' effort to retain continuity with the longstanding CRA
framework while improving clarity, consistency, and proportionality.

I also encourage continued coordination among the OCC, FDIC, and Board of Governors of the Federal
Reserve System. Institutions and communities benefit when materially similar activities are evaluated
under consistent standards, regardless of charter or primary federal regulator. Where the final rule or
related guidance differs across agencies, those differences should be clearly identified and explained.

The proposal makes meaningful progress in several areas, including updated asset thresholds, a clearer
process for confirming community development eligibility, greater use of digital public files, a more
workable strategic plan option, and a focus on major lending product lines. The following
recommendations are intended to preserve those benefits while reducing uncertainty and avoiding
unintended constraints on activities that meet demonstrated community needs.

1. Provide durable, interagency clarity regarding CRA-eligible activities

I support codifying a publicly available, non-exhaustive illustrative list of qualifying and nonqualifying
community development activities and establishing an optional confirmation process. These measures
directly address one of the most persistent CRA challenges: banks often cannot determine in advance
whether a responsive activity will receive consideration, and similar activities may be treated differently
across examinations.

The final rule should require the agencies to coordinate their illustrative lists to the greatest extent
permitted, publish the reasoning supporting additions and removals, and update the lists on a regular and
predictable schedule. The lists should remain expressly non-exhaustive so that banks are not
discouraged from pursuing novel or locally responsive activities. The confirmation process should include
a clear intake standard, a defined response period, and reasonable reliance protection when a bank
proceeds in good faith based on an agency determination.

2. Retain proportional asset thresholds and provide orderly transitions

I support increasing the small bank threshold to $1 billion and establishing an intermediate bank category
from $1 billion through $10 billion. I also support exempting banks with $10 billion or less in assets from
the large-bank data collection, maintenance, and reporting requirements. These changes better align
supervisory expectations with institutional capacity and allow community and regional banks to direct
resources toward lending and community development rather than data processes that may add limited
evaluative value.
 The final rule should include clear transition provisions for institutions that cross an asset threshold
because of organic growth, a merger, acquisition, or temporary balance-sheet conditions. A reasonable
transition period, coupled with advance notice of newly applicable requirements, would promote orderly
implementation and prevent abrupt changes in examination treatment. The agencies should also explain
how assets will be calculated and how annual inflation adjustments, if any, will operate.

3. Adopt a major product line approach that reflects local credit needs

I support focusing retail lending evaluations on major product lines because examinations should reflect
a bank's actual business model rather than compel institutions to manage immaterial product lines
primarily for CRA purposes. Of the two approaches described in the proposal, the assessment-area-level
approach provides greater ability to recognize products that are especially important in a particular
community, even if they are not among the bank's largest products at the institution level.

Whichever approach is adopted, the final rule should establish objective selection criteria, disclose the
selected product lines early in the examination process, and avoid evaluating product lines with
insufficient volume for meaningful analysis. The agencies should also permit a bank to provide
documented evidence that a product line is material to a particular assessment area because of identified
credit needs, market conditions, or the bank's capacity and strategy.

4. Preserve meaningful consideration of delivery channels and credit access

The proposal appropriately refocuses the retail service analysis on credit services rather than deposit
services. At the same time, the method by which consumers and small businesses access credit has
changed substantially. Branches remain important, but online and mobile applications, remote
assistance, call centers, loan production offices, and community partnerships may materially expand
access to credit, particularly for customers who face transportation, scheduling, or geographic barriers.

The final rule and examination procedures should explain how examiners will evaluate the availability,
affordability, accessibility, and effectiveness of credit delivery channels. Digital delivery should not
automatically receive positive consideration merely because it exists, nor should branch delivery
automatically receive greater weight. The analysis should focus on evidence that a channel helps meet
identified credit needs of the bank's assessment area, including the needs of low- and moderate-income
individuals and communities.

5. Reconsider the proposed restrictions on community development grants

I support the objective of ensuring that grants and donations provide a direct and demonstrable
community development benefit. However, the proposed 15 percent indirect-cost limitation for recipients
of grants from large banks could unintentionally exclude effective nonprofit organizations whose
legitimate operating costs exceed that threshold. Smaller organizations and organizations serving rural
or deeply underserved communities may have limited scale yet may be uniquely positioned to deliver
essential services.

The final rule should avoid a rigid, all-or-nothing eligibility standard based solely on an organization's
indirect-cost rate. A more workable approach would permit consideration based on the portion of funds
demonstrably devoted to a qualifying program, allowing an exception where the bank documents the
recipient's effectiveness and the absence of a reasonable alternative, or provide a safe harbor using a
recognized grant-specific cost methodology. The agencies should also clarify how shared costs, fiscal
sponsors, pass-through entities, multiyear grants, in-kind contributions, and grants supporting
organizational capacity will be treated.

Documentation expectations should be proportionate and should not require a bank to perform a quasi-
audit of a nonprofit recipient. Standard attestations and a uniform optional information template would
improve consistency without discouraging partnerships or imposing costs that reduce the funds available
for community work.

I support maintaining a strong expectation that banks meet needs within their assessment areas. Once a
bank has demonstrated satisfactory responsiveness to those needs, however, the rule should permit
appropriate consideration of community development activities outside assessment areas, especially in
rural areas, Native areas, persistent-poverty areas, disaster areas, and other places with limited access
to capital.

The phrase used to determine when local needs have been adequately or substantially met should be
defined through objective factors and examples. The final rule should also explain how statewide,
multistate metropolitan statistical area, regional, and bank-level activities will be allocated and considered.
Greater clarity would encourage banks to support high-need activities without creating uncertainty about
whether those activities will receive CRA consideration.

7. Make the strategic plan option a genuinely practical alternative

I support the proposed prefiling consultation process, clearer standards for measurable goals, written
notice when a plan is technically complete, a defined process for denial and resubmission, and greater
flexibility to amend plans after material changes. These changes could make strategic plans useful for
institutions whose business models are not appropriately evaluated under standard tests.

To make this option workable, the agencies should provide model plan elements, examples of acceptable
performance measures and levels, and transparent standards for determining whether goals are
substantially met. Prefiling feedback should be timely and sufficiently substantive to identify material
concerns without implying preapproval. Where an amendment is narrow or results from circumstances
outside the bank's control, the agencies should not require the bank to repeat the entire public
participation and approval process.

8. Promote examination consistency, transparency, and reasonable implementation

Even well-designed rules can produce uncertainty if examination procedures, examiner training, and
performance evaluations are not aligned. The agencies should issue coordinated examination procedures
and training before the final rule becomes applicable. Banks should receive clear notice of the data,
product lines, assessment areas, and analytical standards that will be used in an examination, along with
a meaningful opportunity to correct factual errors and provide performance context.

The final rule should provide an implementation period sufficient for banks to revise policies, systems,
community development documentation, public files, strategic plans, and training. The agencies should
also conduct periodic reviews of examination outcomes to identify material differences among regions,
agencies, and institution types, and should publish clarifying guidance when recurring inconsistencies are
identified.

Conclusion

The proposal offers a constructive opportunity to improve CRA administration while preserving the
statute's essential focus on meeting community credit needs consistent with safe and sound banking. I
respectfully encourage the agencies to finalize changes that are clear, coordinated, proportionate, and
flexible enough to recognize differences among banks and communities. In particular, the final framework
should provide reliable advance guidance, preserve incentives for responsive community development,
recognize effective credit delivery channels, and minimize documentation that does not materially
improve the evaluation of CRA performance.

Thank you for considering these comments and for the agencies' continued efforts to improve the clarity,
transparency, and effectiveness of the Community Reinvestment Act framework.

Respectfully submitted,

Renee Larrimore

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0096_09000064b9625366.pdf:
My name is Kent M Franzen VP of Compliance for Henderson State Bank. We are a
small community Bank with thirteen locations across Nebraska and have recently grown
past the $500 million asset mark. My own personal experience is that I have worked for
several community Banks in Nebraska since beginning my Banking career in 1985. I
have experience in lending, compliance, operations as well as IT.

 Over my career I have observed that the number of total bank charters in Nebraska
has fallen dramatically from over 300 in 1985 to under 150 at present. Part of this is
market driven, in that as agriculture has consolidated into fewer hands with larger
financial needs Banks have also needed to do the same to service these customers.
However, part of the Bank charter consolidation is driven by the burden of Government
Regulation of which the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) is a part.

 Over the years I have come to appreciate that most regulation was initiated to
manage a certain problem or promote a goal. In my opinion the CRA was originated to
ensure that deposits sourced in a Banks geographic trade area were loaned out
primarily within this same geographic area. Overall, this is a philosophy we agree with.
However, in my personal opinion politics has gradually transformed the CRA into a
mechanism that forces funds to flow towards social programs that have little to no
economic value to the American Society as a whole by control over the donations and
subsidization of lending that political agitators. I will attempt to identify the portions of
the regulation proposal in italics and follow with the comment Henderson State Bank
desires to make in regard to the Small Bank directives in the proposal.

Asset Thresholds: The proposed rule would increase the asset threshold of a small
bank to below $1 billion (up from less than $412 million), or alternatively, to $850 million
or below in alignment with the Small Business Administration ("SBA") standard for
commercial banks (to be automatically adjusted when the SBA size threshold changes);
The small bank threshold would continue to be adjusted annually based on changes in
the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers.

Henderson State Bank (HSB) is extremely glad to see the regulators adjusting these
asset size-based regulations in such a fashion. We support the proposed adjustment to
the $1 Billion asset level for small banks and find the periodic inflation adjustment of this
threshold a vital provision for the future.

Lending Test:
 The Proposed Rule reflects an increased focus on lending activities consistent with the
requirements of the CRA. This change reflects the agencies' view that a community's
credit needs are most directly met through activities that involve lending.

Under the small bank lending test, the agencies would consider only a bank's major
product line(s) when assessing its retail lending. The agencies propose two potential
options for determining a bank's major product lines. Under one option, the agencies
would use a quantitative, bank-level approach to evaluate a bank's retail lending in two
of the four retail lending product lines, and those would be considered the major product
lines. The other option would use an assessment-area-level approach that qualitatively
and quantitatively determines major product lines, similar to the current methodology for
small and intermediate small banks. Under either approach, the agencies would
consider consumer lending to be a major product line only if it constitutes a majority of
the bank's retail lending by both dollar amount and loan count, or at the bank's option.

The Proposed Rule would codify that 30 loans are generally sufficient for a meaningful
lending-performance assessment but permit the agencies to consider fewer loans
where a smaller sample can still support a meaningful assessment. If loan data are
insufficient for a meaningful assessment, the agencies would rely on other lending
criteria that can be meaningfully assessed or on applicable performance-context factors.

In our opinion as long as a small Bank shows that the majority of its lending is done
inside its designated trade area that should be sufficient to satisfy the CRA. The minutia
of looking at consumer lending versus commercial loans or any other parsing of the
data diverts the overall focus from what the CRA is intended to do, and that is keeping
the deposits supplied by the residents of a trade area at work within that same trade
area. Please keep this analysis simple and direct in the regulation.

Service Test:

This change would exclude deposit services and the distribution and availability of an
institution's retail banking facilities, which are currently considered retail banking
services.

HSB supports removing deposit services from the CRA evaluations. It is our experience
that community Banks AKA small banks under the CRA, will need more flexibility to
attract deposits, such as so-called brokered deposits, from outside our trade area for
lending within our trade area, and this change would be a good step in this direction.

Community Development Activities:

Henderson State Bank in regard to the proposed changes to the Community
Development Activities requests that donations made to political subdivisions, such as
school districts or rural fire districts be recognized fully under the CRA without further
 need for any analysis or complicated record keeping. Overall HSB finds these
community development activity rules the most burdensome of the proposed CRA
changes. We encourage the agencies to do all they can to promote CRA credit to
intuitions without the penalty of busy work accounting.

Strategic Plan:

HSB comments on the small bank CRA strategic plan process are that we welcome the
proposed changes to make the process less burdensome. At the risk of "looking a gift
horse in the mouth" we also ask for any further changes that the agencies can make to
ensure this mandate is structured to be as simple as possible for small community
banks. HSB would like to point out that every day we are working to document and
satisfy a regulation requirement such as this strategic planning, is a day we are not
working with and for our clients. We ask that this principle be a major consideration of
those writing this final regulation.

Public File and Notice Requirements:

As I said, my personal banking experience began in 1985. Excluding requests by
examination staff, I have been asked for the Bank's CRA public file precisely two times
over more than 4 decades. Both of those requests were from other Banker's, looking to
oppose an application to establish a new branch location by our Bank. With awareness
that quarterly call reports, with over eighty pages of detail each, are available online
from the FFIEC, on any Bank, the public file does not seem to be of important use to the
citizenry. If regulators must retain this requirement to satisfy law, then please keep the
burden of meeting this requirement to the absolute statutory minimum, especially for
small Banks. We welcome the ability to retain the public file electronically as this is a
way we can provide the information at any HSB location within a few minutes of a
request. So, if this public file information is not highly sought after, what is the purpose
of the public file? Does the public file exist solely to be wielded as a cudgel upon the
Banks by political opportunists looking to force funding of their personal whims by a
privately held Bank?

Point not evident in the request:

HSB would like to bring up one issue in regard to CRA not directly addressed in the
proposed regulation and that is the effect that the internet, internet banking, email,
electronic transactions, electronic signatures, and mobile device deposits are having on
the concept of an identified trade area (AKA Community) for a Bank. At some point in
the not-too-distant future our collective definition of community as a concept in CRA will
 need to adapt to our evolving society. When I joined Henderson state Bank in 2015 we
had five locations in four Nebraska towns. Today we have thirteen locations in twelve
Nebraska towns, literally stretching from the Colorado border to the Iowa border. HSB
has several clients that began their relationship with us as residents of our trade area
but are now residing internationally or in other states, obviously outside our designated
trade area. We have been able to continue to serve them using the technology
mentioned. However, retaining these relationships actually works against us in our CRA
evaluation as these customers are now "out of our trade area." My point is to ask
Regulators and or Lawmakers to ponder how the CRA regulation and/or underlying
legal definitions should be adjusted into the future to take customer relationships like
these into account. If this is not done, the CRA will become a choke collar on the
community reinvestment growth it was intended to foster.

Conclusion:

Henderson State bank agrees wholeheartedly with the general goal of the Community
Reinvestment Act, that the deposits gathered within a community should be used to the
advantage of that community. The clich "A rising tide lifts all boats" comes to mind.
However, we believe that the proof of this concept for a small community Bank should
be measured by its actual lending activity. If most of its activity is being done in its
designated trade area, or even its home state, in the case of rural agricultural banks
then we believe the Bank should be given a satisfactory CRA grade without extensive
accounting tracking of unrelated charity donations or other complicated, time intensive
requirements. We should all be more concerned with meeting customers' needs than
we are with filling out forms, composing public files and writing strategic plans that no
one but regulators and political agitators ask to see or use.

Thank you for your time and attention to our concerns.

Kent M Franzen VP

Henderson State Bank
PO Box 605
Henderson NE 68371
kfranzen@hendersonstate.bank

I am the Executive Director of Clare Housing, an HIV Housing organization that has built and operates over one hundred units of deeply affordable housing for Minnesotans living with HIV, thanks to the current structure of the Community Reinvestment Act Regulations. Like most nonprofit housing providers, partnerships and lending practices with community banks lead to increased availability of housing units and development of multi-family units. However, if the changes to the Community Reinvestment Act Regulations are implemented, nonprofit housing developers, families with low incomes, and small business communities nationwide will be economically harmed. 

With the implementation of the significant changes to the CRA, Minnesota will be the second most impacted state with one hundred seven (107) banks losing requirements for community reinvestments. The changes will mean that the already barrier-laden landscape of securing investments for nonprofit housing developments will become more challenging. According to the 2026 MHP State of Housing Report, there is a gap of over 100,000 available low-income units in Minnesota, and that gap will continue to grow as wage-growth has slowed. With less housing developed and reduced access to dollars to make reinvestments in existing housing for low-income people over time, housing waitlists and competition for affordable and deeply affordable housing will increase. 

It is also critical to consider the role deeply affordable and non-profit owner developers play in our communities. Non-profit developers are able to make units affordable because they are not built to maximize profit, meaning we can provide fair-market rent. Every single person in our community is better off when people are housed – but someone or some organization has to do that work. The lack of affordable housing leads directly to dangerous situations, impacts education, public safety, future job opportunities, and health. All of our social structures relate to housing. The current CRA program is unique, and if the proposed changes take effect there is no replacement program or alternative way forward.

Due to the considerations that will impact housing development, we urge the significant changes to the Community Reinvestment Act not be implemented.
