Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

I am submitting these comments in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
(OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and published in the
Federal Register on August 12, 2026, because the NPRM, as published, fails to satisfy
the legal requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act. To address these failures, the
OCC and FDIC should commit to considering the public comments already received on
the proposed rule and then to publish a new NPRM that gives the public proper notice of
the issues to be addressed by the agencies before moving to a final rule.

I am an attorney with more than 40 years of experience in Federal administrative law
with most of that time spent in helping to develop, publish and defend proposed and final
regulations issued by the agency.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important
in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal
access to mainstream financial services. The proposed rule would substantially reduce or
narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change how regulators evaluate community
development, bank services and support for nonprofit organizations.

The purpose of an NPRM is to give the public adequate notice of an agency's planned
regulations and of the issues involved to allow members of the public to comment
effectively on the proposed rules. The CRA NPRM fails to meet that standard.

 1
 In the preamble to the NPRM, the agencies identify 55 requests for feedback and three
regulatory provisions on which the agencies identify different options. In addition, there
are at least 15 instances in which the agencies specifically request comments on various
issues. The fact that the agencies specifically request feedback and opinions on these
categories of issues would seem to indicate that the agencies recognize the importance of
these questions to implementation of the rule. The provisions of the CRA are not
independent of each other and a change in one distinct regulation is certain to impact the
effect of other proposed changes. Without knowing what choices the agencies will make
on these interrelated questions it is difficult for commenters to understand the impact of
the regulations on regulated financial institutions and the beneficiaries of the CRA and to
comment on these proposed rules.

This concern is particularly glaring in regard to the proposed changes to the standards to
be applied in determining whether a bank is large, intermediate or small. The proposal
would substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated
under the CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks,
while banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated
under the less demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than under the more
comprehensive tests applied to large banks.1 The proposal would also eliminate several
CRA data collection and reporting requirements currently applicable to large banks for
institutions with $10 billion or less in assets, including reporting on small-business,
small-farm and community development lending.2 In explaining this change, the
agencies refer to changes in the banking industry and note that there are fewer small
banks since the initial standards were set in 1995. However, the agencies don't bother to
explain why changes to the industry are relevant to determining a bank's obligations
under the CRA. Nor do the agencies explain how increasing the size standards serves the
statutory purposes of the CRA. In discussing these proposed changes, the preamble fails
to include any discussion of the agencies' expectations on how these changes will affect
the number of institutions subject to various requirements under the proposed rule or on
the level of community reinvestment activities undertaken nationally. On the other hand,
the NPRM identifies five specific requests for feedback and two options for one part of
the relevant proposed regulations. These requests and options relate to significant aspects
of the proposed rules relating to the appropriate categorization of banks by size. Without
knowing how the agencies will address these issues, commenters are significantly limited
in addressing the likely impact of these regulations in addressing the purposes and goals
of the CRA.

1 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,12023 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
2 Id. at 52,120.

 2
 The NPRM also fails to address the fact that, contrary to the history of CRA regulations,
these rules would only be adopted by 2 of the 3 banking regulatory agencies. In the past,
the Federal Reserve joined the FDIC and the OCC in proposing and adopting common
regulations that would provide common CRA standards and rules for the different sectors
of the banking industry. If the FDIC and OCC proceed with these rules without the
Federal Reserve it would result in significantly different rules for different sectors with
no rationale. This would result in significant confusion among both the banking industry
and the affected public. The FDIC and the OCC should withdraw this proposed rule until
they can reach agreement with the Federal Reserve on common proposed rules which
would then be subject to the public rulemaking process.
Sincerely,
Brian Siegel

Dear Chair Hill and Comptroller Gould:

Travois, Inc. appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) rule. For more than 30 years, Travois has worked with American
Indian, Alaska Native, and Native Hawaiian communities to develop and finance affordable
housing and economic development projects, including transactions using the Low-Income
Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) and New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC). Through this work, we
regularly interact with Tribal governments, Tribally Designated Housing Entities (TDHEs),
banks, tax credit investors, syndicators, and other financial institutions seeking to deploy
capital in Native communities.

The stated goals of the proposed rule changes--to increase focus on lending, ensure that
community development grants benefit communities, reduce burdens, and increase clarity
and objectivity--are laudable, but, especially with respect to Indian Country, must be
approached with care and caution.

Our experience working in Indian Country demonstrates both the extraordinary need for
private capital investments in Native communities and the difficulty Tribal nations face
attracting that capital. We appreciate that the proposal expressly recognizes Indian country
and other Tribal and Native lands in portions of the CRA framework. However, those
potentially useful provisions sit within a broader proposal that could materially weaken the
CRA obligations and incentives that drive community development capital. Broader eligibility
for activities in Indian Country has limited practical value if fewer banks have meaningful
community development obligations in the first place.

For that reason, Travois opposes the proposed rule changes in their current form and urges
the agencies to reevaluate their proposal based on public comment and feedback. In
considering how to redraft and reformulate a proposed rule to achieve the stated goals, we
offer the following recommendations in response to the specific questions attached to the
current proposal for consideration.
 Recommendation #1: To best serve Indian Country, preserve meaningful CRA incentives for
Housing Credit and community development investment by retaining the current
intermediate and large bank thresholds (Response to Question 1).

Question 1 asks whether the agencies should consider an intermediate-bank threshold as
high as $30 billion. Travois opposes raising the large-bank threshold from approximately $1.65
billion to $10 billion and strongly opposes the $30 billion alternative. The separate
Investment Test has been a powerful driver of bank investment in LIHTC and other
community development activities. The Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC)
reports that banks provide roughly 75 to 80 percent of Housing Credit equity, underscoring
the importance of CRA to a deep and competitive investor market.

Recent AHTCC survey data make the potential impact concrete. More than 100 OCC- and FDIC-
regulated banks currently investing in the Housing Credit would no longer be subject to the
Investment Test under the proposed $10 billion threshold. Those banks invested at least $1.6
billion - and potentially up to $2 billion - in Housing Credit equity over the five-year survey
period. This is particularly concerning at a time when Congress has expanded the Housing
Credit and additional investor demand will be needed to support that expanded production.

The effect is especially relevant to the communities Travois serves. AHTCC found that
approximately one-third of syndicated Housing Credit equity invested by banks with assets
between $412 million and $10 billion supported rural markets from 2021 through 2024. Tribal
projects frequently compete for capital in these same rural markets, where the loss of even a
relatively small number of active bank investors can have an outsized effect.

We recommend retaining the current large-bank threshold. If the agencies determine that an
increase is necessary, the $3.252 billion alternative is substantially less disruptive than $10
billion. AHTCC estimates that using $3.252 billion instead of $10 billion would reduce the
number of affected Housing Credit investors by approximately 63 percent, from 108 banks to
40, and reduce the estimated five-year Housing Credit equity affected from roughly $2 billion
to $272 million.

Recommendation #2: Preserve meaningful Community Development Test performance for
intermediate banks (Response to Appendix A(d)(3)).

If the agencies expand the intermediate-bank category, the final rule should preserve the
current protection that makes community development performance independently
meaningful. Under the current framework, an intermediate small bank cannot receive an
overall Satisfactory rating unless it receives at least Satisfactory ratings on both the Lending
Test and the Community Development Test.

Travois recommends retaining this minimum Community Development Test requirement for
intermediate banks under the final rule. Satisfactory lending performance should not, by
itself, compensate for inadequate community development performance. Preserving this floor
is particularly important if the intermediate-bank category is expanded, because LIHTC,
NMTC, and other responsive community development investments should remain meaningful
components of an intermediate bank's CRA evaluation.

 2
 Recommendation #3: Make geographic flexibility workable for Indian Country by ensuring
that qualifying community development activities benefiting Indian Country and other Tribal
and Native lands receive CRA consideration outside a bank's assessment areas without
requiring the bank to first satisfy the geographic flexibility standard in every assessment
area (Response to Question 34).

Geography remains one of the most significant barriers to attracting CRA-motivated capital to
Tribal LIHTC and NMTC transactions. Many Tribal communities are outside the assessment
areas of banks with the capacity and expertise to finance these projects. As a result, banks
may favor transactions within their traditional CRA footprints even when Tribal projects serve
communities with significant unmet needs.

The agencies recognize this problem in the proposal, describing "CRA deserts" as areas where
banks engage in little or no CRA activity and acknowledging that the current geographic
framework fails to incentivize community development activity in these areas. Indian Country
is among the clearest examples of this challenge.

In response to Question 34, Travois recommends that qualifying community development
activities benefiting Indian Country and other Tribal and Native lands receive CRA
consideration outside a bank's assessment areas without requiring the bank to first satisfy
the geographic flexibility standard in every assessment area. Requiring satisfaction in every
assessment area risks making Tribal projects technically eligible but practically unattractive.

This requirement also creates uncertainty for investors. Banks commit equity to LIHTC and
NMTC transactions well before the CRA examination that will evaluate them and may not
know at the time of investment whether the outside-area activity will ultimately receive CRA
consideration. A targeted exception for qualifying Native activities would provide greater
certainty while leaving intact a bank's obligation to serve its own assessment areas.

Providing meaningful geographic flexibility for Native communities would help direct CRA-
motivated capital to communities with little or no bank presence and advance the agencies'
stated objective of addressing CRA deserts.

Recommendation #4: Recognize Indian Country residential development as presumptively
promoting economic development (Response to Question 30).

Travois strongly supports an affirmative response to Question 30. Programs supporting
residential development in Indian Country should be presumed to promote economic
development and qualify as community development when applicable requirements are met.
Housing development in Native communities supports construction and permanent
employment, local businesses, infrastructure, community stability, and the ability of Tribal
citizens to remain in or return to their communities.

The agencies should also include the development, rehabilitation, and preservation of
housing among qualifying revitalization and stabilization activities in Indian Country and
other Tribal and Native lands. Housing shortages in Indian Country frequently extend across
income levels, and limiting Tribal housing solely to the affordable housing category does not
fully recognize its broader community development role.

 3
 Finally, to provide a clear pathway for determining when Tribal housing qualifies as
revitalization or stabilization, the agencies should expressly recognize an approved Indian
Housing Plan (IHP) prepared under NAHASDA as a bona fide Tribal government revitalization
or stabilization plan. An IHP is an existing federal planning and reporting framework that can
give banks and examiners an objective basis for evaluating Tribal housing activity without
unnecessary case-by-case uncertainty.

Recommendation #5: Use a comprehensive Native Land Area framework such as the 2023
Native Land Area framework or an equally inclusive approach (Response to Question 55).

Question 55 asks whether the agencies should consider alternative approaches to encourage
banks to meet the credit needs of Indian country and other Tribal and native lands, including
whether the agencies should use the Native Lands definition from the 2023 CRA rules and
whether the proposed definitions create difficulties or unintended consequences. Travois
supports a comprehensive definition that reliably captures the geographies in which Tribal
and Native communities live and undertake community development.

We recommend using the broader 2023 Native Land Area framework, or an equally inclusive
approach, and ensuring that relevant trust lands, restricted-fee lands, Alaska Native areas,
and other Tribal and Native geographies are covered. Geographic definitions should facilitate,
rather than inadvertently exclude, otherwise qualifying Tribal investments.

Recommendation #6: Provide explicit examples for Tribal LIHTC and NMTC investments in the
final rule, illustrative list, and/or Interagency Questions and Answers.

Finally, the agencies should use the final rule, illustrative list, or Interagency Questions and
Answers to confirm that qualifying LIHTC equity investments in Tribal affordable housing and
qualifying NMTC investments serving Native communities receive CRA consideration. Clear
examples would reduce uncertainty for bank CRA officers and examiners and lower the
transaction friction that can discourage a bank from making its first investment in Indian
Country.

Conclusion

The proposed rule appropriately recognizes that Indian Country faces significant and unique
community development challenges. Recognition alone, however, will not move capital. CRA
must preserve meaningful obligations and create practical incentives for banks to invest in
communities that have historically fallen outside traditional bank assessment areas.

Travois therefore urges the agencies not to finalize the proposal in its current form. If the
agencies proceed, they should preserve meaningful community development and Housing
Credit investment incentives, restore stronger Native-focused provisions from the 2023
framework, make geographic flexibility workable for Indian Country, and provide clear
treatment for Tribal housing, LIHTC, and NMTC activity.

Our experience working with Tribal communities demonstrates that there is no shortage of
viable housing and economic development needs in Indian Country. The challenge is
ensuring that private capital has sufficient incentive and a clear regulatory pathway to reach
them. CRA should help close that gap.

 4
 Sincerely,
Phil Glynn
President
Travois, Inc.

grants, and services in communities that need greater access to capital.

We appreciate the Agencies' efforts to reform the CRA regulations, and we support some of the
Agencies' provisions that could improve the CRA framework and increase responsible capital in
underserved communities. However, we are concerned about the increases in the asset thresholds
that determine how banks are evaluated under the CRA. We also have concerns with several
interacting provisions that could further weaken community development incentives that would likely
impair the flow of much needed capital in the most underserved communities.

Greater Minnesota Housing Fund ("GMHF") is Minnesota's largest affordable housing focused
Community Development Financial Institution ("CDFI") dedicated to creating and preserving
affordable housing across the state of Minnesota. GMHF works on behalf of all Minnesotans to address
a range of housing demands including affordable housing production and preservation with an
emphasis on regional population centers, job-growth communities, underserved rural communities,
and Tribal nations. GMHF's investments include funding affordable housing projects, providing
technical support to local communities and developers, linking projects with financial resources,
securing additional resources for affordable housing, and using research and program development
activities to identify new and innovative ways of increasing affordable housing production, including
manufactured housing.

Banks are critical partners in our work. We currently have relationships with banks that provide
loans, participations, investments, and technical assistance. Since 1996 GMHF has made over $1.4
billion in direct capital investments creating nearly 29,000 homes for families, children, and
individuals in low-income, cost-burdened households. Through this work, GMHF has mobilized an
estimated $4.6 billion of capital from all funders, including our banking partners.

Raised Asset Thresholds Jeopardize Community Development Finance:

Section IV.A, "Asset Thresholds"; Questions 13

The NPR defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets, intermediate banks as
institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion in assets, and large banks as institutions with

state based on the number of community development obligations lost.

financial institutions and fewer alternative sources of capital. In Minnesota, construction and
permanent debt/mortgage capital for multifamily housing production and preservation remains
available for larger projects in larger markets but is less available for smaller projects and in smaller
markets and rural communities. Larger projects developed by for-profit and nonprofit developers can
typically access agency lending, including Freddie Mac, Fannie Mae, and HUD-insured products.

I support the OCC and FDIC’s goals of reducing unnecessary regulatory burden, clarifying CRA standards, and ensuring community-development grants benefit the communities they are intended to serve. I support these goals with major changes. Simplification should reduce duplicative paperwork—not weaken meaningful accountability, deposit access, or the public’s ability to evaluate bank performance.

First, I oppose raising the small-bank threshold to $1 billion without preserving a substantive community-development (CD) evaluation for banks between the current approximately $412 million boundary and $1 billion. The proposal would reclassify 604 FDIC-supervised banks from intermediate-small to small, removing a separate CD test for affected institutions. If burden reduction is necessary, simplify documentation while retaining meaningful evaluation of CD lending, investment, and services.

Second, retain deposit services in the retail-service evaluation. Congress expressly found that community needs include credit services as well as deposit services (12 U.S.C. § 2901(a)). The FDIC’s 2023 household survey reported approximately 5.6 million unbanked households, and Philadelphia Fed research found bank branches declined 5.6% from 2019–2023. These data do not prove this proposal will cause additional closures, but they show deposit access remains relevant and should not be excluded without a stronger explanation.

Third, prefer assessment-area-level evaluation of major lending product lines, or permit examiners to consider a product that is locally important even if it is not a major product for the institution overall. A product line can be essential to a particular community’s small businesses, farms, or LMI borrowers.

Fourth, preserve a minimum CD-performance floor for intermediate banks. Under the current framework, satisfactory overall performance generally requires at least satisfactory performance on both lending and CD tests. Allowing stronger lending to fully offset weak CD performance risks weakening incentives to maintain community-development activity.

Fifth, support outside-area CD flexibility only after a bank demonstrates it has adequately addressed identified needs in its assessment areas. Require transparent allocation methods and public explanation of how outside-area activities receive CRA consideration.

Sixth, retain grant accountability and direct-benefit requirements, but make the proposed 15% indirect-cost cap a rebuttable benchmark or allow documented exceptions for necessary, reasonable costs. Explain how the cap’s calculation compares with 2 C.F.R. § 200.414(f); the federal 15% de minimis rate is generally applied to modified total direct costs, not necessarily the entire grant amount.

Seventh, reduce duplicative reporting while preserving a minimum standardized public dataset sufficient to evaluate lending and community-development outcomes, especially in low- and moderate-income communities. Before exempting banks with $10 billion or less from data collection and reporting, explain how regulators and the public will identify geographic disparities and compare performance.

Finally, ground the rule in the CRA’s statutory text and current legal constraints, explain the evidence for expected benefits, distinguish quantified effects from uncertain effects, and monitor outcomes after implementation. I do not assume every provision of the 2023 rule can be restored; I ask the agencies to preserve meaningful accountability wherever legally permissible.

I respectfully request a final rule that reduces duplicative paperwork while preserving substantive community accountability, deposit access, locally responsive lending, responsible community-development activity, and transparency.  Community Reinvestment Act Regulations

 SUPPORT WITH MAJOR CHANGES

Agency Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
 (FDIC)

Comment deadline October 13, 2026

Position Support with Major Changes

Purpose: detailed explanation of requested changes and supporting evidence. The shorter Regulations.gov comment is designed to
accompany this attachment.

CRA Regulations Comment -- Supporting Statement Page 1
 I. Summary and overall position

I support the OCC and FDIC's goals of making Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) supervision clearer, reducing
unnecessary regulatory burden, and ensuring community-development grants produce real benefits. However, administrative
simplification should not weaken the public's ability to evaluate whether banks meet community credit needs, including the
needs of low- and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods.

I recommend reducing low-value paperwork while preserving substantive performance expectations, meaningful
consideration of deposit access, a minimum community-development performance floor where appropriate, comparable
public information, and safeguards against credit being awarded for activity that does not adequately serve a bank's
assessment areas. Where the agencies expect the proposal to shift activity, they should explain the evidence supporting their
predictions and monitor outcomes.

II. Small-bank threshold and community-development accountability

The proposal would raise the small-bank asset threshold from the current approximately $412 million
intermediate-small-bank boundary to $1 billion. Under the proposal, banks below $1 billion would not have a separate
community-development (CD) test. The agencies estimate that 604 FDIC-supervised banks would move from the
intermediate-small to the small-bank category.

These changes may reduce burden, but they also remove a distinct evaluation of CD loans, investments, and services for
affected institutions. Asset size alone does not establish that community-development needs have disappeared. I
recommend retaining the current threshold. If a higher threshold is adopted, preserve a meaningful CD evaluation for banks
between approximately $412 million and $1 billion while simplifying documentation and eliminating duplicative reporting.
Explain what evidence supports removing the separate CD test and how the agencies will detect resulting reductions in CD
activity.

III. Deposit services and banking access

The proposal would narrow the retail banking-services evaluation to credit services and the distribution and availability of
retail banking facilities, excluding deposit services from the substantive evaluation. Yet Congress's CRA findings expressly
state that community needs include credit services as well as deposit services (12 U.S.C. 2901(a)). Deposit access can
affect whether households safely receive income, pay bills, avoid check-cashing costs, and maintain a relationship with a
regulated institution.

The FDIC's 2023 National Survey of Unbanked and Underbanked Households reported approximately 5.6 million unbanked
U.S. households; 66.2% of unbanked households relied entirely on cash. Philadelphia Fed research published in February
2024 reported that branches declined 5.6% from 2019 through 2023 and that branch losses were somewhat greater in LMI
census tracts than in higher-income tracts. These findings do not prove that this proposal will cause more closures, but they
show deposit access remains relevant. Retain deposit services in the retail-service evaluation, or at minimum require
examiners to consider deposit access, branch openings and closures, service availability, and effects on LMI and
underserved communities.

IV. Locally important lending products

The proposal would generally focus institution-level retail lending analysis on two major product lines while also discussing
an assessment-area approach. A product that is not among a bank's largest institution-wide product lines may still be
important in a local market--for example, small-farm lending in an agricultural area or small-business lending where
borrowers have few alternatives.

I recommend identifying major product lines at the assessment-area level, considering local lending volume, business
strategy, capacity, and contribution to local credit needs. If an institution-wide approach is adopted, allow examiners to
consider a non-major product when evidence shows it is materially important to a local assessment area, especially for LMI
borrowers, small businesses, or small farms.

CRA Regulations Comment -- Supporting Statement Page 2
 V. Intermediate-bank community-development test

Under the current framework, an intermediate-small bank generally cannot receive an overall satisfactory rating unless both
lending and CD tests are at least satisfactory. The proposal would allow stronger lending performance to compensate for
weaker CD performance, so an overall satisfactory rating would not necessarily require satisfactory CD performance.

The agencies seek flexibility and a stronger focus on lending, but removing a minimum CD floor risks weakening incentives to
maintain community-development activity. I recommend retaining the requirement that intermediate banks demonstrate at
least satisfactory lending and CD performance for an overall satisfactory rating. Reduce burden through clearer criteria and
proportional documentation rather than allowing weak CD performance to be fully offset by lending.

VI. Community development outside assessment areas

Outside-area flexibility can support projects whose service areas cross municipal or state boundaries and can expand
opportunities to finance regional needs. I support reasonable flexibility provided it remains secondary to a bank's
responsibility to its assessment areas.

Require a documented finding that a bank has adequately addressed identified CD needs in each relevant assessment area
before substantial outside-area activity receives CRA consideration. Require a transparent allocation method and public
documentation of how outside-area activities are credited. Because the agencies acknowledge uncertainty about how activity
may shift among communities and projects, monitor those effects after implementation.

VII. Grants and the 15% indirect-cost cap

I support requiring community-development grants to directly benefit qualifying programs, projects, or initiatives and requiring
recipient commitments and supporting documentation. These safeguards help ensure CRA credit reflects community benefit.

I recommend reconsidering a rigid 15% indirect-cost cap. Financial controls, compliance, program coordination, staffing, and
reporting can be essential to delivering services responsibly, and smaller or newer organizations may have fewer economies
of scale. The federal 15% de minimis indirect-cost rate in 2 C.F.R. 200.414(f) is generally applied to modified total direct
costs for eligible entities without a negotiated rate; that is not necessarily the same as capping indirect costs at 15% of an
entire grant. Explain the proposed calculation and its practical effects. Retain accountability, but make 15% a rebuttable
benchmark or allow documented exceptions where higher costs are necessary, allocable, reasonable, and consistent with
substantial community benefit.

VIII. Public data and transparency

The proposal would generally exempt banks with $10 billion or less in assets from CRA data-collection, maintenance, and
reporting requirements while retaining and revising public-file requirements. Reducing duplicative reporting can be beneficial,
but public files do not necessarily replace standardized, comparable data used to evaluate lending patterns, compare
institutions, and identify geographic disparities.

Retain a minimum standardized public dataset sufficient to assess lending and CD outcomes, especially in LMI communities.
Before adopting broad exemptions, explain how examiners and the public will identify disparities and compare performance
with less data. Assess likely data gaps, keep public files accessible online, and periodically review whether exemptions
impair meaningful evaluation.

IX. Legal alignment and evidence of benefits

The CRA requires regulators to assess a bank's record of meeting the credit needs of its entire community, including LMI
neighborhoods, consistent with safe and sound operations. The agencies are revising their rules in the context of litigation
over the 2023 CRA rule. This comment does not assume every provision of the 2023 rule can or should be restored. It asks
the agencies to preserve substantive accountability wherever legally permissible, clearly explain the statutory basis for major
limitations, and avoid disputed legal interpretations where a more durable alternative is available.

Reduced compliance cost is not by itself proof of improved community outcomes. Identify the evidence supporting expected
benefits and distinguish quantified effects from uncertain or unquantified effects. Establish a review plan tracking lending,

CRA Regulations Comment -- Supporting Statement Page 3
 deposit access, CD activity, and data availability in LMI communities after implementation.

X. Requested changes

I respectfully request that the agencies: (1) retain the current small-bank threshold or preserve a substantive CD evaluation
for banks between approximately $412 million and $1 billion; (2) retain deposit services in the retail-service evaluation; (3)
prefer assessment-area-level major product-line analysis or safeguard locally important lending; (4) preserve a minimum
satisfactory CD-performance floor for intermediate banks; (5) condition substantial outside-area CD consideration on
adequate assessment-area performance and transparent allocation; (6) retain grant accountability while allowing
documented, reasonable exceptions to the indirect-cost cap; (7) preserve minimum standardized public data and assess
data gaps before broad exemptions; and (8) explain the statutory basis, supporting evidence, and monitoring plan for major
changes.

I support reducing duplicative paperwork and tailoring supervision to an institution's size and business model. I oppose
achieving those goals by removing meaningful accountability or public information without adequate evidence and
safeguards. The final rule should make compliance clearer and more proportionate while preserving the CRA's purpose of
encouraging banks to help meet the credit needs of the communities they serve.

To Whom It May Concern:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
(OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposed changes to the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.

CSH is the national leader in supportive housing. For the past 30 years, we have
championed affordable housing paired with essential services like substance use, mental
health, and tenancy support, to help people with disabilities experiencing or at risk of
homelessness get into and stay housed. Active in over 300 communities across 48 states,
CSH has helped create more than 512,500 homes and generated billions in economic
activity. As a certified CDFI, we've invested over $2.2 billion in affordable and supportive
housing and critical community infrastructure over the past decade. We work with
lawmakers and community leaders to advance common-sense, non-partisan policy
solutions grounded in evidence and cost-effectiveness to improve housing outcomes
nationwide.

For nearly fifty years, CRA has played a critical role in directing private capital to low- and
moderate-income communities and supporting investments that would not otherwise
occur at sufficient scale. Affordable housing, community development, small business
growth, community facilities, and neighborhood revitalization have all benefited from a
regulatory framework that encourages banks to help meet the needs of the communities
they serve. Changes to bank asset thresholds, community development investment
incentives, and the treatment of CRA-qualified grants could unintentionally reduce the
availability of capital and support for affordable and supportive housing production,
particularly in underserved communities and smaller markets.
 Maintain meaningful community development responsibilities for banks of all sizes
Raising the asset threshold for large banks from $1.649 billion to $10 billion would
significantly reduce the number of institutions subject to the full CRA examination,
including separate community development investment expectations.

Supportive housing transactions often depend on multiple layers of financing, including
community development loans, equity investments, CDFI participation, public subsidies,
and philanthropic support. Banks with assets between $1.649 billion and $10 billion
currently play an important role in this ecosystem. Reclassifying these institutions as
intermediate banks may reduce incentives for certain forms of community development
activity and diminish the pool of capital available for affordable and supportive housing
development.

This impact could be particularly significant in smaller cities, suburban communities, and
rural areas where there may be relatively few active community development lenders and
investors. In many markets, a single bank's participation can make the difference between
a project moving forward or not. Any reduction in community development responsibilities
should be carefully evaluated for its effects on communities with the fewest financing
options.

Preserve strong incentives for community development investment
Supportive housing developments frequently rely on Low-Income Housing Tax Credit
(LIHTC) equity alongside operating subsidies, rental assistance, state housing resources,
and other financing tools. These transactions are often more complex than conventional
affordable housing developments because they serve people with disabilities with
significant service needs and typically require deeper affordability.

Weakening incentives for community development investment could reduce demand for
Housing Credit equity. If fewer institutions are subject to investment-focused CRA
obligations, competition for Housing Credit investments could decline, resulting in lower
equity pricing and reduced housing production.

A reduction in LIHTC investment would affect the broader affordable housing sector and
could be especially challenging for supportive housing developments, which require more
complex financing structures. At a time when communities across the country continue to
experience housing shortages and rising homelessness, regulatory changes should
strengthen, rather than weaken, incentives for affordable housing investment.

Preserve support for CDFIs and flexible community development financing
Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) provide flexible financing that is
often necessary to advance supportive and deeply affordable housing developments.
 Banks frequently partner with and invest in CDFIs as part of their community development
activities. As a result, changes that reduce incentives for community development
investment could also affect the flow of capital to mission-driven lenders that serve low-
income communities and populations with significant barriers to housing stability.

Many supportive housing projects rely on partnerships among banks, CDFIs, nonprofit
developers, and public agencies. The final rule should continue to encourage robust bank
investment in and partnership with CDFIs and other mission-driven financial institutions
that help finance housing opportunities for people with disabilities and others with
complex service needs.

Protect grants and capacity-building support for nonprofit organizations
The final rule should continue to support CRA-qualified grants and donations that
strengthen local nonprofit capacity. Across the country, nonprofit organizations provide
housing development expertise, homelessness system coordination, housing counseling,
technical assistance, supportive services, and community development activities that are
essential to successful housing outcomes. Many of these organizations rely on grants from
financial institutions that are motivated, in part, by CRA obligations.

The proposal's restrictions on qualifying grants, additional documentation requirements,
and limitations related to indirect costs could unintentionally discourage bank support for
nonprofit and community-based organizations that are essential partners in housing
development and community development efforts. While transparency and accountability
are important, the final rule should recognize that technical assistance, capacity building,
housing development support, and community planning functions are critical components
of successful community development efforts.

Organizations that strengthen local development capacity often make housing production
possible but may not fit neatly within a framework focused exclusively on direct program
expenditures. Reducing support for these intermediaries could weaken the infrastructure
communities rely on to bring affordable and supportive housing projects to fruition.

Keep low- and moderate-income communities at the center of CRA
Supportive housing serves individuals and families facing some of the most significant
barriers to housing stability, including chronic homelessness, disability, and extremely low
incomes. These populations align squarely with CRA's longstanding mission of promoting
investment and access to credit in underserved communities.

The final rule should maintain a strong focus on low- and moderate-income individuals and
communities and ensure that any expansion of eligible activities does not diminish
investment in populations with the greatest housing and service needs. CRA should
 continue to encourage activities that increase housing opportunities, improve
neighborhood stability, and expand access to community development resources for those
with the greatest needs.

CSH has seen firsthand how CRA-driven financing, investment, and grants support
affordable and supportive housing developments that would otherwise struggle to attract
capital. The current housing and homelessness challenges facing communities nationwide
require strong incentives for community development lending, investment, and
grantmaking, not a reduction in those incentives.

Thank you for your consideration of these comments.

Sincerely,

Deborah DeSantis
President and CEO
Corporation for Supportive Housing (CSH)

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

The Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation ( "Department") appreciates
the opportunity to comment on the Proposed Rules issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency ("OCC") and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC"), under the
Community Reinvestment Act ("federal CRA"). As the State of Illinois' banking regulator and
administrator of the Illinois Community Reinvestment Act, the Department is uniquely
positioned to comment on CRA and its implementation to ensure financial institutions meet the
credit needs of the communities they serve.

The federal CRA plays a critical role in fostering investments in low- and moderate-income
("LMI") communities. The Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System notes, "... a
survey of lenders in 1999 showed that the `majority of surveyed institutions engaged in some
lending activities that they would not otherwise have done' without CRA-related guidance."1 For
Illinois, federal CRA-qualified investments from 2010 to 2024 totaled more than $192 billion.

The Department recognizes the agencies' efforts to modernize and streamline the administrative
rules for the federal CRA to adapt to modern banking practices. However, this should not be used

1 Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Community Reinvestment Act of 1977 (May 8, 2023),
Community Reinvestment Act of 1977 | Federal Reserve History.

 1
 as a pretext for undermining, as the Proposed Rules seem to, the purpose and beneficial effect of
the federal CRA. For example, the increase in bank asset size threshold would eliminate data
collection requirements for nearly all Illinois banks. Reducing data collection requirements
would only make it more difficult to identify disparities in lending, the very thing the federal
CRA aims to mitigate. Additionally, consumer advocacy groups have already warned that the
Proposed Rules, specifically the changes to Community Development ("CD"), including how
CD is evaluated, could put billions of dollars in investment at risk when communities are
experiencing a widespread affordability crisis due to the inflated prices of housing, food, student
loans, healthcare, and other necessities. The Department is also concerned that the changes to
how findings of discrimination impact the federal CRA rating will allow institutions engaging in
discriminatory or otherwise illegal credit practices to receive passing federal CRA ratings. The
Department urges the agencies to withdraw the Proposed Rules and re-engage stakeholders to
develop a comprehensive proposal that does not upend civil rights protections provided by the
law. Amendments to the federal CRA necessitate time and strategic analysis to ensure any
changes are not detrimental to communities the law is intended to serve.

 The Importance of Data Collection

The Proposed Rules would increase asset size thresholds, therefore eliminating data collection
reporting obligations for banks of $10 billion and less. In Illinois, that would mean only three
banks would be required to report and collect federal CRA data. This change is consistent with
the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's ("CFPB") final rule implementing Section 1071 of
the Dodd-Frank Act, issued on May 1, 2026, limiting the scope of small business loan reporting
for financial institutions. Together, these measures will result in significant loss of data that is
critical to effectively track trends, including early warning signs of systemic disinvestment.
Proper data collection is a necessary tool to ensure modern-day redlining does not persist and
that regulators can intervene when institutions fail to serve the communities they are located in.

More than 50 years removed from the enactment of the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act
("HMDA"), it is imperative that we recall the fight that ensued to even gain access to lending
data. It was in Chicago that Gale Cincotta galvanized communities, partnering with local and
federal elected officials to advocate against redlining, a practice that was outlawed in 1968 with
the Fair Housing Act. But years after it was outlawed, LMI communities were still being denied
credit to buy homes, start businesses, and revitalize their neighborhoods. The passage of HMDA
in 1975 was the first-of-its-kind legislation that lifted the veil, providing transparency on where
lenders were and were not lending. This acted as a catalyst to the CRA in 1977, which
encouraged financial institutions to lend in communities they acquired and chartered deposits in.
The loss of small business and other investment data under the Proposed Rules will prevent
researchers, state regulators, and the public from being able to effectively determine whether
institutions are lending in their communities. This is a profound setback in the advocacy for data
transparency and fair lending. The Department urges the agencies to maintain CRA data
reporting requirements to ensure access to this vital information is retained.

 2
  Disruptions to the Dual Charter System

In response to changes in consumer lending behavior and reporting that the federal CRA alone
does not address lending disparities in LMI communities,2 Illinois enacted the Illinois
Community Reinvestment Act ("Illinois CRA"), 205 ILCS 735, in 2021. The Illinois CRA
applies not only to Illinois-chartered banks, but also to Illinois-licensed mortgage companies and
Illinois-chartered credit unions. The Illinois CRA builds off the federal CRA and utilizes HMDA
data, in addition to community development, small business, and investment reporting to assess
an institution's record.

Federal changes that significantly reduce the scope of CRA could impact charter decisions.
While the dual banking system allows for divergence in state and federal supervision, those
differences should not create incentives for institutions to select a particular charter based solely
on reduced community investment obligations. State and federal CRA frameworks complement
one another, with the federal CRA providing a baseline for assessing community investment and
the state CRA framework supplementing it. The Proposed Rules will put banks operating in
similar markets with materially different CRA expectations. Charter choices should not come at
the expense of communities' access to credit and reinvestment opportunities.

 Threats to Community Development Funding

Additionally, the increased asset size thresholds would substantially reduce requirements for
banks to invest in LMI communities. In Illinois, from 2010-2024, banks contributed $124 billion
in federal CRA-qualified mortgage lending and $68 billion in federal CRA-qualified lending to
businesses in LMI communities. These investments financed affordable housing, small business
loans, essential funding for Community Development Financial Institutions, and more. For
example, CRA-qualified investments funded mobile home park improvements in Chicago's only
manufactured housing community, start-ups that led to job growth and retention, and food
pantries that serve LMI communities. Federal CRA investment requirements create a regulatory
incentive that cannot be undermined. When banks are moved into less rigorous CRA evaluation
categories, that incentive may diminish, posing a direct threat to CD funding in Illinois.

Several of the proposed amendments to CD run contrary to the purposes of the federal CRA and
its effective implementation. For example, the limits on CD grants would pose a significant
burden to both banks and organizations. Imposing a 15 percent cap on indirect costs of grant
recipients from large banks is based on a "de minimis rate" that is not supposed to serve as a cap.
See 91 Fed. Reg. 52129 n. 131. If implemented, this cap would, notwithstanding the agencies'
stated intent, reduce overall CD investments under federal CRA. This would require institutions
to collect additional reporting metrics on grant recipients, ensuring that the funding does not
exceed 15 percent in indirect costs. This places unnecessary burden on both the recipient and the

2 Linda Lutton, Andrew Fan & Alden Loury, Where Banks Don't Lend, WBEZ (June 3, 2020),
https://interactive.wbez.org/2020/banking/disparity/.

 3
 institution. The proposed cap would also not account for organizations and intermediaries with
diverse structures and multi-service programs and, therefore, would impose unnecessary and
unwieldy data collection requirements in an attempt to track indirect costs. For example, many
organizations adhere to complex compliance reporting requirements and grant funding may
cover, in part, expenses such as staffing, rent, technology infrastructure, and other administrative
costs. Ultimately, the proposed requirement will significantly reduce the number of organizations
able to receive funding and deter banks from issuing CD grants and funding opportunities to
high-impact organizations.

 Effect of Discrimination on Ratings

The Proposed Rules would also diminish or possibly eliminate the negative impact of a bank's
discriminatory or otherwise unlawful credit practices on the bank's federal CRA rating. Under
Option 1, the agencies would limit consideration of evidence of discriminatory practices unless
cited by a public enforcement action or a judicial ruling in a case involving a federal or state
agency--the latter expressly rejecting consideration of judicial rulings in private lawsuits. This
heightened standard serves no legitimate purpose and should be rejected. Public enforcement
actions are governed by different legal standards and therefore should not be necessary to
establish discriminatory practices for purposes of a bank's CRA rating. Even Option 2, which
would permit a finding of discrimination based upon an examination report, would still weaken
this framework by eliminating the requirement that examiners consider "the nature, extent, and
strength of the evidence" of the illegal practices.

Unlawful credit practices are antithetical to the purposes of federal CRA and should always have
the fullest adverse impact on the rating. For example, the federal CRA rating shapes an
institution's supervisory cycle, including how frequently it is examined, its public image and
credibility, and its ability to expand and operate across markets. If a bank's discriminatory or
otherwise unlawful credit practices do not negatively impact its federal CRA rating, this bank
may unfairly benefit by operating for additional years between evaluations, exacerbating the
harm to consumers and communities. Delaying corrective action enables exclusionary and
predatory practices and erodes public trust--the very ill the federal CRA is intended to
ameliorate. If banks can game the system and score passing ratings while engaging in
discriminatory practices, the federal CRA's core purpose will begin to unravel. The Department
urges the agencies to retain the current administrative rule language for the effect of
discrimination when considering a bank's federal CRA rating.

 Conclusion

The federal CRA remains a bulwark against redlining and other unfair or exclusionary lending
practices. The Proposed Rules threaten to upend fifty years of economic and civil rights progress.
They represent a stark reversal in data transparency, community investment expectations, and
supervisory oversight that acts as a safeguard against discriminatory lending practices. These
changes also pose significant threats to the dual charter system. When federal CRA standards

 4
 diverge sharply, a fragmented regulatory landscape incentivizes institutions to switch charters
based on which legal framework is advantageous, rather than choosing a charter based on a
framework that meets an institution's needs and aligns with the communities it serves. This
undermines the parity between state and federal charters that both federal and state law are
designed to preserve. The FDIC and OCC have a responsibility to consider such effects when
seeking to amend the federal CRA rules. For these reasons, the Department urges the agencies to
withdraw the Proposed Rules. At a minimum, the administrative rules implementing CRA should
not be amended unless adequate time is afforded to analyze the potential impacts to ensure CRA
delivers on its intent of ensuring equitable access to credit across all communities.
Sincerely,
/s/ Susana Soriano

1. Purpose

This comment concerns the proposed rule published August 12, 2026 (Federal Register
document 2026-16454, 91 FR 52114).

BRIP -- Banking Reference & Intelligence Platform -- measures the CRA examination record,
investment authority and balance-sheet capacity of FDIC-insured banks from public sources:
Call Reports, the Summary of Deposits, published CRA performance evaluations, and federal
and state banking law. This comment responds to the agencies' request for comment on the
proposed asset-size thresholds and the alternatives to them ( IV.A, 91 FR 5212052123;
Question 1, 91 FR 5212252123). BRIP computes, for every FDIC-insured institution it can
classify, the examination tier each threshold set would assign; this comment reports the results.
It takes no position on whether the agencies should adopt the proposal or any alternative.

Under the proposal's thresholds, 410 of the 512 OCC- and FDIC-supervised institutions that are
large banks today would become intermediate banks, and 843 intermediate small banks would
become small banks. The alternatives the agencies asked about would leave between 49 and
280 institutions in the large tier.

2. Method and data

BRIP applies the proposal's two-observation rule ( IV.A, 91 FR 52121) to total assets reported
at December 31, 2024 and December 31, 2025, using the Call Reports as republished by the
FFIEC on September 15, 2026. The current thresholds are those in effect for 2026, $412 million
and $1.649 billion (OCC Bulletin 2025-48, December 23, 2025; 91 FR 509, January 7, 2026).
Each alternative changes one threshold and keeps the proposal's other; the $10 billion / $30
billion set, as Question 1 poses it, changes both. Every threshold is applied as stated, without

 No institution reported total assets exactly equal to any threshold examined here at either

Capital and surplus is BRIP's measure at December 31, 2025. For institutions that elect the

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency’s (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation’s (FDIC) proposed amendments to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. The Colorado Health Foundation (“CHF” or “the Foundation”) is a statewide, nonprofit and nonpartisan philanthropic organization with a mission to improve the health and well-being of Coloradans. The Foundation recognizes the agencies’ stated goals of reducing regulatory burden for community banks and providing greater clarity in the CRA framework. This proposed rule, however, would substantially narrow CRA examination and reporting requirements by raising the small-bank threshold from less than $412 million to less than $1 billion, establishing an intermediate-bank category of $1 billion to $10 billion, and limiting the full large-bank framework to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. These changes would move hundreds of banks into less intensive examination categories and reduce separate scrutiny of community-development lending, investments, branches, and services. The Foundation is concerned that the proposal could weaken accountability for whether banks are meeting 
local credit and investment needs, particularly in smaller and rural markets where community and regional banks can play an especially important role. 
For these reasons, the Foundation respectfully urges the agencies to withdraw these proposed changes that would significantly narrow community-development, investment, service, and data-reporting requirements. Please see attached letter for our full comments.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0188_09000064b9658fd1.pdf:
October 9, 2026

Jonathan V. Gould
Comptroller of the Currency
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street SW
Washington, DC 20219

Travis Hill
Chairman
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
550 17th Street NW
Washington, DC 20429

Submitted electronically via Regulations.gov

RE: Comments on Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-
AF57; RIN 3064-AG31

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill,

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's
(OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposed amendments to the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. The Colorado Health Foundation ("CHF" or "the Foundation") is a
statewide, nonprofit and nonpartisan philanthropic organization with a mission to improve the health
and well-being of Coloradans. Through community engagement, research, grantmaking, and private
sector investments, the Foundation works to ensure that everyone in Colorado has what they need to be
healthy. The Foundation has a particular interest in ensuring that communities across Colorado have
access to the capital, affordable housing, financial services, and economic opportunities that support
good health and well-being.

The Foundation recognizes the agencies' stated goals of reducing regulatory burden for community
banks and providing greater clarity in the CRA framework. This proposed rule, however, would
substantially narrow CRA examination and reporting requirements by raising the small-bank threshold
from less than $412 million to less than $1 billion, establishing an intermediate-bank category of $1
billion to $10 billion, and limiting the full large-bank framework to banks with more than $10 billion in
assets.
 These changes would move hundreds of banks into less intensive examination categories and reduce
separate scrutiny of community-development lending, investments, branches, and services. The
Foundation is concerned that the proposal could weaken accountability for whether banks are meeting
local credit and investment needs, particularly in smaller and rural markets where community and
regional banks can play an especially important role.

For these reasons, the Foundation respectfully urges the agencies to withdraw these proposed changes
that would significantly narrow community-development, investment, service, and data-reporting
requirements. As outlined below, the Foundation is concerned that:

 Raising the asset thresholds would move hundreds of banks into less intensive CRA
 examination categories, reducing separate scrutiny of community-development lending,
 investments, branches, and services and limiting CRA data collection and reporting to the public.

 The proposed geographic-flexibility standard could establish a benchmark for local community-
 development activity substantially below current levels and weaken incentives for banks to
 remain responsive to needs within individual assessment areas.

 Narrowing consideration of deposit products and branch services could reduce accountability for
 forms of financial access that remain important to low- and moderate-income households and
 communities.

 The proposed restrictions on community-development grants, including the 15 percent indirect-
 cost standard, could make it more difficult for smaller nonprofit and community-based
 organizations to obtain general operating, capacity-building, and other flexible support.

Raising the asset thresholds would substantially reduce community-development accountability and
transparency.

According to the agencies' regulatory analysis, 604 FDIC-supervised banks and 194 OCC-supervised
banks would move from the intermediate category to the small-bank category and would no longer
have a separate community-development test if this proposed rule is implemented. Another 250 FDIC-
supervised banks and 126 OCC-supervised banks would move from large-bank to intermediate-bank
treatment and would no longer be subject to the existing large-bank data collection, maintenance, and
reporting requirements.

Under existing policy, intermediate banks are separately evaluated on community-development lending,
investments, and services, while large banks are evaluated under distinct lending, investment, and
service tests. The proposal would eliminate the separate community-development test for banks below
$1 billion and apply a less rigorous evaluation to institutions between $1 billion and $10 billion.

The National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) estimates that approximately 814 banks
nationwide would no longer receive a separate community-development evaluation and another 417
 would move out of the large-bank framework, leaving only the largest approximately 6 percent of banks
subject to separate reviews of community-development investments and branch services. NCRC also
estimates that the proposal would eliminate approximately 11 percent of currently reported CRA small-
business lending data nationally. These estimates illustrate the scale of the potential reduction in
community-level accountability and publicly available information.

The reduction could be particularly important in Colorado. In the Federal Reserve Banks' 2025 Small
Business Credit Survey, 52 percent of the 98 Colorado employer firms surveyed reported using a small
bank for financial services, compared with 42 percent nationally. The survey defines a small bank as an
institution with less than $10 billion in assets--the same general asset range that the proposed CRA
rule would remove from the large-bank framework.

Reducing the amount of small-business, small-farm, community-development, and assessment-area
data available for these institutions could make it more difficult for regulators, community organizations,
researchers, and financial institutions to identify unmet credit needs and lending gaps. The Foundation
urges the agencies to withdraw this proposal and to preserve meaningful community-development
evaluation and data transparency for institutions that would otherwise move into less intensive CRA
categories.

Reduced scrutiny of community-development investment could have particular consequences for
affordable housing in Colorado.

Access to affordable housing is closely connected to health and economic stability, and Colorado
continues to face substantial affordability pressures. According to the Colorado Housing and Finance
Authority (CHFA), 46.8 percent of Colorado renters are housing cost-burdened and 22.9 percent are
severely cost-burdened. More than one in five Colorado homeowners are also cost-burdened.

Community-development capital is an important part of Colorado's response. Housing Tax Credits have
helped build or preserve more than 83,500 affordable rental homes in Colorado since 1986. In the first
2026 funding round, CHFA awarded credits to 14 developments expected to support 634 affordable
rental homes and generate more than $219 million in private-sector equity across urban, rural, and
Tribal communities.

Moving hundreds of banks out of separate investment evaluations could weaken incentives for
investments such as Low-Income Housing Tax Credits, particularly in smaller markets. Because
affordable-housing projects depend on multiple public and private financing sources, the Foundation
urges the agencies to more fully analyze how reduced investment scrutiny could affect the availability of
private capital before eliminating separate investment evaluations for banks that are currently treated as
large institutions.
 The proposed geographic-flexibility standard could become a ceiling on local community-
development activity.

The proposal would allow a large bank, under one option, to receive CRA consideration for community-
development activity outside an assessment area after reaching annual levels within that area equal to
0.625 percent of allocated Tier 1 capital for community-development loans and a separate 0.625
percent for investments and grants. Intermediate, wholesale, and limited-purpose banks would be
subject to a combined 1.25 percent standard.

Although the agencies describe these figures as geographic-flexibility standards rather than CRA
passing scores, NCRC found a substantial gap between the proposed benchmark and recent activity. In
its review of 69 of the 100 largest banks supervised by the OCC or FDIC, NCRC calculated
approximately $102 billion in annual assessment-area community-development lending, investments,
and grants. Applying the proposed 0.625 percent benchmark to those institutions produced
approximately $14.8 billion, about 85 percent below their observed annual activity.

That approximately 85 percent difference raises concern that the threshold could establish a
substantially lower benchmark for local community-development activity and influence bank and
examiner expectations regarding what constitutes an adequate local commitment. This is particularly
important in communities where projects may be smaller, more complex, or more difficult to finance but
where unmet housing, small-business, infrastructure, and community-development needs remain
significant.

The Foundation urges the agencies to withdraw this proposal and to ensure that any geographic-
flexibility provision preserves strong expectations for responsiveness within each assessment area and
does not reduce incentives for banks to invest above the regulatory minimum where local needs support
greater activity.

Deposit products and branch access remain important components of financial access in Colorado.

The proposal would narrow the large-bank service test to focus on credit services and would no longer
consider deposit services such as checking and savings products. The agencies describe this change as
part of an effort to focus CRA more directly on lending and credit needs. The Foundation is concerned,
however, that affordable and accessible transaction accounts are closely connected to households'
ability to enter and remain in the financial mainstream.

Colorado has made a concerted effort to expand access to safe and affordable banking. Through Bank
On Colorado, the Colorado Office of Financial Empowerment works with financial institutions, local
governments, and community organizations to connect residents to accounts that meet national
standards. According to the Office's January 2026 report, more than 58,780 Bank On accounts were
 opened by Coloradans in 2024 based on data from only about one-third of participating financial
institutions, and approximately 87 percent were opened by customers new to the institution.

The substantial use of these accounts underscores the importance of affordable transaction products to
financial access in Colorado. Removing deposit products from the CRA service evaluation would
therefore eliminate an important mechanism for assessing whether large banks' retail banking services
are responsive to community needs.

NCRC also estimates that more than 5,000 branches in low- and moderate-income census tracts and
more than 4,000 branches in majority-people-of-color census tracts nationwide are operated by banks
that would no longer be subject to a separate large-bank branch evaluation. These figures demonstrate
the scale of branch networks that would lose separate scrutiny and underscore the need to evaluate the
state and local effects of the proposed thresholds, not only the share of national banking assets held by
affected institutions.

The proposed restrictions on community-development grants could reduce flexible support for
nonprofit organizations.

The Foundation is also concerned about the proposed treatment of community-development grants.
Under the proposal, CRA consideration would generally be limited to grants directly used for a specific
program, project, or initiative with a community-development purpose. For grants made by large banks,
recipient organizations would also have to demonstrate that indirect costs associated with administering
the grant do not exceed 15 percent, supported by documentation that could include an IRS Form 990
and annual operating and program budgets.

If implemented, this provision would be especially impactful to community-based organizations that use
operating support and capacity-building resources to maintain staff, develop programs, administer
financing, and deliver services. Importantly, the agencies' own regulatory analysis recognizes this
possible effect. It states that the direct-use requirement, 15 percent operating-cost condition, and
related documentation requirements could mean that general operating support, capacity-building
grants, intermediary grants, and grants to smaller nonprofits receive less CRA-motivated funding.

The 15 percent standard also warrants reconsideration. In explaining its proposal, the agencies point to
OMB's Uniform Guidance. Yet, as the proposed rule itself acknowledges, OMB describes its 15 percent
de minimis indirect-cost rate as a mechanism intended to permit a more reasonable and realistic
recovery of overhead costs, particularly for organizations without the capacity to negotiate a formal
indirect-cost rate. A de minimis rate designed to ensure some recovery of indirect costs does not
necessarily establish that 15 percent is an appropriate ceiling for determining whether a community-
development grant should receive CRA consideration.
 As a philanthropic organization that works with communities and nonprofit organizations across
Colorado, the Foundation recognizes the importance of ensuring that community-development
resources reach their intended beneficiaries. At the same time, project delivery necessarily requires
sufficient administrative capacity within an organization. The Foundation urges the agencies to withdraw
this proposed categorical 15 percent ceiling and to preserve CRA consideration for reasonable general
operating, capacity-building, and intermediary support where the underlying activity has community
development as its primary purpose. The agencies should seek to prevent misuse of CRA credit without
inadvertently creating a standard that makes it more difficult for smaller community organizations to
obtain flexible resources necessary to carry out qualifying work.

Conclusion

The Community Reinvestment Act remains an important framework for assessing whether federally
supervised banks are helping meet community credit needs. The Foundation supports efforts to make
CRA requirements clearer and reduce unnecessary burden, but the proposed changes could
substantially reduce scrutiny of community-development activity, investments, services, public data, and
flexible nonprofit support.

These concerns are especially relevant in Colorado, where communities face significant affordable-
housing needs, small businesses rely on banks below $10 billion in assets, and tens of thousands of
residents are using affordable accounts designed to expand access to mainstream banking.

The Foundation therefore respectfully urges the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the proposed asset
thresholds and related reductions in CRA requirements; to preserve meaningful consideration of
affordable deposit products and branch access; to ensure that geographic flexibility does not weaken
responsiveness within individual assessment areas; and to revise the proposed grant restrictions so that
reasonable operating and capacity-building support remains eligible for CRA consideration. The
agencies should more fully assess the effects of these changes on low- and moderate-income
communities, smaller and rural markets, affordable-housing investment, small-business credit, and
community-based organizations before finalizing policy changes of this magnitude.

The Foundation appreciates your consideration of our comments. If you have any questions, please
contact Kyle Rojas Legleiter, Colorado Health Foundation Senior Director of Policy, at
klegleiter@coloradohealth.org or 303-953-3618.

Sincerely,

Kyle Rojas Legleiter

Senior Director of Policy
 The Colorado Health Foundation
