Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

On behalf of National Housing Trust (NHT), a national affordable housing nonprofit organization, we
appreciate the opportunity to comment on the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment
Act (CRA) regulations issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation (together, the agencies). For nearly 50 years, the CRA has helped
attract private capital to communities across the country and strengthen partnerships between
banks and the community development organizations that serve them. However, several aspects
of the recent proposal would reduce the availability of capital by decreasing the number of banks
subject to meaningful CRA obligations, limit consideration for grants that spur innovation and
catalyze private investment, and redirect investment away from deeply affordable housing that the
CRA is intended to support without durable affordability protections. Together, these changes
would leave low-income residents and communities with fewer resources to build and preserve
affordable housing for generations to come.

Summary of Comments
We urge the agencies to revise the proposal in three principal ways:

 Maintain community development investment and service obligations for banks of all sizes;
 Protect flexible grants and operating support to mission-driven nonprofit organizations as

 qualifying community development activity; and
 Ensure meaningful, enforceable, and durable affordability and tenant-protection

 requirements for naturally occurring affordable housing (NOAH) investments receiving CRA
 credit.

1101 Connecticut Ave , NW Suite 700 202 -333 -8931 (Phone) www.nationalhousingtrust.org
Washington D.C. 20036 202 -833 -1031 (Fax)
 1. Maintain Community Development Investment and Service Obligations for Banks of All Sizes
The proposal to raise CRA asset-size thresholds across small, intermediate, and large banks would
reduce the community development obligations and more comprehensive CRA evaluations that
small, medium, and large banks participate in today. From the perspective of affordable housing
practitioners, these shifts in asset thresholds risk removing important sources of financing from the
community development ecosystem.
For instance, according to the National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders (NAAHL)1, if the
agencies finalize the rule that defines small banks as those with less than $1 billion in assets, more
than 813 banks, or 19% of all banks nationwide, would no longer be subject to separate lending,
investment and service test to determine their CRA rating, rather solely a retail lending test and
community development test. This would, in our view, no longer incentivize small banks to provide
community development loans or investments in the places where they currently do business as a
strong retail lending test would offset a small bank's performance. Smaller and regional banks often
play an outsized role in smaller, rural markets as they are best situated and willing to evaluate
mission-focused projects that may not fit the underwriting preferences or scale requirements of the
largest institutions. Removing the community development evaluations for small banks will mean
that those with total assets less than $1 billion will no longer have comparable incentives to make
direct community development loans or investments. This will result in no obvious substitute
source of capital to fill the gap in places where affordable housing is greatly needed.
Increasing the thresholds for intermediate banks would reduce the number of banks that are
subject to a separate community development investment test and therefore reduce the number of
banks willing to provide project-level investment. This would drive more borrowers toward the same
pool of large-bank capital and weaken pricing and availability for mission-driven borrowers. These
impacts would be especially significant for Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing Credit)
transactions and other deeply affordable housing developments. The Housing Credit program, the
country's most important tool for the production and preservation of affordable rental housing,
relies heavily on investments from banks subject to CRA. According to a 2025 study by the
accounting firm CohnReznick,2 approximately 80% of equity investments in the Housing Credit
each year come from CRA-motivated bank investors. Removing the investment test would
substantially weaken CRA incentives to make equity investments in Housing Credit properties,
especially outside the largest metropolitan markets, meaning affordable housing developers may
face higher costs and less willingness from capital providers to support innovative or mission-
driven deals. At a time when Congress and the President have expanded LIHTC through HR 1 (2025)
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, this rule change goes counter to their priorities and threatens to
weaken the country's most powerful housing production and preservation tool.
For nonprofit Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFI) lenders such as our subsidiary,
NHTCDF, the impact may vary depending on the composition of each organization's bank lender
base. Even where only a subset of current bank lenders are directly reclassified, we believe that the
broader market effect could still be meaningful. If the agencies reclassify large banks as those with
assets over $10 billion, this will reduce the number of large banks by 416, impacting approximately
10% of all banks and reducing the number of banks subject to the full CRA exam.3 These banks may

1 2026 Fact Sheet: CRA Asset Thresholds, National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders.
2 2025 Affordable Housing Credit Study, CohnReznick.
3 2026 Fact Sheet: CRA Asset Thresholds, National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders.

1101 Connecticut Ave , NW Suite 700 202 -333 -8931 (Phone) www.nationalhousingtrust.org
Washington D.C. 20036 202 -833 -1031 (Fax)
 face greater demand from borrowers and intermediaries, while banks with reduced obligations may
have less reason to provide flexible, mission-oriented capital. Increasing the large bank
classification to assets over $30 billion would only exacerbate lending and equity challenges. We
recommend that the agencies retain meaningful CRA obligations for banks with demonstrated
capacity to engage in community development lending, investment, and services, and avoid
changes that would reduce the number and diversity of capital providers supporting affordable
housing.
2. CRA Should Continue to Protect Operating Grants and Nonprofit Capacity Building
The agencies propose to narrow consideration for community development operating grants. While
we support accountability and transparency, we are concerned that an overly restrictive approach
would discourage banks from providing the flexible resources that nonprofit affordable housing
organizations need to serve low- and moderate-income communities effectively. Operating grants
that offer capacity-building support are essential to community development as they allow
nonprofit developers, CDFIs, and policy organizations to respond to emerging community needs
that cannot be financed through project-specific grants alone. Flexible support gives community-
oriented organizations the opportunity to identify unmet needs, develop creative solutions, and
build organizational infrastructure needed to bring promising solutions to scale. If CRA credit is
limited only to grants directly used for a narrow plan, project, or initiative, banks may reduce
support for the very organizations that create and sustain the pipeline of affordable housing and
community development activity. The risk is particularly acute for smaller and rural communities,
where nonprofit capacity is limited and flexible resources can determine whether a project moves
forward at all.
We recommend that the agencies protect and preserve CRA consideration for grants, donations,
and operating support to mission-oriented nonprofit organizations where the recipient's mission,
activities, and use of funds are substantially directed toward community development. Preserving
CRA consideration for this flexible support will enable organizations to develop creative responses
to community needs, test and scale innovative approaches, undertake the early-stage work
necessary to attract private investment, and build a durable pipeline of financeable community
development projects.
3. CRA Credit for NOAH Should Require Meaningful Affordability Protections
NHT is encouraged to see that affordable housing now includes naturally occurring affordable
housing (NOAH), and affordability is determined by rent levels. However, we are deeply concerned
that recognizing naturally occurring affordable housing without strong affordability requirements
could shift CRA-motivated activity away from low-income communities and toward effectively
market-rate middle-income rental housing. While middle-income households face real housing
affordability challenges in many markets, expanding CRA eligibility to NOAH without enforceable
affordability limits could reward activity that does not produce durable community development
benefits, conflicts with the purpose of CRA, and could dilute scarce bank investments that are
needed for deeply affordable homes.
The agencies should avoid a framework in which banks can receive CRA credit for homes affordable
to households well above low-income levels such as 80% of area median income (AMI), particularly
in high-cost markets where lenders are already willing to invest. Broad NOAH eligibility would
reduce the capital available to populations that the CRA is intended to serve. LIHTC and other
restricted affordable housing developments, serving households at 60% AMI or below, would have

1101 Connecticut Ave , NW Suite 700 202 -333 -8931 (Phone) www.nationalhousingtrust.org
Washington D.C. 20036 202 -833 -1031 (Fax)
 to compete for the same capital with lower returns and more demanding affordability obligations.
For example, the broad definition, proposed by the agencies, ties to income levels as high as 120%
AMI and could permit credit for properties serving households far above the income levels CRA is
meant to prioritize. In a high-cost market such as Washington, D.C., that could include rents of
greater than $5000 per month and incomes of more than $196,700 for a family of four statistics
that bear little relationship to the housing needs of low- and moderate-income families. CRA credit
should focus on activity targeted to the low-income households and communities it was intended
to benefit.
If the agencies decide to recognize NOAH activity, they should require clear safeguards that, at
minimum, should include recorded or otherwise enforceable affordability restrictions, rent-growth
limits designed to prevent displacement, income targeting that prioritizes low- and moderate-
income renters, and a meaningful affordability term. The agencies should also consider requiring
sponsor-imposed restrictions or comparable mechanisms where public subsidies are not present.
CRA credit should be calibrated to encourage preservation that would not otherwise occur, deepen

October 13, 2026

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations

As Greater Boston's oldest and largest community foundation, the Boston Foundation is committed
to closing the gaps that drive the region's greatest disparities. Through our civic leadership,
research, grantmaking, partnerships, and advocacy, we work to expand opportunity, advance
equity, and build thriving communities.

Central to this work is the Foundation's Community Wealth pathway, which focuses on increasing
economic mobility and building long-term wealth in historically marginalized communities.
Through this effort, the Foundation advances strategies that advance affordable housing and
homeownership, strengthen community development, and expand access to capital and technical
assistance for underserved small business owners. Together, these investments help create more
equitable, resilient, and prosperous communities throughout Greater Boston.

On behalf of the Boston Foundation, we respectfully urge the withdrawal of the proposed
amendments to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). The proposed changes would weaken
a longstanding and highly effective framework that helps ensure financial institutions meet the
credit, investment, and service needs of low- and moderate-income communities. Collectively,
these changes would reduce transparency, diminish accountability, and weaken incentives for
banks to make meaningful investments in historically underserved communities.

The CRA is one of the nation's most important tools for promoting equitable access to capital,
financial services, and community investment. Enacted to address decades of discriminatory
lending practices and disinvestment, it requires federal regulators to regularly evaluate banks
serving low- and moderate-income communities. Since receiving a poor CRA grade can hinder a
bank's ability to expand, the law incentivizes financial institutions to lend in underserved
communities. These investments have generated billions of dollars in economic activity and
community development financing, expanded pathways to homeownership and entrepreneurship,
and strengthened local economies by providing residents with opportunities that the private market
alone has often failed to deliver.

CRA review requirements vary by bank size, with larger institutions subject to more comprehensive
regulations. The proposed increase in CRA asset thresholds would move roughly 800 banks into the
"small bank" category, eliminating their community development obligations and reducing the
banks subject to those requirements by 40%. More than 400 currently large banks would also be
reclassified as intermediate institutions with less rigorous community development standards,
leaving only 86 banks subject to the highest level of scrutiny. As a result, communities across the
country could face substantial reductions in the investments and services that support economic
mobility and neighborhood stability.
 These investments often fill financing gaps that would otherwise go unmet. Community
development projects and small business lending programs frequently rely on CRA capital to move
forward, including affordable housing projects financed through the Low-Income Housing Tax
Credit program. Weakening community development obligations would likely diminish investment
in these projects, slowing progress toward economic equity, limiting opportunities for wealth
creation, and widening existing racial and economic disparities in addition to a worsening housing
crisis.

The proposal would also weaken oversight of bank branches and financial services in underserved
communities. The over 400 banks that would lose branch evaluation requirements as a result of
being reclassified as intermediate operate approximately 5,000 branches in low- and moderate-
income census tracts (30% of all branches in those communities) and 4,000 branches in majority
people-of-color census tracts (23%). Reducing branch evaluation requirements and eliminating
incentives tied to important banking products could limit access to financial services and further
disadvantage communities.

Nearly five decades after its enactment, the CRA remains a critical safeguard to ensure banks meet
the credit needs of all communities. The proposed rule departs from that foundational purpose by
lowering expectations, reducing accountability, and weaking incentives for meaningful community
reinvestment. At a time of growing housing affordability challenges and persistent racial and
economic inequities, federal regulators should preserve and strengthen this framework that has
helped direct billions of dollars to communities that have been historically excluded from
investment.

Sincerely,

Courtney Brunson
Senior Director, Economic Equity Initiatives

Soni Gupta
Associate Vice President, Community Wealth

Introduction

CBAI and its member community bankers support the CRA, which was enacted by Congress in
1977 and is intended to encourage depository institutions to meet the needs of the communities
in which they operate, including low- and moderate-income ("LMI") neighborhoods, consistent
with the safe and sound operation of such institutions. The CRA requires that each insured
depository institution's record in helping meet the needs of its entire community is evaluated
periodically. That record is taken into account in considering an institution's application for
deposit facilities, including mergers and acquisitions. CRA examinations are conducted by the
banking regulators that are responsible for supervising their depository institutions, which are,
for the purposes of this comment letter, the OCC and the FDIC.

Community banks perform exceptionally well in CRA compliance and examinations precisely
because the mission of community banks is to fairly serve all their customers and communities.
Our members continue to tell us that the community reinvestment makes good business sense
and benefits everyone.

Joint Rulemaking

CBAI welcomes rulemaking which helps to revise and modernize the CRA. Prior rulemaking
efforts to accomplish these objectives included a 2018 advance notice of proposed rulemaking, a
2019 proposed rulemaking, a 2020 finalized rule, a 2021 rescission of that rule, a 2022 notice of
proposed rulemaking, a 2023 final rule, and subsequent litigation which has resulted in the
rescission of that rule. This unfortunate and frustrating whipsawing in the rulemaking process

CRA. This burden falls particularly hard on the nation's community banks and undermines the
spirit of the Regulators' own EGRPRA process with its legal mandate to identify and eliminate
unnecessary or unduly burdensome regulations.

CBAI believes constructive interagency dialogue, collaboration and productive cooperation
between all of the regulators and the banking industry are the surest path to meaningful, lasting
and beneficial changes. CBAI encourages the Regulators to engage in joint rulemaking and agree
on a reasonable final rule to revise and modernize the CRA.

is cause for regulator criticism and even enforcement actions.

The creditworthiness and responsible behavior of borrowers and account holders are several of
the keys to safety and soundness without them, financial services cannot be provided.
Regulations and examinations for compliance with the CRA must never lose sight of or

not be minimized or lost in the modernization of the CRA.

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

The California Community Land Trust Network writes to object to the harmful
changes proposed to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was
passed by Congress in 1977 in response to redlining and creates an affirmative
obligation for banks to help meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of
communities, including low and moderate income (LMI) communities. While the
CRA has successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest and provide services in
underserved communities, challenges related to redlining, discrimination,
underinvestment, and lack of access remain.

The California Community Land Trust Network (CACLTN) is a statewide membership
organization of California community land trusts (CLTs) and allied organizations,
working to support the growth of permanently affordable, community controlled
land and housing in California. Our member organizations - including 50 established
and emerging CLTs - span California from Humboldt County to San Diego,
collectively stewarding over 1,700 permanently affordable homes housing over
3,500 Californians.
 California community land trusts provide permanently affordable homeownership
and rental opportunities to low- and moderate-income residents of California, as
well as opportunities for small business, agriculture, and other community
gathering spaces. CLTs and CLT residents - like other housing and small business
providers - depend on the financial services industry to provide mortgages, as well
as financing for acquisition, rehabilitation, pre-development, and construction.
Some CLTs take advantage of Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) financing,
made possible from bank investments. Additionally, many CLTs have strong
relationships with local and regional banks, who provide EQ2 investments,
donations, grants, and event sponsorships to support the effective work of CLTs to
meet community needs.

The changes proposed will harm the communities that CLTs serve, which are the
very communities CRA was meant to uplift. The proposal does not justify those
changes or consider their expected impact on LMI communities. We request an
extension of the comment period for an additional 60 days so we have time to
better understand how much CRA activity may be lost to communities because of
this proposal an analysis the regulators did not conduct or provide.

The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved
communities in several ways.

 1) Community development (CD) activities for affordable housing
 and small businesses will drop dramatically.

As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities
that support critically needed affordable housing and economic development
projects. These activities often provide the greatest CRA impact in communities as
they strengthen economic stability and mobility, quality of life, and social health of
residents and communities.

The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large"
Banks, such that many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and
expectation to serve the community development needs of their communities.[1]
According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70
California banks would see their reinvestment obligations reduced under the
proposal. Twenty-five California banks would shed their Community Development
 Test responsibilities entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer be subject to
the Investment Test.[2]

The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical
community development programs that have had large impacts in LMI
communities. These include Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) which are a
key driver of affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) which
fuel economic development projects in tribal and other areas; and EQ2 equity
equivalent investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs)
that provide small business lending in underserved areas that banks cannot reach,
and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that take property off of the speculative
market.

Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting
the critical importance of the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable
housing.[3] Approximately half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from CRA
motivated banks.[4] The regulators will even further weaken CD obligations if they
adopt the alternative proposal that Large Banks be defined as those with over $30
billion in assets.

Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance
even where they remain subject to the Community Development and Investment
Tests. The regulators signal to all banks that they can do significantly less CD
lending and investment and still pass their CRA examinations, all while seeking CRA
credit for activity outside of their CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests
that a bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1
capital were devoted to CD loans and CD investments. That percentage is far lower
than the percentage that NCRC determined banks currently devote to community
investments and loans. If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary
to meet the proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by approximately
$87.1 billion, or 85%.[5]

Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have
tremendous negative impacts on affordable housing and small business
development in our state. Asset thresholds should not be raised.


 2) Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.

Another consequence of the proposal's drive to raise asset thresholds is that fewer
banks will be required to report data regarding their small business, small farm,
and community development lending activities. Such data is critical to
understanding not only individual bank performance, but also the needs of local
markets. Rise Economy and its member organizations routinely analyze this CRA
data when meeting with banks and commenting on CRA exams and mergers. The
loss of such data is particularly harmful at a time when the Administration is
walking back efforts to collect and disclose detailed small business lending data
under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank Act. These changes will disproportionately
impact rural communities in our state where banks up to $10 billion in assets make
up a larger part of the small business and small farm lending markets.

 3) Native American communities and Tribal Nations will not see
 sufficient benefits.

The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the needs
of Native American communities and Tribal Nations which have been poorly served
by banks. The current rules focus CRA obligations in areas where banks have
branches, even though there are far fewer bank branches near Tribal lands and in
rural areas where Native Americans may reside. The proposal seeks to address this
CRA gap by encouraging banks to engage in community development and related
activities in "Indian Country" and on "Tribal and Native lands," even if outside of
bank CRA assessment areas. But many members of Tribes in California will not
benefit from this proposal as they do not live in Indian Country or on Tribal or
Native lands, as defined.

CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring within
particular geographies, given the challenges and impacts associated with historic
dispossession and federal policy. Instead, CRA evaluations should also consider
whether banks have established meaningful relationships with, and provided direct
benefits to, federally recognized Tribes as well as non-federally recognized Tribes.
Non-federally recognized Tribes have been acknowledged by, and are able to access
 programs and contracts with, various local and state entities.[11] Such processes
exist.

More specifically, the CRA rules should encourage banks to serve Tribes, nonprofit
organizations or other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned businesses
that are majority owned and controlled by Native American entrepreneurs by
providing:

 Active outreach and engagement
 Community development loans and investments for affordable housing and

 economic development projects
 Small farm and small business loans
 Home mortgage loans
 Grants to meet community needs, including for capacity building for Tribes

 and support for Tribes seeking federal recognition if desired
 Support for cultural, health and other programs
 Bank branches
 Deposit products such as affordable bank accounts, and
 The provision of financial services such as financial literacy, apprenticeship

 programs and technical assistance support

While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities
outside of their branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made to
encourage banks to engage in CRA related activity to directly benefit Tribes,
nonprofit organizations and other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned
businesses that are majority owned and controlled by Native American
entrepreneurs.

A better approach is needed. All banks should be subject to an impact and
responsiveness review factor during their CRA exams that evaluates and tracks
whether banks have engaged in any CRA activity directly with Tribes, Tribally
controlled entities and Native owned businesses.[12] If banks know they will be
examined for their work with Tribes, they will find mutually beneficial ways to work
with Tribes.

 4) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will
 suffer.
 The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by
requiring a demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating
that large banks and their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more
than 15% of these grants on overhead.[13] As if this wasn't enough, the FDIC and
OCC question whether they should end CRA eligibility for bank grantmaking to
nonprofits entirely.

Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian
measures will be except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller
groups, may be impacted.[14]

Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local
needs. They also can be key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and
investment products into communities inclined to trust long established local
organizations. Many nonprofit organizations and programs, such as downpayment
assistance programs, that support CRA related activity, rely on bank contributions
to operate. Smaller, local, and rural organizations will be least able to meet new
reporting obligations, and they risk losing bank support as a result. The proposal
would also end impactful contributions from banks for general operating support,
sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.

Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their
communities on their own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps
in their own capacity seeking assistance with community outreach, borrower
education, credit building and repair, technical assistance, legal services, job
training and placement, tax assistance, affordable housing and other services and
programs which help residents become stable and bankable so that banks can
attract new deposits and make new loans in LMI communities.

The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and will
focus grantmaking on larger organizations that can help them more easily meet
their new FDIC and OCC-imposed regulatory burdens.

Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15%
overhead restriction will negatively affect operations and organizational success. As
one example, in order to secure CRA grants from Large Banks, CDFIs will need to
 pare down costs for critical operational expenses such as underwriting, servicing,
compliance, technology, impact measurement, product development, and borrower
technical assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions,
organizations are put at risk.

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA
activity that contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large
negative impact it will have on nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding,
the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are meant to benefit from the CRA,
and the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

 5) Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.

There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link
between CRA and LMI impact in the name of easing bank burden.

Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their
top two major product lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in,
and profiting from, communities, this lending by banks, subsidiaries and affiliates
must be evaluated. Further, certain products, such as small farm and consumer
loans, are important in many communities, but may not be among a bank's largest
product lines. If regulators give banks a pass and exempt smaller product lines
from CRA oversight, banks will have less incentive to consider how those products
are offered.

Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and
soundness, encourages banks to meet community needs, and engenders greater
trust in banks by the community. Eliminating categories of loan products from
scrutiny will have the opposite effect.

No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test,
which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the
definition of economic development. The CRA should create greater incentives for
banks to support the creation of jobs that pay family sustaining wages for LMI
workers and in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to provisions that would provide
CRA credit for job creation and economic development that may only benefit
 middle- and upper-income workers and communities. Such provisions ignore the
purpose of CRA.

Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA
credit for large scale community infrastructure products that generate profits for
banks, would likely be financed without CRA credit, and provide only incidental
benefits to LMI residents and communities. Such an expansion of what qualifies for
CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities.
For example, banks might choose to more profitably earn CRA credit by financing
larger scale infrastructure projects, like bridges, in lieu of financing less lucrative,
smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local community needs (such as
childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or resilience
projects).

Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA
should require banks to focus their CRA activities on their CRA assessments
areas,[15] where they are subject to more rigorous regulatory oversight (with an
exception made to encourage banks to better serve Tribes, as noted above). Banks
are not doing enough currently to meet the credit and deposit needs in the areas
where they have CRA responsibility, a problem the regulators tried to address in the
2023 CRA Rule.[16] Yet the proposal further encourages banks to seek CRA credit
for projects in areas away from their branches, lending and CRA responsibility. This
will enable banks to get credit for activity outside of their assessment areas, while
providing no accompanying CRA obligation to better serve these areas.

Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal goes
out of its way to encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan option to meet
their CRA responsibilities. The Strategic Plan was meant for financial institutions
that operated under a unique business model that the CRA rules were not designed
to address. The Strategic Plan option provides for minimal public input and
regulatory scrutiny and allows banks to determine the level of reinvestment activity
they need to engage in to earn a passing CRA grade. In our experience, banks with
Strategic Plans tend to reinvest less in the community and in less impactful ways.
The OCC's guidance establishing low community development thresholds for banks
opting for the Strategic Plan, [17] validates this perspective.
 Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community
development efforts with little benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing,
where units are affordable at a point in time but not encumbered by deed or rent
restrictions, are a feature of today's housing market. But CRA rules should not give
banks credit for financing such activities where the benefit to LMI residents and
communities is unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it
can be a driver of bank investment in problematic landlords and displacement. CRA
credit should be given for financing of NOAH only if the project is owned and
operated by mission-driven organizations, where a majority of residents are LMI
tenants, and the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are
compliant with tenant rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents
can reasonably be expected to retain their housing.

 6) Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA
 ratings downgrades.

The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and redline
should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding"
ratings. Under the Biden Administration, at least a dozen banks that passed their
CRA exams were accused of redlining. This proposal will only increase that number
by narrowing what constitutes evidence of discrimination that may be considered
for the purpose of downgrading a bank's CRA rating. Here, regulators should
consider any evidence that a bank, its affiliates, or subsidiaries engaged in
discrimination, redlining, or illegal credit practices as part of their lending, deposit,
branching, or other activities. This evidence should be considered regardless of its
source (public or private parties), or its form (informal complaints, research based
on data, testing results, comment letters, administrative actions, private litigation,
etc.). We also urge the regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity
Act authorizes Special Purpose Credit Programs, and to once again encourage banks
to develop SPCPs to better serve communities that have been redlined, excluded,
and underserved. This is the essence of CRA.

Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information to
allow for meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of
entities and activities, and will undoubtedly harm the communities that the CRA
was meant to support. If finalized in substantially the same form as proposed,
communities will suffer significantly decreased investment in affordable housing and
 CDFI support, more LMI branch closures, higher bank account fees, fewer
community serving nonprofit organizations, and increased bank discrimination and
redlining with no CRA consequence. The CRA will become further removed from its
purpose of encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and
the OCC to reconsider this proposal.

Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Sincerely,

Maddie Ribble
Co-Director
California Community Land Trust Network

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Prosperity Now appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on the Office of the Comptroller of
the Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) proposed amendments to
the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.1

Prosperity Now is a national nonprofit intermediary with nearly five decades of experience working
with financial institutions, community organizations, federal and state agencies, and practitioners to
strengthen household financial stability and expand economic opportunity. Our national network
includes more than 86,000 practitioners and organizations working in housing and homeownership,
entrepreneurship and small business, tax preparation, financial coaching, child and family financial
health, and community finance.

This perspective gives Prosperity Now a practical view of CRA from both sides of the partnership.
We work with financial institutions navigating regulatory requirements and with community
organizations that convert bank lending, investment, grants, and services into resources people use
every day. These include mortgages, small-business capital, affordable financial products, tax
assistance, financial coaching, and housing counseling.

The agencies state that the proposal is intended to better align the CRA framework with the statute,
reduce unnecessary burden, and provide greater clarity. Those are appropriate goals for a durable
regulatory framework. The proposal also recognizes that several changes could alter bank
incentives and create costs or benefits for communities and projects that the agencies do not
currently have enough information to quantify.2

Our comments focus on a key implementation question: how to reduce unnecessary burden while
preserving the incentives, information, and locally responsive partnerships that help translate CRA
into responsible credit and financial services for households and small businesses.

To inform these comments, Prosperity Now also conducted a short survey of 47 community
organizations in September and October 2026. The survey is not nationally representative; we use it
to illustrate how specific provisions in the proposal intersect with current bank-community
partnerships.
 Prosperity Now recommends that the agencies:

 Preserve a meaningful community development component for banks that would move into the
 proposed small-bank category and retain a clear community development standard in the overall
 rating for intermediate banks.

 Adopt the assessment-area approach in Option 2 for determining major product lines, so locally
 significant lending is not excluded simply because it is small relative to a bank's national portfolio.

 Preserve visibility into affordable deposit access and account-opening support to the fullest extent
 permitted by law, even if deposit products are not scored directly under the service test.

 Retain a distinct community development investment component for banks above the current large-
 bank threshold, so that equity and equity-equivalent capital remain visible and separately evaluated.

 Publish the analysis supporting the proposed quantitative geographic flexibility standards and clarify
 that those percentages govern eligibility for outside-assessment-area consideration rather than
 serving as stand-alone performance benchmarks.

 Retain grants and donations as CRA-eligible activities, replace the proposed 15 percent indirect-cost
 ceiling with a more workable standard, and allow general operating, capacity-building, and
 intermediary support when the community development purpose and geography are documented.

 Preserve core standardized reporting for banks that would move out of the large-bank category, using
 a simplified reporting approach where appropriate so that burden can fall without losing the data
 needed to understand local credit conditions.

I. Asset thresholds should be paired with meaningful community development
accountability

Changes to the asset thresholds would reduce compliance and reporting requirements for many
banks, which is an explicit goal of the proposal. They would also move many institutions into
examination categories with fewer community development criteria and less standardized reporting.
The relevant question is whether that relief can be achieved without making locally significant
community development activity less visible or less consequential to CRA performance.

The proposal would define banks with less than $1 billion in assets as small banks, banks generally
between $1 billion and $10 billion as intermediate banks, and banks with more than $10 billion as
large banks. Based on 2024 and 2025 Call Report data, the agencies estimate that approximately
636 of the 3,577 OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks with CRA obligations would fall in the proposed
intermediate category. Only 86 banks, or approximately 2.4 percent, would remain large banks,
although those institutions hold 85.4 percent of industry assets.3

The agencies note that the proposed thresholds would restore roughly the 1995 distribution by asset
share: large banks held 86.2 percent of industry assets in 1995, compared with 85.4 percent under
the proposal. The share of institutions classified as large, however, would fall from 19.6 percent in
1995 to 2.4 percent under the proposal.
 Both measures matter. Asset share supports tailoring regulation by bank size, but institution count
matters in local markets where a bank that is small nationally may still be an important mortgage
lender, small-business lender, community development investor, or nonprofit partner. In Prosperity
Now's survey, 36 of 47 respondents reported current bank support; 23 serve rural areas and 22
serve small cities or towns. These figures are not nationally representative, but they underscore why
local market significance should be considered alongside national asset share. Over 85 percent of
counties with persistent poverty are rural, and any reduction in services funded through CRA
activities are likely to be particularly acute in those communities who are least able to absorb it.

The proposal also requests comment on an alternative intermediate-bank cap of $3.252 billion, the
2020 level adjusted for inflation, rather than $10 billion. The proposal presents that cap as a stand-
alone alternative, although the FDIC analyzes it together with an $850 million small-bank threshold
for economic-analysis purposes. Prosperity Now supports the $3.252 billion intermediate-bank cap
because it would still provide meaningful regulatory relief while retaining the large-bank framework
for more institutions.

The proposal would also remove the investment test for banks between $1.649 billion and $10 billion
that are currently subject to it. Those institutions would be evaluated on lending and community
development performance without a separate assessment of qualified investments.

Investment is not interchangeable with lending. Equity and equity-equivalent capital can play a
distinct role in affordable housing, CDFIs, and other community development transactions and
cannot always be replaced with debt on equivalent terms.

Prosperity Now recommends that the agencies retain a distinct investment component in the
evaluation of intermediate banks above the current large-bank threshold. If the agencies prefer a
single community development conclusion, examinations should at minimum record qualified
investment activity separately within it so that changes in investment activity remain visible.

The proposal would also establish geographic flexibility standards that determine when banks may
receive consideration for community development activities outside their assessment areas. Under
quantitative Option 1, a large bank would need to meet 0.625 percent of allocated Tier 1 capital for
community development loans and 0.625 percent for community development investments and
grants; intermediate, wholesale, and limited-purpose banks would need to meet 1.25 percent in
aggregate. The proposal explains that these standards are based on supervisory experience and
are intended as minimum thresholds for broader geographic consideration, not as stand-alone
measures of community development performance. Because the percentages could nonetheless
influence CRA planning, commenters should be able to understand how they were calibrated and
how they compare with current activity.

Prosperity Now recommends that the agencies publish the supporting analysis used to calibrate the
quantitative standards and state clearly in the final rule and guidance that meeting a geographic
flexibility standard determines eligibility for outside-assessment-area consideration but is not
sufficient, by itself, to determine community development performance.

The proposed threshold changes would also change how community development performance
affects ratings. Banks between $412 million and $1 billion that are intermediate small banks under
the current framework would move into the small-bank framework and no longer receive a separate
community development test. For intermediate banks, the proposal would permit an overall
 satisfactory rating without a satisfactory community development rating when the lending-test
standard is met.4

Prosperity Now supports proportionate supervision. We recommend, however, that the agencies
preserve a simplified community development component for banks between $412 million and $1
billion and retain the current principle that community development performance must be satisfactory
for an intermediate bank to receive an overall satisfactory rating. This would reduce reporting and
examination burden without making community development optional in the overall rating.

II. Major product lines should be determined at the assessment-area level

The proposal presents two approaches for determining which retail product lines receive CRA
evaluation. Option 1 would generally select the two largest product lines at the institution level based
on loan count and dollar volume. Option 2 would determine major product lines in each assessment
area based on the bank's lending volume and business strategy, its capacity to lend in that area,
and whether the product meaningfully contributes to meeting local credit needs. The agencies
specifically ask in Question 7 whether, if Option 1 is adopted, major product lines should instead be
determined by assessment area.5

Prosperity Now recommends Option 2. A product can be small at the institution level and still be
important in a local market. The proposal itself gives the example of small-farm lending that is not a
significant share of a bank's overall portfolio but is significant in a nonmetropolitan assessment area.
The same logic can apply to small-dollar mortgages, manufactured-housing finance, home-
rehabilitation lending, microenterprise credit, and other products that may serve a specific local
need.

Prosperity Now's field survey reinforces the local-product concern. Asked which loan products their
communities depend on but have difficulty finding from other lenders, 25 of 47 respondents selected
small-business microloans, 21 credit-builder loans, 20 small-dollar mortgages, 17 ITIN lending, and
13 manufactured-housing loans. These are examples of products that can be locally significant
without being among a bank's largest national product lines.

This is where examination design reaches the kitchen table. A small mortgage can determine
whether an affordable home is financeable. A rehabilitation loan can determine whether a
homeowner can replace a roof or heating system without relying on higher-cost credit. A small
business loan can cover equipment, payroll, inventory, or a temporary cash flow gap. The local
importance of those products is not always captured by their share of a national balance sheet.

III. Affordable deposit access should remain visible in the CRA framework

The proposal would narrow the retail banking services considered under CRA to credit services and
would exclude deposit products from that portion of the service test. The agencies explain that this
approach reflects their reading of CRA's statutory focus and the litigation surrounding the 2023 rule.6

The practical relationship between deposits and credit still matters. An affordable transaction
account is where wages are deposited, bills are paid, tax refunds arrive, emergency savings are
held, and a banking relationship begins. Fees, minimum balances, overdraft practices, and account
 access affect how much money remains available for housing, food, transportation, childcare, debt
payments, and savings.

Prosperity Now's 2026 Scorecard analysis provides a useful context. Nationally, 14.7 percent of
households lack enough readily accessible financial assets to cover three months of basic
expenses, only 64.2 percent report saving for emergencies, and 36.6 percent report difficulty paying
their usual household expenses. These measures do not show what the proposed CRA change
would cause, but they show why the cost and usability of basic financial products matter to
household financial stability.7

One VITA provider in the survey described a bank partnership that allows clients to open an account
quickly enough to add the account number to a tax return, supporting direct deposit and tax-time
saving. This example illustrates the practical connection between deposit access, and the other
financial services families use.

To the fullest extent permitted by the statute and applicable court orders, the agencies should
preserve visibility into affordable deposit access, account-opening support, and the relationship
between deposit services and local credit needs. If the agencies conclude that deposit products
cannot be scored directly, they should establish a clear monitoring and disclosure approach so
regulators and the public can identify material changes in the availability and cost of basic banking
services over time.

IV. Grants should remain CRA-eligible, and the indirect-cost standard should
measure use of funds rather than organizational worth

The proposal would create a separate definition of a community development grant. A grant
generally would need to be directly used by the recipient for a program, project, or initiative with a
primary purpose of community development and benefit the bank's assessment area, subject to the
proposal's geographic provisions. For a large-bank grant, the recipient's indirect costs for
administering the grant could not exceed 15 percent. The bank would also need written
commitments, an attestation regarding indirect costs, and supporting documentation including IRS
Form 990 information and operating and program budgets.8

The proposal's own example shows the practical consequence: a grant to an organization providing
homeownership counseling and health care services, with approximately 25 percent of the grant
reported as internal expenses, would no longer qualify for CRA consideration for a large bank.
Question 9 asks whether alternative standards should be considered for indirect costs. Question 10
asks whether grants and donations should instead be eliminated from CRA consideration entirely.9

Prosperity Now recommends that grants and donations remain eligible for CRA consideration.
Grants can support activities that lending alone cannot finance, including housing counseling,
financial coaching, free tax preparation, small-business technical assistance, outreach, compliance
systems, and the staff and technology that allow those services to operate reliably.

These funding types are common among survey respondents. Thirty of 47 organizations reported
receiving bank grants. Of those 30, 19 reported general operating support, 11 capacity-building
support, and 24 restricted program or project grants; respondents could select more than one
category. Examples included VITA staffing and supplies, home-repair programs, no-cost small-
business coaching, and year-round tax-preparation outreach.
 The proposed 15 percent limit could make otherwise effective community development grants
ineligible for CRA consideration based on an organization's cost structure rather than the value of
the work being funded. Indirect costs support functions such as financial management, compliance,
technology, supervision, insurance, and facilities that allow programs to operate effectively. These
costs can weigh most heavily on smaller organizations, where fixed costs like audits and insurance
are spread across a smaller budget. The proposed regulatory text applies the limit "consistent with
the Uniform Guidance," under which the 15 percent de minimis rate is applied to modified total direct
costs. The preamble, however, describes the limit as 15 percent "of the grant or donation dollar
amount." Those approaches can produce different results for the same grant. OMB established the
15 percent de minimis rate as an optional method intended to allow more realistic recovery of
indirect costs, particularly for organizations without a negotiated rate, not as a determination that
indirect costs above 15 percent are excessive.10

In the survey, three grant recipients reported that more than 15 percent of their bank grant funding
typically goes toward indirect or overhead costs, six reported about 15 percent, and three were
unsure. Because the survey used a plain-language question about indirect or overhead costs rather
than a Uniform Guidance calculation, these responses should not be treated as a count of
organizations that would fail the proposed standard. They do show that the threshold and calculation
method are material to current grant recipients and should be clear and workable.

Prosperity Now recommends that the agencies remove the fixed 15 percent limit. If a limit is
retained, the agencies should calculate it consistently with the Uniform Guidance and accept an
organization's federally negotiated indirect cost rate, the federal de minimis method, or another
consistent and documented method for allocating reasonable indirect costs.

A more workable standard would require the bank to document the grant's community development
purpose, expected geography, and reasonable allocation of direct and indirect costs, while
permitting recipients to rely on an existing negotiated indirect-cost rate, the federal de minimis
method, or another consistently applied cost-allocation method. General operating support, capacity-
building grants, and intermediary grants should remain eligible when the recipient can document
how the funding supports qualifying community development activity.

The agencies should also avoid duplicative documentation. Existing Form 990s, audited financial
statements, approved budgets, grant agreements, and established indirect-cost policies can provide
evidence without requiring organizations to build a separate compliance system solely for CRA
grants.

V. Reduced reporting should not make local credit conditions harder to see

Standardized data are central to effective CRA oversight and public accountability. The proposal
would reduce data collection, maintenance, and reporting requirements for institutions that move out
of the large-bank category. The OCC estimates that 126 OCC-supervised large banks would be
reclassified as intermediate banks and would no longer be subject to existing and proposed large-
bank data-reporting requirements. The FDIC separately estimates that 250 FDIC-supervised banks
would move from the large-bank to the intermediate-bank framework under the proposed thresholds.
The agencies also recognize that the proposal may reduce standardized CRA data available for
some banks.11
 Standardized data have value beyond compliance. They allow regulators, banks, researchers, local
governments, and community organizations to compare performance across institutions and
geographies, identify changes in mortgage or small-business lending, and determine whether
similarly situated markets are receiving materially different levels of activity.

Prosperity Now recommends that the agencies preserve a core set of standardized public data for
banks that are above the current large-bank threshold but would move into the proposed
intermediate category. A simplified reporting schedule could reduce burden while maintaining the
trend data needed to understand how the new framework is operating in practice.

VI. The public comment record should be used to fill the evidence gaps the agencies
identify

The FDIC states that it does not have enough information to accurately quantify several effects of
the proposal, including potential distributional changes in community development activity. That
uncertainty is a reason to build a stronger record, not to assume either that the changes will have no
effect or that a particular level of funding will disappear.12

The agencies' own regulatory analysis identifies "Reduced Standardized Data and Comparability,"
"Reduced Support for Some Nonprofit and Intermediary Activities," and "Potential Geographic
Reallocation Away From Assessment Areas" as potential secondary burdens. The agencies also
state that the magnitude of these effects is difficult to quantify, making field evidence especially
useful in evaluating the final rule.13

Prosperity Now's survey provides a preliminary view of those mechanisms. Of 47 respondents, 36
reported current bank support and 30 reported bank grants. Respondents described support for
VITA, housing counseling and home repair, financial coaching, small business technical assistance,
and other community services. The survey is not nationally representative, and we do not
extrapolate it to estimate national funding losses. Instead, it provides direct evidence that the
activities the agencies identify as potentially affected are present in current bank-community
partnerships. We also encourage the agencies to publish, where feasible, a post-implementation
plan for monitoring changes in specialized lending, community development activity, grants, and
data availability. A clear measurement plan would allow future adjustments to be based on observed
outcomes rather than assumptions.

Conclusion

CRA modernization presents a legitimate opportunity to improve clarity, consistency, and
administrative efficiency. The proposal also changes several of the mechanisms through which bank
performance is measured, weighted, and reported. Those design choices can influence which
activities receive staff time, capital, grants, and executive attention.

Prosperity Now therefore recommends that the agencies preserve meaningful community
development accountability as bank thresholds change; adopt an assessment-area approach to
major product lines; keep affordable deposit access visible; retain grants while replacing the
proposed 15 percent ceiling with a more workable cost standard; and preserve enough standardized
reporting to measure what happens after the rule changes.
 These recommendations are intended to support a CRA framework that is clear and workable for
financial institutions while remaining connected to the real financial decisions households and small
businesses make every day. We appreciate the agencies' consideration of these comments and the
field evidence included in this record.

Sincerely,

Marisa Calderon
President & CEO
Prosperity Now

Re: Mountain View Community Land Trust opposes the OCC and FDIC proposed CRA
rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould:

The Mountain View Community Land Trust (MVCLT) opposes the changes you have proposed
to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. Congress passed the CRA in 1977 to end
redlining and to require banks to meet the credit needs of the communities where they take
deposits, including low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities. The proposal would weaken
that obligation at the moment our community needs it most. We ask that you extend the
comment period by 60 days so the public, and organizations like ours, can conduct the analysis
that the proposal lacks to determine just how much CRA activity communities stand to lose and
then engage with stakeholders in good faith to review the rules.

MVCLT is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit in Mountain View, California, in the center of Silicon Valley.
We buy existing apartment buildings and hold the land in trust, so the homes stay affordable
permanently and the families who live in them are not displaced. Residents share in governing
the organization through our Leadership Council, which works alongside our Board of Directors.

 1
 We are working with the City of Mountain View, under its Community Ownership Action Plan,
toward our first acquisition: a multifamily building for households earning at or below 50 percent
of area median income. Rents in our model are set at 30 percent of household income. That lets
us house families who earn too little to qualify for most affordable housing.

Our work is CRA in action

The most urgent unmet need in Mountain View is keeping working families in the homes they
already have. Older, unsubsidized apartment buildings house many of the lowest-paid workers in
our community. When those buildings sell, speculative buyers raise rents or redevelop, and long-
time residents leave the city.

A community land trust can stop that only if it can close on a building. Our acquisition financing
will rely on public funds, philanthropic grants, and loans from Community Development
Financial Institutions (CDFIs). Roughly half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from CRA-
motivated banks. When banks pull back, CDFI capital becomes more scarce and more expensive,
and will forestall our ability to invest in the housing our community desperately needs.

Preservation deals are small, slow, and low-return. Banks finance them, directly or through
CDFIs, because CRA examiners count them. If a bank can pass its exam without that work, we
have every reason to expect it will stop doing it.

1. Do not raise the asset thresholds or lower the bar for community development finance.

Raising the thresholds for Small, Intermediate, and Large Banks would cut reinvestment
obligations for 70 California banks, according to NCRC analysis. Twenty-five would shed their
Community Development Test entirely, and 45 would no longer face the Investment Test. These
are the regional and community banks most likely to know a market like ours and to take a first
meeting with a new land trust.

The proposal also signals that a bank can pass with community development loans and
investments equal to just 0.625 percent of Tier 1 capital. NCRC estimates that if banks did only
that much, community development activity would fall by about $87.1 billion, or 85 percent. The
Investment Test is what drives bank capital into CDFIs and into equity-equivalent (EQ2)
investments that help land trusts take property off the speculative market. We urge you to keep
the current thresholds and reject the alternative $30 billion Large Bank definition.

2. Do not restrict bank grants to nonprofits.

The proposal would require grants to be tied to specific community development projects and
would bar Large Bank grantees from spending more than 15 percent on overhead. It even asks
whether grants should lose CRA credit altogether.

 2
 For a young land trust, capacity is the project. Before we can close on a single building, we must
pay for staff, resident organizing, legal work, and the stewardship systems that keep homes
affordable for generations. General operating and capacity-building grants pay for exactly that. A
15 percent cap, and the paperwork to prove compliance with it, would steer bank giving toward
large established organizations and away from small, resident-led groups like ours. Grants are
less than 1 percent of CRA activity; restricting them does serious harm for no evident gain.
3. Limit CRA credit for unrestricted "naturally occurring" affordable housing to mission-
driven owners.
The buildings we aim to preserve are naturally occurring affordable housing. So are the buildings
that speculative investors buy in order to raise rents. Broad CRA credit for financing these
properties would reward banks for funding the buyers we compete against.
Credit should be given only where the owner is a mission-driven organization, a majority of
residents are LMI, and the bank can show the transaction complies with tenant protections and
anti-displacement principles. A community land trust acquisition meets that test. A value-add
investor's does not.
4. Keep CRA activity in the communities where banks take deposits.
The proposal would let banks earn credit for projects far from their branches and assessment
areas. Silicon Valley generates enormous deposits. The CRA should keep requiring banks to
reinvest here, for the LMI residents who live and work here, rather than letting them choose
easier projects elsewhere.
We also share the concerns raised by Rise Economy and its members about lost branches and
affordable bank accounts, reduced data reporting, weak provisions for Tribes, and the narrowing
of evidence of discrimination that can lower a bank's rating.
Conclusion
If this proposal is finalized as written, less bank capital will reach affordable housing
preservation, CDFIs, and the small nonprofits that do this work. In Mountain View, that means
fewer buildings saved and more families displaced. We urge the FDIC and the OCC to withdraw
the proposal and to strengthen, not loosen, banks' obligations to LMI communities.
Thank you for considering our comments.

 3
 Sincerely,
Olga Melo
Olga Melo
Co-Founder
Mountain View Community Land Trust
olga@mvclt.org / 650-669-2641

reinvest here, for the LMI residents who live and work here, rather than letting them choose
easier projects elsewhere.
We also share the concerns raised by Rise Economy and its members about lost branches and
affordable bank accounts, reduced data reporting, weak provisions for Tribes, and the narrowing
of evidence of discrimination that can lower a bank's rating.
Conclusion
If this proposal is finalized as written, less bank capital will reach affordable housing
preservation, CDFIs, and the small nonprofits that do this work. In Mountain View, that means
fewer buildings saved and more families displaced. We urge the FDIC and the OCC to withdraw
the proposal and to strengthen, not loosen, banks' obligations to LMI communities.
Thank you for considering our comments.
