consideration and how those activities are weighted in CRA performance evaluations.

5. The Practical Case for National-Footprint Lending

Axos Bank, as a digital institution with a national lending platform, is well positioned to deploy capital
rapidly to communities affected by major disasters or designated as Opportunity Zones. The Bank's digital
infrastructure enables it to originate and service loans in these areas without the lead time required to
establish physical branch presence. Under the current and proposed frameworks, however, much of this
lending activity receives no or only secondary CRA credit because it occurs outside the Bank's three-city
assessment area footprint. Automatic credit for Disaster and Opportunity Zone lending would align CRA
incentives with the institutional capacity that digital banks bring to these communities, ensuring that the
CRA framework encourages, rather than ignores, the capital flows that Congress intended to stimulate.

III. Additional Comments on Selected Provisions

1. Major Product Line Approach

Axos does support the adoption of a major product line standard for all banks and urges the agency to
review all qualifying activity during the examination process.

2. Exclusion of Deposit Services from the Service Test

Axos supports the proposed narrowing of the service test to evaluate only the range and availability of a
bank's "credit services," excluding deposit products.17 This revision correctly aligns the service test with
the CRA's statutory mandate to assess a bank's record of meeting the "credit needs" of its community. The
CRA is, at its core, a credit statute, and the service test should reflect that focus.

3. Asset Size Thresholds

Axos supports the proposed revision of asset size thresholds to establish three clearly defined categories:
small banks (less than $1 billion), intermediate banks ($1 billion to $10 billion), and large banks (more than
$10 billion).18 These thresholds appropriately realign the CRA framework with the current structure of the
banking industry and with the distribution of banks that existed when the 1995 CRA rules were adopted.
The proposed thresholds will reduce unnecessary compliance burden for community and mid-size banks
while maintaining robust evaluation standards for large institutions, including Axos.

4. Community Development Grants

Axos does not support the Agencies' current 15 percent indirect expense threshold19 as it does not make
allowances for smaller, community organizations that offer housing, job training and placement, and/or
other services that involve substantial indirect costs but meaningfully reach the communities they are

income levels, excluding deposit services).

banks (more than $10 billion). 91 Fed. Reg. at 5212052122.

 intended to benefit. The raw numeric threshold is thus not a reasonable guardrail against rent extraction by
intermediary organizations.

5. CD Activity Confirmation Process

Axos supports the proposed codification of a process under which banks may seek agency confirmation
that a CD activity qualifies for CRA consideration.20 Pre-activity confirmation provides certainty and
enables banks to allocate resources to activities with the greatest community impact. Axos encourages the
Agencies to ensure that the confirmation process operates with reasonable speed and finality.

IV. Conclusion

Axos Bank supports the Proposed Rule as a well-calibrated set of reforms that preserves the core CRA
framework while making targeted improvements to reduce burden, increase clarity, and refocus the
regulatory structure on the statute's credit needs mandate. The Bank particularly commends the Agencies'
fidelity to the deposit-facility-based assessment area framework, which is both legally sound and
operationally effective.
Axos respectfully urges the Agencies to adopt one additional provision: automatic, unconditional CRA
credit for all lending, service, and investment activity within FEMA Major Disaster Declaration areas and
IRS Qualified Opportunity Zones, regardless of whether those census tracts fall within the bank's
assessment area. This mechanism would align the CRA with existing Federal designations of community
need, incentivize capital deployment to the areas Congress has identified as requiring accelerated
investment, and preserve the integrity of the deposit-facility-based assessment area framework.
Your time and consideration are greatly appreciated.

 Very truly yours,

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations Proposed Rule (Docket ID Occ-2026-0694)

To Whom It May Concern:

Thank you for the opportunity to provide feedback on the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposal to reform
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. I am writing to you today on behalf of the
Illinois Housing Council (IHC), a coalition of nearly 300 private businesses and nonprofit
organizations committed to building and preserving affordable housing across Illinois. Our
organization works at the intersection of public efforts and private business, connecting
investors and developers with agencies and nonprofits. Our organization also advocates for
policies that enable the creation of more homes and economic growth across Illinois, including
in rural and under-resourced areas. Several of our members are banks that actively and
enthusiastically participate in community investment and development thanks to the CRA.

For nearly half a century, CRA has driven banks to extend private capital financing to local
communities they serve, combating the legacy of redlining, promoting equitable lending,
and facilitating reinvestment in low- and moderate-income places and people. CRA has
spurred lending and investments in homeownership, small businesses, healthcare,
childcare, and other community needs, but nowhere is its impact more pronounced than in
the effect CRA has had on the production of affordable rental housing through the Low
Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing Credit) program.

The Housing Credit, our nation's most important tool for the production of affordable rental
housing, relies heavily on investments from banks subject to CRA. In fact, approximately 80
percent of equity investments in the Housing Credit each year come from CRA-motivated
bank investors, according to a 2025 study by the accounting firm CohnReznick. Banks
make these investments not only to receive the modest return provided by the tax
advantages associated with investing in Housing Credit properties, but also because the
full CRA examination for large banks includes a distinct investment test. Because Housing
Credit investment yields are typically modest, large banks often could get a more

ADVANCING AFF ORDAB ILITY IN ILLINOIS 310 S Peoria Suite 500 Chicago, IL 60607
 substantial yield from making other forms of investment, but often still choose to invest in
the Housing Credit because Housing Credit investments help banks meet their CRA
obligations.

We are concerned that OCC and FDIC's proposal to reclassify banks with assets ranging
from $1.649 billion to $10 billion as intermediate banks rather than large banks subject to
the full CRA examination, including the investment test, could reduce competition in the
Housing Credit equity market, leading to lower pricing on credits and less housing
produced. Of the 642 banks currently classified as large banks, only 256 would maintain that
designation under the proposal--a decline of over 60 percent, according to the
National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders (NAAHL). This leaves only 6 percent of
banks in the current large bank classification subject to the full CRA exam. According to a
survey by the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC), banks with assets in the
$1.649 billion to $10 billion range invested at least $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity over
the five-year survey period. Extrapolating these results to the full Housing Credit market,
banks in this asset range invested up to $2 billion in Housing Credit equity over the past five
years.

If the OCC/FDIC proposal is made final, newly classified intermediate banks would no
longer need to invest in the low and moderate-income communities they are supposed to
serve because they would no longer be subject to the investment test, despite still having
more general community development obligations as an intermediate-sized bank. This is
because, for various reasons, it is often easier for banks to support community
development activities through lending rather than equity investment.

Moreover, the CRA Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) undercuts recent congressional
action to strengthen and expand the Housing Credit and facilitate more bank investment in
the program. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (also known as the Working Families Tax Cuts
Act) included a substantial increase in Housing Credit authority and expanded the 4
Percent Housing Credit program to increase supply, while the 21st Century ROAD to
Housing Act raised the limit on banks' public welfare investments (PWI) to allow them to
increase their Housing Credit investments. The provision lifting the PWI cap would mostly
impact many of the same banks that would be reclassified as intermediate banks. Thus,
the CRA changes under consideration by the OCC and FDIC could greatly dilute these
legislative accomplishments and undercut congressional goals of providing more
affordable rental homes.

The consequences of this proposal would be most damaging to smaller communities that
now benefit from being in the CRA assessment area of one or more large banks but may no
longer be if the OCC and FDIC change the definition of large bank as proposed. A survey by
Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition finds that approximately one-third of Housing Credit
equity invested through syndicators by banks in the $412 million $10 billion asset range

ADVANCING AFF ORDAB ILITY IN ILLINOIS 310 S Peoria Suite 500 Chicago, IL 60607
 supported rural markets between 2021 and 2024, indicating that these banks play an outsized
role in investing in smaller communities. Credit pricing for properties in many urban areas--
which are more likely to have at least one and often multiple banks competing to invest in
Housing Credit developments because of overlapping assessment areas--tends to be much
higher than pricing in rural and other smaller communities that are not part of assessment
areas for large banks subject to the investment test.

Alternatives to the Primary Proposal

The OCC and FDIC included two alternatives to the primary proposal to set new thresholds
for various bank size classifications related to CRA. The first would raise the large bank
asset threshold from $1.649 billion to $3.252 billion. This alternative would still have far
reaching negative consequences compared to the current large bank threshold but is
substantially less disruptive to Housing Credit investment than the primary proposal to
raise the large bank threshold to $10 billion.

According to AHTCC's survey of bank investment in the Housing Credit, 108 banks would
be reclassified as intermediate banks rather than large banks if the threshold is set at $10
billion, while just 40 would be reclassified as intermediate banks if the large bank threshold
is set at $3.252 billion. Moreover, the banks that would remain subject to the separate
investment test under a $3.252 billion threshold account for approximately 86 percent of
the Housing Credit equity investment by OCC- and FDIC-regulated banks captured in the
AHTCC survey with assets between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.

The second alternative proposal would be far more damaging for affordable rental housing
production than either the primary or first alternative proposals. NAAHL estimates that,
under a $30 billion large bank threshold, 17 states would see the number of large banks
with investment requirements cut by half or more. According to AHTCC, banks with assets
between $10 billion and $30 billion account for more than twice as much Housing Credit
debt and equity investment as banks between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.

Conclusion

The Illinois Hosing Council has seen the impact of CRA firsthand. The Housing Tax Credit
market is fueled by CRA investment. Our rural members, in particular, benefit from the CRA
promoting and ensuring investment in regions that would typically be cut off from bank-
supported community development. Our members report that the proposed changes are likely
to concentrate remaining CRA funds in urban and suburban locations, leaving rural communities
without the investment they need to build new and preserve existing housing. These rule
changes will absolutely increase uncertainty and burden for communities through Illinois, and
do not align with the CRA's statutory purpose.

ADVANCING AFF ORDAB ILITY IN ILLINOIS 310 S Peoria Suite 500 Chicago, IL 60607
 We strongly encourage the OCC and FDIC to leave the thresholds as they currently stand
under the 1995 CRA rule, consistent with the direction the Federal Reserve--the third bank
regulator--appears to be taking. If the OCC and FDIC move forward with changes to CRA
regulations, we strongly urge maintaining the lowest possible threshold for large banks and
adopting policies to strengthen the Housing Credit market in all communities, including
rural and smaller markets.
Sincerely,
Allison Clements
Executive Director
Illinois Housing Council

7. Revise the definition of a "renewal" under the regulation

 a. A common form of financing for small businesses is asset-based
 lending, which is frequently extended in the form of secured
 revolving lines of credit in which assets such as accounts receivable
 and inventory are pledged to secure a loan. To preserve the priority
 and continuity of its security interest a lender will almost always use
 a demand note (otherwise every time a new note is issued the
 lender's secured interest is interrupted and another lender may get a
 priority in the collateral). Historically, the CRA forbids the recognition
 of these loans because they don't meet the definition of a "renewal"
 as applied by the regulation (see A Guide to CRA Data Collection and
 Reporting, "Note: A demand loan that is reviewed on an annual basis
 should not be reported as a renewal because the term of the loan has
 not been extended").21 This results in disqualification of a large
 volume of small business lending from recognition in CRA small
 business loan data.

 b. We also point out that there is a contradiction between this CRA
 practice and the Call Report rules governing reporting small business
 loans. The Call Report rules do not exclude the reporting of secured
 revolving lines of credit that are renewed by banks and evidenced by
 demand notes. This conflict should be resolved. The CRA rules for
 reporting small business loans should be consistent with the Call
 Report rules.

 a. Ever since the 1995 Rule was effective, we've known that examiners
 compare a bank's performance to that of its competitors and to
 certain demographic data in their assessment area. While we've

 calibration points. This lack of clarity has always been a source of

 calibration points, but made it unbelievably complex with all sorts of
 weighting factors and "supporting conclusions" and "recommended
 conclusions" all of which had to be accumulated and adjusted at ever
 increasing geographic levels. We suggest the agencies adopt the
 calibration concept but apply the "KISS" principle, limiting the
 comparisons to each AA.

 It is not clear if that threshold applies to the entire examination
 period or is an annual threshold. Given that small banks and
 intermediate-small banks are now on a 5-year CRA exam schedule,

 entire evaluation period. This needs to be clarified.

 The CRA regulations don't need to be completely overturned. Some minor

take steps toward clarifying community development, what qualifies as
community development and what it is compared against. Those are much
needed changes. But the drastic reduction in reporters offers little if any benefit
(even non reporters are expected to fulfill their CRA responsibilities) and causes

comparisons impossible for all but for 86 of the 3,577 banks regulated by the OCC
and the FDIC. That result is harmful to 98% of all CRA-governed institutions.

by only 2-3% of lenders. At the very least all banks that have community
development responsibilities should be mandated reporters.

community development data that is published. If bankers are required to collect
the expanded data, there is no burden to reporting it. This is a great opportunity
to correct a critical information deficiency.

Len Suzio | GeoDataVision

How 2 Dominant Lenders Distort the CRA "Borrower Characteristics" Benchmark

In my previous article I wrote about how two lenders, American Express and JPMorgan Chase captured a
market share of 53.3% of all small business loans reported by FDIC and OCC-regulated CRA lenders
during 2024. This market dominance has important implications for the other 3,575 lenders examined by
the two bank regulators. With this concentrated loan market, the activity of the two top lenders can easily
distort the benchmarks used by examiners to evaluate a bank's lending to mom and pop businesses.
One of the important lending tests administered in a CRA exam is the "Borrower Characteristics" test which
measures how much lending banks are extending to smaller businesses as measured by "Gross Annual
Revenue" of $1 million or less. Examiners compare the percentage of a bank's small business loans to
smaller mom and pop businesses to the average "penetration rate" of other CRA-reporters within a bank's
local market (assessment area). When a market is dominated by a couple of lenders their activity can
easily distort the performance "benchmarks".
The 2024 CRA national data shows how dramatically two dominant lenders can affect the Borrower
Characteristics Benchmark. The graphic below summarizes the situation.

The table shows that AMEX extended 19.10% of its small business lending to smaller business borrowers.
For JPMorgan Chase, the results were almost diametrically the opposite, with 75.77%, its lending extended
to small businesses.
How did the activity of those two lenders affect the market smaller business borrower penetration rate? The
graphic below provides the answer.

GeoDataVision | geodatavision.com 1
 The smaller business borrower penetration rate for the entire United States was 54.3%. If American
Express's relatively (19.10%) low activity is removed from the calculation for the entire country the
benchmark would increase from 54.3% to 67.4%. Imagine that, a single lender effectively lowered the
national benchmark by 13.1%!

The activity of JPMorgan Chase had an almost equally dramatic impact in the opposite direction. If
JPMorgan's activity were excluded from the national data, the benchmark would decrease from 54.3% to
46.7%. So, the activity of the second most active small business lender raised the bar 8.4% for the entire
country.

If the activity of both lenders were trimmed from the national average the result would show a penetration
rate of 62.7% extended to smaller businesses.

This has big implications for the other 3,575 lenders subject to CRA examination by the OCC or the FDIC.

The 2026 CRA NPR, by reducing the number of mandatory CRA reporters to about 86 will increase the
concentration of lending into only a few banks thereby distorting CRA performance benchmarks all the
more.

There is a big irony in the NPR.

Although the proposal reduces the number of mandatory reporters it does not reduce by a single bank the
number of lenders accountable for performing under CRA.

The "relief" from reporting under CRA is a trap to reduce possible bank opposition to the NPR.

But what sensible and prudent banker would not collect and monitor data that is used by examiners to
determine if they pass or fail their CRA exam?

GeoDataVision | geodatavision.com 2
 As I have said in other articles, the cost of collecting and reporting CRA data for most community banks
should be very small. I estimate $3,000 to $5,000 annually. The FFIEC offers free software and the data
entry time and costs for a bank that originates fewer than 50 loans annually has got to be minimal.

The regulators preach that banks should be monitoring their compliance risk. But the NPR discourages
almost all banks from capturing the data they need to identify and manage that risk.

Could the CRA NPR Eliminate Examination of

Len Suzio | GeoDataVision

The 2026 CRA NPR proposes a concept called "Major Product Line" ("MPL") that potentially would
eliminate the CRA examination of small farm lending by major small farm lenders. The concept, proposed
by regulators as a form of regulatory "relief", would limit CRA examinations to the two most active loan
products offered by a bank. The products include HMDA-reported mortgages, small business loans, small
farm loans, and consumer loans.

A review of the 2024 HMDA and CRA-reported lending activity indicates that for most banks, residential
mortgages and small business loans far exceed the number of small farm loans. Lenders reported almost
6.2 Million mortgages originated during 2024. FDIC- and OCC-regulated CRA-reporters extended almost
8.5 million small business loans but only a little more than 162 thousand small farm mortgages. Clearly,
small farm lending is dwarfed by residential mortgages and small business loans - and that justifies concern
about how often small farm loans would qualify as an MPL and be subject to CRA examination.

A dramatic comparison can be seen in the graphs below that compare small business and small farm
lending.

The average number of small business loans by lender was 16,033 compared to only 503 small farm loans
per lender.

Even when compared based on the median number of loans the contrast is dramatic as can be seen in the
graphs below:

GeoDataVision | geodatavision.com 1
 These numbers would leave one to wonder what the impact of the MPL concept will be on CRA
performance evaluations. It certainly would suggest that small farm lending often would not qualify as a
major product line and therefore would not be examined during a CRA exam.

A review of the top 2024 small farm lenders appears to confirm that small farm lending may not be
examined under the major product line concept for the most active small farm lenders because the volume
of their small business loans far exceeds the volume of small farm loans in 6 of the top 7 small farm
lenders. This shows that under Option 1, at the institutional level, the MPL concept would disqualify small
farm loans from CRA examinations of many of the most active small farm lenders.

GeoDataVision | geodatavision.com 2
 GeoDataVision followed up on this analysis by reviewing the CRA Public Performance Evaluations for 6 of
the 7 lenders with high volumes of small business loans relative to small farm loans. That review identified
only 3 assessment areas in which the lender's small farm lending would qualify under the MPL concept
when compared to the lender's small business and HMDA-reported lending.

The foregoing data appears to confirm the suspicion that many of the biggest and most active small farm
lenders will not have their small farm lending scrutinized by examiners during a CRA exam. Effectively, the
major product line concept would relegate small farm lending to second class status, a highly undesirable
result for markets where agriculture may be the dominant economic sector.

If the major product line concept is adopted it should be applied at the assessment area level under Option
2 for implementing the MPL concept, not the institution level as proposed under Option 1. But even that
may not resolve the problem because, as we discovered after reviewing the CRA performance evaluations
of the #2 to #7 leading small farm lenders, even for the most active small farm lenders their small farm
lending often may not qualify as a MPL. Again, the data captured in those CRA public evaluations indicated
that small farm loans would have qualified as a major product line in only 3 assessment areas!

The major reason given by regulators for the major product line concept was to provide a form of regulatory
relief. But any lender engaged in a significant volume of small farm lending (such as lenders #2 through 7
above) would still be required to capture and report all their small farm lending. So, the relief provided by
adoption of the major product line concept may be illusory, perhaps non-existent.

Regulators may want to reconsider their proposal to adopt the major product line concept. The relegation of
small farm lending to second-class status and the minimal if non-existent regulatory relief undermine any
rationale for adoption of the flawed concept.

The 2026 CRA NPR: The Bombshell in Plain
Sight No One Has Reported

Len Suzio | GeoDataVision

Download

Coverage has focused on the proposed changes in bank-size categories. But the proposed Tier 1-capital
benchmarks for community development may be the far more consequential story.

The reported story

Most news coverage of the 2026 Community Reinvestment Act Notice of Proposed Rulemaking has
focused on the proposed changes in bank-size categories.

That focus is understandable. Under the proposal, a small bank would be an institution with assets of no
more than $1 billion, an intermediate bank would have more than $1 billion but no more than $10 billion,
and a large bank would have more than $10 billion in assets.

Those classifications determine which tests apply, which data must be collected and how a bank will be
examined.

But that may not be the biggest story in the 407-page proposal.

GeoDataVision | geodatavision.com 1
 What's the big story?

Buried in the proposal is a quantitative standard based on Tier 1 capital for community development
lending, investments and grants.

Under the quantitative option proposed by the OCC and FDIC:

 Annually, a large bank would need community development loans equal to at least 0.625% of allocated
 Tier 1 capital in each assessment area.

 Annually, the same large bank would need community development investments and grants,
 collectively, equal to another 0.625% of allocated Tier 1 capital.

 Annually, an intermediate bank would need community development loans, investments and grants
 equal to at least 1.25% of allocated Tier 1 capital.

You read that correctly.

The agencies are proposing explicit numerical standards that appear extraordinarily low when compared
with actual historical community development lending.

The potential consequence is not that banks would be prohibited from doing more. Of course they could do
more. The danger is that a published regulatory number can quickly become an operating target-and these
numbers may reset expectations dramatically downward.

An important clarification: What do the benchmarks actually do?

The proposed percentages are part of what the agencies call a "geographic flexibility standard."

They would determine whether a bank could receive consideration at the State, multistate MSA or bank
level for community development activities conducted outside its assessment areas. The proposal presents
the percentages as one option; a second option would retain a qualitative standard based on whether the
bank has an adequate level of responsive community development activity. Both options stipulate that a
bank must engage in sufficient community development lending and investing to be considered as
"adequate" within the bank's defined communities before any community development activity outside
those boundaries will be considered.

Effectively, the proposed percentages are a prescribed minimum for a bank to attain a satisfactory CRA
rating for its CD lending and CD investing (including grants) in any assessment area.

That makes them important.

The agencies say the quantitative standards generally reflect the minimum level of community development
activity a bank would be expected to conduct-absent other considerations-to avoid a "needs to improve"
rating. They also state that the percentages are not sufficient by themselves to determine a bank's
community development performance.

That distinction is important. But so is the regulatory signal.

Once an agency publishes a numerical minimum and says examiners cannot require a higher level for the
purpose of receiving broader geographic consideration, banks will inevitably compare their programs with
that number.

The question is whether the proposed number bears any reasonable relationship to historical performance.

GeoDataVision | geodatavision.com 2
 How do the proposed standards compare with historical performance?

There has never been a clear official numerical standard for community development activity under the
legacy CRA framework.

In the 2023 CRA rulemaking, the agencies acknowledged that thresholds might improve consistency but
said available data were insufficient to establish them. That rule was later enjoined, and the agencies
subsequently proposed returning to the prior framework.

There is, however, substantial public data about community development lending. CRA-reporting
institutions disclose the number and dollar amount of their community development loans annually.

GeoDataVision reviewed the 2024 CRA data for 565 OCC- and FDIC-regulated reporting banks. Those
institutions reported:

 23,477 community development loans originated;
 approximately $111.97 billion in community development lending; and
 approximately $18.42 trillion in combined assets.
Reported community development lending therefore equaled approximately 0.61% of the banks' combined
assets. Almost half of the institutions in the analysis reported community development lending exceeding
1% of assets.

The broader official FFIEC data, which also includes Federal Reserve-supervised reporters and purchased
loans, shows the same enormous scale. Across all 731 CRA reporters, 646 institutions reported 29,361
community development loan originations totaling approximately $137.2 billion during 2024.

Why does the Tier 1-capital denominator matter?

Tier 1 capital is only a fraction of a bank's total assets.

Consider a simplified example in which Tier 1 capital equals 10% of assets. A community development loan
benchmark equal to 0.625% of Tier 1 capital would equal only 0.0625% of assets.

What happens when the proposed formula is applied to the 2024 data?

Compare the Tier 1 Capital benchmarks with the 0.61% community-development-loan-to-assets ratio in the
GeoDataVision analysis of actual 2024 CD lending.

CD loans originated reported by FDIC- & OCC-regulated banks: $111.97 billion

Required CD loan volume dictated by the Tier 1 benchmarks: $11.69 billion

The actual historical lending results would be almost ten times the proposed minimum.

That is not a small difference. It is an entirely different scale of activity.

JPMorgan Chase offers a striking example. The bank reported approximately $10.526 billion in community
development loans originated during 2024. Applying the proposed 0.625% formula to its Tier 1 capital
produces a benchmark amount of only $1.848 billion.

Again, the proposed percentage is not a cap. It does not compel JPMorgan Chase-or any other bank-to
reduce its activity. But it is a signal from regulators as to what minimum level of activity they will accept to
consider a bank's CD activity as "satisfactory".

GeoDataVision | geodatavision.com 3
 But what happens over time when a bank's historical activity is many times higher than a newly published
regulatory minimum?

That is the question the agencies and the banking industry need to confront.

The difference may be even greater than the reported data suggests

The 2024 CRA lending data reflects loans originated during that year.

The NPR proposes that examiners also consider prior-period community development loans held on a
bank's balance sheet, creating treatment similar to community development investments. The agencies say
this could encourage longer-term lending by recognizing both current activity and qualifying loans from
earlier periods.

That means historical performance under the proposed approach would include more than the $111.97
billion of current-year lending in the GeoDataVision analysis.

Outstanding prior-period loans would be added.

Consequently, the gap between actual activity receiving consideration and the quantitative formula could
be even larger than the current-year comparison indicates.

Why should communities care?

Explicit standards can be highly desirable.

For decades, banks have been forced to estimate examiner expectations without a transparent numerical
reference point. Greater clarity and consistency would benefit banks, regulators and communities.

The problem is not the concept of a published standard.

The problem is whether the standard is realistic.

A benchmark set far below actual historical activity could become a magnet pulling performance downward.
Budgets are reviewed. Programs are compared with regulatory expectations. Management asks how much
activity is necessary. A number that begins as a geographic-flexibility threshold can become, in practice,
the number around which institutions build their programs.

If that happens, affordable housing projects, small-business initiatives, community facilities,
economic-development programs and nonprofit organizations could ultimately receive less financing.

What should the regulators do?

Before adopting any quantitative standard, the OCC and FDIC should:

1. Publish the historical data used to select 0.625% and 1.25%.
2. Compare the proposed percentages with actual community development lending, investment and grant

 activity.
3. Provide bank-level examples showing how the formula would work in practice.
4. Explain why Tier 1 capital is the appropriate denominator.
5. Clarify precisely when the percentage is only a geographic safe harbor and when it may influence a

 performance conclusion.

GeoDataVision | geodatavision.com 4
 6. Test whether the benchmark could unintentionally encourage institutions to reduce activity that already
 substantially exceeds it.

The agencies should also reconcile their present confidence in explicit percentages with the earlier
conclusion that available community development data was insufficient to establish reliable thresholds.

Conclusion

The proposed bank-size changes are important. But they are not the only-or necessarily the biggest-story
in the 2026 CRA proposal.

The proposed community development percentages could become some of the most consequential
numbers in the entire rule.

GeoDataVision's analysis indicates that the amount produced by the proposed formula is almost 90%
below actual 2024 community development lending among the OCC- and FDIC-regulated reporters
studied. Once prior-period loans, investments and grants are considered, the difference could be even
greater.

The agencies may not intend these standards to reduce community development activity. But regulatory
incentives do not depend solely on intent.

They depend on the numbers institutions are given and how those numbers will be used.

Comments on the proposal are due October 13, 2026. Banks, community organizations and other
interested parties should examine the formula carefully and insist that any final quantitative standard be
calibrated to actual historical experience.

Communities have too much at stake for anything less.

 Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on
 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN
 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Centennial Parkside CDC submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of
Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) because it would
significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the
complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before
making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and
moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence
the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60
days.
 Centennial Parkside Community Development Corporation (CPCDC) is a resident-founded,
community-based nonprofit serving East Parkside in West Philadelphia. Founded by East
Parkside residents in 2015, CPCDC works to preserve, promote, and revitalize the neighborhood
through partnerships, resident engagement, and programs that increase opportunity and support a
diverse, thriving community.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring
that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access
to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in
communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to
mainstream financial services.

The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would
change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for
nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without an
adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on
communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In the Philadelphia
metro area, from 2010-2024, banks made over $64 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to
LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and over $22 billion in CRA qualified lending to small
businesses. Investments such as these benefited our community by increasing the number of
affordable mortgages, small business loans, investments in community, including affordable
housing development and preservation. These are all essential resources for the low-moderate
income community that we serve.

We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in our
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital
devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough to receive a
passing CRA rating. This represents a dramatic reduction in what large banks currently devote
to community investments and loans and we fear that this new guidance may operate as a ceiling
instead of a floor. Pennsylvania receives over $3 billion in CRA related investments annually, but
under the proposed rule that could fall to just over $600 million an 80% loss.

Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination
cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans. If
 regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the
communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for communities. For example, in
our community families would struggle to obtain affordable mortgage credit; first-time
homebuyers would continue to face barriers to homeownership; small-business owners would
have difficulty obtaining affordable financing; financing for affordable housing development and
preservation would be more difficult to obtain; our neighborhood would continue to experience
disinvestment; and residents who have limited relationships with mainstream financial
institutions would suffer to access grants and loans.

It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet the needs of communities
like ours. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes
would reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income
communities and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or
disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.

The proposal would also substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while
banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less
demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more comprehensive tests applied to
large banks. The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting
requirements currently applicable to large banks, including reporting on small-business,
community development lending.

A number of banks that operate in Philadelphia will now be considered either intermediate or
small banks under the proposed rule and therefore subject to less rigorous requirements. These
reclassifications and resulting eliminations of community development obligations for over 800
banks and separate investment evaluations for 400 banks across the country, may worsen the
housing crisis by reducing investor interest in buying Low-Income Housing Tax Credits
(LIHTC), and reducing access to mortgages for first-time homebuyers or access to credit for
home repairs.

Similarly, the proposed rule would narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service
test. Today, examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and information
about the costs and features of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit this criterion to credit
services, removing deposit products such as checking and savings accounts from direct
evaluation under the service test. As such, examiners would no longer evaluate whether those
products are affordable and responsive to community needs even though approximately 15% of
 Philadelphians over 100,000 households remain unbanked or underbanked. Moreover,
according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, these households are overwhelmingly
low-income, black, or disabled. CRA review of the cost and features of deposit products has
played an important role in encouraging banks to address these disparities by providing
affordable products, and it must continue to do so.

For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate from
access to credit and economic opportunity. They can determine whether families can safely
receive income, build savings, establish banking relationships and obtain responsible credit. East
Parkside does not have any bank branches within the neighborhood boundaries and residents
often travel substantial distances by public transportation to reach a branch. Many of our
residents have limited access to affordable bank accounts and residents rely on check cashers or
other alternative financial services.

This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and
moderate-income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to
affordable mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible
small-business financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in affordable housing,
small businesses and other community development.

The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply
because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA
obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that
would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the communities those
institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development activity that would receive
less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-income
communities or communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development,
financial counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other
community-based services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit
organizations. These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have deep
relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.

For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and
new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations.
 For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology,
accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the
underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources
over which to spread these costs. In addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with
limited staff and may not maintain financial records or program documentation in the precise
format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller
organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger
organizations whose activities are easier to verify.

Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and partnerships can
play in supporting community development. We have partnered with local banks to bring
resources and information to East Parkside including bank support for housing counseling,
affordable housing, foreclosure prevention, small-business assistance, financial education,
neighborhood revitalization, and operating capacity for our nonprofit.

These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into
tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community
development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond
the banks themselves. These rules should be motivated by the needs of the communities CRA is
intended to serve and not by the perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions.

To be considered economic development under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying
small business must promote economic development by supporting permanent job creation,
retention, or improvement for low- or moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income
communities.

The proposed rule would eliminate this "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks could
earn CRA credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or improves jobs
for low- and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income communities. This
change would weaken the connection between CRA economic-development credit and the
people and communities CRA is intended to benefit. Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying
business expand does not necessarily create jobs, increase economic opportunity in an
underserved neighborhood or address the needs of low- and moderate-income communities.

Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens a
qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank to
demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or neighborhoods.
 We are also concerned that currently, banks above the large bank threshold annually collect and
report data on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans, while
the proposal would limit these requirements to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. Banks
with assets of $10 billion or less would no longer be required to annually collect and report CRA
data on small business loans and community development loans.

Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers would have less information
to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance or understand whether local credit needs
are being met. Local community leaders and elected officials depend on this data for decision
making and for ensuring that the needs of residents are being addressed. This proposed change is
inconsistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs of
entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities, and should not be in the
final rule.

Lastly, prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:

 identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny
 under the proposal;

 quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
 development activities subject to CRA evaluation;

 assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
 including rural communities and communities of color; and

 consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
 meaningful community accountability.

 Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes
 that the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its
 impacts is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs
 considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

 The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for
 meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that
 materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are
 consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities,
 including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.

 We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120
 days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service
evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The
current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.

Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that
do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would
allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather
examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more
complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies
extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.

Sincerely,

Jessi Ray Koch
Executive Director
Centennial Parkside CDC

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

The California Housing Partnership (the Partnership) appreciates the opportunity to comment
on the proposed amendments to the agencies' Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations
published in the Federal Register on August 12, 2026. The Partnership is a private nonprofit
created by the State of California in 1988 with the public mission of increasing the supply of
affordable and sustainable homes through technical assistance and policy education. Since 1988,
the Partnership's on-the-ground technical assistance has leveraged more than $42 billion in
private and public financing to preserve and create more than 102,000 affordable homes.
Additionally, CHP has provided training to more than 52,000 people about affordable housing
finance techniques.

The CRA was passed by Congress in 1977 in response to a long and well-documented history of
financial institutions and real estate interests denying equal access to credit and property
(redlining) to create an affirmative obligation for federal chartered banks to help meet the credit
financial service needs of low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities. While the CRA has
successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest, and provide services in underserved communities
in California, there is still a long way to go before these communities can be said to have
equitable access to capital and financial services. Rather than addressing these persistent gaps,
the proposed CRA rule changes will pull investment and support away from the communities the

49 STEVENSON STREET, SUITE 500 SAN FRANCISCO, CA 94105 WWW.CALHOUSINGPARTNERSHIP.ORG (415) 433-6804
 statute directs federally chartered banks to serve and dramatically worsen California's affordable
housing and homelessness situation, as described below in more detail.

The scale of California's housing need makes the stakes of this proposal especially high for our
state. The California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) estimates in its
statewide housing plan that California needs one million more homes affordable to lower-income
households who cannot afford market-rate homes due to their historic lack of access to capital
and financial services.1

Thanks to the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill (H.R. 1) in July 2025, California has doubled
production of affordable rental homes in the past year. Private bank participation in affordable
home production and preservation has been absolutely critical to this progress. Given that the
participation of federally chartered banks in California has been motivated almost entirely by CRA,
the proposed rule change to exempt many banks from CRA tests would be devastating and
undermine a singular achievement of H.R. 1.

The Partnership estimates that an additional $388.8 billion in CRA loans and investments are
needed to meet these needs over a ten-year period above the amount currently available.
Unfortunately, the proposed CRA rule changes would significantly worsen the situation rather
than improving it by reducing the number of banks incentivized to make CRA loans and
investments in California.

According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70 banks active in
California would see their CRA reinvestment obligations reduced under the proposal, with 25
banks active in California shedding their CRA community development responsibilities entirely.2
Forty-five banks active in California would no longer be subject to the investment test, which has
successfully driven crucial investment in Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC).3 Commercial
banks account for an estimated 85 percent of LIHTC investors nationally, making this test a critical
driver of affordable housing capital.4

Accordingly, we urge you to ensure that the final rule addresses each of the concerns detailed
below.

This is the single most consequential negative change in the proposed rule for California's
affordable housing supply, and its scale is not a theoretical concern, it is a specific, documented,
and immediate shift in the market. According to the National Association of Affordable Housing
Lenders (NAAHL), of the 642 banks currently classified as large banks nationally, only 256 would

found that 376 OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks nationally (126 OCC-supervised and 250 FDIC-

California specifically, NCRC analysis finds that 45 California banks would no longer be subject to

Banks in this asset range play an outsized role in rural and smaller markets that California cannot
afford to lose. AHTCC survey data show that approximately one-third of Housing Credit equity
invested by banks under $10 billion in assets supported rural markets, compared to roughly 8
percent of Housing Credit equity industry-wide, meaning banks in this asset range are
disproportionately responsible for the equity that reaches California's Central Valley, North State,
and other rural regions where few large, multi-state banks maintain assessment areas.

The proposal compounds this problem by weakening how community development performance
is scored for the banks that remain in the intermediate tier. Under the current framework, an
intermediate bank generally must receive at least a "satisfactory" rating on both its lending test
and its community development test to earn an overall satisfactory rating. Under the proposal,
strong lending performance could compensate for weak community development performance in
the overall rating. Because Housing Credit equity serves a function that cannot be replaced with
additional debt, allowing lending to substitute for investment removes the last structural reason
many mid-sized banks would continue making Housing Credit investments at all.

This proposal also runs directly counter to H.R. 1's effective expansion of tax-exempt bonds used
to create affordable homes along with the 4% and 9% Housing Credits that are projected to
finance 1.22 million additional affordable rental homes over the next decade. The proposed rule
also undermines Section 311 of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act which raised the cap on

Development Finance

community development loans, and separately 0.625 percent to community development
investments, to receive a passing CRA rating. This bar is set far below what banks currently do.
NCRC found that among the largest 100 OCC and FDIC supervised banks, the median bank

We ask the agencies to:

current market asking rents in 46 of California's 58 counties are already below this threshold, this

all 58 California counties, would also qualify as CRA beneficiaries, giving banks huge incentives to

any meaningful benefit to the communities the statute is intended to serve.

puts the scale in perspective: as of 2025, California has an estimated 1,076,484
unsubsidized/NOAH affordable homes, compared with only 594,055 government-regulated

of its affordable-housing consideration through ordinary-course lending on buildings it would have

Compounding the deleterious effects of this change, "affordability in NOAH properties, unlike
Housing Credit properties, which carry recorded, government-monitored affordability covenants
lasting 55 years in California, can disappear at the next lease turnover, renovation, or sale. The
Partnership's data shows how unstable this housing is: since mid-2020, an estimated 268,113
formerly unsubsidized affordable homes (19.9 percent of the 2020 stock) have already lost their
affordability, and as of 2025 an additional 78,133 homes are at very high risk of imminent loss,
with 354,332 to 433,166 more at high or moderate risk within five years, a pattern present in 43
of California's 58 counties.9 Crediting banks today for financing volatile NOAH housing would
inevitably mean granting CRA credit for outcomes that evaporate before the next CRA exam cycle.

We recommend that the agencies:

 1. Not adopt the proposed NOAH standard as drafted, or, at minimum,

 2. Require a recorded affordability covenant or regulatory agreement with a duration
 comparable to a Housing Credit extended-use period of at least 30 years so that credit is
 tied to a lasting public commitment rather than a moment in time market snapshot; and

 3. Reject the addition of a "high-cost area" definition up to 120% AMI housing, which not
 only would extend CRA "affordable housing" credit well beyond the LMI populations the
 statute is intended to serve, but also provide no meaningful or lasting community benefit.

Given banks' outsized role as Housing Credit's primary capital source, if the agencies intend to
proceed with adding any version of a NOAH investment or lending standard, they should conduct
and publish an economic analysis of its likely effect on Housing Credit investment and lending
volume and pricing and allow public comment before finalizing the rule.

IV. Preserve CRA-Qualifying Grants and Nonprofit Capacity

The proposal would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by requiring an established
nexus to a specific community development project and capping grantee overhead and
administrative costs at 15 percent, with new documentation requirements to demonstrate
compliance. The agencies also ask whether CRA eligibility for grantmaking should be eliminated
entirely. The Partnership works closely with mission-driven nonprofit developers and service

 providers across California, including organizations that operate downpayment assistance
programs, housing counseling and capacity-building services, that rely on flexible general operating
support and capacity-building grants from banks to keep their doors open. Adding any such
restrictions will lead to most smaller, local, and rural community development organizations (the
ones who are the most important to their communities and the least able to absorb new reporting
burdens ineligible for CRA grants. Bank contributions of this kind represent a small share of overall
CRA activity, but their loss would be felt disproportionately by the organizations best positioned
to do the hardest preservation and community development work in underserved parts of the
state.

We ask the agencies to preserve CRA eligibility for general operating support, capacity-building
grants, and sponsorships to nonprofit organizations engaged in community development, without
imposing new project-level nexus or overhead-tracking requirements that fall hardest on smaller
and rural organizations.

V. Geographic Flexibility Should Complement, Not Replace, Assessment-Area Obligations

The proposed rule changes would allow banks, at their option, to receive CRA credit for
qualifying community development activity outside their assessment areas, up to the state or
multistate level, after adequately meeting needs inside their assessment areas. We support the
goal of directing more private capital to California's rural and underserved "CRA deserts," where
few banks maintain a physical presence or assessment area, and agree this flexibility could help
address the pricing gap between competitive urban "CRA hot spots" and underserved rural
markets. However, this flexibility should not become a mechanism for banks to redirect capital
away from the communities where they take deposits and hold assessment-area responsibility in
the first place.

We ask the agencies to condition any out-of-assessment-area credit on a bank first demonstrating
it has adequately met the community development needs within its own assessment areas, and
prioritize this flexibility for LIHTC, CDFI, and other high-impact investment that would not
otherwise reach underserved rural California communities.

The Partnership has more than 35 years of firsthand experience with how CRA-motivated
investment works and what is jeopardized when that investment weakens. As the state's leading
source of applied research and technical assistance on affordable housing finance, we are available
as a resource to the agencies as you consider the volume of public comment this proposal will
generate. We urge the OCC and FDIC to preserve the standalone investment test, reject the
proposed activity floor, reject the NOAH standard, and ensure that any final rule strengthens,
rather than diminishes, the effectiveness and positive investment that CRA has made possible in

Public comment in relation to OCC-2026-0694

Dear Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation:

I am writing to encourage the OCC and FDIC to preserve a strong Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) and the important role it plays in expanding access to capital
for underserved communities. In particular, I encourage the agencies to maintain the
meaningful incentives the CRA creates for banks to partner with Community
Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs), which help ensure that capital reaches
small businesses and entrepreneurs who might otherwise be overlooked.

I am proud to serve on the Board of WomenVenture, a CDFI serving Minnesota and
Western Wisconsin for the last 25 years. WomenVenture helps entrepreneurs and small
business owners build profitable and sustainable businesses by combining access to
capital with training, technical assistance, and ongoing support. Organizations like
WomenVenture play a critical role in helping entrepreneurs turn promising ideas into
viable businesses, particularly when they face barriers to traditional financing.

My appreciation for this work comes from both my professional and personal
experiences.

I have spent much of my career in finance, including investment banking and private
equity, where I have seen firsthand what it takes for businesses to attract investment
capital. Too often, businesses need to have already achieved significant scale or
demonstrated rapid growth to attract financing. Yet many small businesses need access
to capital precisely to reach that next stage of growth. This creates a difficult cycle for
entrepreneurs with viable businesses but limited access to traditional sources of
funding. This challenge is exacerbated in communities that historically have had less
access to capital.

I also grew up in a family of small-business owners. My grandparents started a business
that my father carried forward and that my brother now leads. Throughout its history,
local banks provided financing to purchase equipment, expand facilities, and support
growth. In turn, our family business has reinvested in the community for generations,
creating jobs, supporting local organizations, and contributing to the local economy.

These businesses may never appear on the cover of The Wall Street Journal, but their
names appear on the jerseys of local youth sports teams. They create jobs, meet
essential needs, and help communities thrive. Their success creates a virtuous cycle of
economic opportunity and community investment.

That experience is a significant part of why I joined the Board of WomenVenture. I
believe that expanding access to capital for small businesses is not simply about
 supporting individual entrepreneurs; it is about strengthening the economic foundation
of our communities.

Bank partnerships are essential to making this possible. The CRA has helped
encourage banks to lend, invest, and provide resources through CDFIs that understand
local needs and can connect capital with entrepreneurs and businesses that might
otherwise struggle to access it. These partnerships extend the reach and impact of
traditional financial institutions while supporting responsible lending and sustainable
economic development.

I recognize the importance of making CRA requirements clearer, more effective, and
less burdensome for financial institutions. Regulatory efficiency is a worthwhile
objective. However, it is important that efforts to simplify the framework do not
unintentionally weaken the incentives that encourage meaningful investment in
underserved communities. A more efficient regulatory framework should preserve
the outcomes the CRA was designed to achieve.

As the agencies are considering changes to the CRA framework, I encourage them to
ensure the final rule:

 Preserves meaningful incentives for banks to lend and invest through CDFIs;

 Recognizes the full value of community development activities that expand
 access to responsible capital and strengthen local economies;

 Supports grants and other resources that help CDFIs build the capacity needed
 to serve communities effectively;

 Maintains meaningful expectations for banks to meet community credit needs;
 and

 Strengthens, rather than reduces, the flow of responsible private capital to small
 businesses and low- and moderate-income communities.

For organizations like WomenVenture, these partnerships translate directly into
financing and support for entrepreneurs to start businesses, create jobs, build wealth,
and reinvest in their communities.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Sincerely,

Jaime Proman
Board Member, WomenVenture
Minneapolis, Minnesota

Jonathan V. Gould
