 Revitalization: Under the current Rule, the definition of "community development" also include
"activities that revitalize or stabilize (i) low or moderate-income geographies; (ii) designated
disaster areas; or (iii) distressed or underserved non-metropolitan middle-income geographies"
with the latter areas limited to those designated by the banking agencies based upon specified
criteria included rates of poverty, unemployment, and population loss.39 The Q&A elaborates on
this by stating that an investment "has as its primary purpose community development when it is
designed for the express purpose of revitalizing or stabilizing low- or moderate-income areas,
designated disaster areas, or underserved or distressed nonmetropolitan middle-income
areas..."40

The proposed rule includes these categories of activities within its definition of "economic
development" so that investments to revitalize or stabilize these areas would continue to qualify
for CRA credit. However, the NPRM adds to this list activities that revitalize or stabilize "Any
other area targeted by a government entity for redevelopment that qualifies for significant
economic incentives, such as tax credits, tax abatements or grants"41 so long as the activities
are for government initiatives that are "consistent with a bona fide government revitalization or
stabilization plan." The section-by-section list as examples of these "opportunity zones, Federal
empowerment zones, State enterprise zones, or city tax incremental financing districts" and
says that "The activities in those areas typically are designed to help attract and retain
businesses and residents."

Of course, to the extent that an investment in an area targeted for economic incentives is
designed to attract and retain businesses and residents within, e.g., an LMI geography is made
to revitalize or stabilize such an area, the investment would qualify for CRA credit under the
preexisting rule. The risk of the proposed expansion in the current revitalization/stabilization rule
is that it would extend CRA credit to investments in areas that are not LMI areas or for
investment in LMI areas that actually have the predictable effect of displacing LMI residents or
small businesses. It is not difficult to envision, e.g., investments in new stadiums or in luxury
hotels or apartments obtaining CRA simply because they are located in an area that is also
receiving tax credits or abatements. That is not what the CRA was designed to encourage.

Our concerns regarding these elements of the NPRM are magnified by another aspect of the
NPRM's treatment of investments. The NPRM proposes to permit a bank to receive CRA credit
for community development investments outside of the bank's assessment that benefit areas
outside of the bank's assessment area as "as long as the institution has been responsive to
community development needs and opportunities in its assessment area(s)."42 The NPRM
proposes two alternative methods for determining what constitutes such responsiveness. The
first alternative would measure the bank's investments in its assessment area against its tier 1
capital and establish a threshold that must be satisfied before outside investments can be
considered; the second alternative would leave it to examiners to determine what constitutes an

39 12 C.F.R. 345.12(g)(4).
40 Q&A ___ 12(H)-8.
41 Proposed 345.12
42 Q&A ___12(h)-6

 11
 adequate level of within-area investments "considering the dollar amount and responsiveness of
community development activities to assessment area community development needs."43

CRL agrees with the principle of permitting a bank to obtain CRA credit for qualified investments
outside of their assessment area so long as the bank is doing a sufficient job within its
assessment area. But the standards for determining when to allow such credit must be carefully
drawn lest banks begin to cherry pick investment opportunities and claim CRA credit. The
comment that the NCRC has submitted in response to the NPRM convincingly demonstrates
that the quantitative metrics set forth in the proposed rule for large and small intermediate banks
are far too lax as they would establish benchmarks substantially below the ratio of banks'
current community development financing relative to their tier 1 capital and thus could lead
some banks to reduce the amount of community development financing they provide down to
the 0.625%/1.25% levels. And, the alternative, qualitative test set forth in the proposed rule is so
indeterminate as to provide no meaningful limitation on when qualified investments outside of
assessment areas can receive CRA credit. Accordingly, we urge the agencies to reconsider and
substantially tighten this element of the proposed rule along the lines proposed by the NRC.

 Consideration of Discriminatory or Other Unlawful Acts

Under the CRA regulation that has been in effect since 1995, "evaluation of a bank's CRA
performance is adversely affected by evidence of discriminatory or other illegal credit practices
in any geography by the bank."44 The regulation lists the specific laws that are relevant for these
purposes and states that an examiner "considers the nature, extent, and strength of the
evidence of the practices" as well as mitigating factors such as "the policies and procedures that
the bank...has in place to prevent the practices; any corrective action that the bank...has taken
or has committed to take, including voluntary corrective action resulting from self-assessment."45

The NPRM proposes to update the list of statutes considered for these purposes to include
1031 of the Dodd-Frank Act which proscribes unfair, deceptive and abusive acts and practices
and also to include the Military Lending Act and the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act.46 We
applaud the agencies for proposing these additions. In response to the agencies' request for
comment as to whether "there are additional examples of discriminatory or other illegal credit
practices that should be identified" in the regulation47 we recommend that the agencies add
violations of 805 of the Fair Housing Act of 1968, 42 U.S.C. 3605, which was inexplicably
omitted from the 1995 Rule. We also urge the agencies to include all violations of the Truth in
Lending Act as was provided for in the 2023 Rule or, at a minimum, at the very least to include
violations of the ability-to-repay and anti-steering incentive provisions of that Act. Those
provisions were added to TILA by the Dodd-Frank Act as a response to, and a means of

44 12 C.F.R. 345.28(c)(1)
45 Id. 345.28(c)(2)
46 Proposed 345.28(c)(1)
47 91 Fed. Reg. at 52151

 preventing the recurrence of, the financial crisis, and violations of those provisions are surely
relevant to CRA assessments.48

At the same time that the NPRM proposes some welcome additions to the range of statutory
violations that can be considered as part of a CRA review, the NPRM severely limits when such
consideration is permissible. In contrast to the current (and long-standing) rule reaffirmed in
2023, that, as noted above, directs examiners to weigh "the nature, extent and strength of the
evidence" of unlawful auctions, the NPRM proposes two alternatives one of which would allow
consideration of a violation only if that violation had been cited in a "public enforcement action
taken by a Federal or State agency or judicial order to which a Federal or State agency is a
party" and the other of which would also allow consideration of supervisory findings of unlawful
conduct.49

The only rationale the NPRM offers for this proposed change is that it "would appropriately focus
the scope of the agencies' consideration of discriminatory or other illegal credit practices on
those violations that are most likely to have a broad impact on the bank's lending activities such
that the benefit those activities may have had in meeting community credit needs would be
adversely affected by the harm the activities caused to the community."50 At most, this rationale
would support the second option in the NPRM as that option at least allows for consideration of
supervisory findings. But the reality is that there is simply no reason to believe that violations
that are the subject, e.g., of judicial orders entered as a result of private litigation or that are
evidenced in private litigation that has not reached a final judgment are ipso facto less "likely to
have a broad impact on the bank's lending activities" than those reflected in public enforcement
actions or supervisory actions. Indeed, some of the most consequential ECOA decisions and
orders have been the result of private litigation.51

Indeed, the NPRM's reliance on public enforcement (and potentially supervisory) actions is
especially untimelyindeed ironicin light of what has happened and is happening to the
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. That agency, of course, has exclusive supervisory and
enforcement authority with respect to consumer protection violations by banks with over $10
billion in assets. Over the past two years that agency's ability to engage in, and appetite for
engaging in, enforcement actions has been severely curtailed. Indeed, the CFPB has initiated
just one enforcement action in the past 18 months (and that action did not involve a depository
institution).52 And whatever CFPB supervisory or enforcement capacity remains would be

RE: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, Docket ID OCC-2026-0694

Catholic Charities USA (CCUSA) appreciates the opportunity to submit comments with respect to
the proposed rule, Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, published on August 12, 2026, that
would make amendments to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. CCUSA is a national
membership organization of 170 diocesan Catholic Charities member agencies, which operate 4,200
service locations across the country. Last year, the Catholic Charities network provided help and
created hope for over 16 million people. Whether talking about housing and community
development initiatives, financial literacy or food and nutrition services offered to individuals and
families in need, or workforce development programs meant to expand economic opportunity, we
write to express concern that the proposed amendments, as written, could limit or even curtail bank
investment in these critical areas. Furthermore, the proposed changes could have the unintended
consequence of more broadly reducing private investment in rural and low- and moderate-income
communities.

Less Capital Available for Housing and Community Development Initiatives.
Last year, the Catholic Charities network helped over 196,000 people access stable housing,
provided homelessness-related services to over 719,000 individuals, provided over 38,000
permanent housing units for families, seniors, and veterans, assisted over 5,000 clients with one-on-
one housing counseling service, and responded to 50 disasters, serving 400,000 individuals. The
ability to provide and offer these services was significantly elevated by bank CRA incentives and
evaluation requirements.

We are concerned that the proposed rule changes, and particularly the increase in the asset
thresholds for small, intermediate, and large banks would eliminate community development
evaluations for 814 banks, resulting in a significant reduction in the demand for Low-Income Tax

 1
 Credits (LIHTCs).1 Reduced bank demand for tax credits, the predominant means by which
CCUSA agencies develop affordable multi-family housing, would undoubtedly result in less
housing being built as agencies will find subsidy to make projects viable less available, especially in
rural and small markets. This would be unfortunate considering the documented need for affordable
housing throughout the country, and particularly in rural areas.2

Less Leveraging of Philanthropic Dollars and Loss of Flexible Operating Support.
Non-profit agencies such as CCUSA and its member agencies oftentimes use CRA-motivated bank
capital to help leverage other investors and resources and to provide critical, flexible operating
support that is not necessarily tied to a specific project or program. Requiring grant funds to be tied
to a specific community development project or program and/or restricting, for banks with assets
over $10 billion, the portion of a grant that can be dedicated to administrative or indirect costs could
significantly reduce a bank's incentive to provide general operating support to non-profits providing
services that address vital community needs. In other words, contrary to the proposal's stated
purpose and as acknowledged in Table 2 and on page 52165, the proposed changes may actually
result in fewer community development grants reaching the communities they are intended to
benefit.

It should also be noted that the provision of grants oftentimes requires technical assistance and
volunteers. Under current rules, banks can receive CRA credit for grants that support community
development including general operational support. If grants funds must be tied to a specific
community development project or program, nonprofits will lose flexible funding needed to
administer the grant effectively.

For instance, a Catholic Charities agency provided this account of the overall impact of a $5,000
CRA-related grant on its financial empowerment program:

 ...we have received a $5,000 grant from a local bank to develop the course and
 instruct. Additionally, the bank has sent volunteers to help during the teaching of [the]
 course. We are looking now to create a hybrid course merging components of our Job
 Readiness Program with the Financial Empowerment Program. With this hybrid, we hope to
 attract employers who are willing to interview our attendees, and hope to use this as a step
 to successful employment...

 Even more worrisome, language in the proposed rule under Question 10 leaves open the possibility
of eliminating CRA credit for all grants and donations.3 CCUSA strongly opposes such a change, as
it could result in significant gaps in non-profits' ability to manage and implement programs that the
broader philanthropic community is unlikely to be able to readily fill.

Reduced Accountability in Underserved Communities. One of CCUSA's biggest concerns is that
the proposed raised asset thresholds would eliminate or reduce scrutiny of branches, community-
development investments, and some banking services. As a faith-based entity working to reduce
poverty in America, we understand the importance of branch presence and investment in low- and
moderate-income communities. The raised asset thresholds would result in hundreds of banks no
longer having to report services, investments, small business loans, and other housing and
community development activities. In addition, the proposed rule would restrict the service test to
credit services and exclude deposit services, such as checking and savings products, from CRA
consideration. The experience of Catholic Charities agencies throughout the country with respect to
offering workforce development, small business, and financial empowerment programs is that these
changes would negatively impact an individual or household's ability to move out of poverty due to
increased challenges involving accessing credit and affordable checking and savings account
products.

Specifically, without regulatory pressure, banks in low- and moderate-income communities may no
longer offer deposit services. If deposit services are not available to families in those communities,
then those families cannot save their money, pay their debts, and qualify for the credit needed to buy
homes, buy or lease cars, or finance businesses. This potential outcome is opposite of the intent of
the proposed rule, as stated in the notice of proposed rulemaking.4 CCUSA urges the agencies to
ensure that banks remain accountable to low- and moderate-income communities via the various
evaluation mechanisms that are currently in place.

In closing, we thank you for the opportunity to submit comments. We believe the current CRA rules
have helped create stronger, less vulnerable communities and have served as an excellent tool and
catalyst for the investment of private and philanthropic dollars. We encourage you to ensure that the
CRA continues to be a tool for positive growth in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods by
making targeted improvements to the CRA regulations.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill,

Thank you for the opportunity to provide feedback on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's
(OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposal to reform the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. My name is Thom Amdur, and I am the Executive Vice President for
Policy & Impact team at Lincoln Avenue Communities (LAC), a mission-driven affordable housing
developer and owner active in more than 34 states. We proudly provide 35,000 affordable rental units to
more than 100,000 residents across the nation. Our organization is dedicated to addressing housing
affordability pressures by developing and preserving high-quality affordable housing through both new
construction and preservation projects utilizing the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (hereinafter "LIHTC"
or "Housing Credit") program. Given our extensive experience with LIHTC, we share the broader
affordable housing industry's deep concern about the potential impacts of the CRA Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking (the "CRA NPR") on affordable housing production and preservation.

The importance of CRA for the Housing Credit:

For more than 50 years CRA has spurred bank lending and investments in homeownership, small
businesses, healthcare, childcare, and other critical community needs. Its positive impact is especially
pronounced in the production of affordable rental housing through the Housing Credit.

The Housing Credit is our nation's most important tool for the production of affordable rental housing,
and it simply could not function at its current scale and impact without the critical investments from
banks subject to CRA. Approximately 80 percent of equity investments in affordable housing communities
financed with the Housing Credit each year come from CRA-motivated bank investors. Banks make these
investments not only to receive the modest return provided by the tax advantages associated with
investing in Housing Credit properties, but also because Housing Credit investments can help satisfy their
obligations under CRA. For large banks, Housing Credit investments typically offer lower yields than many
 alternative investments, making CRA examinations a pivotal incentive to invest in the Housing Credit
despite those comparatively modest returns. If the CRA NPR, as proposed, is finalized, newly classified
intermediate banks would no longer be incentivized to invest in the low- and moderate-income
communities because they would no longer be subject to the investment test, despite still having more
general community development obligations as intermediate-sized banks. This is because it is generally
easier for banks to support community development activities through lending rather than through
equity investments.

The proposed rule:

The CRA NPR proposes to reclassify banks with assets between approximately $1.65 billion and $10 billion
as intermediate banks rather than large banks. As a result, these institutions would no longer be subject
to the full CRA examination framework applicable to large banks, including the separate investment test.

According to a 2026 survey conducted by the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC), of which
we are a proud member, banks with assets between $1.649 billion and $10 billion invested at least $1.6
billion in Housing Credit equity over the five-year survey period from 2021 through 2025. Extrapolating
these results to the full Housing Credit market, AHTCC estimates that banks in this asset range invested up
to $2 billion in Housing Credit equity over the same five-year period.

The concern:

We are deeply concerned that the proposed CRA NPR could dramatically reduce the number of
institutions competing for Housing Credit investments, thereby lowering credit pricing, reducing available
equity, and ultimately resulting in the production and preservation of substantially fewer affordable
homes. This potential investment contraction would come at a time when the nation faces one of the
worst shortages of affordable housing and when Congress has recently acted to expand the resources
available for affordable unit production. The Housing Credit provisions enacted through the commonly
referred to as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act or Working Families Tax Cuts Act, were projected to finance
approximately 1.22 million additional affordable rental homes over the next decade while the bipartisan
21st Century ROAD to Housing Act raised the limit on banks' public welfare investments (PWI) to allow
them to increase their Housing Credit investments. Removing CRA incentives for Housing Credit
investment would dilute the impact of these recent congressional actions by constraining the private
capital necessary to translate expanded Housing Credit resources and investment authority into
affordable homes.

Of the 642 banks currently classified as large banks, only 256 would maintain that designation under the
proposal--a decline of over 60 percent, according to the National Association of Affordable Housing
Lenders (NAAHL). This leaves only 6 percent of banks in the current large bank classification subject to the
full CRA exam.

The negative consequences of this proposal would fall most heavily on smaller and rural communities that
currently fall within the CRA assessment areas of one or more large banks but may no longer do so if the
 OCC and FDIC change the definition of a large bank as proposed. The AHTCC survey found that
approximately one-third of LIHTC equity invested through syndicators by banks in the $412 million $10
billion asset range supported rural markets between 2021 and 2024, indicating that these banks play an
outsized role in investing in smaller communities. Credit pricing for properties in many urban areas--
which are more likely to have at least one and often multiple banks competing to invest in Housing Credit
developments because of overlapping assessment areas--tends to be much higher than pricing in rural
and other smaller communities that are not part of assessment areas for large banks subject to the
investment test.
Assessing the impact:
The OCC and FDIC included two alternatives to the primary proposal to set new thresholds for various
bank size classifications related to CRA. The first would raise the large bank asset threshold from $1.649
billion to $3.252 billion. This alternative would still have far-reaching negative consequences compared to
the current large bank threshold but is substantially less disruptive to Housing Credit investment than the
primary proposal to raise the large bank threshold to $10 billion.

According to AHTCC's survey of bank investment in the Housing Credit, 108 banks would be reclassified as
intermediate banks rather than large banks if the threshold is set at $10 billion, while just 40 would be
reclassified as intermediate banks if the large bank threshold is set at $3.252 billion (Small Business
Administration definition). Moreover, the banks that would remain subject to the separate investment
test under a $3.252 billion threshold account for approximately 86 percent of the Housing Credit equity
investment by OCC- and FDIC-regulated banks captured in the AHTCC survey with assets between $1.65
billion and $10 billion.
 The second alternative proposal would be far more damaging for affordable rental housing production
than either the primary or first alternative proposals. NAAHL estimates that, under a $30 billion large
bank threshold, 17 states would see the number of large banks with investment requirements cut by half
or more. According to AHTCC, banks with assets between $10 billion and $30 billion account for more
than twice as much Housing Credit debt and equity investment as banks between $1.65 billion and $10
billion.

Conclusion

Lincoln Avenue Communities has seen the positive impact of CRA firsthand and strongly encourages the
OCC and FDIC to leave the thresholds as they currently stand under the 1995 CRA rule, consistent with the
direction the Federal Reserve--the third bank regulator--appears to be taking. If the OCC and FDIC move
forward with changes to CRA regulations, we strongly urge maintaining the lowest possible threshold for
large banks and adopting policies to strengthen the Housing Credit market in all communities, including
rural and smaller markets.
Sincerely,

Thom Amdur,
Executive Vice President, Policy & Impact

workforce housing, providing high-quality, sustainable homes for lower- and moderate-income individuals, seniors, and families
nationwide. LAC is a mission-driven organization serving residents across 34 states.

COMMUNITY REINVESTMENT ACT COMMENT LETTER

October 11, 2026

Comment Intake
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street SW, Suite 3E-218

James P. Sheesley

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; FDIC RIN 3064-AG31

On behalf of the banking industry, I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the proposed
amendments to the Community Reinvestment Act regulations issued by the Office of the Comptroller of
the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. I am a Principal at Forvis Mazars which
provides audit, tax, consulting, and advisory services to financial institutions. Our professionals regularly
assist banks throughout the United States with regulatory, risk management, compliance, internal audit,
and operational matters. I have over 22 years experience helping community banks across the nation,
with most of that time with an emphasis on consumer compliance areas including CRA.

We support the agencies' targeted approach to retaining the core CRA framework while reducing
unnecessary regulatory burden, placing greater emphasis on lending, clarifying eligibility for community
development activities, modernizing public-file requirements, and improving the strategic plan process.
We also support the agencies' objective of maintaining meaningful CRA outcomes while improving the
clarity, consistency, and operational efficiency of the regulatory framework. The proposal would
establish asset categories of less than $1 billion for small banks, $1 billion to $10 billion for intermediate
banks, and more than $10 billion for large banks.

Asset-Size Thresholds

I strongly support the proposed changes to the CRA asset-size thresholds. Raising the small-bank
threshold to $1 billion and the intermediate-bank threshold to $10 billion would provide meaningful and
much-needed regulatory relief to community banks.

Community banks invest heavily in the communities they serve through locally originated loans,
community development activities, financial expertise, civic involvement, and longstanding relationships
with local businesses, agricultural producers, nonprofit organizations, and consumers. Regulatory
classifications should recognize that asset growth does not necessarily transform a relationship-based
community bank into a complex large institution. Much of that growth may reflect inflation, consolidation,
economic expansion, or the increasing dollar size of ordinary credit needs.

The proposed thresholds would permit many community banks to devote more resources to meeting
local credit needs rather than administering requirements designed for substantially larger and more
complex institutions. I encourage the agencies to finalize the proposed thresholds and establish a
transparent mechanism for periodically reviewing and, when warranted, adjusting them to prevent
inflation from gradually eroding the relief intended by the rule.

While some stakeholders have expressed concern that the proposal could weaken banks' obligations to
support affordable housing, community development, and economic opportunity, I believe those
concerns overlook the proposal's continued emphasis on meeting community credit needs through

 1|Page
  COMMUNITY REINVESTMENT ACT COMMENT LETTER

lending. Community banks have long demonstrated their commitment to local communities through
relationship-based lending, community development activities, and direct engagement with local
organizations. The proposal does not eliminate CRA obligations; rather, it seeks to refocus CRA
evaluations on activities that most directly address community credit needs while providing greater
clarity and consistency.

By reducing unnecessary compliance burden, establishing more objective community development
standards, and better aligning examination expectations, the proposal may allow community banks to
devote more resources to serving their communities rather than navigating increasingly complex
regulatory requirements. At the same time, I support maintaining strong standards for affordable
housing and community development activities and believe clearer, more objective criteria will ultimately
promote greater participation and more consistent CRA outcomes.

Objective and Consistent Community Development Standards

I support the agencies' efforts to clarify the community development definition and establish an
illustrative list of activities that qualify or do not qualify for CRA consideration, together with an optional
confirmation process.

I strongly encourage the agencies to take as much subjectivity as reasonably possible out of community
development determinations. Banks should receive consistent CRA consideration for substantially
similar activities, regardless of geographic location, examiner assignment, or supervisory agency. In
practice, uncertainty concerning the eligibility or treatment of an activity can complicate CRA planning,
particularly for activities involving multiyear commitments, multiple financing sources, or novel
structures. Uncertainty regarding whether an activity will receive CRA consideration may discourage
banks from undertaking otherwise beneficial projects, particularly when the activity requires a significant
multiyear financial commitment.

A final rule should therefore include clear, objective eligibility standards; practical examples of qualifying
and nonqualifying activities; consistent documentation expectations; and a reliable confirmation
process. An activity that satisfies the regulatory criteria should receive comparable consideration across
examinations and agencies. Examiner judgment will remain necessary to evaluate responsiveness and
impact, but it should not result in inconsistent eligibility decisions for activities with substantially similar
facts. The final rule should also explain the extent to which a confirmation remains reliable when the
underlying facts have not materially changed and identify the circumstances under which an agency
may reconsider a prior confirmation.

Online CRA Public Files and Notices

I agree that the existing physical public-file requirements are outdated. The proposal would allow banks
to maintain their CRA public files on their websites or on websites maintained on their behalf, while
branches would provide notices directing the public to the online information.

This approach reflects how customers and community organizations currently obtain information. Online
access should make CRA information more readily available, easier to search, and more convenient to
review without requiring an individual to visit a branch during business hours. It should also reduce
repetitive paper-maintenance requirements without reducing public transparency. The agencies should
also clarify expectations regarding website availability, accessibility, document retention, and continuity
procedures to follow during temporary service interruptions.

Strategic Plans and Nontraditional Banks

I support the proposed clarification of the strategic plan framework, including greater clarity regarding
required plan content, measurable goals, public participation, prefiling communications, approval,
denial, amendment, resubmission, and performance assessment. The proposal is intended to make

 2|Page
  COMMUNITY REINVESTMENT ACT COMMENT LETTER

strategic plans a more viable and less burdensome option for banks whose operations may not align
well with the standard performance tests.

At the same time, the agencies should proceed cautiously when applying this flexibility to nontraditional
banks. A strategic plan should reflect the institution's business model, but it should not become a
mechanism for avoiding a meaningful obligation to serve community credit and community development
needs. Nontraditional business models may require different measures, geographies, or performance
goals, but the resulting plan should still demonstrate a tangible, measurable, and sustained commitment
to the communities affected by the institution's operations.

Accordingly, the final rule should require strategic plans to include measurable goals, meaningful public
participation, transparent performance standards, and a clear connection between the institution's
activities and the communities it proposes to serve. Flexibility should accommodate legitimate
differences in business models without weakening the fundamental purpose of the CRA.

Small Business and Small Farm Loan Thresholds

I strongly recommend that the agencies consider updating the loan-size thresholds used to identify
small business and small farm loans. The current thresholds of $1 million for small business loans and
$500,000 for small farm loans no longer reasonably reflect inflation, contemporary operating costs, or
current credit-market conditions. Although the proposal does not address the small business and small
farm loan thresholds specifically, the proposal's emphasis on lending and community credit needs
provides an appropriate opportunity for the agencies to evaluate whether the existing thresholds
continue to accurately identify lending to farms and small businesses . When the agencies overhauled
CRA in the mid-1990s, they needed a simple, standardized way to measure lending to small
businesses and farms across all banks. These thresholds have remained largely unchanged since 1995
despite substantial inflation, rising operating costs, and evolving credit market conditions.

The concern is especially significant for agricultural banks. Even relatively small farming operations may
require financing that exceeds $500,000 because of the cost of land, equipment, seed, fertilizer, fuel,
livestock, crop inputs, labor, insurance, and other operating expenses. Gross farm revenues may also
exceed the existing threshold even though the operation remains locally or family owned and is
reasonably viewed as a small agricultural business within its market. A fixed dollar threshold may
exclude loans that, within the context of the local rural economy, support comparatively small or locally
owned agricultural operations.

As a result, agricultural banks may receive insufficient CRA recognition for loans that are central to
meeting the credit needs of rural communities and smaller agricultural operations. This outcome is
inconsistent with a proposal intended to refocus CRA evaluations on lending and community credit
needs.

I urge the agencies to consider increasing both thresholds to levels that better reflect present economic
conditions and lending data, and establish an automatic inflation-adjustment mechanism consistent with
other rules so the thresholds remain relevant. The agencies should also consider whether the definition
of a small farm loan should incorporate additional measures beyond a fixed gross-revenue or loan-size
limitation, particularly where those measurements fail to reflect the economics of modern agricultural
production.

A Uniform Interagency Rule

Finally, I strongly urge the OCC and FDIC to continue coordination with the Board of Governors of the
Federal Reserve System toward adoption of a single, consistent final CRA rule, examination
procedures, and interpretive guidance.

Different CRA standards based solely on a bank's charter or primary federal regulator would create
uncertainty, inconsistent treatment, unnecessary compliance costs, and competitive inequities. It could

 3|Page
  COMMUNITY REINVESTMENT ACT COMMENT LETTER

also complicate charter conversions, merger planning, strategic-plan development, and the structuring
of community development activities. These consequences would be particularly burdensome for
community banks with limited compliance resources.
A unified interagency framework would promote consistent examinations and public expectations while
giving banks greater certainty when making long-term lending, investment, service, and community
development commitments. Interagency alignment should therefore be treated as an essential objective
throughout the rulemaking and implementation process.

Conclusion

I commend the agencies for proposing targeted revisions that preserve the familiar CRA framework
while addressing unnecessary burden and providing greater clarity. I support the proposed asset-size
changes, more objective community development standards, modernization of the CRA public file, and
clarification of the strategic plan process. I encourage the agencies to strengthen the final rule by further
considering updates to the small business and small farm loan thresholds, recognizing the
contemporary economics of agricultural lending, ensuring that strategic plans maintain meaningful
community commitments, and coordinating with the Federal Reserve to promote consistent CRA
standards, examination procedures, and interpretive guidance across the agencies.
Thank you for considering these comments. I would welcome the opportunity to provide additional
information regarding the practical effect of these issues on community banks and the communities they
serve.
Respectfully submitted,

Shaun Harms
Principal, Financial Services
Forvis Mazars

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

Public Counsel writes to object to the harmful changes proposed to the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed by Congress in 1977 in response to redlining
and creates an affirmative obligation for banks to help meet the credit, deposit, and banking
needs of communities, including low and moderate income (LMI) communities. While the CRA
has successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest and provide services in underserved
communities, challenges related to redlining, discrimination, underinvestment, and lack of
access remain.

Public Counsel is a nonprofit public interest law firm dedicated to advancing civil rights and racial,
gender, and economic justice, as well as to amplifying the power of our clients through
comprehensive legal advocacy. Founded on and strengthened by a pro bono legal service model,

Washington, DC 20219
Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations Proposed Rule (Docket ID
OCC-2026-0694)

To Whom It May Concern:

Thank you for the opportunity to provide feedback on the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation's (FDIC) proposal to reform Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA) regulations.

The Housing Advisory Group (HAG), founded in 1993 by the pioneers of
the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC), remains our nation's most
active developer association in expanding and protecting the Credit and has
been at the center of all significant advancements to the LIHTC over the
past 40 years. HAG was specifically created to largely represent the
affordable housing developer's perspective on policy and practices, which
have contributed to the production of over 3 million units of affordable
housing.

The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, our nation's most important tool for
the production of affordable rental housing, relies heavily on investments
from banks subject to CRA. In fact, approximately 80 percent of equity
investments in the Housing Credit each year come from CRA-motivated
bank investors, according to a 2025 study by the accounting firm
CohnReznick.

For a majority of investors, including financial institutions, the LIHTC is an
attractive investment because it offsets tax liability and/or satisfies their
CRA requirements, specifically through the investment test. As we stated
above, minus the investment in the LIHTC by banks, a majority of the
affordable housing developed in the country would not be produced. The
proposed redesignation of banks between $10 billion and $1.6 billion in
assets as intermediate banks, on its own, is not a threat to this investment.
 What will have a significant impact on affordable housing production is the
elimination of the investment test for these banks.

The risk is twofold from our perspective. Developers of affordable housing
need a sufficient amount of equity through syndication of the LIHTC to
offset the capital needs of the development and to limit the debt incurred.
The more debt the development carries, the higher the rent for tenants,
making it very difficult to develop housing for prospective tenants at lower
incomes. Competition for the LIHTC is key to keeping the price of the credit
high enough to secure the equity needed for development. As an example,
an investor paying .94 per credit on a $1million allocation raises $940,000.
If there is less competition for the LIHTC and the investors offer .78, that
equals $780,000, with the development now carrying a $160,000 shortfall.
By eliminating the investment test for intermediate banks, you are
decreasing both the demand and competition for the LIHTC at a time when
the country needs millions of units of housing.

The second risk to the program is the investment deserts that will be
created by eliminating the investment test for intermediate banks. A vast
swath of the country, specifically in rural areas, is served by mid-sized
community banks, most of which would fall into this new intermediate
bank category. If they no longer were required to invest in the communities
in which they do business, these areas could see little or no affordable
housing production and might also see banks close branches as they would
no longer be required to service development in those areas.

Ironically, this NPR reclassifying banks and potentially decreasing
investment in affordable housing undercuts recent congressional action to
strengthen and expand the LIHTC and facilitate more bank investment in
the program. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act included a substantial increase
in the allocation of LIHTCs to the states for production, and it also
expanded the 4 Percent LIHTC program to increase supply. The 21st
Century ROAD to Housing Act raised the limit on banks' public welfare
investments (PWI) to allow them to increase their LIHTC investments. The
provision lifting the PWI cap would mostly impact many of the same banks
that would be reclassified as intermediate banks. Thus, the CRA changes
under consideration could greatly dilute these legislative accomplishments
and undercut congressional goals of providing more affordable rental
homes.
 Alternatives to the Primary Proposal

The NPR included two alternatives to the primary proposal to set new
thresholds for various bank size classifications.

 1. The first would raise the large bank asset threshold from $1.649
 billion to $3.252 billion. This alternative would be substantially
 less disruptive to LIHTC investment than the primary proposal to
 raise the large bank threshold to $10 billion.

 2. It goes without saying that the other proposal to raise the
 intermediate bank threshold to $30 billion would be far more
 damaging for affordable rental housing production. It is estimated
 that under a $30 billion large bank threshold, 17 states would see
 the number of large banks with investment requirements cut by
 half or more. In addition, banks with assets between $10 billion
 and $30 billion account for more than twice as much LIHTC debt
 and equity investment as banks between $1.65 billion and $10
 billion.

 3. Although separate from this rulemaking, we encourage the
 regulators to consider the impact of bank capital requirements on
 the capacity of banks to invest in the LIHTC. The historical
 performance and risk characteristics of LIHTC investments are
 relevant to that work, and the interaction between CRA incentives
 and regulatory capital requirements will influence the amount of
 bank demand for LIHTC equity.

 The CRA proposal and the capital proposals affect different sides
 of that equation. While changes to CRA requirements may reduce
 the incentive for some banks to invest in the LIHTC, more risk-
 sensitive capital treatment could increase banks' capacity to invest.
 The regulators have emphasized that the capital proposals are
 intended to better align regulatory capital with risk, thereby
 allowing banks to invest in communities while maintaining safety
 and soundness. Based on its risk profile, the LIHTC's risk
 weighting should be adjusted downward which in turn could
 materially expand bank's ability to invest equity in the LIHTC
 market. This would decrease the capital charge to banks that invest
 in LIHTC's and increase their appetite for affordable housing
 investments.

Conclusion

The Housing Advisory Group strongly recommends and encourages the
OCC and FDIC to leave the thresholds as they currently stand under the
 1995 CRA rule. If the OCC and FDIC move forward with changes to CRA
designations and regulations, we strongly urge maintaining the lowest
possible threshold for large banks. For newly designated intermediate
banks, we ask that the requirement to invest, as well as lend, in the
communities in which they do business be maintained. Anything short of
this will significantly curtail competition for the LIHTC and affordable
housing production throughout the country.

Respectfully Submitted,

Robert C. Moss
Chairman
Housing Advisory Group

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

Rise Economy submits these comments in opposition to the harmful changes
proposed to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was
passed by Congress in 1977 in response to redlining and to create an
affirmative obligation for banks to help meet the credit, deposit, investment,
and financial services needs of communities, including low and moderate
income (LMI) communities. While the CRA has successfully encouraged
banks to lend, invest and provide services in underserved communities,1

billion in lending to businesses located in LMI tracts in California from 2010 to 2024,

activities that support critically needed affordable housing and economic
development projects. These activities often provide the greatest CRA
impact in communities as they strengthen economic stability and mobility,
quality of life, and the health of residents and communities.

Fewer banks will be subject to Community Development and Investment
Tests. The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate"
and "Large" Banks, such that many banks will be subject to substantially
less CRA scrutiny and expectation to serve the community development
needs of their communities.4 According to National Community
Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, in California, seventy (70) banks

that take property off of the speculative market in favor of the long term
stability of residents and communities.

 4) The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to
 better meet the needs of Native American Communities and
 Tribal Nations.

The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the
needs of Native American communities and Tribal Nations which have been
poorly served by banks. The current rules focus CRA obligations in areas
where banks have branches, even though there are far fewer bank branches
near Tribal Nations and in rural areas where Native Americans may reside.

The proposal seeks to address this CRA gap by encouraging banks to engage
in community development and related activities in "Indian Country" and on
"Tribal and Native lands," even if outside of bank CRA assessment areas.
But many members of Tribes in California will not benefit from this proposal
as they do not live in Indian Country or on Tribal or Native lands, as defined.

CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring
within geographies, given the challenges and impacts associated with
historic dispossession and federal policy. Instead, CRA evaluations should
also consider whether banks have established meaningful relationships with,
and provided direct benefits to, federally recognized Tribes as well as non-

We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation’s (FDIC) proposed revisions to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.
AmPac Business Capital is a community-based, mission-driven nonprofit lender serving small businesses throughout the State of California and in select counties of Arizona and Navada. Through our work as an SBA Community Advantage SBLC, SBA Microlender and SBA 504 lender, we provide responsible financing and technical assistance to small businesses from cradle to legacy in underserved communities, serving startup businesses, rural businesses, LMI communities and first generation entrepreneurs that often face barriers to accessing conventional financing.
We appreciate the agencies’ efforts to modernize the CRA regulations and support provisions that could improve clarity, reduce unnecessary burden, and promote responsible capital in underserved communities. However, we have significant concerns that several proposed changes—including substantially higher asset thresholds, restrictions on community development grants, changes to community development performance standards, and reductions in data collection and transparency—could weaken the incentives that bring banks and mission lenders together.
These changes could have a direct impact on our ability to access the bank capital, investments, grants, lines of credit, deposits, and other financial support that enable us to serve borrowers and communities that conventional financial institutions may not efficiently reach directly.

Our organization’s ability to serve small businesses and communities depends in meaningful part on our relationships with financial institutions. Today, we work with banks that provide support for our organization in the form of loans, investments, deposits, grants, lines of credit, loan loss reserves, and provide referrals. These relationships represent approximately $2 Million or 33% of our total borrowed capital of $6,000,000.  These funds have leveraged guaranteed loan support for AmPac CA 7a SBLC loans totaling greater than $39 Million, and supported loan loss reserve for AmPac’s SBA micro loan program where we have loaned almost $7.5 Million in loans from $5,000 to $50,000 to start-up and early start businesses.   These dollars have created or retained well over $1,700 jobs throughout the State of California and have provided thousands of hours of coaching and technical assistance.  These dollars make communities better and families stronger by advancing entrepreneurial dreams. Dear Deputy Executive Secretary Jones and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency:

We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposed revisions to the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA) regulations, which was published in the Federal Register on August 12, 2026.

AmPac Business Capital is a community-based, mission-driven nonprofit lender serving small
businesses throughout the State of California and in select counties of Arizona and Navada. Through
our work as an SBA Community Advantage SBLC, SBA Microlender and SBA 504 lender, we provide
responsible financing and technical assistance to small businesses from cradle to legacy in
underserved communities, serving startup businesses, rural businesses, LMI communities and first
generation entrepreneurs that often face barriers to accessing conventional financing.

We appreciate the agencies' efforts to modernize the CRA regulations and support provisions that could
improve clarity, reduce unnecessary burden, and promote responsible capital in underserved
communities. However, we have significant concerns that several proposed changes--including
substantially higher asset thresholds, restrictions on community development grants, changes to
community development performance standards, and reductions in data collection and transparency--
could weaken the incentives that bring banks and mission lenders together.

These changes could have a direct impact on our ability to access the bank capital, investments, grants,
lines of credit, deposits, and other financial support that enable us to serve borrowers and communities
that conventional financial institutions may not efficiently reach directly.

BANK PARTNERSHIPS ARE VITAL TO OUR ABILITY TO SERVE LOCAL BUSINESSES
 Our organization's ability to serve small businesses and communities depends in meaningful part on our
relationships with financial institutions. Today, we work with banks that provide support for our
organization in the form of loans, investments, deposits, grants, lines of credit, loan loss reserves, and
provide referrals. These relationships represent approximately $2 Million or 33% of our total borrowed
capital of $6,000,000. These funds have leveraged guaranteed loan support for AmPac CA 7a SBLC
loans totaling greater than $39 Million, and supported loan loss reserve for AmPac's SBA micro loan
program where we have loaned almost $7.5 Million in loans from $5,000 to $50,000 to start-up and
early start businesses. These dollars have created or retained well over $1,700 jobs throughout the
State of California and have provided thousands of hours of coaching and technical assistance. These
dollars make communities better and families stronger by advancing entrepreneurial dreams.

Banks have access to significant pools of private capital and financial expertise, while organizations like
ours have deep knowledge of local markets and longstanding relationships with entrepreneurs who may
not yet have access to conventional financing.

In many cases, we work with business owners before they are ready for a traditional bank loan. We help
them improve financial practices, establish credit, strengthen operations, and build the track record
needed to pursue additional financing as their businesses grow. That work can ultimately create
stronger businesses and future customers for the broader banking system.
Without these relationships, our ability to respond to local credit needs would be more limited. With the
support of investment funds received from a local bank through their CRA investment, AmPac
supported a small business in Volcano, CA. The population of the community is 100 as of the last
census. The company is in the fire prevention and defensible space industry and they provide land
clearing work to support fire prevention initiatives by landowners and local governments. The funds
allowed the business to provide machinery and equipment to support the business. The funds
supported the creation and retention of two new jobs.

We recognize that the CRA is one factor among many that banks consider when deciding where to
direct their resources and build community partnerships. We are concerned that changes to the
proposed framework, particularly changes affecting bank asset thresholds and the treatment of
community development activities, could unintentionally reduce incentives for banks to maintain these
relationships.

For our organization, this is not simply a regulatory issue. It is a question of whether private capital and
local financial partnerships will continue to reach emerging and small businesses that are seeking the
opportunity to grow, create jobs, and strengthen their communities. We encourage the agencies to
preserve a CRA framework that supports these voluntary, market-based partnerships while maintaining
appropriate accountability for meeting community credit needs.

In conclusion, our organization's experience demonstrates that strong partnerships between financial
institutions and mission lenders can expand access to private capital without replacing or competing
with the traditional banking system. Bank relationships provide important resources that allow
organizations like ours to serve creditworthy small businesses and communities that may not yet be well
positioned to access conventional financing.

As the agencies consider modernization of the CRA framework, we encourage a practical approach that
preserves accountability while avoiding unnecessary regulatory changes that could reduce private-
sector investment or limit the flexibility of community-based lenders.

To summarize, we respectfully urge the OCC and FDIC to:
 Retain the current CRA asset thresholds and carefully evaluate whether higher thresholds could
 reduce private-sector incentives to support local communities;
  Preserve CRA consideration for operating and capacity-building support that helps mission
 lenders operate efficiently and responsibly;

 Maintain meaningful incentives for banks to work with mission lenders through lending,
 investments, deposits, grants, loan participations, referrals, and other market-based
 partnerships;

 Continue recognizing small-business lending that addresses genuine gaps in access to credit,
 particularly where businesses are seeking to establish or strengthen relationships with traditional
 financial institutions;

 Maintain appropriate CRA data and transparency so regulators, financial institutions, and
 communities have the information necessary to evaluate outcomes and identify genuine credit
 needs;

 Ensure that CRA continues to distinguish meaningful community development from ordinary-
 course lending, so that CRA incentives remain focused on activities that would otherwise be less
 likely to occur; and

 Preserve flexibility for financial institutions and mission lenders to develop partnerships that
 respond to local market conditions, rather than imposing a one-size-fits-all approach.

 CRA modernization should strengthen accountability while allowing banks and mission lenders
 to use private capital, local knowledge, and established community relationships to address
 legitimate credit needs. The objective should be a CRA framework that encourages greater
 private investment, responsible lending, and measurable community impact without
 unnecessarily increasing regulatory burdens.

4. Remove or narrow exclusions affecting legitimate working-capital and operating loans.

5. Ensure rural lending is considered even when it falls outside a bank's two largest product lines.

 PRELIMINARY STATEMENT

Obelisk Tech Systems Inc. ("Obelisk" or "the Commenter") submits these comments under 5 U.S.C.
 553(c) on the joint proposal of the OCC and the FDIC to amend their Community Reinvestment
Act regulations.1

Obelisk is not a bank and would not be regulated by the rule. It is a small business headquartered

15 U.S.C. 553(c); Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52114 (Aug. 12, 2026) (comments due
 October 13, 2026).

Comments of Obelisk Tech Systems Inc. 16
 OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694, RIN 1557-AF57 -- FDIC RIN 3064-AG31

in Thomas County, Georgia, a nonmetropolitan county.2 It supports a much simpler CRA regime
for small community banks, and it asks that the final rule do more for rural credit, small-business
credit and federally guaranteed lending. It also asks the agencies to keep two things the proposal
puts at risk: accountability for meeting the credit needs of rural communities, and a size framework
that delivers relief to community banks and not to small charters of large organizations.

Congress enacted the Act on October 12, 1977. This Comment is dated October 12, 2026, forty-
nine years later. The operative command has not changed in that time: each agency shall "assess
the institution's record of meeting the credit needs of its entire community, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods, consistent with the safe and sound operation of such institution."3
The asset tiers, the performance tests and the data rules are the agencies' means to that end. This
Comment tests each major provision against that text, the APA and the evidence, including the
evidence that cuts against Obelisk's own position.

Support for small banks is not support for every provision. Obelisk identifies what it asks the
agencies to adopt as proposed, what it asks them to amend, and what it asks them to correct in the
economic analysis. Conclusions that depend on the final rule are stated conditionally, and nothing
here asserts that either agency has violated a statute. This is a comment by a member of the public.
It is not legal advice or a pleading, and James Hunter Poole signs it as an officer of the Commenter,
not as counsel. Filing it creates no standing, cause of action, or right to an individual response or
to citation, and Obelisk claims none.

 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

 IV. STATUTORY AUTHORITY AND SCOPE OF DELEGATION

By what authority? The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit In-
surance Corporation propose to redraw the lines that decide how each of roughly 3,577 banks is
examined for community reinvestment.50 Their authority is a 1977 statute of eight short sections,
one general rulemaking clause, and three related provisions of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act.
That authority is enough for most of what the agencies propose. It is also bounded, and the bounds
decide several questions in this proceeding. This Part maps the authority first, because every propo-
sition that follows depends on it.

A. The Community Reinvestment Act, Section by Section

The Act is title VIII of Public Law 95-128, codified as amended at 12 U.S.C. 29012908.51 Read
in order, it contains a handful of commands to the agencies, three permissions, one consequence
that attaches to a rating, and one line drawn by asset size. It contains no performance test, no
data-collection requirement and, apart from 2908, no size tier.

1. Section 2901: findings and purpose

Congress found that regulated financial institutions "have continuing and affirmative obligation to
help meet the credit needs of the local communities in which they are chartered," and stated the Act's
purpose: "to require each appropriate Federal financial supervisory agency to use its authority when
examining financial institutions, to encourage such institutions to help meet the credit needs of the
local communities in which they are chartered consistent with the safe and sound operation of such
institutions."52 Three features of that sentence govern everything else. The verb is "encourage."
The object is "credit needs." The place is "the local communities in which they are chartered."

Obelisk supports a simpler examination for community banks and supports the $1 billion small-

It opposes two things the agencies are considering: a cross-reference to the Small Business Ad-
ministration's size standard, and the alternative in Question 1. And it asks for one addition, an

A. The Statutory Frame

Proposition S-001. The Act requires assessment of every covered institution's record of meet-
ing the credit needs of its entire community; size tiers are the agencies' creation, except the
one line Congress drew in 12 U.S.C. 2908.

The duty in 12 U.S.C. 2903(a)(1) is to "assess the institution's record of meeting the credit needs
of its entire community, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods." It applies to each
institution examined, and 2906 requires a written evaluation and one of four ratings for each.98 The
Act says nothing about small, intermediate or large banks. The agencies created those categories
by rule in 1995 and 2005 under 12 U.S.C. 2905, and they acknowledge that the statute "does not
require the agencies to tailor the performance tests by asset size."99 Congress drew one size line
itself, the $250 million examination-cycle line in 2908.

Four consequences follow, and they organize the rest of this Part.

 (1) Because the tiers are policy choices within a general delegation, they are judged by the quality
 of the agencies' reasoning and data, not by statutory text. The agencies "must examine the
 relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation."100

C. The Small-Bank Line

Proposition S-003. A fixed $1 billion small-bank line, indexed to the CPI-W, is supportable
on this record. A cross-reference to the SBA size standard is not: eight days after this notice
the SBA proposed $5,031 million for depository institutions.

1. Why $1 billion is supportable

The line tracks the one 1995 margin that still makes sense for small banks. At $1 billion, 79.8
percent of supervised banks are in the lightest tier, against an industry-wide 80.4 percent in 1995.
The 815 banks that move hold 2.9 percent of assets, so community development evaluation still
covers 95.1 percent of assets.116

The figure has a regulatory history. One billion dollars was the outer edge of the small-bank cate-
gory the three agencies adopted in 2005, which "primarily affect[ed] banks with assets of at least
$250 million and under $1 billion."117 The proposal's change is that the community development
test no longer applies below that figure.

The heavier tier imposes a cost that banks act to avoid. The research the OCC cites found that after
1995 banks bunched just below the $250 million line, slowing their growth to stay in the lighter
tier.118 A line that binds fewer growing community banks reduces that distortion.

The burden evidence is real but thin, and Obelisk does not overstate it. The OCC's only per-bank
figure is that intermediate small banks "have indicated that they spend approximately 200 hours
on CRA compliance activities per year," a figure attributed to commenters in earlier rulemakings.

The statute's object is credit. Congress found that regulated institutions "have continuing and af-
firmative obligation to help meet the credit needs of the local communities in which they are char-
tered," and it directed each agency to "assess the institution's record of meeting the credit needs of
its entire community."173 In rural America that credit has a particular shape. It is the farm operating
line that pays for seed, fertilizer and cash rent before a crop is sold; the working-capital loan that
carries a small business between payables and receivables; and the SBA- or USDA-guaranteed loan
that a community bank makes to a borrower who could not obtain credit without the guarantee. A
rule that evaluates rural banks on that credit measures what the statute asks about. A rule that looks
past it measures something else.

Obelisk supports the proposal's reduction of examination and data burden on small community
banks (Proposition S-003). This Part identifies six places where the proposal, as drafted, would
stop evaluating, exclude from consideration or stop measuring the credit that rural communities
use. Each is treated in the same order: the proposal, current law, the defect, the agencies' likely
defense, the contrary evidence, an amendment and a fallback. None of the six amendments restores
the community development test or imposes any data-collection duty on a bank below $1 billion.
Draft regulatory text appears in the Part titled "Proposed Regulatory Text."

The need for these amendments begins with what the notice leaves out. Its treatment of rural credit
is confined to geographic flexibility for community development "deserts," the distressed or un-
derserved tract definition, one illustration involving small farm loans and one example program.
The notice does not mention the SBA 7(a) program, guaranteed loans, the Farm Service Agency,
HUBZones or persistent poverty, and its economic and regulatory-flexibility analyses contain no
rural-specific discussion.174 The Administrative Procedure Act consequence is addressed in Propo-
sition S-013. This Part supplies the substance.

Each amendment in this Part can be made by the OCC and the FDIC in this rulemaking, under

or underserved list across all insured banks requires the participation of the Board. A comment

agencies consider these propositions and give reasons for the choices they make.282

 IX. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEDURE ACT ANALYSIS

This Part states the standards a reviewing court would apply to a final rule and tests the proposal
against them. It is a comment-stage objection. No final agency action exists, no claim under the
Administrative Procedure Act (APA) has accrued, and every defect identified can be cured before
the agencies act; Obelisk does not state that either agency has violated the APA. Each issue carries
a status: ESTABLISHED (a fact about the notice that can be checked against its text), CONDITIONAL
(a defect only if the final rule repeats it), UNRESOLVED (the record permits no conclusion), or NOT
APPLICABLE (screened and set aside).

A. Governing Standards

Notice, comment and the duty to consider. After notice, an agency must "give interested persons
an opportunity to participate in the rule making through submission of written data, views, or argu-
ments with or without opportunity for oral presentation," and, "[a]fter consideration of the relevant
matter presented," must "incorporate in the rules adopted a concise general statement of their basis
and purpose."306 The Supreme Court has put the duty in one sentence: "An agency must consider
and respond to significant comments received during the period for public comment."307 The Dis-
trict of Columbia Circuit states the rule and its limit: "the opportunity to comment is meaningless
unless the agency responds to significant points raised by the public," but "only comments which,
if true, raise points relevant to the agency's decision and which, if adopted, would require a change
in an agency's proposed rule" qualify, and comments that "are purely speculative and do not dis-
close the factual or policy basis on which they rest require no response."308 Each objection below is
drafted to that test: it gives the agency statement challenged, the page, the evidence, and the change
in the rule that would follow.

Scope of review. A court "shall decide all relevant questions of law" and shall set aside agency

A. What the Act Requires of These Agencies

An agency that publishes a notice of proposed rulemaking "shall prepare and make available for
public comment an initial regulatory flexibility analysis" describing "the impact of the proposed
rule on small entities," including "any significant alternatives to the proposed rule which accomplish
the stated objectives of applicable statutes and which minimize any significant economic impact

certification."350 An agency that does not certify must, with the final rule, state "the significant

do not: the first binds only the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and the second binds three

B. How Review of a Final Rule Would Proceed

Finality and timing. Review requires "final agency action," which marks "the `consummation'
of the agency's decisionmaking process" and determines rights or obligations; a proposed rule
is neither.419 The default limitations period is six years, and an APA claim "does not accrue ...
until the plaintiff is injured by final agency action."420 A Regulatory Flexibility Act claim must be
brought within one year by a small entity subject to the rule (Proposition S-014).

Forum. The Hobbs Act does not list the OCC or the FDIC, and no special review statute was
identified, so review of a final rule would lie in a district court under 28 U.S.C. 1331 and 5
U.S.C. 702703, as the challenge to the 2023 rule did.421 Venue lies where a defendant resides,
where a substantial part of the events occurred, or where the plaintiff resides if no real property is
involved.422 Nothing routes such a case to the District of Columbia Circuit by default.

Standards and relief. The standards are those stated under "Governing Standards" in the APA
analysis. An agency may postpone its own effective date pending review, and a court may do so "to
the extent necessary to prevent irreparable injury."423

Who could sue. Regulated banks and their associations could, as they did against the 2023 rule. A
borrower, nonprofit or community organization would have to show a concrete injury fairly traceable
to the rule and not to the independent lending decisions of banks, which is a demanding showing.
Obelisk makes no such claim.

against modified total direct costs, as the Uniform Guidance provides, or against the grant amount,

nonmetropolitan areas, unless the agencies first publish the evidence on which elimination would
rest. The notice reports diversion of grant funds from supervisory experience without figures, and
the OCC's own analysis expects a shift away from grants with uncertain effects on nonprofit orga-
nizations. See Proposition S-012.

Yes. An optional template would reduce the documentation risk for small recipients, provided that
it incorporates the safe harbor in Amendment 8 and is not made a condition of consideration. See
Proposition S-012.

Questions 24 through 30.461

Question 24 (further limits on qualifying businesses or farms). No. The size test already incorpo-
rates the SBA standards in 13 C.F.R. 121.301, whose alternative net-worth and income standard
counts an applicant's affiliates, so affiliation with a larger firm is already addressed.462 Excluding a
start-up because it is expected to grow would exclude the outcome economic development is meant
to produce. See Proposition S-009.

Question 25 (retaining the job requirement for low- and moderate-income persons). Not as a re-
quirement. It should be kept as an alternative route: financing that meets the former purpose test
should continue to qualify even if the agencies retain a use-of-proceeds limit in paragraph (3)(i)(B).
That would keep the proposal from disqualifying activity that qualifies today. See Proposition S-
008.

or enrolled under SBA section 7(a), the SBA 504 program, the USDA Business and Industry pro-
gram, the Farm Service Agency guaranteed farm loan programs and approved State Small Business
Credit Initiative programs, and loans to qualified HUBZone small business concerns. The proposed
list names five kinds of intermediary and no program under which a community bank itself lends.

To Whom It May Concern:

On behalf of The NRP Group, I urge the federal banking regulators to make no change--or
only a minimal change--to the asset thresholds governing which banks remain subject to a
separate Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) investment test. Founded in 1994, The NRP
Group is a vertically integrated developer, owner, builder, and manager of multifamily
housing that creates affordable and market-rate communities at scale. The company has
developed approximately 31,000 affordable apartment homes across the United States
and works with public and private partners to create high-quality rental housing for
individuals and families regardless of income. Raising the large-bank threshold to $10
billion would weaken a proven incentive for banks to invest in Low-Income Housing Tax
Credit properties and diminish the impact of federal affordable housing dollars.

The Housing Credit is the nation's primary tool for creating and preserving affordable rental
housing. Congress expanded the program in 2025, an investment estimated to finance 1.22
million additional homes over the next decade. Banks provide roughly 75 to 80 percent of
Housing Credit equity, and at least 71 percent is CRA-motivated. CRA policy should sustain
this demand, not offset Congress's investment.

An Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC) survey found that 108 banks below the
proposed $10 billion threshold invested at least $1.6 billion over five years--an estimated
$2 billion across the full market. If an increase is necessary, the $3.252 billion alternative
would be far less disruptive, reducing the affected investors from 108 to 40 and estimated
affected equity from roughly $2 billion to $272 million. A $30 billion threshold would place
an estimated $4.5 billion in five-year investment at risk.

The NRP Group has seen the impact of CRA firsthand across the markets where we develop
affordable housing. In San Antonio, for example, lower area median incomes can limit the
rents an affordable community can support even as land, labor, materials, insurance, and
other development costs continue to rise. These economics often cannot generate returns
sufficient to attract private investment without strong CRA-motivated demand for Housing

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Communitas Veterans Agency, Inc (CVA) submits this comment in opposition to the
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of
the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
(FDIC)1 because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also
request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze
the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an
opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting
any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.

CVA provides housing support and homelessness prevention, workforce development and
financial empowerment, and community partnerships that promote stability, independence,
and long-term self-sufficiency in the DMV. We support veterans, their families, and the
community, and CRA is a critical resource in achieving our mission.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important

 in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss, and unequal
