October 12, 2026

Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations -- Docket No. OCC-2026-0694

Dear Comptroller of the Currency and Members of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation:

We are Utah-based nonprofit organizations serving communities throughout our state, and we
appreciate the opportunity to comment on the proposed changes to the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations, particularly the proposed requirements governing
community-development grants.

We strongly support the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA investments produce meaningful
benefits for the communities they are intended to serve. As organizations working directly with
individuals and families--including low- and moderate-income Utahns--we understand the
importance of making sure charitable resources are used responsibly and effectively.

However, we are concerned that the proposed 15% ceiling on indirect costs for community-
development grant recipients of large banks would have the opposite effect from what the agencies
intend. Rather than directing more resources to local communities, the provision could discourage
banks from supporting smaller, community-based nonprofits and shift funding toward larger
organizations that can more easily absorb or allocate costs outside of an indirect-cost calculation.

The Cost of Service
The proposed 15% standard is particularly concerning because it treats a widely used federal
indirect-cost rate as a ceiling when it was established as a minimum rate available to certain
organizations.

Under the federal Uniform Guidance, 2 CFR 200.414(f), eligible organizations may use a de
minimis indirect cost rate of up to 15% of Modified Total Direct Costs (MTDC). That provision
does not establish 15% as the maximum reasonable cost of operating a nonprofit. Organizations
with federally negotiated indirect cost rates may appropriately recover substantially higher
indirect costs.

The distinction matters.

Indirect costs are not synonymous with waste, inefficiency, or money diverted from mission.
They are the costs that make direct services possible and accountable: qualified supervision,
financial management, information technology, facilities, insurance, human resources,
compliance, data collection, evaluation, technology systems, administrative support, and other
infrastructure necessary to deliver services safely and effectively.
 A nonprofit cannot provide excellent services simply by paying for the person standing directly
in front of a client. The systems and people supporting that service are part of what makes the
service possible.

Small Nonprofit Impact
The proposed rule could create a significant unintended incentive for large banks to favor
organizations that can demonstrate overhead below the 15% threshold, regardless of whether
those organizations are the most effective or responsive providers in a particular community.

This is particularly concerning for smaller local nonprofits.

Community-based organizations often operate without the economies of scale available to large
national organizations. A small nonprofit may have to maintain its own accounting, technology,
insurance, human resources, facilities, compliance, fundraising, data systems, and program
administration with a relatively small number of employees and a modest budget.

Those costs may represent a larger percentage of the organization's total expenses than they
would for a much larger institution. Yet that does not mean the smaller organization is less
efficient or that more of its funding is diverted from its mission.

In many cases, the opposite is true: the local nonprofit is the organization with the relationships,
knowledge, trust, and infrastructure to reach people who might otherwise remain underserved.

For example, organizations serving Utah communities may provide literacy instruction, workforce
development, digital skills, education, financial empowerment, health-related services, housing
assistance, food security, and other services directly to low- and moderate-income individuals.
The effectiveness of those services depends on the infrastructure behind them.

A grant that helps a nonprofit maintain the technology needed to communicate with learners, the
staff needed to supervise programs, the insurance needed to protect clients and volunteers, or the
financial systems needed to maintain accountability is still supporting community development.

Project Read: A Utah example
Project Read, a Utah nonprofit providing adult literacy and digital-literacy services, illustrates why
a rigid indirect-cost ceiling can produce a misleading picture of how nonprofit resources are used.

In FY2026, Project Read served 197 adult learners through one-on-one tutoring, small-group
instruction, literacy labs, digital-skills instruction, and virtual programming. Delivering those
services requires substantially more than the direct cost of instructional time. Project Read must
also maintain the systems and infrastructure that make those services possible, including staff
supervision and training, facilities, technology, volunteer coordination, student assessment and
 outcomes measurement, financial management, insurance, compliance, and other
organizational functions.

Project Read's FY2026 expenditures represented an investment of approximately $1,900 per
adult learner served, supporting individualized instruction, small-group learning, digital literacy,
assessment, volunteer coordination, and the organizational infrastructure necessary to deliver
and measure those services.

A rigid 15% indirect-cost ceiling could create a counterintuitive result: an organization serving
hundreds of Utah adults, largely through direct community-based services, could be
disadvantaged in CRA funding decisions simply because the full cost of maintaining the
infrastructure necessary to deliver those services does not fit within an arbitrary percentage.

Project Read's experience is not unique. It illustrates a broader issue facing small and mid-sized
community nonprofits: a low percentage of indirect costs does not necessarily indicate greater
impact, and a higher percentage does not necessarily indicate inefficiency. The appropriate level
of infrastructure depends on the organization's size, mission, service model, geographic reach,
regulatory obligations, and other factors.

Unintended Incentives
A rigid indirect-cost ceiling could also create incentives that undermine transparency.

If legitimate organizational expenses cannot be treated as indirect costs for purposes of CRA
consideration, nonprofits may face pressure to classify expenses differently in order to remain
eligible for bank funding. That would make financial reporting less transparent, not more.

Alternatively, a nonprofit may determine that accepting a CRA-conditioned grant is not worth
the additional administrative burden or risk that the grant will not receive CRA consideration.

Banks could likewise choose to direct their giving toward organizations whose accounting
structures make the 15% threshold easier to demonstrate.

Neither outcome necessarily means that more money reaches the people and communities CRA
is intended to benefit.

Measurement Challenges
The proposal raises important questions about what exactly constitutes "indirect costs" and
how the 15% calculation would be made.

For example:

 What expenses are included in the definition of indirect costs?
  What measurement base is used to calculate the 15%?

 Is the calculation made on the grant itself or on the organization's overall expenses?

 What documentation must a nonprofit provide?

 How frequently must the calculation be performed?

 How should organizations with federally negotiated indirect cost rates be treated?

 How should organizations that use different but accepted accounting methodologies be
 treated?

 How should the standard apply when a bank makes a grant to an intermediary, such as a
 United Way or other community-based funder, which subsequently makes grants to one
 or more nonprofit organizations? Which entity's indirect costs would be subject to the
 15% standard--the intermediary, the ultimate recipient, or both?

 How should the standard apply to multi-year grants if a recipient's indirect-cost rate
 changes during the grant period? Would CRA eligibility be determined based on the
 recipient's rate when the grant is awarded, annually throughout the grant period, or at
 some other point?

These questions matter because 15% of total grant dollars is not equivalent to 15% of Modified
Total Direct Costs under the federal Uniform Guidance.

Creating a new, undefined methodology would also place additional compliance burdens on
nonprofits--particularly smaller organizations that may not have the financial staff or resources
to calculate and document indirect costs under a new bank-specific standard.

Flexible Support Matters
We also encourage the agencies to recognize the importance of general operating and capacity-
building support.

Community organizations need flexible resources to respond to changing community needs,
strengthen their infrastructure, train staff and volunteers, maintain technology, improve
outcomes measurement, and build organizational resilience.

These investments may not always be attributable to a single project or initiative, but they
directly affect an organization's ability to serve its community.

A strong community-development system should not require every dollar to be artificially
assigned to a narrowly defined program expense in order to be considered valuable.
 Regulatory Fragmentation
The Federal Reserve Board did not join this proposal, creating the potential for conflicting CRA
standards for the same community-development activity. This issue is particularly concrete in
Utah, where nonprofits routinely receive community-development grants from national banks
supervised by the OCC, state nonmember banks and industrial banks supervised by the FDIC,
and state member banks supervised by the Federal Reserve--sometimes within the same fiscal
year and for the same program.

If the proposal is adopted as issued, the same nonprofit activity could be subject to different
standards depending on the regulator overseeing the bank providing the grant. A grant
supporting the same program, in the same community, could be subject to the proposed
narrower definition under one bank's CRA framework while being evaluated under the existing
definition by another.

This would create unnecessary administrative complexity for nonprofits that receive funding
from multiple financial institutions. Organizations could need to maintain different
documentation, reporting, or cost-allocation practices for different funders, even when the
underlying community-development activity is identical.

It could also create an unintended situation in which a bank's CRA treatment of an otherwise
identical community-development activity depends more on the bank's charter than on the
activity's actual community benefit.

We urge the OCC and FDIC to coordinate with the Federal Reserve Board before finalizing these
provisions and to preserve, to the greatest extent possible, a consistent interagency standard
for community-development grants. At a minimum, the agencies should explain how they
intend to address the divergence and avoid imposing duplicative or conflicting requirements on
community nonprofits and financial institutions.

Recommendations
We respectfully ask the OCC and FDIC to remove the proposed fixed 15% indirect-cost ceiling.

If the agencies determine that an indirect-cost standard is necessary, we encourage them
instead to:

 1. Clearly define "indirect costs" and the applicable measurement base, so that nonprofits
 and banks can apply the standard consistently.

 2. Provide a safe harbor or exemption for smaller community-based nonprofits, recognizing
 the unique economies of scale and administrative realities they face.
  3. Preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-building grants that
 strengthen an organization's ability to provide qualifying community-development
 services.

 4. Minimize additional documentation and compliance burdens for nonprofit recipients,
 particularly organizations without sophisticated financial or accounting departments.

 5. Provide an appropriate transition period for banks and nonprofits with existing multi-
 year grant commitments.

The CRA exists to encourage banks to help meet the credit needs of the communities they
serve, including low- and moderate-income communities. The proposed 15% ceiling could
unintentionally make it more difficult for community-based nonprofits to access the very
resources that help them meet those needs.

We believe the agencies can achieve their goal of accountability and meaningful community
impact without establishing an arbitrary ceiling that may disadvantage effective local
organizations.

We respectfully urge the OCC and FDIC to remove the proposed 15% indirect-cost cap or
substantially revise it to recognize legitimate, reasonable, and federally accepted nonprofit cost
structures.

Thank you for considering the perspective of Utah's nonprofit community and for your
commitment to ensuring that CRA resources produce meaningful benefits for the communities
they are intended to serve.

Sincerely,

Shaun K. Brown
Executive Director
Project Read
Provo, Utah

Jackie Larson
CEO, Elevate Utah
Provo, Utah

Whitney Bloomquist
Associate Development Director
Wasatch Homeless Health Care
dba Fourth Street Clinic
Salt Lake City, Utah

When more investors compete for a credit allocation, equity pricing improves. Better pricing means less gap financing from scarce public sources and more homes per allocation.
Thank you for considering our comments. We are glad to provide more detail on how these changes would affect our projects.

Norma Dominguez, Chief Financial Officer
Excelerate Housing Group

October 13, 2026

400 7th Street, SW, Suite 1E-216
Washington, DC 20219

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations Proposed Rule (Docket ID OCC-2026-0694)

To Whom It May Concern:

Wendover Housing Partners ("Wendover") appreciates the opportunity to provide feedback on the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's ("FDIC") proposal to reform
Community Reinvestment Act ("CRA") regulations. As a developer of affordable and workforce housing
communities throughout the United States, Wendover is particularly concerned about the proposed increase in
the asset threshold for banks subject to the CRA's separate investment test and the resulting impact on the
availability of financing for affordable housing developments.

Wendover relies on a combination of private investment, conventional financing, and federal and state affordable
housing programs, including the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit ("LIHTC"), to develop housing for low- and
moderate-income families and seniors. Regional and community banks are important participants in these
transactions, providing both financing and equity investments that are often essential to making affordable
housing developments financially feasible.

The proposed redesignation or elimination of the separate investment test for banks with assets between
approximately $1.65 billion and $10 billion threatens to significantly reduce the participation of these
institutions in affordable housing development. Under the current CRA framework, the investment test
provides an important incentive for regional and community banks to invest in LIHTC developments within the
communities they serve. Without that incentive, we are concerned that many of these institutions will substantially
reduce their investment activity or exit the LIHTC market altogether.

From Wendover's perspective, the loss of these banking partners would have meaningful consequences.
Affordable housing developments are inherently complex transactions that depend on assembling multiple
sources of financing. Regional and community banks provide an important source of capital and competition,
particularly in markets where the number of potential investors is already limited. Their participation helps
developers secure competitive LIHTC equity pricing, reduce financing gaps, and move developments forward
that might otherwise be financially infeasible.

Eliminating the separate investment test could reduce competition among LIHTC investors, resulting in lower
equity pricing and increased financing gaps. Unlike conventional market-rate developments, affordable housing
communities are subject to restrictions on rents and tenant incomes, limiting a developer's ability to offset reduced
equity proceeds through increased rental revenue. As a result, even relatively modest reductions in LIHTC pricing
can jeopardize a development's financial feasibility, delay construction, or prevent much-needed affordable
housing from being built.
 We also recognize that the proposed regulations would continue to evaluate certain community development
activities undertaken by intermediate banks. However, community development lending and equity investment
are not interchangeable. While banks may continue to receive CRA consideration for lending activities, the
absence of a separate investment test may encourage institutions to prioritize lending over LIHTC equity
investments. This distinction is particularly important because the availability of equity is often what enables
affordable housing developments to support construction and permanent debt financing in the first place.

These concerns are especially significant in smaller and underserved markets, where regional and community
banks may be among the few institutions willing to invest in affordable housing developments. Reducing their
incentive to participate could further concentrate LIHTC investment among a smaller number of large national
institutions, making it increasingly difficult for developers to secure financing outside the most competitive
metropolitan markets.

At a time when the country faces a significant shortage of affordable rental housing, federal policy should
encourage greater participation by financial institutions in affordable housing investment, not create incentives
for existing participants to withdraw. The proposed changes also risk undermining recent congressional efforts to
expand the LIHTC program and increase the production of affordable rental housing.

Wendover respectfully urges the OCC and FDIC to leave the thresholds as they currently stand, consistent
with the direction the Federal Reserve (the third bank regulator) is taking. If the agencies elect to increase
the threshold, we strongly encourage adoption of the lowest possible increase, together with meaningful
requirements that preserve incentives for newly designated intermediate banks to make community development
equity investments, including investments in LIHTC developments. For newly designated intermediate banks, we
ask that the requirement to invest, as well as lend, in the communities in which they do business be maintained.
Anything short of this will significantly curtail competition for the LIHTC and affordable housing production
throughout the country.

We appreciate the agencies' consideration of these comments and encourage them to carefully evaluate the
potential consequences of the proposed changes for affordable housing production and the communities that
depend on it.

Respectfully submitted,

Jonathan L. Wolf
Founder and Chief Executive Officer
Wendover Housing Partners

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Since 1971, the Housing Authority of Snohomish County (HASCO) has expanded access to
affordable housing for households across Snohomish County. HASCO currently owns and
operates more than 2,000 homes, with hundreds of additional units under construction. Many of
these properties have been developed through the LIHTC program--a public-private partnership
that is essential to affordable housing production nationwide and closely linked to the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).

HASCO joins affordable housing developers and advocates at the national, state, and local
levels in opposing the proposed changes to the CRA. Our principal concerns are as follows:

 1) Although the LIHTC program continues to deliver meaningful results in Snohomish
 County, the widening gap between allowable rents and construction costs increasingly
 threatens project feasibility. At the current tax credit price of approximately $0.78, a
 typical project is financially viable only within the limited number of Qualified Census
 Tracts or Difficult Development Areas (QCTs/DDAs) in the county. By reducing bank
 participation in the CRA and LIHTC programs, the proposed rule could further constrain
 affordable housing production shortly after Congress significantly expanded the
 program through H.R. 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

 2) The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act contains numerous provisions designed to
 encourage housing innovation at the local level. Because innovative approaches are, by
 definition, new and may present unfamiliar risks, banks may be less inclined to support
 them when participation is optional. Washington State currently has 12 banks classified
 as "large"; under the proposed rule, that number would fall to four, substantially reducing
 the pool of institutions positioned to support emerging housing strategies. The
 proposed rule would therefore weaken significant bipartisan efforts to advance practical
 housing solutions nationwide.

 3) HASCO partners closely with community organizations, including Community
 Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs), to address financing gaps in affordable
 housing development. The effects described above could also diminish bank
 engagement with CDFIs, compounding the challenges facing affordable housing
 production and limiting the adoption of innovative housing solutions at a time of urgent
 need.
  For these reasons, together with the concerns raised by our community and national partners,
 HASCO respectfully opposes the proposed rule. We support the FDIC's and OCC's efforts to
 modernize the CRA, streamline its administration, and reinforce the vital role financial
 institutions play in their communities. HASCO welcomes the opportunity to share its local
 expertise regarding the intersection of the CRA, financial institutions, and affordable housing
 development. Based on our experience, however, we believe the proposed rule, as written, would
 materially impede communities across the country in meeting the urgent need for affordable
 housing.

The Neighborhood Development Collaborative (NDC), a coalition of 22 Colorado-based
nonprofit and mission-driven affordable home builders, submits this comment in
opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued
by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC)1 because it would significantly weaken the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the
changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes,
carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities,
provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify
supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60 days.

NDC and its member organizations use CRA-qualified funds to improve the lives of
everyday Coloradans. Grants and other funds required by the CRA are a vital source of
funds for affordable housing construction. CRA-qualified mortgages create affordable
homeownership opportunities, as do the LIHTC investment the CRA drives, the biggest
source of affordable housing in Colorado.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important
in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal
access to mainstream financial services.

 The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and

THIS PROPOSAL REDUCES COMMUNITY INVESTMENT EXPECTATIONS
FOR ALL BANKS

CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In the Denver
Metro Area and Colorado, from 2010-2024, banks invested $49 billion and $85 billion,
respectively, in CRA-qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census
tracts and $25 billion and $13 billion, respectively, in CRA-qualified lending to small
businesses. Investments such as these benefited our community, in the form of affordable
home mortgages for community land trusts and tax credit investments which continue
bringing affordable housing to our state.

We are concerned that the proposed CRA rule upends banks' incentives to make these
investments in the future. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's
Tier 1 capital devoted to either community development loans or investments would be
enough to receive a passing CRA rating.2 However, that percentage is far lower than the
percentage the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the
largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.

NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the
OCC and FDIC supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these
banks currently conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community development
loans and investments inside their assessment areas, and that the median percentage of
annual community development lending in assessment areas was 6.8% of Tier 1 capital,
and a median of 3.6% of Tier 1 capital for annual CRA qualified investments.3 If each
bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet separate thresholds of 0.625%
of Tier 1 capital for community development lending and investments, combined activity
would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually -- a decrease of approximately $87.1
billion, or 85%. Similarly, the proposal encourages banks to use strategic plans to make
their CRA compliance easier and more predictable. Previous proposed guidance also set

Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic
discrimination cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments
and loans. If regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be
accountable to the communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for
communities. In Colorado, for example, homeownership rates have been dropping as
home prices outpace wage growth. 63% of Coloradans owned their homes in 2025, down
4.5% in just 3 years, and well below the 71% at which Colorado's homeownership rate
peaked in 20025. Coloradans need affordable mortgages to be able to unlock the stability
that comes with homeownership. Additionally, Colorado persistently lacks housing
affordable at low incomes. Colorado only has 40% of the homes needed for households
earning less than 50% AMI, a deficit that LIHTC can help fill6.

It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet community needs.
Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes
would reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income
communities and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or
disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.

THIS PROPOSAL ELIMINATES "PURPOSE TEST" FOR ECONOMIC
DEVELOPMENT, WEAKENING CONNECTION TO LMI COMMUNITY
BENEFITS

Under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying small business does not
automatically constitute economic development. The activity must also satisfy a
requirement known as the "purpose test," meaning it must promote economic
development by supporting permanent job creation, retention, or improvement for low- or
moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income communities.7

The proposed rule would eliminate the "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks
could earn CRA credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or
improves jobs for low- and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income
communities. Instead, financing could qualify as economic development based primarily

preserves the business's productive capacity, physical presence or employment base.8

We are concerned that this change would weaken the connection between CRA economic
development credit and the people and communities CRA is intended to benefit.
Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying business expand does not necessarily create
jobs, increase economic opportunity in an underserved neighborhood or address the needs
of low- and moderate-income communities. NDC's members contribute not only to a
greater supply of affordable housing, but also to economic activity in Colorado generally.
From 2018 to 2023, affordable housing construction contributed the following to
Colorado's economy9:

Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens
a qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank
to demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or
neighborhoods.10 The agencies themselves acknowledge that eliminating the purpose test
would expand the universe of activities eligible for CRA credit.11

Before eliminating the purpose test, the agencies should analyze what additional activities
would qualify under the new definition, where those activities are likely to occur, and
whether bank financing could shift away from activities that create or retain jobs for low-
and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income communities. The agencies
should also explain why eliminating the existing connection to these outcomes is
consistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs of
their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities.

PROPOSAL WILL NARROW THE ACTIVITIES SUBJECT TO CRA
EXAMINATION AND HIDE LENDING GAPS

Under the current rule, large banks are generally evaluated on their home mortgage,
small business and small farm lending. The proposal outlines two options for regulators
to focus on products designated as a bank's "major product lines" based either on the
largest two product lines by all lending volume, or based on the type of lending a bank

lending. But if that type of lending is not a major part of a large bank in my community's
business, regulators will not evaluate whether the bank is meeting this crucial community
need. Absent such evaluation, the bank will likely deprioritize making such loans.

In addition, under the current rule banks above the large bank threshold generally collect
and report on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans
and assessment areas. But because of the proposed change in the threshold, banks with
$10 billion or less in assets would no longer be required to collect and report such CRA

Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers will not be able to

Before narrowing the activities subject to CRA examination and eliminating data
reporting requirements, the agencies should analyze the impact of doing so will have for
people with low- and moderate-incomes or low- and moderate-income communities,
including whether it could result in a reduction in the types of lending that would meet
community needs. In addition, the agencies should explain why this change would be
consistent with the CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit
needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.

CONCLUSION

Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:

 Identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA
 scrutiny under the proposal;

 Quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
 development activities subject to CRA evaluation;

 Assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or
 populations, including rural communities and communities of color;

 Consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without
 sacrificing meaningful community accountability; and

Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, NDC believes that the
OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts
is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable
changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

 The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for

consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities,
including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120
days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service
evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The

Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that

examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more
complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies
extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.

I submit this letter on behalf of the Carolina Small Business Development Fund (CSBDF). We appreciate the
opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal Deposit

Register on August 12, 2026.

CSBDF is a thirty-six (36) year old North Carolina non-profit community and economic development
organization that is certified by the Department of Treasury as a community development financial institution
(CDFI). CSBDF is also authorized, regulated and certified to carry out programs of the U.S. Small Business
Administration (SBA). The organization works hand in hand with local, regional, and national banks to
provide responsible financing and technical assistance to underserved small businesses through the SBA
Community Advantage program as well as other publicly and privately supported guarantee programs, while
helping to cultivate a pipeline of bank-ready businesses for conventional financial institutions. Largely because
of debt investments, operating grants and referral relationships with banks of varying sizes who adhere to CRA
rules, CSBDF has deployed over $134M in capital, entered into financial transactions with over 3,400 North
Carolina small businesses and has provided technical assistance to over 9,800 firms throughout the State.
IMPLAN economic development software (which operational grants from banks also help to fund) estimates
that CSBDF financial assistance to small businesses has created and saved nearly 6,200 jobs throughout the
State. In FY25 alone, our estimates showed over $15M in payroll earnings, 734 jobs created and saved and
over $4.6M in tax revenues created.

Debt investments have enabled CSBDF to provide low-cost financing to small businesses who have no other
financing alternatives or costly ones. The operating capital grants from banks have enabled the organization to
provide technical assistance in 1:1, group and digital formats through our online technical assistance platform
called VIVID. Operating capital has also contributed to the organization's clarity and transparency in
reporting, underwriting and data tracking, because it has strengthened the capabilities of our Salesforce and
loan origination platforms. Our capital has been deployed to small businesses in urban and rural areas; to male
and female-owned businesses; veterans and non-veterans; and to all of North Carolina's 10 highest growth

 attract affordable debt capital and operational support from banks. In fiscal year 2026, CSBDF had 14 notes

Re: Comment letter opposing OCC and FDIC proposed CRA rule changes

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

The Community Foundation of Nevada County respectfully submits these comments
in opposition to the changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules
proposed by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency.[1] Congress passed the CRA in 1977 in response to
redlining, creating an affirmative obligation for banks to help meet the credit,
deposit, and banking needs of the communities they serve, including low- and
moderate-income (LMI) communities. The CRA has successfully encouraged banks
to lend, invest, and provide services in underserved communities, yet
underinvestment and lack of access remain real challenges, particularly in rural
regions like ours.

The Community Foundation of Nevada County is a 501(c)(3) community foundation
serving rural Western Nevada County, California, in the Sierra Nevada foothills. Our
 mission is to connect people, resources, and ideas to build a healthy and vibrant
Nevada County. Our strategic priorities are nonprofit effectiveness and capacity
building, community health and wellness, and climate resilience and disaster relief.
Through our Center for Nonprofit Leadership, we provide training, coaching,
leadership development, and fiscal sponsorship to a network of more than 70 local
nonprofits. We steward the Nevada County Relief Fund for disaster response, are
helping build a Community Organizations Active in Disaster (COAD) network for
Western Nevada County, and work to bring new resources to underserved rural
communities such as the San Juan Ridge.

Banks are essential partners in this work. CRA-motivated grants, sponsorships,
lending, and investment help sustain the local nonprofits, affordable housing
providers, community land trusts (CLTs), and Community Development Financial
Institutions (CDFIs) that rural communities depend on. Rural regions also rely
heavily on community and regional banks, the very institutions whose CRA
obligations would be most reduced under this proposal.

We are concerned that the proposed changes would harm the communities the CRA
was meant to serve, and that the proposal does not analyze its expected impact on
LMI and rural communities. We respectfully request a 60-day extension of the
comment period so that the public can better understand how much CRA activity
may be lost as a result. Our concerns center on the following areas.

 1) Support for local nonprofits would decline, especially in rural
 communities.

The proposal would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by requiring
a demonstrated nexus to community development projects, and would require
Large Banks and their grantees to show that no more than 15% of these grants will
be used for overhead.[2] The agencies also ask whether CRA eligibility for bank
grantmaking to nonprofits should end entirely. The proposal itself acknowledges
that general operating support, capacity-building grants, grants to intermediaries,
and grants to smaller nonprofits may receive less CRA-motivated funding as a
result.[3]

This is precisely the funding that sustains nonprofits in communities like ours.
Through our work with local organizations, we see every day how flexible operating
and capacity-building support allows small, often thinly staffed nonprofits to keep
their doors open, retain staff, and deliver services. These smaller, rural
organizations will be least able to meet new documentation requirements, and the
likely result is that banks will make fewer grants overall and concentrate them
among larger organizations. Discouraging grants to intermediaries would also
 weaken one of the most efficient ways philanthropic dollars reach rural areas:
through community foundations and similar partners that pool resources and
regrant them to organizations that banks may not reach directly.

Bank contributions represent a small share of overall CRA activity, yet they have an
outsized impact on nonprofit capacity and on the constructive bank-nonprofit
partnerships that help banks reach and serve LMI residents. We urge the agencies
to preserve CRA eligibility for general operating support, capacity-building, and
intermediary grants, and not to adopt the 15% overhead limit.

 2) Investment in affordable housing, CLTs, and CDFIs would drop.

The proposal would raise the asset thresholds for Small, Intermediate, and Large
Banks, so that many banks would face substantially less CRA scrutiny of how they
serve the community development needs of their communities.[4] According to
National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70 California banks
would see their reinvestment obligations reduced under the proposal; 25 would
shed their Community Development Test responsibilities entirely, and 45 would no
longer be subject to the Investment Test.[5]

The Investment Test has driven critical investment into Low Income Housing Tax
Credits, equity-equivalent investments in CDFIs, and Community Land Trusts that
take property off the speculative market. Commercial banks account for an
estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, and approximately half of nonprofit CDFI
funding comes from CRA-motivated banks.[6] Housing affordability is a pressing
challenge in Nevada County, and any reduction in community development
financing would make it harder for local partners to create and preserve homes that
working families can afford. Asset thresholds should not be raised.

 3) Disaster resilience and rural infrastructure needs could be
 overlooked.

Nevada County is a high wildfire-risk region that has experienced the Jones Fire,
the River Fire, and severe winter storms in recent years. Preparing for and
recovering from disasters depends on strong local partnerships, including with
banks. The proposal would provide CRA credit for large-scale infrastructure projects
that may generate profits for banks, would likely be financed without CRA credit,
and provide only incidental benefits to LMI residents. This could lead banks to earn
CRA credit through large projects in place of smaller, locally driven projects that
better meet community needs, such as childcare facilities, health clinics, rural
broadband, water systems, and resilience projects. CRA credit for infrastructure
should remain clearly tied to meaningful LMI benefit.
  4) Rural branch access and small business lending would be at risk.

By raising the Large Bank threshold to over $10 billion in assets, the proposal would
remove 45 California banks from the Services Test, which reviews whether their
branches serve LMI communities. NCRC estimates that 245 branches in California
LMI areas would be vulnerable to closure under the proposal.[7] Branch presence is
tied to small business lending, and these changes would be felt most in rural areas,
where smaller banks originate a larger share of small business and small farm
loans. Fewer banks would also be required to report small business, small farm, and
community development lending data, information that is essential to
understanding the needs of local markets like ours.

 5) Tribal communities, including non-federally recognized Tribes,
 should be fully considered.

The proposal encourages banks to engage in community development activities in
"Indian Country" and on "Tribal and Native lands," but many California Tribal
members do not live in areas that meet those definitions. In our own community,
the Nisenan Tribe of the Nevada City Rancheria remains without restored federal
recognition since its termination in 1964. CRA evaluations should also consider
whether banks have established meaningful relationships with, and provided direct
benefits to, both federally recognized and non-federally recognized Tribes.[8]

Conclusion. If finalized substantially as proposed, this rule would reduce
investment in affordable housing, CLTs, and CDFIs; weaken the bank-nonprofit
partnerships that rural communities depend on; and make it harder for
communities like ours to prepare for and recover from disasters. We respectfully
urge the FDIC and the OCC to reconsider this proposal and to preserve the CRA's
focus on LMI, rural, and underserved communities.

Thank you for your consideration and for the opportunity to comment.

Sincerely,

Cristine Kelly
Chief Executive Officer
Community Foundation of Nevada County

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Stronger CRA ratings should reflect measurable benefits for communities. The rules should reward
investment in the local capacity that makes those benefits possible.

I submit this comment on behalf of Miles McNeal & Powell LLC (MMP), a social enterprise based in
Vallejo, California. We are developing Upsurge Community toward a future Community Development
Financial Institution serving Solano County. Our perspective comes from community investment,
small-business engagement, and partnerships among public agencies, businesses, and nonprofit
organizations.

I support clearer eligibility standards and proportionate reporting requirements. I oppose the proposed
asset-threshold increases, reduced community development rating requirements, and grant restrictions
because they could discourage banks from funding the organizations and services that prepare
underserved borrowers for financing.

Our strategy through 2035 uses a capital absorption framework. It identifies community priorities,
prepares projects for financing, and establishes the staff, partnerships, and systems needed to manage
investment. Our next stage includes a small-business census and incubator/accelerator programming
to identify financing gaps and prepare entrepreneurs to access capital. This work requires funding
before a loan portfolio can generate revenue.

Asset Thresholds and Accountability | Questions 13; Section IV.B.
MMP/Upsurge supports reducing unnecessary reporting burdens for mission-driven banks, including
CDFI banks. That relief should preserve community development accountability and incentives to fund
the staff, underwriting, compliance, and technology that emerging CDFIs need to serve underserved
borrowers.
 Raising the intermediate-bank ceiling from approximately $1.65 billion to $10 billion would remove
separate investment and service tests for affected banks. Allowing stronger lending performance to
compensate for weaker community development performance would further reduce incentives to
provide grants, investments, and specialized financing.

Retain the current asset thresholds unless a published community impact analysis supports changing
them. Require intermediate banks to earn at least a satisfactory community development rating to
receive an overall satisfactory rating. Preserve lending and geographic data needed to identify
financing gaps and evaluate bank performance.

Grant Eligibility and Indirect Costs | Questions 910.
The proposed grant restrictions could make it harder to fund borrower preparation and the institutions
that deliver it. Emerging lenders must establish financial controls, compliance procedures, and
technology before they have a large portfolio over which to spread those costs.

Direct program expenses and indirect costs must be distinguished. An indirect-cost percentage alone
does not show whether an organization delivers effective services or manages funds responsibly.
Additional documentation also consumes staff time for both banks and recipients. The agencies should
assess those costs, particularly for small grants and emerging organizations.

Preserve CRA consideration for operating and capacity-building grants that support documented
community development purposes, including qualifying activities before CDFI certification. Reject the
alternative of eliminating grants from CRA consideration.

Replace the fixed 15% ceiling with reasonable, documented cost recovery. Recognize applicable
federally negotiated indirect-cost rates and scale documentation to grant size. The federal framework
permits negotiated rates and an optional de minimis rate; it does not establish 15% as a universal
measure of organizational efficiency. See 2 C.F.R. 200.414.

Longer-Term Financing | Question 8.
I support CRA consideration for qualifying community development loans held from earlier evaluation
periods. This can encourage financing terms that match the time borrowers and projects need, rather
than the timing of a bank examination.

For Solano County and surrounding Bay Area counties, the relevant outcomes include businesses
obtaining affordable financing, residents gaining ownership opportunities, and community-serving
facilities being developed or preserved. These outcomes depend on both investment capital and funded
preparation.

I urge the agencies to preserve community development accountability, retain flexible grants, replace
the rigid indirect-cost ceiling, and maintain the data needed to evaluate results. The institutions
expected to deliver community reinvestment must have the resources to do the work.

Respectfully,
R. Shay Miles
Chairwoman, Miles McNeal & Powell LLC
Developing Upsurge Community

 On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA). CRA has helped create a durable incentive for banks to provide loans,
investments, grants, and services in communities that have historically lacked access to capital.

 As the statewide coalition for Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) in
Minnesota, we are proud of the investments and impact that CDFIs have in expanding
opportunity and access across the state. Minnesota is home to almost 40 certified and emerging
CDFIs providing loans and capital investments to communities. CDFIs supplement capital with
critical training and technical assistance for small businesses, childcare providers, home buyers,
affordable housing developers, and community organizations. In the five-year period 2017
2022, CDFIs in Minnesota invested $3.463 billion in capital in rural, suburban, urban, and tribal
communities across the state.

 Page 1
  CRA partnerships are critical to that success, and the changes that the agencies are
proposing would fundamentally alter these partnerships. We have profound concerns with the
increases in the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under CRA and the
restrictions on operating grants, as well as the impacts to bipartisan tools like Low-Income
Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) and New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC). Weakening community
development incentives will impair the flow of much needed capital in the most underserved
communities, and remove the promise of economic mobility and investment from Americans.

Minnesota will be uniquely impacted by proposed changes to community development
obligations

 Minnesota has an active CDFI sector that is vital to ensuring capital moves to
communities. According to original research aggregating the work of CDFIs across Minnesota,
in the year from July 2024 to June 2025, Minnesota CDFIs closed on over 2,399 loans totaling
more than $282M. As of June 30th, 2025, Minnesota CDFIs had Loan Funds totaling more than
$944M and Loans Outstanding totaling more than $700M. Small business development and
affordable housing development simply does not happen in Minnesota at the same scale without
CDFI participation.

 Bank partnerships through the CRA are important sources of capital for CDFIs. The
Minnesota CDFI Coalition's research shows that 74% of Coalition members receive capital from
bank partners. The provisions of the CRA that enable these partnerships would be fundamentally
altered under the proposed changes. According to research from the National Community
Reinvestment Coalition,1 Minnesota would be the second-most impacted state under the
proposed changes. In Minnesota, NCRC estimates:

 50 of 107 banks, or 46.7%, would lose community development obligations
 19 of 36 banks, or 52.8%, would lose large-bank status,
 170 of 343 LMI branches, or 49.6% would be jeopardized

 Based on current asset sizes, NCRC estimates this would roll back all community
development requirements for over 800 banks nationally, reducing the total number of all banks
with CRA-related community development requirements by about 40%, as well as reclassifying
over 400 large banks as intermediate.2 This would change the CRA's framework from one

 where roughly the largest half of all banks have community development requirements, to a
regulatory system where less than one third are evaluated for community development.

 In addition to raised asset thresholds, the OCC and FDIC have also proposed to remove
the requirement that intermediate banks pass both their community development test and their
lending test in order to receive an overall passing CRA rating.3 The OCC and FDIC make a
broad claim that this will lead to banks performing better on both tests without the "artificial

increase their community development even though they no longer have to prove satisfactory
community development performance; and a de-emphasis of community development seems far
more likely.

 The loss of community development obligations and large bank status would remove the
requirements for investing in community that are critical to expanding access to capital across
the state. Without the strong framework of the CRA, the agencies undercut the intent of the
legislation to expand opportunity to all Americans and remove effective community
development and investment tools.

New grant restrictions will harm collaboration and partnerships between banks and
community nonprofits

 The OCC and FDIC are proposing new restrictions on CRA-eligible philanthropy. All
banks will be required to show that grants are "directly used by the recipient for a program,
project, or initiative with a primary purpose of community development" and large banks will
also have to prove that no more than 15% of a grant or donation goes to indirect or

FDIC are proposing a 15% cap on indirect costs since that is the standard the federal government
uses for its grants.

 Banks often support affordable housing, small business development, financial
counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based
services through grants to nonprofit organizations. Grants can be particularly important to local
organizations that have deep relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of

 their communities. A 15% cap may be particularly unrealistic for smaller nonprofit organizations
that are central to community work. Payroll, rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other

 The MacArthur Foundation analyzed data from over 130,000 nonprofits and "found that

 In Minnesota and across the nation, grants often support the organizations and

The Washington State Housing Finance Commission is submitting this comment in opposition to the
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) Regulations because these rules
would significantly weaken the CRA's ability to drive private investment in affordable housing.

Given the complexity of the rule and scope of the proposed changes, we request that the OCC and FDIC
carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an
opportunity to contribute evidence to and comment on the analysis, and extend the current comment
deadline by 60 days.

As the housing finance agency for Washington state, we are concerned about the negative impacts of
these changes on both affordable rental housing and affordable homeownership. Most critically, the
Community Reinvestment Act is a key driver for investment in the federal Low Income Housing Tax
Credit (LIHTC).

The housing credit, established by Congress in 1986, is a highly effective financing tool that brings
millions of dollars in private capital to build and preserve rent- and income-limited apartments across the
country. In Washington state alone, more than 110,000 affordable apartments have been built and
preserved in communities of all sizes for all kinds of renters, from working families to those experiencing
homelessness to seniors.

In the housing credit program, housing developers are allocated credits to sell to investors in return for
capital investment in their projects. Approximately 85 percent of this housing credit investment comes
from banks that are incentivized by the CRA investment test to purchase the credits.

But by raising the asset thresholds for banks, the proposed CRA changes would reduce the number of
banks subject to the investment test requirement, erasing their incentive to invest. The higher the
threshold, the greater the risk to billions of dollars in equity, according to a December 2023 survey of

 RE: NDC OPPOSES THE PROPOSED CRA RULES 2026

The National Diversity Coalition ("NDC") is a national non-profit organization including the
leadership of our nation's major African American, Asian, and Latino organizations as well as major
minority- and women-oriented national nonprofits, and businesses advocating for economic
empowerment and financial equality for low-moderate income (`LMI'), minority, and other
disadvantaged communities.

NDC submits comments opposing the proposed rulemaking ("the CRA proposal"), which aims to
retain the structure of regulations applicable to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
("OCC") and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") supervised banks, but has proposed
major changes in the size of the banks, assessment area, and revised criteria for Community
Development Grants.

Background

Congress enacted the Community Reinvestment Act in 1977 to meet the credit needs of low-income
communities in a manner consistent with banks' safe and sound operations. There is no doubt that
CRA has been one of the transformative laws that has pushed financial institutions to respond to the
credit needs of low-income communities long ignored by traditional institutions.

For a long time, NDC has had concerns about the existing CRA rules, including that almost 90% of
banks received a `satisfactory rating' in CRA examinations.1 However, NDC strongly believes the
proposed changes to the CRA rules would negatively affect low-income communities ("LMI") and
reduce the flow of capital and credit to them.

1 Josh Silver & Jason Richardson, Do CRA Ratings Reflect Differences in Performance: An Examination Using
Federal Reserve Data, NCRC, See at https://ncrc.org/do-cra-ratings-reflect-differences-in-performance-an-
examination-using-federal-reserve-data/
 At the outset, NDC recommends that OCC and FDIC should not proceed with the proposed CRA
rules for the following reasons.

1. NDC Opposes reevaluation of Bank Asset Size Categories

NDC opposes reevaluating asset thresholds used for performance tests. The CRA proposal wants to
define the asset threshold of a `small bank' with assets of 1 billion or less, an intermediate bank with
assets between 1 billion and 10 billion, and a large bank with more than 10 billion in assets. In the
current framework, a small bank has assets of $412 million, intermediate banks have assets between
$412 million and $1.649 billion, and large banks have assets of more than $1.649 billion.

NDC is concerned that the proposed reclassification of assets for large banks and intermediate
banks will exclude many banks currently assessed between $1.649 billion and $10 billion from the
full large bank examination, including the lending, investment, and service tests.2 The impact of
these proposed CRA rules will be devastating for many rural and small-town communities that
heavily rely on these banks for community development initiatives. NDC works closely with LMI
income communities that rely on large banks with assets between $ 1.649 billion and $ 10 billion; we
are seriously concerned that reclassifying asset size for large banks will reduce their regulatory
obligation to report community development investments and small-business lending. NDC strongly
believes this proposed rule would end up treating nearly 80% of OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks
as small banks, while only about 2% would be treated as large banks. As a result, there will be less
money for affordable housing, small businesses, consumer lending, and financial literacy for low-to-
moderate income communities, especially in small towns and rural areas.

Therefore, NDC opposes the proposed CRA rules that reclassify the asset size of small,
intermediate, and large banks.

2. NDC Opposes Revised Criteria for Community Development Grants as it harms Small
 and Medium Community Based Organizations

NDC opposes the CRA proposal that would change community development grants, including the
rule requiring large banks to obtain a written commitment regarding the qualifying use of the
proceeds and to provide documentation sufficient to establish CRA eligibility. NDC also opposes
the rule proposal that would limit consideration for large banks to grant recipients whose indirect
cost for administering a grant or donation does not exceed 15%. This proposed rule would harm
small and medium community-based organizations that provide valuable services to low income
communities, such as affordable housing, small business support, financial literacy, and first-time
homeownership initiatives. Many small community-based organizations operate with fewer than 10
staff members and undertake multiple responsibilities and tasks to provide services for low-income
communities. These small community-based organizations are mostly based in low-income

2 NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters, https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-rollbacks/
 communities and have grassroots connections to their needs. The proposed CRA rule limiting
indirect costs to 15% will severely affect their operations and reduce low-income communities'
access to capital and community development benefits. More importantly, the proposed CRA rule
would lead large banks to prefer large nonprofit organizations that can comply with the
documentation and administrative-cost limits, and thereby refuse to provide community
development grants to small, community-based organizations.

Finally, there is no legal or policy rationale for narrow circumstances in which community
development grants receive CRA consideration. In many federal grants, legal mandates or policy
objectives limit the indirect costs incurred when selecting recipients. However, for community
development grants provided by the financial institution, banks' guiding rationale is to provide
community development funding after understanding the unique needs of low-income communities
and evaluating the competence of community-based organizations. The narrowing of the indirect
cost to 15 percent and the additional requirement of documentation of the grant would result in
reducing the community development initiatives in the low-income communities,

The NDC has a long history of partnering and collaborating with various small community-based
organizations in California, and we all provide important services, including affordable housing,
bridging small business loans, and financial literacy in our communities. Therefore, the NDC
strongly opposes the proposed CRA rules on the revised criteria for community development grants.

3. The proposed CRA Rules would negatively affect the availability of bank branches in
 low-income communities

The proposed CRA rule reclassifying the asset threshold for large banks will harm bank branches in
low-income communities. NDC has always been vocal against closing bank branches in low-income
communities. Closing bank branches creates a `bank desert' in the community, ultimately reducing
access to capital and financial opportunities for small businesses and lending in low-income
communities. In recent years, the number of people living in banking deserts has increased from
11.5 million to 12.3 million.3 Previous studies also show a clear pattern of financial institutions
disproportionately closing bank branches in low-income communities. 4

For the last decades, NDC has been able to challenge banks' attempts to close branches in low-
income communities by using the rules. The CRA branching obligations are the main reason banks
have maintained local branches in low-income communities, fearing that community-based
organizations will challenge their mergers before regulators. However, with the revised classification
of the asset threshold for `large bank', many banks would have less incentive to maintain a fair share

3 Alaina Barca and Harry Hou, US Bank Branch Closures and Banking Deserts, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia,
https://www.philadelphiafed.org/-/media/frbp/assets/community-development/reports/banking-deserts-report-feb-
2024.pdf
4 Jason Richardson, Bank Branch Closures Slow, But Shifting Demographics Cloud the Picture, https://ncrc.org/bank-
branch-closures-slow-but-shifting-demographics-cloud-the-picture/
 of branches in low-income communities, which could accelerate branch closures in LMI areas.
NCRC notes that "large-bank threshold to $10 billion would eliminate separate branch evaluations for 417
banks. More than 5,000 branches in low- and moderate-income census tracts -- 30% of all LMI branches
nationwide -- and more than 4,000 branches in majority-people-of-color census tracts -- 23% of all such branches
--would lose these needed accountability measures."5

NDC also believes that meaningful access to banking services should be evaluated not only through
branch presence and distribution, but also through an institution's commitment to community
engagement, financial education, and the development of banking relationships that address local
credit needs. The proposed or current model of evaluating service test does not properly adequate
the needs of a banking branch operating in the LMI areas.

Therefore, NDC recommends that the OCC and FDIC reevaluate the impact of the proposed rules
on LMI areas and refrain from reclassifying the asset size of large banks.

4. Proposed CRA Rules Reduce the Scope of Challenge to Poor Performing Banks in
 Mergers and Acquisitions

The proposed CRA rule that reclassifies the asset threshold for large banks could negatively affect
community-based organizations' ability to challenge bank mergers that harm low-income
communities. The NDC, along with many other community-based organizations, relies on the CRA
reports to understand the bank's commitment to the credit needs of low-income communities,
including providing capital for small business and community development. Consequently, these
CRA reports play a pivotal role in analyzing bank mergers and acquisitions. However, proposed
changes to large bank asset size would reduce scrutiny of banks, particularly under the service and
investment tests and; community-based organizations would lack sufficient information and
evidence to challenge a bank merger that harms LMI communities.

NDC recommends that the OCC and FDIC not reclassify or change the asset threshold for large
banks, because diluting scrutiny would let poorly performing large banks avoid substantial challenges
to their mergers and acquisitions under CRA.

5. NDC Raises Concern on Continuing Exclusion of Credit Unions from CRA Review

NDC understands the legal limit on including credit unions in the CRA review, as federal statute
excludes credit unions from the CRA. Nevertheless, we still want to highlight the continuing
unfairness of excluding credit unions from the CRA review. Today, credit unions increasingly
operate like big banks. 445 credit unions have assets of more than $ 1 billion. Credit unions are
highly consolidated in the market; the average credit union size has jumped 186% in the past 10

5 Supra note 2
 years. More importantly, in 2025 alone, the National Credit Union Administration approved 157
credit union mergers.

These figures clearly indicate growth and expansion in the credit union sector over the last 10 years.
Nevertheless, credit unions are extremely reluctant to address the credit needs of low-income
communities. CRA regulations require large banks to address the credit needs of low-income
communities, but similarly situated credit unions refuse to do so because they lack those obligations.
In a large bank merger, community-based organizations use their CRA periodic reports to support
or oppose the merger by considering its impact on low-income communities. However, because
there is no legal requirement to invest in low-income communities, community-based organizations
find it extremely difficult to have productive discussions with credit unions to address the credit
needs of low-income communities.

While we acknowledge that this specific issue is beyond the scope of the OCC and FDIC, we submit
this comment to raise awareness of one negative implication of excluding obligations to low-income
communities.

6. Proposed CRA rules do not factor in the importance of institutional investment in long-
 term sustainability of branches in LMI Communities

Establishing a physical banking presence in an LMI community is only the beginning. Sustainable
success requires a strategic commitment to building brand awareness, cultivating community trust,
and developing meaningful relationships with local stakeholders.

Newly established branches, particularly those entering markets where the institution has limited
brand recognition, need adequate corporate marketing support, community engagement resources,
and sufficient time to establish themselves. Without these investments, even well-intentioned branch
expansion efforts risk falling short of their intended community impact.

NDC believes that meaningful access to banking services should be evaluated not only through
branch presence and distribution, but also through an institution's commitment to community
engagement, financial education, and the development of banking relationships that address local
credit needs. The proposed or current model of evaluating service test does not properly adequate
the needs of a banking branch operating in the LMI areas.

CONCLUSION

NDC opposes the OCC and FDIC proposed rewrite of the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA)
regulations. The proposed CRA rules will reduce community development and economic
development for low-income communities and reduce lending to small businesses. Moreover,
proposed rulemaking attempts to reduce the scrutiny of the existing large banks in their
performance in responding to the credit needs of the LMI communities
