Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

We, the undersigned elected officials, organizations and individuals serving
Oregon, urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the proposed Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) rule. Oregon needs more capital to build affordable
homes and preserve the homes people already have. Reducing banks'
incentives to invest would undermine that work and shift more of the financing
burden onto limited state and local housing dollars.

We share a commitment to affordable homes, strong local economies, and fair
access to credit throughout Oregon. State and local housing investments
depend on private financing and capable community partners to deliver results.
CRA helps connect bank capital to those public priorities, supporting rental
housing, affordable homeownership, and the preservation of existing homes,
including manufactured housing communities.

Protect the investment needed to build Oregon homes

Oregon's 2026 Housing Needs Analysis identifies a need for nearly half a
million homes over 20 years. More than 181,000 of those homes must be
affordable to households earning 60% or less of area median income. That need
extends from the Portland metro area and Willamette Valley to Central Oregon,
the coast, and rural eastern and southern Oregon. Production targets cannot be
met without financing that supports rents working families can afford.

Housing Oregon | www.housingoregon.org | P.O. Box 8427, Portland, OR 97207
 The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) supplies equity that reduces how much a
developer must borrow and repay through rent. CohnReznick's 2024 survey found that banks
supplied roughly four out of every five dollars of LIHTC equity, approximately $23 billion
nationwide. It identified CRA as the primary driver of that investment. Weakening CRA
therefore threatens a central source of capital for Oregon affordable housing.

If investor demand falls, the same tax credit allocation can raise less equity. For illustration, a
five-cent decline in pricing on $10 million in total federal credits creates a $500,000 financing
gap. Oregon Housing and Community Services and local governments would then face pressure
to commit more subsidy to each development, leaving less for other homes. Some projects could
be delayed or become infeasible. Strong CRA investment expectations help Oregon's housing
dollars go further.

Keep Oregon banks accountable to local communities

NCRC's Oregon analysis finds that eight of the 31 banks currently subject to community
development evaluation in the state would lose that evaluation: more than one in four. The
affected institutions include Bank of Eastern Oregon in Heppner, Oregon Coast Bank in
Newport, People's Bank of Commerce in Medford, and Citizens Bank in Corvallis. The roster
also includes Pioneer Trust Bank, First Federal Savings and Loan Association of McMinnville,
Evergreen Federal Bank, and Willamette Valley Bank.

Three additional banks serving Oregon--Heritage Bank, 1st Security Bank of Washington, and
Beneficial State Bank--would lose large-bank status and separate investment and service tests.
Combining loans, investments, and services into one community development evaluation
weakens the distinct incentive to supply patient equity, including LIHTC and New Markets Tax
Credit investments. A profitable loan does not perform the same financing function as equity or a
grant.

These changes are especially concerning for smaller Oregon communities where a local
nonprofit may have few financing partners. Our concern is the weakening of standards across the
market; identifying these institutions is not a criticism of their current performance. The agencies
should retain meaningful community development evaluations and separate investment and
service tests, with expectations responsive to local needs.

The proposal also risks setting expectations far below existing investment. NCRC's analysis of
69 large banks compares about $102 billion in annual community development lending,
investments, and grants within their assessment areas with roughly $14.8 billion under the
proposed benchmark scenario: an 85% reduction. The separate 0.625% of Tier 1 capital
benchmarks concern geographic flexibility, not an automatic passing CRA rating. Nevertheless,
such low benchmarks could become banks' practical targets. This is a national scenario, not a
forecast of Oregon losses; the agencies should reject benchmarks that invite such a retreat.
 Sustain New Markets investment in Oregon communities

New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) help finance the jobs and community facilities that support
stable housing. From 2003 through 2024, NMTC-supported projects in Oregon accounted for
$2.64 billion in total project financing across 163 projects, facilities, and businesses. The NMTC
Coalition reports 9,569 permanent full-time-equivalent jobs and 10,789 temporary construction
FTE jobs. These are investments in Oregon communities that conventional financing has not
adequately served.

Oregon examples include St. Vincent de Paul Society of Lane County's workforce development
program in Eugene and the Coquille Indian Tribe's Ko-Kwel Wellness Center near Coos Bay.
Hacienda CDC has used NMTC financing for its headquarters and a public market supporting
Latino food entrepreneurs. Affordable homes are more effective when residents can also reach
health care, training, and opportunities to earn a living.

The agencies should preserve strong incentives for NMTC investment and retain the economic
development purpose test. CRA credit should depend on a demonstrated community benefit.
Allowing routine business financing to qualify without that showing could draw capital away
from projects serving low- and moderate-income residents, including rural and Tribal
communities.

Protect the nonprofits that turn investment into homes

We oppose the proposed 15% indirect-cost cap for qualifying large-bank grants and the
additional documentation requirements. We also oppose eliminating CRA consideration for
grants and donations. Oregon's nonprofit housing organizations need operating support to
assemble financing, manage construction, maintain compliance, and provide housing counseling.
Accounting, technology, and organizational capacity are necessary to deliver these services
responsibly.

A small rural housing organization cannot spread those costs across the same volume of projects
as a larger developer. Culturally specific organizations also need sustained capacity to serve
communities that have experienced redlining and exclusion from homeownership. Restricting
flexible support could leave Oregon with fewer organizations able to develop affordable homes,
even when project funding is available. Preserve CRA credit for operating and capacity-building
grants with a primary community development purpose and use proportionate reporting
requirements.

CRA must continue to address the consequences of redlining and unequal access to capital.
Preserve meaningful public participation, fair-lending accountability, and review of access to
affordable banking services. Rural residents, Tribal communities, and communities of color need
a strong voice in determining whether banks are meeting local needs.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Thank you for your efforts to provide greater clarity, consistency, and predictability in the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) framework, and for the opportunity to comment on the
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's
(collectively, "the agencies") proposed rule.

About NAAHL

The National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders (NAAHL) is the national alliance of
the leading lenders and investors in affordable housing and community development bringing
together banks, community development financial institutions (CDFIs), and other public, private,
and nonprofit lenders, with a mission to expand economic opportunity through innovative
policymaking.

In 2023, NAAHL members made more than $75 billion in housing loans and investments across
all 50 states and Washington, DC, and CRA is central to our members' affordable housing and
community development work. Our unique coalition has allowed NAAHL to bring practitioners'
voices to the table and serve as the honest broker in policy discussions on lending and
community development, particularly in discussions around CRA.

 1
 The Impact of CRA and What's at Stake
CRA has become an essential tool for bringing private capital to meet local credit needs. In 2024
alone, CRA incentivized more than $430 billion in loans and investments for homeownership,
small businesses, and affordable housing and community development in LMI communities
nationwide.

Specifically, in 2024, CRA incentivized:
 Nearly $168 billion in affordable housing and community development lending and
 investments;
 More than $152 billion in small business loans;
 More than $100 billion to support homeownership; and
 More than $10 billion in small farm loans.

In other words, CRA incentivized private capital into communities nearly six times the combined
federal funding for the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), the U.S.
Department of Agriculture's (USDA) Rural Housing Service, the Small Business Administration
(SBA), and the CDFI Fund.1 It has also helped create and strengthen partnerships between banks,
local leaders, nonprofits, and residents as they work toward a common goal: expanding
economic opportunity for the community and the families who live there.

1 Incentive to Impact: How CRA Leverages Private Investments into Affordable Housing, Homeownership, Small
Business, and Local Economies (Center for Affordable Housing Lending, July 2026),
https://naahl.org/s/NAAHL_CRA_Report_072326_V4-Web.pdf.

 2
 CRA is especially irreplaceable for affordable housing and community development. CRA helps
drive loans and investments into housing supply, including through the Low-Income Housing
Tax Credit (LIHTC), and economic development, including through the New Markets Tax Credit
(NMTC), as well as essential community infrastructure. From 2015 through 2024, banks made
more than $1.4 trillion in community development loans and investments benefiting low- and
moderate-income (LMI) people and areas and other underserved geographies.2

Banks of all sizes are essential partners in financing affordable housing and community
development. In 2024, banks with less than $30 billion in assets made nearly $53.5 billion in
community development loans, more than one third of all bank community development lending
by dollar volume that year, and nearly two thirds by number of loans. Banks with less than $10
billion in assets made up the majority of this activity.

Sweeping changes to CRA could jeopardize the partnerships driving our housing, small business,
and community development ecosystems, putting capital for housing supply and local economies
at risk. Without the private capital catalyzed by CRA, communities could see more deals fall
through, fewer business opportunities, and less support for the hospitals, childcare facilities, and
schools serving LMI people and places that make daily life more affordable for families. This, in
turn, means weaker local economies and fewer people and businesses who will be able to access
the credit they need to build opportunity and wealth. Reduced financing and partnerships could
also strain relationships between banks and communities that have formed through years of
collaboration.

While some bank affordable housing and community development activity may continue without
CRA incentives, there is no way to know how much. At a time of significant housing need, we
must carefully consider whether putting nearly two-thirds of this financing at risk is a risk we are
willing to take.

2 Id.

 3
 Areas of Consensus to Strengthen CRA

While recognizing the importance of ensuring CRA continues to successfully incentivize the
flow of capital into communities, our organization and many banks, financial regulators, and
community partners alike have identified the need for targeted updates to account for changes in
our financial system and in customers' and communities' needs, increase clarity, allow for
innovation, and better support communities with significant unmet needs. Targeted updates based
on widespread consensus that has developed over the past decade to address these well-known
issues would create a durable CRA framework that provides the certainty that banks and their
partners need to invest in people and communities. NAAHL generally supports updates in the
following areas, which have developed broad support:

 Increase clarity and transparency through a single non-exhaustive, illustrative list of
 activities eligible for community development consideration, as well as a formal and
 prompt process to receive a prior determination that an activity will qualify for
 community development consideration;

 Allow banks to provide financing based on project needs, not the CRA framework,
 by providing consideration for outstanding balances of community development loans
 paired with appropriate adjustments in the benchmarks examiners use when assigning
 community development ratings to maintain the current level of impact;

 Continue to support activities in underserved markets by providing credit for
 community development activities beyond a bank's assessment area for banks that have
 demonstrated that they met community development needs during their last CRA exam;

 Clarify ways to demonstrate that naturally-occurring affordable housing (NOAH)
 qualifies as affordable housing to incentivize further private capital support for our
 housing supply;

 Provide favorable consideration for financing in partnership with community
 development financial institutions (CDFIs) nationwide;

 Maintain data collection consistent with current levels of coverage to support banks'
 and communities' ability to assess economic opportunities and challenges in each market;

 Maintain consistency across the banking regulators, with all three developing and
 adopting shared regulations and guidance;

 Enhance examiner training and ensure sufficient staffing and head office oversight
 to provide timely, consistent exams for banks of all sizes, regardless of charter type or
 business model; and

 Ensure adequate implementation timelines for industry to adjust to any changes to
 CRA.

NAAHL Recommendations

After thoughtful deliberation with our Sustaining Members, NAAHL is pleased to offer
recommendations to ensure the agencies' updates fulfill their intended purpose and support
lenders' and local partners' shared efforts to expand access to affordable housing and enhance
economic opportunity.

 4
 We support the OCC and FDIC's efforts to clarify CRA implementation and reduce regulatory
burden and support several components of the proposed rule. However, we are concerned that
some proposed changes, taken together, may not have the intended effect and could instead
unintentionally reduce affordable housing and community development outcomes, particularly in
rural areas and smaller markets served by fewer financial institutions.

Our detailed comments begin on page 6 and our responses to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
(NPR) questions begin on page 23.

 I. Establish asset thresholds that support diverse, dynamic markets that meet the range
 of affordable housing and community development needs.

 II. Maintain CRA's focus on lending, investment, and services that expand economic
 opportunity and build wealth.
 a. Set major product lines at the bank level to reduce regulatory burden if a major
 product lines standard is adopted.
 b. Continue to evaluate consumer loans only when they make up a substantial
 majority of lending and measure consumer loan products individually to
 recognize their distinct features and roles.
 c. Establish major product lines prior to the start of the exam period to avoid
 unnecessary burden if a major product lines standard is adopted.
 d. Recognize community development's essential role in helping to meet community
 credit needs by continuing to give appropriate weight to community development
 activities in determining a bank's CRA rating.
 e. Maintain consideration of a bank's record of providing a wide range of products
 and services to meet communities' needs.
 f. Preserve flexibility for banks with unique business models.

 III. Ensure local service providers, community-based organizations, and nonprofits can
 continue to help lenders meet local credit needs.

 IV. Maintain a CRA framework that incentivizes community development financing
 tailored to unique local needs in LMI communities.
 a. Recognize the important and distinct roles of loans, investments, and grants in
 community development financing.
 b. Allow banks to offer financing that responds to community needs, not the CRA
 exam framework.
 c. Preserve eligibility for tax credit equity investments and equity equivalent
 investments.
 d. Clarify eligibility for impactful in-kind donations.
 e. Ensure community development activities support LMI communities and areas of
 unmet need, as intended by statute.

 V. Support access to affordable housing and community development financing in all
 communities through clear, uniform guidance.

 5
  a. Establish clear, uniform interagency guidance on qualifying community
 development activities to support impact and innovation.

 b. Set clear standards for receiving credit outside of assessment areas that give
 banks and communities certainty and align with the realities of community
 development financing.

 VI. Maintain a flexible strategic plan option that prioritizes affordable housing and
 community needs.

 VII. Balance transparency for lenders and communities with regulatory burden.
 a. Maintain data reporting consistent with current levels of coverage to give
 communities, lenders, and researchers a more complete picture of the market.
 b. Maintain existing, well-understood data collection for loans considered under
 CRA.
 c. Right-size data collection and documentation for community organizations.

 VIII. Maintain the Interagency Questions & Answers, which provides clear and well-
 understood guidance on CRA implementation.

 IX. Establish a thoughtful transition process.

We thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed rule and encourage the agencies
to consider providing additional time to engage key stakeholders on the potential changes to
CRA and their industry and community implications before adopting a final rule. We ideally urge
all three banking agencies to work together to adopt a single regulation that maintains strong
levels of community development lending and investment from lenders of all sizes and continues
CRA's longstanding focus on LMI individuals and communities and a durable CRA framework
for banks of all types and sizes.

Detailed Comments

 I. Maintain asset thresholds that support diverse, dynamic markets that meet the
 range of affordable housing and community development needs.

NAAHL does not endorse the proposed changes to bank asset thresholds. At a time when we are
working to lower costs for families and improve neighborhood affordability especially around
housing we view allowing more banks to not be assessed for community development
detrimental to those efforts.

We support maintaining the diverse U.S. banking system that has developed to respond to the
varied credit needs of consumers, businesses, and communities across the country. Just as
communities range in size and in housing and community development needs, there is a need for
banks of different sizes to serve those communities. As noted above, in 2024, banks with less

 6
 than $30 billion in assets made more than one third of all bank community development lending
by dollar volume, and 64 percent by number of loans. Without the credit provided by these
institutions, nearly two-thirds of community development projects supported by CRA-qualifying
loans, including essential affordable housing, may not have been possible. Banks with less than
$10 billion in assets also played a significant role in this lending. These banks were responsible
for more than 60 percent of loans by banks with less than $30 billion in assets, both by dollar
amount and loan count.3 Furthermore, in many smaller markets where larger banks have less of a
physical footprint, banks with less than $30 billion in assets are an irreplaceable lifeline.

Sudden changes to CRA responsibilities for large numbers of banks could have significant
unintended consequences for communities. Increasing the number of banks that are categorized
as "small" and thereby removing their CRA assessment on community development would likely
result in less community development lending and investment. Increasing the number of banks
that are categorized as "intermediate," thereby simplifying their CRA assessment on community
development activities, would also likely result in a net drop of investment activity because
investments would no longer be separately assessed from community development lending and
services.

The consequences of reducing the number of banks assessed on their level of community
development lending and investment could be particularly severe for affordable housing. LIHTC
is the primary financing tool for the construction and preservation of affordable housing. LIHTC
has created or preserved more than 4.28 million affordable units by leveraging private capital,

dollars in the capital stack can keep whole projects from coming together at all. Further, multi-
investor funds that depend on investments from a wide range of investors could shrink. The
result would likely be fewer affordable housing units produced, contrary to recent initiatives
from Congress and the Administration.

Similarly, reductions in the number of banks classified as intermediate or large could diminish
investment through NMTCs and CDFIs, translating into less business growth and less capacity to
support affordable housing, small business lending, homeownership, and other lending to
underserved consumers.

 II. Maintain CRA's focus on lending, investment, and services that expand
 economic opportunity and build wealth.

We urge the agencies to maintain CRA's retail lending evaluation, which primarily focuses on a
bank's record of making mortgage, small business, and small farm loans. Loans to families and
small businesses help drive economic opportunity. Home mortgage loans and small business and
small farm loans, in particular, provide safe and affordable opportunities for customers to build
wealth, with home equity remaining among the largest sources of wealth for the typical
American family.8 While consumer loans meet borrowers' specific needs, they often do not
provide the type of foundational, wealth-building credit that the CRA focuses on promoting.
CRA appropriately focuses on these foundational products which help customers build wealth,
and that focus should be maintained.

 a. Set major product lines at the bank level to reduce regulatory burden if a major
 product lines standard is adopted.

If a the agencies adopt a major product lines standard, determination of a bank's major product
lines should remain at the institution level. Making this determination at the assessment area
level would add significant regulatory burden for banks and examiners, while creating confusion
for communities trying to understand a bank's CRA performance. A single set of major product
lines will facilitate evaluation of how a bank's most significant business lines are helping to meet
community credit needs.

 b. Continue to evaluate consumer loans only when they make up a substantial
 majority of lending and measure consumer loan products individually to recognize
 their distinct features and roles.

 We urge the agencies to retain the longstanding requirement that a consumer loan product make
up a "substantial majority" of a bank's total lending (both by number and dollar amount) to be
evaluated as a major product line, which is currently implemented as a threshold significantly
more than 50 percent of a bank's lending. Current guidance states that examiners will evaluate
consumer lending only if a "lending test evaluation would not meaningfully reflect its lending
performance if consumer loans were excluded," which allows examiners to consider a bank's
total business in determining whether or not to evaluate a consumer product. This standard has
appropriately focused CRA evaluations on a bank's retail product lines that are the most
significant for expanding economic opportunity, while also evaluating consumer loans when they
are the core of a bank's business.

Whether the agencies maintain the existing retail lending evaluation framework or adopt a major
product lines approach, each category of consumer loan should also continue to be treated as a
distinct product for the purposes of determining whether a product line is evaluated as part of a
bank's retail lending. Consumer loans encompass a wide array of products from collateralized,
longer term, amortizing, and larger dollar auto loans, to revolving, non-amortizing credit cards.
Grouping these loans into a single category would obscure the unique role that each product fills
in consumers' finances and make it difficult to demonstrate how a bank is meeting credit needs
through each of these distinct business lines.

 c. Establish major product lines prior to the start of the exam period to avoid
 unnecessary burden if a major product lines standard is adopted.

The agencies should clearly establish the process and timeline for determining a bank's major
product lines before an exam period begins to provide regulatory certainty and maximize impact.
Today, a bank making more than an incidental amount of mortgage, small business, or small
farm loans knows it will be examined on each of these products, and the requirement that
consumer loans represent a "substantial majority" of a bank's retail lending to be considered
establishes a clear exam scope well in advance. This clarity should be preserved if a major
product lines standard is adopted under a revised framework.

 d. Recognize community development's essential role in helping to meet community
 credit needs by continuing to give appropriate weight to community development
 activities in determining a bank's CRA rating.

We urge the agencies to restore the existing standard requiring intermediate banks to receive at
least a satisfactory community development rating in order to be eligible for an overall
satisfactory or outstanding rating. Retail lending and community development activities play
vital and complementary roles in the economic health of communities and should continue to be
weighed equally in intermediate bank exams. Community development loans and investments
are essential to helping to meet the credit needs of communities. While mortgage and small
business loans help individual families build wealth, financing for affordable housing, schools,
childcare facilities, hospitals, and other community infrastructure lifts the entire community,
translating into higher home values, higher incomes, and more financial opportunity for local
residents.

 10
 We also urge the agencies to clarify that longstanding practice and examiner guidance on the
relative weights of the lending, investment, and services tests in determining a bank's rating will
continue to apply. Lending, investment, and services are all critical to helping to meet the credit
needs of communities and should continue to be weighted at 50 percent, 25 percent, and 25
percent, respectively, in the CRA exam.

 e. Maintain consideration of a bank's record of providing a wide range of products
 and services to meet communities' needs.

Banks' record of providing a wide range of products and services, including deposit services, to
LMI customers should remain part of a bank's record of helping to meet community credit needs
through services. Deposit and other banking products and services help customers, particularly
low- and moderate-income customers and small businesses, build wealth. Without access to these
services, individuals and businesses are left more financially vulnerable. Providing well-tailored,
affordable deposit products and other banking services also supports consumers' financial well-
being and can grow into future extensions of credit.

In addition to considering deposit products and services, agencies should also clarify that
deposits from customers residing in LMI area will continue to be considered when determining
the degree to which a branch is serving LMI communities.

 f. Preserve flexibility for banks with unique business models.

Limited Purpose Banks. We urge the agencies to retain the limited purpose designation and
community development test established under the 1995 CRA framework in the final rule. Many
limited purpose banks, including specialized consumer lenders, extend credit nationwide but
have very few assessment areas. This business model does not align with the lending test, and the
lending test would not provide a meaningful evaluation of these banks' record of helping to meet
the credit needs of communities. Further, shifting current limited purpose banks to the traditional
performance tests would add substantial regulatory burden for lenders, including developing new
data collection systems and analysis, without any certainty that this would result in additional
credit in LMI communities since banks' lending would be assessed only in their assessment
areas.

The community development test applicable to limited purpose banks provides a more
meaningful alternative by evaluating banks with specialized business models based on the
community development lending, investments, and services they provide to respond to
community needs, allowing them to deploy resources in ways that can have meaningful impact.

Wholesale Banks. We also urge the agencies to retain the current standard for determining
whether a bank qualifies as a wholesale bank, including retaining the current standard for
determining whether a bank makes retail loans only on an incidental basis. Currently, the 2016
Interagency Questions & Answers state that a bank is considered to extend retail loans on an
incidental basis when those loans make up an insignificant portion of the institution's assets and
income. Under the agencies' proposal, "incidental basis" would instead be defined as retail loans
making up less than five percent of the bank's loans. Establishing a five percent threshold and

 11
 moving from calculating that percentage based on assets and income to a percentage of loans are
substantial shifts from the current policy and could cause significant changes in CRA exams and
additional regulatory burden for banks currently defined as wholesale banks.

 III. Ensure local service providers, community-based organizations, and nonprofits
 can continue to help lenders meet local credit needs.

We strongly oppose the proposed changes to grant making as unnecessarily burdensome and
harmful to the community-based organizations that provide essential services and rely on
operating grants. We urge the agencies to recognize the important work of nonprofits in helping
to meet community credit needs and to maintain the current CRA eligibility for grant funding in
the final rule.

Community-based organizations and nonprofits are essential to the retail and community
development activity at the heart of CRA. A review of bank performance evaluations shows that
banks provide more than $617 million in CRA-qualifying grants each year, with the median
grantmaking bank providing about $47,700 per year in grants.9 CRA-qualifying grants to these
organizations, whether for specific projects, comprehensive initiatives, or capacity, allow local
service providers to help first-time homebuyers qualify for homeownership, guide entrepreneurs
accessing their first small business loan, and build critical affordable housing, among many other
activities that fit squarely within meeting the banking needs of the communities in which they
operate, including low-and moderate income communities. Importantly, grants often provide the
capacity, technical assistance, and infrastructure that make subsequent consumer and community
development lending possible. Not only are these grants essential to community-based
organizations providing services to constituents, but these organizations are also local employers.
Nonprofits employ 12.8 million workers nationwide, accounting for nearly 10 percent of all
private-sector jobs.10

New restrictions on the structure and use of these grants risk not only reducing funding available
for organizational capacity but also discouraging banks from making grants as part of their CRA
strategies at all. This proposal risks reducing local jobs and services benefiting communities,
especially in hard-to-serve areas.

Rather than requiring banks to determine and document how individual grant dollars are
allocated between programmatic and indirect expenses, we urge the agencies to retain the current
standard, which is focused on community development purpose and impact. Where an
organization's mission and activities meet the community development definition and a grant
supports that community development purpose, the grant should remain eligible for CRA
consideration. This well-established standard allows banks to determine which grants best
respond to identified community needs.

NAAHL collected a few anonymous examples of how flexible grant support can directly
generate community development activity and lending.

 grant helped launch a collaboration among several CDFIs seeking to expand specialized

 That capacity enabled the participating CDFIs to originate facility loans for nonprofit

These examples demonstrate why drawing a rigid distinction between programmatic spending
and organizational or administrative capacity does not reflect how successful community

precisely what allow CDFIs and other nonprofits to develop borrowers and projects into viable
lending opportunities.

 13
 The proposed restrictions could work against the agencies' stated objective of increasing CRA's
focus on lending. Grants are often not a substitute for loans or investments; they are what enable
community organizations to develop the borrowers, projects, partnerships, and capacity that
generate additional lending and investment. A CRA framework that makes flexible grant support
substantially more difficult or burdensome could shrink, rather than expand, the pipeline of
viable community development financing.

 IV. Maintain a CRA framework that incentivizes community development financing
 tailored to unique local needs in LMI communities.

 a. Recognize the important and distinct roles of loans, investments, and grants in
 community development financing.

We urge the agencies to maintain emphasis on all three legs of the community development stool
 loans, investments, and grants in the final rule. Community development is foundational in
helping to meet community credit needs. The wide range of community development projects,
from affordable housing for low-income seniors to expanding a small business facility to provide
jobs in an LMI neighborhood, requires a range of financing types. Loans, investments, and grants
each play a unique and essential role in helping to meet the credit needs of communities through
community development. For example, a LIHTC project creating new homes for LMI families
may require equity investment in tax credits; construction and permanent loans; and grant dollars
to come together and remain affordable. If any pieces are missing, the deal falls apart, and
communities lose out on vital housing.

 b. Allow banks to offer financing that responds to community needs, not the CRA
 exam framework.

We support the agencies' proposal to provide consideration for outstanding community
development loans, consistent with the treatment of investments, and urge you to retain a
provision providing consideration for outstanding community development loans at a bank's
option in the final rule. Giving credit for community development loans only in the exam period
in which they were made encourages banks to align lending with their CRA exam cycle rather
than actual need. To ensure banks are incentivized to respond to community needs, we urge the
agencies to clarify that shorter-term loans, including construction loans, can receive additional
consideration for the original loan and for any renewed or expanded credit provided within the
same exam cycle. We also urge the agencies to communicate how they will adjust expectations
on the overall level of community development lending when prior period loans are considered
to ensure that community development loan originations do not diminish. Consideration of prior
period loans should enhance, not weaken, community development outcomes.

We also applaud the agencies' proposal to recognize legally binding commitments to lend,
including legally binding credit enhancements like letters of credit, as equivalent to loans and to
provide CRA consideration equivalent to a community development loan supporting the same
activity. Legally binding commitments to lending, like letters of credit, are genuine extensions of
credit that expose banks to credit risk and require underwriting and ongoing risk management.

 14
 Letters of credit can be essential to bring affordable housing transactions together, particularly
tax-exempt bond financing. Providing equivalent treatment for these legally binding
commitments allows banks and their partners to use the most efficient financing structure for the
transaction, rather than trying to alter financing to meet the CRA exam parameters.

 c. Preserve eligibility for tax credit equity investments and equity equivalent
 investments.

The agencies should clarify that the proposed definition of a community development investment
preserves CRA consideration for banks' investments in funds, limited partnerships, limited
liability companies, and similar entities that finance qualifying community development
activities. These structures are central to financing projects involving LIHTCs and NMTCs,
which drive affordable housing production and economic development. In these transactions, a
bank generally invests in an entity or fund; the tax credit is a benefit associated with that
investment, not itself the security the bank acquires. The proposed definition's reference to a
"security" should expressly encompass direct and indirect ownership interests in these entities,
including interests acquired through multi-investor funds and legally binding commitments to
acquire them. Eligibility would continue to depend on whether the underlying activity has a
primary purpose of community development and satisfies the rule's other requirements.

The final rule should also expressly preserve investment consideration for qualifying equity
equivalent investments (EQ2s) in nonprofit CDFIs and other community development lenders.
EQ2s provide deeply subordinated, long-term capital that supports financing for community
needs in the hardest to serve parts of the market. Long-standing interagency interpretive
guidance recognizes appropriately structured EQ2s that retain equity-like characteristics as
qualified investments, even if they are documented as a note or subordinated obligation. This
clarification would carry forward existing policy.

 d. Clarify eligibility for impactful in-kind donations.

We urge the agencies to clarify that a wide range of in-kind donations will remain eligible for
CRA consideration as qualifying community development investments. In-kind donations can
range from the donation of computers and other office equipment to donations of former branch
locations to other organizations serving the community, including financial institutions serving
LMI populations. These donations are often highly impactful, particularly for smaller recipient
organizations and in smaller markets. If any of the proposed requirements for community
development grants are finalized, the agencies should clarify the ways that banks can
demonstrate eligibility for this range of in-kind donations under the framework.

 e. Ensure community development activities support LMI communities and areas of
 unmet need, as intended by statute.

Each of the four community development purposes should be appropriately tailored to help meet
the credit needs of LMI communities and other areas of unmet need to align with CRA's
statutory requirements and to maximize the impact of CRA activities. In some cases, proposed

 15
 changes to the definitions of each of these four purposes could unintentionally expand eligibility
in ways that could reduce community development benefits for LMI communities.

Affordable housing of all types subsidized, unsubsidized, and naturally occurring is
essential to families' and communities' financial health, yet every part of the country faces an
affordable housing shortage. The resulting cost burdens fall most heavily on lower income
households. Over 80 percent of renter households making under $30,000 are cost burdened,
compared to about 50 percent of all renters.11 Furthermore, rent burdens fall hardest on those
with the lowest incomes because these burdens can cut into spending on basic needs like food
and medicine. It is therefore critical that CRA continue to prioritize the needs of these LMI
households who remain the most underserved, through support for both unsubsidized and
subsidized housing.

While "naturally occurring affordable housing" (NOAH) is eligible for consideration under the
current CRA regulation and guidance, NAAHL has long supported additional clarity on the ways
a bank can demonstrate that NOAH financing qualifies for CRA consideration. We urge the
agencies to clarify ways to demonstrate NOAH eligibility, in addition to ways banks demonstrate
eligibility today, in either regulation or guidance. NAAHL recommends that the agencies define
NOAH as:

 Properties with affordable rents (no more than 30% of 80% AMI) in LMI census
 tracts;

 Properties with affordable rents in census tracts where the median renter is LMI
 and the median rent is affordable to LMI renters; or

 Properties with affordable rents where the owner agrees to maintain affordability
 to LMI renters for the life of financing.

To keep affordable housing financing focused on LMI households while allowing
flexibility for markets with especially high housing costs, rather than creating a new
definition of high-cost markets, we recommend that banks be permitted to use the
Department of Housing and Urban Development's (HUD) Fair Market Rents (FMRs) as
the benchmark for rents when determining whether a loan, investment, or grant financing
a property qualifies for CRA consideration as affordable housing financing. This revised
methodology relies on a widely known and well-understood standard to adjust for high-
cost markets and would focus support on the most acute affordable housing needs.

Civic assistance is an important element of community development and should remain focused
on primarily serving LMI individuals and communities.

Economic development activities should continue to meet a "purpose test"
demonstrating a benefit to LMI individuals or geographies. While financing for
employers can help an individual business, financing does not necessarily translate into
employment or other financial benefits for areas that struggle to access credit. We urge
the agencies to maintain a definition of qualifying economic development that focuses

Revitalization and stabilization activities are an essential component of community

The agencies also discuss examples of qualifying activities that could be particularly impactful in
expanding access to affordable housing. Clarifying that financing for resilience against natural
disasters is a CRA-qualifying activity will help address the growing need to protect families and
communities from extreme weather and rising property insurance costs, and we urge the agencies
to include this in any illustrative list. A shortage of available homes for purchase and
corresponding high home prices in neighborhoods across the country have also made it difficult
for many families to find homes they can afford to buy, making it harder for local businesses to

benefits LMI communities supports affordable homeownership and revitalization and should also
receive CRA consideration under this community development component. The Neighborhood
Homes Investment Act is a widely supported bipartisan tax credit proposal to support the
construction and preservation of affordable homes for owner-occupancy and provides standards
to support impact for modest-income borrowers and communities. We urge the agencies to
include financing for the construction or rehabilitation of owner-occupied homes as another
example of a qualifying activity in an illustrative list.

Essential community infrastructure and facilities are critical components of communities, and we
support maintaining consideration for these activities when they primarily support LMI
individuals or areas. However, we caution against broadly expanding CRA credit for all such
projects, which can be large and are often already financed in the ordinary course of business.
Impactful community development should focus on areas that need additional support accessing
essential private capital. We encourage the agencies to maintain the current standard requiring
demonstrated LMI benefit in most cases, consistent with CRA's intent and the statute.
