  V. Support access to affordable housing and community development financing in
 all communities through clear, uniform guidance.

 a. Establish clear, uniform interagency guidance on qualifying community
 development activities to support impact and innovation.

We appreciate the agencies' efforts to increase clarity and consistency in the CRA process
throughout this proposed rule. We support the agencies' proposal to create a non-exhaustive,
illustrative list of CRA-qualifying activities alongside the regulation. This resource will help
facilitate compliance and expand the use of innovative community development financing across
lenders of all sizes. As the agencies compile this list, we encourage you to include tools banks
use to reach LMI communities today, such as LIHTC, NMTC, and EQ2 investments and loans to
or partnerships with CDFIs, and to clarify that CDFI activities will be credited based on the
CDFI's certification when the financing began, giving banks the certainty they need to invest. To
maximize its impact and support regulatory clarity for banks and their partners, we urge the
agencies to publish and update a single list from all three bank regulators. This will ensure that
all lenders are held to the same standard, regardless of charter type, and facilitate transparency in
CRA implementation.

We also strongly support the agencies' proposal to formally establish a process to determine
whether an activity qualifies for CRA credit. This process will facilitate innovative and impactful
activities, and we urge the agencies to retain this provision in the final rule. To support regulatory
clarity and consistency, we urge the agencies to jointly maintain a list of all activities which
receive pre-approval so that all lenders and community partners know the full range of CRA-
qualifying activities, and so that all three agencies recognize them uniformly.

 b. Set clear standards for receiving credit outside of assessment areas that give banks
 and communities certainty and align with the realities of community development
 financing.

We support the agencies' proposal to clarify when a bank will receive consideration for CRA-
qualifying community development activities outside of its assessment areas. The proposed
geographic flexibility standard offers an opportunity for banks to expand beyond the current
"broader statewide or regional area" (BSRA) limits, which could allow banks to make
community development loans and investments in the areas of need with limited access to the
traditional financial system.

While we support the agencies' efforts to add clarity, we are concerned that the framework under
Option 1, as proposed, may not have the intended effect. Developing a single numerical
threshold for the dollar amount of community development lending and investment in all
assessment areas nationwide is complex. Community development lending and investment needs
and opportunities vary substantially across markets, and the same share of activity is not
appropriate in all markets.

Evaluating activity on an annual basis also does not align with the unique nature of community
development finance. Projects often take months or years to come together and closing dates

 18
 may shift, making it difficult to sustain a steady level of activity each year. Requiring a bank to
meet community development financing thresholds each year does not reflect these realities.
Additionally, annual fluctuations in whether a bank meets the geographic flexibility standard will
not provide the certainty banks need to make community development loans and investments
beyond their assessment areas.

Rather than using a single numerical threshold to determine when a bank will be eligible for
geographic flexibility, we urge the agencies to adopt a standard based on a bank's demonstrated
CRA performance. Under this standard, a bank would be eligible for geographic flexibility if it
received at least a satisfactory on its lending and investment tests in its prior CRA evaluation (at
least a satisfactory on the community development test for an intermediate bank). Agencies
should maintain meaningful lending and investment expectations to ensure that community
development activity in assessment areas is remains at least as strong as it is today. This standard
would give banks and community partners certainty in advance that a bank will receive credit for
activities beyond their assessment areas if they are helping to meet the needs of their
communities, as required by statute and documented by their CRA exam. When a bank does
receive geographic flexibility, community development activities should contribute to the overall
bank rating, as well as state ratings whenever possible, to appropriately reflect a bank's record of
community development in each market.

While geographic flexibility provides the ability for banks to receive CRA consideration for
activities beyond their assessment areas, it does not provide an added incentive to serve the most
underserved areas, including rural and Tribal communities, where there may be extreme need but
where banks have fewer local ties. To support access to credit in the most underserved
communities, we encourage the agencies to consider providing additional qualitative
consideration for activities in these areas.

 VI. Maintain a flexible strategic plan option that prioritizes affordable housing and
 community needs.

We support the agencies' efforts to provide additional clarity on elements of an impactful
strategic plan. Many banks with unique business models have consistently developed strategic
plans to meet the credit needs of their communities. The current approach to strategic plans
provides important flexibilities with respect to assessment areas, in-scope products, test weights,
and measurable goals, coupled with requirements for public comment and regulatory approval to
serve as guardrails to ensure that the flexibilities of the Strategic Plan are used to drive
meaningful outcomes for communities. We support the agencies' proposal to allow banks to
establish measurable goals for the term of the strategic plan as well as annual interim measurable
goals, and welcome the clarification that annual interim measurable goals do not need to sum to
the full plan term goal. This appropriately reflects the less predictable, lengthy nature of
community development financing.

We recommend that the agencies maintain the strategic planning process's current flexibilities.
Any significant changes to the process or substantive new guidance, including adopting elective
goals or illustrative levels of community development activity, should go through the notice and
comment process and include relevant agency data on past performance by banks of all types and

 19
 sizes that were used to develop any elective goals. Additionally, as the agencies enhance the
prefiling communication process, we urge you to prioritize hiring and training staff on the
elements of CRA. Knowledgeable staff are essential to consistent, transparent implementation of
CRA.

 VII. Balance transparency for lenders and communities with regulatory burden.

We appreciate the agencies' efforts to update elements of CRA data and disclosure. As the
agencies make updates, we urge you to maintain balance between providing timely,
comprehensive market information and minimizing compliance burden.

 a. Maintain data reporting consistent with current levels of coverage to give
 communities, lenders, and researchers a more complete picture of the market.

Large banks have reported mortgage, small business, small farm, and community development
loan data for many years. This data serves an important role in helping lenders and the public
assess market opportunities and needs while minimizing burden and protecting borrowers'
privacy and we urge the agencies to maintain current levels of data reporting.

As noted above, we do not support the proposed increases in asset thresholds, which could
reduce focus on affordable housing and community development financing across the country
and would also reduce critical market data, as only large banks are required to report data under
the current and proposed frameworks, and small banks have no data on community development
in their CRA exams. The loss of vital data will make it impossible for communities and
researchers to assess how well private capital is meeting local needs, and large banks that operate
in these markets will be left with incomplete information on which to base their business
strategies.

If the agencies increase the large bank asset threshold, we therefore urge you to decouple data
reporting from the large bank designation so that communities, lenders, and researchers do not
lose vital insights into community development activity and needs. We cannot predict with
certainty how much banks would shift their lending and investment strategy if their community
development financing were to no longer be assessed under CRA. A simultaneous shift in both
CRA consideration and data reporting would make it harder to assess how well rural areas and
smaller markets are being served.

 b. Maintain existing, well-understood data collection for loans considered under
 CRA.

Data collection should continue to reflect the universe of loans that receive CRA consideration
while minimizing compliance burden.

Small Business Loans. We recommend that the agencies retain CRA small business loan
reporting if eliminating such reporting would result in the loss of lending data relevant to CRA
evaluations. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's final rule implementing section 1071
of the Dodd-Frank Act ("1071") does not capture the full universe of institutions and credit

 20
 transactions that meet CRA small business lending requirements. For example, Section 1071 data
reporting requirements exclude transactions that may be relevant to a bank's CRA evaluation,
including agricultural credit, certain small-dollar business credit, and purchases of loans or
participations. Substituting Section 1071 data for CRA data could therefore create gaps in the
information available to examiners and the public and could lead to uncertainty as to whether
loans excluded from section 1071 reporting remain subject to consideration under CRA. The
agencies should retain CRA reporting wherever necessary to ensure that the agencies continue to
receive information on the full range of lending considered in CRA evaluations.

Consumer Loans. While some banks report and are examined on consumer loans today, the
major product lines proposal, if not properly tailored, could significantly increase the data
collection burden for banks who may be required to collect data on whole new business lines. We
urge the agencies to maintain the current standard for data collection on and consideration of
consumer loans.

Community Development Loans. We appreciate the agencies' efforts to further systematize
community development loan data reporting. However, we are concerned that annual reporting
of loan level community development data could pose additional challenges, including making it
more difficult for lenders to identify CRA-qualifying community development loans that may
have been missed as they prepare for their CRA exam. We urge the agencies to balance the need
for transparency and market information with the real challenges of implementation.

 c. Right-size data collection and documentation for community organizations.

The proposed data, documentation, and public disclosure requirements for community
development grants impose significant additional burden and liability for banks and community
organizations and are substantially more onerous than the requirements for any other CRA
disclosures and should not be adopted. Banks already exercise their own due diligence to make
impactful grants to organizations working in their communities. Requiring documentation of
organization budgets, written attestations of operating costs, and bank oversight of operating
expenses will impose new oversight responsibilities that fall outside of banks' areas of expertise
and could raise liability concerns. Further, requiring public disclosure of grantees and award
amounts would compromise both banks' and grantees' privacy. Together, these burdens could
disincentivize grants that amplify impact and drive new credit opportunities nationwide.

 VIII. Maintain the Interagency Questions & Answers, which provides clear and well-
 understood guidance on CRA implementation.

We urge all three banking regulators to continue using the 2016 Interagency Questions &
Answers ("Interagency Q&A"), to update them jointly from time to time, and to jointly issue
additional subregulatory materials and guidance for banks. Adding clarity through regulatory text
is helpful, but subregulatory guidance is essential to ensure consistent implementation that is
responsive to changes in the market. Some elements of CRA, including an illustrative list of
qualifying activities and clarification on how qualitative factors are defined and will be applied,
are best communicated through interagency guidance that can be updated more regularly. The
Interagency Q&A has provided a reliable, consistent source of information on CRA eligibility

 21
 and is frequently used and generally understood by lenders and community partners. The
agencies should build on this successful tool with additional guidance.
As has been the agencies' longstanding practice, all guidance should be issued for public
comment and finalized well in advance of applying that guidance in examinations.

 IX. Establish a thoughtful transition process.
To reduce regulatory uncertainty and ensure successful implementation, the agencies should
outline the implementation timeline and process in any final rule. The proposed changes will
require banks to update their data collection, systems, and public disclosures, and since loans and
investments are often cultivated and run for years, banks will need substantial time to adjust
across business lines as eligibility standards change. To provide sufficient time for banks to
implement these changes, the effective date of the final rule should be January 1 of the calendar
year no sooner than 24 months after the publication of the final rule and after all subregulatory
guidance has been published. For banks operating under a strategic plan, we also urge the
agencies to clarify that strategic plans that are approved as of the implementation date will
remain in place until the end of the plan.
Conclusion
We share your commitment to a CRA framework that is clear, durable, and impactful in
communities across the country. Please contact Sarah Brundage, sbrundage@naahl.org, if we can
be of assistance throughout this process. Thank you for your consideration and we look forward
to our continued engagement with all the banking regulators on CRA.
Sincerely,

Sarah Brundage
President and CEO
National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders

 22
 Response to NPR Questions

Response to Question 1:

Banks of all sizes play an important role in affordable housing and community development
(CD) finance, and we caution that large changes in CRA requirements could have significant
unintended consequences, particularly for rural communities and smaller markets. In 2024, banks
with less than $30 billion in assets made nearly $53.5 billion in CD loans more than one third
of banks' CRA-qualifying CD lending that year by dollar volume, and 64 percent of CRA-
qualifying CD loans by loan count. Banks with less than $10 billion in assets made up more than
half ($27 billion) of that total.13

Reducing or eliminating community development requirements for these lenders could shrink the
amount of critically needed private capital supporting affordable housing and economic
development in LMI communities at a time when our country is focused on those very priorities.
Under the regulation as proposed, banks between $1.649 billion and $10 billion in assets would
now have a combined CD lending, investment, and services test. This combined test reduces the
existing focus on the distinct and complementary roles of loans and investments in CD finance
and could lead to less investment by these institutions, as investment is generally less central to
banks' business models than loans. The result is likely to be most directly felt in rural
communities and smaller markets, where these institutions play a larger role in the local financial
system.

However, the system-wide impacts extend further than simply the loss of investment dollars
from these institutions. For example, banks of all sizes play an important role in the LIHTC
market, making both direct investments and investments in multi-investor funds that support the
production and preservation of affordable housing in their assessment areas. Reductions in direct
investment or in multi-investor pools would have ripple effects for other investors and ultimately
for the amount and location of housing that can be financed. Further, these reductions in
investment would result in a corresponding reduction in CD lending opportunities, as projects
without the necessary investment no longer pencil out.

If the agencies were to increase the small bank threshold to $10 billion in assets and the large
bank threshold to $30 billion in assets, banks with less than $10 billion in assets would no longer
have any community development requirements. These thresholds would further magnify the
impacts outlined above and could threaten affordable housing and other economic development
outcomes.

A change in the large bank definition will also make it more difficult for the agencies and peer
institutions to assess the volume of CD financing happening relative to the unmet need within a
community. Small and intermediate banks do not publicly report information on their small
business, small farm, or community development lending. As a result, it would be impossible for
peer institutions to measure the amount of small business, small farm, or CD finance that small

13 Incentive to Impact: How CRA Leverages Private Investments into Affordable Housing, Homeownership, Small
Business, and Local Economies (Center for Affordable Housing Lending, July 2026),
https://naahl.org/s/NAAHL_CRA_Report_072326_V4-Web.pdf.

 23
 and intermediate banks do in a market and could lead to significant information gaps as larger
banks evaluate market needs for their own CRA exams or strategic plans.

As the agencies consider the revisions to the definition of small, intermediate, and large banks,
we urge you to maintain CRA-specific thresholds, rather than adopting a threshold set by another
agency, such as the Small Business Administration. Other agencies' definitions and
methodologies are tailored to their unique programs and policy purposes. A bank's ability to help
to meet the credit needs of communities is an important and distinct policy objective and should
be assessed separately by agencies with a particular expertise in the business of banking and in
community development.

We urge the agencies to maintain community development responsibilities for banks of all sizes
and to carefully consider the impacts that any changes in asset thresholds could have on rural
areas and smaller markets, as well as the broader community development ecosystem.

Response to Question 3:

CRA addresses banks' service to the communities in the U.S. where they hold deposits
and maintain a presence. If the agencies clarify the definition of assets, we urge you to
adopt a definition that includes domestic assets, not foreign assets, as domestic assets are
uniquely tied to U.S. communities and are available to benefit those communities in
ways that foreign assets are not.

Response to Questions 4-7:

We urge the agencies to maintain CRA's retail lending evaluation, which primarily focuses on a
bank's record of making mortgage, small business, and small farm loans. Home mortgage loans
and small business/small farm loans drive wealth creation and community stability. These
product lines should be prioritized for evaluation if a bank makes them routinely, as they are
today.

The practice of considering a category of consumer loans only when it constitutes a substantial
majority of a bank's total lending, or at a bank's option, and looking at each consumer product
line as a unique category of financial product, strikes an appropriate balance of limiting
regulatory burden for lenders while also assessing a bank's record of lending throughout its
communities when a consumer loan product makes up the vast majority of its business. In our
experience, a consumer product line is treated as making up substantial majority of a bank's
lending when the number and dollar amount of loans is significantly over half of a bank's
lending and would meaningfully impact lending test performance if those loans were excluded.

We caution against lowering the threshold to consider consumer loans in a CRA examination and
grouping disparate loan types into a single consumer category. Unlike mortgage and small
business lending, consumer lending includes a broad array of products with significant
differences between each product line. For example, auto loans are secured, often amortizing,
and for relatively high dollar amounts, while credit cards are unsecured, for smaller dollar
amounts, and have regularly revolving credit lines. Grouping these distinct business lines into

 24
 one bucket would cause technical challenges in trying to determine the loan amount across
different product types and risks equating distinct types of credit that meet very different needs.
Each consumer loan type should continue to be considered as a unique product line when
determining whether and how to evaluate them under CRA.

Clarity is critical to an effective CRA. In all cases, banks should know throughout the entire
period covered by their performance evaluation what retail product lines will be assessed and
how they will be assessed in order to support access to credit, including in LMI communities,
and to reduce regulatory burden. We urge the agencies to clarify that the product lines that will
be evaluated will be determined and communicated by the agencies in advance of the start of a
bank's evaluation period.

Response to Question 8:

Community Development Loans. NAAHL strongly supports providing consideration for prior
period CD loans that are outstanding during a CRA exam at the bank's option. Providing
consideration of prior period CD loans, similar to the treatment of CD investments, will help
ensure that CRA incentivizes CD financing that meets the needs of the community, rather than
being structured to fit the needs of a CRA exam. We also applaud the agencies' proposal to
recognize legally binding commitments to lend, including legally binding credit enhancements
like letters of credit, as equivalent to loans and to provide CRA consideration equivalent to a
community development loan supporting the same activity. Legally binding commitments to
lending, like letters of credit, are genuine extensions of credit that expose banks to credit risk and
require underwriting and ongoing risk management. Providing equivalent treatment for these
legally binding commitments allows banks and their partners to use the most efficient financing
structure for the transaction, rather than trying to alter financing to meet the CRA exam
parameters.

Like CD investments, CD loans should generally be considered on an evaluation-period basis.
However, unlike investments, essential CD financing comes in the form of both short- and long-
term loans, including activities such as short-term construction loans. When there are project
delays, communities often rely on a lender to renew the construction loan to keep the project
moving. Renewals of CD loans or expansions of credit lines within an exam period should be
considered as unique loans issued within the exam period to ensure banks are incentivized to
meet the full range of credit needs of their communities, including critical construction
financing.

We also urge the agencies to communicate how they will adjust expectations on the overall level
of community development lending when prior period loans are considered to ensure that
community development loan originations do not diminish. Consideration of prior period loans
should enhance, not weaken, community development outcomes.

Community Development Investments. In addition to the agencies' clarification of qualifying
CD loans, we also urge the agencies to clarify that the proposed definition of a community
development investment preserves CRA consideration for investments in affordable housing and
economic development defined as qualified investments. Banks' investments in funds, limited

 25
 partnerships, limited liability companies, and similar entities are central to financing projects
involving LIHTCs and NMTCs, as well as EQ2s. These investments are currently qualified
investments and play a central role in housing and community development but may not involve
a "security" as referenced in the proposed definition.

In LIHTC and NMTC transactions, a bank generally invests in an entity or fund; the tax credit is
a benefit associated with that investment, not itself the security the bank acquires. The proposed
definition's reference to a "security" should expressly encompass direct and indirect ownership
interests in these entities, including interests acquired through multi-investor funds and legally
binding commitments to acquire them. The final rule should also expressly preserve investment
consideration for qualifying equity EQ2s in nonprofit CDFIs and other community development
lenders, which provide deeply subordinated, long-term capital that supports financing for
community needs in the hardest to serve parts of the market. Long-standing interagency
interpretive guidance recognizes appropriately structured EQ2s that retain equity-like
characteristics as qualified investments, even if they are documented as a note or subordinated
obligation. These clarifications would carry forward existing policy.

Additionally, we urge the agencies to clarify that a wide range of in-kind donations will remain
eligible for CRA consideration as qualifying community development investments. In-kind
donations can range from the donation of computers and other office equipment to donations of
former branch locations to other organizations serving the community, including financial
institutions serving LMI populations. These donations are often highly impactful, particularly for
smaller recipient organizations and in smaller markets. If any of the proposed requirements for
community development grants are finalized, the agencies should clarify the ways that banks can
demonstrate eligibility for this range of in-kind donations under the framework.

Community Development Services. We further urge the agencies to revise the definition of
community development service to maintain consideration for impactful services performed by
third parties or affiliates. In addition to services performed by bank employees, current
interagency guidance recognizes a range of arrangements, including qualifying services
performed by an affiliate or third party on a bank's behalf as qualifying community development
services. Services performed by a third party or affiliate--for example, a bank contracting with a
community organization to provide homeownership counseling to LMI homebuyers as part of
the bank's mortgage program, or financial education, credit counseling, and technical assistance
to nonprofit and community development organizations can offer significant benefits and help
families access credit on affordable terms. Many nonprofit organizations have professional staff,
established community relationships, specialized infrastructure, and expertise in financial
coaching, credit education, credit reporting, and responsible lending that allow them to offer
services uniquely tailored to consumers' needs. Bank funding can enable these organizations to
deliver qualifying services at far greater scale than a bank could through employee volunteer
activity alone.

Response to Question 9:

We support appropriate accountability for CRA-qualified grants, but do not support the proposed
15 percent cap on indirect or administrative costs or the associated documentation requirements.

 26
 A fixed administrative-cost threshold is not an appropriate proxy for determining whether grant
resources meaningfully benefit a community. Requiring banks to obtain and evaluate Forms 990,
operating and program budgets, attestations, and other documentation would also add significant
complexity and administrative burden to grantmaking without necessarily producing better
community development outcomes.

These requirements could be particularly counterproductive in small and rural communities,
where building the capacity of local organizations is often essential to expanding access to
capital. CDFIs and nonprofit organizations provide local market knowledge, technical assistance,
borrower support, and other infrastructure that can help mitigate risk and develop projects and
borrowers that may not otherwise be financeable. This is particularly important to ensure that
smaller organizations, not just the largest with the most infrastructure, are able to access
financing. General operating support can therefore be an important tool for facilitating
subsequent lending and investment.

Rather than requiring banks to determine and document how individual grant dollars are
allocated between programmatic and indirect expenses, we recommend that the final rule adopt a
simpler standard focused on community development purpose. Where an organization's mission
and activities meet the community development definition and a grant supports that community
development purpose, the grant should qualify for CRA consideration. This approach would
preserve flexibility for general operating support while allowing banks to respond to the
particular needs of their community development partners.

The final rule should similarly preserve appropriate intermediary and subgranting models where
resources ultimately support qualifying community development activities. These models can be
particularly important for reaching smaller organizations and underserved markets.
Documentation requirements should be reasonable and proportional to the nature of grantmaking
so that CRA facilitates, rather than complicates, banks' ability to support organizations meeting
identified community development needs.

Response to Question 10:

We strongly oppose eliminating grants and donations from CRA consideration. As discussed
elsewhere in this letter, we are concerned that the proposal places increased emphasis on
community development lending at the expense of other important forms of community
development activity. Eliminating grants from consideration would further exacerbate this
imbalance. Loans, investments, grants, and services play distinct and complementary roles in
meeting community development needs, and the CRA framework should maintain appropriate
incentives for each. The proposal specifically raises eliminating grants as an alternative in the
context of its broader focus on lending.

Grants fill needs that cannot necessarily be addressed through lending or investment, including
organizational capacity, technical assistance, predevelopment, and program development. They
can also facilitate subsequent lending and investment by strengthening CDFIs and other
community development organizations, developing projects and borrowers, and helping mitigate
barriers to financing. This role can be particularly important in smaller and rural communities,

 27
 where local organizational capacity is often essential to developing financeable opportunities and
mitigating risk. Eliminating CRA consideration for grants in an effort to further increase the
rule's focus on lending could therefore reduce the resources that help make CD financing
possible.

We urge the agencies to maintain a balanced CRA framework that recognizes the important and
complementary roles of lending, investments, grants, and services. The appropriate form of
support should be driven by the identified community development need, not by a regulatory
preference for one type of activity over another. CRA should not incentivize banks or community
development organizations to structure activities around what receives greater consideration on
an examination when another form of support would more effectively meet the needs of the
community.

Response to Question 11:

The primary purpose standard established in the Interagency Q&A is appropriate and clearly
defined. We support maintaining this standard, which has driven impactful CD lending and
investment. It is not necessary to codify this standard, as it is clearly defined in the current
interagency guidance.

If the agencies pursue codifying a definition of "primary purpose," we recommend codifying the
definition as it appears in the Interagency Q&A, including the three-pronged standard that
considers activities where the majority of dollars or beneficiaries are identifiable to a CD purpose
while also allowing for consideration of mixed-income housing that has unique CD benefits for
LMI communities and individuals.

Response to Question 12:

The proposal would require community development activities to be or be tied to a
lending activity to be considered "complex." While we appreciate the agencies' efforts
to add clarity, this revised standard does not necessarily enhance the rule's focus on
community credit needs. Investments including investments in CDFIs and LIHTCs
can be extremely responsive to community credit needs and complex to execute, yet not
directly tied to a loan as part of the transaction.

To maximize impact, the definition of complexity should not restrict the form of
financing banks provide and instead retain flexibility for banks to meet identified
community needs using the most effective products. We also recommend that the
concept of complexity be communicated through interagency guidance or as part of the
illustrative list of qualifying activities, rather than adding complexity as a definition in
the regulation. Maintaining the explanation of complexity in subregulatory guidance
preserves the ability for the agencies to make adjustments and add examples of complex
activities in response to innovations in CD finance.

 28
 Response to Question 13:

CD lending can be complex without being paired with other lending. Loans or
equivalents of loans should not need to be paired with other lending in order to qualify
as complex.

Response to Question 14:

Complexity and other qualitative factors are important incentives to engage in more
difficult but impactful activities. However, requiring all activities to be complex would
add cost and burden for lenders, particularly smaller lenders with fewer complex loans
and investments, and could reduce the overall amount of CD activity in communities.
Loans and investments that may not meet the definition of "complex" are still essential
for community development and should not be disincentivized by removing all CRA
consideration.

Response to Question 15:

All qualitative factors provide important and unique performance context. An activity, like a loan
term flexibility, may be highly responsive to community need and highly impactful without
being complex. CRA's qualitative factors should continue to receive equal weight to ensure that
banks can continue to innovate to meet unique community needs.

Response to Question 16:

The definition of innovativeness established in the Interagency Q&A is appropriate and clearly
defined. NAAHL supports maintaining this standard, which has driven impactful community
development lending and investment. It is not necessary to codify this standard; however, if the
agencies put a definition of innovativeness into the text of the regulation, we recommend
adopting the definition currently included in the Interagency Q&A, which provides appropriate
consideration of bank capacity based on its size.

Similarly, the concept of flexibility is generally understood and does not need additional
definition. If the agencies would like to provide additional guidance on the concept of flexibility,
we recommend that this guidance be made part of the Interagency Q&A or other interagency
guidance, similar to other qualitative factors.

Response to Question 17:

Responsiveness, including flexibility in loan terms, can be particularly impactful in addressing
credit needs in a community. We support the agencies' proposal to maintain the current policy of
considering the responsiveness of both retail and community development activities.

 29
 Response to Question 18:

We caution that significant changes to the definition of affordable housing could have
unintended consequences. The need for affordable housing remains most acute among
LMI households. The number of cost-burdened rental households has reached an all-time
high, with 22.7 million households spending more than 30 percent of their income on
rent and utilities (defined as "cost burdened"), and that percentage is even higher for
poorer households. Over 80 percent of households making under $30,000 are cost
burdened, and over 70 percent of households making between $30,000 and $45,000 are
cost burdened.14

CRA should continue to prioritize the needs of these LMI households who remain the
most underserved through support for both unsubsidized and subsidized housing while
also continuing to allow for appropriate flexibility in truly high-cost markets. The
existing Interagency Q&A provides that certain loans and investments for housing
affordable to middle-income households can qualify for consideration as affordable
housing in certain high-cost markets based on qualitative and quantitative factors. This
measured approach has helped to address housing needs across the income spectrum
based on unique community and project characteristics while prioritizing areas with the
greatest financing needs and should be maintained.

To create a more uniform way to adjust for high-cost markets, we recommend that the
agencies also clarify that properties with rents up to the HUD's FMR for an area qualify
for consideration as affordable housing, even if the FMR exceeds 30 percent of 80
percent of the area median income. HUD's FMRs are adjusted at the local level to
account for high costs, updated annually, and a well-known standard in the market and
easily found online. They are also already used in projects involving HUD subsidies,
which would align requirements across CRA and other funding sources, reducing
complexity for banks and partners.

Response to Question 19:

We caution against setting a new federal standard for high-cost areas. Federal housing
agencies have already established standards for high-cost markets based on detailed
calculations using local factors. Creating a new, separate standard could cause
misalignment with other programs and increase regulatory burden and confusion.

Rather than establishing a new definition of high-cost areas, we recommend allowing
banks to use HUD's existing FMRs, including Small Area FMRs, as the threshold for
affordable rents in high-cost markets. As noted in response to question 18, FMRs are
adjusted for high costs in the local market and are a well-known standard throughout the
country.

14 Joint Center for Housing Studies of Harvard University, America's Rental Housing 2026 (Cambridge, MA: Joint
Center for Housing Studies of Harvard University, 2026), 34, https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/americas-rental-
housing.

 30
 Response to Question 20:

We support consideration of financing housing in a High Opportunity Area or where
housing is difficult to develop as a qualitative factor in the CD evaluation. These
activities are likely to be particularly responsive to community needs because they are in
areas that, by definition, have difficulty attracting private capital or insufficient supply of
affordable housing.

Rather than creating a new category to consider these activities based on their cost of
development, we recommend providing qualitative consideration for loans, investments,
or services tied to housing in these areas. Any adjustments for higher costs should be
made in the same way that adjustments are made in other markets, either by considering
qualitative and quantitative factors as is done today, or by using HUD's FMR for the
area to determine affordable rents.

Response to Questions 21-22:

No, housing partnerships with nonprofits should not automatically qualify as affordable housing.
Housing that qualifies for CD consideration should meet affordability standards, with appropriate
adjustments for high-cost markets, regardless of the partners involved.

Response to Question 23:

No. Home mortgage loans are retail loans and should not be considered under CD. However,
loans for construction or rehabilitation of single-family homes should be considered for CD
credit under the revitalization and stabilization purpose in certain circumstances (see
"Revitalization and stabilization" in our comment letter, above).

Response to Questions 24, 26-28:

Economic development activities, including financing for small businesses and small farms,
should continue to demonstrate a benefit to LMI individuals or geographies in order to qualify
for economic development credit under CRA. Maintaining a "purpose test" will ensure that
economic development activities continue to fulfill CRA's statutory focus on ensuring entire
communities, including LMI communities, are served.

We appreciate the list of government programs, projects, and initiatives that serve small
businesses and small farms that qualify as economic development, including CDFIs that serve
small businesses and small farms. CDFIs play an essential role in helping banks reach small
businesses and small farms that need additional support throughout the loan process. We urge the
agencies to retain this acknowledgment of the important role of CDFIs in reaching underserved
borrowers in the final rule, and also urge the agencies to clarify that financing for or an activity
in partnership with a certified CDFI will receive favorable consideration based on the CDFI's
certification at the time the financing or project began. This would appropriately provide credit
for activities based on the criteria a bank used to make its financing decisions and would give

 31
 banks the certainty they need to make impactful affordable housing and community development
loans and investments.

Response to Question 32:

NAAHL does not object to requiring a bank to retain a notification of eligibility for a CD loan or
CD investment if the bank sought and received a regulatory determination for that loan or
investment. However, to increase transparency and consistency in CRA examinations, we urge
the agencies to publish determinations of CRA eligibility and maintain the list on a publicly
available website. Maintaining such a list will reduce the need for redundant determinations of
eligibility by the agencies and support impactful, innovative lending and investments in
communities.

Response to Question 33:

Agencies should provide notification to a bank within 30 days of receiving a request with no
more than a 15-day extension if needed in order to maximize the benefit for banks and
communities. Community development projects are often complicated and may have limited
windows of opportunity. Undue delay can present costly obstacles or lead to a bank missing out
on a financing opportunity.

Response to Question 34:

As noted in the text of our letter (above), we support the agencies' proposal to clarify when a
bank will receive consideration for CRA-qualifying CD activities outside of its assessment areas.
The proposed geographic flexibility standard offers an opportunity for banks to make community
development loans and investments in the areas of need with limited access to the traditional
financial system.

While we support the agencies' efforts to add clarity by establishing percentages of CD lending
and investment that, once achieved, would make banks eligible for geographic flexibility, we are
concerned that the framework under Option 1, as proposed, may not have the intended effect.
Developing a single numerical threshold for the dollar amount of community development
lending and investment in all assessment areas nationwide is complex. Community development
lending and investment needs and opportunities vary substantially across markets, and the same
share of activity is not appropriate in all markets.

Evaluating activity on an annual basis also does not align with the unique nature of community
development finance, which usually involves long production timelines. Requiring a bank to
meet community development financing thresholds each year does not reflect these realities.
Additionally, annual fluctuations in whether a bank meets the geographic flexibility standard will
not provide the certainty banks need to make community development loans and investments
beyond their assessment areas.

Rather than using a single numerical threshold to determine when a bank will be eligible for
geographic flexibility, we urge the agencies to adopt a standard based on a bank's demonstrated

 32
 CRA performance. Under this standard, a bank would be eligible for geographic flexibility if it
received at least a satisfactory on its lending and investment tests in its prior CRA evaluation (at
least a satisfactory on the community development test for an intermediate bank). This standard
would give banks and community partners certainty in advance that a bank will receive credit for
activities beyond their assessment areas if they are helping to meet the needs of their
communities, as documented by their CRA exam. When a bank does receive geographic
flexibility, community development activities should contribute to the overall bank rating, as
well as state ratings whenever possible, to appropriately reflect a bank's record of community
development in each markets.

While geographic flexibility provides the ability for banks to receive CRA consideration for
activities beyond their assessment areas, it does not provide an added incentive to serve the most
underserved areas, including rural and Tribal communities, where there may be extreme need but
where banks have fewer local ties. To support access to credit in the most underserved
communities, we encourage the agencies to consider providing additional qualitative
consideration for activities in these areas.

Response to Questions 35-36:

NAAHL does not recommend establishing a maximum geographic size for a strategic plan
assessment area. Banks operating under strategic plans often have unique business models that
may make assessment areas of different sizes appropriate.

However, setting an assessment area based on a fixed radius around a physical location would
not align with the availability of public data on the local economy and community needs and is
also not likely to align with the areas in which a bank does business. We recommend continuing
to require assessment areas to be based on geographic areas, rather than a radius, to reduce
confusion and regulatory burden.

Response to Question 37:

No, banks should not be required to submit maps of each assessment area covered by their
strategic plan. Assessment areas are already delineated within a strategic plan, which consists of
geographies that are generally well-known to the communities they cover. While a bank may
provide a map at its option, requiring a visual representation offers no additional benefit.

Response to Question 38:

The agencies should clarify the circumstances in which they expect banks' interim annual goals
to include a growth factor to ensure all banks understand have the information they need to
create a plan that meets the agencies' standards. The agencies should also clarify any
circumstances in which an annual growth factor would not be expected.

 33
 Response to Questions 39-41:

NAAHL supports the agencies' clarification that strategic plans can include both measurable
goals for the entire term of the plan and annual interim goals, and that annual goals do not
necessarily have to sum to the plan term goal. Annual interim measurable goals are helpful
benchmarks, but calendar year metrics do not necessarily align with the long-term and complex
nature of CD finance. CD loans and investments can take months or years to put together and
involve a number of other partners. Unexpected delays can push deals back weeks or months,
making it difficult to project exactly which calendar year financing may close. Further, because
CD transactions are generally for larger dollar amounts than retail mortgage or small business
loans, banks generally do a smaller number of transactions, making each individual transaction a
larger percentage of a bank's overall CRA-qualifying activities.

Goals set for the multi-year term of a strategic plan provide a more reliable estimate of a bank's
CD finance performance and should be used as the primary method to measure a bank's
performance on its strategic plan. As agencies consider interim annual goals, multiple years
should be considered, with any amounts by which a bank exceeds its goals in a given year
carrying forward to future plan years to allow for variations from year to year. A more flexible,
multi-year approach will allow banks to set meaningful goals and pursue more complex and
innovative transactions that may have more unpredictable timelines.

Response to Question 42:

We do not recommend that the agencies pursue a process similar to the OCC's Simplified
Strategic Plan Process for Community Banks for all banks. The strategic plan option provides
flexibility that is particularly useful for banks with unique business models, and uniform elective
goals may not be broadly applicable for these varied models. Larger institutions also have the
necessary capacity to analyze their markets, their peer institutions, and the unique role that they
can plan in their communities.

We urge the agencies to maintain the flexibility that has made the strategic planning process such
an important element of the CRA framework. If the agencies pursue additional written guidance
related to strategic plans, it should be subject to public comment and include any relevant data to
demonstrate how guidelines were developed to ensure the strategic plan framework continues to
support a wide range of banks in providing financing within their communities.

Response to Questions 43-46:

Consideration of a strategic plan bank's CD activities not otherwise considered in connection
with any measurable goals in determining whether a bank should receive an outstanding rating is
appropriate and aligns with the way these activities are treated under the performance tests.
Providing consideration only for an outstanding rating appropriately balances the focus on
meeting credit needs in a bank's assessment areas where it is chartered to do business with
addressing nationwide credit needs, particularly in areas with limited bank footprints. Similar
consideration would not be appropriate to determine whether a bank is eligible for a satisfactory
rating.

 34
 If a bank would like an examiner to consider CD activities not otherwise considered in
connection with any measurable goal in order to help achieve an outstanding rating, the bank
should provide the agency with information on those activities in order for them to be
considered.

Response to Questions 47-48:

We appreciate the agencies' efforts to modernize the strategic plan public engagement process.
The current requirement to solicit public comment through newspapers of general circulation in
each assessment area reflects the state of technology and news at the time the 1995 rule was
finalized and does not account for the many changes over the past 30 years.

We urge the agencies to make clear that all communications about draft strategic plans will
remain directly between banks and community members.

Response to Question 49:

We support the agencies' proposal to clarify the prefiling communications process and we
recommend that this remain an optional resource for banks drafting strategic plans. To ensure
that banks seeking prefiling communications meetings receive those meetings and have time to
complete their strategic plan, the agencies should also provide deadlines by which a bank must
request and an agency must provide a prefiling meeting.

It is also essential that agencies have an adequate number of well-trained staff who are deeply
knowledgeable about CRA to provide meaningful and reliable prefiling communications,
particularly if the agencies expect an increase in the number of institutions electing to use the
strategic plan option. We urge the agencies to prioritize hiring and training as a key component
of this change.

Response to Question 50:

To minimize confusion and provide sufficient time for a bank to achieve its measurable goals,
we recommend that the effective date for a strategic plan be the proposed date, even if that date
has passed by the time the plan is approved. This would align with the current practice and with
examiners' longstanding preference that strategic plans cover full calendar years.

Response to Question 51:

The agencies should establish a maximum extension period for their review of a strategic plan of
15 to 30 days. Timely review of and communication regarding strategic plans is essential for
banks to make business decisions that will allow them to achieve their measurable goals.

 35
 Response to Question 52:

The list of material changes in circumstances that could lead to a plan amendment should be non-
exhaustive as proposed to ensure the agencies can respond appropriately to unforeseen
circumstances.

Response to Question 55:

We strongly support the addition of Indian Country and other Tribal and Native lands to the
areas enumerated for community development revitalization and stabilization. Indian Country
and Native lands experience some of the highest rates of poverty and most extreme housing
needs, including high housing costs, inadequate housing, and lack of housing supply, leading to
overcrowding. CRA should support community development, including affordable housing and
economic development, in these communities.

To ensure the full spectrum of Native lands and Native communities are captured, we encourage
the agencies to adopt the previously finalized definition of Native Lands, as recommended by
Native-serving organizations, including Native CDFIs. To increase community development
activities in Indian Country, new definitions and revitalization and stabilization categories must
be paired with well-defined criteria for when a bank will receive favorable consideration for
these activities outside of its assessment area and must be communicated in advance of the exam
period. Activities in Indian country and other Native lands should also receive additional
qualitative consideration, as these areas are particularly underserved. Additionally, activities with
CDFIs working in Indian country and other Native lands, including Native CDFIs, should
receive CRA consideration.

Response to Questions 56-57:

The agencies should not adopt a radius-based standard to determine assessment areas. In our
experience, the existing standard requiring banks to include census tracts where they do a
"substantial portion" of their loans has rarely raised issues and we urge the agencies to maintain
this standard. If the agencies would like to provide additional clarity on what constitutes a
substantial portion of loans, we urge the agencies to adopt a ratio threshold to determine when a
census tract meets the criteria for inclusion within the assessment area.

A radius-based approach would not align with well-known geographic boundaries, which would
make it more difficult for banks to gather information about the community and its needs and
could lead to significant confusion for loan officers and residents. A fixed radius may also fail to
align with a bank's service areas, which may not be equally distributed around the entire branch.
We therefore urge the agencies to maintain an approach that utilizes census tracts, rather than a
fixed radius, to determine assessment areas.

Response to Question 58:

Interagency subregulatory guidance is essential to facilitate clear, consistent CRA
implementation. The 2016 Interagency Q&A has been a reliable source of information on CRA

 36
 eligibility for a decade and is frequently used and generally understood by lenders and
community partners. We urge the agencies to continue to use and update, subject to review and
public comment prior to finalization, the Interagency Q&A and to provide additional
subregulatory materials and guidance, also subject to public comment and jointly issued by all
three agencies, to provide regulatory certainty for banks and their community partners.

Response to Question 59:

The agencies should prepare a thoughtful transition that provides lenders with the time and
regulatory certainty they need to operationalize updates in a final rule. The proposed changes
will require banks to update their data collection, systems, and public disclosures, and loans and
investments are often cultivated over months or longer and run for years. To provide sufficient
time for banks to implement these changes, the effective date of the final rule should be no
sooner than 24 months after the publication of the final rule and all subregulatory guidance,
which should be separately issued for public comment, consistent with longstanding practice.
The effective date should also be at the start of a calendar year to align with banks' CRA
examination periods, and any community development activities should be assessed under the
CRA framework that was in place when the loan or investment began. Approved strategic plans
have already undergone agency review and should also be grandfathered through the term of the
strategic plan.

Response to Question 60:

We support allowing banks to utilize technology to share information and their public file at the
bank's option. The current regulatory requirement to make paper copies of CRA documentation
available in select locations comes from a time when digital versions were not widely available,
and we urge the agencies to clarify in the regulation that banks may meet these public disclosure
requirements through either sharing files on the bank's website or making files available on a
computer at the bank's branches through its intranet. However, we urge the agencies to allow
banks to continue to fulfill these public disclosure requirements through paper copies at the
bank's option so as not to add new burden if a bank prefers to provide disclosures at the required
locations in paper form.

Response to Question 61:

Banks need a durable CRA framework. This includes predictable asset size thresholds so banks
understand their compliance requirements well in advance. We recommend that the agencies
update the asset thresholds by regulation as needed to allow for notice and comment and to
provide an opportunity to analyze the impact of the proposed changes.

Response to Question 62:

CRA-eligible investments benefiting LMI communities serve the public welfare and are
appropriately categorically defined as qualifying under 12 CFR part 24. We urge all federal
financial regulatory agencies to adopt this standard. We also that urge the agencies to refine the

 37
 definition of community development as detailed above to ensure that the benefit of these
investments for LMI individuals and communities is not diluted.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

The undersigned organizations represent communities across the country and the organizations
and institutions that serve them. We build and preserve affordable housing, finance small
businesses and community facilities, provide critical services, support homeownership and
economic opportunity, and invest in communities of all sizes, including rural and Tribal
communities. We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the proposed rule.

We write because proposed changes to CRA, taken together, could significantly reduce
community development activity and the lending, investment, grants, and other critical resources
available for low- and moderate-income communities. Dramatic drops in CRA-motivated
community development activity would hurt local economies and businesses, exacerbate the
affordable housing shortage, reduce local jobs, and weaken affordability for households,
especially in rural communities and smaller markets, at a time when our country is focused on
those very priorities.

The scale of CRA's impact is significant. In 2024 alone, CRA incentivized more than $430
billion in loans and investments in low- and moderate-income communities, nearly six times the
combined federal budgets of HUD, USDA's Rural Housing Service, the Small Business
Administration, and the CDFI Fund.1

For nearly 50 years, CRA has helped bring private capital into communities and strengthen
partnerships between banks and the organizations that serve them. Through these partnerships,
banks have financed affordable housing and homeownership, small businesses, community
facilities, health care, childcare, economic development, and other essential community needs. At
a time when communities face significant affordable housing shortages, rising costs, and
constrained public resources, the CRA framework should continue to support and strengthen
these partnerships.

1 Center for Affordable Housing Lending, Incentive to Impact (July 2026).
 We urge you to ensure that the final rule does the following:

 I. Maintain meaningful community development responsibilities for banks of all
 sizes. Raising the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under CRA
 would significantly reduce the number of institutions subject to community
 development expectations. For instance, if the "small bank" definition were to be
 raised to banks with less than $10 billion in assets, more than 1,500 banks, or 36
 percent of all banks, would no longer be incentivized to provide community
 development loans or investments. In 2024, these banks reported nearly $27 billion in
 community development loans, representing 35 percent of all community
 development loans made that year.

 In many communities, particularly smaller and rural markets, these institutions are
 important sources of financing and investment. Removing or substantially reducing
 their community development responsibilities would reduce the focus on community
 development financing and risks leaving fewer partners available to finance
 affordable housing, small businesses, community facilities, and other local priorities.

 Furthermore, changes to the evaluation framework should incentivize community
 impact in underserved parts of the country without reducing current levels of
 investment in other markets. At a time when households are struggling to afford basic
 necessities, investments that strengthen local economies and expand housing options
 for families are especially critical.

 II. Preserve strong expectations for community development lending and
 investment. Communities need different types of capital to meet different needs.
 Loans are critical, but they are not interchangeable with investments. Equity
 investments and other forms of capital support affordable housing through the Low-
 Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing Credit), economic development through the
 New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC), CDFIs, and other activities that often cannot be
 supported through conventional lending alone.

 Proposed changes to the evaluation framework, including how community
 development performance contributes to a bank's overall CRA rating, could reduce
 the relative importance of community development investments. The final rule should
 preserve a strong and balanced role for both community development lending and
 investment and not unintentionally reduce investment in affordable housing and other
 critical community development activities. For instance, the Housing Credit, which
 was permanently expanded and strengthened in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act has
 built or preserved 4.13 million affordable homes. However, weakening CRA
 community development requirements risks undermining the very program Congress
 just invested in.2

2 The ACTION Campaign, Low-Income Housing Tax Credit Impact in the United States (Feb. 2026).

 2
  III. Protect grants and other support for nonprofit and community-based
 organizations. Across the country, families, older adults, veterans, and small
 businesses are served by nonprofit and community-based organizations that rely on
 grants to operate. CRA-qualifying grants support housing counseling, financial
 education, small business assistance, food access, health and human services, and
 other essential activities.

 Operating support and capacity building through grants are critical for nonprofit
 organizations that are a lifeline to hard-to-serve communities and that take on difficult
 to develop projects. These organizations are also important local employers.
 Nonprofits employ 12.8 million workers nationwide, accounting for nearly 10 percent
 of all private-sector jobs.3 Reducing support for these organizations could affect both
 the services communities rely on and local jobs.

 The proposed approach to evaluating grants, including restrictions on eligible uses
 and extensive new documentation requirements, would increase compliance burden
 and could force banks to reduce grant support, particularly to smaller organizations,
 including those serving rural and other under-resourced communities. CRA should
 continue to recognize grants and contributions that advance eligible community
 development purposes and respond to demonstrated community needs without
 applying new burdensome regulations.

 IV. Keep low- and moderate-income people and communities at the center of CRA
 as intended by statute. CRA was enacted to address persistent gaps in access to
 credit and investment. Low- and moderate-income communities represent a
 significant share of the country, with more than one in four Americans living in a low-
 or moderate-income census tract.4 The need for affordable housing, access to small
 business financing, and support for other economic and community development
 remains most acute for low- and moderate-income families and communities.
 Expanding CRA's focus to increasingly broader populations or a wide array of new
 activities could unintentionally shift critical private capital away from low- and
 moderate-income households and leave underserved communities behind.

Taken together, changes to income targeting, community development definitions, evaluation
standards, and other provisions could significantly shift where CRA-motivated capital flows and
reduce the focus on low- and moderate-income communities, resulting in less affordable housing
supply, fewer jobs for low- and moderate-income workers, and reduced access to vital
community resources. The final rule should preserve a clear and meaningful focus on the low-
and moderate-income households and communities CRA was intended to serve.

Dear Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and OMice of the Comptroller of the Currency:

Over many years, CRA has helped establish a legacy of bank investment in communities that have
faced limited access to capital. Modernizing CRA requirements and reporting is key. So is recognition
the people with disabilities are an important financial force in America with growing disability finance
needs.

The National Disability Finance Coalition (NDFC) appreciates the agencies' eMorts to reform the CRA
regulations, especially given some of the existing complicated systems and reporting requirements.
NDFC is writing to advocate for incorporating questions about serving the disability community into
the CRA regulations. NDFC also urges the agencies to recognize financing activities that address the
credit and community development needs of people with disabilities as potentially responsive CRA
activities when those activities otherwise satisfy the applicable CRA eligibility criteria and should
ensure that the proposed CD-purpose data framework permits banks and examiners to identify
disability-focused community development activities.

NDFC is a membership organization promoting disability finance, defined as the intentional design
and delivery of financial products, services, and strategies that address the distinct economic realities
of people with disabilities. NDFC builds bridges between Community Development Financial
Institutions (CDFI) and the disability community, ensuring that CDFIs can respond eMectively to the
needs of individuals with disabilities. NDFC oMers policy advocacy, outreach, and trainings on
disability finance to our members, financial institutions, and disability serving organizations. Our
members include CDFIs, credit unions, banks, disability serving organizations, and others interested
in promoting disability finance.

 National Disability Finance Coalition
 Bridging the CDFI and Disability Communities
 Today, more than 70 million Americans--nearly 29% of adults--identify as having a disability, yet most
traditional and mission-driven financial institutions lack the tools or frameworks to serve this
community eMectively. Disability finance has arisen to meet the distinct financial needs of people with
disabilities through intentional product design, tailored services, and strategic partnerships. Disability
finance frequently intersects directly with the CRA's existing community development purposes.
Accessible aMordable housing may qualify as aMordable housing for LMI individuals; disability-serving
community facilities may provide civic assistance to LMI individuals and families; and CDFI financing
for entrepreneurs with disabilities may promote economic development where the financing satisfies
the applicable small-business criteria.

NDFC commissioned a study in 2024 to determine the state and scale of the unmet financial needs of
people with disabilities. The report synthesizes the research findings and oMers a roadmap for CDFIs
and their partners to act. Our assessment reveals both persistent barriers and promising pathways for
mainstream financial systems to include people with disabilities. The report identifies a growing
demand for loans to aMordable, accessible housing projects and community facilities, as well as
products like tailored consumer finance products, assistive technology loans, and flexible small
business financing.

Our findings demonstrate that disability finance does not need to remain a niche endeavor--it is
central to the mission of community-centered lending. As disability prevalence rises across all
demographics and geographies, the CDFI field is uniquely positioned to lead in designing financial
systems that are accessible.

To ensure that CDFIs have the resources to increase their disability finance pipelines, CDFIs need
access to aMordable, flexible financing, which is typically leveraged through project related
investments from mainstream banks. Banks rely on CDFIs to reach people with disabilities and
projects dedicated to serving people with disabilities. CDFIs help borrowers grow, cultivating future
bank customers.

The CRA has long helped created incentives for banks to provide these project related investments,
building and sustaining relationships with CDFIs and strengthening the broader community
development ecosystem. Now is the time to help banks, CDFIs, and disability organizations to work
together and move the disability finance system forward.

 1. To encourage this growth, NDFC is advocating for the new CRA regulations to establish, either
 through the rule, reporting instructions, or subsequent guidance, a standardized means of
 identifying qualifying community development activities whose primary or significant
 purpose is addressing the credit or community development needs of people with
 disabilities. Examples could include accessible aMordable housing, community facilities
 serving people with disabilities, home modification financing, qualifying financing to CDFIs
 operating disability-finance programs, and assistive technology financing. What is the dollar
 value of loans made to projects dedicated to serving people with disabilities, including

Page 2
  accessible aMordable housing, community facilities, and other qualifying community
 development projects?
 2. What is the number and dollar value of loans made to people with disabilities, including
 financing for home modifications, assistive technology, transportation, and small businesses?
 3. What is the number and dollar value of loans made to business owned by people with
 disabilities?
 4. What is the number and dollar value of grants and other investments made to disability
 serving organizations, including CDFIs that focus on disability finance and other community
 development organizations that finance or provide programs and services principally
 benefiting people with disabilities?
 5. NDFC recommends establishing a rule requiring voluntary self-identification of disability,
 with clear privacy and confidentiality protections governing the collection, use, storage, and
 disclosure of that information.

Banks have traditionally financed projects dedicated to serving people with disabilities through Low
Income Housing Tax Credit and New Market Tax Credit equity investments; direct loans, often with
second position mortgages from CDFIs, for the acquisition and construction of aMordable housing and
community facilities; and grants to disability serving organizations. Further, banks have provided
banking services to people with disabilities, loans and grants to consumer finance-focused CDFIs,
and loans to people with disabilities to do home improvements, purchase cars, start businesses, and
more. These financing paths need to continue and grow stronger. By tracking these financial
investments, we can identify underwriting successes and challenges; recognize banks with strong
disability finance portfolios and learn from their approaches; and connect banks with lower levels of
disability financing success to local CDFIs and disability-serving organizations to strengthen those
banks' disability finance outcomes.

CRA has helped create a powerful partnership among banks, CDFIs, and disability serving
organizations. Modernization of the CRA reporting process is key. Matching CRA incentives with the
growing number population of disabled Americans is also key. Adding the suggested tracking metrics
and recognizing disability finance as a community development purpose indicator will be critical steps
in promoting a strong, vibrant disability finance system.

Thank you for your time and consideration.
