OCC RIN 1557-AF57; FDIC RIN 3064-AG31

To Whom It May Concern:

I. Introduction and Scope of Comments

The Community Opportunity Alliance (COA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency's and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's proposed amendments to the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. The proposal would make significant changes to how banks
are categorized and evaluated, how community development activities receive CRA consideration, how grants
are treated, and how banks' geographic responsibilities are defined.

COA is a national field builder for community development. Through our network of state and regional
associations, we support a field of almost 6,000 community development organizations (CDOs) working in
urban, rural, and suburban communities across the country. These organizations develop and preserve
affordable housing, support small businesses and economic opportunity, provide essential community
services, strengthen neighborhoods, and help residents shape the futures of their communities.

COA's role is not simply to represent those organizations in Washington. We work to strengthen the
infrastructure of the community development field itself. We build the capacity of state and regional networks;
connect leaders and organizations across markets; develop and spread effective practices; conduct research
and build knowledge about the field; convene practitioners, funders, financial institutions, and policymakers;
and help ensure that local CDOs have the relationships, resources, and voice they need to succeed. In that
sense, COA is a field builder for a national system of locally rooted organizations.

Our members - state and regional community development associations - occupy a particularly distinctive
place in that system. They sit between individual CDOs and the larger institutions that shape community
development capital and policy. They connect local organizations to one another and to banks, public agencies,
funders, and policymakers; identify needs that may not be visible through lending data alone; strengthen
organizations so they are prepared to deploy capital effectively; and help successful approaches spread from
one community to another.

This network and field-building perspective is particularly important to understanding CRA. State and regional
associations convene practitioners, provide training and technical assistance, coordinate research, policy, and
data work, connect smaller and rural organizations to resources, and build relationships between banks and
community partners. COA (formerly NACEDA) has made this point in prior CRA proceedings: investments in
these networks are themselves investments in community development capacity.
 Put together, these organizations form an ecosystem. Local CDOs turn capital into housing, businesses,
services, and stronger neighborhoods; state and regional associations build their capacity and connect them to
resources and institutions; and COA strengthens and connects that infrastructure nationally. CRA is one of the
most important sources of private-sector partnership and capital within that ecosystem.

This perspective matters in evaluating the proposed rule. CRA does not operate only through individual loans
or investments. Its impact also depends on relationships, organizational capacity, local knowledge, technical
assistance, and institutions capable of connecting capital with community needs. A rule that recognizes
transactions while weakening the organizations and networks that make those transactions possible risks
measuring community development too narrowly.

COA therefore approaches CRA modernization from a straightforward starting point: the regulatory framework
should strengthen banks' responsibility to understand and respond to identified community needs, with the
needs of low- and moderate-income (LMI) people and places at the center. Before asking what activities
should count, CRA should preserve the responsibility of banks to know the communities they serve and to
respond to their needs.

Our comments are intentionally focused. COA and our members have particular experience with banks'
community development responsibilities and with the organizations, partnerships, grants, investments, and
services through which those responsibilities are carried out. We focus primarily on community development
activities and tests, bank asset thresholds and community development obligations, grants and nonprofit
capacity, assessment areas, strategic plans and community engagement, economic and affordable housing
development, racial disparities and discriminatory practices, and interagency consistency. We generally defer
to organizations with deeper expertise on the technical design of retail lending tests and individual retail
product evaluation.

Several parts of the proposal offer opportunities for greater clarity and modernization. COA supports clearer
rules where they make CRA easier for banks, regulators, and communities to understand and implement. But
simplification should not come at the expense of meaningful community development responsibility. Nor
should greater objectivity substitute for community impact, local accountability, or the judgment necessary to
distinguish an activity that genuinely meets an identified LMI need from one that merely satisfies a regulatory
definition.

This concern is particularly acute in the proposal's treatment of grants. Flexible grants and operating support
sustain not only individual CDOs, but also the state and regional associations that provide training, technical
assistance, coordination, research, advocacy, and connections across an entire community development
ecosystem. A CRA framework that narrowly distinguishes project expenses from organizational infrastructure
risks undermining precisely the institutions that help banks identify community needs, develop effective
partnerships, and put capital to work successfully.

Accordingly, COA asks the agencies to evaluate the proposed rule against three basic questions: Does it
preserve meaningful community development responsibility? Does it direct bank activity toward identified
needs of LMI people and places? And does it strengthen, rather than weaken, the community institutions and
relationships necessary to turn capital into lasting community benefit?

In developing these comments, COA also asked our members to share examples of how the proposal could
affect their organizations, their bank partnerships, and the communities they serve. We include several of
those examples below. They are practical examples of how the proposed changes could play out on the
ground.

 Page 2
 II. Priority Recommendations

COA supports modernization of CRA where it makes the law clearer, more responsive to the way banks
operate today, and more effective at directing capital toward identified community needs. But modernization
should not reduce meaningful community development responsibility, weaken the institutions that connect
capital to communities, or make it easier for banks to receive satisfactory ratings while doing less community
development work.

Most importantly, the needs of LMI people and places should remain at the center of CRA community
development activity. Modernization can provide greater flexibility and recognize changing markets, but that
flexibility should not dilute CRA's focus on communities that face the greatest barriers to credit, investment,
services, and opportunity.

Across these recommendations, COA is particularly concerned about the effects of reduced community
development responsibility on rural areas, small cities, and other markets where fewer financial institutions
are available to provide loans, investments, grants, and services. These communities are often especially
dependent on intermediate and regional banks, state and regional community development associations, and
locally rooted CDOs to connect them to capital and financial institutions.

1. Preserve meaningful community development responsibilities across bank sizes - and keep those
responsibilities centered on LMI needs.

COA recognizes that bank size categories can reasonably change over time. We do not believe every bank
should be subject to identical requirements regardless of its size, business model, or capacity. But changes to
asset thresholds should not result in large numbers of institutions losing meaningful community development
responsibilities.

Those responsibilities should remain clearly focused on meeting the credit and community development needs
of LMI people and places. The question is not simply whether a bank engages in some form of community
development activity, but whether its loans, investments, grants, services, and partnerships meaningfully
address needs that the market does not adequately meet on its own.

The proposal raises concern in two ways. First, the agencies ask whether the intermediate-bank category
should extend to institutions with as much as $30 billion in assets and whether, under that approach, the
small-bank threshold should rise as high as $10 billion. COA does not support thresholds approaching those
levels if the consequence is substantially reducing the community development obligations of institutions that
have significant market presence and capacity.

Second, the proposal would weaken the importance of the Community Development Test for intermediate
banks. Under the current framework, an intermediate small bank must receive at least a Satisfactory rating on
both its lending and community development performance to receive an overall Satisfactory rating. The
proposal would require a Satisfactory rating only on the Lending Test, explicitly allowing stronger lending
performance to compensate for weaker community development performance. COA opposes that change.

Community development lending, investments, grants, services, and partnerships serve purposes that retail
lending alone cannot replace. They help finance affordable housing, strengthen small businesses and
community institutions, build nonprofit capacity, and address needs in LMI communities that conventional
markets frequently do not meet. Those activities should retain independent weight in CRA evaluations.

The potential consequences are particularly serious in rural communities and smaller cities. COA (formerly
NACEDA) raised this concern in 2022, noting that intermediate banks often make community development
investments and provide services in nonmetropolitan and rural markets where larger financial institutions may
have less presence. Reducing those banks' obligations can therefore have effects that are larger than their
share of national banking assets might suggest.

 Page 3
 CRA requirements can be right-sized. However, right-sizing should not weaken the law's focus on LMI
community needs.

2. Protect grants, flexible operating support, and the infrastructure that makes community development
possible.

The proposed treatment of community development grants is one of COA's most significant concerns.

The proposal would require qualifying grants to be directly used for a specific community development
program, project, or initiative and, for large banks, would generally disqualify grants to recipients whose
indirect costs exceed 15 percent. Banks would also have to obtain written commitments, attestations, and
supporting documentation from nonprofit recipients. The agencies separately ask whether grants and
donations should be eliminated from CRA consideration altogether.

COA strongly opposes eliminating grants from CRA consideration and believes the proposed 15 percent
indirect-cost framework is fundamentally inappropriate for CRA.

Community development does not occur only through discrete projects. Strong projects depend on strong
organizations, relationships, systems, and networks. General operating support, capacity building, technical
assistance, staff development, financial management, technology, research, coalition building, and other forms
of organizational infrastructure allow CDOs to develop housing, support small businesses, respond to changing
community needs, and become effective long-term partners for financial institutions.

Those investments are especially important in LMI communities, where community-based organizations often
must assemble complicated sources of capital and operate in markets where conventional investment is
limited. Strengthening the organizations that serve those communities is itself an important part of
strengthening their ability to attract and deploy capital.

This is particularly important for COA's members. State and regional community development associations do
not typically build one housing development or administer one neighborhood program. Their value lies in
strengthening an entire field of organizations. They convene practitioners, provide training and technical
assistance, connect smaller and rural CDOs to resources, coordinate policy and data work, spread promising
practices, and help banks and other institutions understand local and regional community needs.

A grant supporting this infrastructure should not be treated as less valuable merely because its impact cannot
be allocated neatly among individual projects or because the organization has legitimate administrative costs
above an arbitrary percentage. Nor should banks be encouraged to impose federal-grant-style cost-allocation
and documentation requirements on nonprofit partners as a condition of receiving CRA consideration.

COA therefore urges the agencies to continue recognizing grants, including flexible and general operating
support, when they support organizations whose primary mission is qualifying community development and
service to LMI people and places. Rather than attempting to determine an organization's community
development value through an indirect-cost calculation, the agencies should establish credible standards for
identifying mission-based CDOs and other community development organizations with demonstrated purpose,
governance, accountability, and history of serving LMI communities.

The rule should recognize the entire community development ecosystem - not simply the transaction at the
end of it.

3. Tie CRA consideration to identified community needs and meaningful LMI benefit.

The needs of LMI people and places should remain the central organizing principle for determining the value of
community development activity under CRA.

A recurring concern throughout the proposal is the risk that clearer definitions of eligible activities could
become substitutes for determining whether an activity actually responds to an LMI or community

 Page 4
 development need. COA supports greater clarity. Banks, community organizations, and regulators all benefit
from knowing what activities are likely to qualify. But eligibility should be the beginning of the analysis, not the
end of it.

As a general principle, CRA consideration should reflect the portion of an activity that actually serves a
qualifying community development purpose and benefits LMI people or places. If a project produces only a
limited LMI or community development benefit, the fact that it falls within an eligible category should not
automatically justify full CRA consideration.

At the same time, the rule should explicitly recognize the role of mission-based CDOs. Where an organization
exists for the purpose of serving LMI people and places, is accountable to the communities it serves, and has a
demonstrated history of community development activity, that mission and track record should provide strong
evidence of primary purpose. CRA should distinguish between incidental LMI benefits attached to otherwise
conventional transactions and activities undertaken by organizations whose reason for existing is community
development.

This principle should also guide how the agencies evaluate responsiveness. The most important qualitative
question should be whether an activity responds to an identified community need, particularly a need
affecting LMI people and places. Complexity, novelty, transaction structure, or connection to a bank loan
should not be treated as inherently more valuable than a simpler activity that meets an urgent local need.

That distinction matters particularly for grants, equity investments, technical assistance, and services. A
flexible operating grant to a trusted CDO, technical assistance that allows a rural organization to undertake its
first development, or patient investment in a difficult community project may be highly responsive even
though it is not a component of a complicated loan transaction.

The same principle applies to economic development. COA supports clearer and more objective standards for
determining eligibility, but objectivity should clarify the connection to community development, not eliminate
it. Business size can serve as a useful guardrail, but the more important questions are why CRA-motivated
support is needed, how it advances an identified community need, and how LMI people or places will benefit.

CRA should reward meaningful response to community need - not simply the ability to fit an activity inside a
regulatory category.

4. Modernize assessment areas so responsibility follows where banks actually do business.

CRA assessment areas should reflect modern banking while preserving accountability to LMI communities.

The traditional branch-based framework increasingly fails to capture where banks conduct significant business.
Banks can originate substantial volumes of loans in communities where they maintain little or no physical
presence. CRA responsibility should follow that activity.

The agencies ask whether assessment areas should be determined through a quantitative standard based on a
substantial portion of lending or through an alternative radius around branches and other facilities. COA favors
an approach based primarily on meaningful lending activity. A radius may be administratively simple, but it
continues to anchor accountability to physical facilities rather than to where a bank actually conducts business.

Assessment-area modernization should therefore be one of the affirmative accomplishments of a new CRA
rule. A bank that does meaningful lending in a community should have meaningful responsibility to that
community, including responsibility for understanding and responding to the needs of its LMI residents and
neighborhoods.

At the same time, COA supports allowing community development activity outside required assessment areas
under appropriate circumstances. Such flexibility can help address one of CRA's persistent challenges:
communities that receive insufficient CRA-motivated capital despite significant need. Rural communities, small

 Page 5
 cities, Native communities, and other less competitive markets can become CRA deserts, while institutions
compete to finance activities in a relatively small number of markets with abundant qualifying opportunities.

Geographic flexibility can help correct that imbalance - but only if it expands responsibility rather than
weakening it. Banks should first demonstrate satisfactory community development performance in their
required assessment areas. Outside-area activities should then receive consideration when they respond to an
identified, significant community need, particularly one affecting LMI people or places.

The goal should be straightforward: modernize where banks are accountable and use flexibility to bring capital
to LMI communities and other places that are otherwise being missed.

5. Strengthen community voice, racial accountability, and consequences for discrimination.

CRA works best when banks understand the communities they serve and communities have a meaningful role
in identifying their own needs - especially LMI communities that historically have had less influence over where
capital flows.

Community engagement should therefore be more than a procedural requirement. Banks should engage
CDOs, residents, local governments, and other stakeholders early enough for that engagement to influence
strategies, investments, and measurable goals. Publishing a nearly completed plan and accepting comments is
not a substitute for meaningful engagement while decisions are being made.

This is particularly important for banks choosing to operate under strategic plans. COA supports the strategic-
plan option as a source of flexibility for institutions with different business models, but it should not become
an easier route to a Satisfactory CRA rating. Regulators should have clear authority to reject or require revision
of plans that do not adequately address identified community needs, including the needs of LMI people and
places.

Strong community engagement should also receive affirmative qualitative consideration in CRA examinations.
COA (formerly NACEDA) proposed such an approach in 2022 because the process through which banks identify
community needs is itself important to effective CRA performance.

CRA modernization must also continue to confront racial disparities in access to credit and investment. COA
does not propose an extensive new racial-data framework in these comments. But racial disparities remain an
important part of the context in which CRA operates and should not disappear from consideration simply
because CRA eligibility is generally structured around income.

The agencies should also ensure meaningful consequences when discriminatory or illegal credit practices are
substantiated. COA supports Option 2 in the proposal, which would preserve regulators' ability to consider
violations identified through examination reports as well as public enforcement actions and judicial orders.
Significant substantiated discrimination should materially affect a bank's CRA rating.

Community voice, an explicit focus on LMI need, and accountability for discrimination are not peripheral to
CRA. They are central to determining whether banks are actually meeting the credit needs of the communities
they serve.

6. Maintain one coherent interagency CRA framework.

CRA should operate under a coherent national regulatory framework that maintains consistent expectations
for serving LMI communities.

The current proposal is being advanced by the OCC and FDIC without the Federal Reserve. COA believes the
three banking regulators should administer materially consistent CRA standards and does not believe the OCC
and FDIC should finalize a fundamentally different framework unless the Federal Reserve participates or the
agencies otherwise reach substantive alignment.

 Page 6
 This is not simply a question of regulatory elegance. Fragmented CRA rules create practical costs for the
community development field. A CDO seeking financing should not need to determine which regulator
supervises a particular bank before it can know what types of investments qualify, what documentation a bank
may require, how an activity will be evaluated, or which geographic standards apply. For state and regional
associations working with many financial institutions and hundreds of local organizations, those burdens
multiply quickly.

Different rules also create the risk of regulatory arbitrage. If materially different CRA obligations attach to
banks based on charter and primary federal regulator, banks have an incentive to consider those differences
when choosing or changing charters. We do not suggest CRA is the only, or necessarily the principal, factor in a
bank's charter decision. But the agencies should not create another reason for similarly situated institutions to
shop for the regulator whose CRA rules they prefer.

For COA and its network of state and regional field-building organizations, consistency matters because their
work routinely crosses the boundaries of individual banks, regulators, and assessment areas. They build
relationships across financial institutions, coordinate statewide and regional strategies, and help local CDOs
navigate the capital system. Regulatory fragmentation makes that work harder without producing a
corresponding benefit for LMI communities.

COA therefore urges the OCC and FDIC not to finalize a materially different CRA framework unless the Federal
Reserve participates or the three agencies otherwise reach substantive alignment. Communities should have
one understandable set of expectations for what CRA requires of banks, and similarly situated banks should
operate under comparable community development obligations regardless of which federal agency supervises
them.

III. Responses to Selected Questions

The recommendations above describe COA's basic approach to the proposal. The responses below apply those
principles to the questions where our network has the most direct experience and expertise. We do not
attempt to answer every question in the NPR.

Question 1 - Asset thresholds

COA supports reasonable adjustments to asset thresholds over time, but does not support changes that
substantially reduce the number of banks with meaningful community development obligations.

The agencies specifically ask whether the intermediate-bank category should extend to institutions below $30
billion and whether, under that approach, the small-bank threshold should rise as high as $10 billion. COA does
not support thresholds approaching those levels.

Our principal concern is not identifying one perfect dollar threshold. It is preserving meaningful community
development responsibility. A bank with substantial assets and market presence should retain obligations not
only to make retail loans, but also to provide the community development loans, investments, grants, services,
and partnerships that help meet needs of LMI people and places.

For that reason, COA also opposes the proposed change to the overall rating framework for intermediate
banks. Under the current framework, an intermediate small bank must receive at least a Satisfactory rating on
both its Lending Test and Community Development Test to receive an overall Satisfactory rating. The proposal
would allow an intermediate bank to receive an overall Satisfactory rating while receiving less than Satisfactory
performance on community development. The agencies should retain the current requirement that an
intermediate bank demonstrate satisfactory performance on both dimensions.

This issue is particularly important in rural areas and smaller cities, where intermediate banks may be among
the most significant financial institutions engaged in local community development. COA (formerly NACEDA)

 Page 7
 raised this concern in 2022, emphasizing the importance of intermediate-bank investments and services in
nonmetropolitan and rural markets.

That concern is concrete in Ohio. The Ohio Community Development Association reports that 37 banks
currently operating in Ohio would move from the large to intermediate bank category under the proposal, thus
facing reduced scrutiny on community development investing and retail services.

The Ohio Community Development Association's analysis also shows that the threshold change would fall
disproportionately on rural communities. While just 38 percent of Ohio's population lives in rural counties, 55
percent of the banks that would move from the large to intermediate category are headquartered in rural
communities. The disparity is even greater when looking at the full branch footprint of impacted banks, which
defines the communities in which they have CRA obligations: 58 percent of the branches of impacted banks
are located in rural counties. Those figures illustrate why reducing community development responsibilities for
intermediate banks can have an outsized impact in rural places.

Questions 9 and 10 - Community development grants and indirect costs

COA strongly opposes eliminating grants and donations from CRA consideration. We also oppose the proposed
15 percent indirect-cost limitation.

The proposal would require qualifying grants to be directly used for a particular community development
program, project, or initiative. For large banks, the proposal would additionally require the recipient's indirect
costs associated with administering the grant to remain at or below 15 percent and would require attestations
and documentation from recipients.

This approach fundamentally misunderstands how effective community development operates.

Grants support more than project expenses. They support the organizations that make projects possible: staff,
financial management, technology, fundraising, partnership development, compliance, training, technical
assistance, planning, research, and other organizational capacities. These are not incidental to community
development. They enable CDOs to develop housing, support businesses, deliver services, attract capital, and
respond to emerging community needs.

The proposed indirect-cost framework is also particularly poorly suited to state and regional community
development associations. These organizations create value across many CDOs, projects, communities, and
bank relationships. Their work may include training dozens of organizations, coordinating statewide policy,
connecting rural CDOs to financial institutions, gathering information about community needs, or developing
partnerships that eventually lead to individual transactions. Attempting to divide those functions into project
and 'overhead' categories does not measure their community development value.

The proposal would also predictably push new administrative burdens onto nonprofit recipients. Even if the
formal compliance obligation rests with the bank, banks would need information and documentation from
grantees to demonstrate compliance. Smaller CDOs in particular may be asked to create or certify cost-
allocation systems that have little connection to whether the grant produces meaningful community benefit.

A COA stakeholder in Southwest Florida, which asked not to be identified, reported that at the same point last
year it had received more than $400,000 in CRA-related bank grants supporting its mission, compared with $0
this year. The organization develops affordable rental housing for veterans, seniors, and people with
disabilities, and reported that it has laid off five staff members as bank grant support has fallen. We do not
suggest that the proposed rule is the only cause of that change. But the example shows how quickly a
reduction in flexible bank grant support can translate into lost nonprofit capacity and fewer resources for
people and communities already facing significant needs.

The Housing and Community Development Network of New Jersey (HCDNNJ) described a different but related
concern. HCDNNJ reported that two major bank community agreements totaling $3 billion have supported

 Page 8
 first-time mortgages, housing counseling, LIHTC and other community investments, as well as direct operating
support for HCDNNJ and partner organizations. HCDNNJ estimates that the proposed changes could put at
least $1 billion in investment in New Jersey's affordable housing market and community development sector at
risk. The proposed 15 percent indirect-cost standard is also directly relevant to its work: HCDNNJ reports that
most of its grants provide more than 15 percent for administrative costs. In practice, the new standard could
make those grants more costly to administer, reduce the amount of support HCDNNJ receives, or reduce bank
engagement altogether. That is exactly the wrong direction for a rule intended to strengthen community
development.

Instead, COA recommends that the agencies continue to recognize grants and donations as qualifying CRA
activities; explicitly recognize flexible and general operating support to organizations whose primary mission is
qualifying community development; eliminate the proposed 15 percent indirect-cost limitation; and establish
clearer standards for identifying mission-based CDOs and other qualifying community development
organizations.

COA (formerly NACEDA) has previously urged CRA regulators to adapt an existing federal framework for
identifying Community Development Corporations (CDCs). Under the Community Economic Development
framework administered by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, qualifying organizations are
private nonprofits whose governing documents establish a principal purpose of planning, developing, or
managing low-income housing or community development projects, and whose boards include representation
from community residents, business leaders, and civic leaders. COA believes the agencies should adapt this
framework for CRA purposes. A nonprofit that can demonstrate through its mission, governing documents,
board composition, and record of work that its principal purpose is community development serving LMI
people and places should be recognized as a qualifying mission-based CDO.

That designation should provide banks and examiners with a strong presumption that grants and other
support to the organization have a community development purpose. This is far better aligned with CRA than
an arbitrary indirect-cost test. It asks the question that matters: is this an organization whose mission,
governance, and work are directed toward community development and LMI needs? If so, CRA should allow
banks to support the organization itself, including its staff, capacity, and operations, rather than requiring
every grant dollar to be traced to a discrete project or forcing the organization to stay below a 15 percent
administrative-cost threshold. The same designation should also matter beyond grants: participation by a
qualifying mission-based CDO should serve as strong evidence of community development primary purpose
when evaluating housing, economic development, and other activities whose LMI benefits cannot always be
captured by a simple numerical threshold.

Question 11 - Primary purpose

COA supports clearer guidance regarding primary purpose, but the guidance should remain centered on
meaningful community development benefit to LMI people and places.

The proposal would generally continue current primary-purpose guidance. An activity qualifies where a
majority of dollars or beneficiaries serve a community development purpose. An activity below that majority
threshold can nevertheless receive full consideration when it has a bona fide community development intent,
is specifically structured to accomplish that purpose, and does or is reasonably certain to accomplish it.

COA recommends a general principle of proportionality. Where an identifiable portion of an activity produces
a qualifying community development benefit, CRA consideration should ordinarily reflect that portion. An
incidental LMI benefit should not transform an entire transaction into a qualifying community development
activity.

At the same time, the rule should preserve substantial flexibility for activities carried out by mission-based
CDOs. COA believes that the identity and mission of the organization carrying out an activity can itself provide

 Page 9
 important evidence of community development purpose. A CDO whose primary organizational mission is to
serve LMI people and places, whose governance reflects community accountability, and whose history
demonstrates sustained community development activity is fundamentally different from an entity
undertaking an otherwise conventional transaction that happens to produce an incidental LMI benefit.

For those organizations, regulators should not rely exclusively on transaction-by-transaction income
percentages to determine whether an activity has a community development primary purpose. CDOs
frequently undertake mixed-income, mixed-use, neighborhood-scale, or long-term revitalization strategies in
which the benefits to LMI residents cannot be allocated neatly to a single percentage. A housing development
may intentionally include households at several income levels to make the project financially sustainable. A
neighborhood revitalization project may benefit residents, businesses, and institutions simultaneously. An
economic development initiative may strengthen a commercial district while also serving LMI entrepreneurs
and residents. These activities can have a clear community development purpose even when a majority-
benefit calculation does not capture their full impact.

COA (formerly NACEDA) took this position explicitly in its 2022 CRA comments, recommending full
consideration where an activity is performed by a community-based development organization with a history
of serving LMI people and places. In the housing context, we argued that such organizations have the mission
and experience to assess mixed-income housing needs in the communities they serve.

The agencies should therefore establish a clear mission-based CDO pathway for demonstrating primary
purpose. Relevant indicators could include the organization's stated mission and governing documents, a
demonstrated history of serving LMI people and places, community representation or accountability in
governance, and a record of developing housing, economic development, or other qualifying community
development activities. COA (formerly NACEDA) has previously pointed to existing federal CDC definitions as a
useful starting point.

This should function as a meaningful presumption, not merely another factor buried in examiner discretion.
Where a qualifying mission-based CDO is responsible for developing, owning, managing, or substantially
carrying out an activity, its mission and track record should create a strong presumption that the activity has a
community development primary purpose, absent evidence to the contrary. That preserves an important
distinction between incidental LMI benefit, which should not generate full CRA credit, and community
development carried out through a mission-driven organization, where the organization itself provides
evidence that serving LMI communities is the reason the activity is being undertaken.

This clarity matters in practice. Banks are understandably cautious when CRA eligibility is uncertain. Ambiguity
around whether CDO activity qualifies can discourage support even when the activity is strongly aligned with
CRA's purpose. A defined CDO pathway would make the rule both more objective and more effective: it would
give banks greater confidence to support trusted community institutions while preserving CRA's focus on LMI
people and places.

Questions 12-17 - Complexity, responsiveness, innovation, and flexibility

COA supports the agencies' effort to clarify qualitative consideration of community development activities. We
particularly support placing responsiveness to community need at the center of qualitative review.

However, COA does not support defining the complexity or value of grants, investments, and services primarily
through their relationship to lending. Under the proposal, an investment, grant, or service could be considered
'complex' based on whether it is a necessary or beneficial component of a multicomponent financing
transaction involving a loan. That approach risks privileging activities because of their transaction structure
rather than because of their community impact.

A general operating grant that allows a CDO to expand its housing pipeline may be more responsive than a
complicated financing transaction. Technical assistance to a small or rural organization may unlock future

 Page 10
 projects that otherwise would never occur. Patient equity may address a need for which a conventional loan is
inappropriate.

 Question 12: No. Linking grants, investments, and services to lending does not inherently make them more
 responsive to community credit needs.

 Question 13: COA does not have a strong view on this question standing alone. Our larger concern is that
 the definition of complexity not elevate loan-linked structure over responsiveness to an identified
 community need.

 Question 14: The agencies should not require investments or services to be tied to complex lending
 transactions as a condition of receiving meaningful consideration.

 Question 15: Complexity should not automatically receive greater consideration than innovation,
 flexibility, impact, or other evidence of responsiveness.

 Question 16: Additional definitions may improve consistency, but the governing principle should remain
 the extent to which the activity helps meet an identified community development need.

 Question 17: Responsiveness should remain an important concept in evaluating community development
 activity. The strongest evidence of responsiveness is that a bank identified a genuine community need -
 particularly a need of LMI people or places - and designed activity that meaningfully addresses it.

The proposal already recognizes that responsiveness can include impact and success in meeting an identified
credit or community development need. COA encourages the agencies to make that concept the center of the
qualitative framework rather than subordinating it to transaction complexity.

Questions 18-20 - Middle-income and workforce housing

COA believes CRA affordable-housing activity should remain primarily focused on LMI households.

Question 18 asks whether affordable housing should be expanded to include middle-income rental housing in
high-cost areas. Question 19 asks how high-cost areas should be defined, and Question 20 asks whether
development cost or location in a high-opportunity area should affect CRA consideration.

COA (formerly NACEDA) expressed caution in 2022 about broadly expanding CRA affordable-housing eligibility
to middle-income households and continues to hold that general position. We are concerned that broad
middle-income eligibility could compete with housing serving households whose incomes and access to capital
are more squarely within CRA's traditional focus.

However, we support greater flexibility where middle-income or workforce housing is being developed or
preserved by a mission-based CDO with a demonstrated history of serving LMI communities. In those
circumstances, the organization's mission, community accountability, and long-term stewardship provide
safeguards that are not present in an unrestricted middle-income housing category.

COA does not take a position on whether the appropriate high-cost threshold is 40 percent or 50 percent.

On Question 20, difficult development conditions should be considered as part of responsiveness rather than
used independently to establish eligibility. Producing qualifying affordable housing in a market where land,
construction, or other costs make development especially difficult can merit greater qualitative consideration.
Difficulty itself, however, should not transform otherwise nonqualifying housing into a CRA-eligible activity.

Questions 21 and 22 - Nonprofit partnerships and naturally occurring affordable housing

COA supports greater flexibility for naturally occurring affordable housing developed or preserved in
partnership with nonprofit and mission-based CDOs.

The proposal asks whether nonprofit partnerships should receive exceptions from the proposed rent standards
tied to 80 percent AMI and, in high-cost areas, 120 percent AMI. COA supports such flexibility, including in the

 Page 11
 high-cost-area framework reaching 120 percent AMI, when a qualifying CDO or nonprofit is materially involved
and appropriate affordability protections are present.

Mission-based nonprofit stewardship matters. These organizations generally have an ongoing purpose of
preserving affordability and serving communities rather than simply maximizing the short-term value of the
property. Their involvement should therefore be recognized as an important indicator of community
development purpose.

Question 23 - Direct mortgages to LMI borrowers

COA does not support treating direct home mortgage loans to LMI individuals as community development
loans merely because mortgage lending is not a major product line for the bank.

Retail mortgage lending and community development financing serve related but distinct functions within
CRA. The agencies should preserve that distinction rather than reclassifying ordinary retail loans based on a
bank's product mix.

LMI homeownership remains an important CRA objective, but it should be evaluated through the appropriate
retail framework rather than redefining individual mortgages as community development loans.

Questions 24-30 - Economic development

COA supports the agencies' effort to make the economic-development definition clearer and more objective.
However, we do not support eliminating the connection between economic-development activity and
meaningful benefit to LMI people, places, or identified community needs.

The proposal would eliminate the existing purpose test, including the requirement that an activity create,
improve, or retain jobs for LMI individuals or in LMI areas, and replace it with more objective qualifying
categories.

 Question 24: The agencies should not exclude a genuinely small startup merely because it is expected to
 grow rapidly. Helping small businesses grow is itself a legitimate economic-development objective. The
 agencies should, however, be cautious about extending CRA consideration to nominally small businesses
 that are affiliates of much larger companies. CRA-motivated economic-development activity should focus
 on independent small businesses and enterprises for which access to capital or support represents a
 meaningful community development intervention. Existing size standards can serve as a guardrail, but size
 alone should not determine community development value.

 Question 25: Yes. COA supports retaining a meaningful, though flexible, LMI nexus. That nexus need not be
 limited to one narrow job-creation test. It might be established through jobs created or retained for LMI
 individuals, meaningful benefit to an LMI community, responsiveness to an identified local need, or
 activity carried out through a qualifying mission-based CDO.

 Question 26: COA does not recommend removing the existing examples of government programs. Any
 additional programs should have a clear community development purpose and a meaningful connection
 to LMI needs or other qualifying community development objectives.

 Question 27: Greater objectivity can improve CRA administration, but objective criteria should clarify the
 community development nexus rather than replace it. A transaction should not become qualifying
 economic development merely because the recipient falls below a size threshold.

 Question 28: Routine operating liquidity should not receive CRA consideration merely because it is
 provided to a small business. CRA consideration should be more closely connected to capital access,
 expansion, productive capacity, technical assistance, job creation or retention, or another identifiable
 community development need.

 Page 12
  Question 29: In developing the final definition, the agencies should avoid excluding activities that serve
 legitimate economic development purposes simply because they do not fit neatly into the new objective
 categories. Mission-based intermediaries and CDOs can be useful evidence of such purpose.

 Question 30: COA supports reasonable presumptions for credible government and mission-based
 programs that demonstrably address community development needs. Such presumptions should simplify
 administration without eliminating the underlying expectation that the activity produce a genuine
 community development benefit.

The overarching principle is that business size is a useful guardrail, but the more important question is why
CRA support is needed and who benefits from it.

Question 34 - Community development outside assessment areas

COA supports allowing banks to receive CRA consideration for qualifying community development activity
outside their required assessment areas, but only after they have demonstrated satisfactory community
development performance within their own assessment areas.

The proposal asks whether banks should be permitted to receive consideration outside assessment areas
without first meeting geographic performance standards everywhere and, if so, what standard should apply.
COA believes local responsibility must come first.

A bank should not be able to compensate for weak community development performance in communities
where it has a clear obligation by accumulating qualifying activities elsewhere. Geographic flexibility should be
additive, not substitutive.

Once a bank has demonstrated satisfactory local performance, however, greater flexibility can be valuable. It
can direct capital toward communities with significant needs but fewer CRA-active institutions, including rural
areas, smaller cities, Native communities, and other markets that can function as CRA deserts.

Outside-area consideration should be transparent, tied to an identified significant community need, available
only after satisfactory performance within required assessment areas, and structured to encourage investment
in underserved markets rather than additional concentration in already competitive CRA markets.

Question 48 - Strategic-plan public engagement

COA supports modernization of the strategic-plan process, but public notice and a comment period alone are
not sufficient community engagement.

Banks seeking strategic-plan treatment should affirmatively engage affected communities before the plan is
substantially complete. That engagement should include CDOs, residents, local governments, and other
organizations with direct knowledge of community credit and development needs.

The purpose should not simply be to document that comments were accepted. The process should help
determine the plan's priorities and measurable goals.

COA also recommends that strong and sustained community engagement receive affirmative qualitative
consideration in CRA evaluation. COA (formerly NACEDA) has previously recommended recognizing exemplary
community engagement because the process through which banks identify community needs is itself
important to effective CRA performance.

Question 53 - Adequacy of strategic-plan goals

Yes. The agencies should make clear that they may deny or require resubmission of a strategic plan when its
measurable goals, viewed in the aggregate, fail to address the credit and community development needs of its
assessment areas.

 Page 13
 That authority is essential if strategic plans are to remain an alternative method of demonstrating CRA
performance rather than an easier route to Satisfactory.

The agencies should retain flexibility to consider different business models, but strategic-plan goals should
demonstrate meaningful attention to identified needs of LMI people and places and should be informed by
meaningful community engagement.

Questions 55 and 56 - Assessment-area modernization
COA strongly supports modernizing assessment areas so that CRA responsibility follows meaningful lending
activity, not simply branch location.

Question 55 asks how the agencies should determine when a bank conducts a substantial portion of lending in
an area. Question 56 asks whether that approach should instead be replaced with a radius around physical
facilities. COA prefers a lending-based approach.

Branches remain important to many communities and should continue to matter in CRA evaluation. But a
branch-only or branch-radius geography is no longer sufficient to determine the full geographic scope of a
bank's responsibility. A bank may make substantial volumes of loans in a community without maintaining a
branch there. Where that occurs, the bank should have meaningful CRA responsibility to that community.

COA does not recommend one particular numerical threshold in response to Question 55. The agencies should
develop a transparent standard for identifying meaningful concentrations of lending and ensure that the
standard captures significant bank activity without allowing incidental lending to create unworkable
assessment areas.

The final rule should also take account of differences among rural, suburban, and urban markets. But those
differences should inform the design of a lending-based standard rather than cause the agencies to retreat to a
purely physical radius.

A core objective of CRA modernization should be simple: bank responsibility should increasingly follow where
banks actually conduct business.

Discriminatory and other illegal credit practices
Although this issue is not presented as one of the proposal's numbered questions, COA believes it warrants
explicit comment.

The agencies propose two alternatives for determining what discriminatory or other illegal credit practices can
affect CRA performance. Option 1 would generally require a violation to appear in a public enforcement action
or qualifying judicial order. Option 2 would also allow regulators to consider violations identified in
examination reports, including confidential supervisory findings.

COA supports Option 2.

A bank's CRA rating should not depend on whether substantiated discriminatory conduct ultimately resulted in
a public enforcement action. Supervisory examinations can identify significant violations that are directly
relevant to whether a bank is meeting community credit needs fairly.

At the same time, the agencies should provide greater clarity and transparency regarding how discriminatory
practices affect CRA ratings. Significant, substantiated discriminatory or illegal credit practices should
materially affect CRA performance ratings. Regulators should retain judgment to distinguish among
circumstances and severity, but consequences must be meaningful enough that a bank cannot receive
substantial CRA benefit from activity occurring alongside serious discriminatory conduct.

 Page 14
 More broadly, CRA modernization should continue to recognize persistent racial disparities in access to credit
and investment. COA is not proposing a detailed new demographic-data regime in this letter, but race and
racial disparities remain relevant context for understanding whether communities are being served equitably.

Interagency consistency

Finally, although the proposal does not pose a numbered question on interagency consistency, COA believes it
is fundamental to the rulemaking.

The proposal is being advanced by the OCC and FDIC rather than all three federal CRA regulators. COA urges
the OCC and FDIC not to finalize a materially different CRA framework unless the Federal Reserve participates
or the three agencies otherwise reach substantive alignment.

Different CRA frameworks would create unnecessary complexity not only for financial institutions but also for
CDOs and the state and regional associations that support them. Organizations seeking bank financing, grants,
or partnerships should not need to maintain separate regulatory playbooks depending on which federal
agency supervises the institution across the table.

COA (formerly NACEDA) raised this same practical concern when prior divergent CRA rulemaking created the
prospect of multiple frameworks. Community organizations and local governments should not have to become
proficient in different CRA systems simply to obtain resources and capital.

Divergent rules also create another problem: an incentive for regulatory arbitrage, or regulator shopping. If
materially different CRA obligations attach to banks based on charter and primary federal regulator,
institutions may consider those differences when choosing or changing charters. We do not suggest CRA is the
only, or necessarily the principal, factor in a bank's charter decision. But the agencies should not knowingly
create a CRA framework in which similarly situated banks face materially different community development
obligations depending on the regulator they choose.

That risk cuts against the basic logic of an interagency CRA framework. A bank should not be able to reduce or
reshape its community development obligations by moving to a regulator with rules it prefers. Nor should
community organizations have to ask who regulates a bank before they can understand the bank's CRA
responsibilities.

For COA and its network of state and regional field-building organizations, consistency also matters because
their work routinely crosses the boundaries of individual banks, regulators, and assessment areas. They build
relationships across financial institutions, coordinate statewide and regional strategies, and help local CDOs
navigate the capital system. Regulatory fragmentation makes that work harder without producing a
corresponding benefit for communities.

COA therefore urges the OCC and FDIC not to finalize a materially different CRA framework unless the Federal
Reserve participates or the three agencies otherwise reach substantive alignment. A modern CRA should be
understandable to the communities it is intended to serve, should impose comparable obligations on similarly
situated institutions, and should not create incentives for institutions to select among regulators based on
which CRA obligations they prefer.

Conclusion

CRA has always worked best when it does more than tell a bank what counts. It should require banks to
understand the communities in which they do business, identify unmet needs, and respond with lending,
investments, grants, services, and partnerships that make a difference for LMI people and places. COA
supports modernization, clearer rules, and reasonable flexibility. But those goals should strengthen community
development responsibility, not narrow it. The final rule should preserve meaningful obligations across bank
sizes, protect grants and the CDO infrastructure that makes community development possible, maintain a real

 Page 15
 LMI nexus, modernize geographic responsibility to reflect where banks actually lend, preserve meaningful
community voice and accountability, and operate under one coherent interagency framework.
COA and our state and regional association members have spent decades working with banks, regulators,
public agencies, funders, and local CDOs to make CRA work in communities. We welcome the opportunity to
continue that work with the OCC, FDIC, and Federal Reserve as the agencies consider the future of the law.
Thank you for considering our comments.
Sincerely,
Frank W. Woodruff
Executive Director & CEO
Community Opportunity Alliance

1557-AF57; FDIC RIN 3064-AG31

To the Comptroller of the Currency and the Board of Directors of the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation:

Ohio CDC Association appreciates the opportunity to provide comment on the proposed
regulatory changes to the Community Reinvestment Act. Our association serves 250
members working in affordable housing, community economic development, financial
education, and food access across all 88 counties of Ohio. Our nonprofit members
particularly focus on serving low- and moderate-income communities, and work closely
with covered financial institutions in order to make sure the needs of their communities are
served.

Because our members work in communities that have experienced decades of
disinvestment, the revitalization of those places is complex and requires long-term patient
investment. Banks are close partners in that work, and the current flexibility afforded to
covered financial institutions under the CRA provides them the ability to serve the multiple
and varied needs of these communities. Given these important partnerships, we are writing
to express concern with two key aspects of the proposed rules.

Asset-size threshold changes could reduce investment, especially in rural Ohio

Banks with asset sizes between $1 billion and $10 billion clearly make an impact on low-
and moderate-income Ohio communities. A mid-sized bank with branches in rural Ohio
invested in a Low-Income Housing Tax Credit project that built 56 units of affordable
 housing in a rural community in Southwest Ohio. A bank headquartered in Southwest Ohio
financed a new food hall in Columbus that allows entrepreneurs to build their food
businesses. A bank headquartered in Northwest Ohio has been working with an affordable
housing nonprofit to explore purchasing its portfolio of home mortgage loans, and
potentially providing loans directly to first-time homebuyers.

Given this impact, the proposal to raise the large bank asset threshold to $10 billion is an
area of concern for our membership. Under the proposal, 37 banks currently operating in
Ohio would move from the large to intermediate bank category, thus facing reduced
scrutiny on community development investing and retail services. Community
development investments are essential to meeting the pressing housing needs of our
communities, as these dollars finance the construction and preservation of much-needed
affordable rental homes through the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC). The New
Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) and investments in CDFIs are also crucial in helping to build
community facilities and provide credit access to a variety of more challenging qualified
borrowers. While banks make a return through these investment programs, the tools are
complex and require investor patience and sophistication and research shows that banks
participate in these programs in large part due to their Community Reinvestment Act
obligations. We are concerned that reducing requirements for community development
investment may disincentivize banks from engaging in these complex programs and result
in a lower overall amount of dollars invested into communities for housing and economic
development.

In Ohio, this change would disproportionately impact rural communities. Rural places
often already struggle to access traditional financing and investment due to the smaller
nature of projects and limited presence of regional or national banks. As such, local banks
play a crucial role in supporting community development lending in rural Ohio. Yet the
proposed change in asset threshold for the large bank test will substantially impact banks
headquartered in rural communities. While just 38% of Ohio's population lives in rural
counties, 55% of the banks that would move from the large to intermediate category are
headquartered in rural communities. The disparity is even greater when looking at the full
branch footprint of impacted banks, which defines the communities in which they have
CRA obligations: 58% of the branches of impacted banks are located in rural counties.

We ask that the regulatory agencies maintain the current asset thresholds in order to
ensure ongoing access to crucial community development investments, especially in rural
areas.
 Removing grant flexibility could increase bureaucracy and reduce results

We are also concerned by the proposal to restrict the purpose of grants to nonprofit
organizations or to even eliminate them entirely from CRA consideration. Financial
institutions act as more than just funders in a healthy community development ecosystem
 they are vested partners in producing tangible outcomes for low- and moderate-income
communities. As such, many banks provide flexible grants to help grow the capacity of
nonprofits in the ecosystem to make sure they are efficiently and effectively delivering
results. Limiting CRA consideration only to grants that are tied to a specific community
development project or program and capping operating expenses at 15% of the grant would
severely limit banks' ability to invest in the partners and projects that align with their own
community development goals.

Flexible bank funding has created lasting results for low- and moderate-income
communities in Ohio. A grant from an Ohio-based bank supported Ohio CDC Association's
Peer to Peer program, which matches more experienced nonprofit staff with a mentee to
work together on an identified organizational challenge. The grant funds support travel and
time stipends for both organizations, giving them the ability to work on building their skills
without worrying about covering staff time with other grants. The program has resulted in
new programs that directly serve low- and moderate-income populations, including the
creation of a home repair program in Cleveland, a new small business assistance center in
Columbus, and a workforce development program for people in recovery in Northeast
Ohio.

Grants from local banks are particularly important in rural Southeast Ohio, where the
decline of industry left small coal mining communities with very limited access to capital.
CRA-motivated giving has been extremely important in helping communities build upon
their assets and allowing local nonprofit organizations to develop innovative projects. One
regional nonprofit received support from a bank to collect and redistribute durable medical
equipment to residents in need or without insurance, saving participants thousands of
dollars. Another Southeast Ohio business development nonprofit organization worked with
entrepreneurs to develop actionable business plans, and support from a local bank
provided the businesses with a small seed grant to get their ideas off the ground. These
grants show what CRA-motivated giving makes possible in communities with few other
sources of capital. Narrowing the grants eligible for CRA credit, or adding allocation and
documentation requirements, risks reducing this support where it is hardest to replace.

Defining program versus administrative time in grants is a challenge familiar to many
nonprofits, particularly related to programs intended to build the capacity of an
organization to deliver a service. Requiring banks to define and document this distinction
 will not result in dollars better spent instead it will require substantially more
administrative time on the part of both banks and nonprofits to ensure compliance with
this rule. Ultimately, that means time and resources focused on paperwork instead of
meeting the continuing and affirmative obligation to serve low- and moderate-income
communities, as the Community Reinvestment Act intended.
We ask that the regulatory agencies preserve CRA credit for flexible and general operating
grants to nonprofits, and drop the 15% operating cap.

Conclusion
Ohio's community development organizations depend on strong, flexible partnerships with
the financial institutions that serve their communities. We urge the agencies to retain asset
thresholds that preserve meaningful community development investment obligations for
mid-size banks, particularly those serving rural Ohio, and to maintain CRA consideration
for flexible grants that build nonprofit capacity without imposing burdensome allocation
and documentation requirements. These changes would keep the Community
Reinvestment Act focused on its core purpose: ensuring that banks continue to meet the
credit, investment, and service needs of low- and moderate-income communities. We
appreciate your consideration of these comments and welcome the opportunity to provide
additional information or Ohio-specific data.

Sincerely,

Torey Hollingsworth
Executive Director
Ohio CDC Association

To Whom It May Concern,

On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA). CRA has helped create a durable incentive for banks to provide safe, sound, and profitable
loans and investments in CDFIs across the country. In addition, grants to support operating
expenses and program expansion have been critical to supporting services in communities that
have historically lacked access to capital.

We appreciate the agencies' efforts to reform the CRA regulations and applaud some of the
provisions that could improve the CRA framework and increase responsible capital in underserved
communities. However, we have major concerns with the increases in the asset thresholds that
determine how banks are evaluated under CRA and the restrictions on grants. We also have
concerns with several interacting provisions that could further weaken community development
incentives that will undoubtedly impair the flow of much needed capital in the most underserved
communities.

Southeast Community Capital Corp, dba Pathway Lending has been a certified Community
Development Financial Institution (CDFI) in Tennessee since 2001. As a state-wide, not-for-profit
CDFI loan fund headquartered in Nashville with full-service regional offices in Memphis,
Chattanooga, and Knoxville, our primary lending and educational services have been focused on
low- and moderate-income communities throughout rural and urban communities in Tennessee.

Financial Institutions are vital partners in the work that we do. The impact of raising the threshold
of the asset size of banks would be significant as 40% of our investing banks are between $1B and
$10B. Further, it would significantly increase the pricing of our borrowings and potentially
eliminate operating grant support for CDFIs. While we all would like to think banks would still do
transactions with CDFIs without CRA regulatory supervision banks will do the absolute minimum
and will take the least burdensome route to achieve minimum requirements which will mean for
banks below $10B buying securities.

 201 Venture Circle Nashville, TN 37228 Phone: (615) 425.7171 Fax: (615) 425.7172 www.pathwaylending.org
 We currently have relationships with 45 banks that provide us with Equity Equivalent Investments,
community development loans, and grants for program expansion. These partnerships are
mutually reinforcing. In addition to providing critical capital and resources to CDFIs, banks rely on
CDFIs to reach underserved communities, develop borrowers, and cultivate future bank customers.

Approximately 60% of our small business originations are from our partner bank referrals. These
businesses are provided much needed capital and technical assistance and typically return to the
financial mainstream withing 36-60 months as a sustainable credit opportunity for the bank that
referred them to us.

To date, we have been provided with approximately $185 million in Equity Equivalent Investments
(EQ2) that have created over $1 billion in economic impact across Tennessee. The lending and
grant capital provided by our bank partners has generated over $641MM in loan originations,
preserved or developed 2,700 affordable housing opportunities, and funded over 1,800 businesses.

CRA has long helped create the motivation for banks to build and sustain these relationships,
strengthening the broader community development ecosystem. We are therefore concerned that
several provisions in the proposal could weaken these incentives, reducing bank engagement with
CDFIs and ultimately the flow of capital to the communities we serve.

The Community Reinvestment Act was created to ensure low-income communities would receive
the critical lending resources needed to grow. The proposed changes to CRA will greatly reduce the
flow of capital to low-income communities. The presence of the CRA has created innovative
solutions and partnership among banks, CDFIs, and low-income communities to ensure the original
intent of access to financial services are available to all communities. We appreciate the agencies'
efforts to improve clarity and flexibility. Modernization, however, should result in more responsible
capital reaching communities with unmet credit needs, as the CRA statute was intended.

We therefore urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the raised asset thresholds and to withdraw the
restrictions on CD operating grants as proposed.

Thank you for considering these comments and for understanding the impact of the proposed
changes on the communities we serve.

Sincerely,

Clinton B. Gwin, CEO

Southeast Community Capital Corp, dba Pathway Lending

 201 Venture Circle Nashville, TN 37228 Phone: (615) 425.7171 Fax: (615) 425.7172 www.pathwaylending.org

To Whom it May Concern:

On behalf of Montgomery Housing Partnership (MHP), I am writing to express our opposition to the Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency
(OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) because it would significantly weaken the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes,
we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely
consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis
and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-
days.

By way of background, MHP is a nonprofit affordable housing developer based in Silver Spring, Maryland, just
outside of the nation's capital. We are also a member of the NeighborWorks America network, a national
affiliation of more than 200 nonprofit community development organizations committed to community
revitalization. Our mission is to preserve and expand quality affordable housing throughout the Washington
metropolitan region. Our success has been a result of taking a comprehensive approach to developing affordable
housing that integrates three things: Housing people; Empowering families; and Strengthening Neighborhoods.

The CRA has been a vital source of capital formation for our organization and the affordable housing industry
as a whole. The vast majority of our lenders are banks that are subject to the CRA. The CRA has been
successful in many respects, none more so than when it comes to financing and constructing affordable housing.
In conjunction with the federal government's Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) program, the CRA has
been the driving force behind the creation of new affordable rental housing in this country. If not for the
CRA, many of the banks that provide capital to our projects would almost assuredly exit the affordable
housing space or require a higher rate of return on their investments.

In addition to motivating banks to invest in affordable housing for low-to-moderate-income households, the
CRA has inspired lenders to become philanthropically engaged in organizations that serve the
communities where they have customers. Many of the banks we work with have chosen to make charitable
contributions to our organization after being exposed to the work we do, which has enabled us to have an even
greater impact in local communities.
 The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change how
regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for nonprofit organizations. We are
concerned that these changes are being considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low-
and moderate-income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination and
disinvestment.

In particular, we are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in communities.
For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital devoted to either community
development loans or investments would be enough to receive a passing CRA rating. However, that percentage
is far lower than the percentage the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the
largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.

NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the OCC and FDIC
supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these banks currently conduct approximately
$102 billion annually in community development loans and investments inside their assessment areas, and that
the median percentage of annual community development lending in assessment areas was 6.8% of tier 1
capital, and a median of 3.6% of tier 1 capital for annual CRA qualified investments. If each bank instead
conducted only the amount necessary to meet separate thresholds of 0.625% of Tier 1 capital for community
development lending and investments, combined activity would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually -- a
decrease of approximately $87.1 billion, or 85%.

In closing, MHP strongly supports efforts to modernize the CRA. The CRA can play a key role in economic
recovery efforts and help ensure that investment continues to flow to historically disinvested communities. As
we look to the future, maintaining a strong CRA program will be critical to helping neighborhoods hit
hardest obtain the capital they need to rebuild and recover.

Thank you for your consideration of our views on this important matter.

Sincerely,
