Dear Sir(s)/Madam(s):

The Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC) appreciates the opportunity to comment
on the notice of proposed rulemaking issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
(OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) (together, the Agencies) regarding
proposed amendments to their Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.1 The AHTCC's
comments focus on the provisions most directly affecting community development investment
and, in particular, investment in affordable housing financed with the Low-Income Housing Tax
Credit (Housing Credit).

Established in 1988, the AHTCC is a leading trade association in the affordable housing
industry, comprised of more than 280 organizations and businesses representing the full
spectrum of stakeholders involved in affordable housing financed with the Housing Credit,
including investors, syndicators, developers, state allocating agencies, and affiliated businesses
and nonprofits. Together, AHTCC members have financed or developed well over half of our
nation's more than four million Housing Credit rental homes.2,3

The Housing Credit is key to addressing our nation's affordable housing crisis and was recently
expanded to meet the growing need. In 2025, Congress increased its investment in the Housing
Credit, which is estimated to finance 1.22 million additional affordable rental homes over the
next decade. We urge the adoption of a CRA framework that supports robust demand for the
Housing Credit to realize the promise of that investment.

A broad and competitive market of private investors is essential to the success of the Housing
Credit. Banks are central to that market. In 2024, banks supplied roughly 80 percent of Housing

1 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52114 (Aug. 12, 2026).
2 The ACTION Campaign, Low-Income Housing Tax Credit Fact Sheet (Feb. 2026),
https://rentalhousingaction.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/ACTION-NATIONAL-FEB-2026.pdf.
3 See the full list of AHTCC members at https://www.taxcreditcoalition.org/about/member-organizations/.
 Credit equity,4 and a recent CohnReznick analysis estimated that approximately 71 percent of
Housing Credit equity surveyed in 2025 was CRA-motivated.5 The CRA investment test in
particular has helped create a deep, competitive, and efficient market for the Housing Credit. The
structure of CRA examinations therefore has a direct relationship to the depth and breadth of the
Housing Credit investor base and to the amount of private capital available to finance affordable
rental housing.

The proposed rule would make changes to the CRA framework for community and regional
banks that would substantially impact the Housing Credit. Most significantly for the Housing
Credit, it would increase the large bank threshold from $1.649 billion to $10 billion in assets,
moving hundreds of OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks that currently have a separate investment
test into a new category with reduced requirements under the intermediate bank community
development test. The proposal also asks for comment on alternative thresholds, including a
$3.252 billion large bank threshold and a $30 billion threshold. The AHTCC surveyed Housing
Credit syndicators to assess how these alternatives correspond to actual Housing Credit
investment activity. Those results provide a market-based record of the amounts of private
capital and number of active investors associated with each threshold.

Our survey found that the lower the large bank asset threshold, the less of an impact there would
be on the Housing Credit investor market. Removing the investment test requirement for banks
under the $10 billion threshold would remove an incentive for a significant number of banks to
invest in the Housing Credit. In an AHTCC survey, over 108 banks below the $10 billion
threshold invested at least $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity over the five-year survey period.
Extrapolating these results beyond just those surveyed by AHTCC, to the full Housing Credit
market, banks under the $10 billion threshold invested approximately $2 billion in Housing
Credit equity over those five years.

Banks under the $10 billion threshold also play a particularly important role in financing
affordable housing in rural communities. AHTCC survey data show that approximately one-third
of Housing Credit equity investments from banks under $10 billion in assets supported rural
markets, indicating that banks in this asset range play an outsized role in investing in rural
communities. By comparison, roughly 8 percent of all Housing Credit equity in a CohnReznick
industry-wide sample was invested in nonmetro counties, a proxy for rural and small-town
markets.

If the Agencies increase the large bank threshold, the $3.252 billion alternative threshold would
be substantially less disruptive to Housing Credit investment than the proposed $10 billion large
bank threshold. On the other hand, the alternative $30 billion large bank threshold that the
Agencies requested feedback on would be significantly more damaging to Housing Credit
investment. Our detailed results are below.

 2
 The Housing Credit Market and the Role of CRA

The nation's shortage of affordable rental housing remains severe. According to the Joint Center
for Housing Studies of Harvard University, the stock of units renting for less than $1,000 per
month in inflation-adjusted terms fell by more than 7 million units between 2014 and 2024.6 The
National Low Income Housing Coalition reports a shortage of more than 7 million homes
affordable and available to extremely low-income renters.7 At the same time, input costs for
residential construction have increased 48.9 percent since 2020, making new affordable housing
more difficult to finance.8

The Housing Credit is the nation's primary tool for creating and preserving affordable rental
housing. The Housing Credit is widely regarded as one of the nation's most successful public-
private partnerships, mobilizing private capital while giving states flexibility to establish
priorities based on local housing needs.9 Last year, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed into
law by President Trump, included the most significant expansion of the Housing Credit in the
program's history, an expansion estimated to finance approximately 1.22 million additional
affordable rental homes over the next decade. Realizing the production potential of that
expansion will require continued support for robust private investment in the Housing Credit.10

Congress has also recently increased banks' capacity to make public welfare investments,
including Housing Credit investments, by raising the public welfare investment cap from 15
percent to 20 percent in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Many of the institutions
positioned to benefit from that additional capacity are community and regional banks. At the
same time, the proposed increase in the large bank threshold could alter the CRA incentives for a
number of these institutions.

CRA has long been one of the principal drivers of the Housing Credit investment market.
CohnReznick estimated that approximately $21.4 billion of Housing Credit equity surveyed in
2025 was CRA-motivated.11 CohnReznick separately reported that banks supplied roughly $23

 billion of Housing Credit equity in 2024, or approximately 80 percent of the market.12 The
separate investment test has helped create a distinct incentive for qualifying community
development investments while leaving banks flexibility to determine which investments best fit
their business strategy and communities. That distinction is important because Housing Credit
equity performs a different function in an affordable housing capital stack than debt, and cannot
be replaced on a dollar-for-dollar basis by additional lending.

A broad investor base also supports a more efficient market. Competition among investors
supports stronger equity pricing, which can increase the amount of private capital generated by
each Housing Credit allocation and reduce the amount of other financing needed to complete a
development. Strong Housing Credit pricing can also improve the financial feasibility of
developments that would otherwise not proceed, allowing Housing Credit allocations to support
additional affordable housing production.

AHTCC Survey Methodology

The purpose of the AHTCC survey was to understand the number of Housing Credit investors
and amount of Housing Credit investment that could be affected if banks lose the incentive that
the large bank investment test currently provides. Because Housing Credit investments by banks
with less than $30 billion in assets are predominantly made through syndicators, the AHTCC
surveyed Housing Credit syndicators to measure affected bank participation and investment.

We received responses from 28 syndicators. Twenty-five provided bank-level investment data
for 2021 through 2025, and other respondents provided portfolio-level information. Of the
respondents providing bank-level detail, 23 also participated in CohnReznick's 2025 volume
survey and represented 79.2 percent of the syndicated Housing Credit market measured by that
survey. Two additional respondents providing bank-level information were not included in the
CohnReznick survey, making 79.2 percent a conservative measure of the AHTCC survey's
market coverage. The breadth of these responses provides a robust and comprehensive view of
Housing Credit investment activity by banks at the asset thresholds under consideration by the
Agencies.

The analysis matched reported Housing Credit investors to 2026 first quarter consolidated asset
data and identified institutions supervised by the OCC or FDIC. Because the survey was
designed to measure actual participation in the Housing Credit market rather than the universe of
all banks, the results should be read as a conservative count of active investors captured by
participating syndicators. Where noted below, the AHTCC also extrapolated reported investment
amounts to 100 percent of the syndicated market using the survey's measured market coverage.

Impact of the Proposed $10 Billion Threshold

Under the proposal, 376 OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks currently classified as large would
move to the intermediate bank framework and would no longer be subject to a separate
investment test. The Agencies identify 126 OCC-supervised banks and 250 FDIC-supervised
banks in this category. The AHTCC survey captured more than 108 active Housing Credit
investors from banks within the affected asset range. Those banks invested at least $1.595 billion

12 CohnReznick, 2025 Affordable Housing Credit Study, accessed Sept. 18, 2026,
https://creditstudy.cohnreznick.com/credit-study.

 4
 in Housing Credit equity during the five-year survey period. Extrapolated to the full syndicated
market, the corresponding five-year amount is approximately $2.0 billion.

These institutions are not incidental participants in the Housing Credit market. Community and
regional banks frequently invest through multi-investor funds alongside larger institutions. Their
commitments can help complete fund raises that deploy capital across multiple properties and
markets and, by sharing exposure across a broader investor pool, can support additional
participation by larger institutions, broadening the reach of Housing Credit investments.
Because multi-investor funds often limit each investor's share of the fund, the loss of one
investor cannot always be replaced dollar-for-dollar by other investors, meaning the departure of
community and regional banks can reduce the overall amount of equity a fund is able to raise,
with effects that can extend beyond the banks directly affected by the proposed threshold change.

Industry experience also indicates that many community and regional banks have entered the
Housing Credit market in recent years and have become repeat investors, broadening the investor
base over time. Limiting their participation now by removing their incentive to invest in the
Housing Credit could also have effects that extend for years to come.

Impact of Alternative Large Bank Thresholds

The Agencies requested comment on alternative large bank thresholds of $3.252 billion and $30
billion. AHTCC survey data show that the choice among these thresholds would have materially
different implications for both the number of banks investing in the Housing Credit and the
amount of Housing Credit equity investment implicated.

Applying the $3.252 billion threshold instead of the proposed $10 billion threshold reduces the
number of affected banks investing in the Housing Credit over the survey period from more than
108 to 40, a reduction of approximately 63 percent.

The distribution of investment within the affected range is also concentrated above $3.252
billion. AHTCC survey data show that approximately 86 percent of Housing Credit equity
investment from OCC- and FDIC-regulated banks with consolidated assets between $1.65 billion
and $10 billion comes from banks with assets above $3.252 billion. Accordingly, the associated

 5
 estimated five-year Housing Credit equity impact declines from approximately $2.0 billion under
the proposed $10 billion threshold to $272 million under the $3.252 billion alternative.

The $3.252 billion alternative would have a significantly less damaging impact on Housing
Credit investment by leaving the separate investment test in place for banks representing a
much larger share of the Housing Credit equity market.

The $3.252 billion figure also has a distinct historical basis in the CRA framework. It is the
inflation-adjusted equivalent of the OCC's 2020 $2.5 billion threshold, which was calibrated to
preserve the relative shares of banks classified as small and intermediate.

The Agencies also requested comment on a $30 billion large bank threshold, which our survey
results show could significantly reduce Housing Credit investments. The AHTCC survey
captured more than 140 banks with consolidated assets between $1.65 billion and $30 billion and
found that these institutions invested at least $3.575 billion over the five-year survey period.
Extrapolated to the full syndicated market, that amount is approximately $4.5 billion, more than
twice the amount associated with the proposed $10 billion threshold and roughly 16 times the
amount associated with the $3.252 billion alternative.

Recurring direct Housing Credit investment is concentrated among banks with more than $30
billion in consolidated assets. Direct Housing Credit investment by banks with less than $30
billion in assets is generally made on a one-off basis, while direct investments facilitated through
syndicators may already be reflected in the AHTCC survey responses, providing a high degree of
confidence in the representative coverage of this sample.

The AHTCC strongly encourages the Agencies to adopt a lower large bank threshold in order to
minimize the loss of a significant number of investors and their associated investments from the
Housing Credit market who would no longer be subject to a separate investment test. To the
extent that the CRA requirements related to the investment test will change for certain banks, the
$3.252 billion large bank threshold would be significantly less damaging to the Housing Credit
than the $10 billion threshold, and dramatically less damaging than the proposed alternative $30
billion threshold.

Community and Regional Banks Play an Outsized Role in Rural Housing Credit Markets

In addition to the number of banks affected and the amount of their investments in the Housing
Credit, the geographic distribution of investment is especially relevant to the threshold
discussion. Our survey found that community and regional banks direct a disproportionately high
share of their investments to rural areas, which could be diminished if these banks lose the
current incentives to invest in the Housing Credit.

For the analysis of impacts in rural areas, the AHTCC was able to identify geographic
investment activity for a subset representing 54.9 percent of the Housing Credit equity reported
by survey respondents providing bank-level data. Within that subset, approximately one-third of
Housing Credit equity supported rural markets during the period 2021-2024: 34.2 percent of
equity from all banks in the $412 million to $10 billion asset range, and 31.6 percent of equity
from OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks in that range. By comparison, 8.1 percent of Housing
Credit equity in a CohnReznick industry-wide sample during the same period was invested in
USDA-defined nonmetro counties. Although the two measures are not identical, the contrast is

 6
 directionally significant and indicates that community and regional banks in the affected asset
range account for a comparatively large share of investment in rural markets.

The AHTCC measure reflects rural investment estimates reported by syndicators providing bank-level data; the CohnReznick comparison reflects
 Housing Credit investment in counties classified as nonmetro under USDA Rural-Urban Continuum Codes. The measures are presented as
 complementary indicators rather than identical geographic classifications.

This pattern is consistent with how the Housing Credit market operates. Community and regional
banks often have business relationships and market knowledge in smaller communities.
Maintaining a broad and deep investor base therefore matters not only for aggregate equity
demand but also for the geographic distribution of that demand.

CRA incentives help encourage bank investment and promote competition in rural Housing
Credit markets, where the pool of potential investors is often limited. Weaker investor
competition can result in lower equity pricing, reducing the amount of private capital available to
finance affordable housing developments. Freddie Mac has illustrated how weaker equity pricing
can create substantial financing gaps, including an example in which lower pricing would leave a
rural development with a $540,000 shortfall that would need to be filled through additional
financing or other sources.13 Reducing incentives for community and regional banks to invest in
these markets could further constrain investor competition, exacerbating existing financing
challenges and potentially making otherwise viable developments infeasible.

The AHTCC encourages the Agencies to adopt a lower large bank threshold so that these
community and regional banks retain the incentive to make investments in the Housing Credit,
particularly in underserved rural areas.

Preserve an Evenly Weighted Community Development Test

The proposal would also change how intermediate bank CRA performance is combined into an
overall rating. Under the current intermediate small bank framework, a bank generally must
receive at least a Satisfactory rating on both the lending test and the community development test
to receive an overall Satisfactory rating. Under the proposal, stronger lending performance could
compensate for weaker community development performance. The Agencies acknowledge that
this change may increase the relative incentive for banks to devote CRA resources to lending
activities. That change would necessarily weaken the relative incentive to devote resources to
community development activities.

That interaction becomes more consequential if substantially more banks are moved into the
intermediate bank category. Housing Credit equity is a community development investment that

13 Freddie Mac, Duty to Serve Underserved Markets Plan, 20182021, revised December 18, 2020, 84,
https://www.freddiemac.com/sites/g/files/ynjofi111/files/about/duty-to-serve/docs/Freddie-Mac-Underserved-
Markets-Plan.pdf.

 7
 performs a function not supplied by additional debt. If the separate investment test no longer
applies to a bank, the structure of the community development test becomes the principal
mechanism within the CRA evaluation for recognizing the bank's investment activity. The final
rule should therefore ensure that community development performance receives even and
distinct weight alongside lending performance in the overall evaluation of intermediate banks.

Geographic Flexibility Can Improve the Allocation of Private Capital

The proposal would provide additional flexibility for banks to receive CRA consideration for
qualifying community development activities outside their assessment areas after satisfying
applicable geographic standards or where performance context demonstrates that local
community development needs have been adequately addressed. The Agencies note that the
existing framework can contribute to distortions in the market known as CRA "hot spots" and
"deserts," including in rural areas where relatively few banks have a physical presence.

A framework that preserves a bank's responsibility to serve its local assessment areas while also
recognizing qualifying activity beyond those areas can broaden the pool of capital available to
communities with fewer CRA-motivated investors. In the Housing Credit market, greater
geographic flexibility can also reduce localized pricing distortions. Where more investors are
able to compete for investments outside their immediate footprints, pricing can become more
consistent across markets, strengthening the efficiency of the national Housing Credit market
without displacing the importance of local performance.

The proposal presents more than one method for implementing this flexibility. From the
perspective of Housing Credit investment, the key consideration is that the final framework
provides a workable and predictable path for meaningful CRA consideration of qualifying
community development investments outside a bank's assessment areas. Either a qualitative or
quantitative framework can be evaluated against that objective.

The final rule should provide a clear and predictable pathway for qualifying community
development activities conducted on a broader statewide or regional basis to receive CRA
consideration. A bank that received a Satisfactory or Outstanding rating on its most recent CRA
evaluation should be presumed to have adequately served the needs of its assessment areas and
therefore be eligible to receive consideration for qualifying activities outside those areas
throughout its next examination cycle. This approach would preserve accountability for meeting
local needs while supporting sustained investment in rural and underserved communities where
affordable housing needs and financing markets often extend beyond individual assessment-area
boundaries.

Related Bank Capital Rules Will Also Affect Housing Credit Demand

Although separate from this rulemaking, we encourage the Agencies to consider the impact of
bank capital requirements on the capacity of regulated institutions to invest in the Housing
Credit. The AHTCC has separately submitted comments regarding the capital treatment of
Housing Credit investments in the Agencies' Basel III rulemaking. The historical performance
and risk characteristics of Housing Credit investments are relevant to that work, and the
interaction between CRA incentives and regulatory capital requirements will influence the
amount and composition of bank demand for Housing Credit equity.

 8
 The CRA proposal and the capital proposals affect different sides of that equation. Changes to
CRA requirements may reduce the incentive for some banks to invest in the Housing Credit,
while more risk-sensitive capital treatment could increase banks' capacity to invest. The
Agencies have emphasized that the capital proposals are intended to better align regulatory
capital with risk, reduce burden, and better support banks' ability to deploy capital while
maintaining safety and soundness. Applying those principles to Housing Credit investments
could materially expand bank capacity to supply equity to the market.

The AHTCC therefore encourages the Agencies, as they consider these related regulatory
changes, to recognize the combined effect of CRA incentives and capital requirements on
Housing Credit demand. A lower risk weight that more accurately reflects the demonstrated
performance of Housing Credit investments would complement the Agencies' broader
deregulatory and risk-sensitive objectives and could significantly expand banks' capacity to
invest in Housing Credit equity.

Conclusion

The AHTCC supports the Agencies' broader efforts to modernize bank regulations, reduce
unnecessary regulatory burden, and better tailor requirements to institutions of different sizes and
business models. Those objectives can be advanced while preserving and, where appropriate,
strengthening the incentives and capacity for private investment in affordable housing through
the Housing Credit.

CRA has long been an important driver of bank demand for Housing Credit equity. As the
Agencies consider changes to bank classifications, examination standards, and geographic
flexibility, the final framework should preserve meaningful incentives for community
development investment and avoid unnecessarily weakening demand for Housing Credit equity.
The AHTCC's survey data provide important market context for the Agencies' consideration of
these changes and show that the alternatives under consideration would have materially different
effects on the number of active Housing Credit investors and the amount of equity investment
affected. We therefore urge the Agencies to adopt a lower large bank threshold that minimizes
disruption to the Housing Credit market.

Related capital reforms should likewise reflect the strong historical performance of Housing
Credit investments and support banks' capacity to invest.

The AHTCC appreciates the Agencies' consideration of these comments and welcomes the
opportunity to provide additional information regarding the Housing Credit market, our survey
data, or the potential effects of the proposed changes. Please do not hesitate to contact us at
emily.cadik@taxcreditcoalition.org.

Sincerely,

Emily Cadik
Chief Executive Officer
Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition

Centrant is a mission-driven lending consortium that provides long-term, fixed-rate permanent
financing for affordable multifamily housing across the Southeast. Centrant originates loans that
qualify for CRA community development consideration, selling participation interests in those loans
to our membership of over 90 bank partners throughout the region. This model allows banks of all
sizes to help meet the financing, community development and affordable housing needs of low- and
moderate-income (LMI) communities.

Our participating banks include entities ranging from $20 million in assets to nearly $250 billion in
assets. Over the past 35 years, loan participation commitments provided by these banks have allowed
Centrant to close over $550 million in loans, financing more than 27,000 affordable apartment units
across nine Southeastern states. We currently hold a pipeline of $90 million in approved loans fully
subscribed by member bank participation commitments that will finance another 3,000 apartment
units over the coming 24-36 months. This degree of support for Centrant's lending program is just
 one example of the financial impact that banks have in addressing affordable housing and community
development needs and much of that support is incentivized under the CRA.

Centrant occupies a unique position as a funding bridge between our bank members and the
communities we collectively serve. In this context, we ask the Agencies to consider these comments
as a means of supporting and recognizing banks that commit themselves to vitally important
community development activities.

 1) We Commend the Agencies' Efforts to Modernize and Clarify the CRA Framework

 First, we offer our support for the Agencies' efforts to modernize the language of the CRA
 rules, foster greater transparency, and reduce unnecessary complexity for banks of all sizes.

 Time and again, financial institutions have demonstrated their sincere interest in serving the
 needs of their customers and their communities by providing the capital that creates
 affordable housing and homeownership, nurtures small businesses, and supports essential
 community needs such as community facilities, healthcare, childcare and economic
 development activities. Concurrently, many of these same activities have allowed banks to
 meet their obligations under CRA. Unfortunately, we hear often from our members that clear
 regulatory guidance is not always forthcoming, and banks may not be certain of receiving
 positive CRA consideration for qualifying activities undertaken in good faith.

 Clear rules, consistently applied, benefit both banks and the communities they serve. We
 therefore support the Agencies' objective of ensuring that the CRA framework operates as
 effectively and efficiently as possible so that banks remain incentivized to participate in this
 vital community financing activity. We also recommend that any changes to the CRA be
 adopted and codified consistently by all three federal banking agencies.

 2) Bank Lending and Investment Incentivized by the CRA Is Critical to Meeting
 Community Needs

 The banking industry plays an indispensable role in meeting the lending, investment, and
 service needs of the communities in which banks operate. As you consider updates to the CRA
 framework, this support must be recognized, encouraged and rewarded.

 A recent study by the National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders (NAAHL) found
 that, in 2024 alone, the CRA incentivized more than $430 billion in loans and investments to
 low- and moderate-income communities -- an amount nearly six times the combined federal
 budgets of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, the USDA's Rural
 Housing Service, the Small Business Administration, and the CDFI Fund. This is not a marginal
 contribution to the nation's community development infrastructure; by a wide margin, it is
 the largest source of capital directed to LMI communities in the country.

 We raise this point because, although the proposal seeks to reduce burden and increase
 clarity, it could inadvertently--and significantly--reduce the volume of bank loans and
  investments flowing to these communities at precisely the moment this capital is most
 urgently needed.

3) Community Development Efforts Should Encompass a Broad Range of Activities, With
 Greater Certainty and Transparency Regarding CRA Eligibility

 Given the extensive role that banks play, the Agencies should refine the proposed definitions
 of community development, including affordable housing, financial education, economic
 development, essential infrastructure, disaster recovery, and grants. They should also
 develop and publish a single, non-exhaustive illustrative list of activities eligible for
 community development consideration and establish a clear, timely process through which
 banks may obtain a prior determination that an activity will qualify.

 The final rule should also provide flexibility in allocating activities that benefit multiple
 assessment areas and should permit consideration of activities outside a bank's assessment
 area(s) when the bank received a rating of Satisfactory or better on its prior examination.

 For loans originated by or purchased from a lending consortium, including those originated
 by Centrant and similar organizations across the country, we recommend that the final rule
 avoid limitations on how or where such loan participations or comparable investment
 structures may receive consideration.

4) Lending and Investment Activities to Support Affordable Housing Should Be Rewarded
 Under Any Revised CRA Framework

 As demonstrated by the recent bipartisan passage of the 21st Century Road to Housing Act,
 the shortage of quality affordable housing is consistently identified as one of the most critical
 needs facing communities across the country today. Any effort to update the CRA regulations
 -- however well-intentioned in its aim to reduce burden -- must protect, encourage, and
 reward the bank lending and investment activities that support the preservation and creation
 of affordable housing.

 We are concerned that several elements of the proposal, taken together, could work against
 that objective by reducing, redirecting or disincentivizing the volume of bank investment and
 lending activity that comprises the majority of capital supporting affordable housing
 development today. As a constructive alternative to narrowing the conditions for CRA credit,
 we would suggest that the CRA revisions adopt new incentives specifically designed to
 encourage and reward banks that support affordable housing initiatives.

5) Affordable Housing Activity by Banks Should Be Recognized Under the CRA, Regardless
 of Location

 We understand and appreciate the Agencies' goal of refocusing CRA evaluations on core
 lending activity within a bank's assessment areas and providing clear guidance regarding
 performance thresholds. While this is an important goal, we recommend that the Agencies
 provide positive CRA consideration for any affordable housing lending or investment activity,
  regardless of location, without requiring a bank first to satisfy a dollar-denominated or
 percentage-based performance threshold within its assessment area(s) as proposed under
 the geographic flexibility standard.

 In our experience, affordable housing developments are often located adjacent to the high-
 demand markets that make up the core of the banking industry's service areas. This is not a
 coincidence; land and construction costs are often prohibitive within the highest-demand
 submarkets themselves, pushing new affordable housing development into adjacent, lower-
 cost communities. The LMI workforce that commutes into a bank's assessment area to fill
 essential jobs -- in healthcare, education, retail, hospitality, and other sectors -- very often
 lives in these nearby communities.

 A rule, calculation or regulatory expectation that continues to focus disproportionately on
 assessment area requirements for an issue like affordable housing, which transcends
 arbitrary boundaries, may discourage banks from pursuing worthwhile affordable housing
 financing or investment activities simply because they believe they may not receive positive
 consideration for their efforts.

 This concern affects not only lending activity, but potentially banks' willingness to provide
 investment capital for projects financed via the federal Low Income Housing Tax Credit
 (LIHTC) program--the single most important federal funding vehicle for affordable housing
 development today. Any deterioration in banks' support for affordable housing finance
 ultimately works against the LMI population that helps sustain economic activity within
 adjacent assessment areas.

 We would propose that banks be allowed to receive positive consideration for out-of-
 assessment area lending and investments that support affordable housing so long as they
 receive and maintain an overall CRA rating of "Satisfactory" or better. This approach would
 provide clarity for banks and regulatory staff alike and would create incentives for banks to
 continue supporting affordable housing developments regardless of location.

6) The Same Concern Applies to Rural Communities

 We share a related, and in some respects more acute, concern for rural communities. The
 proposal's increased emphasis on assessment areas could have a significantly detrimental
 effect on rural communities, where there are fewer banks, less overall CRA-motivated
 investment activity (often referred to as "CRA deserts"), and fewer alternative sources of
 capital available to fill any resulting gap.

 Of the roughly $550 million in loans that Centrant has closed to date, approximately 13%
 financed properties located in rural counties. In our experience, the overall reduction in the
 number of banks through mergers and consolidation has already had a clear impact on
 community development funding in rural areas. Our member funding response is far stronger
 in urban and metropolitan counties, where we often receive significantly more commitments
 than needed, than in rural counties, where we may not receive sufficient commitments
 without follow-up outreach for additional support.
  Providing incentives that recognize and reward banks for community development activities
 in rural and other underserved areas ensures that these communities will continue to benefit
 from the vital support that flows from the banking industry.

 7) Create Structures and Incentives for Banks to Pursue Community Development
 Activities Based on Their Specific Goals and Objectives

 The final rule should preserve flexibility for banks with unique business models. For example,
 the Agencies should strengthen alternatives such as the strategic plan option by
 grandfathering existing plans and ensuring consistent examiner support. The rule should also
 preserve the wholesale and limited purpose designations and avoid changes that would
 subject these institutions to retail-focused examination frameworks that do not reflect their
 operations.

 The proposed adjustments to the CRA asset classifications should not become default
 designations that may inadvertently alter or limit the community development activities
 banks undertake in response to market-specific opportunities, portfolio goals, or other
 strategic objectives. Although the proposed changes, if adopted, will likely prompt some
 institutions to revise their CRA-oriented policies and procedures, others may choose to
 maintain their current approach. The final rule should therefore provide greater clarity
 regarding examinations of Small and Intermediate Banks and should permit--or even
 incentivize--Small Banks to elect evaluation under the Intermediate Bank framework when
 doing so aligns with past practice or future business objectives.

Centrant appreciates the Agencies' willingness to consider these comments and their broader effort
to ensure that the CRA framework continues to fulfill its statutory purpose. A balanced approach to
CRA reform will provide the financial industry with the clarity and consistency it needs to operate
effectively while creating new incentives to strengthen partnerships and protect the community
development outcomes made possible through CRA-related activities over the past five decades.

We would welcome the opportunity to discuss these comments further and to provide any other data
or perspective from our experience financing affordable housing across the Southeast that may assist
the Agencies as they finalize this rulemaking effort.

Sincerely,

David R. Bennett
President
Centrant Community Capital, Inc.

October 13, 2026

Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
550 17th Street NW 400 7th Street SW
Washington, DC 20429 Washington, DC 20219

RE: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
 FDIC: RIN 3064-AG31
 OCC: Docket ID OCC-2026-0694

To the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and Office of Comptroller of the Currency:

Thank you for this opportunity to comment on the proposed amendments to the implementing
regulations for the Community Reinvestment Act of 1977 issued in the joint Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking (NPR).

Introduction

The undersigned organizations are part of the Illinois CRA Coalition, a group dedicated to
protecting and strengthening the federal Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) as a tool for
community development. We believe that the proposed rules fail to conform to the legislative
intent of the CRA and also fail to fulfill the agencies' stated justifications for updating the
implementing regulations.

As indicated in the NPR, the FDIC and the OCC have proposed changes to the CRA to
supposedly reduce regulatory burden, improve clarity, and better align with the statute. With
respect to both improving clarity and reducing regulatory burden, the absence of the Federal
Reserve Board of Governors from the NPR will serve to only increase the lack of clarity and
increase burden on stakeholders if the rules are implemented as proposed. Creating two distinct
regulatory frameworks for the CRA would establish different standards governing how financial
institutions meet their CRA obligations in the communities they serve and make community
oversight, an integral part of CRA enforcement, more difficult.

With respect to the statutory alignment, as noted by the agencies in the NPR, the CRA was
enacted because financial institutions have a "continuing and affirmative obligation" to meet the
 credit needs of the communities where they operate. The law then placed a requirement on the
Federal financial supervisory agencies to examine those financial institutions. These two
provisions place responsibility for implementing and enforcing the CRA on regulated financial
institutions and their supervising agencies. These proposed regulations, as noted multiple times
by the agencies, seek to reduce that burden, but disregard the potential impact on the
communities the CRA is intended to support.

In the NPR, the agencies are quite clear on the positive impact these rule changes will have on
regulated financial institutions and identify the areas in which administrative burdens and
compliance costs are expected to decrease. However, as noted above, the purpose of the CRA is
to ensure that financial institutions serve the needs of the communities where they do business,
and the NPR does not include the same clarity on how the rules will impact those communities.
Throughout the NPR, the agencies point to supervisory experience to justify their proposed
changes, but fail to cite supporting evidence. The Economic Analysis sections include express
language acknowledging that neither the OCC nor the FDIC can determine the direction or the
magnitude of the impact that the proposed changes will have on "LMI communities, small
business, small farms, nonprofit organizations, and other community development stakeholders,"
essentially all of the stakeholders the CRA was enacted to benefit. Given this lack of clarity and
understanding, we strongly urge the agencies to delay any changes to the CRA until they can
conduct a thorough analysis of the potential impacts of the proposed changes on the communities
the CRA is intended to serve. Only then could the agencies accurately assess whether the
proposed rules would in fact align with the intent of the statute.

The remainder of this letter will focus on three broad areas within the reform proposal that
further demonstrate the proposal's lack of alignment with the purpose and intent of the CRA: (1)
changes to entity size thresholds; (2) impacts on community development activity; and (3)
impacts on state CRA frameworks and the Illinois Community Reinvestment Act.

Changes to Entity Size Thresholds

Under the CRA, larger banks get more extensive exams that come with higher standards for
community development activity in particular. Large banks (currently at least $1.6 billion in
assets) are examined on both their community development lending and community
development investments, while intermediate small banks (currently between $416 million and
$1.6 billion in assets) are evaluated under a general community development test that combines
lending and investment activity. Size thresholds are adjusted modestly each year to account for
inflation.

The proposed rule would make drastic changes to the size thresholds that would disrupt the
community development activity that communities across the country have come to rely on from
large and intermediate banks. Raising the large bank threshold to over $10 billion in assets and
the medium (aka intermediate) bank threshold to over $1 billion in assets, as proposed by the
OCC and FDIC, would have grave consequences for Illinois communities. Illinois is currently
served by 171 banks that fall in the intermediate or large categories, triggering community
development obligations. Should this proposed rule go into effect, 68 of those banks, or 39.8% of
them, will be bumped down to the small category and will lose their community development
obligations. Out of the 81 banks currently classified as large banks in Illinois, 50 of them would
 drop down to medium and see their community development requirements severely lightened.
Banks moving down a size category are disproportionately located in rural areas of Illinois,
meaning that rural communities will lose access to a crucial tool for holding banks accountable
to serving unique local needs.

Community development investment and lending activities include a wide range of financial
supports. Investments in nonprofit lenders like community development financial institutions
(CDFIs) can provide affordable mortgage loans to LMI borrowers, provide a key piece of
financing for an affordable housing development, or provide affordable credit products to the
small businesses that fuel local economies. Banks often get CRA credit for investing in
developments that utilize Low Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) or New Markets Tax Credit
(NMTC) funding, or for purchasing municipal bonds that support affordable housing programs.
Banks also get CRA credit for offering grants to nonprofits that provide financial education
programming to communities to help families budget, save, and build wealth. At an even more
detailed level, the community development tests under the CRA reward banks for innovative
activities that are especially responsive to unique, local community needs.

All of those activities are essential to building thriving communities that empower low- and
moderate-income consumers to prosper. This proposed rule drastically lowers the bar for what
banks must do to make that happen.

Further, only large banks must report data on their small business lending activity under the
CRA. Data on small business lending is thin already, section 1071 of the Dodd-Frank Act has yet
to be implemented, which means informed policymaking is made all the more difficult by a lack
of publicly available small business lending data. The small business lending data that banks
report under the CRA, while not nearly as detailed as Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA)
data or the data that would be collected under Section 1071, is the best that we currently have
access to. The change in threshold defining large banks mean that we would lose the data
reported by the 50 large banks operating in Illinois that would drop into the medium size
category, leaving only 31 large OCC- and FDIC-regulated banks that are obligated to report this
crucial data. It furthers CRA's purpose and is in the general public interest to know exactly how
many dollars are being used for small business lending, how effectively certain banks are using
their dollars to invest in the communities they serve, and which communities are in need of more
small business investment. Effective policymaking is informed by comprehensive data. Not
collecting data does not mean that the realities reflected by the data cease to exist.

Impacts on Community Development Activity

In addition to reducing the number of banks subject to community development requirements, as
discussed above, the NPR includes proposals to reduce the importance of community
development activities in the CRA exam process, change how community development activities
are considered, and restrict eligibility for community development grants, all of which create
incentives for financial institutions to reduce the resources they direct to local communities.
Specifically, the FDIC and OCC propose to remove the requirement that intermediate banks
receive at least a "satisfactory" rating on both their lending and community development tests to
receive an overall rating of "satisfactory." As discussed in greater detail below, the NPR also
establishes minimum standards for community development activity that are substantially below
 the current levels of activity performed by financial institutions. Taken together, these changes
would reduce both the incentives for financial institutions to engage in community development
and the resources available to organizations and communities that rely on CRA activity. The
following sections illustrate these impacts through the proposed changes affecting CDFIs,
community development grants, and community development performance expectations.

 Impact on CDFIs

Since the inception of the CDFI designation in 1994, these institutions have played a pivotal role
in helping banks fulfill the intent of the CRA, to eradicate redlining and ensure that banks were
investing equitably in all the communities that they serve. According to analysis by the CDFI
Coalition, banks provide $15$25 billion to CDFIs annually in loans, deposits, and equity-
equivalent investment1. This sizeable investment is not made out of charity but is driven, in large
part, by the CRA and the proven efficacy of these institutions in doing something that these
financial institutions have long struggled with, driving capital into the historically underserved
communities that are hardest for traditional financial institutions to reach within their assessment
areas. CDFIs are experts in turning these bank dollars into catalysts for the creation of small
businesses, affordable housing, cornerstone community facilities like schools, healthcare centers,
and cultural museums, grocery stores, and farms, to name a few examples, typically in areas
where these projects often mark major community milestones.

The work of CDFIs has been particularly impactful in Illinois. From 2005 to 2021, CDFIs
poured over $4.52 billion into undercapitalized Illinois neighborhoods, which created almost
100,000 jobs, developed over 60,100 affordable homes, and supported nearly 12,000 small and
micro businesses statewide. In that same timeframe, the need for CDFIs has continued to grow
with lending increasing annually by an average of 25%. But all of this progress is threatened to
be upended by this proposed rule. The proposed changes to CRA asset thresholds, restrictions on
bank grantmaking activity, and the devaluation of the community development test, among many
other critical components, all create a chilling environment for bank investment in historically
marginalized neighborhoods.

CDFI activity, through both technical assistance and lending, is a lynchpin for community
stabilization and revitalization. Through their ability to leverage $8 in private sector investment
for every $1 they receive in public funding, CDFIs are sought-after partners for community
development initiatives at the state, local, and federal levels. Loosening the obligation that banks
have to partner with CDFIs not only reduces the dollars that flow to economically depressed
communities and undermines the intent of the CRA, but it also diminishes the leverage ratio that
is critical to making government programs work, including the New Markets Tax Credit and the
Opportunity Zones programs that were made permanent this year by this administration. It also
harms competitiveness for other programs like the Capital Magnet Fund which require a set level
of public and private sector partnership. All of which serves to disrupt stated goals by President
Trump to spur economic mobility and affordable housing supply growth. It also creates
unnecessary uncertainty in a regulatory environment that is in need of greater stability to thrive.

1 h#ps://cdfi.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/khic22.pdf
  Community Development Grants and Donations

In the NPR, the agencies propose two new restrictions on the CRA eligibility of community
development grants and donations: first, that grants made by regulated financial institutions are
"directly used by the recipient for a program, project, or initiative with a primary purpose of
community development," and second, for large banks, that they ensure that no more than 15
percent of a grant or donation goes to a recipient's indirect or administrative costs.

These proposals fundamentally misunderstand the role that nonprofit organizations play to
support community development initiatives and act as critical partners for banks in their efforts
to meet their community needs and CRA goals. The current standard, which makes grants and
donations eligible for CRA consideration when the receiving nonprofit organization and its
activities have a primary purpose of community development, already ensures that resources are
directed to organizations serving underserved communities, especially LMI individuals and
households, small businesses, and small farms. Nonprofit organizations also have their own
incentives to ensure they are responsible stewards of all funds received, including programmatic
and financial reporting requirements.

The agencies express concern about alleged "rent extraction," through the diversion of funds
from local communities, and the allocation of resources to "middlemen," although they fail to
provide any supporting data for these allegations. Nonprofit organizations with a mission of
community development are focused on building the economic resources of the communities
they serve, not pulling resources from those communities for profit. In contrast to the agencies'
characterization, nonprofits, including organizations that do not provide direct services, are
members of the communities they serve, as are their staff. While the agencies express an interest
in directing funds away from "middlemen," the organizations that would fit this description are
offering services and playing a role in the community that the financial institutions do not,
including CDFIs as described above. Their role as so-called "middlemen" between financial
institutions and LMI communities, small business, small farms, and other nonprofit organizations
is not extractive, it is a critical piece of the puzzle in deploying CRA eligible funds. So-called
"indirect service" nonprofits not only pass funds through to direct service organizations, but also
administer programs to build the capacity of direct service organizations and provide
administrative support for resource development, program compliance, and technical assistance,
all of which reduces downstream costs.

Although the NPR focuses heavily on reducing regulatory burden for financial institutions, these
changes would actually increase reporting burdens for them, as well as on nonprofits that serve
the communities the CRA was enacted to benefit. In the end, fewer resources will reach
underserved communities, undermining a key purpose of the CRA.

The increased restrictions and regulatory burden associated with these proposed changes would
shift CRA activity away from community development grants, reducing a critical source of
flexible funding for community development nonprofits. This would directly reduce the
resources reaching local communities and could destabilize organizations that provide both direct
and support services. It would also undermine the effectiveness of other funding sources by
limiting nonprofits' ability to maintain the organizational infrastructure necessary to deploy those
resources effectively. The FDIC and OCC acknowledge this possibility in their Economic
 Analysis but do not give it proper weight. Given the likely impact of these changes and the lack
of analysis conducted by the agencies regarding their effects on communities and nonprofit
organizations, we urge the agencies to retain the current eligibility standards for community
development grants and donations.

 Community Development Performance Expectations

This proposed rule would also lower expectations for Satisfactory performance for the large
banks that will still be obligated to provide full scope community development lending and
investment under the FDIC's and OCC's version of the CRA. Currently, banks can get CRA
consideration for community development activities that do not fit neatly within their assessment
areas. This proposed rule maintains that practice and formalizes standards for how much banks
must do within their assessment areas before the regulators will consider their activity outside
those assessment areas implicitly establishing a presumptive Satisfactory level for inside
assessment area activity. Under the proposed rule, a large bank would need to invest only
0.625% of Tier 1 capital in community development grants and investments and 0.625% in
community development lending to avoid a failing rating.

There is ample evidence that the percentages of Tier 1 capital that the proposed rule uses to set
that presumptive Satisfactory level are too low they are well below current average
performance for banks and they are lower than the percentages that the OCC used for their recent
rulemaking regarding strategic plans (which were also too low). Even the OCC's proposed rule
on a "Simplified Strategic Plan Process for Community Banks," that set sample "elective goals"
for banks considering CRA strategic plans did not set the benchmarks as low as this proposed
rule. The strategic plan proposal stated that 3% of Tier 1 capital invested in community
development lending would be an appropriate Satisfactory goal for a larger bank. According to
analysis by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) of the 69 largest banks
regulated by the OCC and FDIC, the median amount of Tier 1 capital dedicated to community
development lending was 6.83%; for community development grants and investments, the
median was 3.58%. Setting a minimum threshold, especially one so far below the current norm,
will inevitably result in a race to the bottom among banks, stripping communities of these
essential investments.

Impacts on State CRA Frameworks and the Illinois CRA

In recent years, states across the country have enacted state level CRAs. These regulatory
frameworks are designed to supplement the federal CRA without adding undue burden to
financial institutions. The Illinois CRA, for example, was written to align with the federal rules
where possible, specifically, through alignment of the entity size thresholds and consistency in
the scope and intent of the performance tests. By holding other major players in the mortgage
lending industry, such as nonbank mortgage companies, to similar standards as banks, the Illinois
CRA and other states' CRAs even benefit banks by leveling the regulatory playing field. Lack of
alignment among the federal banking regulators and movement away from the purpose of the
CRA, which create their own concerns as discussed above, will have downstream effects with
state regulations, including the Illinois CRA, creating further confusion and increased regulatory
burden for communities and covered financial institutions.
 This confusion is compounded by the absence of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors from
the NPR, which will extend to the Illinois CRA. Under the current Illinois CRA framework, the
state's entity-size thresholds align with the federal standards, meaning that an institution's
classification under the Illinois CRA will correspond with its classification under the applicable
federal regulatory framework. As a result, if the proposals in the NPR are implemented, similarly
situated state-chartered banks will face different regulatory standards depending on which federal
regulator supervises the institution. However, if Illinois updates its rule to establish a single
entity-size standard while the federal regulators maintain different thresholds, financial
institutions could be categorized differently under state and federal law. This would increase
regulatory burden as financial institutions monitor and respond to two separate standards and
could create further confusion for other CRA stakeholders. Banks are already being examined
under the Illinois CRA, and other states, like Massachusetts, have had state CRAs in place for
decades. This NPR would throw these state laws into disarray.

Similarly, the changes proposed in the NPR to the performance tests, specifically as they relate to
community development, depart significantly from the purpose of the CRA such that they would
no longer align with performance tests under the Illinois CRA. This again will increase the
regulatory burden by creating two standards for what activities are CRA eligible, increasing the
costs for financial institutions and making CRA engagement more difficult for local
communities.

While the agencies are not directly responsible for state regulatory frameworks, they should be
aware of the increased burden and reduced clarity their proposed changes will create given the
lack of consistency among the federal banking regulators and their movement away from the
language and intent of the CRA. Based on these likely outcomes, we urge the agencies to retain
the current entity size thresholds and performance tests.

Conclusion

Thank you again for the opportunity to comment on this rulemaking. Based on the issues
presented above, we ask that the agencies rescind the NPR and refrain from moving forward with
any changes to the CRA at this time. The changes proposed by the FDIC and OCC are not in
alignment with the statutory language or the legislative intent of the CRA and do not satisfy the
justifications identified by the agencies for the rulemaking. We believe all three federal banking
agencies must be aligned, and these two agencies should not move forward with changes that
increase uncertainty and burden for community stakeholders without first conducting the
necessary review and analysis to understand their potential impacts, particularly when the
proposed changes have not been demonstrated to advance the CRA's statutory purpose.

Sincerely,

Varo Bank, N.A. ("Varo") appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Notice of

V aro Bank is the first all-digital, de novo, U.S. national consumer bank built from the
g round up, designed to make financial inclusion and opportunity a reality for all. Varo
B ank is headquartered in Draper, Utah with offices in San Francisco, California,
C harlotte, North Carolina and New York. The OCC is our primary regulator. Varo
M oney, Inc., the parent company of Varo Bank, is a bank holding company that is
regulated by the Federal Reserve.

V aro reimagines the modern banking experience by providing customers with the tools
they need to build financial resilience and realize their financial power. Products such as
V aro Believe, a secured card, help our customers build their credit profile. Varo Advance
h elps them stretch hard-earned dollars between paychecks on affordable terms. Varo
L ine of Credit allows qualifying customers to access cash when needed through a
straightforward and user-friendly borrowing experience without the hidden fees,
complicated terms, or accumulating interest of other personal loans. We also offer the
ability to earn cashback at thousands of merchant locations nationwide. Our automated

 11781 South Lone Peak Parkway, Suite 150, Draper, UT 84020
 savings features, Save Your Pay and Save Your Change, help our customers utilize our
high yield savings account. In all, we are committed to helping our customers achieve
greater financial stability and a path toward building wealth.

Everything Varo does is tied to our mission of helping customers find financial
resilience--a mission that is consistent with the purpose of CRA. As an inclusive,
mission oriented de novo bank chartered by the OCC, and a digital-only bank currently
operating in all 50 states, we are in a unique position to offer our thoughts on a few key
areas of this CRA proposal.

Geographic Flexibility
As a digital bank with customers in all 50 states, Varo provides financial products,
education, and service to individuals in communities across the country, and is not tied
to any particular physical location. We employ individuals across the country who often
join Varo for its mission and strong culture of volunteerism. In addition to providing CRA
s ervice in our assessment areas, Varo provides eight hours of paid volunteer time each
q uarter for employees to serve and make an impact in their own communities. This
s ervice is especially important because many communities are CRA deserts that receive
little CRA activity due to the technicalities of assessment area determinations, a
c hallenge the agencies acknowledge in the proposal. This problem may be exacerbated
u nder the methodology proposed for allocating community development activities to
p articular assessment areas--which are often already "CRA hotspots." Instead, Varo

d evelopment activities conducted nationwide. This approach would result in banks
h elping meet the needs of low- and moderate-income (LMI) individuals in more

Product Diversity Metrics
Under the proposed rule, all categories of consumer lending would be aggregated for
evaluation when consumer lending constitutes a major product line for a bank. This
aggregation may skew the picture of a bank's performance through its individual
products and may not result in a clear and meaningful metric of comparison across

accommodating business models that do not fit within the standard CRA framework.

 emphasize its importance. In response to Question 59, we also recommend that
e xisting CRA Strategic Plans be grandfathered in until the expiration of their term.

Conclusion
Varo Bank is an ardent supporter of a strong CRA, and we appreciate the agencies'
efforts to modernize its implementation. In the interest of all communities and the banks
that serve them, CRA regulations must be durable, stable, and certain. Thank you for

To: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC). Re: Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57 — Community Reinvestment Act Regulations (91 FR 52114, Aug. 12, 2026). Full comment attached.

This comment takes no position on the proposed thresholds, the major-product-line approach, deposit services, the grant provisions, strategic plans, or any other substantive choice in the proposed rule. It asks how the agencies will learn which way the rule's effects went.

I am a member of the public with no financial interest in any bank, holding company, trade association, community development organization, or grant recipient, and I am employed by none of them. This comment was prepared after reading the proposed rule and all 161 comments posted to this docket as of October 9, 2026, with their attachments. Where existing practice already supplies what a request asks, saying so would answer it.

Four features of the proposed rule deserve credit. It says what it does not know: the effects on communities "are uncertain" in direction and magnitude. It names five ways they could go wrong (Table 4). It proposes to standardize the community development records that reported aggregates do not supply, and to publish grant information. And it contemplates a later look at one threshold, "if warranted." Each stops one step short. The first Table 4 channel is the agencies' own: "less standardized CRA data for banks that would no longer be evaluated as large banks," 126 OCC-supervised and 250 FDIC-supervised large banks by the analyses. The proposed rule does not say how the agencies will see the five effects for those banks, or when they will say so. Three commenters come close: one asks for "a mechanism to assess this return on regulatory investment after implementation" (0031); one would keep intermediate-bank data so the agencies can "assess the impact of any future changes" (0143); one asks of every reporting cut, "What will we no longer be able to know?" (0092). None names an interval, a place, or a baseline.

Request 1 — Say how the agencies will know which way the uncertain effects went. For each Table 4 channel, state which reported data or examination records the agencies expect to use, what banks and period they cover, and what they cannot show, distinguishing what is reported from what is seen only at examination. For reclassified banks, say which sources remain (performance evaluations, HMDA, Call Report Schedule RC-C Part II, section 1071 data when available) and what will no longer be visible. If existing supervisory data are sufficient, say so and say which.

Request 2 — Publish the comparison, by tier and for the reclassified banks, at a stated interval, in a place the agencies already use. Follow the banks reclassified at implementation as a group. Elements, each with source and coverage stated: reported CD loan totals and grant fields, with investment information from examinations summarized by examination period; CRA small business and small farm lending where still reported; mortgage lending shares in LMI areas for HMDA-reporting banks; bank counts by tier; and the agencies' best account of burden relief and transition costs, estimates told apart from experience. Baseline: the year before the effective date where comparable data exist, otherwise the first usable period. Favorable, adverse, and inconclusive results with equal prominence; missing information named and the rest published.

Request 3 — Say what findings would prompt a second look in either direction, and set a first checkpoint. Examples: grants or loans to nonprofits falling in reclassified banks' assessment areas, or LMI lending shares falling against the baseline; or activity holding at or above the baseline beside burden relief, which could support further threshold changes (reliance on section 1071 data is a separate decision needing its own assessment). Three years after the effective date, publish a first assessment with its coverage stated, say whether it supports a next step or leaving the rule as adopted, and if coverage is too thin, say what is unresolved and set the next date. No threshold and no automatic action is requested.

Request 4 — State the experience the grant provision rests on. The preamble illustrates the 15 percent limit with one grant of which "Approximately 25 percent" went to internal expenses. State what the examination record shows about how common that case is, with banks, period, and calculation base, or state that no aggregate exists and what the proposed records could and could not show later; the reported recipient, address, and amount would not by themselves show it.

These requests do not ask the agencies to change any provision, delay the rule, or add data requirements. I ask that the final rule state the agencies' disposition of each numbered request and, for any request not adopted, the reason. The attachment contains the full comment, sources, and a table of what each request would require.

 I. Background

 Banks enjoy a special status in the American financial system and, accordingly, receive
special privileges. First, bank deposits are insured by the FDIC. Without this, depositors would
demand higher rates to compensate for the risk of losing their deposits or almost certainly pull
their deposits out altogether in times of stress, causing bank runs, failures, contagion, and
financial crises. Second, banks with a federal charter benefit from the preemption of state laws,
which allows them to avoid certain state laws such as interest caps and consumer protections
where they are more stringent than federal standards. Even banks with state charters enjoy
special treatment within their chartered state that other corporations do not. Third, banks have
access to special services from the Federal Reserve System in its role as the country's central
bank. Specifically, banks have access to central bank deposit accounts on which banks earn
interest, national payments systems that allow for banks to easily and cheaply transfer
funds, and access to central bank lending and liquidity facilities that provide a government-
supplied source of funding when the private sector fails to do so. Additionally, the largest
banks make substantial profits from the financial transactions conducted with the Treasury and
Federal Reserve as well as benefit from the ultimate backstop: a virtual guarantee that if they
come to the brink of failure, they will be bailed out by the U.S. taxpayer.7

 Banks are afforded these privileges because they are foundational to the functioning and
growth of the economy. While they provide payments and other financial services that greatly
improve the efficiency of economic activity, their most important contribution is the provision of
affordable credit to borrowers across the economic spectrum by lending out deposits, which are
the cheapest major source of funding in the financial system. That credit fuels the economy,
creates jobs, and enables wealth creation, thereby improving financial well-being and making the
American Dream widely available. That credit is used for everything from personal purchases
such as groceries or other day-to-day necessities to home purchases, which for many people is
the most significant source of wealth. It is also used to fund the creation and continuation of
businesses small and large that provide employment and serve as a source of wealth for business
owners. Simply put, it is nearly impossible to achieve any measure of economic success without
banks.

 Unfortunately, the access to or cost of banking products and services has never been fair
or equal in America. Congress passed the CRA in 1977 for the purpose of addressing that fact
and to ensure that banks fulfill the public purpose that justifies their many privileges--i.e., to
provide all Americans, especially those that are economically marginalized, the opportunities
that access to credit, banking, and the broader financial system afford. The CRA essentially
requires the Agencies to evaluate a bank's records of meeting the needs of the communities they
serve, especially low- and moderate-income ("LMI") individuals and businesses within those
communities. Congress was explicit that "the convenience and needs of communities include the

 II. The Proposal Has a Fatal Procedural Defect by Modifying the 1995 CRA
 Regulations (which are not currently in effect)

 The Proposal has a fatal procedural defect. It purports to modify the 1995 CRA
regulations as if those rules are currently operative. However, they are not. The 2023 CRA
regulations are the version of the CRA rules currently in the Code of Federal Regulations. The
OCC and FDIC may not disregard them until they have been rescinded.16

 An existing regulation may be rescinded either by way of a standard notice-and-comment
rulemaking, Fox TV, 556 U.S. 502, or by judicial vacatur in a contested proceeding.17 But the
OCC and FDIC admit directly that they have completed neither step to rescind the 2023 CRA
Regulations. First, the Agencies issued a proposal in 2025 to rescind the 2023 CRA Regulations
but "decided not to finalize the rescission proposal but to issue this new proposal instead."18

 Second, no court has vacated the 2023 CRA regulations, and the case that remains is no
longer a proceeding where vacatur can be obtained since it is no longer adversarial. The OCC
and FDIC note that they "are now moving the District Court for the entry of a final judgment
against them" with the consent of the trade associations that challenged them regarding the 2023

 III. The Current CRA Framework Fails to Meet the Goals of the CRA

 As Better Markets has repeatedly emphasized,21 the current CRA framework is a failure
and therefore is a poor benchmark and starting point for the Proposal. Congress imposed a
continuing and affirmative obligation on banks to help meet their communities' credit needs and
directed the banking agencies to assess their performance across their entire communities,
including LMI neighborhoods. The Agencies' ongoing statutory responsibility is to make that
obligation effective. Weakening an already woefully inadequate framework--as the Proposal
would do--is inconsistent with that responsibility.

 The existing framework remains largely rooted in rules adopted in 1995. Its age alone
does not establish its inadequacy. The primary issue has been and remains that the framework
fails to capture whether banks are serving their communities in the way intended by the CRA.
Indeed, as discussed above, it is clear that many banks, especially the largest banks, are not
serving the needs of their communities and yet are still passing CRA assessments. Beyond that,
the age of the rules does play a role in their failure in that the banking system has changed
materially since then, and the current framework fails to account for those changes. Most
importantly, a bank's physical footprint no longer fully describes its lending relationships. When
a bank conducts substantial business in a community without maintaining a branch there, an
evaluation centered on physical facilities risks overlooking that community's experience. Current
gaps in the framework must be closed, not entrenched.

 The framework must also distinguish between a bank's business priorities and the needs
of its community. In other words, the community should define its own needs through demand
rather than the banks in that community defining it through curated supply. Types of lending that
represent only a modest share of a bank's business may be critically important to local
households, small businesses, or farms. An effective CRA evaluation must examine whether the
bank responds to those needs, rather than allow the bank's preferred business model to define the
limits of the assessment. Otherwise, the evaluation implicitly rewards banks for the activities
they already choose to pursue while overlooking the true community needs banks neglect. For
example, the proposed change to limit the lending test to only a bank's two most material
business lines would do exactly that.

 Meaningful accountability also requires adequate information and consequences for poor
performance. Examiners and the public need to understand where credit is flowing, which
borrowers are being served, and whether community development activity responds to local
needs. Narrower examinations and reduced reporting can make those questions harder to answer.
Satisfactory ratings should reflect satisfactory performance.

 The agencies should therefore begin with an assessment of where the current framework
falls short and how to correct those shortcomings. Instead, the Proposal simply uses the current
framework and would raise asset thresholds and narrow the activities subject to review, among
other highly problematic changes that weaken the current framework. Making an inadequate
framework less demanding does not make it more effective. The proper measure of reform is
whether it strengthens banks' responsiveness to community needs for credit and banking
services.

 More specifically, the current framework allows for too much examiner discretion
throughout the assessment process and too little measurement, transparency, and oversight.
Although examiners utilize some quantitative metrics in certain areas of the assessment process,
most notably in the so-called lending test, there are no defined rules or thresholds that map from
quantitative metrics to assessment conclusions, defying replication and measurability and

promote obfuscation and maximization of bank assessment ratings. Assessments under the CRA
rule must be more meaningful and effective by making them quantitative, transparent, and
