 IX. Conclusion

 The CRA was enacted by Congress because banks took deposits from communities and
declined to lend in them. Fifty years later, the lowest-income Americans own homes at a lower
rate than they did then, banks are withdrawing from the lending the statute covers, and the
Agencies rate nearly every bank a success. That is the underwhelming record the Proposal
should have started from.

 Instead, the Proposal starts from the perspective of the CRA's "burden" on banks and
works backward, removing evaluation from hundreds of institutions, narrowing what the
remaining ones are examined on, striking deposit services, capping community development
grants, setting the community development bar at the floor, and eliminating the data that would
show any of it. It offers no evidence that any change will help a single LMI household, and it
asks a court to make sure the Agencies never have to revisit the questions the statute poses.

 The Agencies should withdraw the Proposal. If they want to modernize the CRA, they
should start with an empirical assessment of how the CRA has performed and attempt to address
the clear deficiencies in the lack of credit in the communities the CRA was designed to help. The
communities the CRA was written for have waited long enough.

 Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

 Family Promise of Philadelphia submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
 referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit
 Insurance Corporation (FDIC) because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).

 We also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely
 consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis
 and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60
 days.

 Our mission is to end family homelessness through direct aid, direct service and advocacy. Since 1991 our
 organization has provided temporary shelter, transitional housing, eviction prevention and shelter diversion for
 children and families.

 The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change how regulators
 evaluate community development, bank services and support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that
 these changes are being considered without adequate analysis of their impact on low- and moderate-income
 communities that have experienced discrimination and disinvestment.

FAMILY PROMISE OF PHILADELPHIA
formerly Philadelphia Interfaith Hospitality Network PIHN
7047 Germantown Ave, Phila, PA 19119
TEL: (215) 247 4663 WEB: www.familypromisephl.org
  To do our work we depend heavily on donors. Among our most important supporters are banks, for which CRA
 provides an important incentive to be community partners, as well as financial investors. In particular, bank
 support helped 131 families avert eviction in 2025, saving the City an estimated $100,000 in shelter costs.

 It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet the needs of communities like ours. Before
 finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce lending, services or
 investment available to low- and moderate-income communities and whether communities that have
 experienced historic discrimination or disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.

 We are especially concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and nonprofit
 organizations. The change threatens bank support for affordable housing, small-business development, financial
 counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based services through
 grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations. These resources can be particularly
 important to local organizations that have deep relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of
 their communities.

 For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and new
 documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations. Smaller
 organizations like ours have fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs. Like many
 community-based nonprofits we operate with limited staff and may not maintain documentation in the precise
 format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations like
 ours are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger organizations whose
 activities are easier to verify.

 Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and partnerships can play in
 supporting community development. One of our bank partners brings bank officers to teach financial literacy,
 and coach families struggling to sustain safe housing.

 Our organization believes that the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its
 impacts is prepared and released for public comment. We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment
 period to a total of at least 120 days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
 significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit
 grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
 An extension would allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather
 examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more complete record on which to
 base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at
 least 60 days.

 Sincerely,
 Robert Byrne, Executive Director

asset thresholds, tailoring evaluations to business models, and replacing ambiguous guidance with
clearer standards. We offer the following recommendations so that improved clarity does not come
at the expense of the flexibility that made the 1995 framework successful.

I. Principles for a Successful Final Rule
The final rule should be built to last. CRA reforms are most durable when developed on an
interagency basis, adhere closely to the statute, and avoid rigid or overly complicated requirements.
The agencies should continue tailoring performance tests to bank types and business models and
be cautious about relying on metrics and comparative measures. Because changes to one part of
the framework often affect how others operate, the agencies should weigh the proposal's
cumulative effect, not just each change in isolation, and provide an appropriate transition.

II. CRA Regulation Should Reflect the Diversity of the Banking System
Thresholds. We support raising the Small and Intermediate Bank thresholds to $1 billion and $10
billion, respectively, and recommend indexing them to Gross Domestic Product so they keep pace
with industry growth rather than consumer prices alone.

Comparative data. Banks moving from the Large to the Intermediate category are accustomed to
examinations that rely on market-share and peer data. The agencies should explain when
comparative information may be considered, how similarly situated lenders would be identified, and
how much weight it would receive. The current Small and Intermediate Small Bank procedures are
 the right model: peer information informs performance context but is not an independent measure of
performance. The statute asks whether a bank helps meet its communities' credit needs, not
whether it outperforms other lenders. Examination procedures and training should make clear that
Large Bank CRA data will not be used to evaluate Intermediate Banks.

Strategic plans. We support making strategic plans more usable. The final rule should expressly
permit combining community development loans and investments in a single goal, allow carry-
forward of excess community development performance, grandfather existing plans, provide out-of-
assessment-area credit for plan banks rated Satisfactory or better, and support examiner training
on plan review.

III. Focus Retail Lending Evaluations on Material Lending Activities
We support evaluating banks on their major product lines and favor Option 1, which determines
those lines at the bank level using both loan count and dollar volume. This approach is predictable,
allows banks to monitor their position during the evaluation period, ensures consistent treatment
across assessment areas, and largely codifies existing practice.

We urge the agencies to retain the existing "substantial majority" standard for consumer lending
rather than the proposed 50 percent threshold. The proposal does not explain why the longstanding
standard should be replaced or show that the added data burden would produce more meaningful
evaluations. Significant questions also remain unresolved. The preamble says consumer lending
would be evaluated in the aggregate, but the regulatory text does not; aggregating diverse products
could obscure performance differences and make ratings hard to replicate; standardized consumer
lending data and benchmarks are limited; it is unclear how borrower and geographic distribution
analysis would apply across product types; and indirect auto lending raises additional
complications. Until these issues are addressed, the current framework remains the better
approach.

IV. Community Development
Definitions. We support the proposed affordable housing standards of 30 percent of 80 percent of
AMI and, in high-cost areas, 30 percent of 120 percent of AMI. Banks should be able to
demonstrate high-cost conditions with objective data, including HUD Difficult Development Areas
and FHFA High Opportunity Areas, and later changes to an area's designation should not affect
credit for existing loans, investments, or binding commitments. The final rule should also recognize
financial education that benefits consumers across income levels, treat operating liquidity as
economic development, credit community-wide infrastructure projects, and recognize all FEMA
disaster designations as well as state-declared disasters.

Eligibility confirmation. The agencies should maintain a single, coordinated illustrative list of
qualifying activities and respond to advance confirmation requests within 30 days.

infrastructure to deliver services and should be eliminated. The agencies should rely on a bank's
reasonable assessment that funds serve a bona fide community development purpose and on
information already disclosed under the CRA Sunshine Act, rather than creating new compliance
requirements.

Long-term financing. We support counting prior-period loans and investments that remain on the
balance sheet. The final rule should also treat legally binding letters of credit and forward
commitments as community development loans and credit outstanding balances.

Multi-area activities. Banks should be permitted to use reasonable internal deposit-allocation

Community development data should remain a collection and maintenance requirement, and
community development grants should not be subject to public reporting. The agencies should not

disabilities. Our residents have an average annual household income of less than $20,000.

POAH appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed amendments to the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. We are concerned that several provisions would weaken
incentives for community development investment, particularly investment through the Low-Income
Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC). Established in 1986, LIHTC is the nation's largest source of equity for the
construction and preservation of affordable rental housing serving households with incomes generally at
or below 50 or 60 percent of area median income. In 2025, Congress expanded LIHTC by lowering the
bond-financing threshold for 4 percent credits and increasing allocations of 9 percent credits. As
Congress seeks to increase affordable housing production, CRA regulations should continue to provide
strong and reliable incentives for banks to invest in LIHTC-financed developments.

Negative Impacts on Community Development

Under the current regulations, banks with assets of at least $1.649 billion are evaluated as large banks
and are subject to a separate investment test. The proposal would raise the large-bank threshold to $10
billion and classify banks with assets from $1 billion to $10 billion as intermediate banks. This change
would substantially reduce the number of institutions subject to a separate investment test. According to

 the National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders, only 256 of the 642 banks currently classified
as large banks would retain that designation--a decline of more than 60 percent.

Banks reclassified as intermediate banks would no longer be evaluated under a separate investment test
that distinctly measures community development investments. Without that test, institutions are likely to
emphasize lending while reducing equity investments, since equity investments though much more
impactful tend to be more challenging to underwrite and execute. This effect could be especially
pronounced in smaller and rural communities currently located within the assessment areas of banks that
would be reclassified. Those communities could lose an important source of accountable, locally
focused community development investment.

Congress acted in 2026 to expand banks' capacity to make public welfare investments in order to
promote expanded investment in affordable housing. Reclassifying many banks as intermediate banks
and removing the separate investment test could reduce the incentive to use that additional capacity,
undermining the policy objective of encouraging greater investment in affordable housing and other
community development activities.

Negative Impacts on LIHTC

The LIHTC is responsible for nearly all of the affordable housing built and preserved in the US since the
program was authorized in 1986 a total of 4.3 million affordable housing units to date, providing
homes for roughly 9.6 million low-income Americans. And the CRA motivates the vast majority of
LIHTC investments: total Housing Credit investment reached $28.9 billion in 2024, an estimated 80%
or $23 billion of which came from banks motivated by CRA requirements.1

The effect of CRA on Housing Credit investment can be clearly seen in Housing Credit pricing, which
determines the amount of equity invested into Housing Credit financed affordable housing construction
or renovation projects. Housing Credit pricing can vary by $0.20 for each $1.00 of Housing Credit
between areas where CRA-driven demand is highest that is, where several major banks must meet
CRA Investment Test requirements and areas outside of banks' assessment areas where CRA-driven
demand is lowest.2 As a result, properties with the least CRA demand can receive 20% less equity for
the same amount of Housing Credits as properties with the highest CRA demand, rendering many
properties with low CRA demand financially infeasible. With such a significant portion of Housing
Credit investment impacted by CRA, our nation's ability to address the growing affordable housing
crisis is closely tied to CRA.

CRA Consideration for Community Development Grants

The proposal would also restrict CRA consideration for community development grants to local
nonprofit organizations. Under the current framework, nonprofit recipients may use grant funds for

administration, compliance, technology, and other operating functions are essential to successful
delivery. A rigid cap would force organizations to seek separate funding for necessary overhead,
diverting time and resources from community development work. The agencies should preserve
flexibility for banks to support reasonable operating costs when those costs are necessary to carry out
qualifying community development activities.

POAH appreciates the OCC's and FDIC's consideration of these comments. We would welcome the
opportunity to provide additional information regarding the role of CRA-motivated investment in
financing affordable rental housing.

Revise the proposed 15 percent indirect-cost limit. Indirect costs are shared expenses
required to operate programs and sustain the organization that houses them. For our

critical components of delivering services effectively, securely, and responsibly.

recipient's indirect costs exceed 15 percent. This hard limit could disqualify valuable
community development grants based solely on an organization's internal cost structure,
completely divorced from the actual value and impact of the work being funded. Indirect
costs support core functions like financial management, compliance, technology,
insurance, and facilities. These expenses weigh most heavily on smaller organizations,

 The Community Preservation Corporation (CPC) respectfully submits this comment in
response to the proposed revisions to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations
published at 91 FR 52114 (RIN 3064-AG31) (the proposed rule). CPC appreciates the
opportunity to engage on this important rulemaking and commends the Office of the Comptroller
of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) (together, "the
agencies") for their ongoing efforts to modernize and clarify CRA regulations.

 CPC is AA- rated by S&P and is one of the largest Community Development Financial
Institutions (CDFIs) in the nation solely focused on financing and investing in multifamily
housing. Since 1974, CPC has served as a bridge between private bank capital, public capital,
and communities in need of affordable housing and economic development. In its over 50-year
history, CPC has invested $16 billion dollars in furtherance of its mission and facilitated the
creation of 247,000 units of affordable housing

 As a financial partner to banks, developers, government agencies, and community
organizations, CPC is uniquely positioned to assess how regulatory changes affect the flow of
capital to affordable housing projects. Based on our practical experience, we offer these
comments with the shared goal of ensuring that the CRA continues to serve as a meaningful
vehicle for equitable investment, expanded housing supply, and affordability for all Americans.

 1
 The Affordable Housing Finance Ecosystem

 Affordable housing projects are not typically financed by any single source of capital.
Rather, projects rely on a carefully assembled combination of private debt, public subsidies,
equity, and grants drawn from multiple institutions operating at different scales and playing
complementary roles. This layered financing structure is a model for how affordable housing
gets built and preserved in the United States. At a time when the country has a national housing
supply shortage, this model should only be strengthened.

 In order to finance affordable housing projects, CPC works closely with government
partners and private financial institutions to create a blended capital stack that supports the future
cash flow of the property. We are often one of several parties in the capital stack, which consists
of construction and permanent debt, LIHTC or other equity, government subsidies, and other
capital, and are well versed in how the layers of capital can be structured to make a development
financially viable. This kind of financing depends on an active and engaged banking ecosystem.

 CPC relies significantly on bank capital to support our financing, and the banks we
partner with benefit from CRA credits for the work we do and the markets in which we lend.
Given our robust knowledge of the affordable housing finance ecosystem, CPC cautions the
agencies to carefully assess the aggregate, ecosystem-level impact of the proposed rule. In
particular, the proposed changes to bank size thresholds and investment requirements, discussed
in further detail below, could reduce community development incentives for many mid-sized
institutions. Even if the effect on any one bank may be relatively modest, the cumulative
withdrawal of engagement across this category of institutions could have a meaningful and
lasting impact on the supply of affordable housing capital.

 When bank participation contracts, the ecosystem does not simply adjust, transactions
fail, and we lose a number of the partners we need to do our work. Whether it is a large bank,
CDFI, or mid-sized lender, when an institution disengages in investing, replacement capital is
rarely available on equivalent terms, on the same timeline, or at all. In the affordable housing
sector, a financing gap of even a few million dollars can be fatal to a project.

Proposed Threshold Increases

 The proposed rule would substantially revise how banks are classified for CRA
examinations by increasing the asset thresholds for each category. It would reclassify "large
banks" as financial institutions with assets over $10 billion, up from the current threshold of
$1.649 billion. It would create a new "intermediate bank" category with an asset range of $1
billion $10 billion, which would replace the current "intermediate-small bank" category with
its asset range of $412 million $1.649 billion. Lastly, it would reclassify "small banks" as
banks with assets under $1 billion, up from the current threshold of $412 million. While we
appreciate the agencies' attempt to modernize decades-old thresholds, the proposed changes are

 2
 too sudden, too substantial, and could destabilize housing production and preservation at a
critical moment.

 The practical consequence of these threshold changes is straightforward: a large number
of banks that were previously subject to stronger CRA requirements would now fall into
categories with reduced obligations. According to a survey by the Affordable Housing Tax Credit
Coalition (AHTCC), banks under the $10 billion threshold play a particularly important role in
financing affordable housing in rural communities. AHTCC survey data show that approximately
one-third of Housing Credit equity investments from banks with under $10 billion in assets
supported rural markets, indicating that banks in this asset range play an outsized role in
investing in rural communities.

 CPC urges the agencies to consider whether both the "large bank" and "intermediate-
small bank" threshold levels are appropriately calibrated given the current banking landscape.
For CPC, increasing, not decreasing, the number of institutions from which we can access capital
is essential to our work. We therefore encourage the agencies to adopt lower thresholds for both
categories. In particular, the proposed alternative $3.252 billion threshold would be substantially
less disruptive than the proposed $10 billion "large bank" threshold or the even more damaging
$30 billion alternative threshold.

Meaningful Incentives

 Among the most consequential features of the current CRA framework is the investment
test, which requires qualifying institutions to demonstrate meaningful investment in LIHTC
transactions and other community development activities. This requirement has served as a
powerful and effective tool for directing private capital toward affordable housing and economic
development initiatives that might not otherwise attract bank investment.

 Under the proposed rule, banks in the new intermediate category would not be subject to
an investment test. CPC is concerned that eliminating this requirement for a broad range of
institutions, namely banks under $10 billion, could meaningfully suppress LIHTC and New
Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) investment activity. Reducing CRA incentives may also undercut
the investment Congress has recently made in the very financing tools that CRA-motivated bank
investment support. Expanding LIHTC in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and increasing the
Public Welfare Investment (PWI) cap in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act reflect the
judgment that more private capital, not less, must flow into affordable housing.

 The investment test has historically served as a catalyst for institutional engagement. In
our experience, banks subject to the investment test develop internal expertise in tax credit
investments and build long-term relationships with developers and intermediaries like CPC.
Eliminating the investment test could discourage these institutions from maintaining the
expertise they have built over many years. Moreover, CPC has sustained relationships with these
institutions, which has led to additional financing activity, both CRA-motivated and other. Over

 3
 time, shifting incentives could lead to the departure of institutions from these markets,
representing an erosion of market knowledge, institutional relationships, and transactional
capacity that would be difficult to rebuild.

 CPC strongly urges the agencies to retain a meaningful investment test for the
intermediate bank category. The investment test is a catalyst for community development
investment and removing it risks diminishing the very activity the CRA was designed to
encourage.
Conclusion

 CPC appreciates the work the agencies are doing to modernize and strengthen the CRA
regulations. However, we caution that this is not the moment to weaken CRA incentives.
Congress has invested in expanding LIHTC and raising the PWI cap to address a national
housing crisis. CDFIs, developers, and communities are ready to put that expanded capacity to
work, and need more partners to do so, not fewer. The CRA framework must ensure that bank
capital flows into the ecosystem to match.

 CPC urges the agencies to: (1) leave unchanged the "large bank" threshold or adopt the
$3.252 billion alternative threshold, and (2) maintain the investment test for banks under the
"large bank" threshold. We also urge the agencies to take seriously the ecosystem-level
consequences of reducing CRA incentives at a time when those incentives are most needed. We
remain committed to working constructively with the agencies toward a CRA framework that
supports housing creation and strengthens communities through capital investment, thereby
improving affordability for all Americans.
Respectfully submitted,
The Community Preservation Corporation

The National Association of Government Guaranteed Lenders (NAGGL) respectfully submits the attached comment letter regarding the proposed Community Reinvestment Act regulations (Docket ID OCC-2026-0694).

Please see the attached letter for NAGGL's full comments and recommendations.

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; 91 FR 52114 (August 12, 2026); OCC
Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; FDIC RIN 3064-AG31

To Whom It May Concern:

On behalf of the National Association of Government Guaranteed Lenders (NAGGL), we
appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's (OCC)
and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposed revisions to the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. We commend the agencies for thoughtfully reconsidering
the CRA framework to place greater emphasis on lending, recognize meaningful economic-
development activity, reduce unnecessary regulatory burdens, and provide greater clarity to
financial institutions working to meet the credit needs of their communities.

NAGGL is the national trade association representing lenders who originate approximately 93%
of all 7(a) loan volume in the U.S. Small Business Administration's (SBA) 7(a) Loan Program.
Our membership reflects the breadth of the nation's small-business lending community,
including large national financial institutions, regional and community banks, credit unions,
Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs), Minority Depository Institutions
(MDIs), Community Advantage Small Business Lending Companies (CA SBLCs), and nonbank
Small Business Lending Companies (SBLCs). Together, these institutions form a nationwide
network delivering federally guaranteed small-business financing to communities throughout
America.

NAGGL's comments focus on two complementary recommendations. First, we urge the
agencies to expressly recognize the SBA 7(a) Loan Program as a qualifying federal
economic-development program under the proposed CRA regulations, ensuring that SBA's
flagship small-business lending program is not omitted from the list of qualifying government
  2

programs that already expressly identifies other SBA financing programs. Second, and equally
important, we request that the agencies establish a distinct regulatory treatment permitting
qualifying 7(a) loans to receive community-development loan consideration in lieu of retail
small-business lending consideration, even when small-business lending is a major retail
product line for the originating institution. Together, these changes would ensure that the 7(a)
Loan Program's congressionally mandated economic-development purpose is not only
recognized in the regulatory definition, but meaningfully reflected in CRA examinations, without
allowing the same loan to receive credit under both retail and community-development lending
evaluations.

The SBA 7(a) Loan Program: Advancing the Core Purpose of CRA

Established by Congress in 1953, the SBA 7(a) Loan Program is the federal government's
flagship small-business lending program and one of its most consequential tools for expanding
access to capital, supporting job creation and fostering economic development in communities
nationwide, with a significant share of its lending reaching minority-owned borrowers.

Over the past decade, the 7(a) Loan Program has delivered more than $302 billion in financing
through over 649,000 loans, supporting more than 3.4 million jobs. In Fiscal Year 2025
(FY25) alone, 7(a) lending facilitated more than $37 billion in lending through approximately
78,000 loans, supporting more than 760,000 jobs.

The 7(a) Loan Program's reach into communities that have historically faced barriers to
accessing capital is equally significant. First, the 7(a) lending commitment to smaller-dollar
lending is unmistakable in the composition of its portfolio. In FY2026, nearly 22% of all 7(a)
loans approved were for $50,000 or less, nearly 44% were for $150,000 or less, 67% were for
$350,000 or less, and nearly three-quarters (73.4%) were for $500,000 or less. By contrast, loans
exceeding $2 million accounted for just 7.7% of total approvals. This distinctive concentration of
smaller-dollar financing sets the 7(a) Loan Program apart from other SBA business loan
programs and underscores its indispensable role in meeting the everyday capital needs of Main
Street businesses, as Congress intended.

In FY26 alone, approximately $1.2 billion in 7(a) financing went to Black-owned businesses,
$2.1 billion to Hispanic-owned businesses, and $6.4 billion to Asian-owned businesses. In fact,
minority-owned small businesses consistently account for approximately 30 percent of 7(a)
lending annually. In FY2026 alone, the 7(a) Loan Program delivered nearly $5.6 billion in
financing to rural small businesses--the largest volume of rural lending of any SBA business
loan program. These results demonstrate 7(a) lending's ability to reach entrepreneurs who have
historically faced barriers to accessing conventional financing.

No other SBA business loan program comes close to matching the 7(a) Loan Program's annual
volume of job creation and retention, its concentration of smaller-dollar loans within the overall
lending portfolio, or its reach into underserved and rural small-business markets.

But perhaps most importantly, the 7(a) Loan Program is distinguished as an economic
development program by its statutory "credit elsewhere" requirement, established under
  3

section 7(a) of the Small Business Act, 15 U.S.C. 636(a). This requirement has historically
been understood and applied as a defining feature of 7(a) lending: SBA-guaranteed financing is
available only when an applicant cannot obtain the desired credit on reasonable terms and
conditions from conventional sources.

In other words, the 7(a) Loan Program is expressly designed by Congress to reach creditworthy
small businesses whose financing needs are not being adequately met by the conventional
lending marketplace. This is not merely an aspirational objective or one that must be met at a
certain percentage of overall loan production; it is a core eligibility requirement for every single
7(a) loan and embedded in the Program's statutory framework.

That mission aligns directly with the purpose of the Community Reinvestment Act. Congress
enacted CRA to encourage federally regulated financial institutions to help meet the credit needs
of the communities in which they operate, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods,
consistent with safe and sound banking practices.

The 7(a) Loan Program puts that principle into practice every day. Its statutory credit-elsewhere
requirement, nationwide lending network, substantial job creation and retention, and
demonstrated reach into underserved and rural markets make it a natural and compelling fit
within the CRA economic-development framework.

Express Recognition of the SBA 7(a) Loan Program Under the Proposed Economic-
Development Definition

NAGGL strongly supports the agencies' proposed revisions to the definition of "economic
development" in proposed 12 CFR 25.12 and 345.12, particularly the establishment of three
independent pathways for qualifying activities: (i) financing that supports the productive
capacity, physical presence, or employment of eligible small businesses or farms; (ii) technical
assistance and support services; and (iii) activities involving federal, state, local, or Tribal
government programs, projects, or initiatives serving small businesses or small farms.

The third category is particularly important. Proposed 12 CFR 25.12 and 345.12, definition of
"economic development," paragraph (3)(iii), recognizes government programs serving small
businesses as defined by those programs and provides a non-exhaustive list of examples,
including SBA Certified Development Companies, Small Business Investment Companies,
qualified Community Development Entities, USDA Rural Business Investment Companies, and
CDFIs financing small businesses or small farms.

NAGGL respectfully requests that the agencies expressly add the SBA 7(a) Loan Program
to this non-exhaustive list and clarify that qualifying loan originations through the 7(a)
Loan Program satisfy the economic-development definition under paragraph (3)(iii).

The 7(a) Loan Program squarely meets the proposed category's stated purpose. It is a
congressionally established federal program expressly designed to serve small businesses,
promote economic development, focus on small dollar loans, facilitate credit availability where
conventional financing is insufficient, and support impressive job creation and retention
  4

throughout the United States. Its extensive network of participating lenders makes it an essential
component of the nation's small-business credit infrastructure and an important tool for the
federal government to foster economic development. Including the 7(a) Loan Program in the list
of federal programs that qualify under economic development recognizes this fact.

Explicit recognition is particularly important because many participating institutions offer
multiple SBA financing products, sometimes to the same borrower for different financing needs
or as part of a coordinated financing arrangement. Identifying other, smaller SBA programs
while omitting explicit reference to the flagship 7(a) Loan Program could introduce unnecessary
uncertainty to participating lenders and the regulatory examinations concerning the CRA
treatment of otherwise comparable federal small-business lending activities. Regulatory clarity
and consistent treatment are essential to encouraging continued lender participation in the 7(a)
Loan Program and ensuring that CRA considerations do not inadvertently favor one federally
authorized financing structure over another.

Response to Question 26

Question 26 specifically asks whether additional government programs, projects, or initiatives
should be included among the examples in the third category of economic development.

In direct response to Question 26, NAGGL strongly recommends that the agencies add the
SBA 7(a) Loan Program, authorized under section 7(a) of the Small Business Act (15
U.S.C. 636(a)), to the examples enumerated in proposed 12 CFR 25.12 and 345.12,
definition of "economic development," paragraph (3)(iii).

Expressly including the 7(a) Loan Program in this list would ensure that the agencies
consistently recognize qualifying 7(a) lending as eligible economic-development activity under
proposed 12 CFR 25.12 and 345.12, definition of "economic development," paragraph
(3)(iii).

Distinct Community-Development Treatment for SBA 7(a) Lending

NAGGL further urges the agencies to recognize that SBA 7(a) lending is distinct from
conventional retail small-business lending and warrants consideration under the community-
development framework. Congress established the 7(a) Loan Program with a specific economic-
development mission and statutory eligibility requirements, including the credit-elsewhere test,
which ensures that 7(a) financing serves small businesses unable to obtain conventional credit on
reasonable terms. Unlike other SBA programs identified in the proposed economic-development
definition, 7(a) financing is delivered through a nationwide network of participating lenders, the
vast majority of which are federally regulated banks subject to CRA examination. For many of
these institutions, 7(a) lending represents a substantial component of their small-business lending
portfolios.

While expressly including 7(a) among qualifying government programs would establish
important clarity regarding its economic-development eligibility, an additional regulatory
distinction warrants consideration. The proposed rule continues to evaluate retail lending
  5

based on a bank's major product lines, regardless of asset size, under proposed 12 CFR
25.21(g) and 345.21(g). Further, proposed 12 CFR 25.12 and 345.12, definition of
"community development loan," paragraph (2), generally exclude loans already considered in a
bank's retail small-business lending evaluation from receiving community-development loan
consideration, subject to limited exceptions. Although the proposal allows otherwise qualifying
loans outside a bank's evaluated major retail product lines to receive community-development
consideration, this flexibility may not extend to 7(a) loans originated by institutions for which
small-business lending is a major retail product line.

As a result, similarly situated 7(a) loans could receive different CRA treatment based on the
originating institution's broader lending portfolio rather than the underlying economic-
development purpose of the loan. NAGGL believes that the 7(a) Loan Program's distinct
congressional mandate warrants a more consistent approach, particularly where the
proposed framework otherwise recognizes qualifying government-program lending as economic-
development activity.

NAGGL therefore requests that the agencies establish an express regulatory exception or
alternative classification permitting qualifying SBA 7(a) loans to receive community-
development loan consideration in lieu of retail small-business lending consideration, even
when small-business lending is a major retail product line for the originating bank. This
treatment would apply to 7(a) loans qualifying under the government-program pathway in
proposed 12 CFR 25.12 and 345.12, definition of "economic development," paragraph
(3)(iii), consistent with the proposal's broader community-development eligibility requirements.
NAGGL is not seeking duplicative CRA credit for 7(a) loans or automatic community-
development qualification for every 7(a) loan; rather, we request a mutually exclusive
classification that allows otherwise qualifying 7(a) loans to be evaluated under the
framework that most accurately reflects their congressionally mandated economic-
development purpose.

This targeted regulatory change would complement the express recognition of 7(a) as an eligible
federal economic-development program, ensuring that its statutory purpose is meaningfully
reflected in CRA examinations while preserving the integrity of the agencies' retail lending and
community-development evaluation frameworks.

Geographic Flexibility for Nationwide 7(a) Lending

NAGGL supports proposed 12 CFR 25.13(e) and 345.13(e), which would allow qualifying
community-development activities outside a bank's assessment areas to receive CRA
consideration, subject to applicable geographic standards. Many 7(a) lenders operate nationally,
delivering financing to small businesses in communities far beyond their branch networks. A
CRA framework that recognizes qualifying community-development lending beyond traditional
facility-based assessment areas, while preserving banks' responsibilities to the communities they
serve locally, better reflects modern small-business lending and encourages expanded access to
capital in underserved markets nationwide. NAGGL strongly encourages the agencies to
clarify that otherwise eligible 7(a) loans considered as community-development loans may
receive such geographic flexibility, consistent with the proposed standards.
  6

Support for Additional Proposed Revisions

NAGGL also supports several related provisions that would strengthen CRA's effectiveness in
encouraging small-business lending.

Independent qualification under the government-program pathway. NAGGL supports
establishing paragraph (3)(iii) of the proposed economic-development definition in 12 CFR
25.12 and 345.12 as an independent category, without requiring qualifying government-program
activities to separately satisfy the financing or technical-assistance criteria of paragraphs (3)(i)
and (3)(ii). Federally established small-business programs are designed to address identifiable
financing and economic-development needs. Recognizing those statutory and programmatic
purposes provides a more consistent and objective basis for determining economic-development
eligibility.

Recognition of applicable program size standards. NAGGL strongly supports the proposed
language allowing small businesses to be defined according to the applicable government
program. SBA's size standards reflect differences across industries and business types. Applying
those standards to qualifying 7(a) activities would promote regulatory consistency, reduce
duplicative eligibility determinations, and avoid unnecessarily excluding eligible small-business
borrowers solely because their annual revenues exceed a separate CRA threshold. This approach
would govern qualification under the economic-development definition without displacing
distinct borrower-characteristic measures applicable to retail small-business lending
examinations.

Greater emphasis on lending and credit services. NAGGL supports the agencies' proposed
revisions to the CRA service test, including proposed 12 CFR 25.24(c)(4) and 345.24(c)(4),
which would focus the evaluation of retail banking services on the range and availability of
credit services rather than deposit products. This approach appropriately reinforces CRA's
statutory emphasis on meeting community credit needs. For SBA 7(a) lenders, whose
congressionally mandated mission is to extend financing to creditworthy small businesses unable
to obtain conventional credit on reasonable terms, this shift is particularly meaningful. We
encourage the agencies to carry this same emphasis on the substance and purpose of lending into
the treatment of qualifying 7(a) originations, recognizing their distinct economic-development
character under the community-development framework.

Elimination of the traditional economic-development purpose test. NAGGL strongly
supports eliminating the existing purpose test and replacing it with clearer, more objective
criteria. The current requirement to separately demonstrate specified job-creation or retention
outcomes for low- and moderate-income individuals or qualifying areas can create unnecessary
documentation burdens and uncertainty, even when financing supports genuine small-business
growth and employment. The 7(a) Loan Program's substantial record of job creation and
retention demonstrates why CRA should recognize meaningful economic-development activity
without imposing an additional subjective test that can discourage participation or complicate
financing decisions.

Federal Reserve Participation
  7

Finally, NAGGL encourages the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System to join the
OCC and FDIC in adopting a consistent interagency CRA framework. NAGGL's bank members
are supervised by all three federal banking agencies, and uniform regulatory treatment is
essential to avoiding inconsistent examination expectations, unnecessary compliance burdens,
and uncertainty for institutions participating in the same federal small-business lending program.

Conclusion

NAGGL appreciates the agencies' willingness to thoughtfully reconsider the CRA framework in
a manner that emphasizes meaningful lending activity, regulatory clarity, and the delivery of
credit to communities throughout the country.

The SBA 7(a) Loan Program's statutory purpose, nationwide lender participation, demonstrated
reach into underserved markets, and extraordinary record of small-business financing and job
support embody the economic-development objectives that CRA is intended to advance.

NAGGL respectfully urges the agencies to expressly recognize the SBA 7(a) Loan Program
as a qualifying federal economic-development program; establish a clear exception
permitting qualifying 7(a) loans to receive community-development loan consideration in
lieu of retail small-business lending treatment, even when small-business lending is a major
retail product line for the originating institution and without giving those loans duplicative
CRA credit; and clarify that qualifying 7(a) lending by nationwide lenders may receive
CRA consideration beyond traditional assessment areas, consistent with the proposal's
geographic eligibility standards.

Together, these changes would ensure that CRA recognizes not only the 7(a) Loan Program's
statutory economic-development purpose, but also the distinct nature of its financing, delivered
by federally supervised institutions that simultaneously provide conventional small-business
lending within their broader portfolios.

We thank the OCC and FDIC for their consideration and look forward to continued engagement
as the agencies finalize these important revisions.

Sincerely,

Kristen Granchelli

Chief Advocacy Officer
National Association of Government Guaranteed Lenders

revise their Community Reinvestment Act regulations.

For 40 years, Costella Kirsch has provided venture debt to emerging growth companies, with
investments of $500,000 to $15 million. We manage an SBA-licensed Small Business Investment
Company. Our loans reach companies that are often too early or too asset-light to qualify for
conventional bank credit, which is the gap the SBIC program was created to fill. Since 2009 alone,
we have financed more than 150 small businesses. Because our fund also uses SBA-guaranteed
leverage, each dollar a bank commits reaches small businesses at a multiple. Banks are among our
most important limited partners, and CRA consideration is a central reason many of them invest.

We support the Agencies' proposal to codify CRA eligibility for SBIC investments, and we support
the comments submitted by the Small Business Investor Alliance (SBIA). We write to ask that the

 www.costellakirsch.com
 final rule preserve the practical value of that eligibility, particularly for wholesale and limited
purpose banks, so the codification does what the Agencies intend.

1. Codifying the SBIC presumption is the right step

We support moving the presumption that bank investments in SBICs meet the economic
development purpose test from interagency guidance into regulation. Codification gives banks
certainty when making long-term fund commitments, which typically run ten years or more.

That certainty matters because SBICs are a proven channel for bank capital to reach small
businesses. SBA licensing, examination and reporting already confirm that SBIC capital goes to
eligible small businesses. Banks can rely on that oversight rather than build their own verification for
each investment. For the same reason, the full range of bank investments in SBICs should qualify
under the government programs prong of the economic development definition (proposed __.12,
definition of economic development, paragraph (3)(iii)).

2. Preserve broader regional credit for wholesale and limited purpose banks1

The proposal would replace the current consideration of community development activities in a
broader statewide or regional area with geographic flexibility standards that credit activities outside a
bank's assessment areas once it has adequately met needs inside them. We support a clear path to
that credit. We ask that whichever standard the Agencies adopt work for wholesale and limited
purpose banks, so they continue to receive credit for SBIC investments in a broader statewide or
regional area that includes their assessment areas. Many of these banks invest in SBICs, and many
have small or single assessment areas and no retail branch network.

SBICs invest where qualifying small businesses are, not where a given bank investor is
headquartered. Sound portfolio construction requires diversification, and SBA rules limit
concentration in any single business. No SBIC can promise to confine its investments to one limited
partner's assessment area.

1 A wholesale bank is a bank that is not in the business of extending retail loans to retail customers. A limited
purpose bank is a bank that offers only a narrow product line, such as credit card or motor vehicle loans, to a
regional or broader market. Each must request and receive its designation from its regulator. Because these banks do
not serve their communities primarily through branch-based retail lending, they are evaluated under a standalone
community development test rather than the lending, investment and service tests that apply to traditional banks.
Under the current rules, they may also receive consideration for community development activities outside their
assessment areas once they have adequately addressed the needs of those areas. See 91 Fed. Reg. at 52117 & nn.42
45; id. at 52118 & n.64.

 www.costellakirsch.com
 The number of banks with this profile is growing. The FDIC approved deposit insurance this year for
Ford Credit Bank and GM Financial Bank, both Utah-chartered industrial banks, and PayPal and
others have applied. Banks like these typically serve customers nationwide from a single
headquarters. How the final rule treats regional credit will shape whether they can invest in SBICs at
all.

If regional credit narrows, these banks face the choice our bank investors describe: shift to direct
lending in their assessment areas, or negotiate a strategic plan. Either path makes SBIC commitments
less efficient for CRA purposes. The likely result is fewer bank dollars in SBICs, which would
undercut the codified presumption the Agencies propose in the same rule.

We also ask the Agencies to retain the limited purpose bank designation. Although the proposed rule
text retains it, the preamble asks whether the Agencies should eliminate the category altogether. The
Agencies recognize that elimination would be a significant change for the banks now evaluated only
under the community development test.2 Without the designation, these banks would be evaluated
under the tests for their asset size, including on their consumer lending. A credit card bank lending
nationwide from a single office, for example, would likely be evaluated on consumer loans it cannot
concentrate in its assessment area. A strategic plan is not an equivalent substitute, because it requires
measurable goals, public participation and agency approval. The predictable result is that these banks
shift toward retail activity in their assessment areas and away from community development
investments such as SBICs.

We respectfully recommend that the final rule:

 1. Adopt a geographic flexibility standard that credits community development activities in a
 broader statewide or regional area that includes the assessment areas of wholesale and limited
 purpose banks.

 2. Continue to treat an investment in an SBIC that invests in that broader area as benefiting the
 bank's assessment area.3

 3. Grandfather CRA treatment of SBIC commitments made before the effective date, for the life
 of the commitment.

 4. Retain the limited purpose bank designation.

2 91 Fed. Reg. at 52125 (Section IV.B, "Limited purpose bank category")
3 This is consistent with current OCC guidance, under which a bank receives consideration for the full dollar amount
of an investment in an SBIC that serves the bank's assessment area(s) or a broader statewide or regional area that
includes them, whether or not the SBIC invests directly in the bank's assessment area. See Office of the Comptroller
of the Currency, Web and Telephone Seminar Q&As, Small Business Investment Companies: An Investment
Option for Banks (Feb. 15, 2012).

 www.costellakirsch.com
 3. Keep fund investments worthwhile under the new size categories

The proposal would reclassify banks as small (under $1 billion), intermediate ($1 billion to $10
billion) and large (over $10 billion). Many banks that invest in SBICs will change categories and
tests.

We ask the Agencies to confirm that SBIC investments receive meaningful consideration for
intermediate banks under the community development test, and remain eligible for consideration for
small banks, which would no longer be evaluated under that test. Because the proposal could allow
an intermediate bank to receive an overall "satisfactory" rating based on its lending test alone, the
final rule should ensure fund investments still meaningfully affect a bank's rating. We also ask for a
transition period so reclassified banks can plan around existing multi-year fund commitments.

4. Coordinate with the Federal Reserve

The Federal Reserve Board has not joined this proposal. SBICs raise capital from banks supervised
by all three agencies, sometimes within a single fund. We encourage the Agencies to work with the
Board toward consistent treatment of SBIC investments, so a bank's regulator does not determine
whether its investment earns CRA consideration.

Conclusion

Codifying the SBIC presumption will strengthen a channel that has moved bank capital to small
businesses for decades. We ask that the final rule keep that channel open for the banks most likely to
use it. We would welcome the chance to discuss these comments and to share our experience
financing small businesses alongside our bank partners.

The Community Development Alliance of the Capital District opposes the OCC and
FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) regarding the Community Reinvestment
Act (CRA) because it would weaken bank accountability and responsibility in our low
and moderate income communities.

The Community Development Alliance is comprised of the Affordable Housing
Partnership Homeownership Center, Albany Community Land Trust, Community Loan
Fund of the Capital Region (a CDFI), and United Tenants. These organizations have
decades of experience working with tenants, home buyers, homeowners, nonprofit
agencies, housing developers and small businesses to benefit the Capital Region of NY.

The Community Reinvestment Act has been essential to our work of providing equal
access to resources and for community development and revitalization efforts. Thanks to
the CRA, our CDFI has capital for lending and in turn funds for creating affordable
housing and small businesses. Because of the CRA, there are area financial institutions
with products for first time homebuyers in low-income neighborhoods. Parts of our
region struggle with disinvestment, housing shortages, poverty and a lack of access to
financial services. Serious efforts need to be made to strengthen CRA regulations not to
weaken them..

The Community Development Alliance is very concerned about the proposal to raise the
asset thresholds that determine how banks are regulated. By raising the small banks

 1
 threshold to below $1 billion too many banks would no longer have CRA evaluations.
And to propose treating banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion as
`intermediate' reduces their reporting requirements and their community obligations.
Because a bank falls below the new proposed higher asset threshold should not mean they
have less responsibility to meet community needs for affordable mortgages, small
business loans, and neighborhood revitalization. Reclassifying banks as small and
intermediate banks would reduce community reinvestment activity.

Rigorous CRA reports help communities identify lending gaps. It is important to have
data on what financial institutions are lending to farms, small businesses, CDFIs and
community development projects and which are not. Reducing reporting requirements
makes it difficult to compare bank performance for underserved populations.

Our community has 1 credit union left still serving in a low-income neighborhood. Other
financial institutions have moved to wealthy suburbs. For example, in one suburban
neighborhood there are 9 banks/credit unions in a 1-mile stretch in a high-income car
centric community. While people without cars in low-income communities have no banks
that can be easily reached. Without legitimate financial institutions, neighbors resort to
check cashers and alternative methods instead of being able to safely receive income,
build savings, establish banking relationships and obtain responsible credit. The first-
time homebuyers, entrepreneurs and tenants we work with need access to affordable bank
accounts. Proposing to remove evaluation of checking and deposit accounts would be
detrimental to our efforts to find good products for our clients that will help them become
stronger financially and build credit. CRA review of cost and features of bank products is
an important role. We need regulations that reward banks for keeping branches open and
providing services to unbanked and low income people. Prioritize the opening of
branches and penalize the closing of branches in underserved areas. Access to financial
institutions and useful affordable products is critical to building assets in underserved
communities. Access to physical banking is still essential for LMI people, communities
and small businesses.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill,

Partners for Rural Transformation (PRT) is a coalition of six Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs)
working in rural regions and Native communities experiencing persistent poverty. By connecting local expertise with
national capital, policy, and partnerships, PRT expands economic opportunity, scales proven solutions, attracts
investment, and advances systems change to strengthen communities across rural America. We appreciate the
opportunity to comment on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking amending the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA)
regulations, jointly issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC).

PRT Partners live in and serve regions and communities of persistent poverty, including Appalachia, the Mississippi
Delta, Tribal communities, the Deep South, the Rio Grande Valley, and the Rural West. A Persistent Poverty County is a
federal designation1 for counties where 20% or more of a county's population has lived at or below the federal poverty
line for at least 30 years. PRT Partners and other rural-serving CDFIs partner with banks daily to mobilize capital in the
most chronically disinvested markets in the country. The Community Reinvestment Act is one tool that can be leveraged
to pull private capital into these places. While we broadly support the idea of greater clarity and reduced burden, the
proposed changes miss the opportunity to strengthen incentives in rural and Tribal regions experiencing persistent
poverty and move away from the CRA's original intent: fair access to credit for underserved people and places 2.

Maintain Current Asset Thresholds for Small, Intermediate, and Large Banks
Raising the asset thresholds that define small, intermediate, and large banks would result in a sharp decline in bank
investment in community development. The proposal to increase thresholds for small banks to <$1 billion, intermediate
banks to between $1 billion to $10 billion, and large banks to >$10 billion, and all higher proposals, poses a risk to the
communities that stand to benefit the most from bank investments. By the agencies' own estimates, one in three banks3
would no longer be evaluated on Community Development tests, and 47% of those banks are headquartered in rural
areas4. Twenty-eight states stand to lose the requirement for the Community Development test for at least one third of
their low- to moderate-income area branches5. This is significant, given that in 2024 alone, the CRA incentivized
hundreds of billions across the country in private capital ($168B in affordable housing and community development
loans, $10B in small farm loans, $152B in small business loans, and $100B in home mortgages)6.

 Partners for Rural Transformation
 www.pfrt.org
 The impacts become even steeper when considering regions experiencing persistent poverty. For example, PRT Partner
HOPE covers a six-states region in the Deep South which covers nearly half (45%) of all persistent poverty counties in the
country. HOPE's analysis of the proposed threshold changes in these six states found that if the proposed thresholds
were to be finalized, there would be a 90% drop in large FDIC/OCC banks (from 39 to 4), and 83% of FDIC/OCC banks
would now be considered small (up from 57% of banks now). In Oklahoma, home to 38 tribal nations, as few as three
banks could remain subject to Community Development testing under these proposed thresholds.

Partners for Rural Transformation recommend that the regulators maintain the current asset thresholds. The proposed
increases would remove the primary incentive, the Community Development test as a form of evaluation, for about
1,500 banks that serve rural and tribal markets to engage in community development.

Recognize Operational Grants as Eligible CRA Activity in the Community Development Definition
The proposal prohibits operating grants and imposes a restriction on funding that supports operational and other
ancillary costs. This would effectively cut off the operating and capacity-building support that rural and Native CDFIs rely
on. PRT supports the comment submitted by Local Initiatives Support Corporation and the Credit Builders Alliance. They
share that the proposed rule would require a community development grant to be used directly by the organization
receiving the funds from a bank, rather than as pass-through grants. For large banks, it would limit the recipient's
indirect administrative costs to 15% and require extensive supporting documentation. These provisions prevent banks
from receiving CRA credit when they fund nonprofit intermediaries that distribute grants or low-cost capital to other
nonprofits carrying out Community Development activities on the ground. Additionally, operating grants are essential
infrastructure in regions of persistent poverty. Treating flexible support as separate from eligible investment ignores
how community development finance fundamentally works and will result in reduced volume of CRA-eligible activity.
Partners for Rural Transformation recommends that the FDIC and OCC keep grants in the Community Development
investment definition and remove the 15% cap on administrative costs.

Increase Clarity on Community Development Eligibility and Response Timeliness
PRT welcomes the proposal's recommendation to publish an illustrative list of activities eligible for Community
Development consideration, which would provide greater clarity for banks, intermediaries, and community developers.
PRT applauds the definitions of government-designated redevelopment areas (e.g. Opportunity Zones) as potentially
qualifying for CRA consideration. However, such designations should not substitute for accurately identifying
communities with demonstrated needs. The agencies should ensure that geographic criteria used to identify eligible
investment areas meaningfully capture underserved rural, Tribal and persistent poverty communities7. Additionally, a
current bottleneck for project deals is the response time from the regulators and examiners for confirming eligible
Community Development activities of a proposed loan or investment. This is especially true for rural projects and deals
with several entities involved in the financing of a single project, especially with the time-sensitivity of New Market Tax
Credit and other similar transactions. The currently proposed 30-day response window is far too long for deals that
depend on certainty to close and move forward.

Partners for Rural Transformation recommend an illustrative list of qualifying community development activities is
published, ensure that geographic eligibility criteria accurately identifies underserved rural, Tribal and persistent-poverty
communities, and establish a 10-business day response window for community development eligibility inquiries to
provide greater certainty and help community development transactions move forward.

 Partners for Rural Transformation
 www.pfrt.org
 Maintain Rating Requirements for Limited Purpose Banks
We support the general narrowing of the limited purpose bank designation, but not full elimination. The proposal
mentions the removal of a bank's record of meeting the credit needs of highly economically disadvantaged areas and
low-income individuals when assigning a rating to a limited-purpose bank. There should be built-in safeguards so rural,
Tribal and persistent poverty mission lenders are not penalized by operating in leaner markets that do not fit standard
benchmark criteria. Removing this factor when calculating a rating shifts focus away from the places with the greatest
need for access to fair credit.

Partners for Rural Transformation recommends requiring CRA ratings to account for a limited-purpose bank's record of
serving highly disadvantaged areas, low-income individuals and small businesses in persistently poor rural and Tribal
areas.

Support Revitalization and Stabilization in Indian Country
PRT echoes and supports the comment by the Native CDFI Network, including establishing Native Land Areas (NLAs) as
their own place-based category for Community Development and investment with additional consideration for bank
branches and Community Development activities that serve Native communities. Tribal and Native lands face significant
barriers to accessing capital, and the CRA should provide meaningful incentives for banks to address these disparities.
We encourage the agencies to retain the comprehensive Native Land Area framework established in the 2023 CRA Final
Rule8, which included enhanced consideration for branches located on Native Lands and an impact and responsiveness
factor for Community Development activities that benefit residents of NLAs. The definition of Native Land Areas should
also recognize the service areas of certified Native CDFIs that extend beyond these geographic boundaries, ensuring that
CRA incentives reflect the actual reach of trusted, locally rooted institutions serving Native communities.

Partners for Rural Transformation recommend that the Native Land Area framework established in the 2023 CRA Final
Rule be incorporated to strengthen incentives for bank branches and community development investments that serve
Native communities.

Transparency and Accountability for Strategic Plans, and Maintain Strong Data & Reporting
The proposed change to the strategic plan option has potential to be a meaningful vehicle to bring bank investment into
rural, Tribal and persistent poverty communities, but only with accountability and transparency. Without accountability
and transparency, strategic plans could be used as a vehicle to circumvent incentives and tests that harm communities
who already experience chronic disinvestment. Public posting of strategic plans and bank performance in executive
plans within a timely manner is critical to creating meaningful accountability for strategic plans. In the same vein, we
appreciate the expanded reporting for large banks that the proposal suggests, with intermediate and small bank
reporting remaining largely unchanged. However, this modest step forward is offset by the proposed asset threshold
changes described earlier in our letter: raising the threshold would remove far more banks from the large bank status
than the new large-bank reporting would ever illuminate.

The Partners for Rural Transformation recommend that the final rule maintain current asset thresholds for large-bank
reporting requirements to preserve transparency, strengthen accountability, and enable regulators and the public to
assess how changes to the CRA evaluation criteria affect lending and investment in rural, Tribal and persistent poverty
communities.

 Partners for Rural Transformation
 www.pfrt.org
 The Partners for Rural Transformation thank you for considering our comment. The CRA has remained one of the tools
that directs private capital into persistent poverty rural and Tribal communities, and we urge the FDIC and OCC to
consider these places as more than an afterthought, but of places where proposed changes carry the most weight.
Please reach out to Emily Simmons at emily@prft.org with any questions.
In Partnership,

on behalf of the Association for Enterprise Opportunity, AEO respectfully submits the attached comment letter regarding the proposed Community Reinvestment Act regulations issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation under OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694, RIN 1557-AF57, and FDIC RIN 3064-AG31.
