Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

Inclusive Action for the City writes to object to the harmful changes proposed to the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed by Congress in
1977 in response to redlining and creates an affirmative obligation for banks to help
meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of communities, including low and
moderate income (LMI) communities. While the CRA has successfully encouraged
banks to lend, invest and provide services in underserved communities, challenges
related to redlining, discrimination, underinvestment, and lack of access remain.

Inclusive Action for the City is a Community Development Financial Institution
based in Boyle Heights and serving communities throughout Los Angeles County.
For the past 15 years, we have supported thousands of small businesses and
entrepreneurs with loans and grants. Many small businesses in our communities
struggle to access affordable capital, making strong CRA requirements essential to
ensuring banks invest in underserved neighborhoods. We are members of RISE
 Economy, advocating for economic equity and access to capital for underserved
communities.

The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift.
The proposal does not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on
LMI communities. We request an extension of the comment period for an additional
60 days so we have time to better understand how much CRA activity may be lost
to communities because of this proposal an analysis the regulators did not
conduct or provide.
The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved
communities in several ways.

 1) Community development (CD) activities for affordable housing
 and small businesses will drop dramatically.

As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities
that support critically needed affordable housing and economic development
projects. These activities often provide the greatest CRA impact in communities as
they strengthen economic stability and mobility, quality of life, and social health of
residents and communities.

The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large"
Banks, such that many banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and
expectation to serve the community development needs of their communities.[1]
According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70
California banks would see their reinvestment obligations reduced under the
proposal. Twenty-five California banks would shed their Community Development
Test responsibilities entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer be subject to
the Investment Test.[2]

The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical
community development programs that have had large impacts in LMI
communities. These include Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTCs) which are a
key driver of affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) which
fuel economic development projects in tribal and other areas; and EQ2 equity
equivalent investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs)
that provide small business lending in underserved areas that banks cannot reach,
and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that take property off of the speculative
market.

Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting
the critical importance of the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable
 housing.[3] Approximately half of nonprofit CDFI funding comes from CRA
motivated banks.[4] The regulators will even further weaken CD obligations if they
adopt the alternative proposal that Large Banks be defined as those with over $30
billion in assets.

Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance
even where they remain subject to the Community Development and Investment
Tests. The regulators signal to all banks that they can do significantly less CD
lending and investment and still pass their CRA examinations, all while seeking CRA
credit for activity outside of their CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests
that a bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1
capital were devoted to CD loans and CD investments. That percentage is far lower
than the percentage that NCRC determined banks currently devote to community
investments and loans. If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary
to meet the proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by approximately
$87.1 billion, or 85%.[5]

Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have
tremendous negative impacts on affordable housing and small business
development in our state. Asset thresholds should not be raised.

 2) Banks will shed branches and BankOn.

The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and maintain
branches in LMI and BIPOC neighborhoods. By increasing the asset threshold for a
Large Bank to over $10 billion, forty-five banks in California will no longer be
subject to the Services Test and reviewed to ensure that their branches are serving
LMI communities. In California alone, NCRC estimates that 245 branches in LMI
areas and 497 branches in neighborhoods of color would be vulnerable to closure
due to this proposal.[6]

Branch presence has been tied to increased small business lending in communities.
Fewer branches will result in less small business lending. These changes will be
particularly hard hitting in rural areas of our state where smaller banks originate a
larger portion of the small business loans.

The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to
offer deposit products that are accessible to LMI residents.[7] Deposit accounts are
a gateway to credit access, financial stability, and wealth building, especially for
families who are otherwise preyed upon by predatory financial institutions. As one
important example, the BankOn program has provided access to no or low fee bank
accounts for over fourteen million people.[8] California is home to several BankOn
 coalitions that establish effective partnerships among banks, community-based
organizations, and local governments. The proposal jettisons this work.

Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million
are underbanked.[9] National banks regulated by the OCC charged billions of
dollars in overdraft and non-sufficient fund fees in 2025, and in California alone,
state-chartered banks charged over fifty-six million dollars ($56 million) in OD and
NSF fees to California consumers in 2025.[10]

 3) Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.

Another consequence of the proposal's drive to raise asset thresholds is that fewer
banks will be required to report data regarding their small business, small farm,
and community development lending activities. Such data is critical to
understanding not only individual bank performance, but also the needs of local
markets. Rise Economy and its member organizations routinely analyze this CRA
data when meeting with banks and commenting on CRA exams and mergers. The
loss of such data is particularly harmful at a time when the Administration is
walking back efforts to collect and disclose detailed small business lending data
under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank Act. These changes will disproportionately
impact rural communities in our state where banks up to $10 billion in assets make
up a larger part of the small business and small farm lending markets.

 4) Native American communities and Tribal Nations will not see
 sufficient benefits.

The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the needs
of Native American communities and Tribal Nations which have been poorly served
by banks. The current rules focus CRA obligations in areas where banks have
branches, even though there are far fewer bank branches near Tribal lands and in
rural areas where Native Americans may reside. The proposal seeks to address this
CRA gap by encouraging banks to engage in community development and related
activities in "Indian Country" and on "Tribal and Native lands," even if outside of
bank CRA assessment areas. But many members of Tribes in California will not
benefit from this proposal as they do not live in Indian Country or on Tribal or
Native lands, as defined.

CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring within
particular geographies, given the challenges and impacts associated with historic
dispossession and federal policy. Instead, CRA evaluations should also consider
whether banks have established meaningful relationships with, and provided direct
benefits to, federally recognized Tribes as well as non-federally recognized Tribes.
Non-federally recognized Tribes have been acknowledged by, and are able to access
 programs and contracts with, various local and state entities.[11] Such processes
exist.

More specifically, the CRA rules should encourage banks to serve Tribes, nonprofit
organizations or other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned businesses
that are majority owned and controlled by Native American entrepreneurs by
providing:

 Active outreach and engagement
 Community development loans and investments for affordable housing and

 economic development projects
 Small farm and small business loans
 Home mortgage loans
 Grants to meet community needs, including for capacity building for Tribes

 and support for Tribes seeking federal recognition if desired
 Support for cultural, health and other programs
 Bank branches
 Deposit products such as affordable bank accounts, and
 The provision of financial services such as financial literacy, apprenticeship

 programs and technical assistance support

While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities
outside of their branches and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made to
encourage banks to engage in CRA related activity to directly benefit Tribes,
nonprofit organizations and other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned
businesses that are majority owned and controlled by Native American
entrepreneurs.

A better approach is needed. All banks should be subject to an impact and
responsiveness review factor during their CRA exams that evaluates and tracks
whether banks have engaged in any CRA activity directly with Tribes, Tribally
controlled entities and Native owned businesses.[12] If banks know they will be
examined for their work with Tribes, they will find mutually beneficial ways to work
with Tribes.

 5) Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will
 suffer.

The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by
requiring a demonstrated nexus to community development projects and mandating
that large banks and their grantees demonstrate that grantees will not use more
than 15% of these grants on overhead.[13] As if this wasn't enough, the FDIC and
 OCC question whether they should end CRA eligibility for bank grantmaking to
nonprofits entirely.

Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian
measures will be except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller
groups, may be impacted.[14]

Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local
needs. They also can be key partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and
investment products into communities inclined to trust long established local
organizations. Many nonprofit organizations and programs, such as downpayment
assistance programs, that support CRA related activity, rely on bank contributions
to operate. Smaller, local, and rural organizations will be least able to meet new
reporting obligations, and they risk losing bank support as a result. The proposal
would also end impactful contributions from banks for general operating support,
sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.

Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their
communities on their own. Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps
in their own capacity seeking assistance with community outreach, borrower
education, credit building and repair, technical assistance, legal services, job
training and placement, tax assistance, affordable housing and other services and
programs which help residents become stable and bankable so that banks can
attract new deposits and make new loans in LMI communities.

The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and will
focus grantmaking on larger organizations that can help them more easily meet
their new FDIC and OCC-imposed regulatory burdens.

Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15%
overhead restriction will negatively affect operations and organizational success. As
one example, in order to secure CRA grants from Large Banks, CDFIs will need to
pare down costs for critical operational expenses such as underwriting, servicing,
compliance, technology, impact measurement, product development, and borrower
technical assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions,
organizations are put at risk.

The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA
activity that contributions represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large
negative impact it will have on nonprofit organizations that rely on bank funding,
the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are meant to benefit from the CRA,
and the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.
  6) Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.

There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link
between CRA and LMI impact in the name of easing bank burden.

Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their
top two major product lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in,
and profiting from, communities, this lending by banks, subsidiaries and affiliates
must be evaluated. Further, certain products, such as small farm and consumer
loans, are important in many communities, but may not be among a bank's largest
product lines. If regulators give banks a pass and exempt smaller product lines
from CRA oversight, banks will have less incentive to consider how those products
are offered.

Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and
soundness, encourages banks to meet community needs, and engenders greater
trust in banks by the community. Eliminating categories of loan products from
scrutiny will have the opposite effect.

No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test,
which has encouraged the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the
definition of economic development. The CRA should create greater incentives for
banks to support the creation of jobs that pay family sustaining wages for LMI
workers and in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to provisions that would provide
CRA credit for job creation and economic development that may only benefit
middle- and upper-income workers and communities. Such provisions ignore the
purpose of CRA.

Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA
credit for large scale community infrastructure products that generate profits for
banks, would likely be financed without CRA credit, and provide only incidental
benefits to LMI residents and communities. Such an expansion of what qualifies for
CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities.
For example, banks might choose to more profitably earn CRA credit by financing
larger scale infrastructure projects, like bridges, in lieu of financing less lucrative,
smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local community needs (such as
childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or resilience
projects).

Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA
should require banks to focus their CRA activities on their CRA assessments
 areas,[15] where they are subject to more rigorous regulatory oversight (with an
exception made to encourage banks to better serve Tribes, as noted above). Banks
are not doing enough currently to meet the credit and deposit needs in the areas
where they have CRA responsibility, a problem the regulators tried to address in the
2023 CRA Rule.[16] Yet the proposal further encourages banks to seek CRA credit
for projects in areas away from their branches, lending and CRA responsibility. This
will enable banks to get credit for activity outside of their assessment areas, while
providing no accompanying CRA obligation to better serve these areas.

Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal goes
out of its way to encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan option to meet
their CRA responsibilities. The Strategic Plan was meant for financial institutions
that operated under a unique business model that the CRA rules were not designed
to address. The Strategic Plan option provides for minimal public input and
regulatory scrutiny and allows banks to determine the level of reinvestment activity
they need to engage in to earn a passing CRA grade. In our experience, banks with
Strategic Plans tend to reinvest less in the community and in less impactful ways.
The OCC's guidance establishing low community development thresholds for banks
opting for the Strategic Plan, [17] validates this perspective.

Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community
development efforts with little benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing,
where units are affordable at a point in time but not encumbered by deed or rent
restrictions, are a feature of today's housing market. But CRA rules should not give
banks credit for financing such activities where the benefit to LMI residents and
communities is unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it
can be a driver of bank investment in problematic landlords and displacement. CRA
credit should be given for financing of NOAH only if the project is owned and
operated by mission-driven organizations, where a majority of residents are LMI
tenants, and the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are
compliant with tenant rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents
can reasonably be expected to retain their housing.

 7) Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA
 ratings downgrades.

The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and redline
should not be allowed to pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding"
ratings. Under the Biden Administration, at least a dozen banks that passed their
CRA exams were accused of redlining. This proposal will only increase that number
by narrowing what constitutes evidence of discrimination that may be considered
for the purpose of downgrading a bank's CRA rating. Here, regulators should
 consider any evidence that a bank, its affiliates, or subsidiaries engaged in
discrimination, redlining, or illegal credit practices as part of their lending, deposit,
branching, or other activities. This evidence should be considered regardless of its
source (public or private parties), or its form (informal complaints, research based
on data, testing results, comment letters, administrative actions, private litigation,
etc.). We also urge the regulators to acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity
Act authorizes Special Purpose Credit Programs, and to once again encourage banks
to develop SPCPs to better serve communities that have been redlined, excluded,
and underserved. This is the essence of CRA.

Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information to
allow for meaningful public comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of
entities and activities, and will undoubtedly harm the communities that the CRA
was meant to support. If finalized in substantially the same form as proposed,
communities will suffer significantly decreased investment in affordable housing and
CDFI support, more LMI branch closures, higher bank account fees, fewer
community serving nonprofit organizations, and increased bank discrimination and
redlining with no CRA consequence. The CRA will become further removed from its
purpose of encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and
the OCC to reconsider this proposal.

Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Very Truly Yours,

Amy Chong
Senior Policy Associate

Summary of Individual Public Comment — Nicholas D. Hawkins
OCC Docket OCC-2026-0694 | RIN 1557-AF57 | FDIC RIN 3064-AG31

I submit the attached comment as a resident of Grand Prairie, Texas, a senior General Studies major at Texas Southern University, and an Irvin M. Henderson Fellow with the National Community Reinvestment Coalition, placed with Hip Hop Caucus. I write solely in my individual capacity; the views and recommendations are my own.

I request revision of the proposed Community Reinvestment Act regulations to preserve public lending information, meaningful community-development scrutiny, and documented benefits for low- and moderate-income communities. I recognize the agencies’ goal of reducing regulatory burden and support eliminating duplicative reporting and using existing records. Relief should preserve the information and examination standards needed to assess whether banks meet community credit needs.

My comment offers five concrete recommendations:

Preserve comparable annual small-business lending disclosure until the agencies demonstrate that replacement data provide adequate public coverage, geographic detail, and timely access.

Maintain consequential community-development examinations, including identifiable findings on loans, investments, grants, and services and a meaningful relationship to overall CRA ratings.

Replace the rigid 15% indirect-cost condition for qualifying large-bank grants with reasonable-cost documentation, proportionate accountability, and demonstrable community benefit.

Retain a clarified economic-development purpose test or an equivalent documented benefit standard connecting qualifying financing to low- and moderate-income people or communities.

Require accountable infrastructure consideration, with documented service access, affordability, cost allocation, and relevant risks. Private data centers are not automatically eligible for CRA consideration.

Exhibit 1 reports NCRC’s modeled Texas reclassification of 141 bank records: 81 losing mandatory distinct community-development test status and 60 losing large-bank status. These figures describe regulatory classifications, not observed financing losses or predicted bank behavior. The comment also uses Broadway National Bank’s historical OCC evaluation and nonprofit-cost research, preserving their respective scope and limitations.

I ask the agencies to address these recommendations, publish institution- and geography-specific impact evidence, and allow meaningful public review before removing existing protections.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0407_09000064b9668baf.pdf:
Individual Comment on the Proposed Community Reinvestment Act
Regulations

October 12, 2026

Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; OCC Docket OCC-2026-0694, RIN 1557-AF57; FDIC
RIN 3064-AG31

To the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation:

I urge the agencies to revise the proposal to preserve comparable public lending information,
consequential community-development examinations, and a documented connection between CRA
consideration and community benefit. The CRA's focus on low- and moderate-income (LMI)
communities guides these requests. I submit five requests under three themes: public information and
meaningful examination; demonstrable community benefit; and accountable infrastructure investment.

I am Nicholas D. Hawkins, a resident of Grand Prairie, Texas, a senior General Studies major at Texas
Southern University, and an Irvin M. Henderson Fellow with the National Community Reinvestment
Coalition (NCRC), placed with Hip Hop Caucus. My research concerns small-business access to capital,
community-development accountability, and the financial and infrastructure relationships associated
with development in Dallas-Fort Worth. I submit this comment solely in my individual capacity. The
views and recommendations are my own and do not represent or imply endorsement by Hip Hop Caucus
or NCRC.

My interest in this rulemaking is practical: residents and small businesses need information that lets
them assess whether banks are meeting local credit needs, and examiners need standards that distinguish
qualifying activity from meaningful performance. My Texas analysis uses NCRC's modeled bank
classifications and an official OCC performance evaluation. These sources identify changes in scrutiny
and illustrate historical activity; they do not establish future financing losses or predict bank behavior.

I recognize the agencies' objectives of clearer eligibility standards, a stronger focus on community credit
needs, and proportionate compliance costs. The Conference of State Bank Supervisors has documented
disproportionate compliance costs among smaller community banks and urged modernization of
regulatory thresholds. The OCC has also made tailored supervision and reduced community-bank
burden explicit priorities. Those concerns deserve a substantive response. I support eliminating
duplicative reporting and using existing records for examinations. The agencies should demonstrate that
replacement safeguards function before removing information or performance requirements on which
community accountability depends. [1-3]

Public information and meaningful examination

1 Preserve comparable annual small business reporting

The proposal would generally classify banks below $1 billion as small, banks from $1 billion through
$10 billion as intermediate, and banks above $10 billion as large, subject to the specified prior-year asset
rules. Proposed 12 CFR 25.42 and 345.42 generally exempt small and intermediate banks from
annual CRA small-business and small-farm reporting. The agencies cite compliance burden and discuss
using data collected under section 1071 of the Dodd-Frank Act to avoid duplication, including the
alternative of relying exclusively on that data. [1, IV.A and IV.G]

Reducing the mandatory CRA reporting population would narrow that reporting channel even if every
affected bank maintained its lending. Any replacement must be evaluated for comparable public
coverage rather than assumed to supply it. NCRC's Texas roster identifies 60 bank records modeled as
moving from large-bank to intermediate-bank treatment. This figure describes examination-category
changes. It is neither a count of missing loan records nor a percentage decline in Texas disclosure.

 Nicholas D. Hawkins | OCC-2026-0694 | Page 1
 Periodic examination findings cannot substitute for a comparable annual public record when residents,
researchers, and small-business organizations need to identify local credit gaps. [1, 4]

I ask the agencies to retain annual reporting for currently covered banks until they demonstrate an
adequate and timely public replacement. Publish a crosswalk comparing institution coverage, loan
products, business-size information, geographic detail, reporting years, release schedules, and public
accessibility under current CRA disclosure and any section 1071 substitute. Identify gaps using explicit
institution, loan-count, and dollar denominators at the state, county, and assessment-area levels. Permit
equivalent fields to be reported once and provide a transition that prevents missing years. Preserve
comparable analytical utility with justified borrower-privacy protections. This approach makes burden
relief depend on available replacement information rather than assumed future equivalence.

2 Preserve consequential community development scrutiny

Under the currently applicable framework described in the proposal, intermediate small banks receive a
distinct community-development test, while large banks receive separate Lending, Investment, and
Service Tests. The proposed thresholds and 25.26 and 345.26 would move some banks into small-
bank treatment without mandatory distinct community-development testing. Banks moving from large to
intermediate treatment would retain community-development evaluation but lose the separate large-bank
Investment and Service Tests. NCRC's Texas model identifies 81 bank records in the first group and 60
in the second, totaling 141 modeled bank records. Exhibit 1 reports the two categories and explains the
method. The figures describe modeled regulatory classifications. [1, IV.A-B; 4]

The agencies explain that higher thresholds reflect banking-industry growth and reduce the cost of
comprehensive examinations. They also propose changing appendix A(d)(3)(i) so an intermediate bank
could receive a Satisfactory overall rating without Satisfactory community-development performance,
provided the lending-test requirement is met. The agencies expect greater flexibility to encourage
stronger performance. My concern is that an overall Satisfactory rating could communicate adequate
responsiveness while the bank's community-development performance remains weaker. CRA records
also matter in specified branch, relocation, merger, acquisition, charter, and deposit-insurance
applications; the applicable provisions permit the record to support denial or conditioning of approval. A
rating does not automatically trigger a particular penalty. [1, IV.B and 25.29 and 345.29]

The Urban Institute's September 29, 2026 analysis similarly identifies weaker reporting and examination
incentives, including the possibility that combining community-development lending and investment
evaluation could reduce investment incentives. This is an analytical concern, not an observed response
to the proposed rule. Empirical research supplies a separate reason to examine the mechanism carefully.
Philadelphia Federal Reserve researchers studied a 2013 change in neighborhood CRA eligibility and
found evidence supporting small-business lending, particularly originations, with larger estimated
effects from losing eligibility than from gaining it. Mee Jung Kim's study estimated approximately 0.8
percent higher small-business employment in CRA-eligible areas relative to ineligible areas, with larger
effects among young firms and firms in minority neighborhoods. Neither study evaluates the proposed
2026 bank thresholds or forecasts Texas outcomes. [5-7]

Broadway National Bank's November 6, 2023 OCC evaluation illustrates the activity made visible by
separate tests. The evaluation covered January 1, 2020 through December 31, 2022 and recorded 65
community-development loans totaling $58.301 million across its examined Texas assessment areas. Its
investment table, including regional investments, reported 399 qualified items totaling $266.417 million:
91 prior-period investments totaling $233.389 million still outstanding and 308 current-period items
totaling $33.028 million. The $266.417 million total therefore is not newly originated investment during
2020-2022. Approximately 254 San Antonio donations totaling $1.4 million were already included in
current-period investment totals. The evaluation also recorded approximately 5,061 community-
development service hours. Broadway's Dallas branch, opened in late 2022, was not evaluated. These
figures are historical examination evidence, not DFW-specific amounts or annual flows. [8, printed pp.
2-4, 10, 15, 18 and 21]

 Nicholas D. Hawkins | OCC-2026-0694 | Page 2
 NCRC's public Texas roster classifies Broadway in the group modeled as losing large-bank status. Its
historical record supports making loans, investments, grants, and services identifiable in examination
findings; it does not establish that Broadway would reduce any activity. I ask the agencies to preserve
distinct community-development review for banks currently subject to it or demonstrate equivalent
scrutiny before changing their treatment. Retain the requirement of Satisfactory community-
development performance for a Satisfactory intermediate overall rating, calibrated to institutional
capacity, safety and soundness, and available opportunities. Equivalent scrutiny should retain
identifiable findings on loans, investments, grants, and services; assess responsiveness to local needs and
opportunities; and preserve a consequential community-development component in the overall rating.
Publishing activity totals alone would not establish equivalence. Explain institution-level and local
effects alongside expected compliance savings. [1, 4, 8]

Demonstrable community benefit

3 Retain qualifying grants with proportionate documentation

The proposed community-development grant definitions in 25.12 and 345.12 require direct use for a
qualifying program, project, or initiative and benefit to the bank's assessment areas, subject to
25.13(e) and 345.13(e). For a large bank's grant or donation to receive CRA consideration, the recipient's
indirect costs for administering the award may not exceed 15 percent, calculated consistently with
Uniform Guidance for Federal Awards, 2 CFR part 200, or a comparable standard. The preamble
describes the ceiling as 15 percent of the grant or donation dollar amount. Under proposed 25.42(a)
(3) and 345.42(a)(3), the bank must collect and retain through completion of its next CRA examination
the recipient's written commitment to qualifying activities, written attestation of compliance, and

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

On behalf of Harborlight Homes, I am writing to comment on the proposed changes to the
Community Reinvestment Act regulations.

Harborlight Homes is a non-profit, Massachusetts-certified Community Development Corporation.
We develop, manage, and advocate for high quality, service-enriched housing that is affordable for
people of all ages across Boston's North Shore region. We support families in achieving economic
stability and growth, making spaces for children to thrive, and homes for our seniors to age-in-
place safely, well, and with dignity. We ensure those who have struggled with homelessness are
able to regain independence, and essential workers have access to homes which allow them to live
in the communities in which they work and raise their families.

CRA has played an important role in encouraging financial institutions to meet the credit and
community development needs of the communities they serve. Bank lending, investments, grants,
and services supported through CRA all play a pivotal role in financing the affordable housing we
develop, manage, and for which we provide services.

We are concerned that several provisions of the proposed rule, particularly when considered
together, could significantly weaken the regulatory framework supporting banks' engagement in
these activities. We urge your agencies to consider not only how individual provisions affect
financial institutions, but also their cumulative impact on the communities, projects, and
organizations that rely on CRA-incentivized capital and partnerships.

Impact on Our Community and Work
 In recent years, CITC and LIHTC funding has been an enormous asset in our capacity to advance
projects and gap-fill unmet needs throughout the organization. The examples are countless in our
projects. Every development, building, and home we build is touched in some way by CRA support.
We are worried that the change in CRA status will prompt the local banking industry, including our
primary local investor, to adjust their giving and investments. This creates an added burden on
Harborlight to secure new donors and alternative tax credit investors, who may require higher
returns, resulting in less equity financing to affordable housing projects. This is especially
burdensome for small teams like ours.

Additionally, even where banks may initially continue their community investments in line with
prior Investment Test requirements, we worry over time they will relax to the less demanding
Intermediate Small Bank standard.

We work in Essex County, which is currently served by 37 banks evaluated on their community
development activities within our communities. If the proposal to increase the intermediate bank
threshold to $1 billion and the large bank threshold to $10 billion was adopted, just 30 banks would
be evaluated on their community development activities. In the alternative proposal to increase the
intermediate bank threshold to $10 billion and the large bank threshold to $30 billion, just 20 banks
would be evaluated on all three criteria (Lending, Investment, and Service) which are all critical to
community development. This could lead to significant changes in the level of lending and
investment we see, making it more difficult for our non-profit to develop needed affordable housing
in our communities.

CD Lending, Investment, and Grants

Community development corporations like Harborlight rarely rely on a single source of funding and
often require multiple forms of capital working together. Loans, equity investments, tax credit
investments, and other financing tools serve different purposes within that capital stack. We are
concerned that the proposed framework could reduce incentives for some banks to make
community development investments, even where those investments are critical to meeting local
needs. A reduction in one source of capital can affect the feasibility of an entire project and
increase pressure on other limited sources of financing.

Bank grants and equity equivalent investments also play a distinct role in the community
development ecosystem. Grants and investments support activities that generally cannot be
financed through traditional loans, including crucial early-stage predevelopment work, technical
assistance, resident services, staffing, and organizational capacity.

We are very concerned about proposals that could make it more difficult for banks to receive CRA
consideration for grants that support the operating capacity necessary to deliver community
development outcomes. Strong local organizations are often what make subsequent lending and
investment possible, particularly in smaller and historically underserved communities.
 Conclusion

We appreciate your agencies' efforts to provide greater clarity and proportionality within the CRA
framework. At the same time, changes intended to reduce regulatory burden should not
inadvertently reduce the lending, investment, grants, and services that CRA helps bring to
communities.

We urge the OCC and FDIC to preserve strong incentives for the full range of community
development activities and to consider the cumulative effects of the proposed changes on
nonprofit organizations, affordable housing, small businesses, CDFIs, and communities across the
country.

Specifically, we respectfully request that the OCC and FDIC preserve the dollar limits of banks in
their current categories and testing requirements, with Large Banks categorized as having over
$1.649 in assets, Intermediate Banks having between $412 million and $1.649 in assets, and Small
Banks having less than $412 million in assets. If this request cannot be met, we request that the
OCC and FDIC then preserve the Community Development Investment and Lending assessments
as separate and meaningful criteria for formerly Large Banks.

Additionally, given the size and impact of the proposed changes to the CRA programs, we request
the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period for the proposed changes to the CRA program 60
to 90 additional days.

Thank you for considering our comments.

Sincerely,

Harborlight Homes

For nearly half a century, CRA has driven banks to extend private capital financing to local
communities they serve, combating the legacy of redlining, promoting equitable lending, and
facilitating reinvestment in low- and moderate-income places and people. CRA has spurred
lending and investments in homeownership, small businesses, healthcare, childcare, and other
community needs, but nowhere is its impact more pronounced than in the effect CRA has had on
the production of affordable rental housing through the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing
Credit) program.

The Housing Credit, our nation's most important tool for the production of affordable rental
housing, relies heavily on investments from banks subject to CRA. In fact, approximately 80
percent of equity investments in the Housing Credit each year come from CRA-motivated bank
investors, according to a 2025 study by the accounting firm CohnReznick. Banks make these
investments not only to receive the modest return provided by the tax advantages associated with
investing in Housing Credit properties, but also because the full CRA examination for large banks
includes a distinct investment test. Because Housing Credit investment yields are typically modest,
large banks often could get a more substantial yield from making other forms of investment, but
often still choose to invest in the Housing Credit because Housing Credit investments help banks
meet their CRA obligations.

We are concerned that OCC and FDIC's proposal to reclassify banks with assets ranging from
$1.649 billion to $10 billion as intermediate banks rather than large banks subject to the full CRA
examination, including the investment test, could reduce competition in the Housing Credit equity
market, leading to lower pricing on credits and less housing produced. Of the 642 banks currently
classified as large banks, only 256 would maintain that designation under the proposal--a decline
of over 60 percent, according to the National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders
(NAAHL). This leaves only 6 percent of banks in the current large bank classification subject to

Dear Comptroller and FDIC Board Members:

On behalf of Community HousingWorks (CHW), I am writing to express our concerns regarding
the proposed amendments to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), particularly the proposal
to increase the large-bank asset threshold to $10 billion. While we recognize the agencies'
objective of reducing regulatory burdens on financial institutions, we are concerned that this
change could unintentionally weaken a critical source of investment in affordable housing.

Headquartered in San Diego, California, CHW is a nationally recognized nonprofit affordable
housing developer, owner, and operator that has been serving working families, seniors, and
individuals with disabilities for 38 years. Our portfolio includes more than 5,000 affordable
apartment homes across California and Texas, serving over 12,000 residents. In addition to
developing and preserving affordable housing, CHW provides resident-centered services focused
on financial stability, health and well-being, and educational success. Our mission is grounded in
the understanding that stable, affordable housing is essential to creating economic opportunity
and strengthening communities.

The Importance of CRA-Driven Investment in Affordable Housing

For nonprofit developers like CHW, access to LIHTC equity is fundamental to the financial
feasibility of both new construction and preservation projects. These developments typically
require complex financing structures that combine tax credit equity with public subsidies,
conventional debt financing, and other funding sources. Strong investor demand helps maximize
the equity available to support each development, reducing financing gaps and limiting the need
for additional public resources.

CHW has worked with large financial institutions, including US Bank, to support the financing
of affordable housing developments. Our ability to engage a diverse pool of financial partners,
including regional and mid-sized banks, is important to maintaining competitive financing
options and advancing our development pipeline.
 Our work has benefited from partnerships with regional and mid-sized institutions such as
California Bank & Trust, Banc of California, Banner Bank, City National Bank, and Western
Alliance Bank. These relationships demonstrate the important role that regional and mid-sized
financial institutions also play in supporting affordable housing financing. Further, this illustrates
the need to preserve CRA initiatives that encourage continued investment in LIHTC-supported
development projects.

Potential Consequences of Raising the Large-Bank Threshold

Under the proposed rule, increasing the large-bank asset threshold to $10 billion would move a
substantial number of financial institutions out of the separate CRA investment test. Although
these institutions would remain subject to CRA obligations, the change could reduce a significant
regulatory incentive for the affected institutions to provide direct investment in LIHTC
developments.

For CHW, reduced participation by regional and mid-sized banks could have direct consequences
on our ability to finance affordable housing. Fewer investors competing for tax credits could
place downward pressure on LIHTC equity pricing, resulting in less equity being made available
to individual developments. Even relatively modest reductions in tax credit pricing can create
significant financing gaps, requiring developers to secure additional subsidies, restructure
projects with less-sustainable terms, or delay (or even prevent) construction. Reduced tax credit
equity could further constrain the production and preservation of housing for low-income
households, seniors, and other vulnerable populations.

Recommendations

We respectfully urge the OCC and FDIC to reconsider the proposed $10 billion large-bank
threshold and evaluate alternatives that better preserve incentives for affordable housing
investment.

CHW supports efforts to modernize the CRA and reduce unnecessary regulatory burdens.
However, these objectives should not come at the expense of the financial incentives that have
helped facilitate affordable housing investment for decades.

Thank you for considering our comments and for your continued commitment to ensuring that
financial institutions meet the credit and investment needs of their communities.

To Whom It May Concern:

The Independent Community Bankers of America1 (ICBA) appreciates the opportunity to
comment on the joint notice of proposed rulemaking issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) (together, the Agencies)

ICBA has long supported the goals of the CRA while advocating for a framework tailored to the

framework that is faithful to the statute, focused on lending, and proportionate in its demands on

targeted modifications would make it stronger.

 General Comments

Community banks are the foundation of the nation's local economies. They make up roughly 90
percent of the nation's insured depository institutions, and they are often the only physical banking
presence in rural towns and underserved neighborhoods.2 Community banks are relationship-
based lenders. They make credit decisions based on local knowledge, long-standing customer
ties, and a personal stake in the borrower's success, rather than on a distant algorithm.

2 See Fed. Deposit Ins. Corp., 2023 Annual Report 54 (2024).

2
 As a result, community banks provide a share of small business and agricultural credit far larger
than their share of industry assets, and they keep local deposits working in the communities that
generated them.3

Yet the community banking sector is being constrained and contracted by onerous regulations
and market pressures. The number of banks has fallen from more than 18,000 in the mid-1980s
to roughly 4,200 today,4 and new bank formation has slowed to a trickle since the 2008 financial
crisis. This trend is, in large part, due to the cumulative weight of regulatory burden.

Compliance costs are largely fixed, so they consume a far larger share of operating expenses at
small institutions than at large ones, and each new reporting requirement, examination procedure,
or data collection mandate falls hardest on the banks with the fewest resources to absorb it.
Regulations that are not tailored to the size and risk of community banks thus inadvertently
accelerate the very consolidation that undermines access to credit in the communities the CRA
was meant to protect.

It is against this backdrop that ICBA strongly supports the purpose of the CRA. Enacted in 1977
in response to redlining, the CRA affirms that regulated financial institutions have a continuing
and affirmative obligation to help meet the credit needs of the local communities in which they are
chartered, including low- and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods, consistent with safe and
sound operations. Properly implemented, CRA regulations encourage lending that strengthens
neighborhoods, supports homeownership, and finances the small businesses and farms that drive
local economic growth.

ICBA believes the Proposal largely strikes this balance. The proposed changes would preserve
every bank's obligation to serve its community while ending one-size-fits-all requirements
designed for the largest, most complex institutions. ICBA commends the Agencies for this effort
and offers the following recommendations to ensure that the final rule achieves the CRA's goals
while right-sizing the regulatory burden on the community banks that have long been the CRA's
most natural practitioners.

 Proposed Changes to Bank Category Thresholds Would Better Achieve Proportionality

Of all the changes proposed by the Agencies, ICBA is most appreciative of the proposed revisions
to the asset thresholds that set the bank category boundaries. Inflation and consolidation have
pushed hundreds of community banks into exams built for the largest banks.

ICBA has long advocated for thresholds that reflect the size and structure of today's banking
industry, and the Proposal is a meaningful step toward restoring the proportionality the Agencies
originally built into the CRA framework. Recalibrating these boundaries would allow community
banks to redirect scarce compliance resources toward what the CRA is ultimately meant to
promote. The Proposal also rightly recognizes that evaluation methods designed for the largest,

summary-deposits-annual-survey

 most complex institutions should not be applied wholesale to banks whose business models are
inherently local.

While every bank would remain subject to the CRA, the proposed thresholds would provide relief
for approximately 800 community banks by reclassifying them as small banks, subject only to the
lending test. Nearly 400 additional banks would be reclassified from large banks to intermediate
banks, relieving them of stringent requirements that should be reserved for only the largest
financial institutions.

The need for this recalibration is evident in the structure of today's industry. Community banks
make up roughly 90 percent of the nation's insured institutions, yet they hold only a small fraction
of its assets. Subjecting hundreds of community banks to the most intensive evaluation methods
does little to expand the reinvestment footprint of the industry as a whole, while imposing real and
disproportionate costs on the institutions least equipped to bear them.

"Small Bank" Threshold

When the Agencies adopted the 1995 framework, they set the small bank threshold at $250
million, capturing approximately 80 percent of all banks, which together held roughly 14 percent
of industry assets, and reserving the more rigorous large bank evaluation for the minority of
institutions that held the remaining 86 percent.5

The 2005 amendments reaffirmed that approach, raising the small bank threshold to $1 billion,
creating the intermediate small bank category for institutions between $250 million and $1 billion,
and indexing both thresholds to inflation so that the vast majority of banks would remain outside
the most onerous categories.6

However, after decades of inflation and consolidation, that balance has eroded. Under current
CRA definitions, "small banks" represent only about 57 percent of institutions.7 The proposed
thresholds would restore the original allocation, with small banks again representing
approximately 80 percent of institutions and the large bank category once more covering roughly
85 percent of industry assets.8

While ICBA strongly supports the proposed thresholds, the Agencies should consider whether
going further would better reflect today's marketplace and the intrinsically different nature of
community banks. Community banks relationship-based model, local funding, local decision-
making, and concentrated geographic footprints mean that reinvestment in the community is

These structural differences also mean that compliance burdens fall disproportionately on
community banks. The largest institutions can spread the cost of dedicated CRA staff, data
systems, and outside consultants across enormous balance sheets. A framework that properly
accounts for these differences would also allow examiners to focus their resources where the
capacity to meet unmet credit needs is greatest.

ICBA believes that $10 billion is a more appropriate threshold for "small banks." The threshold is
a commonly-accepted practice to differentiate smaller banks and larger institutions. , and
"community bank" is the natural regulatory counterpart to the more colloquially used "small bank."
Congress has repeatedly drawn the line at $10 billion, including in the Dodd-Frank Act for
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau supervision and the debit interchange fee cap. The
Economic Growth, Regulatory Relief, and Consumer Protection Act of 2018 used the same
threshold for the community bank leverage ratio and the Volcker Rule exemption. And the Federal
Reserve likewise defines community banking organizations as those with $10 billion or less in
total assets, and the Agencies themselves rely on the $10 billion figure.

ICBA therefore urges the Agencies to set the small bank threshold at $10 billion, ensuring that
community banks are evaluated under the streamlined lending test that best reflects their
business model.

In the alternative, should the Agencies decline to adopt a $10 billion threshold, ICBA recommends
that the small bank threshold be set at no less than $5 billion. Support for this threshold comes
from the Small Business Administration's recent proposal to raise its size standard for small banks
from $850 million to $5 billion.

The Proposal itself acknowledges the divergence between the two standards, observing that
since 2005 the SBA's small bank standard has increased approximately 466.7 percent while the
CRA thresholds, adjusted only for inflation, have increased approximately 64.8 percent. Aligning
the CRA small bank threshold with the SBA's proposed standard would promote consistency
across federal definitions of a small bank, reduce regulatory complexity, and provide meaningful
relief to community banks that, by any reasonable measure, are small institutions.

"Intermediate Bank" Threshold

While ICBA appreciates the Agencies' proposal to increase the asset threshold of "Intermediate
Banks" to $10 billion, we encourage the Agencies to increase that threshold even further, set at
$30 billion. The intermediate category was created to bridge the gap between the streamlined
small bank evaluation and the full large bank framework, giving growing institutions a measured
transition rather than an abrupt jump in compliance obligations as they expand. That bridge works
only if it spans a meaningful range of asset sizes. A $30 billion threshold would keep that structure
intact, so that a bank crossing $10 billion is not immediately pushed toward the most intensive
evaluation methods while it is still, by any practical measure, a regional institution with a local or
regional footprint.

The $30 billion threshold also has a basis elsewhere in the FDIC's recent rulemaking from June
2026, where the Corporation proposed raising the asset threshold for deposit insurance
assessment purposes from $10 billion to $30 billion, with periodic inflation adjustments.9 Aligning

FDIC's regulations and reserve the large bank evaluation for the institutions with the scale,
resources, and market reach it was designed to assess.

Increasing the `Intermediate Bank" limit to $30 billion would also accommodate the Agencies'
potential increase of the "Small Bank" threshold at $10 or $5 billion. If the Agencies adopt a $10
billion small bank threshold, the intermediate bank category must be rescaled to match, or it would
shrink to a narrow band and lose its purpose.

 Focusing Performance on Credit Services and Lending Incentivizes Banks to Increase
 Access to Capital in their Communities

The Agencies propose targeted revisions to the performance tests and standards to better align
examinations with the statute's core objective of assessing how effectively banks meet their
communities' credit needs, to account for differences in banks' business models, and to reduce
regulatory burden. Retail lending evaluations for banks of all sizes would focus on a bank's major
product lines and evaluations would consider the range of retail credit products and services
offered, rather than retail deposit services. Finally, community development activities and retail
banking services not evaluated under another test would be considered as performance context,
with an emphasis on the responsiveness of a bank's activities to community needs. ICBA supports
this refocusing, which ties CRA examinations more closely to the lending that most directly meets
community credit needs.

Part of this approach will require the Agencies to identify a bank's major product lines. Rather
than leaving the selection of evaluated products largely to examiner discretion, the Proposal
would establish a clearer standard for small, intermediate, and large banks and offers two
alternatives.

Under Option 1, examiners would evaluate the bank's two largest product lines among home
mortgage, small business, small farm, and consumer lending, measured across the whole bank
by both dollar volume and loan count over the evaluation period; a bank lending in only one
product line would be evaluated on that line alone.10

Under Option 2, examiners would identify major product lines separately in each assessment
area, weighing the bank's overall lending volume and business strategy, its capacity to lend in
that area, and whether the product meaningfully contributes to local credit needs, so that a bank
could have more or fewer than two major product lines and they could differ by area.11

Under either option, consumer lending would qualify as a major product line only if it accounts for
more than half of the bank's retail lending by both dollar volume and loan count, or if the bank
elects to have its consumer lending evaluated.12 The Agencies explain that the change would
tailor examinations to each bank's business model and reduce the burden of evaluating products
that are not meaningful to it, and they seek comment on a de minimis loan floor, the treatment of
consumer loans, whether to measure lending by dollars, count, or both, and whether the method
should differ by bank size.13

Because the two major product lines would be determined using objective, bank-wide criteria,
banks could anticipate the scope of their CRA examinations, examiner discretion would be limited,
and the lending test would be applied consistently across agencies and examination teams. By
capping the review at two major product lines, the approach would also reduce the burden of
evaluating lending activities that represent a relatively small portion of a bank's business. The
treatment of consumer lending would further prevent examinations from expanding to cover
incidental consumer portfolios, while preserving a bank's ability to seek CRA consideration for
those activities. These features are consistent with ICBA's long-standing support for a tailored,
predictable examination framework that reduces unnecessary compliance burden.

Illustrative List

Since the Agencies first set out to reform CRA regulations more than a decade ago, ICBA has
stressed banker frustration with the predictability of receiving community development credit.
Under the existing framework and subjectivity of examiner discretion, community banks have not
had clear guidance on which activities would qualify for CRA consideration as community
development.

Based on subjective, examiner discretion, activities that received CRA credit varied by region and
by examiner.14 Without a published standard, banks gravitated toward the loans and investments
the agencies had previously credited, rather than toward activities that might best meet local
needs.15

The OCC sought to address this long-standing problem in its 2020 final rule, which established a
list of activities that would receive CRA credit16 and required the OCC to maintain that list on its
website.17 Although the OCC rescinded its 2020 rule in 2021, it retained its activity confirmation
process as a matter of policy, and the 2023 final rule adopted by the Federal Reserve, FDIC, and
OCC, since enjoined, again called for an illustrative list, to be jointly maintained, issued, and
updated by the agencies.18

The Proposal departs from that approach. Proposed __.13(a) would instead require each
Agency to separately maintain, and periodically update, its own publicly available, non-exhaustive
illustrative list of qualifying community development activities, and the Agencies state only that
they "intend" to coordinate.19

ICBA strongly supports codifying the illustrative list, which would promote transparency and give
banks the confidence to plan and invest in their CRA programs. However, ICBA's members are
concerned that permitting separate lists falls short of the Proposal's goal of modernizing the CRA
framework. Nothing in the Proposal would prevent the OCC and FDIC from developing divergent
lists over time, and the Federal Reserve, which has not joined the Proposal, would maintain no
list at all. The result could recreate the very uncertainty that existed before 2020, when banks
lacked clear regulatory guidance, except that the qualifying status of an activity would now turn
on a bank's charter rather than on the CRA's definitions.

For example, a holding company that owns both a national bank and a state nonmember bank

The Agencies already have a proven model for avoiding these problems in the Interagency

 Proposed Changes to Assessment Areas will Adhere to Statutory Intent and Comport
 with the Judicial Settlement

Just as the Proposal clarifies how a bank's performance is measured, it also preserves a sound
approach to where that performance is measured. Assessment areas are built from whole
metropolitan areas or political subdivisions, a bank may adjust them to the portion of a political
subdivision it can reasonably be expected to serve, and they generally may not extend
substantially beyond an MSA or State boundary or arbitrarily exclude LMI census tracts.

The 2023 CRA rules would have upended this framework by requiring large banks to delineate
facility-based assessment areas from whole counties and, more significantly, by creating "retail
lending assessment areas" wherever a large bank's mortgage or small business lending
exceeded specified volume thresholds, regardless of whether the bank had any physical presence
there.

However, recent court rulings have found that prior interpretation of "entire community" clashed
with the statutory text. Now the Proposal reflects this limit, stating plainly that "consideration of
retail lending outside of a bank's assessment area(s) would exceed the agencies' statutory
authority." ICBA strongly supports this approach and urges the Agencies to codify the limit in the
text of the final rule, so that the statutory boundary does not depend on future rulemakings or
examiner discretion.

While the Proposal has not explicitly included language that would alter the existing framework,
the preamble poses several questions for stakeholder feedback.

Of these, revisiting the "substantial portion" standard would help the largest number of community
banks. ICBA supports replacing the undefined standard with an objective numerical threshold that
banks can apply themselves before an examination.

Ideally, that threshold would operate as a safe harbor measured at the county level over a multi-
year period, so that a single anomalous year does not redraw a bank's assessment area.

In contrast, ICBA does not support a mandatory radius test. While a radius is simple, it would
potentially ignore rivers, mountains, highways, commuting patterns, and the bank's actual
customer base. In rural markets in particular, even a density-adjusted radius could sweep in large
areas that a community bank has no realistic capacity to serve.

ICBA also opposes an absolute prohibition on assessment areas that cross MSA boundaries.
Such a rule would fall hardest on rural and exurban community banks whose natural markets
straddle metropolitan and nonmetropolitan counties, forcing them to split a single, coherent
market into multiple assessment areas, each requiring separate analysis and documentation, with
no corresponding benefit to the communities involved.

Finally, ICBA recommends several additional protections. The Agencies should grandfather
existing assessment areas absent a material change in a bank's branch network. This would defer
to a bank's reasonable delineation and require a written rationale before an examiner expands or
rejects an assessment area. ICBA also encourages the Agencies to consider how branchless and
internet-based banks that gather deposits nationwide will be held to comparable reinvestment
obligations, so that the facility-based framework does not become a competitive advantage for
institutions with no physical presence at all.

The Proposal's revisions to the community development definitions would bring welcome clarity
and codify long-standing guidance, and ICBA supports them. ICBA offers several
recommendations that would further encourage the partnerships, investments, and local
institutions that expand access to credit in underserved communities. A recurring theme is the
role of mission-focused depository institutions, including CDFIs, MDIs, and mutual banks, which
convert capital and deposits directly into lending in LMI, minority, and rural communities.

Specific to CDFIs, ICBA urges the Agencies to restore the broader CRA eligibility for activities
supporting all types of CDFIs, regardless of geography. The 2023 proposal appropriately

consideration without regard to the geographic areas served by the CDFI. This approach provided
CDFIs with treatment comparable to that long afforded to minority depository institutions, women-
owned depository institutions, and low-income credit unions and was broadly supported by the
banking industry and the regulatory agencies.

The proposed 2026 rule would narrow this treatment by expressly providing geographic flexibility
for activities supporting nonprofit organizations, including nonprofit CDFIs, as well as MDIs, WDIs,
and LICUs, while subjecting activities supporting other CDFIs to the general assessment-area
requirements or proposed geographic flexibility standards. This distinction is difficult to justify
given the role and mission of CDFIs. CDFIs are specifically chartered or certified to expand access
to capital and financial services in underserved communities, often across geographic boundaries
that do not align with a supporting bank's assessment areas. Requiring traditional banks to satisfy
geographic requirements before receiving CRA consideration for supporting these institutions
could unnecessarily limit the pool of potential partners and reduce access to capital for smaller
CDFIs, particularly CDFI banks operating in areas without large or regional banking institutions.

The agencies should therefore explicitly recognize support for all CDFIs as a qualifying community
development activity and align the treatment of CDFIs with the proposed treatment of MDIs, WDIs,
and LICUs. Loans, investments, and grants to CDFIs should be eligible for CRA consideration
regardless of the geography served by the CDFI. This would provide greater clarity, eliminate an
unnecessary regulatory distinction, and better advance the CRA's objective of promoting access
to credit and investment in low- and moderate-income communities.

of $1 million or less. ICBA recommends that the preamble to the final rule also make clear that

qualify for CRA consideration. These institutions are themselves frequently small businesses,
operate with lean staffing, and deploy their resources almost entirely in the communities the CRA

For example, a community bank might lend its compliance officer to help a newly certified CDFI

of these activities strengthens an institution whose lending directly reaches LMI borrowers, small
businesses, and small farms, and each fits naturally within the statutory directive in 12 U.S.C.

Proposed paragraph (3)(iii) of the "community development" definition would also recognize
