depositors and communities rather than outside shareholders. Both are similarly mission-based,
and both are significant sources of credit to small businesses and small farms.

For example, a community bank's participation in a small business loan originated by an MDI
serving a predominantly minority neighborhood, or its purchase of a portion of a mutual bank's
small farm loan portfolio to free up the mutual's lending capacity, should be presumed to promote
economic development in the same manner as comparable activities with a CDFI. Expressly
listing MDIs and mutual banks would give banks the same certainty the Agencies intend to provide
for activities with SBA Certified Development Companies, Small Business Investment
Companies, Qualified Community Development Entities, and USDA Rural Business Investment
Companies, and would encourage partnerships that channel capital to small businesses that
might not otherwise qualify for traditional bank financing.

Every dollar invested in an MDI, CDFI bank or mutual bank becomes a multiple of new lending in
LMI, minority and rural communities, and the definitions should reward that partnership instead of
overlooking it.

Revitalization or stabilization of targeted geographic areas.

The proposed definition would include "any other area targeted by a government entity for
redevelopment that qualifies for significant economic incentives, such as tax credits, tax
abatements, or grants." ICBA supports this addition.

ICBA recognizes that the Agencies considered, but decided against, specifically naming areas
such as qualified opportunity zones in order to preserve flexibility as government programs
evolve. ICBA nonetheless recommends that the final rule expressly identify Qualified Opportunity
Zones and Persistent Poverty Counties as non-exhaustive examples of qualifying areas while
retaining the general category. Doing so would provide certainty for banks and examiners without
limiting the category's flexibility.

The case for naming Persistent Poverty Counties is particularly strong. These counties, generally
defined as those in which 20 percent or more of the population has lived in poverty over the past
30 years, are already targeted by Congress and Federal agencies, including the CDFI Fund and
USDA, for prioritized investment. Yet many of these counties do not have a formally adopted
redevelopment plan with tax credits, tax abatements, or grants attached, and many contain
metropolitan or moderate-income census tracts that would not fall within the existing "distressed
or underserved nonmetropolitan middle-income" category.

A community bank financing a grocery store, a rural health clinic, or other essential facility in a
Persistent Poverty County should not have to demonstrate that a local redevelopment designation
also applies. Likewise, explicitly naming Qualified Opportunity Zones, which the preamble already

11
 cites as an example, would ensure that examiners treat financing of a manufacturing facility or
mixed-use project within a zone as qualifying without case-by-case debate.

Community development grants.

The proposed definition of "community development grant" would require that a grant or donation
(1) be directly used by the recipient for a program, project, or initiative with a primary purpose of
community development; (2) benefit the bank's assessment area(s); and (3) when provided by a
large bank, go to a recipient whose indirect costs for administering the grant or donation do not
exceed 15 percent, calculated consistent with the Uniform Guidance for Federal Awards, 2 CFR
part 200. Large banks would also need to obtain the recipient's written commitment, a written
attestation of the 15 percent limit, and supporting documentation such as IRS Form 990 and
annual operating and program budgets.

While ICBA appreciates the Agencies' goal of ensuring that grant dollars reach local communities
rather than intermediaries, ICBA is concerned that smaller, local nonprofit organizations will have
difficulty meeting this limitation. A cap built on minimum overhead rate for small nonprofits would
end up punishing the very organizations that rate was designed to promote.

While larger nonprofits benefit from economies of scale, small, local organizations do not. Many
smaller nonprofits also lack the accounting systems to calculate and document indirect costs
under the Uniform Guidance. Perversely, compliance may require a nonprofit to purchase
software or hire outside accountants, which would itself be an indirect cost and make the limit
even harder to meet. The requirement would also increase cost and documentation burden for
the grantor bank, which would need to collect, review, and retain evidence of each recipient's
adherence.

ICBA therefore urges the Agencies to consider one or more of the following alternatives:

 (1) a de minimis exception under which the indirect cost limit and its documentation
 requirements would not apply to grants or donations below a specified dollar amount, such
 as $25,000 per recipient per year;

 (2) an exemption for small nonprofit organizations, such as those eligible to file IRS Form
 990-EZ or 990-N, or those with annual revenues below a set threshold;

 (3) a safe harbor allowing banks to rely on a recipient's good-faith written attestation,
 without further supporting documentation, absent information indicating the attestation is
 inaccurate;

 (4) recognition of a recipient's existing negotiated indirect cost rate agreement with a
 Federal agency as satisfying the standard;

 (5) measurement of indirect costs at the organization level using the functional expense
 allocation already reported on Form 990, rather than grant by grant; or

 (6) a categorical exclusion for grants supporting disaster relief and for in-kind donations,
 where indirect costs are inherently minimal or difficult to separate. ICBA also urges the
 Agencies to confirm that the indirect cost limit will continue to apply only to large banks
 and will not be extended to small or intermediate banks.

Nonprofit intermediaries

12
 The proposed definition of "community development grant" would require the organization
receiving a bank's grant to use the funds directly. This proposed limitation could deny CRA
consideration whenever a bank funds a nonprofit intermediary that passes grants or low-cost
capital on to the local organizations doing the community development work. ICBA is concerned
about this provision as it will make it more difficult for a community bank to deliver needed funds
to LMI communities.

Rather than standing between banks and communities, intermediaries can be an efficient and
accountable way for banks to reach certain communities. A well-run intermediary can serve
several purposes for the benefit of both the bank and end-beneficiary of the grant. Intermediary
organizations can pool funds from several banks and vet community organizations that individual
banks may lack the capacity to evaluate. They also provides technical assistance, monitor how
funds are used, and consolidate reporting. This enables a community bank to support a wide
network of small local nonprofits without building its own grantmaking operation. A rule that treats
intermediary groups as an obstacle would shrink the pool of organizations banks can practically
support.

Instead, ICBA recommends that the final rule create a defined category of "qualified nonprofit
intermediary" that addresses the Agencies' accountability concerns without excluding these
arrangements. Both the intermediary and each downstream recipient would have to be tax-
exempt nonprofits, and each downstream activity would have to qualify as community
development on its own merits. The intermediary would document the amount of the bank's
funding it deployed, the tax-exempt purpose of each recipient, how the funds were used, and
where the activity took place or whom it served. The downstream recipient's use of the funds
would satisfy the direct-use requirement. CRA consideration would follow the location or
beneficiaries of the downstream activity rather than the intermediary's headquarters, and it would
be limited to the dollars shown to have reached qualifying uses.

Federal Home Loan bank Affordable Housing Grants

ICBA also urges the Agencies to address a long-standing gap in how CRA treats grants that
community banks deliver through the Federal Home Loan Bank (FHLB) system. These include
Affordable Housing Program (AHP) direct subsidies and comparable FHLB homeownership,
special-needs, and disaster-recovery grants. Under the existing framework, a grant generally
counts as a qualified investment only when the bank funds it from its own resources. Because
AHP dollars come from the FHLB, examiners have typically treated the member bank as a
conduit. At most, they credit a few hours of community development service for preparing the
application. Neither the current regulations nor the Proposal speaks to these programs directly.
Their treatment is left to examiner discretion, which produces the same inconsistency the
illustrative list is meant to resolve.

Project sponsors cannot apply for AHP funds on their own. A member institution must submit the
application, disburse the subsidy, and monitor the project for compliance over its retention period.
Under the governing AHP agreement, the bank must also repay the FHLB if the project falls out
of compliance. The FHLB may collect directly from the bank's accounts, even when the bank
cannot recover from the sponsor. A bank that carries this administrative burden and balance-sheet
exposure is acting as the grantor, and not merely as a pass-through. Yet the existing framework
gives it little or no recognition for the work.

ICBA therefore recommends that the Agencies confirm that AHP subsidies and comparable FHLB
grants qualify as community development grants, or as another qualifying activity. This should
apply when the member bank administers the award and bears repayment risk. The Agencies

13
 should also recognize that these awards are often one layer of a larger financing package and
credit the bank's role in assembling it.

For example, a rural community bank financing a small LMI rental project may be unable to lend
the full amount because of its legal lending limit or concentration limits. By sponsoring an AHP
application, the bank can close the funding gap with an FHLB subsidy. The banks then administers
that subsidy for the life of the project and remains liable if the project falls out of compliance.

Clear recognition would also add new resources rather than simply steer existing ones. Federal
law requires each FHLB to set aside 10 percent of its annual earnings for AHP. In 2023 that
produced roughly $750 million, alongside approximately $1 billion in voluntary FHLB housing and
community development commitments. Encouraging community banks to take part in these
programs would grow the pool of future affordable housing dollars. These grants are also among
the few community development tools that scale for smaller banks without the size to take part in
tax-credit equity or national funds.

Community development investments.

ICBA supports the proposed definition of "community development investment," which would
include a deposit or membership share in a financial institution that has as its primary purpose
community development and that benefits the depositing bank's assessment area(s). MDIs, CDFI
banks, and mutual banks engage in significant community development activity, driven in part by
their own CRA obligations and mission. However, many of these institutions do not have a charter
or bylaws that expressly states community development as their primary purpose, even though
their lending and deposit activity is overwhelmingly directed to LMI and rural communities.

ICBA recommends that the Agencies presume that a depository institution has a primary purpose
of community development if it (1) is a certified CDFI or a designated MDI, or (2) is otherwise
predominantly engaged in LMI lending, or a predominant share of its borrowers and depositors
reside in LMI or nonmetropolitan rural areas. This approach would mirror the target market criteria
the CDFI Fund applies in certifying CDFIs, which generally require that at least 60 percent of an
institution's financing activity be directed to eligible target markets.

For example, a community bank that places a certificate of deposit with an MDI headquartered in
its assessment area, or with a mutual savings bank whose mortgage and small business lending
is concentrated in LMI and rural census tracts, should be able to receive CRA consideration
without first having to establish that the receiving institution's governing documents name
community development as its primary purpose.

Such deposits provide stable, low-cost funding that the receiving institution can lend out locally,
and they reflect the same type of partnership that Congress encouraged in 12 U.S.C. 2903(b) and
that the Agencies would continue to recognize in proposed __.21(e). A clear presumption would
reduce documentation burden for both institutions and encourage more banks to support mission-
focused depositories.

Complexity.

The Proposal would define "complexity" to focus on lending: an investment, grant, or service
would be complex if it is a necessary or beneficial component of a multicomponent financing
transaction involving a loan, and a loan or loan-equivalent investment would be complex if it
requires specialized expertise to consummate, such as an activity "not routinely provided by
private investors." ICBA recommends that the definition, or the accompanying preamble,
expressly recognize that investments, grants, services, and deposits made in or for MDIs, CDFI

14
 banks, and mutual banks meet this standard. These institutions consistently struggle to access
capital, and every dollar of capital they raise supports a multiple of new lending in their own
communities. Capital investments in these institutions are, by their nature, not routinely provided
by private investors and require specialized expertise to structure and evaluate.

For example, mutual banks have no shareholders, and generally cannot issue common stock.
They must rely on retained earnings to build capital. Mutual capital certificates (MCCs) offer an
alternative, and regulators have recently taken steps to make them more usable, including
October 2025 OCC and Federal Reserve guidance clarifying when MCCs qualify as regulatory
capital and a July 2026 Federal Reserve proposal to modernize Regulation MM and expand
capital-raising options for mutual holding companies.

Yet MCCs are rarely issued or purchased, and no robust or liquid market for them exists.
Recognizing a bank's purchase of MCCs as "complex" would increase the attractiveness of these
instruments, improve their marketability, and give mutual banks a more viable path to raise capital
beyond retained earnings. A community bank that purchases MCCs issued by a mutual savings
bank to fund expanded residential lending in LMI tracts, or that invests in a CDFI bank's
subordinated debt to support small business lending, is engaging in precisely the kind of
specialized, non-routine transaction the complexity factor is meant to reward.

Many mutual organizers also seek to raise capital to charter de novo institutions, which itself
should be recognized as a complex and non-routine transaction. Investments that help capitalize
a de novo mutual, MDI, or CDFI bank require significant expertise, carry meaningful risk, and are
almost never provided by conventional private investors. Recognizing them as complex would
help reverse the multi-decade drought in de novo mutual bank formation and expand access to
locally controlled banking in underserved markets.

Essential community facility.

ICBA appreciates the inclusion of the defined term "essential community facility," meaning a facility
that is open to the public and provides a valuable resource or service, including a school, library,
park, supermarket, hospital or other healthcare facility, public safety facility, or youth or community
center.

There is nothing more essential to a community than the presence of a locally owned community
bank. Locally-owned community banks are uniquely positioned to fill vital roles because their
relationship-based lending relies on local knowledge, local decision-making, and long-standing
ties to borrowers that distant institutions cannot replicate.

The FDIC's Community Banking Studies have likewise found that community banks are often the
only physical banking presence in rural and underserved counties.

Accordingly, ICBA recommends that the Agencies clarify that a community bank branch, or a de
novo community bank, located in or serving a targeted geographic area meets the definition of an
"essential community facility."

For example, financing or other support that enables a community bank to open or retain a branch
in a distressed or underserved nonmetropolitan middle-income census tract, in a Persistent
Poverty County, or in an LMI neighborhood that has lost its last bank branch should qualify as
revitalization or stabilization activity, just as financing for a supermarket or health clinic in that area
would. The Proposal already recognizes the value of preserving banking access by crediting
banks that donate, sell on favorable terms, or make available rent-free a branch to an MDI or
women's depository institution in a predominantly minority neighborhood. Extending that logic to

15
 recognize local community banks themselves as essential community facilities would help stem
the loss of banking access in the communities that need it most.

 ICBA Welcomes Flexibility on Credit for Outside Assessment Area Activity

While the Proposal appropriately anchors CRA evaluations to a bank's assessment areas, it also
offers welcome flexibility for community development activity beyond them. Proposed __.13(e)
would establish a general framework under which the Agencies would consider community
development loans, investments, and grants that benefit or serve areas outside a bank's
assessment area(s). This consideration would be entirely at the bank's option, and it would
replace the current "broader statewide or regional area" concept.

The Agencies explain that the current geographic limitations have produced "CRA hot spots,"
where many banks compete for a limited pool of qualifying activities, and "CRA deserts," including
many rural areas, where little community development activity occurs. To receive consideration
for activities outside its assessment areas, a bank would first need to show that it is meeting the
community development needs of its assessment areas by satisfying a "geographic flexibility
standard," for which the Agencies propose two alternatives.

Under Option 1, a quantitative standard, a bank would need to devote a minimum share of its tier
1 capital, allocated to each assessment area by weight, to community development activities in
that assessment area for each year of the evaluation period.

Under Option 2, a qualitative standard, a bank would qualify if it has an adequate level of
community development activities in each assessment area over the evaluation period,
considering both the dollar amount and the responsiveness of those activities to local needs, a
level the Agencies align with what has historically been considered "low satisfactory."

Under either option, a bank that meets the standard in all of its assessment areas would receive
consideration for outside-area activities in its State, multistate MSA, and institution-level ratings,
while a bank that meets the standard in only some areas would receive consideration only in
those States or multistate MSAs where it met the standard in every assessment area.

Importantly, a bank would never be required to engage in activities outside its assessment areas
to achieve a "satisfactory" or "outstanding" rating. ICBA supports this optional framework, which
would allow banks to comply with the CRA more efficiently, provide certainty about the level of
assessment area activity needed to unlock broader consideration, and help direct capital to
underserved areas without diluting the statute's focus on the communities where banks maintain
a physical presence.

While this flexibility is appreciated, ICBA suggests further refinement. A bank that wants to send
a modest share of its community development dollars to a CRA desert shouldn't first have to prove
itself in every assessment area it serves, especially when the recipient is a mission-driven lender
already reaching underserved borrowers.

Consistent with its recommendation for a de minimis exception to the indirect cost limit on
community development grants, ICBA urges the Agencies to adopt a de minimis exception to the
geographic flexibility standard.

Under this exception, a bank could receive consideration for a limited amount of community
development activity outside its assessment areas without first demonstrating that it has met the
standard in every assessment area. The exception could be capped at a modest level, such as a
fixed annual dollar amount or a small percentage of the bank's tier 1 capital or total community

16
 development activity, so that it would not displace the Agencies' assessment of performance
inside the bank's assessment areas.

Because a bank's ratings would continue to rest on its assessment area performance, a narrow
exception would remain consistent with the statute's focus on the communities surrounding a
bank's physical locations. Many worthy recipients of community development activity fall outside
a bank's assessment areas yet generate meaningful benefits for the communities they serve, and
mission-focused depository institutions, including MDIs, CDFI banks, and mutual banks, are
among the most important of them.

There is already a statutory and regulatory foundation for this approach. Under 12 U.S.C. 2903(b),
carried forward in proposed __.21(e), the Agencies consider capital investments, loan
participations, and other ventures undertaken in cooperation with minority- and women-owned
financial institutions and low-income credit unions, and the proposed rule expressly provides that
"such activities need not also benefit the bank's or savings association's assessment area(s)."
ICBA urges the Agencies to confirm in the final rule that activities qualifying under __.21(e) are
not subject to the geographic flexibility standard, and to extend comparable treatment to CDFI
banks and mutual banks, whose missions and community impact are closely analogous.

As an example, an intermediate community bank in suburban Ohio that places a $250,000
certificate of deposit with an MDI serving a predominantly minority neighborhood in Detroit could
receive consideration under __.21(e) regardless of where that neighborhood is located.

But if the same bank instead invests in subordinated debt issued by a CDFI bank in the Mississippi
Delta that is not minority-owned, or purchases mutual capital certificates issued by a rural mutual
savings bank in another State to support that bank's residential and agricultural lending, it would
receive no consideration unless it first meets the geographic flexibility standard in every one of its
own assessment areas, even though each activity directly expands credit in an underserved
community.

 Reduced Burden Associated with Data Collection

Small Business and Small Farm Data

Under the current rules, CRA small business and small farm data are defined by the size of the
loan rather than the size of the borrower. A "loan to a small business" is a loan with an original
amount of $1 million or less that is reported on the Call Report as either a loan secured by nonfarm
nonresidential property or a commercial and industrial loan,20 and a "loan to a small farm" is
similarly defined as a loan of $500,000 or less. Because these definitions turn on loan size rather
than the borrower's gross annual revenue (GAR), a loan of $1 million or less to a large business
with substantial revenues counts as a small business loan for CRA purposes, while a larger loan
to a genuinely small business may not. The purpose of the CRA is to ensure that banks help meet
the credit needs of their local communities, including their small businesses and small farms, and
community banks thrive when those businesses succeed and can obtain credit. A data framework
that conflates small loans with small businesses does not measure that purpose well.

The Proposal recognizes an opportunity to address this mismatch. The Agencies note that the
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau recently amended its small business lending data rule
under Section 1071 of the Dodd-Frank Act, and they ask whether it would be feasible to partially

FFIEC031_FFIEC041_202512_i.pdf.

 or fully discontinue CRA small business and small farm data collection and rely on Section 1071
data instead. ICBA supports discontinuing duplicative CRA small business data collection in favor
of Section 1071 data to the fullest extent possible. The revised Section 1071 rule, finalized in May
2026, defines a small business as one with GAR of $1 million or less, the same revenue
benchmark examiners already use to evaluate the distribution of a bank's lending to businesses
of different sizes. Relying on Section 1071 data would therefore measure lending to businesses
that are actually small, rather than lending in small amounts, and would spare covered banks from
collecting and reporting two overlapping data sets on the same loans.

Because Section 1071 applies to covered lenders regardless of charter, including nonbank
lenders and larger CDFI loan funds that meet its coverage threshold, its data would offer a broader
view of local small business credit markets than bank-only CRA data, helping banks and
examiners better understand unmet credit needs as part of performance context.

Additionally, Section 1071 captures information about applications as well as originations, offering
richer insight into the demand for credit in a bank's community. Finally, eliminating duplicative

18

example, a $750,000 equipment loan to a manufacturer with $40 million in annual revenue counts
today as a CRA small business loan, while a $1.2 million loan to a family-owned business with
$900,000 in annual revenue is excluded from CRA small business loan data, even though only
the latter plainly serves a small business.

The Agencies should, however, account for two limits of the revised Section 1071 rule: it excludes
agricultural lending, and it applies only to lenders with at least 1,000 covered originations in each
of two consecutive years. Because Section 1071 will not generate small farm data, the Agencies
should streamline, rather than expand, small farm data requirements, and they should not impose
new CRA data collection on any bank that falls outside Section 1071's coverage.

Consumer Lending Data

Community banks are built around localized credit delivery, focusing primarily on home mortgage,
small business, and agricultural lending tailored to the needs of their communities. For most
community banks, consumer lending is secondary to these core products. Under the Proposal,
large banks for which consumer lending is a major product line would be required to collect and
maintain consumer loan data, while other banks could continue to collect such data at their option
in order to have their consumer lending evaluated. The Agencies ask whether, to the extent banks
may continue to opt into a consumer lending evaluation, the optional data collection provisions
should be retained. ICBA urges the Agencies to retain them. A mandatory consumer data
collection standard would impose substantial administrative burden for a loan category that, for
most community banks, is not a core product, while an optional framework honors the principle of
proportionality and the emphasis on flexibility that run throughout the Proposal.

Optionality also serves a real purpose for the community banks that do emphasize consumer
lending. For some, small-dollar consumer loans are among the most responsive products they
offer to LMI borrowers. A rural community bank that makes hundreds of used-vehicle loans so
that LMI residents can commute to work, or a bank that offers small-dollar installment loans as an
affordable alternative to high-cost payday lending, should be able to demonstrate that
responsiveness by electing to collect data and have its consumer lending evaluated. Eliminating
the option would deny these banks credit for meaningful activity, while mandating collection would
burden the many banks for which consumer lending is incidental. ICBA also asks the Agencies to
consider allowing a bank that opts in to collect data only for the consumer loan categories it wishes
to have evaluated, as the current rules permit, rather than requiring data for all categories.
Preserving an optional, flexible approach would best match data obligations to each bank's size,
business model, and risk profile.

 Downgrades in Consumer Protection Violations Create Duplicative Standards for Banks

The current rules require a bank's CRA rating level to be downgraded by one point if the bank
violates CRA rules and consumer protection laws such as the Truth in Lending Act, unfair,
deceptive, or abusive acts or practices (UDAAP), the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, and the
Military Lending Act. Past Treasury reports have acknowledged that CRA is not a consumer
protection law and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) does not have authority
over CRA.21 Treasury added that the agencies' policy is not to downgrade a bank by "more than
one level" unless there is a logical connection between a bank's CRA rating and the evidence of

21 The Dept. of the Treasury, Community Reinvestment Act Findings and Recommendations, pg. 19, (Apr. 3, 2018),
4-3-18 CRA memo.pdf.

19
 discriminatory or other illegal credit practices in the bank's CRA lending activity.22 In the event
there is strong qualitative and quantitative evidence of violations, the OCC would consider any
remedial actions taken by the bank in the agency's evaluation.23

The OCC later updated its 2018 Policies and Procedures Manual, which departed from Treasury's
treatment of downgrades to a bank's CRA level by changing the language from "by more than
one level" to the current language, "by only one rating level unless the agencies find egregious
illegal practices."24 An egregious finding still depends on whether there's a nexus between a
bank's CRA rating and the evidence of discriminatory or other illegal credit practices in the bank's
CRA lending activity.

The Proposal expounds on several aspects of the OCC's 2018 Manual. The Proposal would
include and codify UDAAP, the Military Lending Act, and the Service Members' Civil Relief Act in
the list of violations. Most importantly, the Agencies propose two alternatives for how they consider
discriminatory and other illegal credit practices. The first alternative requires evidence that a
discriminatory or other illegal credit practice violates a law, rule, or regulation cited in a public
enforcement action by a Federal or State agency or in a judicial order. The second alternative
proposes that a discriminatory or other illegal credit practice violates a law, rule, or regulation cited
in a Federal or State agency examination report, enforcement action, or judicial order. The second
alternative would also allow Agencies to withhold confidential supervisory information from the
public section of the bank's CRA Performance Evaluation.

Both options place greater emphasis on objective, clearly defined criteria for CRA downgrades,
which would benefit both banks and examiners by allowing institutions to better understand the
specific violations and material information underlying an adverse rating determination. Of the
alternatives presented, Option 2 appears more comprehensive because it considers examination
findings in addition to judicial orders and enforcement actions. Although banks may be concerned
about the inclusion of examination findings as a factor in downgrades, limiting consideration to
findings involving specific violations of law identified in the regulation would promote greater
objectivity and consistency.

ICBA recommends the agencies should clarify whether "regulatory actions" encompasses both
formal and informal actions, as the current language does not clearly distinguish between them.
Defining the types of actions that may be considered would provide banks with greater
transparency and predictability in how consumer protection violations affect their CRA
evaluations.

ICBA also recommends that the Agencies should consider how changes to downgrades in
consumer protections have not addressed the differences between consumer protection laws and
CRA regulations. For example, Treasury's 2018 Findings and Recommendations acknowledge
that banks still receive double downgrades for consumer protection and CRA violations, even
after the agency's clarification. The double downgrades also occurred even when a bank's
products were not part of its CRA performance evaluations.

 Improvements to the Presentation of the Public File

The current rules require banks to maintain a physical CRA public file containing information
related to their CRA performance, such as branch locations and services, assessment area
information, public comments, and the most recent performance evaluation, with the full file
available at the main office and portions available at each branch. The Proposal would modernize
this requirement by requiring banks to maintain the public file on the bank's website or on a
website maintained on the bank's behalf, eliminating the requirement to keep paper files at the
main office and branches, and allowing banks to satisfy their public notice obligations by
identifying the website where CRA information is posted.

ICBA supports this approach. Most banks already maintain websites where customers can find
information about their products, staff, operations, and regulatory status, and moving the public
file online simply aligns the CRA with the way the public now accesses information. The Agencies
note that approximately 96 percent of U.S. adults use the internet, and community banks' adoption
of websites has followed the same trajectory. In a 1999 Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis
survey of Ninth District community banks, only 22 percent reported having a website, although 66
percent planned to develop one within two years.25 Today, nearly all South Dakota banks maintain
a website, according to the FDIC's BankFind database.26

To ensure the transition delivers its intended burden reduction, ICBA recommends several
clarifications. First, the Agencies should develop a model public file or standardized template
illustrating the required content and organization. Many community banks will be posting this
information online for the first time, and some bank websites today offer little guidance on what
CRA public disclosures should look like. A model would promote consistency, help the public
navigate files across institutions, and reduce the risk of technical violations.

Second, the Proposal would require banks to provide a means of viewing the online public file at
their branches, such as a computer or other device. The Agencies should clarify that this
requirement may be satisfied through staff-assisted access on an existing branch device or by
providing a copy upon request, rather than through a dedicated public terminal that could raise
cybersecurity concerns and impose unnecessary costs on small branches.

Third, for the small number of banks that do not maintain a website, the Agencies should confirm
that a simple page hosted by a third-party vendor satisfies the requirement, consistent with the
Proposal's allowance for a website maintained on the bank's behalf, and should consider offering
an FFIEC-hosted option. Finally, the Agencies should provide a reasonable transition period and
confirm that minor formatting or posting errors will be treated as matters for correction rather than
as deficiencies affecting a bank's CRA rating. Under this approach, a small agricultural bank with
three branches could comply at minimal cost by posting a single, template-based public file on its
existing website and directing branch visitors to that page on a lobby tablet.

Dakota banks covers roughly 300 banks).

21
  ICBA Stresses the Need for Harmonization Across all the Federal Banking Agencies

If finalized, this Proposal would dramatically improve the CRA framework from its current state.
However, in many respects, this dramatic improvement is only achievable if every federal banking
agency promulgates a harmonized rule. ICBA urges the Agencies to finalize the rule jointly with
the Federal Reserve Board (FRB), and to consider providing extended period of time between
finalization and the rule's effective date so FRB might have additional time to adopt the Agencies
final rule through its own interim final rule.

The CRA was designed to work as a single interagency framework, and for most of its history, the
banking agencies have jointly issued regulations, examination procedures, and the Interagency
Questions and Answers.

Unfortunately, FRB has not joined the Proposal. If the Agencies finalize the rule without FRB's
involvement, state member banks would stay under the existing regulations while national banks
and state nonmember banks move to a new framework. Asset thresholds, product-line evaluation,
assessment area rules, and the definition of a qualifying community development activity would
then depend on a bank's primary federal regulator rather than on its size, business model, or
service to its community.

This split would undercut the clarity, consistency, proportionality and overall benefit that the
Proposal is meant to deliver. If the Agencies decide to proceed without FRB involvement, ICBA
recommends the Agencies institute a longer effective date than they would otherwise adopt. This
added time would let FRB adopt the final rule on an interim final basis or through an expedited
rulemaking before the new framework takes effect.

Banks, examiners, and communities would then move to a single set of standards at the same
time rather than through a period of divergent treatment that could prove disruptive and hard to
unwind. It would also ensure that the reforms the Agencies have carefully developed reach every
community bank, whatever its regulator.

 Conclusion

The Proposal marks a significant and welcome turn toward a CRA framework that is faithful to the
statute, focused on lending, and proportionate to the size and business model of the institutions
it governs. By modernizing bank category thresholds that inflation and consolidation have left
behind, grounding assessment areas in a bank's physical presence, clarifying how major product
lines and community development activities are evaluated, and giving banks optional flexibility to
support underserved areas beyond their footprints, the Agencies would preserve every bank's
obligation to serve its community while relieving community banks of requirements designed for
the largest institutions.

ICBA's recommendations would build on that foundation. Setting the small bank threshold at $10
billion, or at a minimum $5 billion, would align the CRA with the line Congress and the banking
regulators have long used to identify community banks. Adopting major product lines, with modest
safeguards, replacing the ambiguous language, codifying the physical-presence requirements,
and recognizing the distinctive role of MDIs, CDFIs, mutual banks, and locally owned community
banks throughout country will provide substantial benefit to this country's community banks and
the towns and cities they serve.

concerns community bankers have raised over many years. ICBA appreciates the opportunity to
comment and stands ready to work with the Agencies as they finalize the rule.

To Whom It May Concern:

The Massachusetts Bankers Association (MBA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed
changes to the regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) as published in the
Federal Register August 12, 2026. (CRA NPR)

The MBA serves as the premier partner and trusted resource for banks throughout Massachusetts and New
England. We represent more than 120 depository institutions operating in the Commonwealth and advocate
as a unified voice to promote success in a dynamic and evolving industry. Our membership includes a
diverse range of banks, from single-location community institutions to some of the nation's largest financial
organizations, providing a broad perspective on the opportunities and challenges facing the banking sector.

We appreciate the thoughtful approach to updating the CRA to reflect the new financial services
environment in a modern era and the goal to reduce regulatory burden for our member banks. We also
appreciate the opportunity to provide our thoughts on several of the provisions outlined within the proposed
rule and encourage the agencies to reevaluate the proposed rule prior to implementation of a final rule.

Consistency between Regulators

The prospect of different CRA frameworks applying to institutions supervised by different federal banking
agencies creates significant challenges for consistency, fairness, and regulatory effectiveness. Through the
CRA NPR, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
 proposed revisions without participation from the Federal Reserve, creating the possibility that banks with
different primary regulators will operate under materially different CRA standards. This fragmented
approach departs from a longstanding principle of CRA administration: regulators should hold similarly
situated institutions to comparable expectations regardless of charter type or supervisory agency. When
regulators apply divergent standards, they increase the likelihood of inconsistent examination outcomes,
create confusion among community groups and other stakeholders, and make it more difficult to compare
CRA performance among institutions that compete in the same markets.

A bifurcated federal regulatory framework would also increase compliance burdens and operational
complexity for multi-bank holding companies and institutions operating across multiple regulatory
jurisdictions. Different federal agencies could require organizations with multiple bank subsidiaries to
develop and maintain separate CRA compliance programs, policies, reporting processes, and examination
preparation strategies to meet varying regulatory expectations. Rather than reducing regulatory burden,
multiple CRA frameworks would increase costs and divert resources away from community development
activities and toward regulatory administration. Likewise, community organizations and local leaders
would face greater difficulty understanding how banks are evaluated, reducing transparency and limiting
their ability to engage effectively with financial institutions on community credit and development needs.

The Massachusetts Bankers Association's membership consists primarily of state-chartered institutions in
Massachusetts. Consequently, most member institutions must comply with both federal and state CRA
requirements. For decades, state and federal regulators have maintained substantial consistency in their
CRA frameworks and examination approaches. This alignment enables financial institutions to understand
regulatory expectations clearly and implement compliance programs efficiently without unnecessary
administrative burden. Consistent standards also provide community groups with greater transparency,
allowing them to better evaluate and compare bank performance across institutions and markets.

The MBA strongly advocates for all federal agencies with CRA oversight to adopt and maintain a unified
regulatory framework. Consistency across agencies promotes fairness, transparency, and effective
supervision while minimizing unnecessary compliance burden. A coordinated approach ensures that
regulators evaluate institutions under comparable standards, supports meaningful performance
comparisons, and allows banks to focus more resources on meeting the credit and development needs of
their communities.

The MBA strongly supports a unified approach by all federal agencies with oversight of CRA.

Asset Thresholds

The Association supports the proposal to increase the "small bank" asset thresholds to include institutions
under $1 billion and "intermediate bank" asset threshold to between $1 billion and $10 billion, and index
them to nominal gross domestic product so they remain relevant over time. It is also important to note that,
while they continue to support their communities in a variety of ways, institutions with assets under $1
billion will not be subjected to burdensome data collection and reporting requirements. These are welcomed
updates to the CRA.
 Community Impact

The proposed rule could unintentionally shift administrative burdens from financial institutions to
community-based organizations. By narrowing the range of activities eligible for CRA consideration and
increasing documentation expectations for certain community development grants and donations, the
proposal may require nonprofit organizations, community development corporations, and other local
partners to provide more detailed records, certifications, and evidence demonstrating that funds directly
support qualifying community development purposes. Rather than allowing banks to bear primary
responsibility for documenting CRA eligibility, the proposal could encourage institutions to seek additional
information from community partners to support examination requirements. Smaller nonprofit
organizations often operate with limited staff and resources, making it difficult to absorb new reporting and
compliance obligations without diverting time and funding away from serving low- and moderate-income
communities.

The proposal may also discourage partnerships between banks and community organizations by increasing
the complexity of obtaining and maintaining CRA consideration. Banks may perceive greater regulatory
risk associated with grants, donations, or community development activities, may require community
partners to complete extensive due diligence, provide ongoing performance reporting, or demonstrate
compliance with detailed eligibility standards. As a result, community organizations could face higher
administrative costs and longer funding approval timelines, particularly when working with institutions
now needing to further document CRA credit. This outcome would be inconsistent with the CRA's
traditional objective of fostering collaboration between banks and community stakeholders to address local
credit and development needs. Instead of streamlining community investment, the proposal could create
barriers that reduce the efficiency and effectiveness of community development partnerships, ultimately
limiting the flow of resources to the neighborhoods and populations the CRA was designed to benefit.

Conclusion

The Massachusetts Bankers Association appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed
revisions to the Community Reinvestment Act and supports efforts to modernize CRA regulations to
reflect today's financial services environment. We also appreciate the opportunity to provide our thoughts
on several of the provisions outlined within the proposed rule and encourage the agencies to consider our
views prior to implementation of a final rule.

As always, please do not hesitate to contact us if we can be of further assistance or if we can further
clarify any points made within.

Sincerely,

To Whom It May Concern:

The Kentucky Bankers Association (KBA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposal of the
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
(collectively, the Agencies) to amend their regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA).1 The KBA is a trade association representing banks of every size and charter type doing business
in the Commonwealth of Kentucky.

After consulting with representatives from the Kentucky Bankers Association's one hundred and fifty-one
(151) member institutions ranging in asset size from twenty-one million dollars ($21,000,000) to over
three hundred and seventy billion dollars ($370,000,000,000.00), the Kentucky Bankers Association
submits its comments to the Proposal as set forth below.

The KBA has joined the comment letter submitted by the American Bankers Association and other state
banking associations. We write separately, and briefly, to address matters of particular consequence to
Kentucky's banks and to the rural communities a great many of them serve. We support the proposal
generally, and we commend the Agencies for recalibrating the CRA asset classifications and for
grounding this rulemaking in the statute's focus on community credit needs.

1Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52114 (Aug. 12, 2026).
 Page 1 of 8
 I. Introduction

The banking industry faces many challenges. However, until recently, none of those challenges included
CRA compliance.

While the KBA is not currently aware of any member banks rated "Needs to Improve", that was not the
case just several months ago. Several KBA member banks were designated "Needs to Improve" along
with the onerous restrictions and reputational labels that come with such a designation.

As discussed in more detail below, this was not a result of banks failing to properly serve their
communities; rather, these designations were a result of wayward examinations, artificial ratios that fail to
account for community demographics, and conclusions that were not justified by law, regulation or
otherwise.

While those banks have now been properly examined and given appropriate ratings, that does not mean
that we can forget the errors of the current regulation in causing damage to these banks and their
communities.

Consequently, the KBA appreciates the opportunity to share its insights on CRA and the proposed
changes to CRA through its comment letter.

II. The KBA Supports the Modernization of CRA

The purpose of the Community Reinvestment Act of 1977 (CRA) is to "encourage banks to help meet the
credit needs of the local communities in which they are chartered, consistent with banks' safe and sound
operations, by requiring federal banking regulatory agencies to examine banks' records of meeting the
credit needs of their entire community including low- and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods."2
"Specifically, in passing the CRA, Congress found that (1) banks are required by law to demonstrate that
their deposit facilities serve the convenience and needs of the communities in which they are chartered to
do business; (2) the convenience and needs of communities include the need for credit services as well as
deposit services; and (3) banks have a continuing and affirmative obligation to help meet the credit needs
of the local communities in which they are chartered."3

As noted in the 2020 proposal, "The current CRA regulatory framework has not kept pace with the
transformation of banking and has had the unintended consequence of incentivizing banks to limit some
of their CD loans and investments to shorter terms that otherwise may be best to meet the needs of their
communities."4

"The Community Reinvestment Act is more than 40 years old and has only been significantly amended
once, in the mid-1990s when cellphones still played the snake game and there was a Blockbuster on every
corner."5 CRA hasn't "received a major update since the Clinton administration."6 "Technology has
changed since then. Consumer needs have changed since then. Banking has changed since then. But the

2 Department of Treasury, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Notice of Proposed Rulemaking: Community
Reinvestment Act Regulations, 85 Federal Register 1204, January 9, 2020, page 1205.
3 Department of Treasury, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Notice of Proposed Rulemaking: Community
Reinvestment Act Regulations, 85 Federal Register 1204, January 9, 2020, page 1205.
4 Department of Treasury, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Notice of Proposed Rulemaking: Community
Reinvestment Act Regulations, 85 Federal Register 1204, January 9, 2020, page 1205.
5 Richard Hunt, BankThink CRA Reforms Must Go Beyond Branch Banking, AMERICAN BANKER, October 7, 2019.
6 John Kimble, Response from Community Groups to OCC/FDIC Joint CRA Proposal, BALLARD SPAHR LPP
CONSUMER FINANCE MONITOR, December 27, 2019.

 Page 2 of 8
 CRA has not and the 1977 law is no longer working. Modernization is needed for the law to continue
working for communities across the country."7

The KBA believes that CRA modernization is long overdue and commends the OCC and Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") for their efforts. The KBA believes that many of the proposed changes
referenced below will allow banks to better serve their communities in line with the purpose of CRA.

III. CRA Performance Should Be Measured by a Bank's Actual Record, Not by Ratios That Do
Not Measure Community Reinvestment.

The KBA's broadest concern with the CRA framework, both as it exists today and as the proposal would
revise it, is the weight placed on ratios. A ratio is easy to examine and easy to compare across institutions.
It is not, for that reason, a measure of whether a bank is helping to meet the credit needs of its community,
and several of the ratios embedded in the CRA framework can be improved by doing less for the
community rather than more.

While the KBA understands the baseline approach to having some formula to measure CRA, the reality is
that these formulas do not account for any communities' actual needs. The KBA and its member banks
have been fortunate to spend time with the leaders of each agency setting forth these proposed changes
and one common theme emerged: the best test for whether a bank is meeting its CRA requirements is the
fact that they are doing business in their communities.

Simply put, banks do not stay in business when they fail to serve their communities. They do not
aggregate deposits, they do not make loans, and they have no relationships if they are not serving their
communities.

There is no ratio to address that fact, but conversely, it is a measure that should serve as the baseline of
any assessment. CRA itself was based on community service, not ratios. In issuing any final rule, the
Agencies should not stray from that original purpose.

"As Senator William Proxmire, who authored the CRA legislation, testified when discussing its purpose:
By redlining let me make it clear what I am talking about. I am talking about the fact that banks and
savings and loans will take their deposits from a community and instead of reinvesting them in that
community, they will actually or figuratively draw a red line on a map around the areas of their city,
sometimes in the inner city, sometimes in the older neighborhoods, sometimes ethnic and sometimes
black, but often encompassing a great area of their neighborhood."8

Kentucky banks are not redlining. Kentucky banks are reinvesting in their communities. No bankers are
drawing redlines around any city or area and staying out of that area. They continue to serve all of their
communities in all one hundred and twenty (120) counties.

Despite those facts, that does not mean that Kentucky banks are not facing artificial pressures by means of
the rations set forth below. In some Kentucky counties, there are virtually no mortgages being made.
Importantly, it is not because banks will not make them; it is because there is no demand. It is an
unfortunate part of our Commonwealth's reality, and something we are all working on addressing, but,
conversely, it leaves many banks in these communities with a choice between failing an artificial ratio
they cannot meet because loan demand does not exist and closing the one institution that serves as the
lifeblood of the community. That is not CRA.

7 Richard Hunt, BankThink CRA Reforms Must Go Beyond Branch Banking, AMERICAN BANKER, October 7, 2019.
8 Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, Request for Comment: Request for Comment Regarding Community
Reinvestment Act, 87 Federal Register 33884, page 33888, June 3, 2022.

 Page 3 of 8
 The proposed CRA framework includes ratios, but those ratios should only serve as one metric in the
process, not a determinative metric that places banks in peril as seen in Kentucky previously. We address
each of those ratios below.

A. The loan-to-deposit ratio. Among the quantitative criteria applied to smaller institutions, none
illustrates the difficulty better than the loan-to-deposit ratio. Because Option 1 would place approximately
103 of Kentucky's 120 banks under the Small Bank test, any ratio retained in that test will be the most
widely applied measure of CRA performance in the Commonwealth. To the extent the final rule carries
the loan-to-deposit ratio forward, we urge the Agencies to be explicit about what it does and does not
show. A bank's loan-to-deposit ratio is determined as much by the character of its deposit base and the
credit demand in its market as by its willingness to lend. A community bank that gathers deposits from an
entire rural county, or one serving a county with an aging and declining population, will carry a low ratio
however aggressively it lends, because deposits are abundant and qualified credit demand is not. A
number of Kentucky counties present precisely that profile. The bank in such a county is not failing its
community; it is serving a community whose deposits exceed its borrowing capacity -- evidence of local
trust, not of withheld credit.

The converse is more troubling still. A bank can raise its loan-to-deposit ratio by purchasing loan
participations originated hundreds of miles away, by buying into syndicated credits, or by lending outside
its market altogether. Each of those steps moves the ratio in the favorable direction while moving capital
out of the community. A measure that rewards an institution for exporting credit, and penalizes it for
holding local deposits it cannot prudently lend locally, is not measuring community reinvestment.

B. The inside-assessment-area lending ratio. A related difficulty attends any criterion measuring the
percentage of a bank's lending inside its assessment area. Kentucky's trade areas do not follow county
lines. A bank in a county-seat town commonly serves farms, small businesses, and households across two
or three adjoining counties in which it maintains no office and which it cannot reasonably delineate.
Lending to those customers -- who are its neighbors in every sense that matters to them -- reduces the
ratio. The measure penalizes the bank for serving the community it actually has in favor of the community
a map has assigned it.

C. Other ratio-based measures. We share the concerns the ABA letter expresses regarding the proposed
geographic flexibility standard, and add only this: in rural Kentucky a county may see one qualifying
affordable housing or infrastructure project in three years and three in the fourth. A bank that funds all of
them has met its community's needs, but a bank measured against an annual percentage of Tier 1 capital
will be found wanting in three years out of four, for reasons entirely outside its control. We likewise
endorse the ABA letter's treatment of comparative data, and add one observation particular to our
markets: in much of rural Kentucky the comparator set is very small, and it consists in substantial part of
credit unions and nonbank lenders that are not subject to the CRA at all and that do not report the data
against which a bank would be measured. A comparison drawn on that basis tells the examiner little about
the bank and less about the community.

We do not ask the Agencies to abandon quantitative analysis; numbers discipline examinations and
promote consistency. Asset-size thresholds, which determine which performance test applies rather than
whether a bank has passed it, are a different matter altogether, and we support their recalibration below.
What we ask is that the final rule, the examination procedures, and examiner training state plainly what
the 1995 framework has always assumed: that these ratios are diagnostic rather than dispositive, that
performance context governs their interpretation, and that no ratio operates as a threshold an institution
must clear to earn a given rating. Where a ratio and a bank's actual record of lending point in different
directions, the record should control.

IV. The KBA Supports Option 1 and a $30 Billion Intermediate Bank Threshold.

 Page 4 of 8
 The KBA strongly supports Option 1, which would define Small Banks as those with less than $1 billion
in assets and Intermediate Banks as those with between $1 billion and $10 billion. The effect in Kentucky
would be substantial. Under the thresholds in effect for 2026 -- $412 million and $1.649 billion9 --
approximately 10 of the 120 institutions headquartered in Kentucky are evaluated under the Large Bank
framework, 39 as Intermediate Small Banks, and 71 under the Small Bank test. Under Option 1, a single
Kentucky-headquartered institution would be a Large Bank, 16 would be Intermediate Banks, and 103 --
roughly 86 percent -- would be evaluated under the Small Bank test. Nine Kentucky banks would move
out of the Large Bank framework and its associated data collection and reporting obligations, and 32
would move from the Intermediate to the Small Bank test. That realignment restores, in Kentucky, very
nearly the distribution the Agencies themselves contemplated in 1995. We also support indexing both
thresholds to nominal gross domestic product, for the reasons the ABA letter sets out.

The preamble asks whether the Intermediate Bank threshold should instead be set at $30 billion. The
KBA supports that alternative and encourages the Agencies to adopt it. At $30 billion, no bank
headquartered in Kentucky would be subject to the Large Bank framework. More to the point, an
institution holding between $10 billion and $30 billion in assets -- large by Kentucky standards -- still
operates a relationship-based, geographically concentrated business that bears little resemblance to that of
the largest banks in the country, and the full Large Bank apparatus of silo-by-silo community
development testing, loan-level data collection, and grant-level documentation is poorly matched to it.

To be clear, the KBA does not believe that altering these thresholds will alter Kentucky banks'
community investment. Kentucky banks have always remained, and will always remain, invested in their
communities. They will continue to fund the broad and diverse needs of their communities. In light of that
commitment, these adjusted thresholds mean only that Kentucky's banks can be more flexible in ensuring
their communities' needs are met rather than focusing solely on rations and math equations that may not
address the communities' true needs.

V. The Exclusion of Operating Liquidity Financing Would Fall With Particular Force on
Agricultural Lenders.

Agriculture is a defining feature of Kentucky's economy, and agricultural lending is a core business line
for many Kentucky banks. We join the ABA letter's request that the definition of economic development
include financing used for ongoing operating liquidity, and write to explain why the exclusion would be
felt most acutely by farm lenders.

A farm operating line of credit is, by its nature, seasonal working capital: it funds seed, fertilizer, fuel,
feed, and labor in the spring and is repaid at harvest. It does not expand productive capacity, acquire
equipment, or enlarge a physical footprint, and so would not qualify under the first proposed subcategory
of economic development; neither would it qualify as technical or supportive services or as participation
in a government program. The exclusion would therefore remove from CRA consideration the single
most consequential credit product a rural Kentucky bank offers -- not at the margin, but entirely, and by
operation of a definition that appears to have been drawn with commercial rather than agricultural
borrowers in view.

VI. Assessing Solely Banks for CRA is Misguided

The purpose of CRA is clear; CRA is designed to assess whether institutions are meeting the credit needs
of their community. However, when a large populace of institutions lending in these communities are
exempt from the proposed rule, it is fatally flawed.

 The Community Reinvestment Act became effective in 1977.10 "During the last two decades, the lending
landscape has transformed. Traditional providers- namely banks-consolidated, leading to branch closures.
The number of banks in the U.S. has declined from over 18,000 in 1986 to under 5,200 today. The
number of branches declined by 14 percent from 2009 to 2020."11

"In the past, small businesses principally sought credit from banks; however, as banks have merged and
consolidated, particularly in the wake of the Great Recession, they have provided less financing to small
businesses. As noted earlier, the number of banks has declined significantly since a post-Great Depression
peak in 1986 of over 18,000 institutions to around 5,200 institutions today, while 13,500 branches closed
from 2009 to mid-2020, representing a 14 percent decrease. Although nearly half of counties either
gained bank branches or retained the same number between 2012 and 2017, the majority lost branches
over this period. Out of 44 counties that were deeply affected by branch closures, defined as having 10 or
fewer branches in 2012 and seeing five or more of those close by 2017, 39 were in rural counties. Of
rural counties, over 40 percent lost bank branches in that period; the rural counties that experienced
substantial declines in bank branches tend to lower-income and with higher proportion of African
American residents relative to rural counties, raising concerns about equal access to credit."12

Meanwhile, new providers and products, such as fintechs and merchant cash advances (MCAs), have
become increasingly prevalent in the small business lending market. Financing by MCA providers is
estimated to have increased from $8.6 billion in volume during 2014 to $15.3 billion in 2017. From 2017

estimated to have increased from $1.4 billion in outstanding balances in 2013 to approximately $25
billion in 2019.13 "Credit unions increased their small business lending from $30 billion in 2008 to at
least $55 billion in 2019."14

"During a period in which depository institutions have been providing relatively less funding, small
businesses have increasingly relied on other nondepository institutions for financing. Since
nondepositories typically do not report their small business financing activities to regulators, there are no
authoritative sources for either the number of such entities or the dollar value of financing they provide to
small businesses. However, what data is available makes it clear that fintech firms are rapidly increasing
their share of the small business financing market."15

"The Bureau estimates that the market for small business financing products totaled $1.4 trillion in

of the small business financing market up to $2.4 trillion."16 "$190 billion in outstanding balances for
private term loans and lines of credit was extended by various non-depository institutions, namely
commercial finance companies, fintechs, and non-depository CDFIs"17

While many of the above statistics are limited to small businesses, these numbers could continue for
pages. Nonetheless, the summation is the same: large groups of lenders that are not banks are extending
significant amounts of credit. However, unlike banks, these lenders are not subject to CRA. Simply put,
if the FDIC or any other agency really wants to accomplish the purpose, these lenders must be subject to
CRA. Otherwise, the rule remains outdated, inaccurate, and provides no true measure as to whether
lenders are truly meeting the needs of their communities.

A lot has changed since 1977. Many community banks have closed and alternative forms of lending now
occupy substantial portions of the lending space. If the FDIC and others are serious about accomplishing
the purpose of CRA, alternative lenders must also be subject to CRA. Otherwise there is simply no
means of understanding whether communities are truly being served. As long as CRA remains a metric
solely for banks, it will remain an archaic law with limited information and demographics as to the true
market and will not resolve any issues on which communities need additional assistance.

While the KBA understands the statutory limitations of the FDIC and OCC, the KBA disagrees with CRA
as it applies solely to banks.

VII. Several Further Provisions Warrant Particular Support in Rural Kentucky.

Disaster recovery. Kentucky has experienced repeated and severe natural disasters. The December 2021
tornado outbreak in western Kentucky and the July 2022 flooding in eastern Kentucky each caused
catastrophic loss of life and property, and in both events Kentucky banks were among the first institutions
to extend credit, restructure existing loans, and fund recovery in the affected counties. We support
eliminating the exclusion of FEMA Public Assistance Categories A and B, and we urge the Agencies to
expand "designated disaster area" to include areas subject to state disaster declarations. Kentucky's
Governor regularly declares states of emergency for flooding, ice storms, and localized windstorm events
that devastate a handful of counties without meeting the thresholds for a federal Major Disaster
Declaration. For the bank in the affected county, the recovery need is identical.

VIII. The Board of Governors Should Join This Rulemaking So That Kentucky's State Member
Banks Are Not Placed at a Competitive Disadvantage.

The proposal would amend only the OCC's CRA regulation at 12 C.F.R. part 25 and the FDIC's at 12
C.F.R. part 345. The CRA regulation of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 12 C.F.R.
part 228, would remain as it is. The consequence is that every state member bank in the Commonwealth
would be excluded from the relief this rulemaking affords, while the institutions with which it competes
most directly would receive it.

This is not a theoretical concern. Of the 120 FDIC-insured depository institutions headquartered in
Kentucky, 18 are state member banks supervised by the Federal Reserve, and they include several of the
largest banks headquartered in the Commonwealth.19 Under the asset thresholds the Agencies set out as
Option 1, which the KBA supports, the disparity appears repeatedly and across every size band in which

threshold may classify differently.

roughly $7 billion in assets would remain subject to the Large Bank framework, while an FDIC-
supervised Kentucky bank somewhat larger than it would be evaluated as an Intermediate Bank. The
same pattern recurs at roughly $4 billion, where a state member bank would remain a Large Bank while a

A bank's decision whether to become a member of the Federal Reserve System turns on considerations --
correspondent and payment services, capital and liquidity management, and in some cases charter
decisions made generations ago -- that have nothing to do with its record of helping to meet the credit
needs of its community. The CRA performance test applied to a bank, and the data collection and
reporting burden that accompanies it, should not be allocated among comparable institutions on a basis
unrelated to size, business model, or performance. For as long as part 228 remains unamended,
Kentucky's state member banks will be examined under a materially different and more burdensome
CRA regime than the banks across the street.

The KBA therefore urges the Agencies to coordinate with the Board of Governors so that a single,
uniform CRA framework applies across all three agencies' supervised institutions. We do not suggest that
the Agencies withhold or delay relief for the institutions they supervise in order to wait for the Board; the
relief in this proposal is overdue and the banks that stand to receive it should not be made to wait longer.
We ask instead that the Agencies pursue conformity actively, state in the preamble to any final rule their
intention to do so, and make clear that they will not treat the resulting disparity as a settled feature of the
framework.

IX. Conclusion

We urge the Agencies to adopt Option 1 and to consider a $30 billion Intermediate Bank threshold; to
make clear that the performance tests' ratios are diagnostic rather than dispositive; to recognize operating
