Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

The Urban Economic Development Association of Wisconsin, Inc. (UEDA) is submitting this comment in opposition
to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of
Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)1 because it would significantly weaken the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).

In addition, given the complexity and of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that before making the
proposed changes, the OCC and FDIC carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income
communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting
any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.

UEDA is a 501(c)(3) membership organization dedicated to the professional development of individuals and groups
working in economic and community development in Wisconsin. Incorporated in 1997, we focus on and advocate
for sustainable homeownership and housing, financial empowerment and economic mobility, small business
growth, community investment, and regional workforce and transportation strategies.

We are an active member of the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) and National Low Income
Housing Coalition (NLIHC). On behalf of our members, we work in collaboration across sectors, and at local,
regional, and national levels to advocate for continued investment in lending products and services to individuals
and businesses in the communities we serve.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that banks meet
the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also
recognized that communities depend on access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain
especially important in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss, and unequal
access to mainstream financial services.

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).

 Page 1 of 5
 The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change how regulators
evaluate community development, bank services, and support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that
these changes are being considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-
income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

UEDA leads and supports two coalitions that have active participation from financial institutions, community-based
organizations, and public entities: Take Root Milwaukee (sustainable homeownership & neighborhoods), and Bank
On Greater Milwaukee (banking access & financial education). These two programs exemplify how community
groups and banks can work together through public-private partnerships to have long-range impact by investing in
underserved communities and this happens largely through the CRA.

Our chief concerns with the proposed rule include:
 1. A reduction in community investment expectations for all banks.
 2. Setting a low community development benchmark that effectively turns into a goal for financial services.
 3. Putting affordable housing and community development investment and financing at risk.
 4. Undermining the financial health of unbanked and underbanked communities.
 5. Restricting CRA credit for grants that support local nonprofit operating costs.

REDUCING EXPECTATIONS, SETTING LOW BENCHMARKS, AND PUTTING MUCH-NEEDED INVESTMENT AT RISK

CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In Wisconsin, from 2010-2024, banks made
over $63.16 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts helping people
and families build wealth through homeownership. Banks also made over $27.74 billion in CRA qualified lending to
small businesses a huge investment in both urban and rural communities in the State.

Investments such as these have benefited our community in many ways. For example, since 2013 UEDA has worked
with Take Root Milwaukee (TRM) members (takerootmilwaukee.com) on an annual analysis of Home Mortgage
Disclosure Act (HMDA) data for the City of Milwaukee and the Milwaukee-Waukesha Metropolitan Statistical Area
(MSA). In 2025, banks made over 35,000 home loans in the Milwaukee MSA; 42% of them were for home purchase.
In the City of Milwaukee, over 8,000 home loans were made in 2025 and 48% of them were for home purchase.
Additionally, 55% of the loans in Milwaukee were to LMI borrowers, and 46% of the loans were to borrowers of
color. TRM is a program that is strongly aligned with the CRA, and its bank members provide a greater percentage
of their home loans to LMI borrowers and people of color than their peers. This is critically important as the City of
Milwaukee has lower rates of homeownership compared to the MSA.

We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends the incentives for banks to invest in communities. For
example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital devoted to either community development
loans or investments would be enough to receive a passing CRA rating2. However, that percentage is far lower than
the percentage that NCRC determined the largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.

For example, NCRC found that the median percentage of annual community development lending in CRA
assessment areas was 6.8% of tier 1 capital3. If banks chose to meet the 0.625% threshold, that would represent a
reduction of 85% in their community development lending activity. Setting such a low regulatory floor could lead to
a de facto benchmark with significant and negative consequences for rural and urban communities.

2 The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit for outside their assessment areas if the banks surpass a benchmark of 0.625% of
its tier 1 capital for community development loans and likewise 0.625% for investments. 91 Fed. Reg. 52121, 52140 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
We are concerned that the practical effect of this proposal is that the benchmark will serve not as a floor, but a ceiling.
3 NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk, (Sept. 10, 2026), https://ncrc.org/cras-
new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-development-activity-at-risk/.

 Page 2 of 5
 For example, in our Take Root program, we continue to see persistent challenges in terms of low-income borrowers
and communities accessing credit in a challenging homeownership market. In the Milwaukee MSA this would likely
look like fewer LMI families obtaining affordable mortgage loans, or small business owners struggling to access
capital either directly through banks or Community Development Finance Institutions (CDFIs), who are a critical part
of the lending landscape for small and micro businesses in our state.

It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet community needs. Before finalizing the rule,
the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce lending, services or investment available
to low- and moderate-income communities and whether communities that have experienced historic
discrimination or disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.

BANK BRANCHES AND ACCESS TO BANKING SERVICES
By raising the large-bank threshold to $10 billion, 417 banks would no longer receive the full large-bank
examination, which includes separate testing that evaluates branch delivery systems and banking services. We are
concerned that approximately 5,000 branches in low- and moderate-income census tracts would no longer be
evaluated as part of the large-bank CRA service test under the proposal, and more than 4,000 branches in majority-
people-of-color census tracts would also lose CRA consideration.

In 28 states, at least one-third of branches located in LMI census tracts would no longer receive any CRA
evaluation.4 In Wisconsin, this would put nearly 46% of LMI branches and 33% of branches in communities of color
in jeopardy. This means that our state is the 4th highest out of 54 in terms of banks losing community development
obligations if the proposed threshold levels are put in place.

The proposal would also narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service test. Today, examiners may
consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and information about the costs and features of deposit
accounts. The proposal would limit this criterion to credit services, removing deposit products such as checking and
savings accounts from direct evaluation under the service test.

As such, examiners would no longer evaluate whether those products are affordable and responsive to
community needs even though 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million are
underbanked. CRA review of the cost and features of deposit products has played an important role in encouraging
banks to address these disparities and increase access to banking.

Since 2019, UEDA has hosted Bank On Greater Milwaukee (bankonmilwaukee.org/), joining over 100 coalitions
across the country to promote safe, affordable accounts and trustworthy financial education to consumers. We
work with 55 members (including 21 financial institutions) and assist banks to partner with service providers to
connect clients to safe and affordable accounts and provide financial education/resources.

For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate from access to credit and
economic opportunity. They can determine whether families can safely receive income, build savings, establish
banking relationships, and obtain responsible credit. According to recent Prosperity Now and FDIC data, 7% of
Milwaukee County households are unbanked, and 16% are underbanked nearly a quarter of households in the
County are not using safe, affordable bank products at all or paying more in fees to use alternative services.

4 NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3, 2026), https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-rollbacks/.

 Page 3 of 5
 Cities for Financial Empowerment (CFE) Fund research indicates that unbanked Financial Empowerment Center
clients are half as likely to increase savings and more than one-third less likely to establish a credit score. Bank On
National Data Hub findings show that opening an account can lead to broader use of bank and credit union services,
supporting goals such as higher education and homeownership.

We strongly believe that regulators should review the quality of all bank credit and deposit products, especially in
the consumer arena, which changes rapidly. This includes marketing, language access, terms, rates, fees, defaults,
and collections. By reducing the importance of deposit services and branch performance in CRA evaluations, the
proposal eliminates incentives for banks to offer basic products that help unbanked and underbanked households.

SUPPORT FOR LOCAL ORGANIZATIONS

We are concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and nonprofit organizations.
Banks are a significant source of support for affordable housing, small-business development, financial counseling,
workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based services through grants,
investments, loans, and partnerships with nonprofit organizations. Through the CRA infrastructure, local
community-based organizations are able to build important and often transformative relationships with banks,
working with them to understand the specific needs of their communities.

For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and new
documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations5. For smaller
nonprofit organizations, this limit may be unrealistic they have fewer programs and funding sources over which to
spread necessary costs such as staff, rent, technology, accounting, compliance, etc. If banks conclude that grants to
smaller organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger
organizations whose activities are easier to verify, with detrimental impact to community-based organizations.

Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments, and partnerships can play in supporting
community development and smaller organizations. UEDA is a small nonprofit, with an annual budget of around
$500,000 and four full-time staff. Along with our Take Root homeownership and Bank On programs, we provide
capacity building and technical assistance to local nonprofits. Often CRA-focused grants from banks are how small
organizations are able to secure support for community initiatives that stabilize neighborhoods.

These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into tangible benefits
for residents. Many community-based organizations operate with limited staff and infrastructure they may not
maintain program documentation in the format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. Rules governing
what kinds of grants and community development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have
consequences well beyond the banks themselves.

Before finalizing these provisions, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule primarily in terms of reducing
perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also determine what the changes mean for the
communities CRA is intended to serve there could be impacts that ultimately reduce resources available to low-
and moderate-income communities.

SUMMARY
Although progress has been made by banks in serving low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities and
communities of color as a result of CRA, there is still much work to be done to ensure that people have access to
fairly priced credit and financial services they can trust to serve their needs.

5 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,129 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).

 Page 4 of 5
 Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:
 identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny under the proposal;
 quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community development activities subject

 to CRA evaluation;
 assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations, including rural

 communities and communities of color; and
 consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing meaningful

 community accountability.

Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes that the OCC and FDIC
should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and released for public
comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting community credit
needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that accountability without first
demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire
communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.

Milwaukee's continues to be one of the most segregated cities and metro areas in the country due to a legacy of
past redlining practices that denied certain groups of people access to credit and underinvested in specific
geographic areas. UEDA works with a diverse cross-section of members and other partners that include nonprofits,
financial institutions, CDFIs, government agencies, small businesses, neighborhood associations, funders, and
individuals concerned with these issues. Working to reverse the impact of these historical disparities requires
consistency and intention, with contributions from the private, public, and nonprofit sectors the CRA is a critical
tool that helps us develop relationships and innovative strategies to meet the needs of our community.

Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from community
organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates, and other stakeholders that do not have dedicated regulatory
staff, additional time is warranted. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit
grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. An extension would allow affected organizations to
evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather examples from the communities they serve, and provide the
agencies with a more complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies
extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days, for a total of 120 days.

Sincerely,

 Consistent with the Agencies' objectives of creating better alignment with the statute,
reducing unnecessary burden, and improving clarity, AENB respectfully recommends that the
Agencies make the following targeted changes to the Proposal:

 Retain the limited purpose designation and standalone CD test. Eliminating the

 Retain the current, qualitative approach to incidental lending. The proposed five

 Do not adopt the 1.25 percent Tier 1 capital threshold for banks with one AA. Under

  II. The Agencies Should Retain the Limited Purpose Bank Designation and Community
 Development Test

 AENB strongly opposes eliminating or narrowing the limited purpose bank designation.
The Agencies have not identified a deficiency in the existing framework that warrants
eliminating it, and AENB's experience demonstrates why the designation continues to serve an
important regulatory purpose. Under the standalone CD test, the OCC found that the Bank
exhibited excellent responsiveness to the credit and CD needs of its AA and recognized
approximately $2.22 billion in loans and investments.2 If the limited purpose bank designation is
not retained in the final rule, AENB would be evaluated primarily on its retail lending in a single
AA, instead of how it actually helps fulfill CD needs in LMI communities. As a result, the
Proposal would reduce AENB's ability and incentive to conduct CD activity outside of the AA,
potentially reducing over $869 million3 in CD activity relative to the activity recognized in
AENB's last performance evaluation.

 The Proposal recognize that eliminating the limited purpose designation would be a
significant change for the small number of banks now evaluated solely under the CD test, but
suggest that the retail lending test ("RLT") would be suitable because those banks' consumer
lending would no longer be omitted from the retail evaluation.4 However, the limited purpose
designation was never intended to address this issue; indeed, under the existing CRA regulations,
the RLT can already evaluate consumer lending. Instead, the limited purpose designation
addresses a more fundamental and continuing structural mismatch: AENB conducts a nationwide
card business through a bank with one AA, and the RLT is focused on performance within a
bank's AAs. Adding credit cards to the categories of loans evaluated under the RLT does nothing
to resolve that structural mismatch. For AENB, designating consumer lending as a MPL would
mean that the Bank's nationwide portfolio would be evaluated through a framework centered on
its single AA, which accounts for less than one percent of AENB's consumer-lending activity.
The proposed RLT exacerbates the very geographic mismatch that the limited purpose
framework was designed to address.

 A CRA evaluation framework should measure how a bank serves its community within
its established business model; it should not require the bank to redesign that model to avoid a
negative result driven by the structure of the test. AENB's nationwide card platform, single
office, and limited physical footprint are longstanding features of a business model that is subject
to ongoing prudential supervision. The Proposal could create incentives to alter lending, product,
or legal-entity decisions merely to improve CRA metrics, which would contradict Congress's
explicit statutory direction to the Agencies to evaluate performance consistently with safe and
sound operations.5 The most direct and administrable solution is to retain the limited purpose
designation and continue evaluating designated banks under the CD test.

percent of the data collected would inform the RLT's AA-based analysis of AENB. That effort

To Whom It May Concern,

On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") together, (the "Agencies") promulgated a Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA). The CRA statute, combined with one common regulatory structure
among all three prudential regulators, has helped create a durable incentive for banks to
provide loans, investments, grants, and services in communities that have historically lacked
access to capital.

We appreciate the Agencies' efforts to reform the CRA regulations and support some of the
Agencies' provisions that could improve the CRA framework and increase responsible capital in
underserved communities. However, we have grave concerns that the increases in the asset
thresholds, related changes in how banks are evaluated under CRA, and the unwarranted
restrictions on operating grants will undermine the statutory goals of CRA. We also have
concerns with several interacting provisions that could further weaken community
development incentives that the current CRA statutory and regulatory framework creates and
reinforces, by impairing the flow of much needed capital in the nation's most underserved
communities.

Who We Are

OFN is the nation's leading network and intermediary focused on community development
investment, managing over $1.3 billion in total assets and a membership of about 500
community development financial institutions (CDFIs). OFN's membership includes community
development loan funds, credit unions, banks, and venture capital funds. OFN is a trusted
investment partner to the public, private, and philanthropic sectors and, for nearly 40 years,
has helped partners invest in communities to catalyze change and create economic
opportunities for all.
 OFN members are vital CRA stakeholders because they turn capital into impact by channeling
CRA-motivated investments into low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities. Banks are
critical partners in our work, by providing loans, investments, grants, and technical assistance.

Investing in CDFIs is an investment in the economic health and vitality of communities.
Through their specialized lending models, deep community relationships, and local expertise,
CDFIs serve as catalytic financing partners, making possible projects that might otherwise
never materialize. These investments, in turn, strengthen local economies, create new
opportunities for lending and investment, and expand the pipeline of viable customers and
projects for banks. Based on most recent annual member data available, conservative
estimates show that banks lend at least $6.2 billion to our members, comprising 46% of the
total borrowed amount. With a focus on people over profit, CDFIs leverage bank capital to fill
credit gaps, extending the reach of mainstream lenders that they not be able to reach one
their own and complement conventional sources of capital.

Since its founding in 1986, OFN members have originated about $137 billion in financing,
helping to create or maintain more than 3.8 million jobs, start or expand more than 1.2 million
businesses and microenterprises, and support the development or rehabilitation of more than
3 million housing units and more than 14,000 community facility projects in rural, urban, and
Native communities across the United States. With cumulative net charge-off rates about one
percent, OFN members lend prudently and productively in the LMI communities that have
always been the focus of CRA. These statistics clearly demonstrate that CDFIs are a vital part
of the country's financial infrastructure, by supporting healthy local and regional economies,
providing economic returns to communities, and improving financial conditions in which banks
operate.

Symbiotic Relationship Between CDFIs and CRA-Motivated Banks

Bank partnerships with CDFIs take many forms, including direct lending and investments in
CDFIs or CDFI-financed projects, equity-equivalent investments, deposits, and grants
supporting CDFI lending and operations. Banks also collaborate with CDFIs through loan
participations, borrower referrals, joint product development, and technical assistance. Many of
these activities qualify for CRA consideration when they serve a community development
purpose or meet the needs of low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities.

These partnerships are mutually beneficial. CDFIs are themselves bank customers, generating
revenue through borrowing, deposits, and other banking services. More importantly, CDFIs
extend banks' reach into underserved markets by making possible financing opportunities that
conventional lenders may not be able to undertake independently. CDFIs leverage their
specialized underwriting, flexible loan terms, and ability to combine public, private, and
philanthropic capital to structure complex transactions, address financing gaps, and mitigate
risks that might otherwise prevent bank participation. As the Federal Reserve Bank of
Cleveland has documented, CDFIs play a catalytic role in bringing together financing and
partners to make projects possible that otherwise might not move forward, helping bring

Page 2
 complex, "but for" projects to fruition by coordinating with banks, economic development
organizations, and developers to assemble financing from multiple sources.1

CDFIs also help develop the next generation of bank customers and investment opportunities.
Through smaller-dollar financing, technical assistance, and relationship-based lending, CDFIs
help individuals and businesses build credit histories, strengthen financial capacity, and
eventually qualify for conventional financing. Beyond individual borrowers, CDFIs can help
cultivate entire markets by demonstrating the viability of investments in underserved
communities and building the financing infrastructure necessary to attract mainstream capital.

While these partnerships offer tangible business benefits to banks, those benefits do not
necessarily translate into sufficient private-sector investment absent CRA incentives. The
higher transaction costs, longer development timelines, and additional risks associated with
underserved markets can make community development financing less attractive than
conventional lending, even where it produces long-term business opportunities. CRA helps
bridge this gap by encouraging banks to commit capital and resources to partnerships that
may not otherwise compete for investment on purely commercial terms.

CDFI partnerships generate real business value for banks, but CRA provides the incentive for
banks to undertake community development activities whose benefits may be longer-term,
indirect, or less immediately profitable than conventional lending opportunities. In this way,
CRA not only incentivizes individual transactions, it catalyzes bank capital, supports the
development of underserved markets, and strengthens the broader community development
finance ecosystem. Weakening these incentives risks reducing the flow of capital to CDFIs and
the communities they serve, while also limiting the longer-term business opportunities that
these partnerships help create for banks.

Process Concerns Give Rise to Uncertainty and Unfounded Analysis

Before turning to the substance of the proposal, we raise concerns with the process used to
develop and release this proposal. Any proposal that is finalized without the participation of the
Federal Reserve would not benefit from a full picture of CRA-incentivized banking activities and
would result in the fracturing of the CRA framework between the three banking agencies.
Different rules and policies mean communities and CDFIs could face substantially different
treatment of community development activities depending on which regulator oversees the
banks serving them.

Moreover, we are concerned that the proposal introduces additional uncertainty at a time when
banks and other CRA stakeholders have already experienced repeated shifts in the regulatory
framework. The OCC adopted a new CRA rule in 2020, then reconsidered and rescinded it in
2021. The three banking agencies jointly adopted another comprehensive rule in 2023, and
that rule was subsequently stayed by litigation and slated for rescission. This repeated cycle of
rulemaking, implementation planning, litigation, and reversal has required banks and

 community development stakeholders to continually adjust to changing expectations. Major

perpetuating that uncertainty rather than providing the stable, predictable framework banks
and communities need to make long-term investments. Business planning becomes harder and

Another concern is that the proposal does not appear to fully account for its downstream
effects on communities and community development markets, while prioritizing the reduced
burden on banks. CRA is consequential for affordable housing, small business finance, rural
development, Indian, Tribal and Native communities and the broader ecosystem of bank-CDFI
partnerships. Changes of this scale warrant enough time and careful analysis to understand
those effects before they are finalized. However, the fact that there has been limited time for
public comment and the lack of empirical data grounding the Agencies' arguments has made it
difficult to fully capture the potential implications and unintended consequences for
communities. While we recognize that the goal of the CRA proposal is to reduce compliance
obligations on banks, the CRA statute is clear that its purpose is to ensure the flow of
responsible capital to communities with unmet credit needs. We urge the Agencies to approach
any changes to the CRA with a detailed analysis of community impact and alignment with
statutory objectives.

Raised Asset Thresholds Jeopardize Community Development Finance: Section IV.A,
"Asset Thresholds"; Questions 13

The proposal defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets,
intermediate banks as institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as
institutions with more than $10 billion. About 800 banks that currently face a separate
community development test as intermediate small banks would become small banks and no
longer be subject to that test or responsive to the incentives it creates. Another approximately
400 banks that are currently evaluated as large banks would become intermediate banks,
losing the separate large-bank lending, investment, and service tests and many associated
data-reporting requirements.

States with large rural populations would be disproportionately affected as they would
experience the highest rates of transitioned banks in the country. In Louisiana, Minnesota,
Georgia, Wisconsin, Iowa, Alaska, Mississippi, and Indiana, more than 40% of banks operating
in the state would no longer be subject to community development obligations under the
proposal. The states with the highest number of full-service branches in LMI census tracts that
would be lost due to the proposal are Texas, Illinois, California, Missouri and Louisiana.2 In
these communities, the loss of even one or two CRA-motivated bank partners can materially
affect whether critical community development projects are financed. For communities with
fewer financial institutions and fewer sources of private capital to begin with, losing even a
handful of CRA-motivated lenders and investors could have an outsized effect on whether

 affordable housing is built, small businesses are established and grow, and whether needed
community facilities get financed.

Harm to Communities from Loss of Community Development Finance

The asset-size thresholds determine whether and how a bank's community development
performance is evaluated and therefore affect the strength of banks' incentives to engage in
community development activities. The Agencies acknowledge in the proposal that when banks
become subject to a CD test under the current framework, the explicit evaluation of their CD
activities typically results in banks adjusting their CRA programs.

Banks moving down the threshold ladder and losing incentives for community development
activities would have a direct impact on our partnerships. Based on the proposal to redefine
the asset-size thresholds for small and large banks at $1 billion and $10 billion, respectively,
and using a limited sample of OFN members, we conservatively estimate that $283 million in
member bank debt is at risk from the bank funders that would move from the large or
intermediate categories into lower asset-size categories. For some members, the share of bank
debt at risk under this proposal approaches 50%, including CDFIs serving states such as Idaho
and North Dakota.

Misalignment with Congressional Priorities on Affordable Housing and New Markets
Tax Credit (NMTC)

The change also undermines Congress's recent efforts to address the growing affordability
crisis, including the nation's severe shortage of affordable housing. Through the One Big
Beautiful Act, Congress expanded the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) and made New
Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) permanent-- two bipartisan, popular federal tax credit programs
with a long track record of success in communities. In conjunction with the raising of the Public
Welfare Investment (PWI) cap through the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, these recent
legislative passages demonstrate that Congress is committed to tackling rising housing,
construction and financing costs. Meanwhile, the proposal undermines these important
investment tools which could further strain already challenging the project economics.

LIHTC and NMTC are considered equity investments that are evaluated under the standalone
investment test for large banks which currently have a distinct 25%-weighted component of
their CRA evaluation devoted to qualified investments. Moving banks into the lower size
category would mean these transitioned banks would only be subject to a diluted evaluation
that considers all CD in one test. This means a bank may have less reasons to engage in
complicated LITHC and NMTC deals because investment performance no longer receives a
separate rating. Through this weakened regulatory incentive, bank demand for these
investments would decrease.

According to Novogradac, CRA-motivated banks contribute more than 80% of annual LIHTC
and NMTC equity. In competitive markets where there is high demand for CRA eligible projects,
tax credit pricing can be higher due to the increased demand and other costs associated with
such projects. Conversely, in "CRA deserts" such as rural areas and Indian Country/Tribal

Page 5
 lands, fewer banks pursue CRA credit, leading to lower equity pricing and financing gaps.3 The
proposal fails to adequately consider the nexus between CRA-motivated banks and
participation in these tax credit programs, thereby risking major disruptions to affordable
housing and community development projects that will disproportionately impact rural and
underserved communities that already struggle with access to capital.

Significance of CRA data and transparency: Section IV.G, "Data Collection, Reporting,
and Disclosure"

The threshold changes would also substantially reduce the number of institutions subject to
large-bank CRA data requirements. This would make it harder for communities, CDFIs,
policymakers, and regulators to identify credit gaps, compare bank performance, assess
geographic disparities, and understand whether community credit needs are being met the
very foundational purpose of the CRA statute. We are concerned that aggregate community
development finance data is already difficult to track and the proposal would exacerbate the
lack of coverage from existing data, making it even more difficult to identify and understand
where credit is flowing.

The data is also critical to evaluate the effects of regulatory changes such as those
contemplated in this proposal. If fewer banks are required to report community development
activity, regulators and stakeholders will have less visibility into whether reclassified banks
reduce, maintain, or shift their community development lending and investments over time.
That would make it more difficult to determine whether changes to CRA are affecting the
overall volume, geographic distribution, or types of community development financing reaching
underserved communities. Reducing the number of institutions required to report these data
would therefore diminish policymakers' and the public's ability to identify trends, evaluate the
effectiveness of CRA, and assess the real-world consequences of future changes to the
regulatory framework.

Recommendation

For all the reasons cited above, we urge the Agencies to retain the current asset size
thresholds and reject all alternatives offered (including the substantially higher thresholds
raised for consideration in Question 1). The current thresholds are already annually indexed to
Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, so they are not beholden

Agencies use in the proposal does not adequately explain why raising asset thresholds better

communities are met. For the small bank threshold, the proportionality metric rests on the
distribution of the number of banks such that nearly 80% of all banks would be considered
small, similar to what the percentage was in 1995. While that may be a true statement of
percentages, by the same logic, nearly 20% of banks in 1995 were considered large whereas
under the proposed large bank threshold, only a little over 2% of all banks would be

 considered large. Instead of using the same logic across the board, the Agencies selectively

Interacting Provisions That Could Further Reduce Community Development
Incentives

Preserve meaningful consequences for intermediate-bank CD performance: Section
IV.B, "Performance Tests -- Intermediate Bank Ratings"

Under the current framework, an intermediate small bank generally must receive at least a
Satisfactory rating on both its lending test and its CD test to receive an overall Satisfactory
rating. The proposal would require a Satisfactory or better lending-test rating but would allow
lending performance to compensate for weaker CD performance.

This change is particularly concerning when combined with the proposed asset thresholds,
which would move hundreds of banks currently evaluated under the large-bank framework into
the intermediate category. If weak CD performance does not prevent an overall Satisfactory
rating, banks may have less regulatory incentive to make CDFI loans and investments, provide
grants, or undertake other community development activities. We urge the Agencies to retain
a requirement that intermediate banks demonstrate at least Satisfactory CD performance to
receive an overall Satisfactory rating.

Complexity definition anchored to lending is too narrow: Section IV.C, "Qualitative
Factors"; Questions 1217

The proposal would define complexity for CD investments, grants, and services largely by
whether an activity is a necessary or beneficial component of a multicomponent financing
transaction involving a loan. We oppose establishing a lending-centric definition of complexity.
Investments in CDFIs can involve specialized expertise, layered capital, subordinate positions,
public subsidies, risk sharing, guarantees, tax-credit structures, patient repayment terms, or
other features that make transactions complex even when they are not directly paired with a
particular bank loan. We also oppose requiring CD investments or services to be complex as
contemplated in Question 14 or treating complexity as categorically more responsive than
innovation, flexibility, or impact as contemplated in Question 15.

The Agencies should assess complexity, innovativeness, flexibility, impact, and responsiveness
based on the characteristics and community value of the activity itself, rather than its
association with a lending transaction.

Page 10
 Prevent ordinary retail lending from substituting for specialized CD lending: Section
IV.B, "Retail Lending Product Lines," Questions 47; and Section IV.C, "CD Loans"

The proposal would evaluate retail lending only in a bank's major product lines. It would also
allow a loan in a retail product line that is not evaluated as a major product line to receive
consideration as a CD loan if the loan otherwise satisfies the community development
definition. We agree that genuine community-development-oriented financing should not lose
CRA consideration simply because a product line is excluded from the retail evaluation.

However, this interaction creates a risk that ordinary-course small-business, small-farm, or
other retail lending could substitute for more specialized community development lending,
including multilayered transactions and investments and high-impact community development
financing that may be less commercially attractive without CRA incentives. The Agencies
should require a meaningful community development nexus and ensure that the provision does
not allow banks to satisfy CD expectations primarily through activity they would undertake in
the ordinary course of business.

Retain small business definition: Section IV.D, "Economic Development", Question
24

The proposal would revise the CRA definition of economic development by creating three
categories of qualifying activity. Under the first category, financing could qualify if it supports a
business or farm that either meets the size-eligibility standards for the Small Business
Administration (SBA)'s Development Corporation or Small Business Investment Corporation
programs or has gross annual revenues of $1 million or less, and the financing expands,
improves, or preserves the business's productive capacity, physical presence, or employment
base. The proposal would also remove the current purpose test requiring the activity to
support job creation, retention, or improvement for LMI individuals or in an LMI area.

We recommend that the agencies retain, for CRA purposes, the SBA size standards that are
currently in effect. This approach would better serve the regulatory purpose behind the
definition of "economic development" than automatically incorporating future increases to
those size standards as separately proposed by SBA. SBA estimates that its August 2026
proposal would expand eligibility to approximately 114,500 additional firms, including through
significant increases in some employee- and revenue-based thresholds.8

Automatically allowing future SBA increases to flow through to CRA could materially expand
the universe of businesses whose financing qualifies as community development without the
OCC and FDIC independently determining whether those larger businesses are appropriate
indicia of CRA-related economic development. The risk is especially significant because the
CRA proposal would simultaneously eliminate the existing LMI-focused purpose test. Taken
together, a broader size standard and a weaker nexus to LMI individuals or communities could
allow increasingly large, ordinary commercial transactions to qualify as community

8 U.S. Small Business Administration, Proposed Rule on Small Business Size Standards, 91 Fed. Reg. 53,741
(Aug. 20, 2026). https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/20/2026-17042/small-business-size-
standards

Page 11
 development, potentially diluting CRA incentives for financing smaller businesses and
communities with the greatest unmet credit needs.

Accordingly, with respect to Question 24, we recommend that the Agencies anchor CRA
eligibility to the SBA size standards currently in effect. This would ensure that changes made
for SBA programs do not automatically and unintentionally redefine the scope of CRA
community development.

Essential community infrastructure and facilities should retain a meaningful CD
nexus: Section IV.D, "Community Development Definition -- Revitalization and
Stabilization", Question 25

We support CRA consideration for essential community facilities and infrastructure, particularly
in rural communities, Indian Country, distressed areas, and other markets with limited access
to conventional capital. The proposal, however, would broaden eligibility for essential
community infrastructure and facilities serving specified targeted areas. These activities would
no longer necessarily need to demonstrate that they help attract or retain businesses or
residents, and community-wide infrastructure may receive consideration without allocating a
particular share of the benefit to LMI individuals.

We are concerned that large infrastructure transactions routinely financed in the conventional
market could compete with affordable housing, CDFI financing, small-business lending, and
other activities more dependent on CRA incentives. The Agencies should preserve flexibility
where infrastructure addresses a genuine community development or financing gap while
ensuring that ordinary-course infrastructure transactions do not displace more targeted CD
activity.

Strategic plans require strong guardrails: Section IV.F, "Strategic Plan"; particularly
Questions 3853

We support efforts to provide greater clarity regarding strategic plans and measurable goals.
However, because strategic plans allow banks to develop individualized CRA performance
standards, strong guardrails and oversight are essential to ensure that use of such plans does
not circumvent rigorous and reasonably consistent expectations applied to similarly situated
institutions.

The agencies should require strategic plan goals to be responsive to demonstrated community
needs, sufficiently rigorous to approximate performance expected under the standard CRA
tests, transparent and measurable, subject to meaningful public engagement and evaluated
against clear standards for determining whether the goals adequately address assessment-
area credit needs.

We particularly urge the Agencies to establish strong standards in responding to Question 53,
which asks when measurable goals should be considered inadequate to address assessment-
area needs.

Page 12
 Geographic flexibility for CD activities outside assessment areas: Section IV.E,
"Consideration of Community Development Activities -- CD Activities Outside
Assessment Areas"; proposed __.13(e); Question 34

The Agencies are considering both quantitative and qualitative approaches for determining
when a bank has sufficiently served its assessment areas to receive consideration for outside-
AA activity. We support the goal of enabling CRA-motivated capital to reach communities with
significant unmet needs but relatively few bank assessment areas. With respect to Question
34, we support greater geographic flexibility where it can help direct CRA-motivated capital to
rural communities, Indian Country, and other underserved areas that may fall outside
traditional assessment areas. This flexibility can be especially important for statewide and
regional CDFIs and other intermediaries that aggregate capital, diversify risk, and efficiently
deploy financing across multiple markets, including to smaller organizations and communities
that individual banks may not be able to reach directly.

The proposal appropriately recognizes that outside-assessment-area activity should receive
consideration only after a bank has demonstrated that it is helping to meet community
development needs within its own assessment areas. We therefore recommend a hybrid
approach that preserves the predictability and administrative efficiency of a quantitative
benchmark while also considering the responsiveness of a bank's activities to identified
community development needs and relevant performance-context factors. A quantitative
threshold can provide banks and their community development partners with greater certainty
regarding when outside-assessment-area activity will receive consideration, but that threshold
should be calibrated to meaningful community development performance and not merely the
minimum level associated with avoiding a failing rating. Incorporating responsiveness would
also help ensure that the standard reflects whether a bank is addressing the actual needs and
opportunities within its assessment areas rather than simply meeting a dollar-based minimum.

We therefore support appropriate flexibility where a bank has substantially met the applicable
standard if performance context demonstrates that the shortfall reflects limited community
development opportunities or other market conditions rather than material unmet needs within
the assessment area. Outside-assessment-area activity should supplement, rather than
displace, meaningful community development activity in the communities a bank is already
obligated to serve. This approach would preserve the benefits of greater geographic flexibility
while maintaining a strong connection between CRA consideration and a bank's record of
meeting community development needs within its own assessment areas.

Page 13
 Support for Provisions That Could Strengthen Community Development Finance

Consider prior-period community development loans: Section IV.C, "CD Loans";
Question 8

We strongly support providing CRA consideration for qualifying CD loans that remain
outstanding from prior evaluation periods, similar to the existing treatment of prior-period
investments. Community development borrowers frequently need long-term, patient financing.
CRA should encourage banks to structure loans around community needs rather than
examination cycles.

With respect to Question 8, we recommend evaluation period-based consideration because it
better recognizes patient, long-term CD financing and provides a more representative measure
of capital committed throughout the CRA examination period than an annual snapshot and
brings parity to the treatment of loans and investments. The agencies should base
consideration on the average outstanding balance or otherwise account for both the amount
and duration of the outstanding exposure, and should treat repeated renewals of substantially
the same loan as a single exposure.

Establish an illustrative list and advance-confirmation process: Section IV.E,
"Illustrative List" and "Confirmation of CD Activity Eligibility"; Questions 3233

We strongly support establishing a publicly available, non-exhaustive illustrative list of eligible
CD activities and a formal process for advance confirmation of eligibility. The Agencies,
together with the Federal Reserve should seek to maintain consistent standards and, ideally, a
single interagency illustrative list.

With respect to Questions 3233, we support requiring banks to retain eligibility
determinations for as long as the applicable activity remains on their balance sheet and
establishing a maximum 30-day extension beyond the proposed 90-day review period.

We also encourage the Agencies to pair this with a confirmation process that provides timely
certainty while maintaining accountability for genuine community development impact.
Eligibility determinations should include a clear written rationale and, where appropriate,
identify the facts or conditions on which eligibility depends. The agencies should provide a
process for reconsideration where banks or community development partners can supply
additional information, as well as a mechanism for community stakeholders to raise material
concerns regarding activities that have been determined to be eligible. Nonconfidential or
anonymized determinations and their rationales should be made public to promote
transparency and consistent treatment across institutions. Eligibility determinations should also
remain subject to verification during CRA examinations where the activity is ultimately
implemented differently than represented.

Page 14
 Recognize Indian Country and other Tribal and native lands: Section IV.D,
"Revitalization and Stabilization"; Section IV.I, "Indian Country and Other Tribal and
Native Lands"; Question 54

We strongly support expressly recognizing Indian Country and other Tribal and native lands as
targeted geographies within the revitalization and stabilization component of community
development.

Recognize disaster preparedness and resilience: Section IV.D, "Revitalization and
Stabilization -- Designated Disaster Areas"; Question 31

We support expressly recognizing qualifying activities that help communities prepare for, adapt
to, and withstand natural disasters. CDFIs frequently provide financing before and after
disasters to affordable housing developments, homeowners, small businesses, and community
facilities. CRA should recognize responsible investments that strengthen vulnerable
communities before disasters occur, not only financing provided after damage occurs.

Conclusion

CRA has helped create a powerful partnership among banks, CDFIs, and the communities we
serve. We appreciate the agencies' efforts to improve clarity and flexibility. Modernization,
however, should result in more responsible capital reaching communities with unmet credit
needs, as the CRA statute intended.

We therefore urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the raised asset thresholds proposed and to
withdraw the restrictions on CD operating grants and several other provisions that weaken
community development incentives at the expense of LMI communities around the country.
Notwithstanding some notable instances where we support the changes proposed, we
generally support the retention of the current 1995 framework to best support a robust,
stable, unified CRA framework that is implemented consistently by all three banking regulators
including the Federal Reserve.

Thank you for considering these comments and for considering the impact of the proposed
changes on the communities we serve. We are grateful for the opportunity to submit this in
support of and on behalf of our almost 500 members. For questions, please contact me at
dwilliams@ofn.org or Susie Han, Vice President, Regulatory Affairs at shan@ofn.org.

Sincerely,

Susie Han
Vice President, Regulatory Affairs
Opportunity Finance Network

Dafina Williams
EVP, Chief Policy Officer and Head of Government Affairs
Opportunity Finance Network

 To Whom It May Concern,

 IFF appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the
 Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)'s joint Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) on the Community
 Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.

 IFF is a large mission-driven Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) serving the Midwest. IFF
 provides capital and technical assistance to strengthen nonprofits and underserved communities across a ten-
 state region that includes Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Ohio, Wisconsin, and
 Kentucky. Since 1988, IFF has made over 2,400 loans for more than $1.95 billion leveraging a total investment in
 communities of $6.98 billion and supporting tens of thousands of jobs. We have developed 44.6 million square
 feet of real estate and created more than 18,900 child care slots, 160,900 school seats, 864,700 new patient visits,
 and 23,200 units of affordable housing.

 IFF brings a unique regional perspective to this rulemaking. Across the Midwest, the CRA serves as a vital
 regulatory incentive for regional banks and major financial institutions to channel capital from primarily
 metropolitan financial centers and directly into the heartland's underinvested micropolitan, small-town, and rural
 communities. Two-thirds of IFF's debt capital is provided by bank partners who invest not only to satisfy CRA
 obligations, but because they recognize that mission-driven CDFIs provide the specialized expertise and hands-on
 support needed to deploy capital effectively where traditional commercial banking models cannot easily reach.

 While we support efforts to modernize the CRA, the proposed NPRM could disrupt this balanced community
 development ecosystem. Issuing a rule without the participation of the Federal Reserve creates a fractured
 regulatory framework, while proposed changes to asset thresholds, evaluation standards, and grant eligibility
 threaten to constrict the flow of patient capital to low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities. We offer the
 following comments and recommendations to ensure the final regulatory framework remains predictable,
 effective, and durable.

 1. Reclassifications and Weakened Standards May Undercut the Intent of the CRA
 The CRA recognizes the importance of meeting a community's credit needs. Doing so requires both direct
 bank lending and specialized, long-term equity and patient capital investments. Direct bank lending alone
 Docusign Envelope ID: 7455E3DC-62EA-8CCE-80D4-8B8816204640

 cannot replicate the specialized reach of CDFIs, which serve LMI communities by financing early childhood
 education centers, schools, federally qualified health centers, and other essential facilities.

 The CRA is one of the most effective drivers of private investment in the nation's community development
 infrastructure. In 2024 alone, the CRA incentivized over $430 billion in private capital for affordable
 housing, homeownership, small businesses, and small farms--nearly six times the combined annual
 appropriations for the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the Department of Agriculture's
 Rural Housing Services, the Department of Commerce's Small Business Administration, and the CDFI
 Fund.1 Between 2015 and 2024, the CRA incentivized $168 billion in public welfare investments
 nationwide, primarily through public-private partnerships, the Low Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC), the
 New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC), and direct investments into CDFIs.1

 The proposed rule could weaken the core framework of CRA in two critical ways:

 First, raising the large-bank asset threshold to $10 billion would remove the standalone investment test
 for many midsized and regional institutions, weakening incentives for intermediary partnerships that
 expand their ability to meet community needs. These partnerships are especially important in
 micropolitan and rural communities. As a lender whose financing is not constrained by appraised value,
 IFF complements banks' conventional lending and serves as a problem-solving partner for critical projects
 that cannot move forward with traditional financing alone. Banks can retain their depository relationships
 and provide appraisal-based lending, while IFF aggregates capital and brings specialized underwriting, real
 estate expertise, and hands-on support to essential human service and community-anchored projects.
 Together, CDFIs and smaller banks can finance projects that respond to community need and that neither
 could readily deliver on its own. Regional and community institutions are among IFF's most engaged, long-
 term funding partners; weaking incentives for these relationships could reduce the flow of patient capital
 that CDFIs rely on to package and execute complex local development projects.

 Second, the proposed weakened evaluation standards could reduce overall investment in community
 development nationwide. Allowing intermediate banks to achieve an overall "Satisfactory" CRA rating
 without receiving a satisfactory rating on their Community Development (CD) evaluation fundamentally
 weakens their incentive to participate in CD and investment. This structural change will disproportionately
 affect small towns and rural communities that rely heavily on intermediate and regional banks for
 community financing. America thrives on innovation and the incentive to do more, and the evaluation
 standards should reflect this--encouraging banks to innovate, deepen partnerships, and continually
 improve how they meet local needs and support long-term community and economic health.

 2. Proposed Changes Risk Unintended Consequences for Investments into LMI and Rural Communities
 The need for affordable housing and community development capital across the country has never been
 clearer. Public-private partnerships are essential to addressing this challenge, but they rely on regulatory
 structures that are stable, responsive, and oriented toward long-term community impact.

 As written, the proposed rule could inadvertently weaken the mechanisms that drive private capital into
 LMI and rural areas. This could directly counteract the recent congressional and administration actions
 focused on expanding the nation's housing supply and fostering economic development. This includes the
 expansion of the LIHTC and the permanency of the NMTC, passed in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025.
 The proposed rule could also counteract the raising of the Public Welfare Investment (PWI) cap passed in

 the ROAD to Housing in the 21st Century Act of 2026, which could otherwise drive more investment into
 these tax credit programs.

 Financial institutions account for 80% of LIHTC equity and 98% of NMTC equity nationwide, with banks
 providing virtually all annual NMTC investment.1 Furthermore, institutions with assets between $1.65
 billion and $30 billion play an outsized role in sustaining rural housing and economic growth. Sudden or
 blunt modifications to CRA evaluation standards risk dampening bank appetite for these equity
 investments. Any contraction in participation directly threatens the supply of new affordable housing and
 risks delaying vital community infrastructure projects mid-stream.

 To avoid unintended disruptions to LMI families and rural markets, we encourage the agencies to align
 CRA implementation with shared federal goals by maintaining strong, explicit incentives for LIHTC and
 NMTC participation within any revised framework.

 3. Interagency Alignment and Regulatory Stability Are Essential for Community Investment
 Community development relies heavily on long-term predictability, certainty, and consistency. Complex
 community development real estate projects typically require a 2- to 5-year packaging and execution
 timeline. Regulatory swings can cause financial institutions to pause long-term equity or grant
 commitments while awaiting final rules.

 A final rule issued solely by the OCC and FDIC without corresponding participation from the Federal
 Reserve Board is a departure from the agencies' historically unified approach to CRA implementation.
 Given that this marks the fourth major effort in less than a decade to revise the federal CRA framework,
 separate regulatory standards introduce operational complexity and heighten the risk of future instability.

 A single, uniform federal framework across all three regulatory agencies is critical to minimizing
 confusion, preserving competitive fairness, and ensuring that vital community development capital flows
 uninterrupted to the neighborhoods that need it most.

 4. Flexible Grant Funding Drives Pipeline Development and Capital Deployment in Underserved Markets
 Effective community development relies on a multi-tiered capital ecosystem where debt, equity, tax
 credits, and grants work in concert. CDFIs operate on the "inefficient frontier" of community finance:
 serving markets, building capacity, and structuring customized transactions that traditional commercial
 banking models are not designed to reach. In this ecosystem, grant funding and general operating support
 do not replace lending; rather, they serve as the catalytic seed capital required to build project pipelines,
 deliver technical assistance, and absorb early-stage risk so that debt capital can follow.

 The NPRM proposes new restrictions on grant eligibility, including eliminating general operating support in
 favor of project-specific grants and capping administrative cost allocations at 15%. While intended to

 pipelines are actually built.

 High-impact community facilities, such as early childhood education centers, health clinics, and cultural
 spaces, rarely arrive loan-ready. They require intensive predevelopment support, custom underwriting,
 and organizational capacity building. Restricting general operating support and imposing rigid
 administrative caps creates operational friction that discourages banks from funding the very
 infrastructure required to turn community priorities like these into bankable projects.

 A collaboration among Midwest CDFIs illustrates how flexible grant funding can unlock community

 We remain deeply committed to our bank partners and to the communities we serve across the Midwest. We

 Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on
 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN
 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

I submit this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above
(CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) because it would significantly weaken the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the
changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes,
carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide
an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting any
changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60 days.

I am a self-employed Realtor, working for Elfant Wissahickon REALTORS for the past 40 years
and have helped many Pennsylvanians become homeowners due in part to the CRA. Today's
required savings and rising costs have created a barrier not seen in my many years. What I have
also seen is the dilution and disillusion of "The American Dream" to own your own home. There
is not enough housing, but what is visible is new construction of apartments here. When I moved
to Philadelphia 50 years ago, 85% of Philadelphians were homeowners. Today only 50% are
homeowners.
 For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring
that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-
income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both
credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in communities that
have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream
financial services.

The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would
change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for
nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without an
adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on
communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In the Philadelphia
metro area, from 2010-2024, banks made over $64 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to
LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and over $22 billion in CRA qualified lending to small
businesses. Investments such as these benefited our community by bringing occupants with a real
reason to maintain the integrity of the community in which they own property.

We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in our
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital
devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough to receive a
passing CRA rating. This represents a dramatic reduction in what large banks currently devote
to community investments and loans and we fear that this new guidance may operate as a ceiling
instead of a floor. Pennsylvania receives over $3 billion in CRA related investments annually,
but under the proposed rule that could fall to just over $600 million an 80% loss.

Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination
cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans. If
regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the
communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for communities. For example, in
our community as I've seen whole blocks becoming largely rentals of absentee owners. The
block continues a downhill slide in these cases.

It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet the needs of communities
like ours. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes
would reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income
communities and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or
disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.
 The proposal would also substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while
banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less
demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more comprehensive tests applied to
large banks. The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting
requirements currently applicable to large banks, including reporting on small-business,
community development lending.

A number of banks that operate in Philadelphia will now be considered either intermediate or
small banks under the proposed rule and therefore subject to less rigorous requirements. These
reclassifications and resulting eliminations of community development obligations for over 800
banks and separate investment evaluations for 400 banks across the country, may worsen the
housing crisis by reducing investor interest in buying Low-Income Housing Tax Credits
(LIHTC), and reducing access to mortgages for first-time homebuyers or access to credit for
home repairs.

Similarly, the proposed rule would narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service
test. Today, examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and
information about the costs and features of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit this
criterion to credit services, removing deposit products such as checking and savings accounts
from direct evaluation under the service test. As such, examiners would no longer evaluate
whether those products are affordable and responsive to community needs even though
approximately 15% of Philadelphians over 100,000 households remain unbanked or
underbanked. Moreover, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, these
households are overwhelmingly low-income, black, or disabled. CRA review of the cost and
features of deposit products has played an important role in encouraging banks to address these
disparities by providing affordable products, and it must continue to do so.

For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate from
access to credit and economic opportunity. They can determine whether families can safely
receive income, build savings, establish banking relationships and obtain responsible credit. I've
seen people with no experience of banking as any "typical" American would do because they see
no purpose in travelling outside their neighborhood to bank, let alone having a savings account.

This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and moderate-
income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to affordable
mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible small-business
financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in affordable housing, small
businesses and other community development.
 The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply
because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA
obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that
would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the communities those
institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development activity that would receive
less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-income
communities or communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development,
financial counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-
based services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations.
These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have deep relationships
with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.

For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and
new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations.
