To Whom It May Concern:

On behalf of Columbia Bank (OR), we appreciate the opportunity to comment on the
proposed rulemaking to amend the regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment
Act ("CRA"). We support the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation's efforts to provide greater clarity, reduce unnecessary
burden, and preserve the CRA's core objective of encouraging banks to help meet the credit
needs of their communities.

Serving our communities is central to Columbia Bank. We support affordable housing in
growing metropolitan markets, provide credit to small businesses and farms in agricultural
communities, invest in nonprofit organizations throughout the Pacific Northwest, Pacific,
and Mountain West, and partner with tribal communities across our footprint. These
communities have different needs and opportunities, and effective CRA regulation should
recognize those differences.

At its core, CRA modernization should give banks greater certainty, tell us what counts, avoid
unnecessary burden, and not punish effective community development activity. Columbia
Bank supports features of the Proposal that advance those principles. We are concerned,
however, that several provisions could introduce new complexity without a corresponding
community benefit.

Tell Banks What Counts
Banks should not have to guess whether an activity will receive CRA consideration before
committing capital, personnel, or other resources. Columbia Bank supports maintaining a
single interagency illustrative list of qualifying activities, strengthening the advance-
confirmation process, and responding to eligibility requests within 30 days. These reforms
would allow institutions to spend less time interpreting regulations and more time serving
their communities.

The list should remain non-exclusive, and examiners should retain authority to recognize
activities that meet demonstrated local needs. Consider a loan supporting a rural hospital
 in Eastern Oregon, a wastewater project serving an agricultural community in Idaho, or a
tribal economic development initiative in Washington. These activities may not fit neatly
within a predefined category, but they are often among the most important investments a
bank can make in a community. Columbia Bank has seen firsthand that impactful
community development activity does not always look the same across markets.

The Agencies should also provide notice before removing an activity from the qualifying list
and protect commitments made in reliance on existing guidance. Community development
loans, investments, and grants are often negotiated over many months. Banks and
community partners should not be penalized because regulatory treatment changes after
they have committed to a worthwhile project.

Provide Certainty Around Performance Ratings
Banks need a clear understanding of the standards associated with every CRA rating, not
merely the minimum necessary to receive a Satisfactory rating. The Agencies should publish
benchmarks, representative scenarios, and examination guidance explaining how
quantitative and qualitative considerations will be weighed.

Banks should not have to wait until an examination to learn that an examiner interprets a
performance measure differently than the institution reasonably expected. Guidance
delivered after the fact is not regulatory clarity.

Evaluation standards must also recognize differences among markets. Affordable housing,
small-business credit, and community development opportunities look very different in
Seattle, Portland, Sacramento, Los Angeles, Boise, Phoenix, or Denver than they do in Walla
Walla, Yakima, Yuma, St. George, or tribal communities across our footprint. CRA should
measure whether a bank is helping meet community credit needs in the markets it serves,
not whether it has matched or outperformed another institution operating under different
conditions.

Do Not Punish Effective Community Development Activity
Columbia Bank agrees that community development grants should benefit the communities
they are intended to serve. The proposed 15 percent overhead condition, however, is the
wrong way to make that determination and should be removed.

The relevant question should be whether an organization performs a substantive community
development function and produces meaningful results. An organization providing housing
counseling, workforce development, financial education, or small-business assistance
across communities such as Flagstaff, Prescott, Cedar City, and Moses Lake, or across
dispersed communities throughout our footprint, may reasonably incur administrative costs
above an arbitrary threshold while still delivering significant community benefit.

Banks should be permitted to rely on reasonable certifications and existing documentation.
Requiring institutions to independently validate nonprofit expense allocations will direct
 resources toward compliance administration rather than community impact. It may also
disadvantage smaller organizations that perform valuable work but lack extensive
administrative capacity, especially in more rural communities.

The final rule should clearly recognize activities that expand access to the banking system in
the Service test, including Bank On certified accounts, Individual Development Accounts,
financial education, and digital literacy. Banks should continue to have a clear place within
the CRA regulatory framework for these activities to qualify for CRA consideration.

Columbia's community strategy includes financial mobility, access to capital, technical
assistance, financial education, housing stability, and rural entrepreneurship. These are
practical ways banks help individuals, families, and communities become financially
stronger.

Ensure Significant Lending Activities Continue to Count
Columbia Bank is concerned with the proposed Major Product Line concept. While intended
as a form of regulatory burden reduction, the proposal could result in significant lending
activities being excluded from CRA evaluation. For agricultural lenders in particular, small
farm lending may not qualify as a Major Product Line simply because residential mortgages
and small business loans originate in greater volume.

This would create the anomalous result that some of the nation's most active small farm
lenders, including institutions serving agricultural communities across Columbia Bank's
footprint, could have their small farm lending excluded from CRA review. In markets where
agriculture is a dominant economic driver, relegating small farm lending to secondary status
would be inconsistent with the CRA's objective of evaluating how well banks meet local
credit needs.

Consider agricultural communities throughout Idaho, Eastern Oregon, Central Washington,
California, Arizona, and Utah. In these markets, access to farm credit is a fundamental
component of economic development and community vitality. Lending that supports
farmers and ranchers should not receive diminished CRA consideration simply because
other loan categories originate in greater volume.

Moreover, the burden reduction associated with the Major Product Line concept appears
limited. Banks would still be required to capture, maintain, and report small farm lending
data. If the reporting burden remains while the regulatory recognition is reduced, the
rationale for the proposal becomes difficult to justify.

Columbia Bank encourages the Agencies to reconsider the Major Product Line concept and
ensure that significant lending activities, including small farm lending, continue to receive
meaningful CRA consideration.
 Do Not Replace Regulatory Relief with New Burden
The Proposal includes meaningful efforts to reduce burden, but those gains should not be
offset by new documentation, verification, or operational requirements that offer limited
supervisory value.

Implementation may require system changes, vendor programming, employee training,
policy revisions, and testing. Institutions cannot responsibly operationalize new
requirements before the Agencies have issued final examination procedures and clear
implementation guidance.

Burden-reducing provisions should become available promptly, while genuinely new
obligations should be phased in. The Agencies should update the Interagency CRA
Questions and Answers, publish examination procedures well before mandatory
compliance, and allow adequate time for implementation.

Adopt a Durable Interagency Framework
Columbia Bank strongly encourages the OCC, FDIC, and Federal Reserve to work toward a
single, coordinated CRA framework. The Federal Reserve did not join the current Proposal,
creating the prospect that institutions could remain subject to different CRA regimes
depending on their regulator.

The industry has spent years responding to proposed changes, implementation planning,
litigation, and regulatory reversals. It does not need another temporary framework. The
Agencies should pursue a rule that is clear, practical, coordinated, and durable enough to
remain workable through changes in agency leadership and policy direction.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment. Columbia Bank supports thoughtful CRA
modernization, but the measure of success should be straightforward: banks should know
what counts, understand how they will be evaluated, and be able to direct resources toward
communities rather than unnecessary compliance activity.

Respectfully submitted,

Trent Wright
SVP / Director of Government Relations

roughly 3,577 banks the agencies supervise (2.4 percent) would remain large banks and subject
to the investment test, compared with more than 450 today.2 The OCC alone estimates that 126
of its large banks would become intermediate banks, and 194 of its intermediate small banks
would become small banks that are "no longer assessed on CD activities."3

These changes would fall hardest on affordable housing equity. About 80 percent of Housing
Credit equity comes from banks that invest in part to meet their CRA obligations, and the large
bank investment test is a main reason banks accept the modest returns those investments offer.4
The National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders estimates that the number of large
banks would fall from 642 to 256. According to the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition,
banks with assets between $1.649 billion and $10 billion invested at least $1.6 billion in Housing
Credit equity over the five-year period covered by its survey.5

For PHAs, fewer investors means lower prices for tax credits and larger financing gaps in RAD
and Section 18 transactions. PHAs must fill those gaps with scarce Capital Fund dollars and local
resources, or the deals do not close. About one-third of the Housing Credit equity that banks with
$412 million to $10 billion in assets invested through syndicators went to rural markets in 2021
2024. ACTION says this shows those banks "play an outsized role in investing in smaller
communities.

Today, an intermediate small bank cannot earn an overall "satisfactory" rating unless it is rated at
least "satisfactory" on both the lending test and the CD test. The proposal would require only a
"satisfactory" lending test.6 Combined with the new $10 billion threshold, a $5 billion bank
would move from an investment test that makes up 25 percent of its rating to a CD test that no
longer affects whether it is rated "satisfactory." For most banks between $1 billion and $10
billion, community development would become optional.

1Letter from the ACTION Campaign Steering Committee to the OCC and FDIC, Community Reinvestment Act
Regulations Proposed Rule (Docket ID OCC-2026-0694) (Oct. 2026) (ACTION Campaign Letter).
2Proposal, sec. IV.A ("Large bank threshold" and "Intermediate bank threshold").
3Proposal, sec. VI.A (OCC Expected Effects).
4ACTION Campaign Letter (citing CohnReznick, 2025 Affordable Housing Credit Study).
5ACTION Campaign Letter (citing analyses by the National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders and the
Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition).
6Proposal, sec. IV.B ("Intermediate bank ratings"); proposed appendix A, paragraph (d)(3).
 This is the wrong moment to weaken these incentives. Congress has just expanded Housing
Credit authority in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and raised banks' public welfare investment
limit in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, in both cases to draw more bank capital into
affordable housing.7

CLPHA recommends that the agencies:

 Leave the asset thresholds as they currently stand.8

 If the agencies move forward with changes, maintain the lowest possible threshold for
 large banks. The $3.252 billion alternative would be substantially less disruptive to
 Housing Credit investment than the $10 billion proposal: banks that would stay under the
 investment test at that level account for about 86 percent of the Housing Credit equity
 from banks between $1.65 billion and $10 billion in the Affordable Housing Tax Credit
 Coalition's survey. The $30 billion threshold raised in the proposal would be far more
 damaging, because banks between $10 billion and $30 billion account for more than
 twice as much Housing Credit debt and equity as banks between $1.65 billion and $10
 billion.9

 Keep community development a meaningful part of every bank's rating, with a strong
 role for investments as well as loans. Today, a mid-sized bank must earn at least
 "satisfactory" on both its lending test and its CD test to be rated "satisfactory" overall.
 The proposal would drop the CD test requirement, so a bank could be rated "satisfactory"
 even with weak community development performance. The agencies should keep both
 requirements.

 Adopt policies that strengthen the Housing Credit market in all communities, including
 rural and smaller markets.10

II. Protect Equity Investment and Credit for Complex, Publicly Subsidized Transactions

The proposal's stated aim is to increase the focus on lending. But in PHA redevelopment, loans
and equity are not interchangeable. A typical RAD or mixed-finance transaction combines
Housing Credit equity, a construction loan, permanent debt, PHA and local soft funds, and a
HUD rental subsidy contract. Without the equity, the loans cannot be made.

Under the current rules, examiners can give a bank more credit for community development
activities that are complex, innovative, flexible, or responsive. These qualitative factors can raise
a bank's rating beyond what the dollar amount of its activities alone would earn. But the current

7ACTION Campaign Letter.
8ACTION Campaign Letter.
9ACTION Campaign Letter.
10ACTION Campaign Letter.
 rules do not define them, and the agencies acknowledge that examiners have applied them
inconsistently.11 The current investment test also gives weight to investments that are "not
routinely provided by private investors."

CLPHA supports the proposed definition of "complexity." Its first component recognizes
investments that are a necessary part of a multi-component financing that includes a loan. Its
second component gives as an example "a community development activity that is not routinely
provided by private investors, such as an activity that relies on public subsidies."12 PHA
transactions fit both components.

CLPHA recommends that the agencies:

 State in the rule or the illustrative list that Housing Credit equity, loans, and bond
 purchases in RAD conversions, Section 18 repositionings, Faircloth-to-RAD
 developments, and mixed-finance public housing are complex activities.

 Not require that CD investments or services be complex to receive credit. Many highly
 responsive activities, such as a grant to a resident services program, are not complex but
 meet real needs.

 Not rank complexity above impact. Preserving deeply affordable units for extremely low-
 income households is high-impact whether or not the financing is complex.

 Support the proposal to credit prior-period CD loans that remain on a bank's balance
 sheet, as investments are credited. This would better recognize the long-term financing
 that affordable housing requires.

III. Recognize Public Housing Clearly in the Affordable Housing Definition

A. Name PHA programs and transactions

CLPHA supports proposed paragraph (1)(i)(D) of the CD definition, which qualifies rental
housing "undertaken in conjunction with an explicit Federal, State, local, or Tribal government
affordable housing program for low- or moderate-income individuals or families." Banks and
examiners would still benefit from naming the programs PHAs use, so that a PHA transaction
does not depend on an individual examiner's judgment.

CLPHA recommends that the rule text or the illustrative list expressly include:

 Public housing (Section 9 of the U.S. Housing Act of 1937), including Capital Fund
 financing;

 RAD conversions to project-based rental assistance or project-based vouchers, Section 18
 demolition and disposition, and Faircloth-to-RAD development;

11Proposal, sec. IV.C ("Qualitative factors").
12Proposal, sec. IV.C ("Qualitative factors"); proposed __.12 (definition of "complexity").
  Mixed-finance public housing development and Choice Neighborhoods transformation
 plans;

 Housing assisted with project-based or tenant-based Housing Choice Vouchers, including
 activities of Moving to Work agencies;

 Bonds and other obligations issued by PHAs or their instrumentalities for affordable
 housing; and any other local, state, or federally assisted affordable housing program.

B. Give full credit to PHA-led mixed-income redevelopment

The proposal would give pro rata credit for mixed-income housing based on the share of units set
aside for low- and moderate-income households. Many PHA redevelopments are mixed-income
by program design. Choice Neighborhoods, for example, requires one-for-one replacement of
public housing units and supports mixed-income communities that include market-rate and
workforce units. Pro rata credit would make these transactions less attractive to banks than
single-use projects, even though they are carried out under a government affordable housing
program.

CLPHA recommends that the agencies clarify that qualifying activities receive credit for the
full activity even when the development includes unrestricted units. At a minimum, the pro rata
share should count every unit with a public subsidy or recorded affordability restriction,
including units with project-based vouchers.

C. Add affordability safeguards for unsubsidized housing

Banks can receive CRA credit today for financing unsubsidized rental housing with affordable
rents, often called naturally occurring affordable housing (NOAH). But the current rules do not
mention NOAH, and the agencies acknowledge that their guidance is "not sufficiently clear"
about whether it qualifies or how to show that a property is affordable.13 Unlike subsidized
housing, where a government program or recorded restriction keeps rents affordable for a set
period, NOAH stays affordable only as long as market conditions and the owner's decisions
allow.

The proposal would qualify NOAH that is "likely to be inhabited by low- or moderate-income
individuals or families as demonstrated by median rents that do not and are not projected at the
time of the transaction to exceed 30 percent of 80 percent of the area median income." In high-
cost areas, the limit would be 30 percent of 120 percent of area median income.14 The agencies
explain that clearer standards "would help encourage banks to engage in efforts to preserve and
add to the nation's affordable housing stock."

CLPHA supports that goal. NOAH is an important source of housing for voucher holders and
other low-income renters. But the proposed test applies only at the time of the transaction. It does
not ask whether rents will stay affordable after the financing closes or whether current residents

13Proposal, sec. IV.D ("Affordable housing").
14Proposed __.12 (definition of "community development," paragraphs (1)(i)(A) and (C)).
 can stay. As a result, a property could qualify even if the acquisition plan depends on raising
rents afterward, which would reduce the affordable housing stock rather than preserve it.

CLPHA recommends that the agencies:

 Require a reasonable commitment that rents will stay affordable for the loan term or the
 evaluation period, whichever is longer, not only at closing;

 Exclude financing for acquisitions whose business plans depend on rent increases above
 the affordability standard or that result in displacement of current residents;

 Give banks more weight under the new responsiveness standard for financing NOAH
 properties whose owners accept Housing Choice Vouchers. These commitments help
 ensure the housing actually reaches low-income families; and

 Extend the exemptions to PHAs, their affiliates, and properties with recorded
 affordability restrictions, not only to nonprofit partnerships.

IV. Revise the Grant Provisions So They Do Not Cut Off Resident Services

Grants pay for what loans cannot: Financial coaching, workforce programs, homeownership
counseling, digital inclusion, youth programs, and resident council capacity. These services are
usually delivered by PHA nonprofit affiliates and local partners. The agencies' own analysis
recognizes that the new grant requirements "may reduce CRA incentives for general operating-
support grants, grants to intermediaries, or grants to organizations with higher operating-cost
ratios, which could affect nonprofit capacity."15

CLPHA has joined the national sign-on letter organized by the National Association of
Affordable Housing Lenders (NAAHL), which raises the same concern.16 That letter warns that
the proposed limits on eligible uses and the extensive new documentation requirements "would
increase compliance burden and could force banks to reduce grant support, particularly to
smaller organizations." It urges the agencies to "continue to recognize grants and contributions
that advance eligible community development purposes and respond to demonstrated community
needs without applying new burdensome regulations." CLPHA agrees and offers the PHA-
specific concerns below.

A. Do not eliminate grants

CLPHA strongly opposes the proposal to remove all grants and donations from CRA
consideration. Grants are a key source of support for housing counseling, financial education,
and other services that help residents prepare for and use credit.17 The proposal itself cites

15Proposal, sec. VI (Economic Analysis).
16NAAHL Sign-On Letter.
17NAAHL Sign-On Letter.
 financial literacy programming and homeownership counseling as examples of activities that
grants can support.18

B. Credit grants made through local intermediaries

The "directly used" requirement would exclude grants to intermediaries that regrant within the
bank's assessment area, such as community foundations, CDFIs, United Ways, and PHA-
affiliated nonprofits that fund resident councils and small partners. These intermediaries let
banks reach organizations too small to manage bank grant requirements themselves. CLPHA
recommends that grants made through local intermediaries count toward CRA when the
intermediary passes the funds on to community development programs in the bank's local
community.

C. Confirm that resident services qualify

The proposed civic assistance definition lists childcare, education, workforce development, job
training, housing assistance, financial literacy, and homebuyer counseling. CLPHA
recommends that the illustrative list confirm that grants to PHAs and their affiliates for these
services to public housing and voucher households qualify, including Family Self-Sufficiency,
Jobs Plus, and Resident Opportunity and Self-Sufficiency programs.

V. Keep Low-Income People and Neighborhoods at the Center of CRA

A. Retain explicit consideration of low-income people and highly disadvantaged areas

The proposal would remove the rating factors that specifically recognize a bank's record of
serving highly disadvantaged areas and low-income people, reasoning that the term `highly
disadvantaged areas' is undefined and that the borrower and geographic distribution factors
already cover these needs. CLPHA urges the agencies to keep explicit recognition of service to
low-income people. Many households in public housing and the voucher program are extremely
low-income, earning 30 percent of area median income or less, and many earn well below that
level. Many have limited credit histories and need small-dollar loans, low-cost accounts, and
flexible underwriting products that are less profitable for banks to offer without specific
recognition under CRA. Rather than drop the factor, the agencies could define `highly
disadvantaged areas:' for example, by reference to poverty rates or the distressed census tract
criteria.

B. Keep the retail services evaluation meaningful

The proposal would limit the retail services evaluation to the "range of credit services,"
excluding deposit products. The CRA statute itself finds that "the convenience and needs of
communities include the need for credit services as well as deposit services."19 For many public
housing residents, a safe, low-cost account is the first step toward credit. It is how families

18Proposal, secs. III.B and IV.C ("CD grants").
1912 U.S.C. 2901(a)(2).
 receive wages and benefits by direct deposit, receive Family Self-Sufficiency escrow payments,
and build the credit history that lenders require. Households without one pay a high price. In
2023, 4.2 percent of U.S. households had no bank account, with higher rates among lower-
income households. One-third of these households cited fees or minimum balance requirements
as the main reason, and 18.2 percent used nonbank check cashers, most often to cash a paycheck
or a government check.20 Check-cashing fees average almost 4 percent of a check's value. In
2012, Americans paid an estimated $1.8 billion in fees to cash $52 billion in checks.21 At that
rate, a household cashing $15,000 a year in paychecks would pay about $600 in fees.

CLPHA recommends that the agencies continue to consider the availability of affordable
accounts and branch access in low- and moderate-income areas.

VI. Geographic Flexibility and Transition

A. Geographic flexibility

CLPHA supports giving banks credit for CD activities in underserved areas outside their
assessment areas, provided they have first met the needs of their own assessment areas. Large
urban PHAs still face capital needs measured in billions of dollars, and flexibility should add
capital to underserved areas rather than draw it away from cities.

B. Transition provisions

PHA projects take years to put together, and grants for resident services often run for several
years. CLPHA supports the proposal's plan to keep crediting activities that qualified when they
were made. We also ask the agencies to review activities committed before the new rule takes
effect under the current rules, and to phase in the new thresholds and grant requirements over a
reasonable period of time.

C. Analyze the effect on affordable housing before finalizing

The agencies' economic analysis measures how much the proposal would reduce banks'
compliance costs, but not how it would affect community development lending, investment, and
grants. CLPHA recommends that the agencies estimate these effects, including on Housing
Credit investment and PHA redevelopment, before issuing a final rule.

Conclusion

For nearly 50 years, CRA has helped bring private capital into the communities where public
housing residents live. CLPHA supports a clearer and more workable CRA rule. However, the
measure of success should be whether affordable homes are built and preserved, residents can
get fair and well-serviced credit, and the organizations that serve them can keep doing their

20Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, 2023 FDIC National Survey of Unbanked and Underbanked Households,
Executive Summary (Nov. 2024), https://www.fdic.gov/household-survey.
21Duke University Fuqua School of Business, "New Research Could Improve Check-Cashing Industry for
Customers and Businesses" (Apr. 18, 2016) (citing FINRA Investor Education Foundation data).
 work. We urge the agencies to keep meaningful CD obligations for banks of all sizes, protect
equity investment and grants, recognize public housing clearly, and measure the quality of credit
as well as its quantity.
Thank you for considering these comments.

Sincerely,

La Shelle Dozier
CEO
Council of Large Public Housing Authorities

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations

To Whom It May Concern:

The American Bankers Association (ABA)1 and 45 state banking associations appreciate the
opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's (OCC) and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) (collectively, the Agencies) proposal to amend their
regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).2

For nearly five decades, bank CRA lending and investment has been a catalyst for economic growth
and opportunity. In 2024 alone, banks provided roughly $340 billion in capital to low- and
moderate-income communities in the form of mortgages, community development, and small
business and small farm loans.

While many aspects of the current regulatory framework continue to work well and should be
preserved, ABA supports updating the regulations to incorporate longstanding guidance and
interpretations and to ensure that CRA evaluations remain appropriately tailored to the diversity of
the financial institutions subject to the CRA. We also share the Agencies' goal of aligning the
regulation with the CRA statute and appreciate the proposal's renewed focus on credit needs, not
deposit products. We also support the Agencies' goal of reducing regulatory burden.

1 The American Bankers Association is the voice of the nation's $26.5 trillion banking industry, which is
composed of small, regional and large banks that together employ over 2 million people, safeguard $20.7
trillion in deposits and extend $13.9 trillion in loans.
2 90 Fed. Reg. 52114 (Aug. 12, 2026).

 1
 In addition to these goals, we urge the Agencies to consider the following as they update the CRA
regulation:

The final rule should provide long-term regulatory certainty. The Agencies should adopt a rule
that provides clear and durable expectations, thereby reducing the uncertainty and disruption
associated with repeated rounds of regulatory change. A rulemaking that includes all three
regulatory agencies is more likely to stand the test of time.

The final rule's asset classifications for CRA evaluations should be increased. The proposal
appropriately recognizes that a bank with a few billion dollars in assets should not be subject to the
same CRA framework as a bank with hundreds of billions of dollars in assets. ABA supports
increasing the Small and Intermediate Bank thresholds to $1 billion and $10 billion, respectively,
and indexing those thresholds to Nominal Gross Domestic Product to ensure they remain relevant
over time. Doing so would meaningfully differentiate regulatory expectations among institutions of
varying sizes and realign the distribution of banks subject to the rule's asset classifications with the
distribution the Agencies adopted in 1995. The Agencies should also provide greater clarity
regarding Small and Intermediate Bank examinations and permit Small Banks to elect evaluation
under the Intermediate Bank framework.

The final rule should preserve examination options tailored to different business models.
Strategic plans remain an important tool for aligning CRA responsibilities with local community
needs and a bank's business strategy. The Agencies should strengthen that option by preserving
flexibility, grandfathering existing plans, and providing consistent examiner support. Likewise, the
rule should preserve the wholesale and limited purpose designations and avoid changes that
would force these institutions into retail-focused examination frameworks that do not reflect how
they operate.

Retail lending evaluations should focus on material lending activity. Major product lines should
be determined at the bank level, and the Agencies should retain the existing substantial-majority
standard by defining it as 75 percent of a bank's total lending.

The community development framework should support a broad range of activities and
provide greater certainty regarding CRA eligibility. The Agencies should refine the proposed
definitions of community development and provide greater clarity regarding the eligibility of
activities, including affordable housing, financial education, economic development, essential
infrastructure, disaster recovery, and grants. The final rule should also provide flexibility for
allocating activities that benefit multiple assessment areas and permit consideration of outside-
assessment-area activities when a bank receives a Satisfactory or better rating on its prior
examination. The Agencies should also publish an illustrative list of qualifying activities and
establish a timely process for confirming CRA eligibility.

 2
 Retail service evaluations should remain focused on credit. The proposal appropriately aligns
the retail service evaluation with the CRA's statutory focus on helping to meet community credit
needs.

Assessment area requirements should preserve flexibility. Assessment area delineations
should continue to reflect the communities a bank can reasonably serve. Any full-county
requirement should apply only to Large Banks, and the Agencies should retain flexibility in applying
the substantial portion standard.

Data collection and implementation requirements should support examinations without
creating unnecessary burden. Community development information should continue to be
collected and maintained for examination purposes, but the Agencies should avoid new reporting
requirements that provide limited supervisory value. In addition, community development grants
should not be subject to public reporting requirements.

The Agencies should provide an orderly transition to a new rule. Large Banks should receive at
least two years before becoming subject to new data collection and reporting requirements. Banks
that move to a different asset classification should have the option either to transition to the
applicable framework on January 1 of the following calendar year or to complete the current
evaluation period under the existing rules. For all other banks, examinations should not transition
between frameworks mid-cycle, and the Agencies should provide updated guidance and
examination procedures well before implementation.

I. Principles for a Successful Final Rule

This proposal is the third attempt to update the CRA regulation in eight years, and we appreciate
the Agencies' continued work to modernize the rules. While the two prior rulemakings did not result
in lasting regulatory change, they generated meaningful public comment regarding what works
under the 1995 rule, where improvements are needed, and what is permissible under the CRA
statute. The following lessons should guide the Agencies in this rulemaking.

 A. Approach this rulemaking with an eye toward durability.

Banks, regulators, customers, and communities are best served by a stable regulatory framework.
To that end, the Agencies should strive to finalize a rule that is grounded in the statute and will
withstand changes in political administration. Prior CRA reform efforts suggest several principles
for achieving this objective.

First, history demonstrates that CRA reforms are successful when developed on an interagency
basis. On two prior occasions, amendments to the rule that were issued without the support of all
three banking Agencies were not long-lasting. We urge the OCC and the FDIC to coordinate with
the Federal Reserve to develop a unified CRA rule.

 3
 Second, durability requires restraint. The Agencies' responsibility is to implement the CRA statute,
not rewrite it. If Congress determines that CRA obligations should be expanded or decoupled from
a bank's physical location, Congress--not the banking Agencies--should make that policy
judgment. The same principle applies to extending CRA obligations beyond banks to other financial
services providers, such as credit unions, fintechs, stablecoin issuers, and nonbank mortgage
lenders. Likewise, any decision to expand CRA beyond its traditional focus on lending and
community development to encompass a bank's deposit products is a policy choice for Congress,
not the Agencies.

Third, successful regulations are not rigid or overly complicated. Prior reform efforts relied on
formulas and metrics that were difficult to understand and were not workable for the full range of
bank business models.

 B. Balance greater consistency with the need for flexibility and tailoring.

The 1995 rule has endured for more than three decades because it recognizes the diversity of both
the banking system and the communities that banks serve. Banks differ in their capacity and
business models, just as communities differ in their credit needs and economic circumstances. An
updated CRA framework must be flexible enough to account for both.

As the Agencies move forward, a principal challenge will be balancing improved clarity and
consistency with the flexibility that has been central to the success of the 1995 framework.
Objective standards and metrics promote more consistent evaluations, but they should not
become bright lines that fail to account for differences in business models, market conditions, and
community needs. Therefore, the Agencies should further tailor the rule's performance tests to
different bank types and business models and avoid overreliance on bright lines and comparative
measures that may not accurately reflect a bank's performance.

 C. Evaluate the proposal as an integrated framework.

While the proposal preserves the core structure of the existing CRA framework, it would make
significant changes to several elements of the rule. In analyzing the comments and fashioning a
final rule, the Agencies should not evaluate those changes in isolation. Revisions to one aspect of
the CRA framework often affect other provisions, and a change that appears modest on its own
may have significant--and unintended--practical impacts when viewed in combination with other
elements of the proposal.

For example, eliminating the limited purpose designation while also adopting the proposed
geographic flexibility standard for out-of-assessment-area activities would exacerbate existing
CRA hot spots by requiring institutions to direct additional resources to markets where demand for
qualifying community development opportunities already exceeds supply. This would further

 4
 increase competition and pricing for community development opportunities without generating
additional community development activity or additional benefit for communities.

The Agencies should consider not only the individual merits of each proposed change, but also how
the proposal's components operate together. With these key principles in mind, we offer the
following comments on the proposal's specific provisions.

 II. CRA Regulation Should Reflect the Diversity of the Banking System

The CRA framework has long recognized that banks of different sizes and business models serve
their customers and communities in different ways. The 1995 rule tailors performance standards
and evaluation methods based on bank asset size, business model, and performance context. We
appreciate that the proposal largely preserves this flexibility and we offer the following
recommendations to strengthen this tailoring.

 A. Increase the thresholds for Small and Intermediate Banks to $1B and $10B
 respectively and index them to Gross Domestic Product.

One of the most important ways the CRA framework tailors regulatory expectations is through
asset-based performance tests. Asset thresholds determine the CRA performance tests and the
data collection and reporting requirements to which a bank is subject. As a result, where the
Agencies draw these lines has significant implications for both regulatory burden and CRA
administration. ABA supports the proposed increase of the asset thresholds for the Small and
Intermediate Bank performance tests.

 1. The proposed thresholds appropriately realign the distribution of
 institutions with the Agencies' original goal of reducing burden on
 smaller banks.

The proposal requests comment on multiple options for updating the thresholds. ABA supports
Option 1, which would define Small Banks as banks with less than $1 billion in assets in either of
the prior two calendar years and Intermediate Banks as banks with between $1 billion and $10
billion in assets in either of the prior two calendar years. Banks with more than $10 billion in assets
in both of the prior two calendar years would be Large Banks. Option 1 would adjust the $1 billion
Small Bank threshold annually based on the Consumer Price Index, but it would retain a fixed $10
billion threshold for Intermediate Banks.

Option 1 would realign the distribution of institutions subject to these standards with the Agencies'
1995 vision for a tiered CRA framework and its adjustment in 2005. In 1995, the Agencies set a
Small Bank threshold of under $250 million in assets as a means of holding Small Banks
accountable for meeting credit needs, but sparing them the disproportionate burden of data
collection and reporting--a burden the Agencies believed was not necessary to fulfill the statute's

 5
 requirements. As the Agencies noted, that data would be of less value in determining the
distribution of borrowers and loans, given that the communities served by Small Banks tend to be
geographically compact.3

In 2005, after 10 years of implementing the 1995 rules, the Agencies concluded that the 1995
threshold still subjected community banks to unnecessary and burdensome data collection and to
an overly rigid community development approach.4 Thus, the Agencies raised the Small Bank
threshold to banks with assets under $1 billion, and they created a class of small banks called
Intermediate Small Banks--those with assets between $250 million and less than $1 billion.
Intermediate Small Banks were relieved of data collection, with the Agencies noting not only the
disproportionate burden data collection imposes on community banks, but also the low benefit of
the data, citing the availability of Call Report and other data with which to evaluate these banks'
responsiveness to community credit needs.5 The Agencies also adjusted the community
development test for Intermediate Small Banks, so that they were no longer competing with multi-
billion dollar banks for qualified investments, to "reduce burden on these banks while making the
evaluation of their community development records more effective."6

The Agencies' objective to reduce regulatory burden on community banks remains critical today
and underscores the need to realign the thresholds set decades ago. Regulatory burden on
community banks has significantly increased since the thresholds were established and has been
recognized as a key driver of industry consolidation, resulting in fewer credit options for
communities across the country.

In 1995, approximately 80 percent of institutions qualified for the Small Bank test, which
represented about 9 percent of industry assets.7 Today, only about 57 percent of institutions are
classified as Small Banks for CRA purposes.8 Many Intermediate Small Banks and banks currently
classified as "Large" are community banks that struggle to compete with larger institutions.

In addition, community banks currently classified as Large must collect and report CRA data; these
banks would face increased data collection and maintenance costs under the proposal, as the
Agencies propose to require Large Banks to increase data collection and maintenance for
community development lending and investments, grantmaking, and potentially for consumer
lending.

Thus, ABA supports Option 1, which would readjust the CRA asset thresholds so that, once again,
nearly 80 percent of institutions would be evaluated under the Small Bank standards, while the

4 70 Fed. Reg. 44256 (Aug. 2, 2005).
5 Id. at 44258.
6 Id. at 44260.
7 90 FR at 52120.

8 Id.

 6
 most complex requirements would be reserved for the largest institutions. These smaller banks
may be numerous, but according to the Agencies, under Option 1, OCC and FDIC Small Banks
would hold only 4.9 percent of industry assets.9 Similarly, Option 1's adjustment to the threshold
for Intermediate Banks would result in about 17.8 percent of OCC and FDIC banks being
Intermediate, with these banks holding 9.7 percent of total industry assets. Together, banks
reclassified under Option 1 would hold about 14.6 percent of total industry assets, while banks
classified as Large would hold the vast majority of banking assets. Option 1 would ensure that
banks of all sizes would continue to serve community credit needs, while recognizing, as the
Agencies have since 1995, the differences in capacity and business model amongst banks of
different asset sizes.

Option 1's realignment is entirely appropriate and consistent with the Agencies' goal of reducing
burden. A bank with $5 billion in assets, which is Large now but would be Intermediate under
Option 1, simply should not be subject to the same CRA framework as a bank with $500 billion in
assets. Yet under the current thresholds, both are evaluated under the Large Bank framework and
must collect and report data, despite significant differences in scale, staffing, and resources.
Option 1 appropriately aligns CRA requirements with institutional size and capacity and helps
preserve the community bank business model.

 2. Adjust the thresholds annually based on Gross Domestic Product.

In addition to recalibrating the asset thresholds, the Agencies should include in the final rule a
requirement to adjust them annually. Today, the Small and Intermediate Small Bank thresholds are
adjusted annually based on the Consumer Price Index (CPI). Under the proposal, the Small Bank
threshold would continue to be adjusted automatically, but the Intermediate Bank cap would
remain fixed.

This approach will inevitably result in the Intermediate Bank cap becoming outdated. Moreover,
banks need a predictable means of determining when they may transition to a new CRA
performance test rather than relying on periodic rulemakings that occur on an unpredictable
timeline. And, an annual adjustment requirement would reduce the need for repeated rulemakings
to recalibrate the thresholds.

In addition, although the Agencies adjust the current thresholds annually for inflation, this process
does not capture the fundamental changes that have occurred in the banking industry over the last
three decades. Consolidation and growth in average asset size have far outpaced inflation-based
adjustments. As a result, many institutions have been pushed into a more complex CRA evaluation
framework even though they remain community banks.

9 91 FR at 52121.

 7
 ABA therefore recommends indexing both the Small and Intermediate Bank thresholds to nominal
Gross Domestic Product (GDP). Unlike an inflation-based adjustment, nominal GDP reflects both
inflation and economic growth and thus provides a more comprehensive measure of changes in
the banking industry and the broader economy. This approach would help to preserve the intended
distinctions among Small, Intermediate, and Large banks over time.

ABA does not agree that the proposed threshold increases will reduce CRA activity. All banks will
continue to have CRA responsibilities and will continue to be examined for CRA compliance; none
will be "exempt" as some commentators have alleged.

Second, allowing more institutions to qualify for the Intermediate Bank test would not eliminate the
community development responsibilities of these institutions. Unlike the Large Bank test, which
requires banks to fill separate "buckets" of community development lending and investments, the
Intermediate Bank test evaluates those activities on a combined basis. As a result, rightsizing the
asset cap for Intermediate Banks would reduce burden on these banks to fill each bucket and
allow more institutions to determine the appropriate mix of community development loans and
investments based on the needs of the communities they serve. This is consistent with the
Agencies' goal when they established the Intermediate Small Bank classification--to provide
flexibility to institutions in how they serve community credit needs.

For example, one community may have a robust pipeline of affordable housing investments, while
another may have greater need for healthcare facilities or other community infrastructure. The
argument that banks will reduce community development investment activity because they are no
longer required to fill a separate investment bucket presumes that regulators, not local banks,
should determine the optimal mix of community development activities. Community development
financing should be driven by community needs, not by a government preference for one qualifying
activity over another. The relevant question is whether a bank is helping to meet community
development needs, not whether a bank's community development dollars are allocated among
community development categories in proportions preferred by regulators or other external
parties. A change in activity mix does not equate to a reduction in community development activity.

Third, there is no evidence that Small Banks do not engage in community development activities
because they are not required to do so. Indeed, a survey of ABA members found that 63% percent
of Small Banks (as defined by the current regulation) made community development loans or
investments during their current or most recent evaluation period. These institutions undertake
such activities because they have developed expertise in community development financing or
have access to local opportunities that align with their business strategies.

Moreover, as discussed in Section II. C., below, some institutions that would be reclassified from
Intermediate Banks to Small Banks under the proposal have stated that they would prefer to
continue being evaluated under the Intermediate Bank framework because they have established
community development programs and want those activities to be fully recognized in CRA

 8
 examinations.10 Not all Small Banks have the resources, expertise, or community development
opportunities necessary to maintain a community development program. However, some do and
assertions that banks of $1 billion in assets and below do not engage in community development
activities are incorrect and ignore the diversity of community bank business models.

Finally, the proposed rule inquires whether the Intermediate Bank threshold should be raised to
$30 billion in assets and the Small Bank threshold should be raised to $10 billion in assets. These
thresholds are not part of the proposed text; rather, the Agencies pose the question in the
preamble. We appreciate that the Agencies are taking the calibration of asset classifications
seriously and are open to exploring a range of alternatives. Before considering this threshold
further, the agencies should consider such a change in conjunction with their refocusing the rule
on the statute's objectives as well as the cumulative regulatory burden and competitive pressures
facing community banks.

The proposal also invites comment on a third option: whether to align the Small Bank threshold
with the Small Business Administration's (SBA) size standard for commercial banking organizations
and savings institutions. Under this approach, banks with less than $850 million in assets would be
Small Banks and banks with between $850 million and $5 billion in assets would be Intermediate
Banks.11 Under this alternative, the thresholds would track changes to the SBA's size standard for
commercial banking organizations, which the SBA reviews periodically and adjusts at least once
every five years. We do not support this approach because it would delegate CRA threshold-setting
to an agency with no responsibility for CRA examination or supervision. The banking Agencies--not
the SBA--should determine the asset thresholds that govern CRA evaluations.

 III. Clarify and Adjust Small and Intermediate Bank Examinations

Recalibrating the asset thresholds is only one part of ensuring that CRA evaluations remain
appropriately tailored. The final rule should build on that approach by providing Small and
Intermediate Banks with additional flexibility and examination options that recognize the diversity
of institutions within these categories.

 A. Clarify the role of comparative data in Small and Intermediate Bank
 examinations.

The proposal would retain the longstanding--and important--focus on performance context as
part of the CRA evaluation framework. Under both the existing rule and the proposal, performance
context includes consideration of "the performance of similarly situated lenders."12 However,

10 Under the proposal, community development activities conducted by Small Banks generally would receive
consideration only as part of performance context rather than as a distinct component of the evaluation.
11 After the banking agencies issued the CRA proposal, the SBA proposed increasing the size standard from
$850 million to $925 million.
12 91 FR 52186 and 12 CFR __.21(b)(5).

 9
 neither the regulation nor the proposal defines "similarly situated lenders," and bankers report
significant variation in the degree to which examiners incorporate this information.

This issue takes on added importance in light of the proposed increase of the Intermediate Bank
threshold. Institutions currently evaluated as Large Banks that would be reclassified as
Intermediate Banks are accustomed to evaluations that consider aggregate, market-share, market
rank, and other comparative lending data. 13 Naturally, they have questions about how evaluations
would be conducted when they are no longer required to report CRA data. Therefore, we urge the
Agencies to explain when comparative information may be considered, how similarly situated
lenders would be identified, and the weight comparative information would receive in the
examination process.

The current Small and Intermediate Small Bank examination procedures provide a useful model in
this regard. They treat information about similarly situated institutions as a tool for understanding
performance context, rather than as an independent measure of performance.14 The exam
procedures expressly state that peer information may help examiners understand local market
conditions, opportunities, and constraints, but they do not suggest that a bank's CRA performance
should be judged based on how it compares to other lenders.

The Agencies should reaffirm this principle in the final rule, updated examination procedures, and
examiner training materials. Comparative information can provide valuable insight into local
market conditions, but the CRA statute requires regulators to evaluate a bank's record of helping
meet the credit needs of its communities--not whether it meets or outperforms other lenders.

The Agencies should also ensure that revised examination procedures and examiner training make
clear that data reported by Large Banks will not be used to evaluate Intermediate Banks. Once an
institution transitions to the Intermediate Bank category, examiners should not rely on peer
comparator data derived from CRA reporting by Large Banks. Doing so would reintroduce Large
Bank data into a framework that does not require Intermediate Banks to collect or report CRA
information. If comparative information is considered, it should be based on institutions that are
truly similarly situated and only as part of the performance context analysis. This clarification is

Performance Evaluations, OCC Bulletin 2018-17 (June 15, 2018) (addressing the use of demographic,
aggregate, and market share data in CRA evaluations).
14 As part of the performance context analysis, examiners review financial information and prior CRA
evaluations of institutions of similar size serving the same or similar assessment areas. The procedures then
incorporate comparative information into particular aspects of the lending analysis. For example, in
evaluating a bank's loan-to-deposit ratio, examiners consider, as applicable, "the capacity of other similarly-
situated institutions to lend in the assessment area(s)," together with the bank's own lending capacity,
economic conditions, and lending opportunities. When evaluating areas of low loan penetration, the
procedures similarly direct examiners to consider information about other lenders serving the same or

 particularly important because the proposal does not define which institutions qualify as "similarly
situated lenders" for purposes of evaluating Intermediate Banks.

 B. Provide Small Banks the option of being evaluated under the Intermediate Bank
 test.

In addition to raising the thresholds for the Small and Intermediate Bank tests, the Agencies
propose to revise the Small Bank lending test. Under the current rule, examiners evaluate a Small
Bank's loan-to-deposit ratio, lending within its assessment area, lending to borrowers of different
income levels, the geographic distribution of the bank's loans and, as appropriate, "other lending-
related activities, such as loans originated for sale to the secondary markets, community
development loans, or qualified investments" (emphasis added). The proposal removes this
provision and instead permits examiners to consider community development activities as part of
performance context under proposed __.21(b). It does not explain how examiners would
recognize loans originated for sale in the secondary market for Small and Intermediate Banks.

This change could reduce the recognition that Small Bank community development activities and
loans originated for sale into the secondary market receive in CRA exams. Many institutions
welcome being classified as a Small Bank and the reduced compliance burden that accompanies
that designation. At the same time, banks do not operate the same CRA programs. For some
institutions--particularly those that would move from the Intermediate Bank framework to the
Small Bank framework--community development activities are an important way that they meet
local credit needs. These activities often require substantial time, expertise, and resources and
can represent a meaningful commitment to the communities a bank serves. Under the proposal,
however, those activities would no longer receive consideration as a distinct component of the
evaluation and instead would be considered only as part of the bank's performance context.

The proposed change could affect ratings. Once a bank achieves Satisfactory performance under
the Small Bank test, examiners may be less likely to undertake a detailed analysis of performance
context when determining whether the institution's performance merits an Outstanding rating. As a
result, community development activities may receive less recognition, potentially making it
difficult for Small Banks with strong community development records to be meaningfully
differentiated or recognized. Over time, this could further concentrate Outstanding ratings among
larger institutions.

To address these concerns, the final rule should permit Small Banks to elect evaluation under the
Intermediate Bank framework. Although they may elect evaluation under the Large Bank framework
today and under the proposal, that option carries additional complexity and data collection
requirements. An Intermediate Bank election would allow Small Banks with significant community
development activity to receive direct consideration for that work without assuming those
additional burdens.

 11
 Finally, the proposal would eliminate consideration of "loans originated for sale into the secondary
market" without explaining how these activities would be treated. Community banks often
originate mortgage loans for sale to manage interest-rate and liquidity risk and generate liquidity for
additional lending. The Agencies should clarify how these activities will be evaluated under the
revised Small and Intermediate Bank lending tests.

 IV. Preserve and Strengthen the Strategic Plan Option

The strategic plan option tailors a bank's CRA performance evaluation to its business model. ABA
has long maintained that banks and the communities they serve benefit from the regulatory
certainty and flexibility of design that strategic plans provide, and we have consistently advocated
for improvements to the strategic plan approval process.

We support the proposed changes to improve the strategic plan option. The need for the CRA
framework to accommodate different business models will continue to grow as community banks
partner with fintechs, offer specialized lending products, or operate hybrid business models that
combine local and digital banking activities. The agencies should ensure that the strategic plan
option remains sufficiently flexible to account for bank business models.

The proposal appropriately recognizes that strategic plans are underused and seeks to make them
a viable option for more banks. These are worthwhile objectives, and we offer the following
recommendations for improving the strategic plan option.

 A. Permit banks to continue combining community development loans and
 investments within a single strategic plan goal.

The proposal would revise the strategic plan framework to require a bank to address all three CRA
performance categories--lending, investments, and services--while permitting the exclusion of
measurable goals for a category if supported by the bank's performance context. This creates
uncertainty regarding whether banks may continue to combine community development lending
and community development investments within a single community development finance goal, or
whether the proposal requires separate goals or separate justification for each category.

Requiring banks to establish separate goals for community development loans and investments
would reduce flexibility and make strategic plans less responsive to local market conditions.
It could also discourage use of the strategic plan option. The final rule should preserve this
flexibility and expressly state that banks may combine community development lending and
investment activities into a single community development finance goal.

 12
  B. Clarify that strategic plan banks may carry forward excess community
 development performance from one year to the next.

The proposal requires banks to establish annual interim measurable goals for each year of a
strategic plan. We request that the Agencies clarify that banks may carry forward excess
community development performance to account for common fluctuations in community
development markets, such as project pipeline variability, availability of tax credit allocations, and
the timing of complex closings. Each year, community development opportunities vary markedly
between lending and investment, which can make it difficult for banks to meet annual interim goals
if the bank has established separate goals for lending and investments. Broader economic
conditions also shift from year to year and can directly affect the lending and investment goals a
bank is able to achieve. Together, these factors often cause community development activity to
occur unevenly over time.

For these reasons, a bank that exceeds its annual community development goal in one year should
receive credit for that performance in subsequent years. A bank's community development rating
should reflect its cumulative performance over the full evaluation period, not year-to-year
variability driven by market conditions that are beyond the bank's control.

 C. Grandfather existing strategic plans.

The proposal does not address the treatment of institutions currently operating under approved
plans. Banks need certainty that previously approved plans will remain valid through the duration
of the approved term. The final rule should expressly provide that existing plans remain effective
and may be completed under the framework that applied at the time of approval.

 D. Invest in examiner education and training regarding strategic plans.

One reason the strategic plan option remains underused is that many examiners encounter
strategic plans infrequently and may not be familiar with their development, approval, or
evaluation. Likewise, our members report significant variation in examiner familiarity with strategic
plans and the role that performance context plays in evaluating plan goals. Updated examiner
training would promote consistency, improve the regulatory consultation process, and help ensure
that banks receive meaningful feedback when operating under strategic plans. Enhanced examiner
expertise would also reinforce the Agencies' stated objective of encouraging broader use of the
strategic plan option.

 E. Prioritize local community input.

Proposed __.27(c) would continue to require a bank seeking to adopt a strategic plan to informally
seek suggestions from members of the public in assessment area(s) covered by the plan during

 13
 plan development and to formally solicit public comment on the draft strategic plan for at least 30
calendar days.

We recommend that the Agencies specify that greater weight will be accorded to comments
submitted by individuals or organizations within the bank's local community and that a bank is not
required to respond to public comments submitted by individuals or organizations outside its
assessment area. Banks should remain focused on the credit needs of the communities they are
chartered to serve, and commenters outside those communities should not unduly influence a
bank's strategic plan or impose additional procedural burdens. Clarifying this principle would
ensure that public participation enhances the relevance of the strategic plan and the degree to
which it is tailored and responsive to local community needs and conditions. This is also consistent
with the statute's focus on a bank's physical footprint and its local community.

 V. Preserve Wholesale and Limited Purpose Business Models

Today, regulators evaluate Wholesale and Limited Purpose institutions under a standalone
community development test rather than the standard lending, investment, and service tests. This
approach recognizes that Wholesale and Limited Purpose Banks have specialized, often
nationwide lending models which cannot be fairly assessed under standards designed for
traditional retail banks.

The proposal, however, would fundamentally reshape the CRA framework for Wholesale and
Limited Purpose Banks. CRA examinations should evaluate how a bank serves its communities
within the context of the business it has chosen to operate--not pressure institutions to engage in
retail lending activities in order to achieve satisfactory CRA performance. Significant changes to
the current treatment of Wholesale and Limited Purpose Banks would only introduce new burden,
which is at odds with the Agencies' stated goal in this rulemaking. Any updates to the CRA
regulation should continue to recognize the specialized operations of Wholesale and Limited
Purpose Banks rather than forcing them into lending that is outside of the scope of their business
models.

 A. Retain the phrase "to retail customers" in the definition of a Wholesale Bank.

The current rule defines a Wholesale Bank as an institution that "is not in the business of extending
home mortgage, small business, small farm, or consumer loans to retail customers" (emphasis
added). The proposal would remove the phrase "to retail customers."

The wholesale designation is used by industrial and corporate banks, institutional service banks,
private and wealth management banks, and custody banks. These institutions provide custody,
trust, clearing, treasury, securities, and correspondent banking services and may also engage in
commercial lending, capital markets activities, or other specialized financing. None of these
activities constitutes retail banking, nor are they marketed to the retail public.

 14
 By removing the phrase "to retail customers," the definition would no longer focus on whether a
bank is engaged in retail banking. Instead, a bank could lose wholesale status simply because it
originates loans that fall within certain loan categories, even when those loans are provided only as
an accommodation to existing clients and are ancillary to the bank's specialized business lines. As
a result, institutions that do not market to or serve the retail public would be evaluated under a CRA
framework that was designed for retail banks. Retaining the phrase "to retail customers" preserves
the distinction between wholesale and retail banking.

 B. Retain the existing approach to incidental lending for Wholesale and Limited
 Purpose Banks.

The proposed definition of "incidental basis" would further narrow the eligibility criteria for
wholesale and limited purpose designation. As proposed, a bank would qualify as a Limited
Purpose Bank if it offers only a narrow product line (such as credit card or motor vehicle loans) and
provides other types of loans only on an incidental basis. Similarly, a bank would qualify as a
Wholesale Bank if it is not in the business of extending home mortgage, small business, small farm,
or consumer loans, other than on an incidental basis. Under the proposal, lending is incidental if it:

 Is provided infrequently as an incident to the institution's specialized operations or as an
 accommodation to the institution's customers;

 Is not advertised or marketed to the public or the institution's customers; and
 Constitutes no more than 5 percent of the institution's total lending as of December 31 of

 each of the prior two calendar years.

The consequences of the proposed definition of "incidental basis" would be significant;
institutions that have long been evaluated as Wholesale or Limited Purpose Banks could be
disqualified, thereby requiring that they be evaluated as a retail bank even though they remain
fundamentally non-retail institutions. This is at odds with the Agencies' goal of reducing burden.
The proposal does not explain why such a significant narrowing of the eligibility criteria is necessary
or otherwise justified, or why the Agencies propose replacing it with a more restrictive and
prescriptive standard.

ABA has the following concerns with the proposed definition of incidental basis.

First, the Agencies state that this definition is intended to "largely codify guidance in the
Interagency Questions and Answers," specifically Q&A __.12(n)--2. That Q&A, however, asks
whether "only an insignificant portion of the institution's total assets and income result from the
other lending" (emphasis added).

The proposed definition is a significant departure from the current measure used to determine
whether retail lending is "insignificant." Rather than focusing on portfolio characteristics--

 15
 specifically, the assets and income attributable to the "other lending"--it applies a calendar-year
threshold based on loan production. Because lending volume and composition can vary
substantially from year to year due to factors outside an institution's control, annual production
may not reliably reflect the institution's business model. By contrast, the proportion of assets and
income attributable to accommodation lending is generally more stable.

Second, the test's proposed restriction on marketing to customers is overly broad. Non-retail-
focused institutions should remain free to discuss loan products with their existing clients. The
relevant question is not whether a bank provides information about lending products to its clients;
it is whether a bank markets products to the general public. For example, a wealth management
client may inform a relationship manager that he or she is considering building a custom home.
Providing information about available mortgage products in response to that conversation is a
natural extension of the existing wealth management relationship; it is not retail marketing. A bank
should not lose its wholesale designation because it responds to a client's expressed financial
needs.

Third, we understand that the historical rule-of-thumb threshold for accommodation lending, while
not codified or addressed in public guidance, was 10% of total assets and income. Yet, the
Agencies do not explain why they are proposing to cut this percentage in half, and they do not
provide evidence that the existing wholesale and limited purpose designations have been applied
too broadly.

For these reasons, we recommend that the Agencies not adopt the proposed definition of
"incidental basis." Instead, the Agencies should retain the current approach, under which
wholesale and limited purpose eligibility is evaluated based on the institution's overall business
model and whether other lending activities are insignificant in relation to the institution's
operations. The existing framework provides sufficient flexibility to accommodate specialized
business models while allowing the Agencies to distinguish appropriately between retail and non-
retail institutions.

 C. Retain the Limited Purpose Bank designation.

The current rule defines a Limited Purpose Bank as an institution that offers a narrow product
line--such as credit card or motor vehicle loans--to a regional or broader market. The preamble
requests comment on eliminating the limited purpose designation, even though the proposed
regulatory text retains it. The Agencies also inquire whether the proposed major-product-line
approach could accommodate institutions currently evaluated as Limited Purpose Banks.

The proposed major product line approach would not be workable for banks currently designated
as Limited Purpose Banks. Eliminating the designation would subject these institutions to retail
lending and service standards that are often poorly aligned with their business models and delivery
channels. This result is not consistent with the Agencies' goal of reducing regulatory burden.

 16
 The Agencies adopted the limited purpose designation in 1995 because they recognized that the
CRA standards applicable to retail banks (including the geographic distribution of loans and
availability of branch-based services) did not fit Limited Purpose Banks. For example, the preamble
to the 1995 rule explains that Limited Purpose Banks "typically draw their resources from, and
serve areas well beyond, their immediate communities" and have a "different operational focus"
than traditional retail banks.15 The 1995 rule "encourages an institution that does not itself engage
in the categories of lending evaluated under the lending test to seek designation as a Wholesale or
Limited Purpose Bank so that the institution's CRA performance can be evaluated under criteria
appropriate to the institution."16

Eliminating the limited purpose designation would therefore recreate the very mismatch it was
designed to address.

First, retail-oriented lending and service tests would not provide a meaningful CRA assessment of
Limited Purpose Banks. These institutions typically offer a specialized lending product on a
regional or nationwide basis while maintaining only one or a small number of physical locations
and corresponding assessment areas. As a result, the borrower and geographic distribution
analyses that comprise the lending test would be applied to only a small portion of the lending
activity that comprises a bank's business. A Limited Purpose Bank could have a strong record of
serving borrowers nationwide yet receive a weak CRA rating because its evaluation would focus
exclusively on lending within the bank's assessment area(s). Likewise, retail-service measures
would evaluate delivery channels the institution was never designed to provide. The result would
not be a more accurate CRA evaluation, but one that distorts the performance of specialized
nationwide lenders.

Second, the bank's nationwide lending could adversely affect its ratio of lending inside versus
outside its assessment area, even though a bank's ratio would reflect the institution's specialized
national business strategy rather than a failure to meet local credit needs.

Third, eliminating the limited purpose designation, together with the resulting data collection
requirements applicable to Large Banks, would require these institutions to collect and maintain
consumer loan data across large nationwide portfolios even though CRA performance would only
be evaluated where the bank has a physical location. This outcome would be inconsistent with the
proposal's objective of reducing regulatory burden, and would provide minimal benefits.
