  VI. Focus Retail Lending Evaluations on Material Lending Activities

The proposed lending test would evaluate a bank's record of meeting community credit needs by
evaluating its retail lending in its major product lines. The proposal would apply a major-product-
line framework to banks of all sizes and requests comment on two alternatives for identifying the
retail lending products subject to examination.

Under Option 1, the Agencies would evaluate a bank's two largest retail lending product lines,
determined at the bank level, based on both loan count and dollar volume. Under Option 2, the
Agencies would identify major product lines separately in each assessment area based on the
bank's overall lending volume and business strategy, its capacity to lend in the assessment area,
and the extent to which lending in a product line meaningfully contributes to the bank's record of
meeting the credit needs of that assessment area. Option 2, therefore, could result in the
evaluation of more or fewer than two product lines, and different product lines could be evaluated
across a bank's assessment areas.

Under either alternative, the relevant product lines could include home mortgage, small business,
small farm, and consumer lending. However, consumer lending generally would be evaluated only
if it represents more than 50 percent of the bank's retail lending by both loan count and dollar
volume, or if the bank elects to have it considered.

 A. Determine major product lines at the bank level.

ABA supports focusing CRA retail lending evaluations on a bank's major product lines. This
approach would concentrate examinations on the lending activities that most meaningfully define
a bank's business model, and therefore, would be an effective and efficient approach to evaluating
a bank's record of meeting the credit needs of its community.

Of the two options proposed for defining major product lines, ABA recommends that the Agencies
adopt Option 1, which would determine major product lines at the bank level based on loan count
and dollar volume. Unlike Option 2, which could result in different major product lines being
evaluated in different assessment areas, Option 1 would result in the same major product lines
being evaluated across all assessment areas. Banks could monitor these metrics during the
evaluation period, which would provide predictability as to whether a product will be assessed.
Option 1 would also largely codify existing practice.

In contrast, Option 2 poses multiple challenges that would create burden and uncertainty for
institutions, undermining the goals of the rulemaking. First, it would introduce significant
uncertainty by requiring major product lines to be determined in each assessment area based on a
combination of quantitative and qualitative factors. As a result, banks would have limited ability to
predict with confidence which product lines ultimately would be evaluated in a particular

 18
 assessment area. Option 2 could also result in a more complex evaluation if a bank were to be
evaluated on different product lines in different assessment areas.

Second, uncertainty regarding whether consumer lending will be identified as a major product line
in a particular assessment area would effectively convert Option 2 into a de facto universal data
collection requirement. Proposed __.42(a)(4) would require a Large Bank for which consumer
loans are a major product line to collect and maintain machine-readable, loan-level data (i.e., loan
identifier, amount, location, and the borrower's gross annual income) for every consumer loan that
the bank originates or purchases during the evaluation period, across all consumer loan
categories.

Today, banks do not systematically capture or refresh borrower income data for many consumer
loan products, and that information cannot be reconstructed after the fact. A bank facing
assessment-area-by-assessment-area major product line determinations would therefore have no
practical choice but to collect and maintain evaluation-ready data on its entire consumer portfolio,
in every assessment area throughout the evaluation period as a hedge against the possibility that
examiners could later designate consumer lending as a major product line in a particular
assessment area at exam time. This burden is especially acute and unwarranted for credit-card
and auto lenders that serve national markets from one or a small number of assessment areas
because these institutions would be required to collect and maintain data across their entire
nationwide consumer portfolio even though only a small portion of that lending may ultimately be
relevant to assessment-area-level CRA evaluation.

Option 1 avoids this concern by establishing a single bank-level determination based on objective
measures of loan count and dollar volume that institutions can monitor throughout the evaluation
period, which would allow banks to plan for any future consumer-lending data collection
requirements if consumer lending becomes a major product line.

 B. Retain the existing substantial majority standard and define it as 75 percent of
 total lending.

The proposed rule would evaluate a bank's consumer lending if it represents more than 50 percent
of the bank's retail lending by both loan count and dollar volume or if the bank elects to have it
considered. This approach would significantly expand the role of consumer lending in the CRA
evaluations for some banks.

Under the current framework, examiners evaluate a bank's consumer loans when they constitute a
"substantial majority" of a bank's business, although a bank may elect to have consumer lending
considered even if the bank does not reach the substantial majority threshold. The proposed "more
than 50 percent" threshold is a departure from this practice. The Interagency Questions and
Answers (Interagency Q&A) interpret "substantial majority" to mean a volume of consumer lending
so significant that a CRA evaluation "would not meaningfully reflect" a bank's lending performance

 19
 if consumer loans were excluded.17 Three decades of examination practice have applied this
standard. Yet, the Agencies offer no explanation for replacing it, including why the current
substantial majority framework is inadequate or why a simple majority is the appropriate
alternative. Nor does the proposal demonstrate why the resulting increase in data collection
burdens would produce more accurate and meaningful CRA assessments. The proposed change is
also notable given that recent CRA rulemakings recognized the unique data collection and
evaluation challenges associated with consumer lending.18

The proposal also raises a number of significant implementation and supervisory questions
regarding how consumer lending would be evaluated against a broader set of institutions.

First, consumer lending encompasses a diverse range of products--including credit cards,
automobile loans, personal loans, and student loans--with distinct purposes, risk characteristics,
and delivery channels. The preamble states that when consumer lending constitutes a major
product line, examiners would evaluate all categories of consumer lending in the aggregate.
However, this approach is not reflected in the proposed regulatory text.

Moreover, the Agencies do not explain how examiners would conduct a meaningful performance
evaluation and draw consistent ratings across such diverse forms of credit. Unlike mortgage, small
business, or small farm lending, consumer lending consists of multiple product categories that
often serve different customer populations and business objectives. Aggregating these products
into a single consumer-lending category could obscure important differences in performance and
make rating outcomes difficult to understand or replicate.

These concerns are compounded by the limited availability of standardized consumer-lending data
and the absence of reliable benchmarking information across product types. Accordingly, if
consumer lending is evaluated under the CRA, the Agencies should evaluate consumer lending
separately by product category rather than as a single aggregated product line. This approach
would produce more meaningful performance evaluations and improve the comparability of
examination results.

Second, it is unclear how the proposal would apply the Lending Test's borrower and distribution
analysis to the full spectrum of consumer loans. These analyses were developed for home
mortgage and small business/small farm lending, where borrower income and geography are
collected, verified, and factored into underwriting decisions. In contrast, consumer loan products
typically are originated nationally and are not targeted to specific geographic markets. Moreover,
assessment areas typically represent only a small portion of a consumer lender's nationwide
footprint. For institutions that originate consumer loans on a national basis, lending activity within

18 85 Fed. Reg. 34,73940 (June 5, 2020).

 20
 a particular assessment area may not be representative of the bank's overall consumer lending
business or the distribution of borrowers across its entire portfolio. As a result, the Lending Test's
distribution analyses may provide limited insight into a bank's record of meeting the credit needs of
its assessment area.

Third, indirect auto lending presents additional complications. Unlike home mortgage, small
business, or small farm lending, indirect auto loans are typically originated through dealer
networks rather than bank-directed delivery channels. Banks generally do not market directly to
borrowers or control dealer locations. For these reasons, a bank's role in the transaction often
differs significantly from its role in originating home mortgage, small business, or small farm loans,
making direct comparisons under the Lending Test difficult. Moreover, banks compete with finance
companies, captive auto lenders, and credit unions that are not subject to CRA and would not be
required to report auto lending data. The proposal does not explain how examiners would account
for these market dynamics when evaluating bank lending performance.

For these reasons, ABA recommends that the Agencies retain the existing substantial-majority
standard, under which consumer lending is evaluated only when consumer loans represent such a
significant portion of a bank's business that excluding them would not support a meaningful
evaluation of a bank's CRA lending performance. To provide greater certainty and promote
consistent application, the Agencies should define "substantial majority" as consumer lending
representing at least 75 percent of a bank's total lending activity measured by both loan count and
dollar volume over a two-year period.

A total-lending measure is the appropriate benchmark because the purpose of the substantial-
majority inquiry is to determine whether consumer lending is sufficiently important to the bank's
overall business to warrant CRA evaluation in the first instance. If consumer lending constitutes
only a relatively small portion of a bank's total lending activity, there is little reason to devote CRA
examination resources to evaluating that product line. By contrast, measuring consumer lending
solely against a bank's retail lending portfolio could result in consumer lending being designated a
major product line even when it represents a relatively small share of the institution's overall
lending business and therefore would not meaningfully affect an assessment of the bank's CRA
lending performance as a whole.

A 75 percent threshold also is consistent with the ordinary meaning of a "substantial majority" as
compared to the proposed "simple majority" standard. Three decades of examination practice
have recognized that consumer lending should be evaluated only when it constitutes a dominant
component of a bank's lending business. Establishing a clear 75 percent threshold would preserve
that principle while providing institutions and examiners with a more objective and predictable
standard. Measuring the threshold over a two-year period would further reduce volatility and
ensure that consumer lending is identified as a major product line based on sustained business
activity rather than temporary fluctuations in a bank's portfolio.

 21
 Finally, this approach would provide greater clarity than the current Interagency Q&A, which refers
to a "substantial portion" of a bank's "total business" without defining those terms with precision.
A 75 percent threshold based on total lending activity would maintain continuity with the existing
framework while giving banks and examiners a clear, administrable standard for CRA planning and
examination purposes.

 VII. Update the Community Development Framework

ABA appreciates the Agencies' efforts to clarify and improve the CRA rule's community
development framework. We support several aspects of the proposal, including revisions to
affordable housing and financial education, recognition of legally binding commitments and
outstanding community development loans, and mechanisms designed to provide greater
certainty regarding CRA eligibility. Certain provisions, however, warrant refinement to preserve
flexibility and avoid unnecessary burden.

 A. Refine the proposed definitions of community development.

The proposal would amend the definition of "community development," by revising the core
categories of community development--affordable housing, civic assistance, economic
development, and revitalization and stabilization. ABA generally supports these changes but
recommends the following modifications.

 1. Adopt the proposed affordable housing standards and clarify high-cost
 area eligibility.

The proposed definition of affordable housing has two components: (1) a baseline affordability
standard and (2) affordable housing in high-cost areas, which includes middle-income housing in
high-cost markets.

 Baseline Affordability Standard. Rental housing that is inhabited by LMI individuals or
 families where median rents do not and are not projected to exceed 30 percent of 80
 percent of area median income (AMI).

 High-Cost Areas. Rental housing that is likely to be inhabited by LMI or middle-income
 individuals or families where median rents do not and are not projected to exceed 30
 percent of 120 percent of AMI in high-cost areas.

ABA supports the proposed baseline standard. It provides a clear and objective framework for
determining whether rental housing qualifies as affordable housing and will promote consistency

 22
 across examinations. It also aligns with existing federal housing policy, including the 2026 housing
goals for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.19

Similarly, we support the proposed standard for affordable housing in high-cost areas. Middle-
income households in these markets often face significant housing cost burdens despite earning
incomes above those traditionally associated with CRA-eligible housing activities. The proposed
standard of 30 percent of 120 percent of AMI in high-cost areas recognizes these market realities
and would encourage additional investment in communities experiencing acute affordability
challenges.

While the Agencies do not propose to define what constitutes a high-cost area, the preamble
requests comment on whether one should be adopted. ABA agrees that additional clarity would be
beneficial. Rather than prescribing a single definition, however, the Agencies should permit banks
to identify high-cost market conditions using any objective and supportable methodology
appropriate to the activity. For example, banks should be permitted to rely on HUD Difficult
Development Areas, FHFA High Opportunity Areas, HUD Fair Market Rents, and similar federal
metrics. However, these methods should be treated as permissible and illustrative rather than
mandatory or exclusive.

We also note that although not defined in the current rule or the Interagency Q&As, the Agencies
have historically considered a county to be high-cost when more than 40 percent of households
are housing cost burdened. This standard has significant limitations.20 If the Agencies retain this
county-based approach, they should lower the threshold to more than 30 percent and permit
banks to rely on the American Community Survey cost burden measure most relevant to the
activity, such as renter cost burden for rental housing activities. A threshold of more than 30
percent would better capture high-cost markets such as Suffolk County, Massachusetts (39.8
percent), New York County, New York (39.4 percent), Dallas County, Texas (36.0 percent), and San
Francisco County, California (33.0 percent), which should not be excluded merely because they
fall slightly below a 40 percent threshold. We also recommend the Agencies clarify that
subsequent changes in an area's cost designation will not affect CRA consideration for existing
loans, investments, or legally binding commitments.

proposed thresholds are also consistent with the Federal Housing Enterprises Financial Safety and

be determined based on rents that `[do] not exceed 30 percent of the maximum income level of such income

the threshold to more than 30 percent and permit banks to rely on the American Community Survey cost
burden measure most relevant to the activity, such as renter cost burden for rental housing activities.

 23
 Finally, ABA strongly supports the proposal's inclusion of mixed-income housing within the
definition of affordable housing and recommends preserving the current approach for mixed-
income projects. Under the existing Interagency Q&A, when more than 50 percent of a project's
units are affordable to low- or moderate-income individuals and the project has a primary purpose
of community development, the entire project should receive CRA consideration. When less than
50 percent of a project's units are affordable to low- or moderate-income individuals, the project
should receive pro rata consideration based on the affordable portion. This approach preserves full
consideration for projects with a primary community development purpose while appropriately
recognizing the affordable housing component of other mixed-income projects.21

 2. Recognize financial education activities that benefit consumers across
 income levels.

The definition of community development would also include various forms of civic assistance,
including financial literacy and homebuyer counseling programs that serve, assist, or are
reasonably expected to serve or assist LMI individuals and families. ABA is pleased that the
proposal recognizes these activities and recommends that the final rule state that they need not be
targeted to, or provided primarily for the benefit of, LMI individuals. Financial education benefits
individuals across all income levels and helps consumers navigate an increasingly complex
financial system, including fraud prevention and digital financial literacy. Banks should therefore
receive CRA consideration for providing these services on a generally available basis.

Under the current rules and Interagency Q&As, CRA credit is limited to programs that serve LMI
individuals or schools where more than half of students qualify for free or reduced-price meals.
Requiring financial literacy initiatives to have a principal purpose of serving LMI individuals is
inconsistent with school boundaries in many communities. Urban magnet and rural schools
typically draw students from a wide geographic area, and many rural counties have only one high
school. Moreover, some school districts in small cities and suburban areas intentionally draw their
attendance maps so that the student population is economically diverse. These realities make it
difficult to target financial education solely to LMI populations. Instead, financial education is
offered to all, including LMI individuals.

Banks also play an important role in adult financial education, offering housing counseling,
budgeting instruction, digital financial literacy, or programs to prevent fraud and elder financial
exploitation. Today, a bank does not receive CRA consideration for making these presentations to
organizations that do not qualify as having a community development purpose (e.g., Rotary Club,
Lions Club, Chamber of Commerce, etc.), even if the audience includes LMI individuals. Senior
citizens in all income brackets are at heightened risk of fraud and financial abuse, and

21 See Interagency Q&A __.12(h)--8.

 24
 policymakers encourage banks to provide programs to prevent financial exploitation. Therefore, all
adult financial education activities should receive CRA credit.

 3. Retain consideration for operating liquidity financing and activities with
 CDFI banks as part of economic development.

The proposal would replace the current "purpose test" outlined in the Interagency Q&As22 with
three sub-categories of economic development. The first proposed sub-category would include
financing for small businesses or farms that expands, improves, or preserves the business's or
farm's productive capacity, physical presence, or employment bases. It would expressly exclude
financing primarily used for ongoing operating liquidity. Nor would operating liquidity financing
qualify under the remaining two categories of economic development, which focus on technical
and supportive services and participation in government programs. The exclusion of operating
liquidity financing would represent a meaningful change from current practice and would narrow
the range of CRA-qualified economic development activities.

We request that the Agencies revise the definition of economic development to include financing
used for ongoing operating liquidity. Working capital and operating-liquidity loans can be essential
to small businesses, particularly during seasonal fluctuations and periods of inflation or other
economic uncertainty. The Agencies recognized the importance of such financing during the
COVID-19 pandemic by providing CRA consideration for Paycheck Protection Program ("PPP")
loans and related activities.23 And, even under normal economic conditions, many small
businesses depend on operating liquidity financing to purchase inventory and retain employees.
These loans help to sustain local economies and preserve jobs. They are no less important to local
economies than financing used to acquire equipment or expand physical facilities. The definition of
economic development should encourage banks to provide these loans, not exclude them from
CRA consideration.

In addition, the proposed definition of economic development would list U.S. Small Business
Administration Certified Development Companies, Small Business Investment Companies,
Qualified Community Development Entities, U.S. Department of Agriculture Rural Business
Investment Companies, and Community Development Financial Institutions that finance small
businesses or small farms as examples of government programs, projects, or initiatives that
receive positive CRA consideration. ABA supports this approach, which is consistent with the
existing Interagency Q&A. In particular, activities involving CDFI banks that receive CRA
consideration under the current regulations and Interagency Q&A should continue to receive CRA
consideration under the final rule.

22 See Interagency Q&A __.12(g)(3)--1.
23 OCC, FDIC & FRB, CRA Consideration for Activities in Response to the Coronavirus FAQs (May 27, 2020).

 25
 Bank Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) are longstanding participants in the
community development ecosystem and often serve as effective channels for delivering financing
and other resources to underserved communities. The current Interagency Q&A has long
recognized the role that CDFIs play in providing credit to underserved communities.24 Activities
involving CDFIs that receive CRA consideration under the current regulations and Interagency Q&A
should continue to receive CRA consideration under the final rule.

 4. Refine the treatment of essential infrastructure and disaster recovery.

The proposal would revise the revitalization and stabilization component of community
development by codifying relevant guidance from the Interagency Q&As.25 We support these
amendments and recommend additional modifications to the treatment of essential infrastructure
and disaster recovery activities.

 a. Provide CRA consideration for community-wide infrastructure
 projects.

The proposal would codify guidance from the Interagency Q&As and provide CRA consideration for
activities that finance or support essential community facilities or essential infrastructure. ABA
supports this addition. However, the proposal does not sufficiently address longstanding
interpretive challenges regarding whether infrastructure financing must be targeted to LMI
individuals or LMI areas.

Under existing CRA regulations and guidance, banks have generally received CRA consideration for
infrastructure projects where the primary purpose of the activity benefits LMI individuals and/or
LMI geographies or revitalizes or stabilizes a nonmetropolitan middle-income geography.26 In
practice, this has discouraged banks from making loans or investments to build or improve roads,
hospitals, schools, water/sewer utilities, broadband, and similar infrastructure projects because
they frequently benefit entire communities or residents spread over multiple counties rather than
discrete LMI populations. This interpretation works at cross purposes with the CRA statute, which
requires banks to serve the credit needs of their entire community, including (but not limited to)
LMI individuals. These projects will benefit LMI individuals and should receive consideration.

The proposal's treatment of essential infrastructure creates additional uncertainty because the
proposed regulatory text and preamble are in tension. On the one hand, the proposed regulatory
text could be read to require that infrastructure activities fully benefit one of the enumerated

25 Where practicable, the Agencies should align the CRA rule's treatment of underserved rural areas with
existing federal rural-development program definitions.
26 See Interagency Q&A __.12(g)(4)(ii)--2, 12(g)(4)(iii)--3, and __.12(g)(4)(iii)--4.

 revitalization and stabilization geographies.27 On the other hand, the preamble acknowledges that
essential infrastructure projects are often "community-wide projects for which it is not feasible to
allocate the benefit to specific populations or areas."28 If the final rule is interpreted to require that
infrastructure projects be targeted exclusively to qualifying geographies or demonstrate a
particular percentage of LMI benefit, the result could be more restrictive than current practice and
undermine the Agencies' stated objective of encouraging infrastructure investment.

Therefore, the Agencies should clarify that infrastructure activities may receive CRA consideration
when they benefit LMI individuals, LMI census tracts, or other targeted areas, even if the activity
also serves a broader community and the benefits cannot be precisely allocated among specific
populations. CRA consideration should not depend on whether a project satisfies a particular
percentage threshold or exclusively benefits an enumerated geography. This would be consistent
with the Agencies' rationale as provided in the preamble to the proposal:

 The addition of an express reference to essential infrastructure in the Proposed
 Rules would acknowledge the importance of these types of projects to communities
 by ensuring that essential infrastructure activities receive CRA consideration if they
 benefit LMI census tracts or other targeted areas.29

We also recommend a targeted revision to the definition of "essential infrastructure." As currently
drafted, the definition includes "mass transit," which may not adequately encompass shuttle bus
or van service arrangements that are common in rural areas. These services typically operate
through a limited number of pick-up locations, on-demand scheduling, or direct transportation to a
resident's home. They provide access to grocery stores, pharmacies, healthcare facilities, and
other necessities, but may not fit traditional concepts of mass transit. To ensure that these
services receive appropriate CRA consideration, we recommend that the Agencies replace "mass
transit" with the term "public transportation."

 b. Recognize all FEMA disaster designations as well as state-
 declared disasters.

The proposal would build upon the current revitalization and stabilization framework by codifying
the treatment of designated disaster areas and broadening CRA eligibility for disaster recovery
activities that may not qualify under existing guidance.

nonmetropolitan middle-income census tracts; (iii) Indian country or other Tribal and native lands; or (iv) any
other area targeted by a government entity for redevelopment that qualifies for significant economic
incentives, such as tax credits, tax abatements, or grants. Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed.
Reg. 52114, 52182, 52202 (Aug. 12, 2026).
28 Id. at 52135.
29 Id. (emphasis added).

 27
 ABA supports eliminating the Interagency Q&A's exclusion of disaster recovery assistance
pertaining to FEMA Public Assistance Emergency Work Category A (Debris Removal) and Category
B (Emergency Protective Measures). The original rationale for excluding Category A and Category B
designations was that such conditions were viewed as temporary. But even temporary conditions
can have long-term impacts on affected communities. When FEMA determines that a disaster
warrants federal assistance, the banking Agencies should not impose a separate judgment as to
whether the disaster is sufficiently permanent or significant to justify CRA consideration.

We also note that the proposal would define a "designated disaster area" as a geographic area that
is the subject of a Major Disaster Declaration by FEMA. We recommend that the Agencies expand
this definition to include areas subject to state declarations, as not all state declarations with
significant local impacts are designated by FEMA. While such situations are relatively uncommon,
the consequences of excluding these areas can be substantial. For example, wildfires do not
always receive a federal disaster declaration, particularly if the damage is largely limited to land
and livestock. Yet, these events can have considerable economic consequences for affected
communities that warrant CRA-supported recovery and stabilization efforts.

 5. Preserve the existing treatment of community development grants.

The proposal would create a new category for community development grants. A bank would be
permitted to receive CRA consideration only for grants and donations directly used by the recipient
for a program, project, or initiative with a primary purpose of community development. For Large
Banks, the proposal would also impose a 15 percent cap on the indirect costs that recipients incur
as a part of administering a grant or donation. In addition, Large Banks would be required to obtain
a recipient's written commitment regarding the use of grant funds, a written attestation that
indirect costs do not exceed 15 percent, and supporting documentation such as the organization's
IRS Form 990 and operating budget information. Certain grant information would be required to be
reported to the Agencies and could be included in a public database.

CRA consideration should not be limited to grants that fund a discrete program, project, or
initiative. Many nonprofit organizations rely on unrestricted operating support to carry out their
community development mission, yet such funding is often among the most difficult to obtain.
Salaries, technology, rent, and other organizational infrastructure are not ancillary to community
development--they are often what make community development activities possible in the first
place. The proposal's focus on project-specific funding would create an artificial distinction
between support for a particular activity and support for the organization carrying out that activity.
In practice, both forms of funding can produce meaningful community development benefits.

The proposal also elevates indirect cost calculations over community impact. CRA credit should
focus on whether the recipient carries out a bona fide community development activity, not
whether the organization satisfies a particular bright line accounting threshold. Nonprofits organize
and report expenses in different ways, and administrative costs alone are not a reliable measure of

 28
 effectiveness. The Agencies should instead focus on whether the grant supports a qualifying
community development purpose and allow banks to reasonably demonstrate that fact based on
the same methodologies that they use today.30

Finally, we note that the proposal's treatment of grants could inadvertently discourage banks from
partnering with nonprofit intermediaries that play a critical role in delivering community
development resources to local communities. Intermediaries help banks identify community
needs, conduct due diligence, provide technical assistance, monitor performance, aggregate
outcome data, and distribute funding efficiently through trusted local networks. As a result, they
often enable banks to reach organizations and communities that would otherwise be difficult to
serve.

The final rule should preserve CRA consideration for grants made through qualified nonprofit
intermediaries, provided that the underlying activities independently satisfy the CRA's community
development requirements. CRA credit should be based on the community development purpose
of the downstream activity and attributed to the location of the ultimate beneficiaries. Rather than
discouraging the intermediary model, the Agencies should recognize its role in expanding the
reach, effectiveness, accountability, and long-term impact of community development
investments while maintaining appropriate safeguards and documentation requirements.

 B. Provide positive CRA consideration for legally-binding commitments to lend and
 prior period community development loans.

The proposal would amend the definition of community development loans to include legally-
binding commitments to lend and outstanding balances on prior period community development
loans. ABA supports these proposed changes.

Including legally-binding commitments to lend in the definition of community development loan
recognizes both the financial and legal reality of these arrangements. Once a bank issues a letter of
credit, it is legally obligated to honor it and must hold capital against that exposure.31 When a bank
is committed to provide financing for a qualifying community development purpose in the same
manner as a loan, it should receive positive CRA consideration as a community development loan.

30 In addition to demonstrating that grants and donations meet a qualified community development purpose,
banks also commonly maintain internal due diligence processes for vetting recipients prior to making a
donation, including reviewing an organization's mission, activities, governance, financial condition, and
anticipated use of grant proceeds.
31 In certain markets, letters of credit are essential to affordable housing finance. In New York City, for
example, affordable housing projects are often financed through bond issuances rather than direct bank
loans. In these situations, banks often provide a letter of credit during the construction period to obtain the
credit ratings necessary to attract investors.

 29
 Similarly, providing positive consideration for outstanding balances on prior period community
development loans would encourage banks to provide long-term financing that is often key to the
success of community development initiatives. In many cases, longer-term loans have a greater
community impact than short-term revolvers (depending on conditions) and should be recognized
accordingly. Tracking outstanding balances on prior period community development loans for CRA
purposes should be at the bank's option, not a requirement.

 C. Do not require complexity as a condition of CRA eligibility.

Although the proposal states that complexity is not required to achieve a particular rating, it
provides that activities deemed complex would be considered responsive and receive greater
weight in the CRA evaluation. The Agencies inquire whether community development investments
and services should be required to be complex and whether complex activities should be
considered more responsive than innovative, flexible, or impactful activities. The Agencies should
not require complexity as a condition of CRA eligibility for community development loans,
investments, grants, or services. The appropriate eligibility standard is whether the activity has a
qualifying community development purpose. Complexity may be considered as a qualitative factor,
but simple and scalable activities that meet community needs should receive full CRA
consideration.

 D. Provide flexibility for allocating community development activities across
 multiple assessment areas.

The proposal would provide two methods for allocating credit when a community development
activity benefits more than one assessment area. Examiners would allocate community
development activities based on either (1) the physical address of the recipient of the proceeds or
the beneficiary of the activity or (2) based on the weight assigned to each assessment area as a
proportion of deposits. The proposal would also permit a bank to use another reasonable
methodology that has been approved by the bank's regulator.

We support allocation based on the physical address of the recipient of the proceeds or beneficiary
of the activity. Banks collect and maintain this information for many types of community
development activities. This approach is straightforward to administer and generally avoids the
complexities associated with deposit-based allocation methodologies.

Under the deposit-based allocation method, examiners would assign a weight to each assessment
area based on the proportion of deposits in that assessment area as determined by the FDIC's
Summary of Deposits (SOD) survey data. While SOD data may be a useful allocation measure for
some banks, it has significant limitations for CRA deposit-allocation purposes for other banks and
therefore should remain an option, not a required allocation methodology. Banks have substantial
flexibility in assigning deposits for SOD reporting, and those assignments are often based on
operational or business considerations unrelated to CRA. For example, some institutions assign

 30
 brokered, wholesale, online, or centralized corporate deposits to a single branch or administrative
location. As a result, SOD data can create artificial concentrations of deposits in particular
assessment areas and may not accurately reflect where deposits are actually sourced or
maintained.

In addition to the physical-address and deposit-based methodologies, the proposal would permit a
bank to use another reasonable methodology approved by its regulator. We support this flexibility
and recommend that banks be permitted to seek approval for an alternative methodology at any
time during the evaluation period. Regulators should provide a timely response so that banks have
certainty regarding how their community development activities will be allocated. Approving a
proposed methodology only at the time of the evaluation would create unnecessary uncertainty
and could deprive banks of a meaningful opportunity to make adjustments.

 E. Provide consideration of outside-assessment-area activities if a bank receives a
 Satisfactory or better on its prior exam.

The proposal would replace the current CRA approach to out-of-assessment-area activities with a
new geographic flexibility standard. Under the current rule, banks may receive consideration for
activities that benefit a broader statewide or regional area that includes their assessment area(s).
Under the proposal, however, banks would receive consideration for activities outside their
assessment area(s) only if they satisfy a geographic flexibility standard.

The agencies propose two alternatives. Under Option 1, a bank would be required to conduct a
specified level of community development activity in each assessment area each year, measured
as a percentage of Tier 1 capital allocated according to the assessment area's weighting. 32 Under
Option 2, a bank would be required to demonstrate an adequate level of community development
activity in each assessment area over the evaluation period based on dollar volume and
responsiveness. In either case, a bank would be required to satisfy the applicable standard in every
assessment area in each state or multistate MSA in which it seeks consideration for an out-of-
assessment-area activity.

We appreciate the Agencies' effort to provide certainty regarding when a bank may obtain positive
CRA consideration for out of assessment area activities. However, the proposed geographic
standards do not consider the ebb and flow of community development pipelines and would
exacerbate CRA hotspots. In addition, they would not provide the certainty banks need when
making community development decisions.

32 Large banks would be required to expend 0.625 percent of Tier 1 capital on community development loans
and 0.625 percent of Tier 1 capital on community development investments and grants. Intermediate,
Wholesale, and Limited Purpose institutions would be required to expend 1.25 percent of Tier 1 capital.

 31
 Community development opportunities do not arise in a predictable or linear manner. Project
pipelines fluctuate over time based on an assessment area's unique economic conditions,
community development opportunities, and funding needs. Affordable housing projects,
infrastructure investments, and other qualifying activities often emerge sporadically rather than on
an annual schedule. Yet Option 1 would require banks to satisfy a quantitative threshold in every
assessment area every year. That approach does not reflect the nature of community development
activity and is inconsistent with evaluating CRA performance over a multi-year examination period.

Option 1 could also discourage participation in some of the most effective community
development financing vehicles. Nationwide and regional investment funds deploy capital across
multiple geographies rather than within a single assessment area. Conditioning credit for out-of-
assessment-area activities on compliance with bright-line annual assessment-area-specific
thresholds would make participation in these funding mechanisms less attractive, potentially
reducing capital available for communities nationwide.

Option 1 would also intensify CRA hotspots. Pursuant to Interagency Q&A __.25(e)-1, a Wholesale
or Limited Purpose bank that has adequately addressed the needs of its assessment area(s) may
receive consideration for qualified community development activities conducted on a nationwide
basis. If these institutions were required to direct 1.25 percent of Tier 1 capital to their assessment
areas to receive nationwide consideration--or if other aspects of the proposal caused them to lose
their designations--many nationally operating institutions with only a single assessment area
would be forced to concentrate substantial amounts of community development capital in already
saturated CRA markets.

Salt Lake City illustrates this potential problem. By one estimate, Option 1 would require banks to
make $2 billion in community development loans and investments in Salt Lake City each year
before receiving consideration for activities elsewhere. Salt Lake City does not have enough
community development opportunities to absorb that level of annual activity. Rather than directing
capital to communities with the greatest need, the proposal would further concentrate activity in
existing CRA hotspots and drive up the cost of community development financing without
advancing community benefit.

A simpler and more effective approach would be to permit banks to receive consideration for
qualifying out-of-assessment-area community development activities if they received an overall
CRA rating of "Satisfactory" or better on their most recent examination. This standard would be
predictable and would ensure that institutions are meeting the needs of their own communities
while avoiding the complexity and unintended consequences of the proposed geographic flexibility
standards. Institutions with less than Satisfactory performance would remain ineligible to receive
consideration for out-of-assessment-area activities during the subsequent examination cycle.

Additionally, the agencies should explicitly recognize support for CDFI banks located outside of a
bank's assessment area(s) as a qualifying community development activity, provided that the bank

 32
 adequately meets the credit needs of its own assessment area. The majority of CDFI banks are
located in rural communities and provide essential financial services in areas with limited access
to capital. Recognizing investments in, deposits with, and other partnerships involving CDFI banks
outside of a bank's assessment area(s) would be an effective means of supporting community and
economic development in these locations.

 F. Strengthen the proposed mechanisms for confirming CRA eligibility.

Under the proposal, the Agencies would maintain an illustrative list of qualifying community
development activities and establish a preapproval process through which banks could request
confirmation that a specific activity qualifies for CRA credit before undertaking it. We strongly
support these aspects of the proposal.

When CRA eligibility for a new or novel loan or investment product is unclear, banks have had
varying degrees of success obtaining feedback from examiners regarding whether the activity will
receive positive CRA consideration. The proposed creation of an illustrative list and a preapproval
process may help to reduce some of this friction.

To improve the utility of an illustrative list, we recommend that it be cumulative, searchable, and
organized by topic rather than date. The list should be understandable by frontline personnel who
do not specialize in compliance, such as branch managers, commercial lenders, and community
development officers. We also recommend that the Agencies make clear that the list is not
exhaustive and that changes to the list will operate prospectively. In other words, if a loan or
investment qualified for CRA consideration when it was originated or purchased, the bank should
continue to receive CRA consideration for that activity as long as it remains on the bank's books.
Finally, the Agencies should commit to updating the list regularly.

With respect to the preapproval process, the value of the preapproval mechanism will hinge on the
timeliness of an agency's response. A 90-day response period is too long. Community
development lending and investment opportunities often move quickly, and a response received
three months after a request is submitted may arrive after the window to invest has closed. For this
reason, ABA recommends a 30-day response period.

 VIII. Retail Service Evaluations Should Reflect CRA's Statutory Focus on Credit

The proposal would revise the retail banking services criterion to better align CRA evaluations with
the statute's focus on credit. Under the current rule, examiners consider the range of retail services
offered across the bank's assessment area(s). The Interagency Q&A further provide that examiners
may evaluate factors such as loan and deposit products, transaction fees, and the costs and
features of deposit accounts.33 The proposal would narrow that inquiry by directing the Agencies to

33 81 FR 48542-43.

 33
 evaluate the "range and responsiveness of the credit services provided" (emphasis added) and by
adding the term "credit" throughout the retail services criterion. In doing so, the proposal would
supersede the Q&A's treatment of deposit products and clarify that retail service evaluations
should focus on services that help meet community credit needs.

ABA supports this aspect of the proposal because it more closely adheres to the text and purpose
of the CRA. Congress directed the banking Agencies to assess an institution's record of "meeting
the credit needs of its entire community" and repeatedly framed CRA performance in terms of
community credit needs.34 Not a single operative provision of the CRA authorizes the Agencies to
evaluate deposit products. This focus on the provision of credit reflects the concern that Congress
sought to address by enacting the CRA--the mismatch between banks accepting deposits from
LMI communities but not serving those communities with their credit products.

The proposal refocuses the Service Test on this statutory purpose. If policymakers wish to expand
the scope of CRA beyond the provision of credit, that decision belongs to Congress, not the
banking Agencies.

 IX. Preserve Flexibility in Assessment Area Delineation

The proposal would largely retain the existing assessment area framework. Assessment areas
must generally consist of one or more metropolitan statistical areas, metropolitan divisions, or
contiguous political subdivisions, and must include the census tracts where a bank maintains its
main office, branches, and deposit-taking ATMs. Assessment areas also must include the
surrounding census tracts where the bank originates or purchases a substantial portion of its loans
in its major product lines. ABA appreciates the Agencies' focus on the CRA statute, which requires
the Agencies to assess banks' performance in helping to meet the credit needs of the local
communities where they are physically located.

While not part of the proposed regulatory text, the Agencies request feedback on whether Large
Banks should be required to delineate full counties and whether the "substantial portion" standard
should be clarified or replaced with a more objective measure. We offer our comments on these
requests below.

34 The statute provides that institutions shall "help meet the credit needs of the local communities in which
they are chartered." 12 U.S.C. 2901. The FBAs shall "assess the institution's record of meeting the credit
needs of its entire community, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods." Id. 2903(a)(1). They
may consider as a factor "capital investment, loan participation, and other ventures undertaken by the
institution" provided that these activities "help meet the credit needs of local communities." Id. 2903(b).
And each rating assigned to an institution -- "Outstanding," "Satisfactory," "Needs to improve," or
"Substantial noncompliance" -- are predicated on how well the institution met "community credit needs."
Id. 2906(2).

 34
  A. Any full-county requirement should apply only to Large Banks.

ABA supports preserving flexibility in assessment area delineation and opposes requiring all banks
to serve entire counties regardless of size, capacity, or branch footprint. While a full-county
approach may be appropriate for institutions above the proposed $10 billion Large Bank threshold,
it would be impractical for smaller institutions. Community banks with only one or a few branches
located near a county border often cannot reasonably serve that entire county. The CRA rule
should continue to recognize these realities.

The same concern applies in states, where regional planning districts or similar constructs serve as
county-equivalent geographic units.35 The final rule should expressly recognize county-equivalent
geographic areas and make clear that the same flexibility available for delineating partial counties
applies to those areas.

 B. Retain flexibility for applying the "substantial portion" standard.

The proposal would require a bank to delineate the surrounding census tracts in which the bank
has originated or purchased a "substantial portion" of its loans in its major product lines. Thus, it
would retain the same "substantial portion" standard that exists in the current rule. We generally
concur with this approach, which provides a bank with flexibility to apply a methodology that
reflects its business model, branch footprint, and lending patterns. However, the Agencies should
consider the "substantial portion" standard in conjunction with the proposed major product line
and consumer lending provisions. Because the proposal applies the "substantial portion" standard
to a bank's major product lines, rather than to its lending activity as a whole, changes to the criteria
for identifying major product lines--or to when consumer lending is treated as a major product
line--could significantly affect whether a bank is required to delineate additional census tracts as
part of its assessment area(s).

We also note that the preamble to the proposal inquires whether the agencies should replace the
substantial portion standard with a new concept whereby banks would include all census tracts
within a radius of the bank's main office, branches, or deposit-taking ATMs or remote service
facilities. ABA does not support this approach. A fixed radius requirement would create artificial
assessment areas and may be inconsistent with the CRA statute.

35 We are aware of county-equivalents in Connecticut and Massachusetts. Other states may have similar
arrangements.

 35
  X. Data Requirements Should Support CRA Examinations While Avoiding
 Unnecessary Reporting and Duplication

The proposal would establish new community development data requirements for Large Banks.
Those requirements should be designed to facilitate CRA examinations without creating
unnecessary reporting burdens.

 A. Community development data should remain a collection and maintenance
 requirement.

The proposal would require Large Banks to collect and maintain standardized data on community
development loans and investments, including information regarding the amount, location,
community development purpose, and other characteristics. Notably, these requirements are
designed to facilitate CRA examinations; they are not a reporting requirement. That distinction is
critical and must be preserved.

Transforming the new data collection and maintenance requirements into a reporting obligation
would create significant operational and policy concerns. Unlike retail lending data, community
development activities often require individualized CRA eligibility determinations that may depend
on facts that are not fully developed at the time an activity is originated or funded. Requiring banks
to make final community development determinations on a fixed reporting timetable would compel
banks to classify activities before all relevant information about a transaction is available. In
addition, community development lending and investment opportunities may vary significantly
across markets and over time, making activity levels alone an incomplete picture of CRA
performance. This could lead to misleading comparisons if viewed outside the examination
process and performance context.

 B. Community development grants should not be subject to public reporting
 requirements.

The proposal would require Large Banks to collect and maintain additional documentation for each
community development grant, including: (1) a written commitment from the recipient regarding
the use of grant funds; (2) a written attestation that indirect administrative costs will not exceed
fifteen percent of the grant amount; and (3) supporting documentation, including IRS Form 990 and
related budget information. The proposal would also require standardized reporting of grant-
related information as part of the community development data framework.

Public reporting of grant data raises significant concerns. Disclosure of recipients and funding
amounts could subject banks to increased pressure from organizations seeking funding, scrutiny
of individual grant decisions, and disputes from organizations that were not selected to receive
support. Banks often have legitimate strategic, operational, reputational, or risk-based reasons for
allocating charitable resources in a particular manner. Public reporting requirements could

 36
 discourage bank participation in community development grant programs and reduce banks' ability
to support local organizations effectively. Accordingly, information regarding community
development grants should be collected and maintained for examination purposes but should not
be publicly reported.

 C. The Agencies should not rely exclusively on Section 1071 data for CRA
 examinations.

The proposal would not modify the existing CRA data collection and reporting requirements for
small business and small farm loans. The Agencies do, however, request comment on
opportunities to reduce duplicative requirements arising from CRA reporting and the Consumer
Financial Protection Bureau's Section 1071 small business lending data collection rule. The
Agencies state that there may be opportunities to amend the CRA rules to eliminate or minimize
duplicative data collection, maintenance, and reporting requirements and that, "to the fullest
extent feasible," they "intend to leverage Section 1071 data and discontinue duplicative CRA data
collection and reporting requirements."

We appreciate the Agencies' willingness to explore opportunities to reduce burden and eliminate
duplication and urge them to take the following considerations into account as they evaluate
potential approaches.

Section 1071 data does not capture all lending activity that is relevant to CRA evaluations. For
example, farm loans, purchased loans, and renewals that do not involve an extension of new credit
receive positive CRA consideration but are not included in Section 1071 reporting. Therefore,
exclusive reliance on Section 1071 would create gaps in the information needed to evaluate a
bank's small business and small farm lending performance

In addition, the Agencies should consider the risks of tying CRA reporting requirements to a data
collection regime designed to serve a different statutory purpose. While one of section 1071's
stated purposes is to help identify community development opportunities, it was codified in the
Equal Credit Opportunity Act, not the CRA. As a result, the agency that administers section 1071 is
the CFPB, which does not have CRA oversight as one of its responsibilities. Future revisions to
Section 1071 may therefore be driven by policy objectives unrelated to CRA, which would leave the
banking Agencies dependent on a dataset that does not align with CRA examination needs.

 XI. Evidence of Discriminatory or Other Illegal Credit Practices

The proposal would retain the existing rule's treatment regarding the adverse effect of
discriminatory or other illegal credit practices on a bank's CRA rating. Congress directed the
banking agencies to evaluate how well institutions meet the credit needs of their communities.
Consistent with that statutory focus, the proposal appropriately continues to limit evidence of
discriminatory or other illegal practices to "credit practices."

 37
  XII. Provide an Orderly Transition to a New Rule

An orderly and well-coordinated transition will be critical to the successful implementation of any
final rule. ABA supports a phased transition that allows banks to promptly realize the benefits of
regulatory relief while providing sufficient time to implement new requirements.

Banks that move to a different asset category because of revised thresholds should have the option
either to transition immediately to the applicable framework on January 1st of the following
calendar year or to complete the current evaluation period under the existing rules. This flexibility
would allow these institutions to balance the benefits of earlier regulatory relief against the
burdens of a hybrid examination.

By contrast, new data collection, maintenance, and reporting requirements will require substantial
systems, operational, and governance changes and should not become effective for two years.
New reporting requirements also should take effect at the beginning of a calendar year, allowing
institutions to collect and report a full year of data under a single framework.

The Agencies also should address how the final rule will apply when a CRA evaluation period spans
both the current and revised frameworks. For Large Banks that remain subject to the Large Bank
framework, the Agencies should complete the evaluation period under the existing rules rather
than combining performance standards from two regulatory frameworks in a single examination.
Doing otherwise would require examiners to reconcile different performance criteria into a single
rating.

ABA also urges the Agencies to retain and update the Interagency Q&A. The Q&A provides
transparency regarding policy decisions and promotes consistency across examinations. It is also
an important training resource for examiners. The Agencies should conform the Q&A to the final
rule and update examination procedures promptly following publication of a final rule. To avoid
interpretive gaps during the transition, the Agencies should issue a redline of the existing Q&A
showing where portions have been superseded.

Finally, the proposal would make significant changes to the CRA framework, and implementation
questions are inevitable. The Agencies should work with industry participants to identify areas
requiring clarification and address those questions through public implementation guidance. That
guidance should be updated as necessary and issued sufficiently in advance of applicable
compliance dates so that institutions and examiners have a common understanding of the
Agencies' expectations.

 38
  XIII. Conclusion

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this proposal. Refreshing the CRA rule and reducing
regulatory burden are worthwhile undertakings, and we appreciate the Agencies' efforts to do so.
As we mentioned at the beginning of this letter, the proposal is the third attempt to revise the CRA
rules in less than a decade. The Agencies should use this opportunity to adopt a framework that
will be long-lasting. A final rule is most likely to stand the test of time if it remains faithful to the CRA
statute, reflects interagency consensus, relies on transparent and well-supported standards, and
provides flexibility for diverse bank business models.

Sincerely,

The Consumer Bankers Association1 and the Bank Policy Institute2 (together, the "Associations")
appreciate the opportunity to provide these comments to the Office of the Comptroller of the

The Associations represent banks that carry out a significant portion of the nation's community
reinvestment activity, across the full range of business models from branch-based retail banks,
regional and super-community banks, wholesale and limited purpose institutions, to banks with
specialized or nationwide lending operations. We support efforts to ensure that the CRA
remains an essential part of the framework for sustaining and revitalizing communities. Based
on our members' decades of experience delivering credit to low- and moderate-income ("LMI")
communities under the CRA, we understand that the value of the CRA framework turns not only
on the substance of its standards but also on its stability, clarity, and consistency across the

three federal banking agencies. To that end, we write to urge the Agencies to ensure that the

requirements, and direct resources to the communities that need them.

I. Executive Summary

The Agencies should build any final rule on four principles:

 1. Durability and consistency over time. The rule should be crafted to survive
 changes in administration and legal challenge, rather than contribute to the back-and-
 forth swinging of CRA policy through repeated reforms that have imposed
 implementation costs without improving community outcomes. Relatedly, the Agencies
 should not discard existing standards that generally work well absent a compelling
 reason.

 2. Consistency across regulators. Similarly-situated institutions should face the same
 standards regardless of their federal regulator. Recent history shows that CRA reform
 without three-agency consensus has not endured.

 3. Clarity and predictability. Banks should know in advance how the Agencies will
 evaluate their activities, so they can plan and commit resources with confidence.

 4. Community impact over compliance. The rule should push resources toward
 communities rather than erect documentation and other compliance requirements that
 serve as obstacles to beneficial activity.

Measured against these principles, which are discussed in greater detail in section II below, the
Proposal gets several things right, but some of its provisions would benefit from refinement or
even a return to the 1995 rules that are now in effect, which have successfully expanded access to
credit, affordable housing, and economic development over several decades. The Associations
support revisions to the Proposal that may be needed to secure Federal Reserve support and
broad stakeholder consensus, even if those revisions require scaling back the scope of the
changes made in this rulemaking.

The following changes to the Proposal would be consistent with these principles and may help
the Agencies achieve a broader consensus on a final rule:

Recommendations to promote impactful activities while accommodating diverse business
models (section III below)

 Keep the existing approach of identifying retail product lines for evaluation in the
 Lending Test, but if the final rule nevertheless contains a formalized major product line
 methodology, it should be a predictable, bank-level methodology that accommodates
 different business models.

 Retain the existing "substantial majority of a bank's business" standard for determining
 when consumer lending will be evaluated under the Lending Test rather than expand it
 as proposed.

 Preserve the existing framework for recognizing community development activity
 outside assessment areas or, at a minimum, revise the proposed "geographic
 flexibility" standard to make it more workable for banks with different business models.

 2
 OCC and FDIC

 Withdraw the 15 percent indirect-cost restriction on community-development grants or
 replace it with a more flexible approach.

 Retain the existing limited purpose and wholesale bank definitions without the proposed
 changes to the eligibility criteria.

 Enhance the performance context framework by allowing a bank to elect for its
 examiners to review the distribution of its HELOCs against other lenders' HELOCs.

 Allow services performed on the bank's behalf, including by affiliates, to qualify as
 community development services.

 Finalize the Proposal's recognition of naturally-occurring affordable housing and rental
 housing for middle-income families in high-cost areas, while preserving flexibility for
 how banks can establish that a project qualifies and that a market is a high-cost area.

Recommendations to promote clarity and consistency (section IV below)

 Keep the existing assessment area delineation framework largely as-is, while eliminating
 the requirement to include census tracts where a bank has originated or purchased a
 substantial portion of its loans, which would better ground that framework in the
 statute's requirements.

 Establish a meaningful qualifying activities list and a binding advance confirmation
 process on which banks can rely without excessive delay.

 Confirm that removing deposit products from evaluation does not curtail recognition of
 alternative delivery systems or of pertinent data showing that a branch serves LMI
 individuals.

 Make strategic plans a genuinely workable alternative evaluation method, including by
 confirming that those plans do not need to include retail lending goals and by
 streamlining the Agency approval process.

 Provide that a public enforcement action is necessary, but not sufficient, to downgrade a
 CRA rating for discriminatory or other illegal credit practices, retain the "nature, extent,
 and strength of the evidence of the practices" factor, and codify OCC PPM 5000-43.

 Confirm that the new definition of community development investment captures existing
 forms of qualified investments.

 Reduce examiner variability through guidance.

Recommendations to balance costs and benefits (section V below)

 Decline to impose new data collection, reporting, and disclosure burdens that lack
 supervisory value, including the proposed new requirements for community
 development activity and consumer loans and a mandatory requirement to post CRA
 public files online.

 3
 OCC and FDIC

 Consider the potential negative consequences of increasing the asset size thresholds and
 avoid further increases to those thresholds, such as a $30 billion large bank threshold
 and a $10 billion intermediate bank threshold.

 Make it optional to count prior period community development loans.

 Provide at least a two-year implementation period, with changes taking effect for any
 given bank at the start of its next evaluation period.

The remainder of this letter provides additional context for why a durable, interagency CRA
framework is critical for the industry and the communities it serves, then describes in greater
detail our recommendations for achieving a final rule that drives banks' CRA resources toward
LMI and other disadvantaged communities. Finally, section VI provides answers to specific
questions posed in the Proposal.

II. Durable Interagency CRA Rules Ensure CRA Dollars Go to the Communities
 That Need Them

We appreciate that the Proposal would leave intact the basic framework for CRA evaluations,
and we encourage the Agencies not to adopt sweeping changes within that framework.

Banks and their community partners need stable rules to plan multi-year lending, investment,
and grant commitments. Repeated changes to the CRA framework impose uncertainty that
undermines banks' incentives to plan long-term CRA initiatives. Regulatory changes also can
divert CRA departments' budgets and attention away from lending, investment, and services
and toward regulatory implementation efforts. And an important lesson of the past decade of
CRA reform is that regulatory changes not supported by broad-based consensus of industry
participants, community partners, and regulators often do not endure, and instead can create a
"whip-saw" effect because future administrations could turn the dials sharply in the opposite
direction.

A rule that only two of the three federal banking agencies adopt compounds that risk.
Divergence among the OCC, FDIC, and Federal Reserve would create operational uncertainty
and opportunities for regulatory arbitrage: it would complicate examinations and compliance
for multi-bank holding companies, mergers and acquisitions involving institutions with
different regulators, charter changes, and consortium investments involving banks operating by
different rulebooks. These issues may give a future administration reasons to roll back the
changes currently being proposed, or worse, to make more sweeping changes.

On this basis, the Associations support the Agencies making revisions to the Proposal that may
be needed to secure Federal Reserve support and broad stakeholder consensus. But even if the
Federal Reserve does not join in this rulemaking, the Agencies should strive for their CRA
regulations to harmonize in substance with the Federal Reserve's CRA regulations. The
Agencies should therefore avoid adopting changes that materially change the substantive
standards for CRA evaluations and eligibility criteria, as opposed to clarifying the meaning of
existing rules. For example, if a group of banks works together to make grants to seed a local
community development organization, those grants should count the same for all the
participating banks, regardless of their regulator.

 4
 OCC and FDIC

III. Recommendations to Promote Impactful Activities While Accommodating
 Diverse Business Models

 A. The Agencies Should Keep the Existing Approach of Identifying Retail
 Product Lines for Evaluation in the Lending Test, but if the Final Rule
 Nevertheless Contains a Formalized Major Product Line
 Methodology, It Should Be a Predictable, Bank-Level Methodology
 That Accommodates Different Business Models

The Proposal sets forth two options for identifying major product lines that would be subject to
evaluation under the retail portions of the Lending Test. Neither option is, from our members'
perspective, necessary to ensure that examiners appropriately focus on a bank's most material
retail lending products in their evaluations. In practice, examiners generally already focus the
retail aspects of the Lending Test on the products that are significant to a bank.

While the Associations do not oppose additional clarity in concept, we strongly oppose the
Proposal's introduction of a major product line framework that would expand the circumstances
in which the Agencies evaluate consumer lending in the Lending Test. Section III.B of this
letter, immediately below, describes our concerns with the Proposal's approach to consumer
lending.

If the Agencies proceed to finalizing a major product line methodology, Option 1, with
adjustments, would provide greater clarity and certainty than Option 2 because Option 1 would
operate at the institution-wide level. The Agencies should make the following adjustments to
Option 1 if they proceed with finalizing it:

 Exclude consumer loans from the framework and instead retain the current "substantial
 majority of a bank's business" standard for evaluation of consumer loans, as discussed in
 section III.B of this letter, immediately below.

 Allow any bank to elect, in specific assessment areas, to have local evaluation of a
 product line that would not meet the Option 1 definition of a major product line where
 doing so would give a more meaningful evaluation of the bank's performance in that
 market.

 Use at least two years of the bank's retail lending data to ensure that annual fluctuations
 in the bank's relative lending volumes do not distort the bank's major product lines, and
 relatedly, provide a transition period so that the designation of a new major product line
 is not retroactive to the beginning of the year in which the Agency identifies the major
 product line.

These changes would align the proposed framework better with current practices, which
generally operate well today, and facilitate better long-term planning.

 B. The Agencies Should Retain the Existing "Substantial Majority of a
 Bank's Business" Standard for Determining When Consumer Lending
 Will Be Evaluated Under the Lending Test Rather Than Expand It as
 Proposed

As part of the Proposal's major product line methodology, the Agencies have proposed to
evaluate consumer loans (a heterogeneous category that includes a wide variety of products with

 5
 OCC and FDIC

vastly different target customers, origination channels, and servicing requirements) under the
Lending Test if consumer loans as a whole represent 50 percent or more of the bank's retail
loans by loan count and dollar amount. This standard represents a significant expansion over
the current standard, whereby the Agencies will only evaluate one or more of the sub-types of
consumer loans if consumer lending represents a substantial majority (not a bare majority) of
the bank's business (not just its retail lending). The Agencies' longtime position has been that
consumer lending should only be subject to evaluation where it would otherwise not be possible
for examiners to conduct a meaningful evaluation of the bank's performance.4 The Proposal
does not offer an explanation for why the Agencies are changing course and expanding the
current standard.

The existing "substantial majority of a bank's business" test provides for evaluation of consumer
lending in narrower circumstances than the Proposal's major product line methodology, and for
good reason. Consumer loans are generally a poor fit for the Lending Test in a number of
respects:

 While consumer loans meet borrowers' specific needs, they often do not provide the type
 of foundational, wealth-building credit that the CRA focuses on promoting and
 incentivizing. For example, consumer loans can include wealth management loans, such
 as securities-backed loans or loans to finance the purchase of art, as well as other loan
 types that are not tailored to the needs of the general retail public and are thus
 misaligned with the CRA's aims of addressing the unmet credit needs of LMI
 communities. Indeed, in its 2020 final rule to revise its CRA regulations, the OCC
 excluded credit card products from consideration under that rule's Retail Lending
 Distribution Test on the basis that credit card loans do not play as significant a part in
 building consumer wealth as other loan types such as mortgages.5

 Banks have far less control over the marketing process for certain consumer loans than
 for home mortgage or small business loans. For example, in indirect automobile
 lending, the dealer, rather than the bank, interfaces with the customer and facilitates
 near-instant credit decisions at the point of sale. Banks generally do not market directly
 to consumers; instead, they provide dealers with the terms on which they are willing to
 purchase loans. After the customer purchases a vehicle and executes a retail installment
 sales contract ("RISC"), the dealer shops the RISC to multiple lenders. The bank may
 approve, counteroffer, or decline the transaction, but the dealer selects the lender and
 assigns the RISC accordingly. This process benefits consumers by allowing dealers to
 identify favorable financing options on their behalf.

`substantial majority' to be so significant a portion of the institution's lending activity by number and

lending and believes that, given the nature of the lending and the impact it has on LMI individuals and

communities, it may not be appropriate for the CRA to be used to incentivize banks' credit card lending. . .

. [T]he final rule . . . removes credit cards . . . from the definition of consumer loan to reduce the burden

associated with information gathering and to ensure that banks have an incentive to engage in a variety of

CRA activities that benefit LMI individuals.").
