 OCC and FDIC

 Banks have much less control over the geographic distribution of their borrowers for
 consumer loans than they do for other types of loans subject to evaluation under the
 Retail Lending Test. To return to the example of automobile loans, consider a bank that
 lends in partnership with a third party responsible for lead generation or origination
 (such as an auto dealer in the indirect lending model). Even if the bank adjusts its
 underwriting criteria to approve more LMI applicants, it is unlikely to have any control
 over whether individuals in a given census tract submit applications in the first place. In
 any given assessment area, the bank's dealer partners could locate their dealerships in
 neighborhoods that attract few consumers from particular census tracts, which may
 make it challenging for the bank to perform well on a geographic distribution test in that
 assessment area. Banks cannot, and should not be expected to, control the dealer's real
 estate decisions to solve this problem. For credit card loans, which may or may not be
 issued in partnership with third parties responsible for lead generation, the dynamic is
 similar: the high-volume, nationwide model of credit card lending means that banks
 have little, if any, control over the census tracts of applicants for credit cards.

 Banks also have less control over the income distribution of their consumer loans than
 other types of loans subject to evaluation under the Lending Test. Consumer loans are
 generally smaller in dollar amount and higher in volume than mortgages. Given these
 characteristics, banks often employ automated underwriting models that rely on stated
 income levels as a proxy for inputs that would be used in a more time-intensive mortgage
 underwriting process.

 Applying the Lending Test to banks' consumer loans could effectively force banks to
 expand into subprime (or lower prime) segments in order to achieve satisfactory CRA
 ratings. Subprime and lower prime lending requires materially different underwriting,
 origination, servicing, and collections processes and procedures that many banks may
 not be willing or able to implement especially for high-volume products like indirect
 auto and credit card lending. Encouraging banks to expand in this way could materially
 increase risk for banks, and potentially lead to worse customer outcomes. Congress
 never intended these results when it enacted the CRA. To the contrary, Congress
 specified in several places in the statute that any evaluation measure must be "consistent
 with the safe and sound operation" of institutions subject to the Act.

 Banks that make consumer loans often do so on a nationwide basis, untethered from
 their branches. Banks with significant amount of consumer lending could therefore fare
 poorly under the Lending Test's factor that evaluates the percentage of loans made inside
 their assessment areas, known as the in/out ratio.

 The Agencies lack reliable market-wide peer lending data for consumer loans, and could
 not obtain such data without a significantly burdensome overhaul of their data collection
 requirements.

 Finally, subjecting consumer loans to the Lending Test could encourage some banks to
 exit or scale back their consumer lending lest they fail the test. In turn, this reaction
 could lead to a contraction of safe, responsible credit available in the marketplace,
 ultimately ceding consumer lending markets to non-bank lenders that are not subject to
 the CRA.

 7
 OCC and FDIC

For all these reasons, banks that have grown their consumer lending to the point where it would
become subject to evaluation under the Lending Test have generally sought designation as
limited purpose banks or adopted strategic plans in lieu of proceeding with such evaluation.

If the Agencies nevertheless finalize a quantitative standard for including consumer loans in the
Lending Test evaluation, that standard should align more closely with the current "substantial
majority" standard. Specifically, such a quantitative standard should provide that a type of
consumer loans will be subject to evaluation only if, by loan count and dollar amount, consumer
lending constituted 75 percent or more of the bank's total lending (including commercial
lending and retail lending) in each of the two consecutive years immediately prior to the
beginning of the evaluation period. If that threshold is met, the bank's most significant type of
consumer lending should be the one subject to evaluation.

It is particularly important that the denominator of any quantitative standard be broader than
"retail lending." A bank with significant commercial lending or other non-retail business may
not have high volumes of mortgage, small business, or small farm loans. Using retail lending as
the denominator may cause the bank's consumer lending percentage to be artificially high under
the proposed formula.

It is also critical for the final rule not to lump all consumer loans together for purposes of the
underlying evaluation. Each sub-type of consumer loan has very different characteristics, risks,
marketing channels, and peer performance. And each bank has different proportions of the sub-
types of consumer loans. Aggregating the sub-types of consumer loans together despite these
differences would make it nearly impossible for examiners to evaluate a bank's performance in a
manner that is both accurate and not superficial. For instance, as noted above, an investment-
secured consumer loan intended to finance the purchase of expensive art is fundamentally
different from a credit card, and treating such loans the same for CRA evaluation purposes
would potentially be misleading. The Proposal offers no clarity on how examiners would
conduct such an evaluation.

Finally, the problems associated with evaluation of consumer loans underscore the importance
of creating a more workable "safety valve" in the form of the strategic plan option for banks
whose consumer loans would otherwise be subject to the Lending Test. We discuss our
recommendations in this regard in section IV.D of this letter, below.

In sum, the Agencies should retain the existing "substantial majority of a bank's business"
standard for including consumer loans in the Lending Test, or at least quantify that existing
standard with a 75 percent of total lending test rather than significantly lowering the bar for
consumer loans to be evaluated as the Agencies have proposed.

 C. The Agencies Should Maintain a Qualitative Standard for Recognizing
 Community Development Activity Outside Assessment Areas, but if
 They Finalize Option 1 of the Proposed "Geographic Flexibility"
 Standard, They Should Make Significant Revisions to Make It More
 Workable for Banks With Different Business Models

The Proposal would replace the existing standard for determining whether community
development activity outside a bank's assessment areas should be considered with a new
geographic flexibility standard. The Agencies are considering two options for the geographic
flexibility standard. The first option would set forth a minimum 1.25 percent of allocated Tier 1

 8

capital requirement per assessment area,6 and the second option would set forth a qualitative
standard. Either option would replace the existing approach whereby examiners will favorably
consider activities that benefit geographies or individuals located somewhere within a broader
statewide or regional area that includes the institution's assessment areas, as long as the
institution has been responsive to community development needs and opportunities in its
assessment areas.7

Insofar as Option 2 does not set forth a uniform, mandatory minimum amount of community
development activity that banks need to conduct in their assessment areas in order to receive
credit for community development activities conducted outside their assessment areas, Option 2
is far superior to Option 1 because it hews closer to the existing approach, which has proved to
be workable in practice. The Agencies should add clarity to Option 2 by presuming that any
bank that has received a Satisfactory or Outstanding bank-level rating in its prior evaluation has
satisfied the geographic flexibility standard for the current evaluation.

Option 1 is particularly problematic for the following reasons:

 Uniform minimum requirements do not take into account differences among banks'
 business models. Some banks operate with few if any branches and thus would have
 significantly higher allocated Tier 1 capital figures in their assessment area(s). Some
 banks have their main offices in urban markets that are CRA hotspots, and some banks
 have their main offices in markets with few community development opportunities. And
 some banks have significant business outside the United States, meaning that a Tier 1
 capital-based measure might overstate those banks' capacities to make loans and
 investments in the United States.

 The 1.25 percent minimum appears to be calibrated far too stringently compared to some
 banks' historical lending and investment activities, and the Proposal does not contain
 adequate justification for how the Agencies arrived at that figure. The Agencies state
 that they set these thresholds based on "supervisory experience," but do not explain
 whether that experience includes a review of historical levels of community development
 activity by banks with different business models, geographies, CRA classification (e.g.,
 wholesale and limited purpose banks), and approaches to branch networks. We believe a
 comprehensive review would reveal that the proposed minimums exceed levels of
 community development activity that some banks have historically performed in their
 assessment areas while earning Satisfactory and Outstanding CRA ratings based on the
 overall context of their performance.

 A requirement to conduct a minimum amount of activity in assessment areas could
 exacerbate, rather than alleviate, the problem of CRA hotspots and CRA deserts, as it
 would reduce some banks' incentives to conduct community development activities in
 rural markets where fewer banks have branches, and instead cause them to focus more
 activity on the market(s) in which their offices are located to avoid undershooting the
 minimum requirement. In particular, because branchless banks would need to allocate

 D. The Agencies Should Withdraw the 15 Percent Indirect Cost
 Restriction on Community Development Grants or Replace It With a
 More Flexible Approach

For large banks, the Proposal would count a community development grant only if the
recipient's indirect costs do not exceed a novel 15 percent limit, and would require banks to
collect grant-level certifications and documentation to demonstrate compliance with this
limitation. Additionally, the Proposal would limit consideration to grants that are directly used
by the recipient for a specific program, project, or initiative.

The Associations support robust CRA recognition of community development grants. Grants
sustain organizations and activities that lending and investment alone cannot; they seed future
lending, investment, housing, counseling, and other critical community development activities;
and they matter most in rural and smaller markets where investment opportunities are scarce.

We recommend eliminating the 15 percent indirect cost restriction and limitation on general
operating and capacity-building support grants, which would serve as an obstacle to the CRA's
purposes for the following reasons:

 Indirect cost ratios do not reliably measure community impact. Necessary operating
 expenses rent, cybersecurity, technology, audit, insurance, compliance, staff
 development, and administrative infrastructure are precisely the costs that let a non-
 profit deliver its mission. For example, banks commonly and appropriately make
 operational grants that stand up a new non-profit's infrastructure. A startup non-profit
 naturally has a higher ratio of overhead than an existing non-profit, but could have a
 greater community impact in the long term. A bank's grant could seed the startup non-
 profit to serve a community that existing non-profits are not serving. Similarly, a smaller
 non-profit may have a higher ratio of overhead than larger non-profits because it does
 not benefit from the same economies of scale.

 The Agencies have not ascertained a relationship between a recipient's indirect cost ratio
 and the community benefit its work produces, which would render the 15 percent
 limitation arbitrary. The Agencies rest the limitation on an analogy to the Office of
 Management and Budget's 15 percent de minimis indirect cost rate under the Uniform
 Guidance. But OMB designed the de minimis rate as a simplifying option, not a cap:
 an organization that has never negotiated an indirect cost rate may claim up to 15
 percent without documenting its actual overhead at all, sparing both the organization
 and the government the expense of a rate negotiation.8 In other words, the de minimis
 rate is a floor allowing documentation-free cost recovery not a ceiling on reasonable
 overhead.

 The Agencies have not conducted an analysis of how many community development
 partners would qualify for community development grants under the 15 percent limit.

 But research shows that high-performing non-profits typically have indirect cost rates
 that exceed 15 percent.9

 The Agencies have also not offered any explanation for why any issues relating to grant

 only apply to large banks, as proposed.

 The proposed limit on indirect costs would impose documentation burdens on non-

 A non-profit organization that has indirect costs in excess of 15 percent may nevertheless

 the bank would be if it attempted to conduct the same community development activity

 Limiting consideration to grants that support a discrete program, project, or initiative

For all of these reasons, the Agencies should withdraw the proposed 15 percent limit and
associated certification and documentation requirements and omit the requirement for a
community development grant to be used for a specific program, project, or initiative.

 The Agencies should establish a dollar-based de minimis threshold for the size of a grant

 including those based in rural areas.

 E. The Agencies Should Retain the Existing Limited Purpose and
 Wholesale Bank Definitions Without Finalizing the Proposed Changes
 to the Eligibility Criteria, and Retain the Community Development
 Test for These Banks

The Proposal would change the standards for qualifying as a limited purpose or wholesale bank,
and indicates that the Agencies are even considering eliminating the limited purpose
designation. The proposed changes include introducing a new definition of "incidental basis,"
with a 5 percent limit on incidental lending that creates more questions than it answers, and
deleting the phrase "to retail customers" from the definition of "wholesale bank."

We strongly oppose any changes to the limited purpose and wholesale bank definitions and any
elimination of the limited purpose designation. The Agencies have no sound reason to eliminate
the limited purpose designation, and there are compelling reasons to keep it, along with the
Community Development Test that applies to these banks:

 Limited purpose and wholesale banks occupy distinct corners of the financial sector by
 virtue of their business models, and can serve the needs of their communities in unique
 and important ways. The Community Development Test allows these banks to focus on
 their unique characteristics and serves as an important safety valve for them due to the
 poor fit of the Lending Test to their business models.

 F. The Agencies Should Enhance the Performance Context Framework
 by Allowing a Bank to Elect for Its Examiners to Review Its
 Distribution of HELOCs Against Other Lenders' HELOCs

Under the existing CRA regulations (and under the Proposal), the Agencies evaluate a bank's
home mortgage lending distribution against home mortgage lending by all HMDA reporters,
with no breakdown by loan type. The HMDA data include both closed-end mortgage loans and
home equity lines of credit. Examiners therefore benchmark HELOCs and other open-end
home mortgage loans against an aggregate HMDA distribution that mostly includes closed-end
mortgage loans, which is arguably a historical accident. HELOCs generally were not part of the
mandatory HMDA dataset used in CRA evaluations until the 2015 HMDA rule expanded
reporting for open-end lines of credit, with data collection beginning in 2018. That change was
intended to expand data collection, but it had the unintended effect of heightening CRA
performance standards for banks that originate significant volumes of HELOCs.

HELOCs differ fundamentally from closed-end mortgages in purpose, structure, and risk.
Whereas closed-end mortgages primarily finance home purchases or refinance existing
mortgage debt, HELOCs provide revolving credit for debt consolidation, unexpected costs, and
short-term cash-flow needs. By combining revolving access, repeated draws, variable balances
and payments, and the borrower's home as collateral, HELOCs can progressively erode equity
and make repayment risk harder to assess. Most importantly, closed-end mortgage distribution
is not an appropriate proxy for expected HELOC distribution: the products serve different
purposes, involve different eligibility requirements, and respond to different borrower demand
 disparities that are amplified in LMI communities, where lower homeownership rates and less
usable home equity may constrain HELOC eligibility and demand.

Benchmarking HELOCs against closed-end mortgages undermines prudent lending and harms
banks and borrowers alike. Because closed-end mortgage distribution reflects a different

 15
 OCC and FDIC

product market, borrower population, purpose, and underwriting framework, it cannot establish
a valid expectation for where or to whom HELOCs should be originated. Using that distribution
as the benchmark can (1) pressure banks to originate marginal HELOCs, subsidize qualifying
loans, or otherwise relax prudent underwriting to address perceived shortfalls; (2) force banks
to incur substantial marketing and subsidy costs to remediate perceived distribution gaps; and
(3) compel banks to purchase loans from other lenders, including nonbanks, at greater cost and
credit risk while shifting lending to less-regulated providers. Encouraging unsuitable HELOC
lending to LMI borrowers who may have less home equity and fewer reserves to absorb
changing payments or income and property-value shocks can heighten default and foreclosure
risk.

The Agencies should use the current rulemaking to fix this error. Specifically, the CRA
framework should allow banks to elect for their examiners to conduct a separate benchmarking
exercise comparing a bank's HELOCs and other open-end mortgages against the aggregate of all
lenders' HELOCs and other open-end mortgages. Running this calculation separately would
give examiners valuable performance context and mitigate the misleading comparisons that
currently burden lenders with significant HELOC volumes.

 G. The Agencies Should Allow Services Performed on the Bank's Behalf,
 Including by Affiliates, to Qualify as Community Development
 Services

The Agencies have proposed to define community development services only to encompass "a
volunteer service performed by a bank employee representing the bank." The final rule should
omit the requirement that the volunteer be an employee of the bank. Some banks use shared
services models whereby an affiliate of the bank may be the employer of record for staff who
provide services to the bank. Additionally, some banks may use an independent contractor
model rather than employment arrangements for certain services. In either scenario, the
volunteer's activities should count as a community development service for the bank if the
volunteer is acting on the bank's behalf, regardless of whether the volunteer has a formal
employment arrangement directly with the bank.

 H. The Agencies Should Finalize the Proposal's Recognition of Naturally-
 Occurring Affordable Housing and Rental Housing for Middle-
 Income Families in High-Cost Areas, While Preserving Flexibility for
 How Banks Can Establish That a Project Qualifies and That a Market
 is a High-Cost Area

We support the Agencies' recognition of naturally-occurring affordable housing and rental
housing inhabited by middle-income families in high-cost areas. Activities that support such
housing address the well-documented affordability challenges that can occur in a wide variety of
markets.

The Proposal does not prescribe a single methodology for establishing that housing is likely to
be inhabited by families with the requisite income classification or for identifying high-cost
areas, and we support the flexibility that the Proposal thereby provides. Examiners should allow
banks to demonstrate that the relevant conditions exist using objective, supportable data
sources appropriate to the transaction.

Different measures may be more relevant than others depending on the nature of the activity.
For example, a homeownership-focused transaction may warrant consideration of home prices,
mortgage affordability, or cost-burden metrics, while a rental housing transaction may be better

 16
 OCC and FDIC

evaluated using rent burdens, affordability thresholds, or housing development cost indicators.
A bank seeking to demonstrate that a market is a high-cost area should be able to rely on the
American Community Survey cost-burden measure that is most relevant to the transaction, such
as homeowner cost burden for homeownership-focused activities or renter cost burden for
rental housing activities. Similarly, a bank should be permitted to rely on established federal
designations, such as HUD Difficult Development Areas or FHFA High Opportunity Areas,
where appropriate to the facts and circumstances of a particular transaction. Subsequent
changes in an area's designation should not affect CRA consideration for an existing loan,
investment, or legally binding commitment, and reasonable transition treatment should apply
when an area gains or loses high-cost status.

When finalizing the rule, the Agencies should also clarify that a market can be considered a
high-cost area even if it does not satisfy the 40 percent standard (i.e., that at least 40 percent of
households have monthly costs greater than 30 percent of their monthly income) that is
discussed in the preamble to the Proposal. If the Agencies determine it is necessary to establish
a minimum threshold percentage of households that have monthly costs exceeding 30 percent of
monthly income, that threshold should be set at 30 percent rather than 40 percent. The
limitations of a county-based 40 percent threshold are evident in markets commonly
understood to have significant housing affordability pressures. For example, using the proposed
methodology, San Francisco, California and Dallas County, Texas, would not qualify because
35.6 percent and 38.5 percent, respectively, of households in those counties are housing cost
burdened, despite the well-documented affordability challenges in these markets.13 A 30
percent threshold would more appropriately capture high-cost markets that should not be
excluded merely because they fall slightly below a 40 percent threshold.

 B. The Agencies Should Establish a Meaningful Qualifying Activities List

The Proposal would codify the existence of a publicly-available, non-exhaustive, illustrative list
of examples of community development activities. As proposed, the Agencies would have 90
days to communicate a response to a bank's request for including a new activity on the list, but
could extend that timeframe indefinitely.

We support the adoption of a qualifying activities list, but our members' experience is that a 90-
day review period let alone a longer review period that the Agencies could take with indefinite
extensions would simply be too long to be practical. The qualifying activities confirmation
process is likely to be most useful when banks are reviewing whether they should participate in a
particular lending or investment opportunity. Banks often have a limited window to evaluate
whether to engage in a fast-moving transaction. Usually the window of opportunity is only a few
weeks, if not a few days. At the same time, the Associations recognize that the Agencies may
have constraints on their resources that make it difficult to provide approvals within days of
receiving a request.

 E. The Agencies Should Provide That a Public Enforcement Action Is
 Necessary, but Not Sufficient, to Downgrade a CRA Rating for
 Discriminatory or Other Illegal Credit Practices, Retain the "Nature,
 Extent, and Strength of the Evidence of the Practices" Factor, and
 Codify OCC PPM 5000-43

The Agencies have proposed to clarify the types of evidence of discriminatory or other illegal
credit practices that would form the basis for a downgrade of a bank's CRA rating. Under one
option under consideration, the Agencies would only consider formal, public enforcement
actions, and under the other option under consideration, the Agencies could consider
supervisory information as well. Additionally, the Agencies have proposed to delete the "nature,
extent, and strength of the evidence of the practices" factor that examiners should consider
when determining the effect of discriminatory or other illegal credit practices on a bank's CRA
rating.

We suggest several improvements to this part of the CRA framework. First, the final rule should
provide expressly that a formal, public enforcement action is necessary, but not sufficient, for a
downgrade based on discriminatory or other illegal credit practices. Discriminatory or other
illegal credit practices cited only in examination reports and not a public enforcement action
should never provide the basis for a downgrade of the bank's CRA rating. Banks are not
accorded adequate due process in the supervisory setting to contest examiners' findings. The
enforcement process often provides banks their only opportunity to present their case to more
senior agency staff. There are several reasons why an examination finding may not become a
public enforcement action, including that the finding pertains to immaterial conduct or is not
adequately supported. And because examination findings are confidential supervisory
information, the disclosure of such findings that have not ripened into an enforcement action
could undermine the full and free exchange of information between banks and their examiners.

21 See 90 Fed. Reg. 59,744 (Dec. 22, 2025).

 20
 OCC and FDIC

At the same time, not all public enforcement actions are created equal. Some public
enforcement actions are based on conduct that should not give rise to a bank-level CRA
downgrade. For example, some enforcement actions may relate to non-core business lines or
geographies for the bank, limited conduct, or fully-remediated practices. The existing
regulations provide the Agencies with appropriate discretion to consider these factors and
potentially decline to downgrade the bank's CRA rating.

Second, to assist examiners in their determination of whether a given enforcement action
provides a sufficient basis for a downgrade, the final rule should retain the "nature, extent, and
strength of the evidence of the practices" factor. Each element of that factor is, and should be,
relevant to whether the Agencies should downgrade a bank's rating based on discriminatory or
other illegal credit practices.

Third, and relatedly, the final rule should codify guidance set forth in OCC PPM 5000-43 that
further describes the circumstances in which the OCC will bring a downgrade.22 PPM 5000-43
contains much more helpful specificity than the CRA regulations and facilitates examiners' and
banks' understanding of how to apply the factors set forth in the regulations. Specifically,
consistent with the PPM, there should be a logical nexus between the assigned rating(s) and
evidence of discriminatory or other illegal credit practices in the bank's CRA lending activities,
and the Agencies should give full consideration to the remedial actions that the bank has taken.
As recognized in the PPM, "a lower rating may not be warranted if a bank self-identifies
violations and voluntarily takes corrective actions in a timely manner." The PPM also sets forth
a general policy of downgrading a bank's CRA rating by only one rating level.

Finally, the Agencies should revise the Proposal to provide that the enumerated list of law
violations that can give rise to a CRA rating downgrade is exhaustive. The current enumerated
list captures the full range of conduct causing material harm to consumers and communities in
the credit context. Making the list non-exhaustive exposes banks to retroactive or novel
interpretations they could not have anticipated, undermining the predictability and clarity that
are essential to effective compliance. And allowing for a downgrade based on non-enumerated
violations would risk conflating CRA-relevant credit practices with general consumer protection
violations a distinction the Interagency Questions and Answers have consistently maintained.

 F. The Agencies Should Confirm That the New Definition of Community
 Development Investment Captures Existing Forms of Qualified
 Investments

The Proposal's definition of the term "community development investment" would capture a
"security or a deposit, or membership share in a financial institution" that has as its primary
purpose community development and meets certain other criteria. The Agencies should clarify
that forms of investment that currently meet the standard for a qualified investment, including
tax credit investments, equity-equivalent investments, and in-kind contributions such as
donations of branches, would continue to meet the new definition of community development
investment (provided that the remaining criteria are satisfied). Additionally, the Agencies
should confirm that an in-kind contribution would not be treated as a community development

grant, as it would be impossible to impose an indirect cost restriction on a recipient's use of non-
cash property.

 G. The Agencies Should Reduce Examiner Variability Through Guidance

The CRA regulations are rife with subjective and undefined terms, such as "responsive,"
"complex," "innovative," "flexible," and "adequate." These terms can produce materially
different outcomes depending on examiner judgment.

The Agencies should not define these terms in any rigid manner, because fixed definitions may
not capture the range of acceptable practices, business models, and performance contexts that
arise in practice. Instead, it would be more constructive for the Agencies to issue additional
guidance that provides examples of how these terms are applied in practice. Additionally, the
Agencies should require examiners to justify their determinations with objective facts and
sound reasoning when applying these terms, just as the Agencies have done in their final rule on
unsafe or unsound practices.23 The Agencies can take these steps through guidance, including
updates to examination manuals and internal operating manuals, rather than changes to the
CRA regulations.

V. Recommendations to Balance Costs and Benefits

 A. The Agencies Should Decline to Impose New Data Collection,
 Reporting, and Disclosure Burdens That Lack Supervisory Value,
 Including the Proposed New Requirements for Community
 Development Activity and Consumer Loans, and a Mandatory
 Requirement to Post CRA Public Files Online

Despite the Proposal's stated goal of "reducing unnecessary burden,"24 the Agencies have
proposed several new and potentially burdensome data collection and reporting requirements.
We oppose any data collection or reporting requirement that is not strictly necessary for the
CRA framework to operate correctly. Each data collection and reporting requirement should
only stand if it (1) fulfills the Agencies' needs for conducting a CRA exam, (2) facilitates
comparability, and (3) addresses gaps in existing data sources. These principles are not only
good regulatory policy, they are requirements of the Paperwork Reduction Act.25 Minimizing
unnecessary data collections also ensures that agencies do not misuse private sector data for
unrelated purposes in the future.

Based on these principles, we have the following recommendations for each of the Proposal's
revised data requirements:

 Community development loans, investments, and grants. The Proposal would
 impose new data collection requirements for community development lending,
 investment, and grant activities. The lending and investment data collection
 requirements are not necessary for examiners to evaluate banks' community
 development activities; examiners have performed such evaluations for decades without

24 91 Fed. Reg. at 52,115.

25 See 44 U.S.C. 3508 (requiring a collection of information to be "necessary for the proper

performance of the functions of the agency" and to "have practical utility").

 22
 OCC and FDIC

 more specific and standardized data. The Agencies should therefore withdraw these new
 requirements. We explain why the Agencies should withdraw the grant-specific
 requirements in section III.D, above. Similarly, for the reasons discussed in section
 III.D, above, the Agencies should not maintain a public database of community
 development grant information, as the preamble to the Proposal indicates they expect to
 do.

 Consumer loans. The Proposal would impose consumer loan data collection on any
 large bank that has consumer lending as a major product line. The Agencies should
 revise this requirement so that consumer loan data collection requirements only apply
 when a bank is actually evaluated on consumer lending (or at the bank's option), not
 when the bank's consumer lending trips the major product line threshold. A bank that
 has consumer lending as a major product line could be a limited purpose bank evaluated
 on the Community Development Test or might adopt a strategic plan that does not have
 goals relating to consumer lending. In either case, consumer lending data would be
 irrelevant to the bank's evaluation. Additionally, banks required to collect consumer
 loan data should not be required to report that data separately from providing it to
 examiners in the context of the bank's own CRA examination. The Agencies have no
 need for receiving that data on an annual basis outside of the examination process,
 especially because reporting of data from such a limited portion of banks would not
 establish reliable peer data.

In response to a request for comment in the Proposal regarding whether the Agencies should
partially or fully discontinue CRA data collection for small business loans and small farm loans
and rely exclusively on section 1071 data, we do not support such a discontinuation. Section
1071 data are not duplicative of CRA small business lending data. For example, the revised
section 1071 rule only requires reporting of loans to businesses with gross annual revenues of $1
million or less, while the CRA rules require the reporting of loans that are $1 million or less in
size. As another example, the revised section 1071 rule excludes agriculture-purpose credit from
covered transactions, while the CRA evaluates (and therefore requires the reporting of) small
farm lending.

Finally, the Agencies should make it optional rather than mandatory for banks to post their CRA
public files on their websites in lieu of providing those files to members of the public upon
request. In our members' experience, public commenters sometimes submit CRA comments
with inaccurate and unsubstantiated allegations, and banks should not be required to host such
comments on their own websites.

 B. The Agencies Should Consider the Potential Negative Consequences
 of Increasing the Asset Size Thresholds and Avoid Further Increases
 to Those Thresholds, Such as a $30 Billion Large Bank Threshold and
 a $10 Billion Intermediate Bank Threshold

The Agencies have proposed to increase the thresholds for a bank to qualify as a large bank or
intermediate bank (formerly an "intermediate small" bank) to $10 billion and $1 billion,
respectively. The Proposal indicates that the Agencies are also considering increasing these
thresholds to $30 billion and $10 billion, respectively.

While the Associations generally support regulatory tailoring in concept, we urge the Agencies to
consider the potential negative consequences of increasing the thresholds so dramatically.
Higher thresholds mean that the Agencies would evaluate fewer banks' community development
lending and investment activities at all (for banks reclassified as small banks), and would also

 23
 OCC and FDIC

evaluate fewer banks' activities using the Community Development Test (for banks reclassified
as intermediate banks). These changes would remove or reduce many banks' incentives to
engage in community development lending and investment. In turn, these changes could
negatively impact the aggregate amount of industry capital that will be available to support the
administration's priorities (such as Low Income Housing Tax Credit investments and other
investments encouraged under the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act). They could also
concentrate the risks associated with such investments among a smaller group of banks. The
Agencies should specifically consider the effects on rural or other small markets, where the
proposed reclassification would leave fewer large banks with strong incentives to engage in
community development activities.

Additionally, the Agencies should consider the potential impact of concentrating CRA reporting
burdens on a smaller group of large banks, which could skew CRA data because reported small
business lending data would represent a smaller cross-section of the industry than they
currently do. Distribution analyses of small business lending already suffer from the fact that
peer data exclude nonbank lenders. Reducing the pool of lenders represented in the peer data
would exacerbate these data quality issues, particularly in smaller markets where there may be
few large banks to report on small business loans.

To address these issues, the Agencies should:

 Adopt higher thresholds only after fully analyzing the potential negative consequences of
 reclassification described above;

 Not raise the large bank and intermediate bank thresholds to $30 billion and $10 billion,
 respectively, as such a dramatic reclassification would clearly have significant negative
 consequences; and

 Allow banks reclassified into intermediate or small bank status to opt into a higher
 category so that they can continue to earn CRA credit for their community development
 and other activities.

 C. The Agencies Should Make It Optional to Count Prior Period
 Community Development Loans

The Agencies have proposed to add a new provision to their regulations that would count
community development loans made in prior periods that remain outstanding during the
current evaluation period. We support this change, which should generally remove a
disincentive for banks to make longer-term community development loans.

We recommend that counting of prior period community development loans be at a bank's
option rather than mandatory. Optional treatment would allow banks to determine whether the
benefits of counting prior period loans in the current period outweigh the costs of implementing
systems to track prior period loans that remain outstanding. Unlike investments, loans may
renew and change in value across multiple years and exam cycles and, therefore, may be more
challenging to report.

 24
 OCC and FDIC

 D. The Agencies Should Provide at Least a Two-Year Implementation
 Period, With Changes Taking Effect for Any Given Bank at the Start of
 Its Next Evaluation Period

The Proposal does not contain any implementation provisions, including information regarding
the compliance period for its changes.

The final rule should provide at least a two-year pathway for compliance, with any changes
taking effect as of the beginning of any evaluation period that is on or after January 1st of the
third calendar year following the effective date of the final rule. This approach would ensure
that banks have a reasonable amount of time to prepare, while not disrupting their plans for
their existing evaluation periods or requiring evaluations to be conducted under two different
sets of standards.

The Agencies should also clarify that any community development loan, investment, or grant
made, or committed to, prior to the compliance date of the final rule will be grandfathered if it
would qualify for consideration under the existing CRA rules.

VI. Answers to Specific Questions in the Proposal

Question 1: To better align with agency policies that establish an asset size of less than $30
billion as a threshold for certain supervisory approaches, such as being considered a
community bank or being subject to the continuous examination process, should the agencies
consider adjusting the intermediate bank asset size threshold to include all banks with an asset
size of less than $30 billion that do not qualify as small banks? If the agencies establish $30
billion as the appropriate threshold to delineate between intermediate banks and large banks,
should the agencies also adopt a larger threshold for small banks, such as the $10 billion
currently proposed as the intermediate bank threshold?

No, the Agencies should not raise the respective thresholds to $30 billion and $10 billion, as
doing so would have significant negative consequences discussed in section V.B, above.

Question 5: Should the agencies consider consumer lending--a. By type of consumer loans,
rather than in the aggregate, when consumer loans constitute a major product line? b. When
consumer loans account for less than a majority of retail lending but is one of a bank's largest
two product lines? In this circumstance, should the agencies permit the optional consideration
of consumer lending? c. At the bank's request, regardless of whether the consumer loans
constitute a major product line?

As discussed in section III.B, above, the Agencies should maintain the current approach to
considering consumer lending. Consumer loans should not be evaluated when they account for
less than a substantial majority of the bank's business overall (not a bare majority of the bank's
retail lending, as proposed). We have no objection to the Agencies only evaluating consumer
loans when a bank has requested that they do so.

Question 7: If the agencies adopt Option 1, should the agencies determine a bank's major
product lines by assessment area, as opposed to at the institution level as proposed?

For the reasons described in section III.A, above, we do not support the adoption of Option 1 in
the form proposed, but if the Agencies adopt Option 1, it should operate at the institution level.

 25
 OCC and FDIC

Question 9: Are there alternative standards the agencies should consider relying on in the
context of limiting indirect costs for CD grants? Do the proposed guardrails do enough to
ensure the majority of grant and donation funds go directly towards benefiting the bank's
assessment area(s)?

A limitation on indirect costs is not necessary and would not serve the purposes of the CRA. If,
however, the Agencies finalize such a limitation, there are alternative approaches that would
better align with the goals of the CRA than the proposed 15 percent indirect cost limitation. We
discuss these alternative approaches in section III.D, above.

Question 10: As an alternative, should the agencies eliminate all grants and donations from
CRA consideration?

No. As discussed in section III.D, above, grants and donations provide flexible means for non-
profit organizations to serve communities and advance the purposes of the CRA.

Question 14: Are there additional opportunities for the agencies to further enhance the rule's
focus on lending, such as by requiring that CD investments and CD services be complex? If so,
should complex CD activities be a requirement for all banks or only banks that exceed a certain
asset size, such as banks that would be large banks under the proposal?

The Agencies should not require community development investments and services to be
complex. The only requirement should be that the investment or service has community
development as its primary purpose.

Question 18: Should the definition of affordable housing be expanded to include rental housing
for middle-income individuals in high-cost areas as proposed? For example, should banks be
incentivized to support affordable workforce housing that would allow public servants, such as
teachers, firefighters, and police officers, to live in the communities they serve?

Yes, the definition of affordable housing should be expanded to include rental housing for
middle-income individuals in high-cost areas.

Question 19: Should the agencies clarify what constitutes a high-cost area, for example by
providing a definition? If so, should the definition be based on the standard for housing cost-
burdened households referenced above? Is the 40 percent threshold appropriate or should it
be set higher to ensure that the definition meaningfully captures counties where middle-
income families or households are housing cost burdened, for instance should it be set at 50
percent? Are there other definitions of "high-cost areas" that the agencies should consider?

The Associations support the Agencies' recognition of high-cost areas and the continued
consideration of community development activities that address affordability challenges in
those markets. However, as discussed in section III.H, above, the Agencies should avoid
prescribing a single methodology for identifying high-cost areas and instead should provide
flexibility for banks to demonstrate high-cost market conditions using objective, supportable
data sources appropriate to the transaction.

 26
 OCC and FDIC

Question 23: Should the rules modify the definition of affordable housing such that home
mortgage loans provided directly to LMI individuals or families would qualify as CD loans if
not considered as a major product line for the bank?

Yes. Home mortgage loans that a bank makes directly to LMI individuals or families should
qualify as community development loans when home mortgage lending is not a major product
line for the bank. Further, the Agencies should adopt a similar approach for a bank's small
business and small farm loans that would otherwise qualify as community development loans if
small business or small farm loans are not a major product line for the bank.

Question 24: Should the agencies further limit the businesses or farms that qualify under the
first category of economic development (proposed __.12, definition of economic development
paragraph (3)(i)(A)), for example, by excluding startups that are expected to quickly exceed
the size test or excluding small businesses that are affiliated with non-small businesses?

A limitation involving the bank's expectations of a small business's growth would be unworkable
in practice and contrary to the goal of helping small businesses grow. A bank may have no way
of knowing whether a startup will quickly exceed the size test, and it would be difficult for the
bank to "prove the negative" and demonstrate that it did not have the expectation that such
growth would occur.

Question 29: Are there activities that would be considered economic development under the
current rules that would not qualify under the proposed definition of economic development?

We are not aware of any lending and investment activities that would be considered economic
development under the current rules that would not qualify under the proposed definition of
economic development, especially with the inclusion of proposed subsection (3)(i)(B) of the
definition of "community development."

While the proposed definition no longer expressly refers to financing provided through
intermediaries, we understand that the proposed definition still captures such funding. Notably,
the definition of "economic development" refers to "financing . . . for businesses" that meet size
standards, thereby capturing financing provided through an intermediary, and does not refer to
"financing . . . to" such businesses, which might imply that the bank provides the financing
directly to the business. Moreover, a loan to, or investment in, an intermediary that provides
the financing to startups or other recently formed small businesses would have as its primary
purpose financing for small businesses, thereby satisfying the definition of "community
development loan" or "community development investment."

Additionally, we understand that the carveout for financing primarily used for ongoing
operating liquidity is not intended to exclude financing that a recipient actually uses to fund
ongoing operating expenses such as payroll and rent, as such financing can be critical to the
recipient's ability to maintain its employment base and productive capacity, especially given the
fungibility of money.

 27
 OCC and FDIC

Question 33: Should the agencies provide an outer limit for the timeframe in which they would
provide a response following any notification to the requestor that additional time is needed to
consider a request? If yes, what would be an appropriate length of time, for example would an
additional 60 days be appropriate? Or a lesser amount of time such as 30 days? Should the
agencies be required to specify the length of the extension in their notification to the requestor
that additional time is needed?

Yes. As discussed in section IV.B, above, the Agencies should shorten the review period to no
longer than 30 days after an Agency's receipt of a request, which the Agencies could extend by 15
days. The request should then be deemed approved if the Agency fails to deny the request by the
end of the 30- or 45-day review period.

Question 50: Should the Agencies allow strategic plans that are approved after the proposed
effective date to go into effect as of the approval date? Should the effective date be the
proposed date in the plan even if that date is in the past?

The Agencies should allow for the effective date of a strategic plan to be a date that is in the past.
There are several valid reasons why the plan's proposed effective date might fall before the
approval date of the plan, including that the reviewing Agency took longer than anticipated to
approve the plan.

Question 55: Are there alternative approaches the agencies should consider to encourage
banks to meet the credit needs of Indian country and other Tribal and native lands? For
example, should the agencies use the definition of Native Lands in the 2023 CRA rules? Are
there any difficulties or unintended consequences that banks might encounter with the
definitions as proposed?

The Agencies should adopt a definition of Native Lands that is based on the definition of Native
Land Areas in the 2023 CRA rules, but is expanded to encompass the Proposal's addition of
Tribal Census Tracts. The 2023 definition covered federal Native American trust lands, state-
established reservations, legally defined Alaska Native villages, and other Native geographies
that may not be expressly retained in the Proposal. A broad geographic definition is appropriate
because tribal economic activity often extends beyond reservation borders, including housing,
healthcare, infrastructure, education, and economic development projects that serve Native
American populations across multiple land classifications.

Question 57: Should the agencies replace the requirement to include census tracts where the
bank does a substantial portion of lending in the bank's assessment area(s) with an alternative
such as the radius-based standard discussed above. If so, how should the agencies determine
the appropriate radius? Should it vary by type of geographic area (e.g., MSA or
nonmetropolitan area)?

No, the Agencies should not adopt such an approach, for the reasons discussed in section IV.A,
above.

 28
 OCC and FDIC

Question 58: Throughout this SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION the agencies referenced the
guidance in the Interagency Questions and Answers. Several aspects of this proposal were
based on codifications of the existing guidance. The agencies request feedback on how to
address the Interagency Questions and Answers going forward.

The Agencies should retain the Interagency Questions and Answers and only make revisions as
necessary to conform to the final rule. Any revisions should be subject to a separate notice-and-
comment rulemaking process.

Question 60: The agencies request comment on whether they should maintain the location of
public information requirements in current 12 CFR __.43(c) or adopt a website requirement
as proposed. The agencies also invite comment on whether requiring banks to include their
public file requirements on a bank's website would impose costs on banks, result in cost
savings for banks, or have a significant impact on public access to banks' public file
information. In addition, the agencies invite comment on whether banks should be required to
provide for inspection of the public file at all branch locations or only at certain branch
locations in a State.

As discussed in section V.A, above, the Agencies should provide banks the option to follow the
existing public file requirements or to post their public files on their websites, rather than
making either approach mandatory.

 The RER and its members lead an industry which generates more than 20 percent of
America's gross national product, employs more than 9 million people and produces nearly two-
thirds of the taxes raised by local governments for essential public services. RER members are
heavily engaged in the ownership, development and management of real estate, and regularly
engage in capital formation and lending activities in support of these investments.

 Many RER members borrow from banks (the "RER Members' Banks") regulated by the
OCC, FDIC and the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System ("Federal Reserve" and
with the OCC and FDIC, collectively, the "Federal Banking Agencies"). The Federal Banking
Agencies promulgate and administer regulations interpreting the CRA.

 Many of the RER Members' Banks lend for real estate development through separate
banking subsidiaries. It is not uncommon for a banking conglomerate to be comprised of
subsidiaries which include, for example, a New York state-chartered Federal Reserve member
bank (regulated for CRA purposes only by the Federal Reserve) and an affiliated national bank
subsidiary (regulated for CRA purposes only by the OCC). In at least those cases and many
others, having a single, clear and harmonious set of CRA regulations would reduce costs and
limit uncertainty, thereby better enabling banks to perform the mission of the CRA, which is to
meet the credit needs of [the banks'] entire commun[ities], including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods."3

Background and District Court Decision as a Prelude to the Rulemaking Proposal

 The CRA became law nearly fifty years ago, in 1977, to among other things eradicate a
practice called "redlining" in which some banks refrained from lending to certain customers,
primarily in low- to moderate income neighborhoods. In 1995, the then-existing Office of Thrift
Supervision jointly issued with the Federal Banking Agencies comprehensive regulations
implementing the CRA (the "1995 Regulations"),4 and in doing so, created a thorough
examination and supervisory framework for regulated banks and thrifts for purposes of
determining CRA compliance. If the Rulemaking Proposal is adopted and finalized in its
proposed form, much of the 1995 Regulations would continue to be in full effect.

 The 1995 Regulations delineated which institutions would be evaluated, which activities
would be considered in examinations, how ratings would be assigned and provided other
regulatory guardrails for purposes of determining compliance with the CRA. While the 1995
regulations were comprehensive, the regulations were geographically, technologically and
substantively bounded.

 As technology and the business of banking advanced --and with that advancement, the
geographic reach of banks in the U.S. lengthened-- the RER gathers that over time the Federal

Banking Agencies increasingly saw the need to revise CRA regulations to make the rules fit the
business of banking after the 20th century.

 In 2024, the Federal Banking Agencies jointly issued comprehensive regulations5 to align
CRA-related regulation with the modern banking system in the U.S., but these regulations were
enjoined by a federal district court6 on the basis that the regulations were outside of the statutory
scope of the CRA and banks were already sustaining "irreparable harm" through
"nonrecoverable compliance costs"7 such as the following:

 An estimated first-year compliance burden of approximately $91.8 million, based on an
 OCC clarification concerning expenditures that would be incurred if full compliance
 were required during the first 12 months;

 Agency estimates of approximately 105,500 to 235,000 hours for reporting,
 recordkeeping, and disclosure obligations; and

 Additional institution-specific expenditures relating to systems changes, database
 updates, program planning, vendor arrangements, personnel, and compliance
 infrastructure.8

 Unlike the 1995 Regulations promulgated by each of the Federal Banking Agencies, only the
OCC and FDIC made the Rulemaking Proposal.9

Executive Summary

 Because of the compliance costs and the potential for conflicting CRA regulations among the
Prudential Regulators as inherent problems of the Rulemaking Proposal, the RER recommends
that CRA rulemaking efforts continue but only with all three Federal Banking Agencies
promulgating CRA rules, and only in a manner which is harmonized by each of the Federal
Banking Agencies. In the meantime, banks under the regulatory jurisdiction of the Federal
Banking Agencies should continue to be subject to existing law and regulations until a
harmonized body of new CRA rules are proposed and put into final form jointly and altogether
by each of the Federal Banking Agencies.10

 There are several compelling reasons for our recommendation, and while one is general,
others are more technical in nature. Generally speaking, if the OCC and FDIC promulgate final
CRA rules without parallel Federal Reserve action, the historically uniform interagency CRA
framework may be replaced with materially different regulatory regimes based solely on the
charters of our REF Member's Banks (because those banks (including subsidiaries of the same
global banks) may be subject to different prudential regulators for CRA compliance purposes).
Undue or unnecessary compliance costs jeopardizes yet additional injunctive relief against the
FDIC and OCC (along the lines of what the district court ordered in Texas Bankers Ass'n in
2024).

Consequences of a Divided CRA Regulatory Regime

 Real estate development by members of the RER are financed by markets and syndicates
irrespective of regulatory silos. A divided CRA regime could make identical loans receive
different treatment, weaken investment incentives for some lenders, complicate mergers and
syndicated transactions, and make the flow of capital into underserved markets less predictable.

A better outcome insofar as CRA regulations are concerned is the following:

 The promulgation of a substantively uniform final rule by all of the Prudential
 Regulators;

 Coordinated transition, examination and interpretive guidance with an eye towards
 minimizing regulatory differences; and/or

 A system of reciprocity under which each Federal Banking Agency recognizes the other's
 rules and decision making and applies consistent standards to multi-bank housing and
 community development transactions.

Real Estate Transactions Require Regulatory Certainty and Harmony

 Affordable housing and community development projects frequently rely on several
regulated banks performing different roles in myriad capacities. The capital stack for complex
real estate transactions may be comprised of multiple sources of grant proceeds, tax credit (i.e.,
low income housing tax credit ("LIHTC")) participants and multiple banks, with one bank
providing at the outset a construction loan, and a different bank lending in a permanent loan,
with still other financial institutions ranging from the provider of a warehouse facility or credit
enhancement, to a community development financial institution or CDFI.

 With multiple banks potentially subject to differing CRA compliance obligations, the overall
regulatory compliance exercise for those banks may over time amount to three dimensional
regulatory chess:

 The lead lender for the real estate development may be an OCC-supervised bank seeking
 CRA credit from the OCC's final rule for its loan;

 A bank regulated by the Federal Reserve with uncertainty as to which regulatory regime
 applies may need to conduct a side-by-side regulatory analysis for purposes of
 understanding whether the same loan qualifies under Regulation BB, the rule of the
 Federal Reserve for the CRA;

 The banks lending to the real estate development might disagree over the geographical
 allocation of CRA credit among assessment areas.

 We recognize that the Rulemaking Proposal by the OCC and FDIC includes a formal process
through which a bank could seek from those regulators confirmation that a community-
development activity qualifies for credit; however, at this point the Federal Reserve has not
proposed an equivalent process for such confirmation.

Assessment Area

 We understand that the OCC and FDIC may be evaluating an "in-assessment area"
benchmark of 1.25% of Tier 1 capital for wholesale and limited-purpose banks, a benchmark
which would need to be met before qualifying activities outside of a bank's assessment area
could receive CRA consideration.

 Although the objective of encouraging meaningful activity within banks' assessment areas is
understandable, the proposed benchmark could have significant unintended market
consequences. In heavily-banked assessment areas, it may drive additional capital toward an
already limited supply of CRA-eligible transactions, increasing competition and placing further
pressure on pricing and deal economics. Conversely, strong projects in markets outside of major
banking centers especially in tertiary metropolitan and rural communities - will be
disadvantaged notwithstanding their underlying credit quality and community impact.

 We gather that these concerns have been discussed on industry trade association (e.g., ABA
and BPI) conference calls, and in those calls, CRA professionals have cautioned that the
resulting market pressures could become unsustainable.

 A more flexible framework may be necessary to avoid reinforcing CRA hotspots while
simultaneously creating or expanding capital deserts in markets that have fewer regulated
banking institutions.

 ***

 As discussed above, the RER appreciates the OCC and FDIC for the Rulemaking Proposal
and believes that this proposed rulemaking represents an important step towards modernizing the
rules for CRA.

 However, given foreseeable compliance costs, the potential for conflicting CRA regulations
among the Prudential Regulators and the possibility of further injunctive action by a federal court
(in light of anticipated compliance costs and the decision in Texas Bankers Ass'n), the RER
recommends that CRA rulemaking efforts continue, but only with all three Federal Banking
Agencies promulgating CRA rules in a clear, harmonized manner.

 The RER looks forward to continuing to serve as a resource to the OCC and FDIC and all
stakeholders to address issues affecting compliance obligations imposed by prudential banking
regulations generally and by the CRA in particular. Thank you.

 RE: Concerns Regarding Proposed Changes to Community Reinvestment Act Asset

 To whom this may concern:

 On behalf of the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Barbara (HASBARCO), I am writing
 to express our significant concerns regarding proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment
 Act (CRA) asset thresholds that would substantially increase the number of banks classified as
 "small" or "intermediate" institutions. As an organization committed to expanding affordable
 housing and community development opportunities, we are deeply concerned about the potential
 impact these changes could have on the availability of financing in underserved communities
 throughout California, particularly in Santa Barbara County.

 California continues to face one of the most severe housing affordability crises in the nation.
 Communities throughout Santa Barbara County are experiencing rising housing costs, limited
 housing supply, increasing development expenses, and growing challenges in providing
 affordable homes for low- and moderate-income households, seniors, individuals with
 disabilities, veterans, and essential workers. Access to capital through CRA-motivated lending
 and investment has been an important component in financing affordable housing developments
 and community revitalization efforts that serve these populations.

 The CRA has historically encouraged financial institutions to provide community development
 loans and investments that support affordable housing, neighborhood revitalization, economic
 development, and community services. Currently, approximately 46 percent of federally insured
 banks are incentivized through CRA requirements to provide community development financing.
 Proposed increases to the asset thresholds for small and intermediate banks would significantly
 reduce the number of institutions subject to these incentives and could result in a corresponding
 reduction in community development investment nationwide.

 These changes are particularly concerning for communities such as Santa Barbara County, where
 affordable housing developments often rely on complex financing structures involving multiple
 public and private funding sources. CRA investments frequently serve as a critical financing tool
 that helps make affordable housing developments feasible. For example, without Wells Fargo
 investment in a previous development, we would not have been able to move forward with the
 project. A reduction in bank participation could further constrain an already limited funding
 environment and make it more difficult to develop, preserve, and rehabilitate affordable housing
 throughout the Central Coast and California.

 The proposed changes would also have a disproportionate impact on rural communities and areas
 outside of major metropolitan centers. This is especially relevant for Santa Barbara County,
 which encompasses both urban centers and large rural and agricultural areas. Communities such
 as Lompoc, Santa Maria, Guadalupe, Buellton, Solvang, and Santa Ynez depend on continued
 investment to address workforce housing shortages, aging housing stock, community facility
 needs, and economic development opportunities. Reduced CRA incentives could further limit
 access to financing in the very communities where investment is needed most.

 Additionally, affordable housing developers throughout California are already facing significant
 challenges related to rising construction costs, insurance premiums, labor shortages, and higher

 housing production and address long-standing housing shortages, it is difficult to reconcile
 reducing incentives for community development investment with the urgent need for additional

 REDUCTION IN COMMUNITY INVESTMENT EXPECTATIONS FOR ALL BANKS

 CRA obligations encourage banks to invest throughout the communities they serve. From 2010 through 2024,
 banks in San Francisco made $84,970,182,000 in CRA-qualified mortgage loans to low- and moderate-income
 borrowers or in low- and moderate-income census tracts, as well as $4,985,180,000 in qualified small-business
 loans. The proposed rule could undermine these incentives. For example, it suggests that a bank could receive a
 passing CRA rating by devoting just 0.625% of its Tier 1 capital to community development loans or investments.
 That threshold is far below the share that the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) found the
 largest banks currently devote to such activity. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should determine whether
 the proposed changes would reduce lending, services, or investment in low- and moderate-income communities
 and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or disinvestment would bear
 disproportionate harm.

 We ask the agencies to:

 1. Reject the proposed 0.625% Tier 1 capital floor, or set any minimum activity threshold at a level consistent
 with current market performance rather than a fraction of it.

 2. Maintain separate, independently binding minimums for community development lending and community
 development investment, so that a bank cannot satisfy its entire community development obligation
 through lending alone.

 SUPPORT FOR LOCAL ORGANIZATIONS

 We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and nonprofit
 organizations. In particular, the proposal would impose a 15% limit on indirect costs, add new documentation
 requirements, and raise the possibility of eliminating CRA eligibility for grantmaking altogether.
 Banks support affordable housing, small-business development, financial counseling, workforce programs,
 neighborhood revitalization, and other community-based services through grants, investments, loans, and
 partnerships with nonprofit organizations. These resources are especially important to local organizations with
 deep community relationships and firsthand knowledge of residents' needs.
 For grants from large banks, the proposal would cap indirect costs at 15% and impose new documentation
 requirements that could place substantial burdens on smaller organizations. Such a cap may be unrealistic because
 staff, rent, technology, accounting, compliance, and other operating expenses are essential to program delivery.
 These investments sustain the organizations and infrastructure that turn capital into tangible benefits for residents.
 As a result, rules governing which grants and community development activities receive CRA consideration can
 affect communities far beyond the banks themselves.

 Before finalizing these provisions, the agencies should assess whether the proposed documentation requirements
 and limits on administrative expenses would reduce or redirect bank support away from smaller nonprofit
 organizations, particularly those with limited administrative capacity. The agencies should also determine
 whether those effects would ultimately reduce resources available to low- and moderate-income communities.

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

The Jefferson Economic Development Institute (JEDI) writes to object to the harmful changes proposed to the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed by Congress in 1977 in response to redlining and creates an affirmative
obligation for banks to help meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of communities, including low and moderate
income (LMI) communities. While the CRA has successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest and provide services in
underserved communities, challenges related to redlining, discrimination, underinvestment, and lack of access remain.

JEDI is a community economic development organization celebrating 30 years of providing entrepreneurial and wealth-
building services in far northern CA for rural low-resourced and diverse individuals in an effort to build more resilient
communities. We are founding members of the Coalition for Responsible Lending and have been a RISE Economy
member over the years.

The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift. The proposal does not justify those
changes or consider their expected impact on LMI communities. We request an extension of the comment period for an
additional 60 days so we have time to better understand how much CRA activity may be lost to communities because of
this proposal an analysis the regulators did not conduct or provide.

 The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in underserved communities in several ways.

 1. Community development (CD) activities for affordable housing and small businesses will drop dramatically.
 a. As currently implemented, the CRA incentivizes community development activities that support critically
 needed affordable housing and economic development projects. These activities often provide the
 greatest CRA impact in communities as they strengthen economic stability and mobility, quality of life, and
 social health of residents and communities.

 b. The proposal would raise asset thresholds for "Small," "Intermediate" and "Large" Banks, such that many
 banks will be subject to substantially less CRA scrutiny and expectation to serve the community
 development needs of their communities.[1] According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition
 (NCRC) analysis, 70 California banks would see their reinvestment obligations reduced under the
 proposal. Twenty-five California banks would shed their Community Development Test responsibilities
 entirely, and 45 California banks would no longer be subject to the Investment Test. [2]

 c. The Investment Test has successfully driven investment into several critical community development
 programs that have had large impacts in LMI communities. These include Low Income Housing Tax
 Credits (LIHTCs) which are a key driver of affordable housing finance; New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC)
 which fuel economic development projects in tribal and other areas; and EQ2 equity equivalent
 investments in Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) that provide small business lending
 in underserved areas that banks cannot reach, and in Community Land Trusts (CLTs) that take property off
 of the speculative market.

 d. Commercial banks account for an estimated 85% of LIHTC investors, highlighting the critical importance of
 the CRA Investment Test in the financing of affordable housing.[3] Approximately half of nonprofit CDFI
 funding comes from CRA motivated banks.[4] The regulators will even further weaken CD obligations if they
 adopt the alternative proposal that Large Banks be defined as those with over $30 billion in assets.

 e. Of great concern, the proposal creates a roadmap for banks to decrease CD finance even where they
 remain subject to the Community Development and Investment Tests. The regulators signal to all banks
 that they can do significantly less CD lending and investment and still pass their CRA examinations, all
 while seeking CRA credit for activity outside of their CRA assessment areas. The proposal suggests that a
 bank could receive a passing CRA rating if just a mere 0.625% of its Tier 1 capital were devoted to CD loans
 and CD investments. That percentage is far lower than the percentage that NCRC determined banks
 currently devote to community investments and loans. If each bank instead conducted only the amount
 necessary to meet the proposed thresholds, CD activity would decrease by approximately $87.1 billion, or
 85%.[5]

 f. Any reduction in community development financing by banks in California will have tremendous negative
 impacts on affordable housing and small business development in our state. Asset thresholds should not
 be raised.

 2. Banks will shed branches and BankOn.
 a. The CRA has been especially effective in encouraging banks to open and maintain branches in LMI and
 BIPOC neighborhoods. By increasing the asset threshold for a Large Bank to over $10 billion, forty-five
 banks in California will no longer be subject to the Services Test and reviewed to ensure that their branches

 Page 2
  are serving LMI communities. In California alone, NCRC estimates that 245 branches in LMI areas and 497
 branches in neighborhoods of color would be vulnerable to closure due to this proposal.[6]

 b. Branch presence has been tied to increased small business lending in communities. Fewer branches will
 result in less small business lending. These changes will be particularly hard hitting in rural areas of our

 c. The proposal would also entirely remove the long-standing obligation for banks to offer deposit products
 that are accessible to LMI residents.[7] Deposit accounts are a gateway to credit access, financial stability,

 institutions. As one important example, the BankOn program has provided access to no or low fee bank

 d. Meanwhile, 5.6 million U.S. households remain unbanked and more than 19 million are underbanked.[9]

3. Critical data on lending transparency will be lost.
