 Such data is critical to understanding not only individual bank performance, but also the needs of local
 markets. Rise Economy and its member organizations routinely analyze this CRA data when meeting with
 banks and commenting on CRA exams and mergers. The loss of such data is particularly harmful at a time
 when the Administration is walking back efforts to collect and disclose detailed small business lending
 data under Section 1071 of the Dodd Frank Act. These changes will disproportionately impact rural
 communities in our state where banks up to $10 billion in assets make up a larger part of the small
 business and small farm lending markets.

4. Native American communities and Tribal Nations will not see sufficient benefits.
 a. The proposal does not go far enough to encourage banks to better meet the needs of Native American
 communities and Tribal Nations which have been poorly served by banks. The current rules focus CRA
 obligations in areas where banks have branches, even though there are far fewer bank branches near Tribal
 lands and in rural areas where Native Americans may reside. The proposal seeks to address this CRA gap
 by encouraging banks to engage in community development and related activities in "Indian Country" and
 on "Tribal and Native lands," even if outside of bank CRA assessment areas. But many members of Tribes
 in California will not benefit from this proposal as they do not live in Indian Country or on Tribal or Native
 lands, as defined.

 b. CRA consideration here should not be limited only to activities occurring within particular geographies,
 given the challenges and impacts associated with historic dispossession and federal policy. Instead, CRA
 evaluations should also consider whether banks have established meaningful relationships with, and
 provided direct benefits to, federally recognized Tribes as well as non-federally recognized Tribes. Non-
 federally recognized Tribes have been acknowledged by, and are able to access programs and contracts
 with, various local and state entities.[11] Such processes exist.
 Page 3
  c. More specifically, the CRA rules should encourage banks to serve Tribes, nonprofit organizations or other
 entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-owned businesses that are majority owned and controlled by
 Native American entrepreneurs by providing:

 i. Active outreach and engagement
 ii. Community development loans and investments for affordable housing and economic

 development projects
 iii. Small farm and small business loans
 iv. Home mortgage loans
 v. Grants to meet community needs, including capacity building for Tribes and support for Tribes

 seeking federal recognition if desired.
 vi. Support for cultural, health and other programs
 vii. Bank branches
 viii. Deposit products such as affordable bank accounts, and
 ix. The provision of financial services such as financial literacy, apprenticeship programs and

 technical assistance support

 d. While banks should generally be precluded from getting CRA credit for activities outside of their branches
 and CRA assessment areas, exceptions should be made to encourage banks to engage in CRA related
 activity to directly benefit Tribes, nonprofit organizations and other entities controlled by Tribes, and Native-
 owned businesses that are majority owned and controlled by Native American entrepreneurs.

 e. A better approach is needed. All banks should be subject to an impact and responsiveness review factor
 during their CRA exams that evaluates and tracks whether banks have engaged in any CRA activity directly
 with Tribes, Tribally-controlled entities and Native owned businesses.[12] If banks know they will be
 examined for their work with Tribes, they will find mutually beneficial ways to work with Tribes.

5. Contributions to local nonprofits that serve communities will suffer.
 a. The proposed rule would tighten CRA eligibility for bank grants to nonprofits by requiring a demonstrated
 nexus to community development projects and mandating that large banks and their grantees
 demonstrate that grantees will not use more than 15% of these grants on overhead.[13] As if this wasn't
 enough, the FDIC and OCC question whether they should end CRA eligibility for bank grantmaking to
 nonprofits entirely.

 b. Here, as elsewhere, the regulators fail to analyze what the impact of such draconian measures will be
 except to acknowledge that community groups, including smaller groups, may be impacted.[14]

 c. Nonprofits play a critical role in communities, helping to meet a variety of local needs. They also can be key
 partners for banks trying to bring deposit, credit and investment products into communities inclined to trust
 long established local organizations. Many nonprofit organizations and programs, such as downpayment
 assistance programs, that support CRA related activity, rely on bank contributions to operate. Smaller,
 local, and rural organizations will be least able to meet new reporting obligations, and they risk losing bank
 support as a result. The proposal would also end impactful contributions from banks for general operating
 support, sponsorships, and capacity-building grants.

 Page 4
  d. Banks cannot always effectively help meet the credit and deposit needs of their communities on their own.
 Most banks rely on nonprofit partners to fill in the gaps in their own capacity seeking assistance with
 community outreach, borrower education, credit building and repair, technical assistance, legal services,
 job training and placement, tax assistance, affordable housing and other services and programs which
 help residents become stable and bankable so that banks can attract new deposits and make new loans
 in LMI communities.

 e. The likely effect of this proposal is that banks will make fewer grants overall and will focus grantmaking on
 larger organizations that can help them more easily meet their new FDIC and OCC-imposed regulatory
 burdens.

 f. Even where nonprofits are able to secure grants from Large Banks, the 15% overhead restriction will
 negatively affect operations and organizational success. As one example, in order to secure CRA grants
 from Large Banks, CDFIs will need to pare down costs for critical operational expenses such as
 underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology, impact measurement, product development, and
 borrower technical assistance. With less support to sustain these operational functions, organizations are
 put at risk.

 g. The regulators' focus on this issue is perplexing given the miniscule share of CRA activity that contributions
 represent (less than 1% of bank CRA activity), the large negative impact it will have on nonprofit
 organizations that rely on bank funding, the harm it will cause to LMI communities that are meant to benefit
 from the CRA, and the disruption it will cause to constructive bank-nonprofit partnerships.

6. Less benefit for LMI communities, more lenience for banks.
 a. There are several provisions in the proposal that will further weaken the link between CRA and LMI impact
 in the name of easing bank burden.

 b. Fewer loans reviewed. Under this proposal, banks may only be reviewed for their top two major product
 lines of business. But if banks are offering loan products in, and profiting from, communities, this lending by
 banks, subsidiaries and affiliates must be evaluated. Further, certain products, such as small farm and
 consumer loans, are important in many communities, but may not be among a bank's largest product
 lines. If regulators give banks a pass and exempt smaller product lines from CRA oversight, banks will have
 less incentive to consider how those products are offered.

 c. Greater scrutiny of loan products and banking practices promotes bank safety and soundness,
 encourages banks to meet community needs, and engenders greater trust in banks by the community.
 Eliminating categories of loan products from scrutiny will have the opposite effect.

 d. No economic development for LMI. The proposal would eliminate the purpose test, which has encouraged
 the financing of projects that create LMI jobs, from the definition of economic development. The CRA
 should create greater incentives for banks to support the creation of jobs that pay family sustaining wages
 for LMI workers and in LMI areas, not fewer. We object to provisions that would provide CRA credit for job
 creation and economic development that may only benefit middle- and upper-income workers and
 communities. Such provisions ignore the purpose of CRA.

 Page 5
  e. Broadening community infrastructure dilutes CRA. The proposal would provide CRA credit for large scale
 community infrastructure products that generate profits for banks, would likely be financed without CRA
 credit, and provide only incidental benefits to LMI residents and communities. Such an expansion of what
 qualifies for CRA credit can significantly dilute CRA's impact on LMI residents and communities. For
 example, banks might choose to more profitably earn CRA credit by financing larger scale infrastructure
 projects, like bridges, in lieu of financing less lucrative, smaller CDFI-led projects that better meet local
 community needs (such as childcare facilities, health clinics, rural broadband, water systems, or resilience
 projects).

 f. Allowing banks to cherry pick projects outside of CRA assessment areas. The CRA should require banks to
 focus their CRA activities on their CRA assessments areas,[15] where they are subject to more rigorous
 regulatory oversight (with an exception made to encourage banks to better serve Tribes, as noted above).
 Banks are not doing enough currently to meet the credit and deposit needs in the areas where they have
 CRA responsibility, a problem the regulators tried to address in the 2023 CRA Rule.[16] Yet the proposal
 further encourages banks to seek CRA credit for projects in areas away from their branches, lending and
 CRA responsibility. This will enable banks to get credit for activity outside of their assessment areas, while
 providing no accompanying CRA obligation to better serve these areas.

 g. Encouraging CRA Strategic Plans encourages less investment. The proposal goes out of its way to
 encourage banks to select the CRA Strategic Plan option to meet their CRA responsibilities. The Strategic
 Plan was meant for financial institutions that operated under a unique business model that the CRA rules
 were not designed to address. The Strategic Plan option provides for minimal public input and regulatory
 scrutiny and allows banks to determine the level of reinvestment activity they need to engage in to earn a
 passing CRA grade. In our experience, banks with Strategic Plans tend to reinvest less in the community
 and in less impactful ways. The OCC's guidance establishing low community development thresholds for
 banks opting for the Strategic Plan, [17] validates this perspective.

 h. Expanding credit for NOAH may dilute affordable housing and community development efforts with little
 benefit. Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing, where units are affordable at a point in time but not
 encumbered by deed or rent restrictions, are a feature of today's housing market. But CRA rules should not
 give banks credit for financing such activities where the benefit to LMI residents and communities is
 unclear or absent. NOAH can be a resource for LMI residents, or it can be a driver of bank investment in
 problematic landlords and displacement. CRA credit should be given for financing of NOAH only if the
 project is owned and operated by mission-driven organizations, where a majority of residents are LMI
 tenants, and the bank can demonstrate that the transaction and the property are compliant with tenant
 rights and anti-displacement principles so that LMI residents can reasonably be expected to retain their
 housing.

7. Discrimination and illegal credit practices should lead to CRA ratings downgrades.
 a. The CRA is the nation's anti-redlining law. Banks that discriminate and redline should not be allowed to
 pass their CRA exams with "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding" ratings. Under the Biden Administration, at
 least a dozen banks that passed their CRA exams were accused of redlining. This proposal will only
 increase that number by narrowing what constitutes evidence of discrimination that may be considered for
 the purpose of downgrading the bank's CRA rating. Here, regulators should consider evidence that a bank,
 its affiliates, or subsidiaries engaged in discrimination, redlining, or illegal credit practices as part of their

 Page 6
  lending, deposit, branching, or other activities. This evidence should be considered regardless of its source
 (public or private parties), or its form (informal complaints, research based on data, testing results,
 comment letters, administrative actions, private litigation, etc.). We also urge the regulators to
 acknowledge that the Equal Credit Opportunity Act authorizes Special Purpose Credit Programs, and to
 once again encourage banks to develop SPCPs to better serve communities that have been redlined,
 excluded, and underserved. This is the essence of CRA.

Conclusion. The proposal is ill-conceived, does not provide sufficient information to allow for meaningful public
comment, ignores its impact on numerous types of entities and activities, and will undoubtedly harm the
communities that the CRA was meant to support. If finalized in substantially the same form as proposed,
communities will suffer significantly decreased investment in affordable housing and CDFI support, more LMI
branch closures, higher bank account fees, fewer community serving nonprofit organizations, and increased bank
discrimination and redlining with no CRA consequence. The CRA will become further removed from its purpose of
encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We urge the FDIC and the OCC to reconsider this proposal.

Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Sincerely,

Nancy T. Swift

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Community
Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN
3064-AG31]

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

The Business Center for Entrepreneurship & Social Enterprise (TBC) submits this comment
in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by
the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
(FDIC) because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In
addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the
OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences
for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis
and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment
deadline by 60 days.

TBC is a Philadelphia-based nonprofit economic development organization providing
entrepreneurship education, individualized business advising, workforce training, and
access-to-capital readiness services to approximately 1,000 small businesses annually.
Through its Innovation and Manufacturing Center in Wayne Junction, and neighborhood
revitalization initiatives, TBC helps entrepreneurs establish and grow enterprises, develop
financial capacity, and create pathways to employment and economic mobility. Its work
serves communities including Germantown, Wayne Junction, East Germantown, and
NicetownTioga, where equitable access to banking, responsible credit, and sustained
community investment is essential to business formation and neighborhood stability.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring
that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-
income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both
credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in communities that
 have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream
financial services.

The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would
change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for
nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without an
adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on
communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In the Philadelphia
metro area, from 2010-2024, banks made over $64 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to
LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and over $22 billion in CRA qualified lending to small
businesses. Investments such as these benefited our community by helping entrepreneurs
obtain working capital, purchase equipment, improve commercial properties, and sustain
neighborhood-serving businesses. For TBC constituents, affordable financing can be the
difference between completing a business plan and opening a storefront, hiring a worker,
or expanding production. Community development lending also supports commercial
corridors such as Wayne Avenue, where reinvestment in existing businesses can strengthen
local employment and neighborhood services.

We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in our
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital
devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough to receive a
passing CRA rating. This represents a dramatic reduction in what large banks currently devote
to community investments and loans and we fear that this new guidance may operate as a ceiling
instead of a floor. Pennsylvania receives over $3 billion in CRA related investments annually,
but under the proposed rule that could fall to just over $600 million an 80% loss.

Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination
cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans. If
regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the
communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for communities. For example, in
our community . TBC works with entrepreneurs who need manageable financing for
startup costs, inventory, equipment, storefront improvements, and business expansion. A
decline in CRA-motivated lending and investment could leave these owners with fewer
affordable options, delay hiring and growth, and increase dependence on costly financing.
It could also undermine efforts to revitalize Wayne Junction and adjacent commercial
corridors by reducing the capital available for building improvements, business retention,
and new neighborhood enterprises.

It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet the needs of communities
like ours. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes
would reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income
communities and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or
disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.
 The proposal would also substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while
banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less
demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more comprehensive tests applied to
large banks. The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting
requirements currently applicable to large banks, including reporting on small-business,
community development lending.

A number of banks that operate in Philadelphia will now be considered either intermediate or
small banks under the proposed rule and therefore subject to less rigorous requirements. These
reclassifications and resulting eliminations of community development obligations for over 800
banks and separate investment evaluations for 400 banks across the country, may worsen the
housing crisis by reducing investor interest in buying Low-Income Housing Tax Credits
(LIHTC), and reducing access to mortgages for first-time homebuyers or access to credit for
home repairs.

Similarly, the proposed rule would narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service
test. Today, examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and
information about the costs and features of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit this
criterion to credit services, removing deposit products such as checking and savings accounts
from direct evaluation under the service test. As such, examiners would no longer evaluate
whether those products are affordable and responsive to community needs even though
approximately 15% of Philadelphians over 100,000 households remain unbanked or
underbanked. Moreover, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, these
households are overwhelmingly low-income, black, or disabled. CRA review of the cost and
features of deposit products has played an important role in encouraging banks to address these
disparities by providing affordable products, and it must continue to do so.

For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate from
access to credit and economic opportunity. They can determine whether families can safely
receive income, build savings, establish banking relationships and obtain responsible credit.
TBC's business education and advising work underscores that access to an affordable
checking account, reliable payment services, and a banking relationship is foundational to
business readiness. Entrepreneurs need these tools to separate personal and business
finances, accept customer payments, document revenue, build credit histories, and qualify
for financing. In neighborhoods served by TBC, reduced access to affordable banking
services can push owners toward higher-cost alternatives and make formal business growth
more difficult.

This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and moderate-
income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to affordable
mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible small-business
financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in affordable housing, small
businesses and other community development.
 The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply
because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA
obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that
would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the communities those
institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development activity that would receive
less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-income
communities or communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development,
financial counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-
based services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations.
These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have deep relationships
with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.

For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and
new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations.
For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology,
accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the
underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources
over which to spread these costs. In addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with
limited staff and may not maintain financial records or program documentation in the precise
format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller
organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger
organizations whose activities are easier to verify.

Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and partnerships can
play in supporting community development. TBC's experience demonstrates why community
development partnerships matter: its business coaching, entrepreneurship cohorts,
workforce training, and Innovation and Manufacturing Center connect residents with
skills, technical assistance, and pathways to enterprise ownership. Sustained financial-
institution support for organizations undertaking this work can help cover the instructors,
facilities, outreach, and advisory capacity necessary to reach smaller and underserved
businesses. Restrictions that discourage banks from supporting community-based
nonprofits could weaken the delivery infrastructure that helps entrepreneurs become ready
to use capital effectively.

These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into
tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community
development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond
the banks themselves. These rules should be motivated by the needs of the communities CRA is
intended to serve and not by the perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions.

To be considered economic development under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying
small business must promote economic development by supporting permanent job creation,
 retention, or improvement for low- or moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income
communities.

The proposed rule would eliminate this "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks could
earn CRA credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or improves jobs
for low- and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income communities. This
change would weaken the connection between CRA economic-development credit and the
people and communities CRA is intended to benefit. Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying
business expand does not necessarily create jobs, increase economic opportunity in an
underserved neighborhood or address the needs of low- and moderate-income communities.
TBC's Wayne Junction business improvement initiative illustrates the importance of
measuring actual community benefits. Proposed investments in neighborhood businesses--
such as upgraded equipment at a local cleaner, accessibility and operating-system
improvements at a pest-control company, and modernization of a hair salon--are designed
to support business retention, stronger operations, and potential employment growth.
These are proposed projects rather than verified completed investments or documented
new jobs; they illustrate why CRA consideration should remain tied to demonstrable
outcomes for local businesses, workers, and neighborhoods.

Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens a
qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank to
demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or neighborhoods.

We are also concerned that currently, banks above the large bank threshold annually collect and
report data on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans, while
the proposal would limit these requirements to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. Banks
with assets of $10 billion or less would no longer be required to annually collect and report CRA
data on small business loans and community development loans.

Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers would have less information
to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance or understand whether local credit needs
are being met. Local community leaders and elected officials depend on this data for decision
making and for ensuring that the needs of residents are being addressed. This proposed change is
inconsistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs of
entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities, and should not be in the
final rule.

Lastly, prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:

 identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny
under the proposal;

 quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
  assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
including rural communities and communities of color; and

 consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
meaningful community accountability.

Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes that the
OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is
prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to
prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that
accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of
meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods.

We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days.
The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant changes
to bank classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit
grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The current comment period closes on
October 13, 2026.

Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that do not
have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would allow affected
organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather examples from the
communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more complete record on which to base
any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment
deadline by at least 60 days.

Sincerely,

Pamela Rich Wheeler, Executive Director
The Business Center for Entrepreneurship & Social Enterprise (TBC)

Deputy Executive Secretary Jones and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency:

I submit this letter on behalf of the Mission Lenders Working Group (MLWG) and its member Community
Advantage (CA) mission lenders working to finance, grow and sustain small businesses and emerging
entrepreneurs in underbanked and underserved communities across the country. We appreciate the
opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, proposing
major revisions to the regulations of the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) published in the Federal
Register on August 12, 2026.

The Mission Lenders Working Group represents a national network of U.S. Small Business Administration
(SBA)-authorized, regulated, community-based, mission-driven nonprofit lenders, including several U.S.
Treasury-certified CDFIs, that work hand in hand with local, regional, and national banks to provide
responsible financing and technical assistance to underserved small businesses through the SBA Community
Advantage program, while helping cultivate a pipeline of bank-ready businesses for conventional financial
institutions.

Our members' experience demonstrates that banks and mission lenders are complementary partners, not
competing sources of capital. Mission lenders frequently serve as an entry point into the financial system for
entrepreneurs and small businesses that may not initially qualify for conventional bank financing. Through
relationship-based prudent underwriting, smaller-dollar lending, technical assistance, and business
development support, mission lenders help borrowers strengthen their businesses and, over time, become
potential customers of conventional financial institutions.

CRA has played an important role in creating the durable incentives that make these partnerships possible.
  The MLWG appreciates the agencies' efforts to modernize the Community Reinvestment Act regulations and
 supports provisions that could strengthen the CRA structure and promote responsible investment in
 underserved communities. However, we are deeply concerned that the proposed increases in asset thresholds,
 limitations on operating grants, and other interconnected changes could significantly weaken incentives for
 banks to invest in, lend to, and partner with mission-based lenders. These changes could reduce access to
 critical sources of capital for mission lenders and, in turn, constrain the ability of SBA Community
 Advantage mission lenders and other community development mission lenders to provide much-needed
 financing and technical assistance to underbanked and underserved small businesses and communities.

 Taken together, these changes could have consequences well beyond CRA examinations. They could affect
 the availability of the bank capital and other resources that mission lenders rely upon to finance underserved
 small businesses.

I. CRA SHOULD CONTINUE TO INCENTIVIZE BANKMISSION LENDER PARTNERSHIPS

 MLWG Recommendation: Any CRA modernization should preserve bank and mission lender partnerships
 to strengthen this critical ecosystem for underserved and underbanked small businesses.

 The CRA has helped establish an important bridge between financial institutions and mission lenders serving
 communities with unmet credit needs.

 Through local partnerships, banks provide mission lenders with capital and other resources that can be
 leveraged into significantly greater community impact. The majority of referrals for small business financing
 also come from local and regional banks to mission lenders. In turn, mission lenders provide these bank
 partners with potential future access to borrowers and markets that can be difficult or costly to reach through
 conventional lending channels. This relationship is particularly important for new entrepreneurship, young
 small and existing small businesses.

 CRA has created a durable incentive for banks to lend, invest, and most importantly, partner with mission
 lenders to expand access to capital for underserved small businesses and communities that have historically
 faced barriers to conventional financing. Banks are essential to the business community, but they can't help
 everyone. Too many small business owners that hear "no" from a bank successfully search online for easy
 money, it's available, it's expensive, often layering multiple lenders that offer loans based on automated
 models until the business owner(s) end up closing their business or working just to pay their minimum debt
 obligations. This is harmful to the business community and the communities they serve. Mission-based
 community lenders offer an affordable alternative, often,the only viable alternative following tenets of
 responsible lending. With the help of SBA Community Advantage mission lenders, these small unbankable
 and many times underserved small businesses are creating jobs, generating economic activity, and paying
 taxes. These small businesses continue to be bank customers and, if they do well enough, will become bank
 borrowers in the future.

 The CRA creates value not only through the direct activities of banks, but also by encouraging banks to
 partner with mission lender organizations that extend their reach and cultivate future bank customers.
  II. PROPOSED ASSET THRESHOLDS COULD WEAKEN BANKMISSION LENDER
 PARTNERSHIPS AND REDUCE ACCESS TO CAPITAL [Section IV.A - Asset Thresholds; Questions
 13]

 MLWG Recommendation: Retain the current CRA asset thresholds rather than substantially increasing the
 thresholds as proposed.

 The MLWG is concerned that the proposed increases in CRA asset thresholds (the proposal defines small
 banks as institutions with at least $1 billion up to $10 billion in assets and large banks as institutions with
 more than $10 billion in assets) could substantially reduce the number of banks subject to meaningful
 community development requirements.

 The proposal would move a significant number of banking institutions, approximately 800 banks, into lower
 CRA evaluation categories. Banks that currently have explicit community development requirements could
 consequently face fewer incentives to make community development loans and investments, provide grants,
 or engage in other community development activities. For mission lenders, the consequences would be
 significant.

 MLWG members depend on relationships with banks of different sizes and business models. A bank's CRA
 obligations are an important factor in its decision to establish or maintain relationships with mission lenders,
 including through lending facilities, investments, grants, deposits, loan participations, and other forms of
 support.

 Reducing those incentives could reduce the amount of private capital available to mission lenders and
 ultimately constrain the amount of financing available to underserved small businesses.

 The agencies should carefully consider the downstream effects of changes to CRA asset thresholds on
 organizations that depend on bank partnerships to reach underserved communities.

III. PRESERVE CRA SUPPORT FOR BANKMISSION LENDER PARTNERSHIPS AND SMALL-
 BUSINESS LENDING [Sections IV.B and IV.C -- Retail Lending Product Lines and Community
 Development Activities]

 The MLWG is particularly concerned about the interaction between the proposed treatment of retail lending
 and community development activities.

 Small-business lending is central to economic opportunity and development in underserved communities. Yet
 the small businesses that mission lenders serve frequently require financing that is smaller, more flexible, or
 more relationship-intensive than conventional lending models provide.

 MLWG Recommendations: CRA should continue to create meaningful incentives for banks to support this
 lending ecosystem.
  The agencies should also recognize that supporting a mission lender can enable a bank to reach substantially
 more underserved small businesses than the bank might otherwise reach directly.

 CRA consideration should extend to appropriate bank activities that support mission lenders, including:
 Lending facilities and lines of credit;
 Loan participations;
 Investments;
 Deposits;
 Operating and capacity-building grants;
 Referrals and strategic partnerships;
 Technical assistance; and
 Other forms of capital or support that expand the ability of mission lenders to provide responsible
 small-business financing.

 The agencies should ensure that ordinary-course lending to larger or lower-risk borrowers does not
 inadvertently substitute for specialized lending and partnerships that are more dependent on CRA incentives.

IV. CRA DATA AND TRANSPARENCY MUST BE PRESERVED
 Section IV.G -- Data Collection, Reporting, and Disclosure

 MLWG Recommendation: Preserve robust CRA data collection and public transparency sufficient to
 evaluate bank performance and identify unmet credit needs.

 The MLWG is concerned that the proposed changes could substantially reduce the number of institutions
 subject to CRA data collection and reporting requirements. Reliable data is essential for understanding
 whether capital is reaching underserved communities and small businesses.

 Mission lenders use data to identify credit gaps with all types of small businesses, business locoation,
 understand market conditions, evaluate potential bank partnerships, and determine where additional capital is
 needed.

 Reduced data availability would make it more difficult for communities, policymakers, regulators, mission
 lenders, and financial institutions to understand where credit is flowing and where gaps remain.

V. GEOGRAPHIC FLEXIBILITY SHOULD EXPAND ACCESS TO CRA CAPITAL
 Section IV.E -- Community Development Activities Outside Assessment Areas; Question 34

 MLWG Recommendation: The MLWG supports appropriate geographic flexibility that enables CRA-
 motivated capital to reach communities with significant unmet credit needs, including rural communities,
 underserved markets, and areas with limited bank presence.

 Mission lenders frequently operate across geographic areas that extend beyond traditional bank assessment
 areas. However, geographic flexibility should supplement, not replace, meaningful community development
 activity within a bank's own assessment areas.
  The CRA framework should encourage banks to partner with mission lenders when those partnerships
 provide an effective means of reaching communities where conventional financial services are limited.

 VI. SUPPORT CLARITY AND CERTAINTY FOR COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT ACTIVITIES
 [Section IV.E -- Illustrative List and Confirmation of Eligibility; Questions 3233]

 MLWG Recommendation: MLWG supports establishing a publicly available, non-exhaustive illustrative
 list of eligible community development activities and a formal process for advance confirmation of CRA
 eligibility.

 Greater certainty would help banks and mission lenders develop partnerships and structure transactions with
 confidence that qualifying activities will receive appropriate CRA consideration.

 We encourage the agencies to establish consistent interagency standards and a transparent process for
 eligibility determinations.

 VII. RECOGNIZE THE LONG-TERM NATURE OF COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT FINANCE
 [Section IV.C -- Community Development Loans; Question 8]

 MLWG Recommendation: The MLWG strongly supports CRA consideration for qualifying community
 development loans that remain outstanding from prior evaluation periods. Mission lenders frequently
 provide patient, long-term financing to underserved small businesses and communities. CRA should
 encourage banks to structure financing around the needs of small business borrowers and communities rather
 than examination cycles.

VIII. CONCLUSION

 The Mission Lenders Working Group believes that effective CRA modernization should strengthen the
 partnerships that already exist among banks, mission lenders, and underserved communities. The CRA
 remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable in meeting the credit needs of the
 communities they serve. The agencies should ensure that any changes to the CRA framework preserve this
 accountability and remain consistent with the statute's core purpose of encouraging financial institutions to
 help meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods
 and underserved small businesses. Modernization should result in more responsible capital reaching
 communities with unmet credit needs, not fewer incentives for banks to engage with the mission lenders and
 small businesses that serve those communities.

 These partnerships produce benefits throughout the financial system.

 Banks provide mission lenders with capital and resources that can be leveraged to reach underserved
 borrowers. Mission lenders provide relationship-based financing, technical assistance, and business
 development support that helps entrepreneurs establish stronger businesses and, in many cases, become
 future customers of conventional financial institutions.
 For these reasons, MLWG urges the OCC and FDIC to ensure that CRA modernization does not
unintentionally weaken the incentives supporting this ecosystem.

Specifically, we urge the agencies to:
 Retain the current CRA asset thresholds;
 Preserve meaningful CRA incentives for banks to partner with mission lenders;
 Maintain meaningful CRA consideration for small-business lending that reaches underserved
 businesses and communities;
 Preserve CRA eligibility for flexible operating and capacity-building grants;
 Maintain meaningful community development expectations for intermediate banks;
 Preserve robust CRA data collection and transparency;
 Allow appropriate geographic flexibility to reach underserved small businesses and communities
 while maintaining meaningful assessment-area performance; and
 Recognize the critical role that mission lenders play in expanding the reach of the banking system
 and cultivating future bank customers.

Changes that reduce meaningful incentives for banks to invest in, lend to, or partner with mission lenders
could weaken the CRA's ability to fulfill that purpose.

Thank you for considering the perspective of the Mission Lenders Working Group and the thousands of
small businesses and underserved communities served by our members.

Sincerely,

Sandy Headley

Sandy Headley, Vice President of Access to Capital for Entrepreneurs, Inc. (ACE)
Access to Capital for Entrepreneurs, Inc.
MISSION LENDERS WORKING GROUP | Vice President

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations -- Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
 Docket ID OCC20260694 | RIN 1557AF57 (OCC) | RIN 3064AG31 (FDIC)

Dear FDIC Representatives:

Northeast Bank appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed amendments to the
regulations that implement the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) published on August 12, 2026. We
support efforts to modernize the CRA framework, reduce unnecessary regulatory burden, and provide
greater clarity and consistency in CRA examinations. At the same time, we believe the regulations must
continue to recognize and encourage the full range of activities through which community banks meet
the credit needs of their communities.

Northeast Bank is a locally owned, business-focused community bank headquartered in Minneapolis,
Minnesota, with approximately $850 million in assets. Since our founding in 1947, we have focused on
building relationships with local businesses, supporting entrepreneurs, and strengthening the
communities we serve. We are particularly proud of our record of nine consecutive Outstanding CRA
evaluations since 1997, reflecting our longstanding commitment to community reinvestment and
supported in part by our performance under the community development test applicable to
intermediate small banks today.

We offer the following comments and recommendations based on our experience serving small
businesses and participating in community development activities and as an institution that would be
directly impacted by the proposed asset-size threshold.

1. Support for Increasing the Small Bank Asset Threshold

As a state-chartered, non-member bank that is supervised by the FDIC, under the proposal Northeast
Bank would be classified as a "Small Bank" institution. Northeast Bank supports the proposal to increase
the Small Bank asset threshold to $1 billion. We believe this adjustment appropriately recognizes the
significant differences in resources, operating models, and compliance capabilities between community
banks and larger financial institutions.
 A higher threshold would reduce unnecessary regulatory complexity for community banks while
preserving their obligation to meet the credit needs of their assessment areas. For relationship-focused
banks such as Northeast Bank, a streamlined evaluation framework would allow more resources to be
devoted to lending, customer service, and community development.

We encourage the agencies to adopt the proposed $1 billion threshold and provide for periodic inflation
adjustments based on CPI-W, as proposed, so that the threshold remains meaningful over time.

2. Modernize the Small-Business Borrower Revenue Threshold (__ .22(b)(3)(ii);
Questions 24, 26, and 27)

We recommend that the agencies increase the longstanding $1 million annual gross revenue benchmark
for evaluating lending to smaller revenue businesses to $5 million. The existing $1 million benchmark no
longer adequately reflects the operating realities of many small businesses. Inflation, rising labor and
occupancy costs, and higher prices for goods and services have substantially increased the revenue
necessary to sustain a business, without necessarily changing its character as a small, locally owned
entity.

Although loans to businesses with revenues above $1 million may still qualify for consideration under
the CRA Lending Test, the borrower-revenue benchmark influences how lending to smaller businesses is
evaluated. Consequently, meaningful lending to local businesses may not receive appropriate
recognition within the borrower-distribution analysis.

We encourage the agencies to modernize this benchmark, provide for periodic inflation adjustments,
and ensure that the evaluation framework appropriately recognizes SBA lending and other financing
that expands access to capital for small businesses.

3. Preserve Voluntary Consideration of Community Development Activities for
Small Banks (__.21(b)(3) and (b)(7); __.26(a)(1) and (d); and Questions 14
17)

Northeast Bank supports a streamlined CRA examination process for Small Banks. However, pursuant to
Appendix A of the proposed rule, a Small Bank's community development activities are considered
towards an Outstanding rating only if a bank meets each component of the lending test standards and
exceeds "some or all" of those standards. We are concerned that placing substantially greater emphasis
on the Lending Test, without an effective mechanism for recognizing exceptional community
development performance, could unintentionally discourage activities that provide significant benefits
 to local communities. The proposal does not provide an effective mechanism for recognizing
community development performance of Small Banks.

By way of example, our bank has consistently demonstrated a strong commitment to community
reinvestment through lending, community development investments, charitable contributions, financial
education, and the provision of technical assistance and financial expertise to community organizations.

We strongly believe that the proposed Small Bank framework should preserve a meaningful path for
banks to demonstrate exceptional performance through these activities.

Importantly, we are not recommending a mandatory Community Development Test for all Small
Banks. We recognize that such a requirement could impose unnecessary burdens on institutions that do
not have the resources or business models to support extensive community development programs.

Instead, we recommend that Small Banks be permitted to voluntarily submit supplemental community
development and qualitative performance information for examiner consideration, particularly when
seeking an Outstanding rating.

We propose that the final rule or accompanying examination guidance include language substantially as
follows:

 A bank may voluntarily submit supplemental qualitative, community
 development, or contextual information that it believes demonstrates its
 responsiveness to community credit needs, even when collection or reporting of
 that information is not otherwise required. Examiners will consider relevant
 information voluntarily submitted by the bank when evaluating CRA
 performance and determining whether the institution's overall performance
 warrants an Outstanding rating.

This approach would preserve the benefits of simplified Small Bank examinations while recognizing and
encouraging exceptional community engagement.

We also support continued consideration of qualitative factors such as responsiveness, flexibility,
complexity, innovation, and community impact. These factors are particularly important when
evaluating activities that address unmet credit needs or serve communities that have historically faced
barriers to accessing financial services.

In sum, Northeast Bank does not object to reclassification as a Small Bank for CRA purposes but asks
that the final rule preserve the ability of Small Banks to receive recognition for community development
activities alongside its performance under the lending test.
 4. Preserve and Strengthen CRA Recognition for CDFI Partnerships (Questions 26
and 29)

Northeast Bank strongly supports continued and meaningful CRA consideration for banks' partnerships
with Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs).

We work with several CDFIs serving our community through a variety of arrangements, including
providing low-interest loans, supporting grants through the Rasmussen Family Northeast Bank
Foundation, and purchasing participations in loans originated by CDFIs. These participations help
replenish CDFIs' lending capacity, enabling them to extend financing to additional entrepreneurs and
businesses.

CDFIs play a critical role in expanding access to affordable capital for entrepreneurs and communities
that have historically faced barriers to traditional financing. Equally important, they combine financing
with trusted relationships, business guidance, and technical assistance that help entrepreneurs start,
stabilize, and grow sustainable businesses.

We appreciate the agencies' recognition of CDFIs in the proposed economic development framework
and encourage them to explicitly preserve CRA consideration for qualifying loans to CDFIs, loan
participations, grants, and related technical assistance. We note that the listed example of "Community
Development Financial Institution" is limited to those "that finances small businesses or small farms"
and would encourage the agencies to confirm and include CDFIs engaged in affordable housing and
other qualifying community development activity to receive comparable consideration.

We also encourage the agencies to recognize that financing a CDFI's lending capacity and supporting its
essential programs can directly advance community development, even when the benefit is delivered
through an intermediary rather than a single identifiable project. Qualifying working-capital financing
that helps entrepreneurs sustain and stabilize their businesses should also receive appropriate
consideration.

The CRA framework should encourage, rather than discourage, partnerships that combine bank capital
with CDFI expertise to expand economic opportunity and address unmet community credit needs. We
urge the agencies to avoid overly restrictive eligibility interpretations or documentation requirements
that could undermine these valuable partnerships.

5. Retain CRA Consideration for Grants and Donations (Questions 9 and 10)

Northeast Bank strongly opposes eliminating grants and donations from CRA consideration, as
contemplated in Question 10. Grants and donations are essential components of community
 reinvestment, particularly when they support nonprofit organizations, CDFIs, financial education, and
community development initiatives that cannot be sustained through lending alone.

Through the Rasmussen Family Northeast Bank Foundation, which receives most of its funding from
Northeast Bank, we support organizations that provide meaningful services to individuals,
entrepreneurs, and communities with limited access to traditional financial resources. Northeast Bank
maintains records identifying the source of funding for each grant and evaluates whether the grant
supports a qualifying CRA community development purpose, including documenting the applicable
category. Only qualifying grants attributable to bank-provided funds are included in our CRA
submissions.

These contributions may be relatively modest in dollar amount but can have substantial community
impact. We support reasonable accountability and documentation standards but caution against
requirements that unnecessarily restrict recognition of legitimate program administration,
organizational capacity, or other costs necessary to deliver effective community development services.

We recommend that the agencies retain grants and donations as qualifying community development
activities and ensure that the final framework recognizes their value without imposing disproportionate
compliance burdens.

6. Promote a Consistent CRA Regulatory Framework Across All Three Federal
Banking Agencies

Northeast Bank strongly encourages the OCC, FDIC, and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve
System to work towards a consistent and coordinated CRA regulatory framework.

We recognize that the current proposal has been issued by the OCC and FDIC. However, we believe that
consistent CRA regulations, examination procedures, and supervisory expectations across all three
federal banking agencies are essential to ensuring fair and predictable CRA evaluations.

The CRA establishes a common obligation for insured depository institutions to help meet the credit
needs of the communities they serve. Banks should therefore be evaluated under substantially
equivalent standards regardless of their primary federal regulator. Differences in CRA requirements or
interpretations among the agencies could create unnecessary regulatory complexity, increase
compliance costs, and result in inconsistent treatment of otherwise similar institutions and activities.

For community banks with limited compliance resources, regulatory consistency is particularly
important. A uniform framework would allow banks to focus more of their resources on lending,
community development, and serving their customers rather than navigating differing regulatory
expectations.
 We encourage the OCC and FDIC to coordinate closely with the Federal Reserve in finalizing these
regulations and to pursue consistent definitions, performance standards, examination procedures, and
guidance. Final regulations should provide a single, appropriately tailored CRA framework
administered consistently by all three federal banking agencies - even if it takes longer to develop.
A unified approach would promote regulatory clarity, fairness, and efficiency while preserving the CRA's
fundamental purpose of encouraging banks to meet the credit needs of their communities.

Conclusion

Northeast Bank supports a CRA regulatory framework that is clear, appropriately tailored to bank size
and business model, and focused on meaningful outcomes for the communities that banks serve.

We respectfully encourage the agencies to adopt the proposed $1 billion Small Bank threshold;
modernize the $1 million small-business borrower-revenue benchmark; preserve voluntary submission
of community development and qualitative performance information for Small Banks and require
consideration of such information when provided; explicitly recognize qualifying CDFI partnerships;
retain grants and donations as eligible community development activities; and work toward a consistent
CRA regulatory framework across the OCC, FDIC, and Federal Reserve. We support the proposed
threshold increase if the final rule preserves a meaningful path for Small Banks to receive recognition for
exceptional community development performance.

We believe these recommendations would help preserve the CRA's effectiveness while reducing
unnecessary regulatory burden and recognizing the diverse ways community banks contribute to
economic opportunity and community development.

We appreciate the agencies' consideration of these comments.

Respectfully submitted,

Eva B. Rasmussen
Chief Strategy Officer / CRA Committee Chair / Member, Board of Directors
Northeast Bank
Minneapolis, Minnesota

To the Comptroller of the Currency and the Board of Directors of the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation:

Dear Comptroller and FDIC Leadership:

On behalf of Green+, I respectfully submit this comment letter opposing
significant elements of the proposed revisions to the Community Reinvestment
Act (CRA) regulations. Green+ urges the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) to
reconsider provisions that would weaken accountability for meeting
community credit needs, diminish transparency, and undermine investment in
affordable housing, small businesses, and economically distressed
communities. Green+ is a non-profit community development corporation
(CDC) working to expand economic opportunity and improve the quality of life

150 E. 1st Street Lancaster, TX 75146
 for low- and moderate-income Texans. Our organization seeks to develop
affordable housing, revitalize neighborhoods, and provide essential
community services. We work primarily in urban, economically distressed
neighborhoods and we understand firsthand that community development
depends on a functioning partnership among banks, nonprofit organizations,
public agencies, and mission-driven financial institutions. The CRA is a
foundational mechanism for encouraging banks to participate in these
partnerships and help meet the credit needs of the communities they serve.
Although we support reasonable efforts to simplify regulations and provide
greater clarity to financial institutions, the proposed rulemaking is not
reasonable, and regulatory efficiency must not come at the expense of
meaningful community investment and public accountability.

I. The CRA Must Continue to Promote Meaningful Investment in Affordable
Housing and Community Development

Affordable housing remains a critical need across Texas. CDCs develop and
preserve affordable rental housing, support homeownership, rehabilitate
deteriorating properties, and revitalize neighborhoods where private capital
alone frequently fails to meet community needs. These activities often depend
on complex financing structures that combine bank loans, grants, philanthropic
resources, public funding, and specialized financing from Community
Development Financial Institutions (CDFI's). The CRA helps encourage banks
to participate in these transactions by recognizing the value of lending,
investments, and services that support community development. Weakening
that incentive could make it more difficult for nonprofit developers to assemble
viable financing packages, increase the cost of affordable housing production,
and limit the ability of communities to preserve existing affordable units.
Green+ is particularly concerned that changes intended to narrow or redirect
qualifying community development activities could create uncertainty for
banks and their nonprofit partners. Banks need clear, predictable rules that
recognize the full range of legitimate community development activities,
including affordable housing development and preservation, rehabilitation of

 2
 distressed neighborhoods, and financing for community facilities serving
low-income populations. We urge the agencies to preserve broad, practical
eligibility for activities that demonstrably benefit low- and moderate-income
communities. Any qualifying-activity framework should be transparent,
sufficiently flexible to accommodate local needs, and responsive to the
realities of financing affordable housing and community development projects.

II. Excluding Deposit Services Would Overlook an Important Dimension of
Community Reinvestment

The proposed rule would narrow the range of retail banking services
considered in CRA evaluations by excluding deposit services. Green+ opposes
this approach. Access to safe, affordable banking is an important component
of economic stability. Low income households and small businesses need
accessible deposit accounts to receive income, save for emergencies, manage
expenses, and establish financial relationships that can support future
borrowing. In communities where traditional banking access is limited, the
availability and affordability of deposit services can be particularly important.
Although deposit services are not a substitute for responsible lending, they
are an essential part of a bank's relationship with its community. Removing
them from consideration risks overlooking whether financial institutions are
providing meaningful access to basic banking services in the neighborhoods
they serve. Green+ urges the agencies to retain a comprehensive assessment
of retail banking services, including deposit access, affordability, accessibility,
and responsiveness to the needs of low- and moderate-income communities.
CRA evaluations should encourage banks to expand responsible banking
relationships, not limit the definition of community service to a narrower set of
activities.

III. Preserve Transparency and Accountability Through Meaningful Data
Collection

 3
 Green+ is concerned about the proposal to exempt banks with $10 billion or
less in assets from certain CRA data collection, maintenance, and reporting
requirements. We recognize that smaller institutions have fewer resources to
devote to compliance. However, reducing reporting requirements without
adequate safeguards could make it harder for regulators and the public to
determine whether community credit needs are being met. Green+ does not
want to see any changes to the current bank asset-size classifications. Reliable
data helps identify underserved neighborhoods, evaluate lending patterns,
measure access to credit, and determine whether community development
investments are reaching the people and places with the greatest need. For
nonprofit housing developers and CDFIs, transparent information about
lending and investment patterns can also support effective partnerships with
financial institutions. Texas includes large metropolitan areas alongside rural
communities, smaller cities, and regions experiencing persistent economic
challenges. Aggregate information can obscure significant differences in
access to capital within these areas. Without appropriate data, gaps in
mortgage lending, small-business financing, and community development
investment may be more difficult to identify and address.

IV. Protect the Role of CDFIs and Community-Based Lending Partnerships

CDFIs are essential partners in expanding access to capital for small
businesses, entrepreneurs and communities that are underserved by
conventional financial institutions. CDFI's frequently collaborate with banks to
structure financing, extend credit to borrowers with limited collateral or credit
histories, and support projects that may not proceed through conventional
underwriting alone. CRA incentives can encourage banks to provide loans,
investments, and other support that enable these partnerships to operate
effectively. The agencies should ensure that the regulations recognize the
community development value of financing delivered through qualified CDFIs
and other mission-driven intermediaries. The proposed rules do not
accomplish this. Community development lending should not be evaluated so

 4
 narrowly that it discourages banks from partnering with organizations that
possess specialized expertise and established relationships with underserved
borrowers. The final rule should clearly recognize qualifying loans,
investments, and other eligible support that help CDFIs finance affordable
housing, small businesses, and community revitalization. It should also
preserve a workable process for confirming eligibility so that banks can make
informed commitments without unnecessary uncertainty or delay.

V. Ensure Community Development Grants Reach Communities Without
Undermining Effective Organizations

Green+ supports appropriate safeguards to ensure that community
development grants benefit their intended recipients and produce meaningful
community outcomes. However, rules governing grants and donations should
recognize that effective nonprofit organizations require qualified staff, sound
financial management, compliance systems, and other reasonable operating
resources to deliver those outcomes. Restrictions that fail to distinguish
between excessive administrative costs and necessary organizational capacity
will weaken the organizations responsible for delivering affordable housing,
small-business financing, and essential services. Smaller community-based
organizations will be especially vulnerable to rules that impose rigid
requirements without accounting for differences in organizational size,
mission, and operating model. We encourage the agencies to adopt clear,
practical standards that prevent misuse of grant funding while recognizing
reasonable administrative and operational expenses necessary to achieve
community development objectives. The focus should remain on measurable
community benefits, sound stewardship, and effective delivery of services to
underserved populations.

VI. Recommendations and Conclusion

Green+ respectfully urges the OCC and FDIC to revise the proposed rule to:

 5
 1. Preserve strong CRA accountability by ensuring that regulatory simplification
does not diminish banks' responsibility to meet the credit needs of their entire
communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.

2. Retain consideration of deposit services as part of a comprehensive
evaluation of access to affordable, responsible retail banking.

3. Maintain meaningful data transparency through aproportionate reporting
requirements and appropriate safeguards that allow regulators and the public
to identify unmet credit needs and disparities in access to capital.

4. Protect community development financing partnerships by recognizing
qualifying activities conducted through CDFIs, CDCs, and other mission-driven
organizations that serve low-income communities and small businesses.

5. Support effective nonprofit capacity by ensuring that grant and donation
standards distinguish necessary operating expenses from improper diversion
of funds.

6. Provide clear and inclusive qualifying-activity standards that recognize the
diversity of affordable housing, community revitalization, and economic
development needs across Texas.

The Community Reinvestment Act is more than a regulatory framework. It is an
important public policy tool for encouraging the financial resources of the
banking system to help meet community needs. For Texas communities facing
housing shortages, limited access to small business capital, and persistent
economic disparities, a strong and effective CRA remains essential. Green+
urges the OCC and FDIC to reconsider the proposed changes identified in this
letter and adopt a final rule that preserves meaningful incentives for
community investment, supports effective partnerships between banks and
community-based organizations, and maintains transparency and

 6
 accountability for the communities the CRA was enacted to serve. Thank you
for considering our comments and for the opportunity to represent the
perspectives of Texas's community development sector.
Sincerely,
Karen Brooks-Crosby
Chief Operating Officer

Lancaster, TX 75146

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the joint notice of proposed rulemaking (NPR) to amend
