successful public policy.

CRA requires regulators to assess a bank's record of meeting the credit needs of its entire community,
including low- and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods and consumers, consistent with the bank's safe
and sound operation. Public CRA ratings provide banks with an incentive to achieve certain goals
described in the framework and criteria established by the agencies. CRA has opened access to credit and

 1
 services for people, small businesses, farms, and community development projects that may not be served
by regulated banks in its absence. CRA incentivized more than $430 billion in loans and investments in
LMI communities in 2024 alone1.

Our letter focuses on the changes that we believe will most directly affect the work of HPN members: bank
asset thresholds, intermediate bank ratings, community development definitions, and community
development grants. We encourage the agencies to consider this feedback and draft a final rule that
preserves efforts to increase the supply of affordable housing for LMI households and maintains a system
that incentivizes banks to invest in LMI communities.

Bank Asset Thresholds

HPN is concerned that the changes to the asset thresholds proposed in Section IV.A of the NPR will
significantly decrease investment in affordable housing at a time when housing affordability is a national
issue. Under the proposed thresholds, 79.8 percent2 of banks would have no community development
obligation while 416 banks would no longer be subject to the investment test, a critical driver of investment
in affordable housing.

Changes to the bank asset thresholds may be most acutely felt in rural or smaller markets where regional
and community banks are the primary financial institutions, making the proposed changes
disproportionately harmful in non-urban communities. When there are fewer sources of capital, changes in
community development investment for certain types of banks could have an outsized impact. A survey
conducted by the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition showed that one-third of Low-Income Housing
Credit (Housing Credit) investment in rural areas comes from banks under the $10 billion asset threshold.

This proposal could undermine recent congressional action to expand the Housing Credit, make the New
Markets Tax Credit permanent, and increase the Public Welfare Investment cap, allowing banks to invest
more in community development. Both the New Markets Tax Credit and Housing Credit are important
development tax credits with track records of success creating affordable housing and investing in LMI
communities while supporting job growth. Banks that are currently subject to CRA account for at least 71

1 Center for Affordable Housing Lending, Incen8ve to Impact (July 2026).
2 hEps://www.federalregister.gov/d/2026-16454/p-171

 2
 percent of equity investments in the Housing Credit, the primary federal program used to develop
affordable multifamily rental housing in the United States. Of those banks, those with assets under $10
billion invested approximately $2 billion in Housing Credit equity over a five-year period. Higher demand for
the Housing Credit through CRA-motivated investment results in stronger equity pricing which in turn
reduces the amount of other financing needed to complete developments.

Intermediate Bank Ratings

The agencies' proposed changes to the treatment of community development (CD) test ratings for
intermediate banks in Section IV.B. would significantly weaken incentives for community development
investment. Under the proposal, an intermediate bank could receive an overall Satisfactory CRA rating
based solely on achieving a Satisfactory or higher lending test rating, regardless of its performance on the
CD test. By removing any minimum community development standard, the proposal effectively elevates
lending performance above all other CRA obligations and diminishes the importance of activities that are
critical to meeting community needs. As a result, intermediate banks may have less reason to make grants,
support CDFIs, or provide community development equity investments through tools such as the Housing
Credit, since a strong lending score could offset weak CD performance. The impact of this change would
be compounded by the proposed increase in the asset threshold for intermediate banks, which would move
more banks into a category with lower community development expectations. Together, these changes
could lead to a greater reduction in meaningful investment in underserved communities.

HPN recommends retaining the current rating structure, which requires intermediate banks to receive a
Satisfactory rating on both the lending and CD tests to receive an overall Satisfactory rating.

Community Development Definitions

Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing

HPN is pleased to see that the proposed definition of affordable housing expressly includes naturally
occurring affordable housing (NOAH) and is determined based on rent levels, not individual income. Given
that 75 percent of low-cost housing in the United States is NOAH, it is important that it is included in the

 3
 definition of unsubsidized affordable housing3. The proposal outlined in the NPR is also in line with the
definition of "low income" by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and other federal
programs, contributing to greater consistency.

HPN supports the NPR's inclusion of NOAH with rents affordable to LMI individuals being set at 30 percent
of 80 percent AMI.

The NPR would also consider NOAH housing in high-cost areas for CRA credit when rents are affordable
to middle-income individuals. While HPN recognizes that housing supply is needed across the income
spectrum, we are concerned that the inclusion of middle-income individuals with no requirements to also
meet the needs of LMI individuals in high-cost areas could detract from the goals of CRA to primarily invest
in LMI communities. Investing in homes for higher income households may be more attractive to banks
because of the potential rate of return and would disincentivize investment in LMI communities.

Given the intent of CRA, HPN recommends maintaining a focus on LMI communities and households in
the final rule to support hard-working Americans across the country.

Inclusion of Nonprofit Partnerships

The agencies ask if it is sufficiently clear that affordable housing activities in partnership with nonprofit
organizations are included in the meaning of affordable housing. While we appreciate the agencies stating
their intent that nonprofit organizations are implied in the definition, it would be helpful if the final rule
included explicit examples of allowable affordable housing activities to provide clarity to regulated banks
and their partners. Such a list could include examples such as investment in housing that is financed,
preserved, or developed in partnership with a nonprofit organization or developments with deed or rental
restrictions.

Community Development Grants

In Section IV.C the agencies propose narrowing the definition of CD grants to those that "will be directly
used by the recipient for a program, project, or initiative with a primary purpose of community development;

3 Preserva8on Compact, NOAH Preserva8on and Research

 4
 benefits the bank's assessment area(s); and for a large bank, is provided to a recipient whose indirect
costs for administering the grant or donation do not exceed 15 percent."4

HPN opposes these limiting changes because grants can serve a wide array of important purposes for
nonprofits and CDFIs in delivering investment and services into communities. Limiting the use of funds in
this manner takes away the flexibility that banks and their CD partners need to appropriately address
unique situations. Our members use operating grants to provide technical assistance to housing projects
and owners facing financial distress, support resident programming such as financial wellness and child
savings programs, strengthen organizational data tools and infrastructure to scale their work, and promote
homeownership opportunities. These uses support our members' ability to preserve housing supply and
access over the long-term, meet ongoing and new community needs, determine scale and depth of
programming, and support resident stability.

A 15 percent cap on administrative costs should not be used as a proxy to determine the impact a grant
will have on a community and arbitrarily limits organizations. Such a restriction could disproportionately
impact small and emerging CDFIs and nonprofit organizations that serve rural communities and other
areas with limited capital through burdensome reporting and restricted operating support. It is important to
preserve flexibility in grant administration costs to account for the variability of organizational size, scope,
and geography.

We recommend retaining the current framework for general operating and capacity-building grants under
the 1995 rule, which has a strong track record of effectiveness. If the agencies pursue the 15 percent cap,
we recommend including a clear definition of administrative costs in the final rule. This will ensure that
programmatic costs are not counted against the cap and provides organizations and banks with more
clarity on what is subject to the proposed limitation on expenses.

Conclusion

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the NPR. To preserve consistency in CRA regulation and
protect the incentives that support affordable housing and community development investment, HPN

to discuss any points in this letter further, please contact us at policy@housingpartnership.net.

loans--thereby developing a pipeline of potential future bank customers. CDFIs, in return,
 receive low-cost capital that enables them to take on the greater financial risks of lending to

Raised Asset Thresholds Jeopardize Community Development Finance:

Section IV.A, "Asset Thresholds"; Questions 13

The proposed changes to the CRA define small banks as those with less than $1 billion in assets,

institutions with more than $10 billion. About 800 banks that currently face a separate

In Pennsylvania, where Bridgeway is headquartered and makes the majority of its loans, it is
estimated that 25 out of 110 banks, representing 23% of all the banks in the state, would no

Bridgeway is concerned not only about the potential loss of individual bank relationships, but
also about the broader effect of reducing the number of institutions with meaningful community
development incentives. Approximately 70% of Bridgeway's external funding comes from
traditional financial institutions in the form of low-cost debt. If fewer banks are incentivized to
provide community development capital, CDFIs may increasingly compete for a smaller pool of
CRA-motivated bank funding. Even where Bridgeway's existing banking relationships remain

Significance of CRA data and transparency: Section IV.G, "Data Collection, Reporting,

 the proposal would exacerbate the coverage of data, making it difficult to understand the flow

Support for Provisions That Could Strengthen Community Development
Finance

 Consider prior-period community development loans: Section IV.C, "CD Loans";

to invest, lend, and serve low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities.

Ceres is a nonprofit advocacy organization with over 35 years of experience working to accelerate
the transition to a cleaner, more just, and resilient economy. Our Investor Network, Company

with whom we work on a range of sustainability-related and policy-related issues. The Ceres
Accelerator for Sustainable Capital Markets aims to transform the practices and policies that
govern capital markets by engaging federal and state regulators, financial institutions, investors,
and corporate boards to address weather-driven risk as a systemic financial risk. The comments
provided herein represent only the opinions of Ceres, and do not necessarily infer endorsement by
each member of our Investor, Company, or Policy Networks.

Ceres Headquarters: 99 Chauncy Street, Boston, MA 02111 ceres.org
California Office: 369 Pine Street, Suite 620, San Francisco, CA 94104
 I. INTRODUCTION

As a longstanding avenue for financial access and wealth-building opportunities, the CRA statute
serves an important purpose that should be strengthened to support communities not weakened
to relieve banks. Ceres has encouraged and supported previous efforts to update CRA rules to
ensure it continues to effectively function within the realities of modern banking practices and the
complex landscape driving reinvestment needs from underserved LMI communities. However,
this proposal falls short of reforming the CRA rules in line with the original purpose of the 1977
statute enacted by Congress to redress the nation's long and painful track record of lending
discrimination and disinvestment. As a crucial driver for banks to provide capital to CRA-eligible
activities including affordable housing, small business financing, and community investments,
rolling back CRA obligations could result in banks of all sizes scaling back CRA coverage and
activity in the very underserved communities meant to be served by the statute. Furthermore, this
proposal risks undermining equitable financial access and resources at a time when people,
communities, and small businesses are already grappling with challenges from housing
affordability, rising inflation rates, and less recognized financial losses driven by frequent and
severe natural disasters and extreme weather events. To prevent significant declines in much
needed CRA-eligible community development activities nationwide, we request that the OCC and
FDIC rescind this current proposal until a thorough analysis of its impacts on LMI communities is
prepared and released for a new public comment.

II. CERES' BACKGROUND AND ENGAGEMENT ON CRA

Federal CRA Engagement

Ceres has demonstrated a consistent track record advocating for timely, critical, and necessary
updates to federal CRA rules. In February 2021, we submitted comments to the Federal Reserve
Board of Governors' (the Fed) advanced noticed of proposed rulemaking on updating the CRA
rules and recommended the explicit inclusion of CRA-eligibility for resiliency activities to address
extreme weather challenges disproportionately impacting LMI communities. This was followed
by our October 2021 comments supporting the OCC's proposal to rescind its 2020 CRA rules in
favor of joint interagency rules developed by the three CRA federal banking regulators, the Fed,
OCC, and the FDIC, to offer consistency and clarity for financial institutions with CRA
obligations. In response to the 2022 interagency notice of proposed rulemaking to update CRA
rules, Ceres delivered comments supporting the proposed inclusion of crucial resiliency provisions
to support underserved vulnerable communities in preparing for and adapting to natural disasters
and extreme weather risks.

We supported the updated 2023 CRA final rules as a positive step forward in addressing common-
sense and beneficial updates poised to strengthen CRA overall for LMI communities and the
financial institutions that serve them. In response to the roll-out of the 2023 final CRA rules, we
hosted a private convening in January 2024 which brought together over a dozen US regional
banks and GSIBs to review and discuss the implications of the "disaster preparedness and weather
resiliency" category under community development. As a follow up to the convening and in
alignment with the critical updates in the 2023 final CRA rules, we developed and distributed a

California Office: 369 Pine Street, Suite 620, San Francisco, CA 94104
 resource guide highlighting the intersection of resiliency and CRA while elevating the opportunity
to support CRA-eligible community infrastructure under the new community development
"disaster preparedness and weather resiliency" category.

Most recently, we submitted comments strongly opposing the agencies' proposed rescission of the
2023 final interagency CRA rules in August 2025. By recodifying the 1995 CRA regulations, the

preparedness and weather resiliency activities were curtailed at a time when geographically
vulnerable LMI communities need it most. We also commented on the review of the Community

Economic Growth and Regulatory Paperwork Reduction Act (EGRPRA) in October 2025. While
recognizing the agencies' procedural mandate to reduce paperwork and improve efficiency under
the routine EGRPRA review process, we emphasized our position then that less regulation does
not necessarily mean better regulation, which appears apt repeating given the agencies current
stated effort "to reduce unnecessary burden", without comprehensively grappling with the scale
and impact that less resources will have on LMI communities.

State-level CRA Engagement

We have also engaged in efforts to support CRA modernization and updates on state-level CRA
rules. In April 2025, Ceres submitted a comment letter to the New York Department of Financial
Services' (NY DFS) proposal to extend coverage of New York's state CRA to nonbank mortgage
lenders, including the expectations for how they will be evaluated at meeting the credit needs of
the communities where they operate. With an increased number of non-bank mortgage lenders in
the New York marketplace and disparities in mortgage access persisting for New Yorkers, the rule
sought to fill a long-standing gap. By expanding coverage of New York's state CRA rules to
mortgage companies, NY DFS is helping to unlock critical access to wealth-building home loans,
aligned with the safety and soundness principles embedded in the CRA rules, while holding
mortgage companies accountable for their lending practices at meeting the credit needs of all New
Yorkers. This alignment is particularly important as New York's LMI and disaster-vulnerable
neighborhoods face rising insurance costs, property-value volatility, and uneven access to
mitigation finance, reinforcing the need for embedding disaster preparedness and weather-
resilience lending into CRA eligibility. As a follow-up, we submitted an additional comment letter
to NY DFS in October 2025, affirming their new updates. By continuing to strengthen its own
state CRA rules, addressing its state-specific needs, and demonstrating a steadfast commitment to
evaluating how changing market dynamics impact the way LMI communities access financial
services, NY DFS set an important example for how to evaluate and update CRA rules. While
states with their own CRA rules have shown agility and responsiveness by prioritizing updates that
represent the needs of their local markets, not every state has its own CRA rules, underscoring the
importance of the federal CRA to be updated with the unmet needs of LMI communities across
the nation as the primary focus in mind.

Coalition and Community Engagement

As part of our CRA advocacy and engagement efforts, we connect with community-based
organizations on a range of policy issues through our membership in the National Community

 3 ceres.org

Ceres Headquarters: 99 Chauncy Street, Boston, MA 02111
California Office: 369 Pine Street, Suite 620, San Francisco, CA 94104
 Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC), a network of over 700 community organizations dedicated to
advancing federal and regulatory policies that expand access to credit, strengthen community
investment, and create fair opportunities for individuals and communities to build wealth. Through
this coalition, we have supported various NCRC-led public comments related to the federal and
state CRA efforts alongside other community-based organizations.

III. ISSUES IN THE CURRENT PROPOSAL

The agencies' stated effort in this current proposal "to refocus on the statutory objective of
encouraging banks to meet the credit needs of their communities" appears counterintuitive and
unlikely based on the potential implications of the proposed changes being advanced. NCRC's
detailed analysis of the current proposal highlights several key areas that risk weakening
community-development obligations for banks nationwide. While we recognize the validity of all
the concerns raised by NCRC, we focus primarily on the following issues:

 1. Reducing community development evaluations

The proposal would substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks of various
sizes are evaluated under CRA and thereby reduce community development scrutiny and therefore
weaken the CRA's primary mechanism for holding banks accountable for serving the needs of the
entire communities in which they operate. The changes could severely reduce regulatory
expectations as shown by analysis conducted by NCRC:

 Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while banks with assets
 between $1 billion and $10 billion would be evaluated under the less demanding

 Approximately 800 banks would no longer receive a community development evaluation

 The proposal would reclassify another 417 banks by raising the intermediate bank

 exams by being evaluated based on their combined community development loans,
 investments, and services.

 As a result, only the largest 6% of banks would face separate reviews of their community
 development loans, investments and branch services or of their CRA small-business loan
 reporting requirements.

The banks that would be reclassified are not marginal participants. The Center for Affordable
Housing Lending reports that banks with $1.564 billion to $10 billion in assets made 11,880
community development loans totaling approximately $32 billion in 2024.

California Office: 369 Pine Street, Suite 620, San Francisco, CA 94104
 The reporting at stake is also substantial. According to the Federal Financial Institutions
Examination Council (FFIEC), institutions with $1.564 billion or more in assets accounted for
99.4 percent of reported small business loan origination dollars in 2024, while the 157 institutions
with $10 billion or more accounted for 70.7 percent. By our calculation from these figures, roughly
29 percent of reported small business origination dollars came from institutions with assets
between $1.564 billion and $10 billion. CRA reporters also account for 77.6 percent (by dollar
amount) of small business loans outstanding at depository institutions. Raising the large-bank
threshold would end mandatory reporting for banks in this range. We distinguish between the loss
of data, which follows directly from the proposal, and a loss of lending, which is the risk the
agencies have not analyzed but should.

Evaluations are an important mechanism for ensuring that banks stay accountable to fulfilling their
CRA obligations. Since banks provide capital through channels that generate CRA credit, by
adjusting asset thresholds in such a way, bank incentives to support CRA-eligible community
development investments may be drastically curtailed. Our concerns are grounded in the risk that
lowering evaluation standards at this proposed scale will reduce measurable progress toward
equitable access to homeownership. These reclassifications for over 800 banks and separate
investment evaluations for 400 banks may worsen the housing crisis by reducing the demand for
other tools such as the Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC) and the New Market Tax
Credits (NMTC). The CRA is often referred to as the main motivator of bank investment in LIHTC
and NMTC, with banks accounting for 85% of LIHTC investment dollars. As such, changes in
bank investments could compromise affordable housing and other development activities
supported by LIHTC and NMTC.

The agencies should also expect effects to differ by geography. A 2026 study of CRA designation
from 2012 to 2019, found statistically significant employment gains in metropolitan tracts (2.5
percentage points) and smaller gains in micropolitan tracts (0.6 percentage points), with positive
spillovers into neighboring tracts that decline with distance, but no statistically significant effect
in small-town and rural tracts, which the authors link in part to banks in those areas being
frequently exempt from the full extent of CRA exams. Combined with evidence that smaller banks
account for a disproportionate share of rural mortgage lending, this means national aggregates
could mask very different local outcomes.

Existing research also indicates that banks respond to CRA incentives, so the agencies cannot
assume that changing those incentives is behaviorally neutral. A 2026 paper on CRA enforcement
finds that the median bank increased its CRA-qualifying lending by more than 15 percent in the
year it sought merger approval, and banks at the 75th percentile by about 50 percent. The authors
characterize this as window dressing and criticize current enforcement, but the pattern shows that
banks adjust their lending when regulatory consequences are at stake. This matters because the
proposal would allow intermediate banks to receive an overall Satisfactory rating without a
Satisfactory community development rating, a change that Urban Institute notes would weaken the
overall rating that agencies weigh in merger applications.

The OCC and FDIC's proposal to alter which banks would be evaluated for CRA compliance risks
undermining how Congress intended the agencies implement the CRA. The accountability the
CRA creates has been successful at ensuring borrowers and LMI communities have access to

a reduction in community development investments and loans.

3. Overlooking clarity on CRA-eligible resilience financing opportunities

The proposal adds the following language to the new definition of community development under
the revitalization and stabilization category: "programs, projects, or initiatives that assist
individuals and communities with preparing for, adapting to, or withstanding natural disasters."
However, the 2023 final rule made "disaster preparedness and weather resiliency," its own explicit
community development category and specifically mentioned community solar projects,
promoting green space, and cooling or warming centers in LMI census tracts as examples. This
proposal mentions neither of those as examples. This risks hindering the flow of capital to
financing much needed resilience projects and offering banks an additional opportunity to earn
CRA credit.

The United States is increasingly confronting extreme weather events, such as flooding, extreme
heat, storm surges, and droughts. The frequency and cost of these events has increased significantly
since 1995. In 1995, there were 7 billion-dollar disasters costing $23.3 billion and resulting in 977
deaths. Jumping forward to 2024, there were 24-billion-dollar disasters costing $182.7 billion and
resulting in 558 deaths. These physical risks have the potential to seriously disrupt not only our
financial system but also the communities being served.

While natural disasters and extreme weather risks affect everyone, they disproportionately impact
low-income communities. Decades of systemic underinvestment and redlining have impeded
access to the most basic financial services for LMI communities. For many of the same reasons,
these communities suffer disparate environmental burdens and disproportionately live on the
frontlines of extreme weather events that are increasing in frequency and intensity. Furthermore,
physical destruction has a disproportionate impact on LMI households as they are also more likely
to live in housing more susceptible to damage, such as older homes, apartment buildings, and

against the impacts of extreme weather events, creating additional financial burden.

The updated 2023 CRA rules were important not only for driving fairness and access in LMI
communities, but also for addressing systemic physical risks. The 2023 interagency final rule
recognized the urgent need to offer CRA-eligible credit opportunities for resiliency activities for
vulnerable communities to better prepare and withstand the devastating impact that these physical
risks pose. This alignment is particularly important as frontline LMI communities confront rising
insurance costs, property-value volatility, and uneven access to mitigation finance, reinforcing the
need for a just transition that embeds weather resilience measures into CRA opportunities.
Incentivizing banks to invest in resiliency reinforces the intended purpose of the CRA while
allowing banks additional opportunities to earn CRA credit and accelerating financial stability in
vulnerable communities.

4. Undermining the affirmative obligation CRA mandates

Proposed changes to community development definitions, evaluation standards, and other
provisions could significantly shift where CRA-motivated capital flows and reduce the focus on
LMI communities, resulting in less affordable housing supply and reduced access to much needed
financial resources. Regulators should preserve a clear and meaningful focus on the LMI
communities that CRA was originally intended to serve. Releasing an updated CRA rule that fails
to strengthen the components that would allow it to more aptly fulfill the original mandate would
be a significant disservice and may result in doing more harm than good. The proposed framework
would seem to run counter to the CRA mandate and ultimately amount to decreased loans,
investments, and services to LMI communities as statutorily required.

When CRA was enacted, banks were not fulfilling their obligations to all communities. The federal
CRA law enacted by Congress in the 1970s was a response to the practice of redlining - a decade's
long practice of refusing to make loans in certain communities based on class, race, or immigrant
status of the residents who lived there. The impact of redlining continues to be felt today. Notably,
CRA was passed as part of a series of civil rights laws, including the Fair Housing Act (1968),
Equal Credit Opportunity Act (1974), and the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (1975), as part of
national pressure to address the deteriorating conditions of American cities--particularly lower-
income and minority neighborhoods.

By law, CRA establishes a "continuing and affirmative obligation" for banks to help meet "the
credit needs of its entire community . . . consistent with the safe and sound operation of the
institution." Through a continuing and affirmative obligation, the law requires regulated financial
institutions to help meet the credit needs of the local communities where they're chartered. A bank
charter is a privilege that comes with special subsidies and benefits, one of them being deposit
insurance and access to discounted loans from the Fed. Those privileges come with obligations.
When a bank takes deposits, it should be reinvesting those deposits by making loans back into the
community, including LMI residents. That reinvestment obligation is part of a bank's public
purpose. Banks are chartered by state and federal governments to serve a public purpose and in

 ensuring safety and soundness measures, they uphold the financial stability of our banking system,
which is critical to the country's stability and economic development. By creating this affirmative
obligation, CRA serves a critical role that should not be undermined.

When CRA functions accordingly, it is apparent. Scholarly research assessing the incentive
mechanisms of the CRA provides evidence of how the CRA works well to influence bank behavior
as intended and how it could better address current realities. Even financial institutions that are not
currently covered by federal or state CRA rules have found merit in the implementation of CRA
for improving their performance. A February 2021 New York DFS report analyzed lending and
redlining in Buffalo, New York, revealing an important finding about a mortgage company that
had a good record of lending to all parts of its market: "...in response to the Department's inquiry
regarding its fair lending policies, Homestead Funding Corp., the non-depository lender...with a
good record of reaching minority populations in the Buffalo area explained that one reason for its
success is that it operates in another state that happens to impose CRA requirements on non-
depository institutions and therefore, analyzing lending data to ensure the lender is reaching all
parts of its markets is a regular practice. Especially with respect to the portion of non-bank
mortgage lenders that are not reaching low- and moderate-income borrowers, application of the
CRA could improve their performance as it has for banks and help ensure continued good
performance for those institutions already serving their whole communities, thereby increasing the
availability of mortgage lending in communities that have heretofore experienced unequal access."
It is notable for a financial institution to acknowledge and give credit to a regulation for positively
contributing to its own performance. The CRA statute can not only benefit LMI communities but
also the financial institutions that serve them. This reinforces the essential and beneficial role that
CRA imposes. Updates should be made to allow the CRA to always achieve its critical statutory
purpose.

IV. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Conduct necessary and needed analysis to determine impact on LMI communities

We are concerned that these changes are being proposed without an adequate analysis of their
likely impact on LMI communities and on communities that have experienced historic
discrimination and disinvestment. Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:

 quantify changes in lending, investments, services and community development activities
 subject to CRA evaluation

 consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
 meaningful community accountability

 show that community needs become less significant simply because a bank falls below a
 higher asset threshold

NCRC conducted their own extensive analysis and mapping in response to the proposal to
showcase the detrimental consequences the changes would have on LMI communities. These
findings warrant careful consideration by the agencies who are ultimately statutorily responsible
for overseeing the CRA and encouraging financial institutions to help meet the credit needs of the
communities in which they do business.

Ceres Headquarters: 99 Chauncy Street, Boston, MA 02111
California Office: 369 Pine Street, Suite 620, San Francisco, CA 94104
 To prevent significant declines in needed CRA-eligible community development activity, the
agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce lending, services, or
investment in LMI communities and whether communities that have experienced historic
discrimination or disinvestment would be disproportionately affected. Before finalizing the rule,
we request that the OCC and FDIC rescind this current proposal until a thorough analysis of its
impacts on LMI communities is prepared and released for a new public comment.

The agencies should also distinguish between the loss of data and the loss of lending. Raising
reporting thresholds changes what regulators and the public can observe about economically
significant activity. The agencies should quantify both effects: (1) the reduction in visibility that
follows directly from the proposal, and (2) any change in lending that may follow from reduced
scrutiny. Additionally, the agencies should examine whether other lenders would fill any gap. The
agencies should analyze impacts separately for metropolitan, micropolitan, and rural markets.

2. Do not raise bank asset thresholds as proposed

We recommend the regulators not move forward with any of their proposals to increase asset
thresholds. Raising asset thresholds would appear to significantly roll back CRA requirements and
significantly reduce the number of institutions subject to community development expectations.
Banks of all sizes play a vital role in community development lending, but scaling back community
development responsibilities risks hindering opportunities to finance affordable housing, small
businesses, and other essential community development. The OCC and FDIC state they are raising
asset thresholds to reduce regulatory burden, however they have not provided sufficient evidence
of the severity of regulatory burden, or that the loss of community development, branches, and
small business lending data will be outweighed by this reduction in burden. Furthermore, the
regulators have not shown that community needs have become less significant simply because a
bank falls below a higher asset threshold.

Studies show that CRA poses minimal compliance costs for financial institutions. A Federal
Reserve Bank of St. Louis report analyzed over 1,500 survey responses from nearly 1,100 unique
banks assessing compliance costs of community banks attributable to specific regulations and
found that CRA accounted for 7.2% of compliance expenses, which is towards the bottom end of
their overall compliance costs. Based on 3 years of community bank surveys, the study found that
compliance costs across all banks, and all years, averaged about 7 percent of noninterest expenses.

On the other hand, CRA benefits to LMI communities are well-recorded and well-established.
Studies demonstrate that the federal CRA is making a beneficial difference in unlocking vital
financial access to LMI communities. Research by The Center for Affordable Housing Lending
showcases the power of CRA to leverage private investments to more fully address the needs of
communities nationwide. In 2024, CRA incentivized more than $430 billion in loans and
investments for homeownership, small businesses, and affordable housing and community
development in LMI communities nationwide. Specifically, CRA drove:

 Nearly $168 billion in affordable housing and community development lending and

investments;

 More than $152 billion in small business loans;

 More than $100 billion to support homeowners; and

  More than $10 billion in small farm loans.

From 2015 to 2024, financial institutions made more than $1.4 trillion in community development
loans and investments benefiting LMI communities. Of that, more than $1.2 trillion was in the
form of loans benefiting LMI communities and individuals, and the remaining $168 billion was in
the form of investments. As of its passage in 1977, CRA has driven $6 trillion in loans and
investments to LMI communities. According to research by NCRC, since 1996, CRA-covered
lending in LMI communities has delivered $883 billion in loans for affordable housing and
economic development projects and $973 billion in 24 million small business loans.

Notably, the CRA does not mandate or encourage risky lending. Rather, financial institutions must
operate consistently with safe and sound practices. Research shows that federal CRA lending has
demonstrated a track record of implementation in line with safety and soundness. Economists
Robert Avery and Kenneth Brevoort affirm that CRA-covered home lending is typically safer and
more sound than non-CRA covered lending. According to their analysis, when a larger share of
lending was issued by CRA-covered banks than by mortgage companies, neighborhoods
experienced lower delinquency rates and less risky lending. A Federal Reserve study likewise
reported that CRA-related mortgage loans had delinquency rates lower than average across all
2006 mortgages and significantly lower than those of subprime loans. The Federal Reserve Bank
of San Francisco examined California loans originated by CRA-regulated institutions and also
found they were significantly less likely to default than those originated by non-CRA-regulated
institutions. These empirical studies provide a strong case for the safe and effective role CRA
serves that must be preserved rather than weakened.

3. Consider clarifying CRA credit opportunities for needed resilience financing under
 community development

The CRA rules are important not only for ensuring fairness and mobilizing financial access in LMI
communities, but also for the potential to address relevant systemic physical risks. Although the
proposal adds language to the new definition of community development under the revitalization
and stabilization category, "programs, projects, or initiatives that assist individuals and
communities with preparing for, adapting to, or withstanding natural disasters," the 2023 final rule
went a step further by making "disaster preparedness and weather resiliency" its own explicit
community development category and referenced examples such as community solar projects and
development of green spaces, and cooling or warming centers in LMI census tracts. This proposal
mentions none of those helpful examples, which risks hindering the potential flow of capital to
financing for much needed resilience projects and offering banks an additional opportunity to earn
CRA credit.

Significant work remains to ensure LMI communities have the resources to protect and guard
against damage to their properties and adequately deal with loss of income from a natural disaster
or adverse weather event. The notable and staggering increase in losses from natural disasters and
extreme weather events illustrates the urgent need for proactively clarifying the full scope of CRA-
qualifying resilience activities. Since many LMI communities are more exposed to extreme
weather threats, such as flooding in coastal and inland areas and extreme heat in urban
neighborhoods, their risk of housing insecurity and financial vulnerability is also further

 exacerbated and compounded. While current regulatory guidance allows CRA credit for activities
designed to revitalize or stabilize federally designated disaster areas, it does not explicitly provide
credit for activities that would proactively minimize the damages of these events before they occur.
Given that the current CRA rules are predominantly reactive to natural disasters and incentivizes
retrofitting properties to be more energy efficient for the benefit of the tenants, those rule changes
would have made a beneficial advancement by allowing banks to proactively undertake activities
that support disaster preparedness and weather resiliency in LMI communities while allowing
banks to receive the credit they seek on CRA exams.

The updated 2023 CRA final rules were a positive step forward in addressing common-sense and
necessary changes poised to strengthen CRA overall for LMI communities and the financial
institutions that serve them. The inclusion of disaster preparedness and weather resiliency as a
community development category would have beneficially awarded CRA credit to banks for
financing critical measures such as construction of flood control systems in flood-prone areas,
retrofitting multifamily affordable housing to withstand future disasters or weather-related events,
financing community solar projects, and upgrades to affordable housing such as energy-efficient
appliances. While remaining responsive to natural disasters, these updates would have importantly
broadened disaster preparedness and weather resiliency to incentivize proactive measures to help
LMI communities prepare for, withstand, and minimize the damage from severe weather events.

The CRA can not only benefit LMI communities but also the financial institutions that serve them.
Rebuild By Design's CRA Bank Guidebook aims to help institutions strategically direct their CRA
investments toward projects that strengthen community-wide infrastructure that minimizes the
damages of extreme weather. It outlines how CRA rules could enable CRA credit for activities
related to disaster preparedness and infrastructure revitalization and stabilization. CRA
investments offer an opportunity to reduce risk exposure for communities and banks by reducing
harm in CRA-eligible LMI communities where banks do business. Since protecting communities
protects bank assets, resilience measures contribute to safeguarding capital investments. CRA can
shift investment from post-disaster recovery to proactive infrastructure that stabilizes assets,
reduces risk, and allows banks to earn CRA credit. Incentivizing banks to invest in resiliency
reinforces the intended purpose of the CRA while allowing banks additional opportunities to earn
CRA credit and accelerating investment in vulnerable communities.

Financial institutions should be incentivized and encouraged to offer CRA-eligible products and
services that respond accordingly in support of local community needs, including physical risks
from increasing and intensifying exposures to extreme weather threats. Given the growing impacts
of extreme weather and disaster risks, we urge the FDIC and OCC to consider uplifting mitigation
and adaptation financing for consideration under CRA.

Illustrative list and pre-approval process

clarity and certainty for financial institutions. As a follow up to the 2023 updated rules, agencies
expressed their intention of jointly publishing an illustrative list of eligible pre-approved
community development activities, which was expected to include examples of disaster
preparedness and weather resiliency activities. Against the backdrop of increasing extreme

The 2023 regulation also offered the prospect of a pre-approval process for banks to seek prior

New York's state-CRA offers a valuable model

Encouraging lending aligned with resilience--particularly in underserved communities--can play
a crucial role in enhancing long-term stability and ensuring that the transition to a more resilient

acknowledging the need for banks and insurance companies to take steps to assess and mitigate
risks from extreme weather and natural disasters. In February 2021, NY DFS released a letter to
New York state-chartered banks describing how resilience activities could receive consideration
as a community development activity during their CRA examination. This was, to the best of our
awareness, the first time a U.S. financial regulator explicitly encouraged CRA to be used for
resilience activities. The NY DFS guidance went a step further by helpfully offering a specific list
of examples of financing activities that support resilience. Examples included: financing
community solar projects that provide energy to an affordable housing project, flood resilience
activities for multifamily buildings, and reducing heat risk via air conditioning installation in

4. Prioritize LMI communities as the focus of CRA

The CRA plays an important role in lifting up underserved communities. CRA functions to
motivate banks to invest in critical areas of need through the promise of earning credit for eligible
CRA activities. Notably, it is not designed or intended to focus on providing regulatory relief to
financial institutions, especially at the expense of the needs of LMI communities. Practically all
banks pass their CRA exams despite evidence of existing lending and credit gaps in LMI
communities that should be addressed. According to NCRC, approximately 98% of banks pass
their CRA exams with just less than 10% receiving an "Outstanding" rating and almost 90% of
them receiving a rating of "Satisfactory." To maximize the CRA's progress and effectiveness,
regulators must refocus the proposal on addressing the unmet credit needs of LMI communities,
rather than on providing regulatory relief to financial institutions.

Financing plays a critical role in helping vulnerable communities build resilience to future
disasters. By spurring the flow of private capital, it can therefore serve as an important part of the
solution to addressing important local community issues including, housing affordability,
workforce development, community infrastructure upgrades, entrepreneurship, and rural
development. However, there are few policies or programs to help build financial resilience, which
requires sufficient liquid resources. Regulatory incentives for banks, such as CRA credit, help
drive investments to frontline communities. Given that extreme weather threats are not distributed
equally, financing for activities that help mitigate and build resilience to these physical risks would
strengthen the CRA for both LMI communities and the financial institutions that serve them.

Support for affordable housing, small business financing, and community development remains
necessary. Housing finance disparities remain a stark issue and contribute to economic inequality,
which aggravates the historic effects of discrimination in housing markets. While homeownership
serves as an important avenue for building wealth and the transfer of wealth across generations,
persistent lending disparities exacerbate economic inequality and frustrate the long-running
purpose of CRA to end the nation's long and painful history of lending discrimination and
disinvestment.

Several crucial and applicable lessons can be gleaned from assessing state-level CRA
modernization efforts. States with their own CRA laws also continuously evaluate any oversight
gaps not being covered by the federal CRA to ensure continued lending and credit access to
underserved communities in their respective states. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
(CFPB) conducted extensive analysis and research on state CRA laws and the availability of credit
access across a range of financial products, including mortgage lending, small business lending,
and others. In their 2023 report, the CFPB found that just as the federal CRA law has been revised
a number of times since its passage, state CRAs have been amended periodically in response to
changing markets to cover additional types of financial institutions, collect additional data to better
understand financial markets, and address state-specific needs. This responsiveness to evolving
market needs is aligned with the evolution and history of federal CRA rule updates. Updating the

 rules for implementing CRA does not diminish or undermine its effectiveness, rather it shows an
ongoing commitment to the statutory purpose of the CRA by proactively adapting to LMI
communities' unmet or evolving credit needs. While states with updated CRA rules have
demonstrated agility and responsiveness, not every state has its own CRA rules, underlining the

CRA is a necessary statute that aims to encourage financial institutions to meet the credit needs of
LMI communities. While we support common-sense updates, changes should be made that enable
the CRA to always achieve its critical statutory purpose. The CRA statute has a proven track record
of implementation in line with safety and soundness and important role to continue serving.
Therefore, it should not be weakened or diminished in pursuit of regulatory relief. We urge the
agencies to ensure that CRA focuses on prioritizing LMI communities as mandated.

V. CONCLUSION

With the goal of increasing lending, investment, and financial services in historically underserved
communities, CRA remains critically necessary and one of the strongest tools available for driving
equitable financial access to the unmet banking needs of LMI borrowers.

However, this proposal undermines the CRA's core mechanisms for holding banks accountable
for serving the needs of LMI communities. While CRA has been proven effective and while it is
a necessary vehicle for driving financial access to LMI communities, there is room for updating it
to ensure it aligns with the current realities of intensifying physical risks, modern banking
practices, and unmet community needs. We have consistently advocated for CRA updates to
address urgent and modern realities being confronted in the financial landscape. This continues to
include the persistent reality of extreme weather events compromising the financial stability of
LMI communities and the pressing need to offer CRA-eligible credit opportunities for resilience
activities to help them better prepare and withstand the devastating impact that these physical risks
pose.

Efforts to weaken CRA regulations could have negative and damaging consequences for LMI
communities frustrating the purpose of the CRA to meet the credit needs of LMI communities.
This current proposal falls short of updating CRA rules in line with the original purpose of the law
and risks undermining equitable homeownership access at a time when Americans and small
businesses are already grappling with historic deepening affordable housing gaps, rising inflation
rates, insurance volatility, and less recognized losses driven by their disproportionate exposure to
increasing natural disasters and extreme weather events. In this current proposal, the regulators
have missed an opportunity to provide necessary and common-sense updates that would have
strengthened CRA for both LMI communities and the financial institutions that serve them.

The OCC and FDIC should rescind the current rule proposal and in keeping with the spirit and
mandate of the CRA law, the agencies should instead conduct an analysis of how the proposed
changes would impact LMI communities that have confronted longstanding disinvestment and
financial disenfranchisement.

See attacheRe: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, OCC-2026-0694 / FDIC RIN 3064-AG31

PEOPLE TRUST, Little Rock, Arkansas, submits this comment. Our full answers to all 63 questions are attached.

KEY REQUEST: State expressly that loans to, investments in, and deposits or shares in Treasury-certified CDFIs are presumed to have a community development purpose in every category, not only economic development. This gives banks certainty and cuts documentation burden (Q11).

We support the illustrative list, the eligibility confirmation process, credit for prior-period loans and binding commitments, and the new Indian country and disaster categories. We oppose changes that weaken the CRA's core obligation:

1. Thresholds (Q1-3): Reject $1B/$10B. About 86 banks would remain large banks, and 376 would lose the investment and service tests and data reporting. Go no higher than $850M/$3.252B. Reject $30B.

2. Product lines (Q4-7): Prefer Option 2, by assessment area. Bank-wide selection drops small farm and small business lending in rural areas. Use both dollar volume and loan count.

3. Intermediate banks: Keep the rule that a Satisfactory overall rating requires a Satisfactory community development test.

4. Grants (Q9-10): The 15% cap misreads 2 CFR 200, where 15% is a de minimis rate, not a ceiling. Accept a negotiated rate or 25%, whichever is higher. Treat grants for loan capital and loan-loss reserves as direct use. Do not eliminate grant credit.

5. Complexity (Q12-17): Name subordinated debt, loan-loss reserves, equity-equivalent investments and co-lending as complex. Do not require investments or services to be complex. Weight impact on LMI people most.

6. Economic development (Q24-29): Keep the LMI job requirement (Q25). Without it, almost any small business loan counts. Add SSBCI, USDA relending and revolving loan funds to the example programs.

7. Housing (Q18-23): Middle-income rentals in high-cost areas only with binding affordability, at lower weight, using a 50% cost-burden test. Count LMI mortgages that are not a major product line.

8. Disasters (Q31): Remove the Category A/B exclusion as proposed.

9. Confirmations and outside-area activity (Q32-34): Cap extensions at 30 days and publish confirmations. Apply "substantially met" at the State or MSA level, never bank-wide. Prefer Option 1.

10. Strategic plans (Q35-54): No declining goals. Require at least one LMI lending goal. Missing annual goals in two or more years should bar "substantially met." Use a 45-day comment period, email notice, approval-date effectiveness, and a new comment period for resubmissions.

11. Deposit services: Keep them in the service test. A low-cost account is the first step to credit.

12. Discrimination: Adopt Option B so confidential exam findings can lower ratings.

13. Data and access (Q58-62): Publish community development grant, loan and investment data. Keep the public file available at branches as well as online. Keep CRA small-business data until Section 1071 data are published. Allow 18-month transitions and grandfather existing commitments.

Arlo Washington, President, PEOPLE TRUST

CRA Comment Letter

Oct 13, 2026 @AWash

To: Chief Counsel's Office, Attention: Comment Processing, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency,
400 7th Street SW, Suite 1E-216, Washington, DC 20219; and Jennifer M. Jones, Deputy Executive
Secretary, Attention: Comments--RIN 3064-AG31, Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, 550 17th
Street NW, Washington, DC 20429

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations -- OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694 (RIN 1557-AF57); FDIC
RIN 3064-AG31; 91 FR 52114 (Aug. 12, 2026)

From: Arlo Washington, President, PEOPLE TRUST, Little Rock, Arkansas

We appreciate the agencies' work to add clarity to the CRA rules. We support the illustrative list, the
eligibility confirmation process, credit for prior-period community development loans and binding
commitments, and the new categories for Indian country and disaster preparedness. We are concerned,
however, that several changes would weaken the law's core obligation: the much higher asset
thresholds, the optional community development test for intermediate banks, the removal of deposit
services, the grant restrictions, and the dropped low- and moderate-income test for economic
development. Our answers to each numbered question follow, in order.

Key request -- CDFI clarity. We ask the agencies to state expressly, in the rule or the illustrative list,
that loans to, investments in, and deposits or membership shares in Treasury-certified CDFIs are
presumed to have a primary purpose of community development. Current guidance applies this
presumption only to economic development. Extending it across all community development
categories would give banks certainty and reduce documentation burden. (See also our answer to
Q11.)

Asset thresholds and major product lines (Q1Q7)

We oppose the $1 billion / $10 billion thresholds. By the agencies' own counts, 250 FDIC-supervised
banks and 126 OCC-supervised banks would lose the investment test, the service test and data
reporting. About 86 banks nationwide would remain large banks. If thresholds must rise, they should go
no higher than the $850 million / $3.252 billion alternative.

Q1. Should the intermediate bank threshold be raised to $30 billion, and the small bank threshold to
$10 billion? No. Supervisory definitions of "community bank" serve safety-and-soundness purposes, not
the CRA's purpose. A $30 billion cap would leave only the largest national banks with full CRA
obligations.

Q2. Should the rules clarify that wholesale, limited purpose or strategic plan status does not override
the asset-based definition? Yes. A large bank should keep large-bank data duties whatever its
evaluation method.

Q3. Should the rules define "assets"? Yes. Use total assets from Schedule RC of the Call Report, or
Schedule RAL for U.S. branches of foreign banks.
 Q4. Under Option 1, should there be a de minimis amount, such as 30 loans, before a product line
counts? Yes. Evaluate a product line when the bank makes 30 or more loans in it overall or in any one
assessment area. Lending that matters to a local market should not be dropped as "incidental."

Q5. How should consumer lending be considered? (a) Yes, by type, because pricing and risk differ by
type. (b) Yes, allow optional consideration when it is a top-two line. (c) Yes, at the bank's request, but
only with full data so the review is not selective.

Q6. Dollar volume, loan count, or both? Both, as in Appendix C. Either measure alone distorts the
result.

Q7. Under Option 1, should major product lines be set by assessment area? Yes. We prefer Option 2
overall. Credit needs are local. Bank-wide selection can drop small farm and small business lending from
rural assessment areas where those loans matter most.

Community development activities, grants and complexity (Q8Q17)

Q8. Should prior-period loans and investments count annually or by evaluation period? Annually,
based on the average outstanding balance, a balance held only on the measurement date does not
count. Renewals should count once per evaluation period.

Q9. Are there better standards than the 15% indirect-cost cap, and are the guardrails enough? The cap
is too blunt. Under 2 CFR part 200, 15% is a de minimis rate a recipient may use without negotiating. It is
not a ceiling, and many established nonprofits have negotiated rates above it. We recommend accepting
a federally negotiated indirect-cost rate or 25%, whichever is higher. Grants for loan capital and loan-
loss reserves at nonprofit lenders, including CDFIs, should count as direct use.

Q10. Should grants be eliminated from CRA consideration? No. Grants fund housing counseling,
technical assistance and first-loss capital that make lending possible. Ending them would reduce lending,
not focus it.

Q11. Should the agencies give guidance on primary purpose for each community development
category? Yes, and they should codify it with examples for each category.

Note to Q11: As stated above, we ask the agencies to state expressly, in the rule or the illustrative list,
that loans to, investments in, and deposits or membership shares in Treasury-certified CDFIs are
presumed to have a primary purpose of community development across all categories, not only
economic development as current guidance provides.

Q12. Does the proposed "complexity" definition improve the focus on credit needs? Partly. Name as
complex: subordinated debt, loan-loss reserves, equity-equivalent investments, and co-lending with
nonprofit or government lenders.

Q13. Should the first part of the complexity definition apply to loans and loan equivalents? Yes. A loan
within a layered transaction is complex because of its structure.

Q14. Should investments and services be required to be complex? No. That would screen out simple,
high-impact support such as deposits in low-income credit unions. Give complex activities more weight
instead.
 Q15. Should complexity count more than innovativeness, flexibility or impact? No. Impact on low- and
moderate-income people should count most.

Q16. Should innovativeness or flexibility be defined? (a) Yes. Codify the Q&A innovativeness guidance.
(b) Scale it to bank size. (c) Define flexibility by terms that widen access to credit, such as longer terms,
below-market rates, subordinate positions and reduced collateral.

Q17. Should responsiveness apply only to community development activities? No. Retail products that
serve low- and moderate-income borrowers should be judged on responsiveness too.

Community development definition (Q18Q31)

Q18. Should affordable housing include middle-income rental housing in high-cost areas? Only
narrowly. Require a binding affordability restriction, count only the restricted units, and give it less
weight than LMI housing.

Q19. Should "high-cost area" be defined, and is 40% the right threshold? Yes, define it. Use 50% of
households that are cost-burdened, not 40%, and publish the list annually.

Q20. Should housing cost or High Opportunity Areas be considered? Yes, as a responsiveness factor
rather than a new category.

Q21. Should nonprofit partnerships for naturally occurring affordable housing be exempt from the
30%-of-80%-AMI rent test? Yes, if the nonprofit commits in writing to keep rents affordable for the
financing term.

Q22. Should the same exemption apply at 120% AMI in high-cost areas? No. That standard is already
broad.

Q23. Should direct mortgages to LMI borrowers count as community development loans when they
are not a major product line? Yes. This keeps an incentive for affordable mortgages at banks with small
mortgage volume.

Q24. Should eligible businesses be further limited? Yes. Exclude businesses affiliated with non-small
firms and startups expected to exceed the size test within two years.

Q25. Should the requirement to create or keep jobs for LMI people or in LMI areas be retained? Yes.
Without it, almost any small business loan, in any neighborhood, could count. A simpler test would
work: the business is in an LMI or distressed tract, or is majority owned by or employs LMI people, or the
financing comes through a government or nonprofit small business program.

Q26. Should any example programs be removed or added? Keep all five. Add the State Small Business
Credit Initiative, USDA Intermediary Relending Program lenders, and state and local revolving loan
funds.

Q27. Will removing the purpose test encourage financing that benefits communities? No. It will mostly
relabel lending banks already do. Clearer criteria are welcome but should stay tied to LMI benefit.

Q28. Should any activities that qualify under the proposal be excluded? Yes. Exclude refinancing with
no new capacity, financing for owner distributions, and acquisitions that consolidate ownership.
 Q29. Would anything that qualifies today lose credit? Yes, for example working-capital lines that keep
microbusinesses open. These should still qualify when they serve small businesses in LMI areas.

Q30. Should other programs, such as Indian country housing, be presumed to qualify? Yes. Presume
qualification for activities with Tribal housing authorities and HUD Section 184 lending. Count them
under both economic development and revitalization.

Q31. Should the exclusion for FEMA Category A/B-only designations be kept? No, remove it as
proposed. Debris-only declarations after tornadoes and floods still leave serious rebuilding credit needs.
Focus credit on LMI households, small businesses and small farms in the area.

Confirmation process and activity outside assessment areas (Q32Q34)

Q32. Should a bank keep an eligibility notice as long as the loan or investment stays on its balance
sheet? Yes. Long-term investments outlast several exam cycles, and credit under __.13(c) depends on
proving eligibility at the start.

Q33. Should there be an outer limit on extended review time? Yes. Allow one 30-day extension and
require the agency to state its length. Publish confirmations, with confidential terms redacted, so every
bank benefits from the answer.

Q34. If outside-area activity is allowed without meeting the standard everywhere, should
"substantially met" apply? Apply "substantially met" only at the State or multistate MSA level, never
bank-wide. Otherwise a bank could neglect a weak market and count distant activity instead. We prefer
the quantitative Option 1. Any use of the performance-context exception should be explained in writing
in the performance evaluation. Extra weight should go to activity in persistent-poverty counties, Indian
country, and distressed or underserved rural tracts.

Strategic plans (Q35Q54)

Q35. Should plans be required to cover whole political subdivisions? Yes, for large banks. (a) Setting
goals in advance does not cure the exclusion of LMI tracts. (b) A radius approach could work for small
banks if it cannot exclude LMI tracts inside the radius.

Q36. Should assessment areas have a maximum size? Yes, the combined statistical area. Larger areas
let averages hide neglected neighborhoods.

Q37. Should plans include maps of each assessment area? Yes. They cost little and help the public.

Q38. Do the measurable-goal rules explain enough, and should there be a growth factor? Add that
annual goals may not fall below the bank's prior-period performance, and that every plan includes at
least one LMI lending goal.

Q39. Do whole-term goals give appropriate flexibility? Yes, if the annual goals stay binding minimums.

Q40. Should whole-term goals be required? Yes, in addition to annual goals.

Q41. How should annual and whole-term goals be weighed? Missing annual goals in two or more years
should rule out "substantially met," so banks cannot backload activity into the last year.
 Q42. Should the OCC's simplified strategic plan process apply to all banks? Only to community banks,
and only as guidance.

Q43. Is the outside-area approach for an Outstanding rating appropriate? Yes, if limited to banks that
met their satisfactory goals in every assessment area.

Q44. Should activities not tied to any goal count toward a Satisfactory rating? No. A bank that misses
its own satisfactory goals should move to the standard tests.

Q45. Should that consideration be at the bank's election or required? Required, and applied
consistently, so banks cannot pick activities after the fact.

Q46. Should plans be allowed to set goals for activity outside assessment areas? Yes, but only
Outstanding goals, and only after in-area satisfactory goals are met.

Q47. How far ahead should a bank give the agency its draft plan? Ten business days before the
comment period starts.

Q48. Do the public engagement changes strike the right balance? Agency website posting is a real
improvement. Also keep the newspaper notice, add email notice to groups that ask for it, and extend
the comment period to 45 days.

Q49. Is the prefiling consultation provision right? Yes. Put the agency's written feedback in the public
file with the final plan.

Q50. When a plan is approved late, which effective date should apply? The approval date. A past date
would let goals be set after results are known.

Q51. Should extensions of the review period be capped? Yes, at 30 calendar days, stated in the
extension notice.

Q52. Should the list of material changes be exhaustive? Keep it non-exhaustive. State that a bank's
voluntary choice to cut activity or close branches in LMI areas is not a material change that justifies
lower goals.

Q53. Should the agencies explain when goals fall short in the aggregate? Yes. Goals fall short when
they are below the bank's recent performance, below similar lenders, or silent on credit needs raised in
public comments.

Q54. Are the denial and resubmission rules clear enough? Mostly. Add that a resubmitted plan with
changed goals needs a new comment period.

Other provisions (Q55Q63)

Q55. Are there other ways to encourage lending in Indian country and Tribal lands, such as the 2023
rule's definition? Yes. Consider the broader 2023 definition, and presume qualification for activities with
Tribal governments and Tribally designated housing entities.

Q56. What should a quantitative "substantial portion of loans" standard be based on? On fair-lending
practice: the areas a bank reasonably serves, without leaving out LMI or majority-minority tracts.
 Q57. Should a radius standard replace it, and how should the radius be set? Yes, as a floor. Vary the
radius by density: smallest in principal cities, largest in rural non-MSA areas.

Q58. How should the Interagency Questions and Answers be handled? Keep them in force until a final
rule takes effect. Then republish an updated set after public comment.

Q59. Should there be transition provisions? Yes. Allow 18 months for new data rules and 12 months for
strategic plan changes. Grandfather existing multi-year commitments so good-faith obligations are not
stranded.

Q60. Should the public file move to a website only? Require the website, but keep access at branches
on request, with free copies. Many rural and low-income residents lack reliable broadband.

Q61. Should the rule state the first year's small-bank threshold? Yes, and publish each yearly
adjustment in the Federal Register.

Q62. How should non-compliant assessment areas be handled? The agency should require a compliant
delineation, evaluate the bank as if it had complied, and treat any arbitrary exclusion of LMI tracts as a
factor that can lower the rating.

Q63. Should the Part 24 cross-reference be changed? Yes. Public welfare investment authority should
depend on whether an investment meets the community development definition.

Other requests for comment

Intermediate bank ratings. Keep the rule that an intermediate bank needs a Satisfactory community
development test to earn an overall Satisfactory. For many $1$10 billion banks, that test is the only
CRA reason to invest or lend for community development.

Deposit services. Keep deposit products in the service test. The statute names deposit services as part
of community needs, and a low-cost account is often the first step to credit.

Limited purpose banks. Do not eliminate the category without a transition. If it changes, keep a
community development component for these banks.

Discriminatory or illegal credit practices. Adopt Option B, so violations found in confidential exams can
still lower a rating. Keep the "nature, extent, and strength of the evidence" factor.

Public data. Yes, publish a database of community development grants with recipient, address and
amount. Extend it to community development loans and investments.

Section 1071 data. Rely on it only once it is actually collected and published. Until then, keep CRA small-
business and small-farm reporting.

Closing

The CRA requires banks to meet the credit needs of their whole communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Clearer rules help, but not at the cost of fewer banks being held to
that standard. We ask the agencies to adopt the changes above.

Respectfully submitted,
 Arlo Washington, President
PEOPLE TRUST

they are below the bank's recent performance, below similar lenders, or silent on credit needs raised in

Q54. Are the denial and resubmission rules clear enough? Mostly. Add that a resubmitted plan with
changed goals needs a new comment period.

Other provisions (Q55Q63)

Q55. Are there other ways to encourage lending in Indian country and Tribal lands, such as the 2023

 Q57. Should a radius standard replace it, and how should the radius be set? Yes, as a floor. Vary the
radius by density: smallest in principal cities, largest in rural non-MSA areas.

Q58. How should the Interagency Questions and Answers be handled? Keep them in force until a final

Q59. Should there be transition provisions? Yes. Allow 18 months for new data rules and 12 months for

delineation, evaluate the bank as if it had complied, and treat any arbitrary exclusion of LMI tracts as a
factor that can lower the rating.

depend on whether an investment meets the community development definition.

Intermediate bank ratings. Keep the rule that an intermediate bank needs a Satisfactory community
development test to earn an overall Satisfactory. For many $1$10 billion banks, that test is the only
CRA reason to invest or lend for community development.

Deposit services. Keep deposit products in the service test. The statute names deposit services as part
of community needs, and a low-cost account is often the first step to credit.

Limited purpose banks. Do not eliminate the category without a transition. If it changes, keep a
community development component for these banks.

Discriminatory or illegal credit practices. Adopt Option B, so violations found in confidential exams can
still lower a rating. Keep the "nature, extent, and strength of the evidence" factor.

Public data. Yes, publish a database of community development grants with recipient, address and
amount. Extend it to community development loans and investments.

Section 1071 data. Rely on it only once it is actually collected and published. Until then, keep CRA small-
business and small-farm reporting.

Closing

The CRA requires banks to meet the credit needs of their whole communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Clearer rules help, but not at the cost of fewer banks being held to
that standard. We ask the agencies to adopt the changes above.
