Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Housing Initiative Partnership, Inc. submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of
Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) because it would
significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the complexity
of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any
proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income
communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies
identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.

Housing Initiative Partnership, Inc. (HIP) is a nonprofit housing organization that expands access
to affordable housing and helps individuals and families achieve housing stability and financial
well-being. Through HUD-certified housing counseling, affordable housing development and
preservation, resident services, and financial empowerment coaching, HIP serves low- and
moderate-income residents and communities. HIP's work advances community reinvestment

 6525 Belcrest Road, Suite 555 | Hyattsville, MD 20782 | phone: (301) 699-3835 | fax: (301) 699-8184 | www.HIPhomes.org
 by partnering with financial institutions and other stakeholders to direct loans, grants,
investments, and services toward affordable housing, homeownership, and neighborhood
revitalization. HIP serves the residents of Maryland--Prince Geroge's' Montgomery, Anne
Arundel, and Howard Counties.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in
communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to
mainstream financial services.

The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would
change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for
nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without an
adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on
communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

REDUCTION IN COMMUNITY INVESTMENT EXPECTATIONS FOR ALL BANKS

CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In our community, from
2010-2024, banks made $134,568,731,000 in CRA qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers
or in LMI census tracts and $32,303,164,000 in CRA qualified lending to small businesses.
Investments such as these benefited our community by increasing the number of affordable
mortgages for first-time homebuyers.

We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital
devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough to receive a
passing CRA rating. However, that percentage is far lower than the percentage the National
Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the largest banks currently devote to
community investments and loans.

NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the OCC and
FDIC supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these banks currently
conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community development loans and investments
inside their assessment areas, and that the median percentage of annual community
development lending in assessment areas was 6.8% of tier 1 capital, and a median of 3.6% of
tier 1 capital for annual CRA qualified investments. If each bank instead conducted only the
amount necessary to meet separate thresholds of 0.625% of Tier 1 capital for community
development lending and investments, combined activity would fall to approximately $14.9
billion annually -- a decrease of approximately $87.1 billion, or 85%. Similarly, the proposal
encourages banks to use strategic plans to make their CRA compliance easier and more

 Housing Initiative Partnership, Inc.
 6525 Belcrest Road, Suite 555 | Hyattsville, MD 20782 | phone: 301.699.3835 | fax: 301.699.8184 | www.hiphomes.org
 predictable. Previous proposed guidance also set strategic plan benchmarks for CRA
performance well-below historical levels of community development activity.

Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic
discrimination cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and
loans. If regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to
the communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for communities. For
example, in our community such as families struggling to obtain affordable mortgage credit,
first-time homebuyers facing barriers to homeownership, and neighborhoods that continue to
experience disinvestment. It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet
community needs. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed
changes would reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income
communities and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or
disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.

LESS COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT SCRUTINY OF BANKS

The proposal would substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while
banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the
less demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more comprehensive tests
applied to large banks. The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and
reporting requirements currently applicable to large banks for institutions with $10 billion or
less in assets, including reporting on small-business, small-farm and community development
lending.

Approximately 800 banks would no longer receive a community development evaluation
because the proposal would raise the small-bank threshold from $412 million to $1 billion. The
417 banks newly classified as intermediate rather than large would no longer be examined
under separate CRA investment and services tests and instead would be evaluated based on
their combined community development loans, investments and services. These
reclassifications and resulting eliminations of community development obligations for over 800
banks and separate investment evaluations for 400 banks, may worsen the housing crisis by
reducing the demand for Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC).

In Maryland 26.2% of banks would lose CD obligations, 30.8% of the state's banks will lose their
large-bank status, 15.2% LMI branches jeopardized, and 9.4% of branches in jeopardy in
communities of color.

This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and
moderate-income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to
affordable mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible
small-business financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in affordable
housing, small businesses and other community development.

 Housing Initiative Partnership, Inc.
 6525 Belcrest Road, Suite 555 | Hyattsville, MD 20782 | phone: 301.699.3835 | fax: 301.699.8184 | www.hiphomes.org
 The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply
because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA
obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks
that would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the communities those
institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development activity that would receive
less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-
income communities or communities that have experienced historic discrimination and
disinvestment.

SUPPORT FOR LOCAL ORGANIZATIONS

We are concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations.

Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development, financial counseling,
workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based services through
grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations. These resources can
be particularly important to local organizations that have deep relationships with residents and
understand the specific needs of their communities.

For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and
new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller
organizations. For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff,
rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to
deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and
funding sources over which to spread these costs. In addition, many community-based
nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain financial records, budgets or
program documentation in the precise format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If
banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations are more difficult or costly to document,
they may redirect funding toward larger organizations whose activities are easier to verify.

Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and partnerships can
play in supporting community development. Bank grants have supported HIP's HUD-certified
housing counseling, HIP's CORES-certified resident services in affordable apartment
communities, and expansion of financial empowerment coaching with HIP's most vulnerable
clients.

These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital
into tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community
development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well
beyond the banks themselves.

Before finalizing these provisions, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed
documentation requirements and limits on administrative expenses would reduce or redirect

 Housing Initiative Partnership, Inc.
 6525 Belcrest Road, Suite 555 | Hyattsville, MD 20782 | phone: 301.699.3835 | fax: 301.699.8184 | www.hiphomes.org
 bank support away from smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those with limited
administrative capacity. The agencies must also determine whether those effects would
ultimately reduce resources available to low- and moderate-income communities.

More broadly, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule primarily in terms of
reducing perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also determine what
the changes mean for the communities CRA is intended to serve.

Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:

 identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny
 under the proposal;

 quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
 development activities subject to CRA evaluation;

 assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or
 populations, including rural communities and communities of color;

 consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without
 sacrificing meaningful community accountability; and

Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes that
the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is
prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to
prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that
accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose
of meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods.

We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120

closes on October 13, 2026.

Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from

affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather examples from
the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more complete record on which
to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026
comment deadline by at least 60 days.

Midwest Housing Equity Group, Inc. ("MHEG") appreciates the opportunity to comment on the
Community Reinvestment Act ("CRA") Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) issued by the
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
(FDIC).

MHEG is a Nebraska nonprofit corporation formed in 1993. Our mission is to change lives for a
better tomorrow by promoting the development and sustainability of quality affordable housing.
We accomplish our mission primarily through the syndication of Federal LIHTC's. More
specifically, we raise private sector equity capital (mostly from banks, insurance companies and
the Enterprises) to invest in affordable housing developments throughout the Midwest. Since
inception, we have raised over $4 billion of capital and helped create more than 30,000 safe, decent
and affordable rental homes in the Midwest. We have invested approximately $1.5 billion of that
amount in communities of 50,000 or fewer people. We are proud to note those dollars have helped
create and preserve more than 12,000 quality rental homes in rural America. Across the entire
portfolio, our average development is comprised of just 38 units and several of our investments
are in 6-, 10- and 12-unit properties. We are honored to play a key role in providing affordable
housing across our footprint.

The need for safe, decent and affordable housing continues to grow across the nation. We are
committed to helping the Midwest, particularly the rural Midwest, meet its affordable housing
needs. It is against that backdrop that we respectfully offer a few comments for consideration as it
relates to the proposed rule. Our core motivation is to ensure that any CRA regulatory rewrite does
no harm to affordable housing and community development investment, especially in rural
communities.

 515 N. 162nd Avenue, Suite 202, Omaha, NE 68118 P 402 334 8899 F 402 334 5599 mheginc.com
 The Housing Credit is the nation's primary financing tool for the development and preservation of
affordable housing for low-income households, including veterans and seniors. As one of the most
successful public-private partnerships, the Housing Credit has financed more than four million
affordable homes since its creation in 1986. The Community Reinvestment Act plays a critical role
in sustaining the Housing Credit market by creating a strong regulatory incentive for financial
institutions to invest in Housing Credit properties. According to a 2025 study by CohnReznick,
approximately 80 percent of annual Housing Credit equity investment comes from bank investors
motivated by CRA considerations. Depository institutions provide this capital not solely for the
modest financial returns generated by Housing Credit tax benefits, but also because the CRA
examination framework for large banks includes a separate, dedicated Investment Test. In short,
banks continue to allocate substantial equity capital to Housing Credit properties because these
investments help fulfill their affirmative CRA obligations.

Affordable housing investment and development are essential to the long-term growth, stability,
and success of communities. Without a safe and stable place to call home, individuals and families
face significant barriers to accessing the other foundations of a productive and healthy life. The
broader community benefits of affordable housing development are also well documented,
including increased economic activity, job creation, improved property values, reduced
incarceration rates, and increased tax revenue. These benefits are especially important in rural
communities, many of which have seen little or no new housing development, affordable or
otherwise, for many years.

The CRA was enacted in 1977 to ensure that banks help meet the credit needs of the communities
in which they operate, particularly low- and moderate-income communities. We recognize the
importance of updating and modernizing CRA regulations to reflect changes in the banking
industry. However, it is equally important to preserve the CRA's vital role as a primary driver of
regulated financial institutions' investment in affordable housing, particularly through the Housing
Credit. We also urge the banking agencies to consider the impact of current economic conditions
on Housing Credit production. Elevated interest rates have increased the cost of capital, while
rising construction costs, supply chain challenges, and inflation continue to create significant
headwinds for affordable housing development.

For these reasons, we respectfully urge the agencies to avoid any CRA regulatory changes that
would reduce investment in Housing Credits or otherwise adversely affect affordable housing
production and preservation. Maintaining strong CRA incentives for Housing Credit investment
is essential to meeting the urgent and growing need for affordable housing, particularly in the rural
and underserved communities that depend on this investment most.

We are deeply concerned that the agencies' primary proposal to reclassify banking institutions
with assets between $1.649 billion and $10 billion as intermediate banks, rather than large banks
subject to the full CRA examination, would substantially weaken the affordable housing finance
ecosystem. By eliminating the separate Investment Test for this cohort, the proposed rule threatens
to reduce competition among investors, depress Housing Credit pricing, and ultimately result in
fewer affordable homes being built.

 Page 2
 Data compiled by the National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders (NAAHL) underscores
the scale of this impact. Of the 642 institutions currently designated as large banks, only 256 would
retain that classification under a $10 billion asset threshold, a net decline exceeding 60 percent. As
a result, only 6 percent of all banking institutions currently subject to the large bank classification
would remain subject to the full CRA examination and its dedicated Investment Test. In addition,
a survey conducted by The Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC) found that banks
in the $1.649 billion to $10 billion asset tier invested at least $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity
over the five-year survey period. Extrapolated across the broader market, institutions in this asset
range deployed up to $2 billion in Housing Credit equity during that same timeframe.

Under the proposed rule, newly reclassified intermediate institutions would no longer be subject
to an enforceable requirement to maintain direct equity investments in the low- and moderate-
income communities they serve. Although these institutions would retain general community
development obligations, depository institutions have consistently found community development
lending to be structurally easier, less resource-intensive, and more operationally convenient than
executing complex equity investments. Without a distinct regulatory imperative to make equity
investments, these institutions can be expected to redirect capital away from Housing Credit equity
and toward debt instruments.

The proposed rule also directly undermines recent bipartisan congressional action intended to
expand the Housing Credit and encourage increased bank participation. The One Big Beautiful
Bill Act (also known as the Working Families Tax Cuts Act) enacted substantial statutory increases
in Housing Credit allocation authority and expanded the 4 percent Housing Credit program to
significantly accelerate housing supply. At the same time, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act
increased the statutory limit on banks' Public Welfare Investments (PWI), enabling institutions to
expand their Housing Credit equity commitments. Notably, the increase in the PWI cap directly
benefits many of the same institutions that the agencies now propose to reclassify as intermediate
banks. The proposed threshold modifications would therefore severely dilute these hard-won
legislative achievements and directly frustrate Congress's intent to expand the national supply of
affordable rental housing.

The negative consequences of the proposed reclassification would be felt most acutely in rural and
smaller communities. According to the AHTCC survey, approximately one-third of all Housing
Credit equity deployed through syndicators by institutions with assets between $412 million and
$10 billion from 2021 through 2024 supported rural markets. This finding underscores the essential
role these institutions play in financing affordable housing in non-metropolitan areas. Eliminating
the standalone Investment Test for banks with assets below $10 billion would deepen existing
geographic pricing disparities, increasing the risk that affordable housing developments in rural
and underserved communities are left stranded and that these communities face reduced access to
private capital.

With respect to the two alternative regulatory frameworks described in the Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking, we offer the following observations:

 Page 3
 The first alternative to increase the large bank asset threshold from $1.649 billion to $3.252 billion
would still have negative effects compared with the current CRA framework. However, it would
be materially less disruptive to the Housing Credit market than the primary proposal to raise the
threshold to $10 billion. Based on the AHTCC survey findings, a $10 billion threshold would
reclassify 108 institutions as intermediate banks, while a $3.252 billion threshold would reclassify
only 40 institutions. Critically, under a $3.252 billion threshold, the institutions that would remain
subject to the separate Investment Test account for approximately 86 percent of all Housing Credit
equity investments made by OCC and FDIC regulated banks captured in the AHTCC survey.

Conversely, the second alternative proposal to raise the large bank threshold to $30 billion would
cause substantially greater harm to affordable rental housing production than either the primary
proposal or the first alternative. NAAHL estimates that, under a $30 billion threshold, 17 states
would experience a reduction of 50 percent or more in the number of large banks subject to
investment requirements. In addition, AHTCC data show that institutions with assets between $10
billion and $30 billion account for more than twice the aggregate volume of Housing Credit debt
and equity investment as banks in the $1.65 billion to $10 billion range. As a result, a $30 billion
threshold would significantly reduce, and in many regions effectively decimate, bank equity
participation in Housing Credit developments.

For these reasons, MHEG respectfully requests the OCC and FDIC to retain the large bank asset
threshold currently established under the 1995 CRA regulations, $1.649 billion, adjusted for
inflation. Equity investment is indispensable to Housing Credit developments, and CRA policy
should preserve incentives for banks to provide that equity rather than allow more readily
achievable lending activity to displace it. Simply put, administrative simplification should not
come at the expense of the affordable homes CRA helps make possible.

MHEG also encourages coordinated and consistent CRA administration across the banking
regulators. Because the Federal Reserve did not join this proposal, careful attention to regulatory
consistency is especially important. If the OCC and FDIC nevertheless proceed with modifications
to the CRA regulations, MHEG strongly urges the agencies to adopt the lowest possible large bank
threshold and to include policies that expressly protect Housing Credit investments in rural and
smaller communities.

Thank you again for the opportunity to comment on the proposed rule. We hope our Midwest and
rural perspective is helpful. As you consider our comments, please let me know if I can provide
additional information.

Kindest regards,

John Wiechmann
President/CEO

 For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that banks

Industrial Cities, Economic Mobility and the National Manufacturing Agenda

The Administration has made expanding domestic manufacturing a national priority, and Kresge shares
the goal of a stronger industrial base. Much of that expansion will happen in older industrial cities like
Detroit and its peers in the Great Lakes region and the South, which have the industrial land, logistics
infrastructure, supplier base and experienced workforce that manufacturers need.

However, new plants alone will not be enough. Workers need affordable housing near the jobs being
created, and small and mid-sized suppliers need working capital, equipment loans and real estate financing
in order to grow. Families also depend on childcare, job training, health clinics and neighborhood
businesses. After decades of disinvestment, conventional lenders do not reliably provide this financing in
industrial cities. Appraisals often come in below development costs, smaller firms may lack the collateral
or credit history that conventional underwriting requires, and many residents have limited relationships
with banks.

The CRA is one of the few federal tools that consistently brings bank capital into these markets, and much
of that capital reaches borrowers through CDFIs. A rule that sharply reduces banks' community
development obligations would make it harder for these cities and their residents to take part in a
manufacturing expansion. We ask that the agencies' analysis take this into account.

1. The Proposal Would Sharply Reduce Community Investment Expectations for All Banks

CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. For example, in metro Detroit,
from 20102024, banks made approximately $28,964,420,000 in CRA-qualified mortgage lending to LMI
borrowers or in LMI census tracts and approximately $25,252,603,000 in CRA-qualified lending to small
businesses. This lending has helped families buy homes in a city hit hard by the foreclosure crisis and has
financed schools, clinics and other facilities that neighborhoods rely on. On the former Marygrove College
campus in northwest Detroit, for example, Kresge has partnered with bank investors on a series of
financings. These included Detroit's first New Markets Tax Credit investment in early childhood education
and a $57.3 million bank financing that converted historic campus buildings into a K-12 school serving
nearly 1,000 Detroit children. The banks' participation in those deals was motivated in large part by the
CRA.

We are concerned that the proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in communities. For example,
it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's tier 1 capital devoted to community development loans,

 2
 and 0.625% to community development investments, would be enough to receive CRA credit.2 That
percentage is far lower than what the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined
the largest banks currently devote to community development. NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA
performance evaluations of all sixty-nine OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks among the top 100 banks by
assets. It found that these banks currently conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community
development loans and investments inside their assessment areas, with median annual community
development lending of 6.8% of tier 1 capital and median annual CRA-qualified investments of 3.6% of
tier 1 capital.3 If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet the proposed 0.625%
thresholds, combined activity would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually, a decrease of
approximately $87.1 billion, or 85%. The proposal also encourages banks to use strategic plans to make
CRA compliance more predictable, and previous proposed guidance set strategic plan benchmarks well
below historical levels of community development activity.4

A reduction of this size would hit industrial cities hard, and philanthropy cannot make up the difference.
Foundation capital like Kresge's is usually structured as subordinate debt, guarantees or first-loss capital
so that banks can lend and invest at a larger scale, and each Kresge dollar typically brings in several dollars
of bank financing. That model only works if banks stay in the deal. In Detroit and similar cities, less bank
participation would mean fewer affordable homes built and fewer small manufacturers and suppliers able
to finance expansion. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes
would reduce lending, services or investment available to LMI communities, and whether communities
that have experienced historic discrimination or disinvestment, including older industrial cities, would be
disproportionately affected.

2. CDFIs and Affordable Housing Production Depend on CRA-Motivated Bank Capital

The relationship between the CRA, CDFIs and affordable housing production is central to Kresge's work,
and we do not think the proposal gives it enough attention. In the cities where we invest, CDFIs make most
of the early-stage housing loans, including predevelopment and acquisition loans, bridge loans for LIHTC
projects, construction loans for small multifamily buildings, and loans to preserve existing affordable
housing. CDFIs fund this lending largely with loans and equity-equivalent investments from banks, which
receive CRA consideration for that support, together with subordinate capital and guarantees from
foundations like Kresge. If the bank capital declines, the rest of the structure does not hold together. It's
important to note that this type of lending and investing by banks motivated by CRA, is not inherently
more risky than traditional lending. In fact, CDFI lending and lending to affordable housing is typically
less risky than traditional small business or multi-family real estate lending as has been documented by
numerous studies but the Federal Reserve system and other national policy experts.5

2The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit for activities outside their assessment areas
if the banks surpass a benchmark of 0.625% of tier 1 capital for community development loans and,
separately, 0.625% for community development investments. 91 Fed. Reg. at 52,140. We are concerned
that the practical effect of this proposal is that the benchmark will serve not as a floor, but a ceiling.
3NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 85% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk
(Sept. 10, 2026), https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-
development-activity-at-risk/.
4NCRC, The Proposed CRA Rule's Strategic Plans: A More Predictable Path to Doing Less (Sept. 1,
2026), https://ncrc.org/the-proposed-cra-rules-strategic-plans-a-more-predictable-path-to-doing-less/.

5 Affordable Housing Financing Is Overpriced, But It Doesn't Have to Be, Shelterforce, June 20th, 2026
https://shelterforce.org/2026/06/30/affordable-housing-financing-is-overpriced-but-it-doesnt-have-to-be/

 3
 Industrial cities depend on this structure even more than high-cost markets do. In much of Detroit, rents
and sale prices do not cover the cost of new construction or major rehabilitation, so projects need several
layers of financing, typically tax credit equity, CDFI loans, public subsidy and philanthropic capital. Banks
provide most LIHTC equity nationally, and the CRA is a main reason they do. Weaker CRA incentives
would lower tax credit pricing and reduce CDFI lending capacity, and fewer homes would be built. For
employers trying to hire, that means fewer places for new workers to live.

The proposal's changes to asset thresholds compound this risk. Banks with assets below $1 billion would
be treated as small banks, and banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be
evaluated under the less demanding intermediate-bank framework.6 The proposal would also eliminate
several data collection and reporting requirements, including community development lending reporting,
for institutions with $10 billion or less in assets.7 Approximately 800 banks would no longer receive a
community development evaluation, and 417 banks newly classified as intermediate would no longer be
examined under separate investment and service tests.8 Regional and community banks in this size range
are important lenders to and investors in local CDFIs, and they buy a significant share of LIHTC equity
outside the largest markets. Without a separate investment evaluation, these banks lose the specific
incentive to make equity investments, equity-equivalent investments in CDFIs and LIHTC purchases,
which are the hardest forms of capital to replace.

We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants. For grants from
large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and new documentation
requirements.9 Many CDFIs and housing nonprofits, especially smaller and newer organizations in the
neighborhoods we serve, use bank operating grants to pay for the underwriting, asset management and
technical assistance staff that their lending depends on. For these organizations, those staff costs are a core
part of delivering the program. If banks decide that grants to smaller organizations are harder to document,
they are likely to shift funding to larger institutions, leaving fewer local lenders in the neighborhoods that
need them.

We urge the agencies to (a) preserve, and state explicitly in any final rule, that loans to, investments in and
grants to certified CDFIs receive CRA community development consideration; (b) retain a meaningful,
separate evaluation of community development investments for banks with assets above $1 billion; and (c)
before finalizing the threshold changes, analyze the volume of CDFI financing and LIHTC equity provided
by banks that would move into less rigorous examination categories, and the effect on affordable housing
production in LMI communities.

3. Eliminating the Purpose Test Would Weaken the Link Between Economic Development Credit
and LMI Workers

Under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying small business does not automatically constitute
economic development. The activity must also satisfy the "purpose test," meaning it must promote

https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-rollbacks/.
991 Fed. Reg. at 52,129.

 economic development by supporting permanent job creation, retention or improvement for LMI people
or in LMI communities.10 The proposed rule would eliminate the purpose test, allowing financing to qualify
as economic development based primarily on the type and size of the business and whether the financing
expands, improves or preserves the business's productive capacity, physical presence or employment
base.11 The agencies themselves acknowledge that this change would expand the universe of activities
eligible for CRA credit.12

Kresge supports CRA credit for financing small manufacturers and suppliers, and we would welcome
guidance confirming that this financing qualifies. The purpose test, however, is what makes sure such
financing benefits LMI workers and neighborhoods. Without it, a bank could receive the same credit for
financing an expansion that creates no jobs accessible to local residents, or that moves jobs out of the
community, as for financing a business that hires and trains people from a struggling neighborhood.
Growth in manufacturing output that does not reach these residents would do little for economic mobility
in industrial cities.

We urge the agencies to keep the purpose test and clarify it, for example by confirming that financing
which creates or retains manufacturing and production jobs accessible to LMI workers, or that is located
in or near LMI census tracts, satisfies the test, and by recognizing workforce housing near industrial
employment centers as responsive to community development needs. Before eliminating the purpose test,
the agencies should analyze what additional activities would qualify, where those activities are likely to
occur, and whether bank financing could shift away from activities that create or retain jobs for LMI people
or in LMI communities.

4. Less Scrutiny and Reporting Would Make Credit Gaps Harder to Identify

Under the current rule, banks above the large-bank threshold annually collect and report data on small
business, small farm and community development loans. The proposal would limit these requirements to
banks with more than $10 billion in assets, meaning that more than 400 banks would no longer collect and
report this data. According to NCRC, the change would eliminate roughly 11% of CRA small business
lending data nationwide.

Kresge conducts due diligence on complex community development transactions, and CRA performance
evaluations and public lending data are among the few consistent sources of information about which banks
are active in a market and where credit needs are unmet. Our CDFI and municipal partners use the same
information to find credit deserts and decide where to direct limited subsidy. Without it, investors, local
governments, researchers and regulators would have a harder time telling whether capital is reaching the
neighborhoods and small manufacturers that national policy is trying to support. Before reducing reporting
requirements, the agencies should analyze the effect on the ability of the public and the agencies themselves
to assess whether banks are meeting the credit needs of LMI communities.

identifying permanent job creation, retention, or improvement for low- or moderate-income persons or in
low- or moderate-income geographies as qualifying purposes).
1191 Fed. Reg. at 52,13334.
12Id. at 52,133.

 5
 Conclusion
Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:

 identify which LMI communities would receive less CRA scrutiny under the proposal;
 quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community development

 activities subject to CRA evaluation, including bank financing of CDFIs and purchases of LIHTC
 equity;
 assess whether the effects would be concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
 including older industrial cities, rural communities and communities of color;
 evaluate how reduced community development activity would interact with the Administration's
 stated goal of expanding domestic manufacturing; or
 consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
 meaningful community accountability.

Given these omissions and the concerns described above, the Kresge Foundation believes the OCC and
FDIC should withdraw this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and released
for public comment. The proposal likely requires considerable changes to prevent significant declines in
CRA-related activity.

The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting community
credit needs, including in the industrial cities where much of a manufacturing expansion will take place.
The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that accountability without first
demonstrating that the changes are consistent with the CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire
communities, including LMI neighborhoods.

We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days. The proposal
is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant changes to bank classifications,
community development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA
implementation. Given the breadth of the proposal, and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
CDFIs, community organizations and other stakeholders that do not have dedicated regulatory staff,
additional time is warranted. We therefore request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment
deadline by at least 60 days.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment. We would welcome the opportunity to share more about our
experience financing housing, community facilities and economic development in Detroit and other
industrial cities.

Sincerely,

The Kresge Foundation

Dear Comptroller and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Representatives:
On behalf of the Baltimore City Youth Action Board (BCYAB), we are writing to express our opposition to the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. We are concerned that this proposal would weaken banks’ obligations to invest in, lend to, and provide essential services to low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities, while reducing transparency and accountability.
BCYAB is a youth-led organization that advocates for young people experiencing or at risk of homelessness and housing instability in Baltimore City. Our work centers the voices and lived experiences of young people who face barriers to safe, stable, and affordable housing, economic opportunity, and access to essential resources. We recognize that strong community investment is critical to addressing these challenges and creating pathways for young people and families to thrive.
The proposed changes threaten the financial resources that communities rely on to support affordable housing, community development, small businesses, and essential services. Reducing banks’ incentives and obligations to serve LMI communities could undermine local organizations and initiatives working to address economic inequality and housing instability. For young people, these investments can help strengthen the neighborhoods, services, and support systems necessary to build stable futures.
We are particularly concerned about the potential consequences for Baltimore and communities throughout Maryland. Equitable community revitalization requires sustained investment, meaningful accountability, and policies that ensure financial institutions serve the needs of the communities in which they operate. Weakening CRA requirements risks widening existing disparities and limiting opportunities for communities that already face significant barriers to economic mobility.
We urge the OCC and FDIC to reconsider the proposed rule and preserve strong CRA requirements that promote responsible lending, community development investment, access to financial services, and transparent accountability. Regulators should prioritize the needs of low- and moderate-income communities and ensure that community members and organizations have meaningful opportunities to understand and evaluate banks’ performance.
As a youth-led organization, we believe that young people deserve to grow up in communities where they can access stable housing, economic opportunity, and the resources necessary to thrive. Protecting strong CRA regulations is an important part of ensuring that Baltimore communities have the investment and support they need, both now and for future generations.
Thank you for considering our comments and for the opportunity to share our perspective on this important matter.
Sincerely,
Baltimore City Youth Action Board

To Whom it May Concern:

Woodforest National Bank ("Woodforest" or "Bank") appreciates the opportunity to
provide the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation (FDIC) with its comments on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
(NPR) for modernizing the regulations of the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). The
Bank recognizes the issuing agencies' efforts to modernize the CRA regulatory
framework in a manner that seeks to align evaluation standards with banks' business
models, promote responsiveness to local community needs, and preserve the CRA's
core statutory purpose of encouraging banks to help meet the credit needs of the
communities they serve.

Headquartered in The Woodlands, TX and operating across 17 states, Woodforest is an
interstate financial institution with total assets of $9 billion, including $8.1 billion in
deposits, as of June 30, 2026. The Bank employs over 4,300 individuals and operates
more than 700 branches. Despite ranking 184th in total assets and 169th in total
deposits, Woodforest ranks within the banking industry's top 10 in number of CRA
assessment areas (AAs) with 198. With branches predominantly located inside major
retail and grocery store lobbies ("in-store branches"), the Bank enjoys unparalleled
opportunities to build customer relationships and provide financial solutions for
residents of all income levels.

Woodforest is not a traditional mortgage lender. Rather, its primary retail products are
small-dollar, patiently termed consumer loans. Described as "innovative" in consecutive
CRA Performance Evaluations, these loans provide responsible, credit-building
alternatives to "payday" and other short-term, high-interest lenders known for creating
 debt traps in low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities. Supplementing
Woodforest's retail lending are innovative, complex and responsive community
development (CD) loans, investments and services that play an essential role in meeting
the credit needs of communities across the Bank's 198 AAs. Together, these retail and
community development activities have enabled Woodforest to earn consecutive
"Outstanding" CRA examination ratings.

Woodforest recognizes aspects of the NPR that would promote greater flexibility within
the CRA framework. Specifically, the Bank supports:

 Providing the option for Intermediate Banks to elect evaluation under Large Bank
 procedures or to pursue a CRA Strategic Plan under a more flexible framework;

 Publishing an illustrative list of qualifying CD activities, along with a process for
 confirming eligibility for activities not included on the list, to increase certainty;

 Providing CRA credit for prior-period CD loans that remain on the balance sheet,
 thereby incentivizing longer-term, patient CD capital so often needed in LMI
 communities.

At the same time, Woodforest believes certain aspects of the proposal would benefit
from refinement. It therefore offers the following recommendations to ensure that CRA
evaluations appropriately recognize the wide range of business strategies that financial
institutions employ to meet community credit needs.

 1. Allow banks to choose between "Option 1" and "Option 2" to determine major
 product lines based on their business models.

 The NPR proposes two alternatives for determining a bank's major product lines
 under the lending test. Option 1 would apply a quantitative, institution-level
 approach that selects a bank's two largest product lines measured by a
 combination of dollar volume and loan count. Option 2 would apply a more
 flexible approach that considers the bank's overall business strategy, capacity to
 lend in the AA, and the extent to which the product line meaningfully contributes
 to meeting local credit needs.

 Rather than prescribing a single methodology for identifying major product lines,
 the agencies should permit banks to elect either Option 1 or Option 2 based on
 their business models and lending strategies. The quantitative approach of
 Option 1 offers predictability that would suit some institutions whose largest
 product lines (mortgages, business loans, etc.), measured by a combination of
 dollar volume and loan count, already align with how they meet community
 credit needs. It is less well suited to institutions whose primary lending products
 address specialized customer and market needs, such as Woodforest's
 responsive small-dollar consumer loans. These loans' lower balances could

 Page 2 of 5
  leave that major product line underweighted in the Lending Test even when loan
 count is substantial. Option 2 would better accommodate unique lending
 strategies by considering how a product line contributes to meeting community
 credit needs within the context of the bank's business strategy. Ultimately, banks
 should be free to design products around the customers they serve. CRA should
 be flexible enough to evaluate those models, not a reason an institution chooses
 to offer or withhold a product. Any final rule should preserve both options.

2. Ensure "meaningful assessment" standards reflect an institution's capacity to
 serve local markets.

 The proposed 30-loan threshold for a "meaningful assessment" is a reasonable
 statistical starting point. Woodforest appreciates, however, that the NPR
 contemplates examiner discretion to analyze fewer than 30 loans when a
 meaningful assessment remains possible. Such flexibility is essential because
 meaningful performance should be evaluated within the context of an
 institution's capacity to serve a market, including factors such as branch
 presence, deposit share, and local market characteristics. This consideration is
 especially relevant for institutions operating across numerous AAs with widely
 varying demographic and economic conditions. Woodforest, for example,
 operates in 198 different AAs, 74 of which (37%) are served by a single branch.
 Despite this broad footprint, the Bank's average FDIC deposit market share
 outside its headquarters AA is only 0.04%. In some rural, sparsely populated, or
 otherwise economically challenged communities, meaningful responsiveness
 may not equate to 30 specific product line originations during an evaluation
 period. Applying the threshold as a cutoff could discourage continued
 engagement in such markets where lending opportunities may be limited even
 though CD financing and service needs remain significant.

 Accordingly, any final rule should establish the presumption that AAs with fewer
 than 30 major product loans will be evaluated, with examiner judgment reserved
 only for situations where a meaningful assessment truly cannot be performed.
 Such evaluations should be conducted relative to the institution's capacity to
 serve the market and other relevant performance context.

3. Strengthen the consideration of CD financing within the Intermediate Bank
 rating framework.

 Under the current Large Bank framework, CD lending has historically
 supplemented retail lending performance and contributed materially to Lending
 Test conclusions. CD loans often involve longer terms, flexible underwriting,
 layered capital sources, and partnerships with Community Development
 Financial Institutions (CDFIs), Minority Depository Institutions (MDIs), and
 myriad other nonprofit partners. Those attributes are typically more innovative,

 Page 3 of 5
  complex, and responsive than conventional lending. As a result, CD lending has
 traditionally received distinct recognition in CRA evaluations capable of
 significantly influencing a bank's overall rating.

 The same is true of CD investments. They frequently complete capital stacks
 and support flexible CD solutions, such as: (1) equity for projects involving
 affordable housing, small business development, and community revitalization;
 (2) partnerships with CDFIs, MDIs, Small Business Investment Companies
 (SBICs), and innovative social impact funds; and (3) other forms of patient
 capital that lending alone often does not provide. In practice, CD lending and CD
 investing often function as essential complementary tools that work together to
 address community needs holistically.

 The proposed Intermediate Bank framework would reduce the influence of both
 CD lending and CD investments on overall CRA rating outcomes. CD loans would
 no longer contribute directly to the Lending Test. Instead, they would be
 evaluated alongside CD investments and CD services within a separate CD Test
 that carries less influence on an institution's overall rating than the proposed
 retail-focused Lending Test. As a result, exceptional CD financing, whether
 through lending or investment, would have less ability to affect overall rating
 outcomes despite often being among a bank's most impactful activities.

 The agencies should ensure innovative, complex, and responsive CD lending and
 investing can meaningfully influence CRA rating beyond the limited confines of
 the proposed CD test. This could be accomplished either by including CD lending
 in the Lending Test while providing distinct, rating-influential consideration for CD
 investments, or by simply ensuring that both CD lending and CD investing are
 capable of influencing an institution's overall CRA rating.

 Preserving long-established incentives for both forms of CD financing is
 essential for the continued flow of flexible, patient capital to LMI communities. It
 would also allow CRA ratings to reflect an institution's responsiveness to
 community credit needs more fully and accurately.

4. Achieve interagency alignment to support durable CRA modernization.

 Woodforest encourages the OCC, FDIC, and Federal Reserve to work toward a
 consistent and coordinated CRA framework. Differing regulatory approaches
 can increase complexity, create uncertainty, and make modernization efforts
 more difficult to implement successfully. A durable CRA framework should
 provide institutions with confidence that expectations will be applied
 consistently, regardless of charter type or primary federal regulator. The Federal

 Page 4 of 5
  Reserve's decision not to join the current proposal highlights the importance of
 continued interagency collaboration as CRA modernization moves forward.
 Greater alignment among the federal banking agencies would reduce the
 potential for regulatory fragmentation while increasing the likelihood of
 successful and durable reform. Woodforest therefore encourages the agencies
 to pursue a final rule that reflects the broadest possible interagency consensus.
Woodforest is hopeful these recommendations will be helpful to the OCC and the FDIC
as the rulemaking process moves forward. The Bank remains committed to helping
meet the credit needs of the communities it serves and encourages a final rule that
preserves flexibility for diverse business models. If you have any questions regarding
the content of this letter or would like additional information, please contact Doug
Schaeffer, Chief CRA Officer, at dschaeffer@woodforest.com. Once again, thank you
for the opportunity to comment.
Sincerely,

For nearly half a century, CRA has driven banks to extend private capital financing to local

spurred lending and investments in homeownership, small businesses, health care,
childcare, and other community needs, but nowhere is its impact more pronounced than in
the effect CRA has had on the production of affordable rental housing through the Low
Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing Credit) program.
The Housing Credit, our nation's most important tool for the production of affordable rental
housing, relies heavily on investments from banks subject to CRA. In fact, approximately
80 percent of equity investments in the Housing Credit each year come from CRA-
motivated bank investors, according to a 2025 study by the accounting firm CohnReznick.1
Banks make these investments not only to receive the modest return provided by the tax
advantages associated with investing in Housing Credit properties, but also because the
full CRA examination for large banks includes a distinct investment test. Because Housing
Credit investment yields are typically modest, large banks often could get a more
substantial yield from making other forms of investment but often still choose to invest in
the Housing Credit because Housing Credit investments help banks meet their CRA
obligations.

the full CRA examination, including the investment test, could reduce competition in the

produced. Of the 642 banks currently classified as large banks, only 256 would maintain
that designation under the proposal--a decline of over 60 percent, according to the

National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders (NAAHL). This leaves only 6 percent of
banks in the current large bank classification subject to the full CRA exam. According to a
survey by the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC), banks with assets in the
$1.649 billion to $10 billion range invested at least $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity over

banks in this asset range invested up to $2 billion in Housing Credit equity over the past five
years.

If the OCC/FDIC proposal is made final, newly classified intermediate banks would no
longer need to invest in the low and moderate-income communities they are supposed to
serve because they would no longer be subject to the investment test, despite still having
more general community development obligations as an intermediate-sized bank. This is
because, for various reasons, it is often easier for banks to support community
development activities through lending rather than equity investment.

Moreover, the CRA NPR undercuts recent congressional action to strengthen and expand
the Housing Credit and facilitate more bank investment in the program. The One Big
Beautiful Bill Act (also known as the Working Families Tax Cuts Act) included a substantial
increase in Housing Credit authority and expanded the 4 percent Housing Credit program
to increase supply, while the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act raised the limit on banks'
public welfare investments (PWI) to allow them to increase their Housing Credit
investments. The provision lifting the PWI cap would mostly impact many of the same
banks that would be reclassified as intermediate banks. Thus, the CRA changes under
consideration by the OCC and FDIC could greatly dilute these legislative accomplishments
and undercut congressional goals of providing more affordable rental homes.

The consequences of this proposal would be most damaging to smaller communities that
now benefit from being in the CRA assessment area of one or more large banks but may no

longer be if the OCC and FDIC change the definition of large bank as proposed. A survey by
the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC) finds that approximately one-third of
Housing Credit equity invested through syndicators by banks in the $412 $10 million asset
range supported rural markets between 2021 and 2024, indicating that these banks play an
outsized role in investing in smaller communities. Credit pricing for properties in many
urban areas--which are more likely to have at least one and often multiple banks
competing to invest in Housing Credit developments because of overlapping assessment
areas--tends to be much higher than pricing in rural and other smaller communities that
are not part of assessment areas for large banks subject to the investment test.

 Churchill provides construction and permanent financing for rural multifamily apartments
throughout the United States. We have seen the tax credit pricing disparity between urban,

competitively with larger banks in more populated areas. Therefore, these new guidelines
will produce an unfair pricing matrix that will diminish the ability to produce rural
multifamily housing.

Alternatives to the Primary Proposal

The OCC and FDIC included two alternatives to the primary proposal to set new thresholds
for various bank size classifications related to CRA. The first would raise the large bank
asset threshold from $1.649 billion to $3.252 billion. This alternative would still have far-
reaching negative consequences compared to the current large bank threshold but is
substantially less disruptive to Housing Credit investment than the primary proposal to
raise the large bank threshold to $10 billion.

Churchill has seen the impact of CRA first-hand. We strongly encourage the OCC and FDIC
to leave the thresholds as they currently stand under the 1995 CRA rule, consistent with
the direction the Federal Reserve--the third bank regulator--appears to be taking. If the
OCC and FDIC move forward with changes to CRA regulations, we strongly urge
maintaining the lowest possible threshold for large banks and adopting policies to
strengthen the Housing Credit market in all communities, including rural and smaller
markets.

The Public Housing Authorities Directors Association (PHADA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the OCC and FDIC’s proposed Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rule. PHADA represents approximately 1,900 public housing authorities (HAs) across the nation that administer the Public Housing, Housing Choice Voucher (HCV), Project-Based Voucher, Rental Assistance Demonstration (RAD), and other federal affordable housing programs. Our members are on the ground across the country serving low- and moderate-income (LMI) households and communities, often providing housing and other services in LMI neighborhoods.

In summary, PHADA opposes this CRA proposal. The proposed rule would subject fewer banks to community development evaluation under CRA, which would reduce bank capital flowing into Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) deals. The rollback of CRA exam criterion for many banks will lead to less investment and lending in the LMI communities served by HA’s nationwide, reducing access to homeownership for residents and hindering local economic growth. This rule could lead to a 120% increase in the number of people living in community development deserts across America. PHADA's specific concerns are detailed in our comment letter.

PHADA thanks the OCC and FDIC for the opportunity to comment and looks forward to working with the regulators to ensure that HAs across the country can continue to receive bank financing to preserve and develop affordable housing units.
