Dear Chair Hill and Comptroller Gould:

PHADA appreciates the opportunity to reply to the OCC and FDIC's proposed new Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) rule. PHADA represents approximately 1,900 public housing authorities (HAs)
across the nation that administer the Public Housing, Housing Choice Voucher, Project-Based Voucher,
Rental Assistance Demonstration (RAD), and other federal affordable housing programs. Our members are
on the ground across the country serving low- and moderate-income (LMI) households and communities,
often providing housing and other services in LMI neighborhoods.

In summary, PHADA opposes this CRA proposal. The proposed rule would reclassify bank asset thresholds
determining how banks are evaluated under the CRA such that fewer banks would be evaluated on
community development investments in low- and moderate-income (LMI) areas, likely leading to less
lending and investment from banks.

Our specific concerns are as follows:

 1
  The proposal would subject fewer banks to community development evaluation under CRA, which
 would reduce bank capital flowing into Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) deals,
 potentially weakening tax credit pricing and ultimately resulting in fewer affordable units
 constructed.

 If OCC and FDIC finalize this proposal, it would cause a 120% increase in the number of people
 living in community development deserts nationwide.1

 By loosening requirements on banks with under $1 billion in assets, the rule would
 disproportionately impact rural communities, many of which are served by PHADA members.

 The rollback of CRA exam criterion for many banks will lead to less investment and lending in the
 LMI communities served by HA's nationwide, reducing access to homeownership for residents and
 hindering local economic growth.

This CRA rule would also blunt positive impacts of recently-enacted legislation. The One Big Beautiful
Bill Act boosted 9% LIHTC allocations by 12% and loosened the 4% bond test from 50% to 25%. Plus, the
21st Century ROAD to Housing Act raised the cap on banks' public welfare investments from 15% to 20%
of capital and surplus. These measures expand the supply of credits and banks' capacity to invest in them,
but this expansion will be greatly undermined if the new CRA rule reduces demand for banks to make those
investments.

Overall, this proposed rule would weaken banks' incentives to finance affordable housing, reduce the
community development investments that power local economies and small businesses, and inhibit many
residents' ability to access banking services. For these reasons and more, PHADA recommends that
regulators:

 Retract this proposed rule and do not finalize a rule which only covers the OCC and FDIC.
 Extend the comment period to at least 120 days.
 Provide broad economic analysis on the projected impacts of the CRA rule on LMI communities.
 The FDIC, OCC, and Federal Reserve should collaboratively promulgate a CRA framework that

 incentivizes banks to direct capital and investment to LMI communities.

The Current CRA Framework
Enacted in 1977 as a response to historical discrimination and redlining, the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA) requires banks to assess and report on how they meet the credit needs of the entire community where
they are chartered. The CRA categorizes banks and applies a regulatory framework based on their size. In
general, larger banks are examined on their lending, investments, and branch services to maintain a strong
CRA rating, while small banks are only evaluated on lending.

1 CRA Coverage Map -- NAAHL

 2
 Under the current CRA framework,2 the appropriate regulatory agency examines a bank's track record of
meeting the credit needs of its community by assessing its retail lending, investment and services, and its
Community Development (CD) activities. A strong CRA rating helps banks to secure approval for mergers,
acquisitions, branch openings, and relocations from federal regulators--making the CRA a powerful
incentive to drive capital into communities that would otherwise be unserved.

Why the CRA matters to Public Housing Authorities
The CRA is a key driver of capital into under-resourced communities that HAs frequently serve. In 2024
alone, the CRA incentivized more than $430 billion in bank loans and investments in LMI communities,3
nearly six times the combined federal budgets of HUD, USDA's Rural Housing Service, the Small Business
Administration, and the CDFI Fund. Of that $430 billion, about $168 billion was in lending and investment
for affordable housing and community development.

HAs that are revitalizing properties through Rental Assistance Demonstration (RAD) or mixed-finance
deals depend upon financing from banks to make transactions viable. The CRA is central to supporting
demand for the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC); a 2025 study estimates that 71% of equity
investments in the LIHTC come from CRA-motivated bank investors.4 Moreover, one-third of LIHTC
equity investments from banks with under $10 billion in assets supported rural markets these banks would
no longer be subject to the investment test under the rule, jeopardizing these investments.5

The proposed rule would reduce the number of banks that are incentivized to invest in the LIHTC, thus
reducing demand for the credits. If this rule were finalized, PHAs that have mixed-finance or RAD deals in
the pipeline could receive less investment from banks, and PHAs' LIHTC deals would attract fewer equity
investments. This translates into fewer affordable units that can be developed amid the ever-worsening
housing crisis, especially in rural areas.

Moreover, as residents improve their employment opportunities and increase their income, they also need
access to reliable and affordable banking services. Families striving for self-sufficiency rely on access to
affordable, small value, loan services provided by bank branches in their communities. For instance, a
household may need to purchase a vehicle to access better employment opportunities, so access to small
dollar used car loans can be important. By its very nature, the CRA influences where bank branches are
located, and it could lead to the closure of banks that serve LMI neighborhoods. The proposed rule weakens
or eliminates the incentives of the CRA regulations to provide these services and meet community needs.

2 Federal Register: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, as most recently codified by the OCC in 2021 and
 preserved in Appendix G to 12 CFR Part 25 (OCC); 12 CFR Part 228 (Federal Reserve); 12 CFR Part 345 (FDIC)

3 Incentive to Impact: How CRA Leverages Private Investments into Affordable Housing, Homeownership, Small
 Businesses, and Local Economies | Center for Affordable Housing Lending

4 2025 Affordable Housing Credit Study | CohnReznick
5 Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC)

 3
 Many households are also striving for the American Dream of homeownership as they pursue upward
mobility, and affordable mortgages for lower-cost homes can be an essential part of that process. The CRA
plays a critical role in incentivizing banks to offer safe, affordable credit through CRA-qualifying mortgage
loans. Nearly one in four mortgage loans in 2024 were incentivized by CRA, as banks financed nearly
504,000 mortgage loans with a total value of more than $100 billion to either LMI borrowers or in the LMI
communities in their CRA assessment areas.6 This proposed rule could jeopardize banks' mortgage lending
to prospective first-time homebuyers in LMI and rural areas.

Overall, this proposed rule could result in residents and HAs losing access to banking services, loss of
investment in affordable housing from banks, and adverse impacts on the ability to develop new units amid
the worsening housing crisis. For these reasons, PHADA believes the proposed rule would be a net harm
to HAs and the residents they serve, and thus we urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw this proposed rule.

Impacts of revised bank size thresholds
The proposed rule would increase the small bank threshold from $412 million to $1 billion, and the top of
the intermediate category would rise from $1.649 billion to $10 billion. Under these changes, nearly 80%
of OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks would be treated as small banks, and banks with $10 billion or less
in assets would be exempt from CRA data collection, maintenance, and reporting requirements.

Ultimately, many banks would be reclassified from a large bank to a small or intermediate bank
classification, thereby reducing their obligations under the CRA. Under the proposal, 79.8% of all banks
would be considered small.7 Only the largest 6% of all banks would remain subject to the full CRA exam.8
Six states would see the number of large banks in their state cut by at least half, and 29 states would see the
number of large banks in their jurisdiction decline by at least one-third.

Analysis by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) illustrates how large the potential
reduction could be. Modeling the proposed rule's effect on 69 OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks, NCRC
estimates annual community development financing would fall to about $31 billion, a reduction of roughly
$71 billion per year--if those banks reduced their activity to the minimum benchmark levels.9 While this
is a modeled scenario, it shows how much the proposal would loosen banks' commitment to lend and invest
in distressed and LMI neighborhoods across the nation.

Further, analysis from the National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders (NAAHL) indicates that,
under the proposed rule, 813 banks would be reclassified as "small" and would have no community
development loan or investment obligations.10 This will have a disproportionate impact on small rural
communities. States like Mississippi would see 41% of banks lose community development obligations,

7 Federal Register: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
8 Community Reinvestment Act | NCRC
9 The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters NCRC
10 CRA National Fact Sheet (August 2026) | NAAHL

 4
 while 42% of banks in Iowa, 44% of banks in Georgia, and 48% of banks in Louisiana would lose all
community development obligations. HAs in those states and other nonprofit groups like housing
counseling agencies would have fewer banks willing to finance their projects or programs.

Raising the large-bank threshold to $10 billion means 417 banks would no longer receive the full CRA
examination,11 which includes lending, investment, and a separate service test that evaluates branch delivery
systems and banking services. The elimination of the full CRA examination for these banks removes their
incentive to provide loans, investments, and retain full-service bank branches. This would mean roughly
5,000 branches in low- and moderate-income census tracts, including 4,000 branches in minority-majority
tracts, would no longer be evaluated under the CRA branch service test and thereby removing incentives
for banks to maintain those branches.

Question 1 of the proposed rule asks whether to go even further and raise the intermediate bank cap up to
$30 billion and raise the small bank threshold up to $10 billion. Under this scenario, more than 1,500 banks
(36% of all banks nationwide) would lose the incentive to provide community development investments or
loans--these 1,500 banks loaned nearly $27 billion for community development in one year, which was
35% of all such loans made that year.12 This would represent a catastrophic hit to the capital available in
under-resourced LMI communities which PHADA members serve.

Impacts of changes to CRA examinations
In addition to the raised asset thresholds, PHADA is also concerned about the targeted changes to CRA
examinations. The proposed rule would let banks earn CRA credit for financing activities without having
to demonstrate that the activity creates, retains, or improves jobs for low- and moderate-income people or
in LMI communities. In addition, the OCC and FDIC are proposing two options for defining a bank's
"major product lines," with the goal of minimizing both the type and amount of lending reviewed for CRA
performance.

The rule also proposes to remove the requirement that intermediate banks pass both their community
development test and their lending test to receive an overall passing CRA rating. The regulators claim,
without support, that requiring intermediate banks to pass both tests to receive a satisfactory rating is an
"artificial constraint"--a dubious claim when nearly 98% of banks are receiving passing scores on their
CRA examinations.13 It is nave to expect that these banks will increase their community development
investments and loans without any incentive to do so. It is far more likely this will result in a reduction in
lending and investments to LMI communities.

The proposed rule would allow an infrastructure project to receive CRA credit if it "benefits or serves" a
CRA-eligible area, even if the project delivers little meaningful benefit to LMI residents and does not help

11 The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters | NCRC
12 NAAHL Cautions Against Changes to CRA that Would Reduce Affordable Housing and Community Development

 Outcomes | NAAHL
13 Do CRA Ratings Reflect Differences in Performance: An Examination Using Federal Reserve Data | NCRC

 5
 preserve or strengthen the community. For example, a data center located in an LMI tract may qualify for
CRA credit, despite creating few permanent jobs and providing little direct benefit to residents. This change
dilutes the power of the CRA's incentive, jeopardizing loans and investments presently going toward
affordable housing. It allows banks to achieve higher returns financing more lucrative projects that merely
"benefit or serve" an area rather than directly serving it, making it more likely they will direct capital away
from projects that truly serve LMI residents.

In highly cost-burdened markets, the proposal would expand CRA consideration to certain middle-income
rental housing activities--directing CRA-motivated capital away from LMI communities. This would allow
banks to shift investments toward middle-income households that would yield higher returns, which dilutes
available bank financing to affordable housing for lower-income renters.

Changes to the treatment of community development grants would curtail bank support for community
development financial institutions (CDFIs), Community Development Corporations (CDCs), housing
counselors, and other local housing-focused organizations. The proposed rule would prohibit large banks
from making grants or donations to recipients that have overhead costs exceeding 15%. This is unrealistic
in the current regulatory environment; overhead costs support staffing, technology, financial management,
compliance, and other resources needed for service efficient delivery.

By redefining whether and how a bank's "major product lines" get CRA consideration, the proposal may
lead to closure of bank branches in LMI areas and loss of banking services for residents in these areas. The
rule proposes two options for defining a large bank's "major product lines", both of which would minimize
both the type and amount of lending reviewed for CRA performance. One option proposes to define a
bank's two largest categories of loans as their major product lines, which would be calculated based on
total lending leaving smaller rural communities that receive a lower lending volume at a disadvantage.
The rule also proposes to incorporate a bank's major product lines into how banks determine their
geographic CRA assessment areas by only requiring banks to include geographies where they have
"originated or purchased a substantial portion of its loans in its major product lines." If a bank does not do
much consumer lending in a given geography, it can exclude that area from its CRA assessment area thus
leaving less incentive for the bank to maintain that physical branch location altogether. This would leave
1,006,648 people in tracts with no CRA coverage a 120% increase in community development deserts.14

FDIC and OCC Should Retract this Proposed Rule
It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet community needs, and this rule has
been proposed with insufficient analytical basis and not enough time to comment. The proposal itself offers
little to no analysis of the impact of reducing the types of lending that are reviewed in CRA evaluations.
Instead, the agencies "preliminarily believe the potential negative impact is unlikely to be significant
because, in many instances, banks provide those loans primarily for business reasons rather than to address

14 NAAHL CRA Comment Letter Final 10/13/26

 6
 CRA obligations." This is a fundamental misreading of the congressional intent of the CRA. The CRA was
passed to give banks an affirmative obligation to serve all communities. Lawmakers in 1977 recognized
that banks needed to be incentivized to make loans and investments in LMI neighborhoods, as banks would
chase higher returns elsewhere and not make investments in LMI areas without the CRA.15

Many PHADA members serve small town and rural areas with few banking services and comparatively
less LIHTC investment from banks, which are further jeopardized by this proposal. Before finalizing any
CRA rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce lending, services or
investment available to LMI and rural communities, how bank investment in the LIHTC would be
influenced by the changes, and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or
disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.

Additionally, PHADA requests that the comment period be extended to at least 120 days. A mere 60 days
is not sufficient for effective analysis and comment on this complex 350+ page proposed regulation, which
poses over 60 specific questions to the public for comment. This rule would have far-reaching impacts that
must be fully understood before a final rule is promulgated. Notably, when the FDIC and OCC proposed a
CRA rule in 2020, the initial comment window was extended.16 In summary, our recommendations are:

 Retract this proposed rule and do not finalize a rule which only covers the OCC and FDIC.

To Whom It May Concern:

 The New York Bankers Association ("NYBA")1 appreciates the opportunity to comment on
the proposed amendments to the regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act
("CRA")2. We appreciate the agencies' efforts to modernize the federal CRA framework, reduce
unnecessary regulatory burdens, and provide greater clarity regarding CRA evaluations and
qualifying activities. At the same time, we encourage regulators to carefully consider the unique
challenges facing New York institutions and ensure that any final rule promotes consistency,
minimizes unnecessary burden, and preserves flexibility for institutions with differing business
models and community footprints.3

 1. Consistency Among Regulatory Frameworks

 New York occupies a unique position as one of only a handful of states with its own state
CRA legislation and regulatory framework applicable to state-chartered institutions. As a result,
many New York banks are regulated simultaneously by the New York State Department of
Financial Services and either the Federal Reserve Board ("FRB") or the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation ("FDIC"). Conformity and cooperation among state and federal regulators
are therefore essential concerns for New York institutions.

 For decades, substantial alignment between state and federal CRA frameworks has enabled
state-chartered institutions to understand regulatory expectations clearly and implement
compliance programs efficiently, helping ensure that their CRA programs remain focused on
serving communities rather than navigating conflicting regulatory requirements. Consistent

 1
 standards have benefited banks, regulators, and community stakeholders alike by creating
transparent expectations and meaningful performance comparisons. NYBA is concerned that
this proposal could fragment CRA oversight at a time when consistency should be a priority.

 The Proposal was advanced by the OCC and FDIC without participation from the FRB,
creating uncertainty and raising a risk that institutions could be subject to materially different
CRA standards and examination frameworks. For New York institutions, this raises the prospect
of three distinct CRA regulatory frameworks: one administered by the OCC and FDIC, another
maintained by the FRB, and New York's existing state CRA framework. The resulting
inconsistencies could create unnecessary complexity and compliance burdens, particularly for
state-chartered institutions subject to both state and federal oversight. A coordinated regulatory
approach has historically served institutions, regulators and communities more effectively.

 A divergent federal-state regulatory framework would also increase compliance burdens and
operational complexity for institutions operating across multiple regulatory jurisdictions. Rather
than reducing regulatory burden, the existence of multiple CRA frameworks would increase
costs and divert resources away from community development activities such as affordable
housing initiatives, community development investments, financial empowerment programs, and
instead redirect them toward regulatory administration.

 The effects would also extend beyond financial institutions. Community organizations,
affordable housing partners, local leaders, and other stakeholders benefit from clear and
consistent standards regarding how CRA performance is measured and evaluated. Divergent
frameworks would make it more difficult for community groups to understand how banks are
evaluated, reducing transparency and limiting their ability to engage effectively with financial
institutions regarding local credit and community development needs. Accordingly, NYBA
strongly encourages federal banking agencies with CRA oversight responsibilities to adopt and
maintain a coordinated and consistent regulatory framework.

 2. Asset-Based Thresholds

 NYBA appreciates the agencies' efforts to recategorize small and intermediate banks and
increase the small bank asset threshold to include institutions under $1 billion and intermediate
bank asset threshold to between $1 billion and $10 billion. We are also supportive of the
Proposal's confirmation that institutions with assets under $1 billion would not be subjected to
burdensome data collection and reporting requirements, providing meaningful relief for smaller
institutions.

 At the same time, asset size alone does not necessarily reflect a bank's business model,
market presence, lending activity, or overall impact on the communities it serves. Some
institutions with assets below $10 billion hold significant deposit market share, operate across
multiple metropolitan areas, or maintain extensive lending operations. Institutions with similar
asset sizes can have dramatically different geographic footprints, market presence, lending
activities, and community development capacity. Thus, asset-based thresholds can quickly
become arbitrary and may not accurately reflect a bank's actual impact within the communities it
serves.

 NYBA has consistently advocated for regulatory approaches that consider both a bank's size
and its community presence when determining the appropriate CRA evaluation framework.
Such an approach would preserve appropriate regulatory relief for smaller institutions while
ensuring that CRA evaluations more accurately reflect a bank's impact. Accordingly, NYBA

 2
 encourages the agencies to incorporate greater flexibility into the proposed evaluation
framework, allowing consideration of an institution's business model, market presence, and
community impact rather than relying exclusively on asset size.

 3. Community Development and Retail Services

 NYBA is concerned that the proposal's reduced emphasis on retail banking and community
development services could unintentionally undervalue an important component of how
institutions meet community needs. By narrowing the focus primarily to lending activities and
excluding most consideration of deposit services and other retail banking services, the proposal
may inadvertently reduce regulatory incentives for banks to maintain branches, invest in service
delivery channels, and provide financial education and technical assistance in underserved
communities. Across New York State, NYBA member institutions devote substantial resources
to financial education, volunteer service, technical assistance, and community partnerships.

 NYBA strongly supports maintaining a meaningful Service Test that recognizes the impact of
bank services on low- and moderate-income households and communities. Collectively, our
membership has committed hundreds of thousands of hours and significant additional resources
over the last decade providing CRA-qualified services throughout our underserved communities.
In particular, community service is at the core of the community banking model and should
maintain significant recognition through CRA evaluations.

 4. Community Impact

 NYBA also encourages regulators to maintain a focus on the actual impact of CRA activities
within local communities. An effective CRA framework should preserve flexibility for institutions
to respond to local community priorities while maintaining clear standards for evaluation.
Regulators should also avoid requirements that discourage community partnerships or divert
resources from community investment to administrative compliance. CRA is most successful
when it promotes meaningful outcomes and allows resources to be deployed where they can
have the greatest impact.

 5. Conclusion

 NYBA appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed revisions to the Community
Reinvestment Act and supports efforts to ensure that CRA regulations remain responsive to
today's financial services environment. Thank you for your consideration of these comments.

would substantially weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).

 The PHRC is the leading civil rights enforcement agency in Pennsylvania, working to ensure
that Pennsylvanians can live, work, and learn, free from unlawful discrimination. The CRA is a
critical tool in advancing fair housing and equitable access to credit and banking services. It ensures
that lending institutions meet the needs of all communities, particularly those historically affected by
redlining, disinvestment, and systemic inequities. Weakening the CRA would undermine decades of
progress and harm communities across Pennsylvania.

 According to the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) the proposed
reclassification of banks would reduce CRA obligations by 87%, significantly decreasing investment
in Pennsylvania communities. It is estimated that 25 out of 100 banks would no longer have
community development obligations. Additionally, 27 out of 62 banks in Pennsylvania would lose
their large bank status. With this proposed rule, fewer banks would have the requirement to have
separate branch evaluations, leaving 159 out of 649 bank branches in Low to Moderate Income
neighborhoods in Pennsylvania at risk of closing, and 29 out of 273 bank branches in communities
of color at risk of closing. Lastly, over 10% of banks would no longer be required to provide data
about who they are lending funds to (https://ncrc.org/cra/).

 If implemented, these changes would significantly reduce investment in affordable housing
and in communities that have long endured the compounded harm of historic redlining. They are
likely to decrease access to banking services in marginalized neighborhoods and obscure lending
activity at a time when transparency around housing opportunities is essential.

 The PHRC recently published an updated edition of its white paper, "The State of Fair
Housing in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania," which examines the significant housing needs that
Pennsylvanians face. This paper analyzes the barriers that Pennsylvanians face in accessing housing
that meets their needs. Findings include a significant shortage in housing that is affordable to
Pennsylvanians that are low or extremely low income and substantial barriers to accessing housing,
including background checks that deny future housing opportunities, based on long-past mistakes,
denial of housing based on a household's source of income, limiting housing opportunities for
survivors of domestic violence, and restrictive zoning that prevents housing diversity, and more.

 In our current housing market, where there is a significant shortage of housing, these urgent
issues lead to Pennsylvanians living in housing that does not meet their needs, such as shelters,
overcrowded dwellings, motels, campers, and substandard housing with significant health hazards.
This prevents individuals and families from being able to gain the stability they need to maintain
jobs, get a quality education, and build strong communities. Lending institutions play a critical role
in ensuring access to financial services that enable individuals to build their credit, savings, and

On behalf of the more than 140,000 members of the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), I appreciate
the opportunity to provide comments in response to the Joint Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (proposal) issued
by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
regarding Community Reinvestment Act Regulations.

NAHB is a Washington DC-based trade association representing, among others, companies involved in the
development and construction of for-sale single-family homes, including homes for first-time and low- and
moderate-income (LMI) home buyers, as well as the production and management of affordable multifamily
housing. The ability of the home building industry to meet the demand for housing, including affordable
housing, is facilitated through CRA-driven loans and investments. Therefore, the regulations that guide these
activities are critical to addressing housing supply needs.

The original purpose of the Community Reinvestment Act ("CRA" or "the Act"), to encourage banks to serve
their communities, is as essential today as it was in 1977 when CRA was first enacted. However, as the financial
services industry evolves so does the need for new approaches to meet the Act's statutory intent and NAHB
agrees it is important to update and modernize the regulations to more effectively meet the needs of LMI
families and communities and develop targeted policies that will enhance CRA's impact on affordable housing
and increase housing supply. However, that process must be done while preserving the incentives that have
supported essential affordable housing development such as the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC). NAHB
also believes that restoring long-term certainty to the CRA framework is essential to encouraging the
investments and partnerships needed for CRA to have the greatest impact.

Background

Page 2

CRA was enacted not only to encourage and incent banks to meet the banking needs of the entire communities
in which they have physical facilities, including LMI neighborhoods, but specifically to combat the practice of
"redlining." Redlining referred to a lender's refusal to make loans or offer financial services in communities
deemed risky or unfit for investment due to the income, racial, or ethnic composition of the area. The Act
requires the Federal Reserve, FDIC and OCC (collectively the "federal banking agencies") to evaluate the CRA
performance of the depository institutions each agency supervises. Based on an institution's performance in
meeting the credit needs of its entire community, including LMI neighborhoods, it is assigned a CRA rating and
issued a public performance evaluation by the examiner from its federal banking regulator.

In 2023, the federal banking agencies finalized a new joint CRA regulation. The primary objectives of this rule
were to modernize the CRA and included expanding assessment areas to adapt to changes in the banking
industry, including mobile and internet banking; tailoring performance standards to account for differences in
bank size, business model and local conditions; providing a list of CRA eligible activities focused on LMI
communities and underserved rural communities; incenting bank collaboration with Minority-owned Depository
Institutions (MDIs), Woman-owned Depository Institutions (WDIs), Low-Income Credit Unions (LICUs) or
Treasury Department-certified Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs); and encouraging bank
investments in disaster preparedness and climate resilience activities in LMI neighborhoods.

Under the 2023 CRA Final Rule, as fully implemented, large banks institutions of $2 billion or more would be
subject to four performance tests: the Retail Lending Test; the Retail Services and Products Test; the Community
Development Financing Test; and the Community Development Services Test. Intermediate banks, assets
between $600 million and $2 billion, would be subject to two performance tests: the Retail Lending Test and the
Intermediate Bank Community Development Test. Small banks, under $600 million would be subject to the
Small Bank Lending Test. The federal banking agencies would continue to evaluate banks' performance in the
areas surrounding their main office, branches, or deposit-taking remote service facilities (i.e., facility-based
assessment areas). In addition, the federal banking agencies would evaluate the retail lending performance of
certain large banks in areas outside their facility-based assessment areas where they have concentrations of
retail loans (i.e., retail lending assessment areas) and the retail lending performance of large banks and certain
intermediate and small banks in the nationwide area outside their facility-based assessment areas and retail
lending assessment areas (i.e., outside retail lending areas). Further, the federal banking agencies would
consider community development loans, community development investments, and community development
services both inside and outside of a bank's facility-based assessment areas.

As adopted, the 2023 CRA Final Rule would have become effective on April 1, 2024; however, most substantive
provisions of the rule would not have become applicable until January 1, 2026, or January 1, 2027. During this
transition period, the 2023 CRA Final Rule specified that the 1995 CRA regulations, as reproduced in Appendix G
of the 2023 CRA Final Rule, would remain applicable.

On March 21, 2024, the federal banking agencies issued a supplemental rule to the 2023 CRA Final Rule which
extended the applicability dates of the facility-based assessment area and public file provisions of the 2023 CRA
Final Rule from April 1, 2024, to January 1, 2026. The supplemental rule also included some technical, non-
substantive amendments to the 2023 CRA Final Rule and related regulations.

The complexity and regulatory burdens of the 2023 CRA rule prompted litigation. On February 5, 2024, several
plaintiffs jointly filed suit against the federal banking agencies in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District
of Texas, and the plaintiffs subsequently requested a preliminary injunction on February 9, 2024. On March 29,
2024, the district court granted plaintiffs' request and enjoined the federal banking agencies from enforcing the
2023 CRA Final Rule against the plaintiffs, pending resolution of the litigation. The district court's order also

extended the 2023 CRA Final Rule's effective date of April 1, 2024, along with all other implementation dates,
day for day for each day the injunction remains in place.

On April 18, 2024, the federal banking agencies appealed the district court's preliminary injunction to the U.S.
Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. However, on March 28, 2025, during the pendency of the appeal, the
federal banking agencies made an unopposed motion to stay the appeal pending completion of a new
rulemaking that would propose rescinding the enjoined 2023 CRA Final Rule and reinstating the CRA framework
that existed prior to the 2023 CRA Final Rule. The federal banking agencies publicly announced this intention the
same day. On April 1, 2025, the Fifth Circuit granted the agencies' motion.

On July 16, 2025, the federal banking agencies proposed to rescind the CRA final rule issued on October 24,
2023, and published in the Federal Register on February 1, 2024, as subsequently amended (2023 CRA Final
Rule). The federal banking agencies also proposed to replace the 2023 CRA Final Rule with regulations adopted
by the federal banking agencies and the former Office of Thrift Supervision (OTS) on May 4, 1995, as amended,
and as published in the Electronic Code of Federal Regulations (eCFR) as of March 29, 2024 (1995 CRA
regulations), with conforming amendments to the agencies definition of "small bank" and technical
amendments to the OCC's definition of "small bank" and transition provisions. The federal banking agencies also
proposed technical amendments to their regulations implementing the CRA sunshine requirements of the
Federal Deposit Insurance Act, and the OCC is proposing technical amendments to its Public Welfare
Investments regulation.

NAHB submitted comments agreeing with the agencies' premise that repealing the 2023 CRA regulation and
recodifying the 1995 CRA rules would restore certainty in the CRA framework for stakeholders, limit regulatory
burdens on banks, and ensure that banks continue to focus on the purpose of the CRA. We commended the
federal banking agencies for working together on this joint proposal, and we urged them to quickly reinstitute
the 1995 CRA rules. We were also pleased that recodifying the 1995 CRA rules would preserve the separate CRA
investment test, which has been an essential driver for banks' LIHTC equity investments in affordable rental
housing.

Proposed Rule

On July 31, 2026, OCC and the FDIC (collectively, the agencies) proposed targeted changes to the 1995
framework aimed at more closely aligning the CRA regulatory framework with the statutory mandate by
focusing primarily on lending which the agencies believe is how a community's credit needs are best met. The
Federal Reserve did not join the proposal.

The proposal would increase asset thresholds for banks to reduce regulatory burden:

 A "small bank" would have less than $1 billion in total assets, up from the current threshold of $412
 million.

 A new "intermediate bank" category would replace the existing "intermediate small bank" category and
 cover banks with assets from $1 billion through $10 billion; the current range is $412 million to $1.649
 billion. These banks would be exempt from data collection and reporting requirements and have more
 flexible supervision;

 A "large bank" would have more than $10 billion in assets, compared with the current threshold of more
 than $1.649 billion. Under the proposal, large banks would continue to be subject to the lending test,
 investment test, and service test.

Additionally, the proposal would:

 Focus only on a bank's major product lines when evaluating its retail lending activities;
 Modify the framework for grants and donations by limiting consideration of community development

 (CD) grants to those directly used for a plan, project, or initiative with community development as a
 primary purpose; and requiring large banks to document that recipients of CD grants do not have
 overhead costs in excess of 15 percent;
 Modifying the strategic plan framework aimed at making it more viable and less burdensome option for
 banks.

NAHB Comments

NAHB members are interested in CRA because it motivates banks to participate in activities that support access
to financing for home builders, developers and remodelers; access to affordable mortgage credit for LMI families
and families in LMI census tracts; as well as the production of affordable owner-occupied and rental housing and
community and economic development.

NAHB's response focuses on the areas most relevant to the expertise of home builders and developers and the
association's commitment to affordable homeownership and rental opportunities for LMI families. Our
comments address aspects of the agencies' proposal that impact access to financing for construction of new
homes, align with NAHB's housing advocacy priorities that call for policies to increase housing supply, increase
affordable housing options, and benefit LMI homeowners and renter households and lessen the compliance
burden for community banks.

CRA is, and should continue to be, a major driver for banks to make loans and investments in affordable and
workforce housing. Compliance with CRA mandates, and the impact of banks' CRA activities on regulators'
approval of their future business or mergers, gives banks powerful motivation to lend in LMI communities. It
also has prompted banks to develop innovative mortgage products that enable LMI households to achieve
homeownership. Examples of these products include mortgage loan enhancements such as closing cost
assistance, interest rate buy downs, and down payment assistance. The importance of CRA as a homeownership
vehicle for LMI and workforce households cannot be overstated, since homeownership is the most
straightforward way for families to build wealth. However, community banks should be incentivized to these
activities without overly burdensome regulatory compliance.

Joint Federal Banking Agency Proposal

For the CRA to be relevant going forward, the regulations must take into account current banking practices,
important public policy interests, and increased data availability. Significant developments in all these areas
indicate the timing is appropriate for updated CRA requirements and new approaches for evaluating a bank's
CRA performance. However, for CRA to continue to be successful, the regulations must provide long-term
certainty to banks and stakeholders. NAHB is deeply concerned that the proposal was not issued jointly by all
federal banking agencies, raising immediate questions about whether a durable final rule can be implemented.

Increase Support for LIHTC Program

The LIHTC program is the nation's largest and most effective federal program for producing affordable
multifamily rental housing. As a public-private partnership, LIHTC exemplifies the type of community
development investment the CRA should continue to support and encourage. According to the National Council
of State Housing Agencies, LIHTC has financed more than four million apartments for low-income households

and adds approximately 100,000 to 150,000 units to the affordable housing inventory each year.1 Because LIHTC
properties generally must remain affordable for at least 30 years, these investments provide long-term rent
stability for low-income households. Banks' LIHTC equity investments are essential to the program's success and
have been strongly supported by the CRA framework. These investments help generate the equity needed to
make affordable rental developments financially feasible, while also advancing CRA objectives by supporting
community revitalization and economic activity. LIHTC developments create well-paying construction jobs,
generate local tax revenue, and support ongoing employment for maintenance staff, property managers, and
local vendors. In many cases, LIHTC properties serve as catalysts for broader neighborhood revitalization.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act substantially increased state LIHTC allocations, which makes it especially important
that CRA regulations continue to strongly encourage and reward banks' LIHTC equity investments. NAHB is
concerned that any changes to the CRA framework could inadvertently reduce bank participation in LIHTC
transactions. Accordingly, the agencies should retain and expand current CRA incentives for LIHTC investments,
including by allowing banks to receive CRA credit for LIHTC investments outside of assessment areas in eligible
states, territories, or regions where the bank has at least one assessment area. NAHB also urges the agencies to
carefully evaluate the final rule's potential impact on LIHTC investment before adoption to ensure it does not
adversely affect the production and preservation of affordable rental housing.

Changes to the asset thresholds in the proposal could have a substantial impact on banks' support for LIHTC.
The Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC) conducted a survey on the potential impact and the
responses indicated that:2

 A $10 billion asset threshold would impact more than 108 banks who invested at least $1.6 billion in
 LIHTC equity during the five-year survey period. Based on these findings, banks below the $10 billion
 asset threshold are estimated to have invested approximately $2 billion in LIHTC equity across the
 broader market over the same period.

 Approximately one-third of LIHTC equity investments from banks under $10 billion in assets supported
 rural markets, indicating that banks in this asset range play an outsized role in investing in rural
 communities.

 Lowering the threshold from $10 billion to $3.252 billion would reduce the number of affected LIHTC
 investors by approximately 63 percent, from 108 banks to 40 banks, and decrease the estimated five-
 year LIHTC equity impact from roughly $2 billion to $272 million.

 A $30 billion asset threshold would affect more than 140 banks that invested at least $3.575 billion in
 LIHTC equity during the five-year survey period. Extrapolated across the broader LIHTC market, these
 banks are estimated to have invested approximately $4.5 billion over the same period.

NAHB recommends the following actions to strengthen support for the LIHTC program:

 Avoid regulatory changes that would weaken banks' incentives to provide LIHTC investments or loans.

 Establish additional incentives for banks of all sizes to invest in LIHTC properties in underserved areas.

Lending Test Should Encourage Acquisition, Development and Construction Lending

The agencies propose that under both the large bank lending test and the small and intermediate bank lending
test, they would consider only a bank's major product line(s) when assessing its retail lending (i.e., consumer,
home mortgage, small business, and small farm loans). These changes are intended to reduce regulatory burden
for banks by tailoring the lending test to focus on the product lines that make up most of a bank's record of
serving community credit needs, thus enabling banks to better focus their resources to more effectively manage
their CRA programs. The agencies provide two options to implement the major product line for all banks. Under
Option 1, the agencies would select the two product lines based on a bank's total retail lending activity,
determined at the bank level and based on both loan count and dollar volume during the evaluation period.
Under Option 2, the agencies would assess a bank's retail lending in major product line(s) based on certain
considerations at the assessment area level. Under this approach, a bank could have more or less than two
major product lines.

The proposal misses the opportunity to address the nation's housing supply shortage, one of the most important
issues the housing industry is facing right now and is expected to face for the next few years. The proposal
should incent banks to support acquisition, development and construction (AD&C) financing to help home
builders and developers increase the supply of single-family homes.

NAHB estimates that the U.S has a housing shortage of roughly 1.2 million homes. The shortage especially hurts
first-time buyers. Access to construction financing is a key ingredient for increasing housing supply.

NAHB recommends that the agencies incent construction loans to home builders and borrowers for the
construction of 1-4 family residential properties in the lending test. This incentive is important because
commercial banks and thrift institutions are the primary source of financing for small to mid-sized builders and
developers. According to NAHB's 2026 Second Quarter Survey on AD&C Financing, 89 percent of survey
respondents indicated that commercial banks and thrift institutions were the primary source of credit for single-
family pre-sold construction; 74 percent for single-family speculative construction; 73 percent for land
development activities and 83 percent for land acquisition. The percentages for construction financing have
been consistent since NAHB began the survey in 2005 which illustrates the outsized role banks have in the
creation of new housing supply. Additionally, 27 percent of respondents reported using bank-provided
construction-to-permanent loans to finance single-family home construction, underscoring banks' important
role in expanding homeownership opportunities.

Clarify Job Training Activities Qualify as Civic Assistance

The proposed rule recategorizes "community services targeted to LMI individuals" activities as civic assistance.
Workforce development and job training programs currently qualify as a component of economic development
as directed by the Interagency Questions and Answers, but the proposal would reclassify these activities as civic
assistance.

NAHB recommends that the agencies clearly state in the final rule that support for job training qualifies as civic
assistance. Job training programs can be extremely beneficial to the workforce needs of LMI communities and
LMI individuals and families. For example, the Home Builders Institute (HBI) is a national organization providing

career training in the building industry. HBI training programs are taught in local communities across the country
to youth, veterans, displaced workers and other underserved populations and provide students with the skills
and experience they need for successful careers through pre-apprenticeship training, job placement services,
mentoring, certification programs, textbooks and curricula. Serving on boards, volunteering, donating or finding
other ways to contribute to organizations that help individuals become skilled at trades will ultimately
contribute to the economic well-being of individuals, their families and their communities.

Assure Evaluation Framework Provides Equal Weight of Lending Test and Community Development (CD) Test

Under the current CRA framework, an intermediate small bank generally must receive at least a "satisfactory"
rating on both the small bank lending test and the CD test to obtain an overall rating of "satisfactory." The
proposal would remove this limitation by allowing stronger performance on the lending test to offset weaker
performance on the CD test when assigning an overall rating. As a result, under the proposal, an intermediate
bank could receive an overall rating of "satisfactory" even if it does not receive at least a "satisfactory" rating on
the CD test.

NAHB strongly urges the agencies to keep equal focus on both the lending test and community development
test. Retaining a meaningful community development test is especially important if more banks are moved into
the intermediate bank framework. Prioritizing lending activities could weaken incentives for important
community development activities, particularly LIHTC equity investments. The unintended consequence of the
proposed change would likely reduce the demand for LIHTCs, which in turn would reduce the equity multifamily
owners need to maintain long-term affordability for low-income tenants and may make some projects
infeasible.

Develop New Policies to Increase Support for Construction and Preservation of Affordable Housing

NAHB urges the agencies to engage with interested stakeholders to develop additional policies that will facilitate
banks' financing of new construction and preservation of affordable single-family homes and apartments. Some
possible ideas include, but are not limited to creating incentives for banks to:

 Support acquisition, development and construction (AD&C) financing to help home builders and
 developers increase the supply of single-family homes affordable to LMI home buyers. The agencies
 should develop policies that encourage banks to make more construction loans for 1-4 family residential
 properties. This incentive is important because commercial banks and thrift institutions are the primary
 source of financing for small- to mid-sized builders and developers.

 Increase affordable housing investments in "CRA deserts" which struggle to attract loans, investments and
 services because they are located outside banks' facility-based assessment areas. Incentives could include
 allowing banks of all sizes to receive CRA credit for LIHTC investments outside of their traditional assessment
 areas and providing CRA credit for the full amount of the loan or investment for a LIHTC-financed project as
 eligible for CRA credit regardless of the number of affordable units.

Questions:

Question 18: Should the definition of affordable housing be expanded to include rental housing for middle-
income individuals in high-cost areas? For example, banks could be incentivized to support affordable workforce
housing that would allow public servants, such as teachers, firefighters, and police officers, to live in the
communities they serve.

 1201 15th Street NW | Washington, DC 20005 | T 800 368 5242 | nahb.org
 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
October 13, 2026
Page 8

NAHB Response
For purposes of the CRA3, LMI refers to individuals whose income is less than 80 percent of the area median
income (AMI), or in the case of a geography, median family income that is less than 80 percent AMI. "Middle-
income" individuals have incomes of at least 80 percent AMI and less than 120 percent AMI, and a "middle
income" geography has a median family income of at least 80 percent of AMI and less than 120 percent of AMI.

Although the focus of CRA should remain on benefits for LMI individuals and areas, NAHB believes it is
reasonable for the agencies to expand the definition of affordable housing to include rental housing for middle-
income individuals in high-cost areas.

Question 21: Should naturally occurring affordable housing partnerships with non-profit organizations be
exempt from the requirement that median rents not exceed 30 percent of 80 percent of the area median income?

Question 22: Should naturally occurring affordable housing partnerships with non-profit organizations be
exempt from the requirement that median rents not exceed 30 percent of 120 percent of the area median
income in high-cost areas?

NAHB Response
Naturally occurring affordable housing (NOAH) often refers to older, unsubsidized apartments that are
affordable to LMI households. NAHB supports efforts to preserve and recapitalize NOAH.

NAHB strongly believes that for-profit and non-profit housing providers should compete on a level playing field.
By extension, if NOAH properties associated with non-profit partnerships are relieved from CRA rent limits, then
NOAH properties associated with for-profit companies should receive the same relief. We are unclear why the
agencies would confer preferential treatment on non-profit housing partnerships solely on the basis of their
non-profit tax status. Exempting non-profits from the rent limits unfairly excludes for-profit housing providers,
despite their significant role in developing and preserving affordable housing. CRA eligibility and relief from rent
limits should be available on a neutral basis for NOAH properties owned by both non-profit and for-profit
providers to ensure a level playing field and maximize investment in affordable housing.

Question 23: Should the rules modify the definition of affordable housing such that home mortgage loans
provided directly to LMI individuals or families would qualify as CD loans if not considered as a major product line
for the bank?

NAHB Response
NAHB believes that mortgage loans including construction-to-permanent loans to LMI individual and families
should be incentivized even if it is not a major product line for the bank. CRA is, and should continue to be, a
major driver for banks to make loans and investments in affordable and workforce housing. Compliance with
CRA mandates, and the impact of banks' CRA activities on regulators' approval of their future business or
mergers, gives banks powerful motivation to lend in minority and LMI communities. It also has prompted banks
to develop innovative mortgage products that enable LMI and minority households to achieve homeownership.
Examples of these products include mortgage loan enhancements such as closing cost assistance, interest rate
buy downs, and down payment assistance. The importance of CRA as a homeownership vehicle for LMI and
workforce households cannot be overstated, since homeownership is the most straightforward way for families
to build wealth.

Conclusion
CRA is important to NAHB members because it motivates banks to participate in activities that support access to
financing for home builders, developers and remodelers; access to affordable mortgage credit for LMI families
and families in LMI census tracts; as well as the production of affordable owner-occupied and rental housing and
community and economic development therefore helping to address housing affordability and increase housing
supply.
LIHTC is the nation's largest and most effective federal program for producing affordable multifamily rental
housing and CRA should remain a key driver incentivized bank lending and investment. Accordingly, the agencies
should retain and expand CRA incentives for banks of all sizes to invest in LIHTC. Before adopting the final rule,
the agencies should assess how any proposed changes, including revised asset thresholds, may affect LIHTC
investment and ensure changes do not reduce support for this critical source of financing for the production and
preservation of affordable rental housing.

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations RIN 3064-AG31 / Docket ID OCC-2026- 0694

To Whom It May Concern,

Locus appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking issued by
the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
(OCC) regarding the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).

Locus is a national community development finance organization that deploys capital through two
certified Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs): Locus Impact Fund, a CDFI loan
fund, and Locus Bank, a CDFI bank. Together, these institutions finance affordable housing, small
businesses, community facilities, economic development projects, and other investments that
expand opportunity in underserved communities, particularly in Virginia.

Our perspective on this proposal is informed by our work as both a CDFI lender and a regulated
bank with our own CRA obligations. We see firsthand how CRA influences the flow of capital
through community development finance ecosystems, including partnerships among banks, CDFIs,
public agencies, foundations, tax-credit investors, and other mission-driven institutions. Because
we operate at multiple points within that ecosystem, we are uniquely positioned to evaluate how
changes to CRA incentives affect the availability of capital in communities.

While we appreciate the agencies' efforts to provide greater clarity in certain areas of CRA
implementation, we are concerned that several provisions within the proposal would weaken the
incentives that currently encourage banks to participate in these collaborative financing
ecosystems. In particular, we urge the agencies to reconsider: (1) proposed changes affecting the
limited-purpose bank designation; (2) the proposed asset-threshold increases; (3) restrictions on
community development grants; and (4) several interacting provisions that collectively shift CRA's
focus away from the broader community development ecosystem and toward a narrower
conception of lending.

110 Peppers Ferry Road, NW locusimpact.org 7814 Carousel Lane, Suite 100
Christiansburg, VA 24073 Richmond, VA 23294
877-214-3564 877-214-3564
 I. Preserve the Limited-Purpose Bank Designation for Community Development-

 Focused Banks

Locus is particularly concerned by proposals that would narrow or eliminate the limited-purpose
bank designation. The agencies specifically request comment on whether the designation should
be narrowed or eliminated entirely.

Locus Bank is a community development-focused institution whose mission is centered on
financing activities that strengthen underserved communities. We believe the limited-purpose
designation remains important because it recognizes that certain specialized institutions cannot be
meaningfully evaluated through examination frameworks designed for traditional retail banks.

This issue is particularly relevant to Locus Bank. The bank has operated under the limited-purpose
framework and was evaluated under the Community Development Test, receiving an Outstanding
CRA rating for our prior three exams. Examiners found strong performance through community
development lending, including innovative and complex financing structures that advanced
community development objectives.

We recognize that relatively few institutions operate under the limited-purpose designation today.
However, that does not diminish its value. The designation exists to accommodate specialized
institutions whose business models do not focus on traditional retail banking and lending.

Recommendation: Maintain the limited-purpose bank designation or a comparable examination
framework for specialized community development-focused institutions such as Locus Bank.

II. The Proposed Asset Thresholds Would Reduce Community Development
 Capacity at the Exact Moment Communities Need More Capital (Section IV.A,

 "Asset Thresholds"; Questions 13)

The proposed asset thresholds would significantly reduce the number of institutions subject to
current community development obligations and would move many currently large banks into a
less rigorous framework. Under the proposal, hundreds of banks nationwide would face fewer
community development expectations and fewer incentives to participate in affordable housing,
small business finance, community facilities, and other community development activities.

In Virginia, it is estimated that 11 banks--approximately 11.1 percent of all banks in the state--
would no longer be subject to community development requirements. Another 16 banks--
approximately 29.6 percent of Virginia banks--would lose large-bank status and face reduced CRA
expectations.

For communities, the consequences are straightforward. Less community development activity
means fewer affordable housing projects getting financed, fewer loans flowing to CDFIs, fewer
investments in community facilities, less flexible capital for small businesses, and fewer resources
available to support workforce development, healthcare, and neighborhood revitalization efforts.
 Reduced CRA motivation can ripple throughout the entire community development finance
ecosystem. The result is not simply fewer CRA-qualified activities. It is fewer affordable housing
projects financed, fewer loans and investments flowing to CDFIs, less capital available for small
businesses and community facilities, and fewer public-private partnerships capable of serving
underserved communities.

Community development projects are often financed through complex capital stacks involving
banks, CDFIs, tax-credit investors, foundations, and public agencies. When bank participation
declines, projects become harder to finance and some projects do not happen at all.

Misalignment with Congressional Priorities on Affordable Housing and New Markets Tax Credit
(NMTC)

The asset thresholds change also undermines Congress's recent efforts to strengthen Low-Income
Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) and New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) which are two bipartisan, popular
federal tax tools with a long track record of success in our communities. While Congress expanded
LIHTC and made NMTC permanent, the proposal undermines these important investment tools.

LIHTC and NMTC are considered equity investments that are evaluated under the standalone
investment test for large banks which currently have a distinct 25%-weighted component of their
CRA evaluation devoted to qualified investments. Moving banks into the lower size category would
mean these transitioned banks would only be subject to a diluted evaluation that considers all CD
in one test. This means a bank may have greater ability to emphasize CD lending rather than
maintain the same level of LIHTC or NMTC investment because investment performance no longer
receives a separate rating. Through this weakened regulatory incentive, bank demand for these
investments would decrease.

Recommendation: The agencies should retain the current CRA asset thresholds and reject the
proposed alternatives.

III. Restrictions on Community Development Grants (Section IV.C, "Community

 Development Activities -- CD Grants"; Questions 911)

Locus strongly opposes the proposal to restrict CRA consideration for community development
grants and to impose a 15 percent indirect-cost limitation.

Community banks, including community development-focused institutions such as Locus Bank,
have deep relationships with the nonprofit organizations, community development corporations,
and local partners serving their communities. Our employees live and work in the communities we
serve. They volunteer with local organizations, participate in community initiatives, and frequently
serve on nonprofit boards and advisory committees. Through these relationships, community
 banks often have a direct understanding of which organizations are effective, where capacity
constraints exist, and how flexible operating support can strengthen community impact.

For that reason, we believe community banks are often better positioned than a uniform regulatory
standard to determine how community development resources should be allocated. A grant
supporting staffing, technology, compliance systems, program expansion, strategic planning, or
fundraising capacity may in many cases generate greater long-term community benefit than a
narrowly restricted project grant.

We are also concerned that the proposal could increase--not reduce--administrative burden. The
proposed indirect-cost limitations and documentation requirements would require banks and
nonprofit recipients to devote additional time and resources to categorizing expenses,
documenting compliance, and demonstrating eligibility. These requirements may discourage
smaller organizations from seeking support and make community development grants more
difficult to administer despite no clear evidence that they would improve community outcomes.
The proposal would therefore risk reducing flexibility while simultaneously increasing compliance
burden.

Recommendation: The agencies should maintain full CRA consideration for community
development grants, including unrestricted operating support and capacity-building grants, and
should not impose the proposed indirect-cost limitations or additional documentation
requirements.

IV. The Definition of Complexity is Too Narrow (Section IV.C, "Qualitative Factors";

 Questions 1217)

We are concerned by the proposal's lending-centered definition of complexity. Many high-impact
community development investments are complex precisely because they involve layered capital
structures, blended finance, tax-credit programs, guarantees, public subsidies, concessionary
capital, and multiple stakeholders.

Examples include New Markets Tax Credit transactions, Low-Income Housing Tax Credit
structures, CDFI equity investments, Loan-loss reserve structures, and Public-private impact
investment partnerships.

The complexity of these transactions often exists whether or not a specific bank loan is attached.
The final rule should recognize that complexity can exist in investments and capital structures
independent of lending.

Recommendation: Expand the complexity definition so that it appropriately recognizes innovative
community development investments, blended-finance structures, tax-credit transactions, and
other catalytic investment vehicles.

V. Protect Community Development Activities from Being Crowded Out by
 Conventional Lending (Section IV.B, "Retail Lending Product Lines," Questions 47; and

 Section IV.C, "CD Loans")
 We support the agencies' goal of increasing transparency and objectivity. However, we are
concerned that several provisions may unintentionally allow conventional lending activities to
substitute for specialized community development activity.

Community development lending, investments, and partnerships frequently involve higher
transaction costs, greater complexity, longer timelines, and deeper engagement with underserved
communities. If conventional retail lending receives comparable CRA treatment, banks may have
fewer incentives to participate in specialized transactions that are more difficult but often more
impactful.

Recommendation: The final rule should ensure that activities receiving community development
consideration continue to demonstrate a meaningful nexus to community development outcomes
and maintain strong incentives for banks to participate in specialized community development
financing. Conventional retail lending should not become a substitute for dedicated community
development activities.

VI. Support for Certain Clarifying Provisions

Locus supports several elements of the proposal that could improve program administration and
increase certainty:

 Creation of a formal process for obtaining advance confirmation of CRA eligibility;
 Development of a publicly available illustrative list of eligible activities;
 Recognition of Tribal lands and Native communities within CRA frameworks; and
 Consideration of qualifying community development loans from prior evaluation periods.

These provisions can improve transparency, create regulatory certainty, and encourage continued
innovation when implemented appropriately.

VII. Final Summary & Recommendations

Locus respectfully recommends that the agencies:

 Maintain the limited-purpose bank designation, or a comparable examination
 framework, for specialized community development-focused institutions like Locus Bank.

 Retain the current CRA asset thresholds and reject the proposed alternatives to preserve
 incentives for community development investment, lending, and partnerships.

 Maintain full CRA consideration for community development grants, including operating
 support and capacity-building grants, and avoid imposing indirect-cost limitations or
 additional administrative requirements.

 Expand the definition of complexity to appropriately recognize innovative investments,
 tax-credit transactions, blended-finance structures, and other community development
 activities that may not involve a direct lending component.
  Preserve strong incentives for specialized community development financing and
 ensure that conventional retail lending does not become a substitute for dedicated
 community development activities.

 Finalize provisions that improve clarity and certainty, including the CRA eligibility
 confirmation process, illustrative list of qualifying activities, recognition of Tribal
 communities, and consideration of qualifying community development loans from prior
 evaluation periods.

CRA has been one of the nation's most successful tools for encouraging private-sector investment
in underserved communities. Locus appreciates the agencies' efforts to provide greater clarity and
consistency within the CRA framework. We respectfully urge the agencies to preserve the
incentives that have made CRA such an effective catalyst for affordable housing, community
development finance, CDFIs, community facilities, and economic opportunity. We appreciate the
opportunity to submit these comments.

Sincerely,

Pravina Raghavan
President & CEO
Locus

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Nearly every affordable home our members build and every small-business loan they close in Minnesota
has bank support in its financing package. That is why the Minnesota Consortium of Community
Developers (MCCD) is writing about your proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA). MCCD is an association of nonprofit community development organizations and CDFIs working
to expand the wealth and resources of Minnesota communities through housing and economic
development -- work that is only possible if we also confront the policies that kept Black, Indigenous,
and other communities of color from stable housing, capital, and generational wealth. Congress passed
the CRA so that banks would "help meet the credit needs of the local communities in which they are
chartered," including low- and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods. We believe that your proposal
moves away from what Congress intended.

MCCD's members have built strong relationships with banks of all sizes to support community
development projects throughout Minnesota. While some of these relationships might continue
informally, CRA provides something voluntary partnerships cannot guarantee: a predictable expectation
that banks will reinvest in lower-income communities. That predictability is the CRA working as
intended, and it fosters a mutually beneficial relationship between banks and community developers.

The biggest risk is that fewer banks will have any community development obligations at all.
Analysis from the National Community Reinvestment Coalition determined that the higher asset
thresholds would end community development evaluations for 50 of Minnesota's 107 banks. As we read
the Proposal, an intermediate bank could also earn an overall "satisfactory" rating on its lending alone,
with community development counting for only about a quarter of its evaluation. A bank could meet its
requirements without any investments in affordable housing. This could render the recently passed 21st
Century ROAD to Housing Act, which expanded the cap for Low-Income Housing Tax Credits
(LIHTC), useless. We request that you keep a real, required community development test for banks of
substantial size, and maintain the requirement that intermediate banks pass both the lending and
community development tests.

Flexible grants stabilize organizations on the ground. Current grants provide enough flexibility to
help cover operational expenses that are necessary to keep organizations open and diligent with
compliance and reporting requirements. These critical funds also help boost loan-loss reserves, cover
deferred maintenance needs in affordable housing properties, and support technical assistance to help set
entrepreneurs up for success as they start or grow their business. By introducing this new 15 percent
overhead cap, organizations will need to find other ways to make up the difference likely cutting staff,
 services, and hours. We ask you to drop the proposed cap and consider grants for their purpose and
impact to communities.

CRA credits should continue to support those the law protects. The Proposal would let large
infrastructure and Opportunity Zone investments count even when their benefit to low- and moderate-
income residents is only incidental, and it would remove the specific rating factor for highly
disadvantaged areas. At the same time, it says nothing about race, even though the CRA was born from
repairing the harm caused by redlining. While progress is being made, Minnesota's racial
homeownership gap remains among the widest in the country. The CRA must continue to require a
direct, primary benefit to LMI communities, keep the highly disadvantaged areas factor, and use race and
ethnicity data in performance context and public reporting.

Banks should be accountable to communities where they do business, and the rules should apply to
online banks. Online banks have grown in recent years and can build a large lending or deposit base in
Minnesota without a branch. The proposed changes do not require community development duties in
Minnesota despite benefiting from the growing customer base. We ask you to create a workable lending-
or deposit-based standard that reaches that activity. We also urge you to preserve the small-business and
community development data we use to spot gaps and hold banks accountable, and to work with the
Federal Reserve, which is not part of this Proposal, so that all three agencies administer one CRA
framework.

For all these reasons, we urge the FDIC and OCC to withdraw the Proposal or, at a minimum, to make
the changes above. Minnesota's ability to finance housing, small businesses, and neighborhood
investment depends on banks staying accountable to the communities they serve. Please do not hesitate
to reach out to us as you consider this rulemaking; we would welcome the chance to share more about
our members' work.

Respectfully,

Kit Fordham
Interim CEO
Minnesota Consortium of Community Developers (MCCD)
